11265-notes-and-queries-number-02-novemb:
The second number of Notes and Queries, dated November 10, 1849, opens with thanks to readers who have already made the new journal a literary exchange. Contributors answer earlier queries and raise new ones: Bishop Aylmer's letter and a poem on the Armada, notes on ancient libraries, a pedlar's song attributed to Shakespeare, and traditions about Hamlet. J. Payne Collier and Bolton Corney are among the correspondents.

The journal's idea was simple and new: a medium where literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists could ask and answer questions in public. This early number shows the formula working, with learning traded in short paragraphs. It is a founding document for the reference culture that later produced far larger works.
11577-notes-and-queries-number-03-novemb:
Notes and Queries number 3 is dated Saturday, 17 November 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. It calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of it.

Notes cover travelling in England, Sanuto's Doges of Venice by Sir F Madden, and letters from Lord Nelson's brother after Trafalgar. Misquotations, Herbert's and Dibdin's Ames, and notes from fly leaves follow. Queries, answers, and minor queries close the number, with a register from East Peckham church in Kent and notes on Queen Elizabeth's household.
11636-notes-and-queries-number-05-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 5 is dated Saturday, 1 December 1849. It cost threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with Lord Chatham and Queen Charlotte. An original letter on Pitt's resignation in 1761 follows. Public feeling and changes at court are covered there.

Ancient tapestry by Planché and travelling in England come next. Prison discipline and execution of justice follow. Queries ask about Sanuto's Doges of Venice and the manuscripts of Sir Roger Twysden. Minor queries cover a bust of Sir Walter Raleigh. Notes on books, catalogues, and sales close the issue, with notices to correspondents.
11651-notes-and-queries-number-07-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 7 is dated Saturday, 15 December 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with a marriage contract of Mary Queen of Scots and a bill of fare from 1626. Moneta Sanctae Helenae and translations of Gray's Elegy follow.

Notes on authors and books by Bolton Corney appear as well. Queries ask about Berkeley's theory of vision and Doctor Johnson with Professor de Morgan. Suppressed passages in Cartwright's poems are queried too. Minor queries cover Christencat, hexameter verses in Scripture, and the festival of Saint Michael. Answers on lobsters in medals and straw necklaces close the round.
11652-notes-and-queries-number-08-decemb:
Notes and Queries number 8 is dated Saturday, 22 December 1849, priced at threepence, fourpence stamped. Notes open with Otloh the scribe, Cunningham's London, wives of ecclesiastics, Tower Royal, and an ancient inscribed dish by Albert Way. Barnacles, Dorne the bookseller, and sermons by Stephen follow in turn.

Queries ask about Love, the king's fool, Mare de Saham, the Advent bells, and the poets, with minor queries on Darnley, coffee, and catsup. One answer quotes Heywood on Love, prince of fools, who made king and queen merry with many good pastimes. The number is a Christmas antiquarian miscellany, brisk and crowded with small learning.
12139-the-gringos-a-story-of-the-old-cal:
B. M. Bower published The Gringos in 1913, a novel of California in the gold-rush year 1849, with help from George W. Lee, a genuine Forty-niner. The story follows American newcomers, called gringos by Californios, into a valley ruled by old Spanish families.

Vigilantes, squatters, rodeos, fiestas, and duels with riatas drive the plot, as Jerry Simpson and his neighbors clash with Don Andres household over land and honor. Bower sympathizes with both sides by turns, and her heroine, called the finest little woman in the world, steadies hot tempers. The novel mixes romance with a rough record of conquest, showing how law gave way to guns when two peoples met on one range.
13513-notes-and-queries-number-04-novemb:
Notes and Queries for November 24, 1849, its fourth number, opens with a statement of progress and prospects for the new journal. John Bruce writes on Luther and Erasmus, Hallam's Middle Ages is discussed, and notes cover writers on fly-leaves, the origin of grog, ancient alms-basins, and Dyce against Warburton and Collier.

Food of the people, bills of fare, Bishop Barnaby, trade editions, and Dibdin's Typographical Antiquities fill the notes. While queries ask about clouds or shrouds in Shakespeare and a medal of the Pretender. A note on Shakespeare manuscripts argues that none survive except his name, save one letter addressed to him. The young journal already shows its lasting pattern.
13521-notes-and-queries-number-09-decemb:
Notes and Queries for December 29, 1849, closes the journal's first year with notes on Sir E. Dering's household book, Berkeley's theory of vision, Bishop Barnaby, mathematical archaeology, and Gothic architecture. Dr. Burney's musical works, ancient alms-basins, and minor notes on Prince Madoc, St. Barnabas, Cromwell's baptism, and the Times fill the rest.

A letter on a song in the style of Suckling, and a note on the contest for the best translation of Gray's Elegy, judged by Mr. Nares of the British Critic, show the journal's literary range. The number looks back on progress made since November and forward to new questions, keeping its promise of a medium where readers answer each other's puzzles.
13550-notes-and-queries-number-06-decemb:
Notes and Queries for December 8, 1849, its sixth number, opens with a few words of explanation from the editor. Notes cover a letter from the Earl of Shaftesbury on Monmouth's ash, Drayton's poems, a passage in Goldsmith, ancient libraries, a defence of a bald head, and royal household allowances.

Adversaria notes printers' couplets, Charles Martel, Bodenham and Ling, and travelling in England, with minor notes on an ancient alms dish, a bishop that burneth, and Sussex ironworks. A royal warrant under the signet at East Hampstead in the fourteenth year of a reign orders household officers to pay allowances. The young journal already mixes documents, books, and curiosities.
16030-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-nine, dated October 14, 1897, under the Great Round World Publishing Company. News, science, and stories fill the paper in words young readers could follow. This number leads with a disquieting rumour about the Seal Conference. The paper kept children abreast of diplomacy.

England, the rumour runs, refused to join the Seal Conference if Russia and Japan were admitted. At the British Foreign Office, officials would not say positively whether Britain had declined. Young readers learn how news travels: rumour, denial, and waiting. Seen now, the issue shows 1897 children meeting world politics in plain, careful words.
1936-letters-from-england-1846-1849:
Elizabeth Davis Bancroft's Letters from England, 1846 to 1849, gathers letters written during her years in London as the wife of the American minister. A portrait of Mrs. Bancroft, probably taken at Brady's National Gallery in New York after her return, fronts the volume, and the letters that follow describe a society at its height.

At a London dinner, Bancroft notes, one may meet so many people, each with a peculiar gift, that one cannot avail oneself of every opportunity. The letters move through dinners, debates, and country houses. The book is a valuable record of Anglo-American society in the 1840s, written by a woman with a sharp eye and a wide circle.
20126-the-cave-of-gold-a-tale-of-califor:
Everett McNeil wrote The Cave of Gold, a tale of California in '49. The gold rush year gives the tale its heat and risk. Bud hears fearful screams from a hill and turns pale at the sound. Yet he vows to find the cause and climbs at once.

With rifle ready, he fixes his eyes on the spot above. Boys' gold rush tales mix mines, caves, and sudden peril freely. McNeil sets greed, courage, and wild country in a fast plot. Readers get a vivid taste of how '49 looked to young readers years later.
23192-gold-seekers-of-49:
Gold Seekers of '49 is an adventure story about the California gold rush, told through a boy named Charley. Its chapter list promises a full journey west: a mysterious stranger, a call to the golden west, an unwelcome companion, and an attack by an enemy early on the road.

The route runs by Panama, up a river, and through the Golden Gate into San Francisco. Later chapters take Charley on to the diggings, where he hears a key talk, follows an enemy's trail, and makes a great discovery. Readers get the rush as a young traveller's string of risks, races, and finds.
27744-remarks-on-clarissa-1749:
Published in London in 1749, this anonymous pamphlet gathers criticisms of Samuel Richardson's novel Clarissa heard in conversation, addressed directly to its author. It reports objections to the heroine's character and conduct from the first volumes to the close.

The writer also records defenses offered by Clarissa's admirers, and adds reflections on the character of Prior's Emma. The pamphlet is a lively record of how Richardson's vast epistolary novel divided its first readers, and of the arguments they had about it. The writer insists he has neither softened objections nor added praise beyond what he heard. The talk went on.
40397-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
One monthly number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 403, dated May 1849, opens with colonisation and Mr Wakefield's theory. The reaction, or foreign conservatism, follows. Madame d'Arbouville's Village Doctor is reviewed in translation. National education in Scotland gets an article. Ararat and the Armenian highlands supply travel.

Legitimacy in France and Austria and Hungary treat the revolutions of 1848. A college sketch in verse and Jack Moonlight lighten the number. Moonlight memories by B Simmons appear in verse. William Blackwood and Sons published from George Street, Edinburgh, and Paternoster Row, London. The number shows Maga's Tory range at mid century.
42412-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-no-:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 401, is dated March 1849, in its sixty-fifth volume. Maga, as its readers called it, was the Tory monthly of Edinburgh, and the contents of this number show its range in 1849.

Scientific and practical agriculture leads. A poem, The Sycamine, follows, and an essay takes stock after a year's republicanism in France. The Caxtons, the serial novel then running, reaches its eleventh part. Proudhon and his economic contradictions get an article, and Mérimée's history of Peter the Cruel another. The Green Hand, a short yarn, supplies the fiction of the sea. A monthly like this was a small parliament of letters: farming, socialism, Spain, and a family serial, debated between the same covers by anonymous gentlemen.
43721-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 405, is the July 1849 issue of the Scottish monthly. The number opens volume sixty six, which runs to December of that year. Its contents mix dialogue essays, travel, serial fiction, and sport. William Blackwood and Sons published the issue at Edinburgh and London.

The lead piece is a dialogue in the voice of Christopher North and his friends, set at a camp in the Highlands. The speakers trade banter about age and looks before settling to talk. An article on the island of Sardinia follows. The Caxtons, a serial novel, reaches its fourteenth part in this number. Other pieces treat the game laws in Scotland and the schooling ideas of Pestalozzi. A postscript closes the issue.
43722-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Number 406 of a famed Edinburgh magazine, volume sixty six, is dated August 1849. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and sold it in London as well. The contents page lists eight pieces, from a life study to war news and a tale told in parts.

Charles Lamb leads the number, with a piece that gives Lamb a quiet, quaint niche in the temple of English letters. The niche, the writer jokes, should hold laughing cherubs and sly carved jokes, like old church work. Part fifteen of The Caxtons, a yarn called The Green Hand, and a piece on the rising in Baden follow.
43814-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The November 1849 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume sixty-six, number 409, leads with The Transportation Question. The article argues that imprisonment has failed both to deter crime and to reform criminals. Government, it says, has been driven back to transportation by the voice of the country and by jails too full to hold the growth in prisoners. An order in council has authorized the return, and the chief difficulty now is finding a colony willing to receive the penal settlers.

Scottish figures from the parliamentary reports back the claim: convictions rose from 2,936 in 1846 to 3,669 in 1848, and those with previous convictions from 858 to 1,043. The rest of the number holds My Peninsular Medal, a poem called Disenchantment, Across the Atlantic, Peace and War Agitators, The French Novels of 1849, and Dies Boreales.
44183-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood Edinburgh Magazine, volume sixty five, number 399, is the January 1849 issue. William Blackwood and Sons printed it at Edinburgh and sold it in London. The Year of Revolutions opens the contents at page one of the number. French Conquerors and Colonists follows as the second piece in the list.

The Caxtons, part nine, continues a serial novel in the middle pages. The White Nile, then art and artists in Spain, fill the next heads. The dodo and its kindred gets a natural history piece in the issue. A tale of 1787 called The Sword of Honour and memoirs of Kirkaldy of Grange close the list. Tory letters, tales, and travel fill the famous Maga in its 1849 form.
44344-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 400, volume 65, for February 1849, leads with Caucasus and the Cossacks, a review of Moritz Wagner's travels of 1843 to 1846. The article marvels at Circassia, a small mountain land holding out against Russia: sixty millions against six hundred thousand, a colossus against a pigmy, yet the dwarf still resists after twenty years.

The contents mix the magazine's range. The Caxtons, a novel then running in parts, reaches part ten. Essays treat the statistical accounts of Scotland, the poetry of sacred art, American thoughts on the European revolutions of 1848, and the English universities. A poem, The Covenanters' Night-Hymn, stands in the number, and pieces on Dalmatia and Montenegro and the Carlists in Catalonia widen the map. Beattie's life of the poet Campbell is reviewed under modern biography. Readers get a full number of the age's great monthly, politics, fiction, and verse in one wrapper.
45693-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for October 1849 is number 408, in volume 66. Blackwood and Sons published it at Edinburgh and London. The contents open with the last part of The Caxtons, a serial novel. Its chapter 101 bids farewell to a beautiful land of exiles. Lynmouth Revisited follows as a travel piece. An article asks what revolutionising Germany has attained.

A sea yarn, The Green Hand, reaches its fifth part in this issue. Physical geography and a remedy for civil revolution in the Canadas come next. The English Mail-Coach, De Quincey's famous essay on the glory of motion, appears here. The number closes with the diary of Samuel Pepys. Fiction, politics, and memoir share the magazine's pages in the Blackwood manner. The issue shows the mid century monthly at full stretch.
46665-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 402 for April 1849, is volume sixty-five of the famed Scottish monthly. Contents include a review of Macaulay's History of England, a notice of Johnston's Physical Geography, and part twelve of the novel The Caxtons. Essays on old painting practice and on Tennyson's poems follow in the number.

The lead review praises the historical and critical essay as a form brought to perfection in one generation. Lighter pieces include verses on sea life and London cries, and the tale Claudia and Pudens. A life of Sir Astley Cooper begins in this issue for medical readers. The number shows Blackwood's mix of politics, letters, and tale telling.
46993-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-no-:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for June 1849 is number 404 of the long-running monthly. William Blackwood and Sons printed it at Edinburgh and sold it through booksellers across the kingdom. The contents list mixes fiction, politics, and church debate in the house style.

The Caxtons, a serial novel, opens the number with its thirteenth part. A romance of Russian history follows, then letters to an Anglo-Catholic clergyman. Austria and Hungary, feudalism in the nineteenth century, and civil revolution in the Canadas fill the middle. In the Caxtons part, the narrator works by soft arts to win his family over to a bold project. He feeds his uncle Roland books on Australian life until the old soldier sighs for the wild himself.
53948-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-1-j:
A famed American monthly opened its thirty fourth volume at Philadelphia in January 1849. Its cover shows a day on the mountains, drawn and cut by Tucker. Steel plates, mezzotints and sheet music dressed the number. The names on its masthead read like a roll of the age.

Bryant, Cooper, Dana, Longfellow and Lowell stand among the chief hands. Sigourney, Sedgwick and Osgood write for it as well. Contents mix tales, verse and essays: the belle of the opera, a corsair's victim, Kate Richmond's betrothal. Game birds of America reach their twelfth part. A history of men's dress, notes on maple sugar, book news and an editor's table close the month.
53949-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-2-f:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-four, number two, for February 1849, opens with a Valentine song cut by W E Tucker. Its lead tale, The Young Lawyer's First Case by John Todd, starts at a death bed in Vermont. A calm, dying mother calls her eldest son home from college. Her dearest wish was a pulpit for him; he chose the law, and she must make her peace with it in their last talk.

The month's list runs wide: Christine, The Ennuyee, The Mirror of Life, and The Wager of Battle. Saint Valentine's Day suits the date, and a piece on Mendelssohn suits the ear. The garb of men through the ages and the wild birds of America give fact its turn. Fans of old monthlies get tale, verse, and lore in the full Graham mix.
53953-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-3-m:
Graham's Magazine for March 1849 makes up volume thirty four, number three, of a well known American monthly of its day. The number opens with a serial tale, The Naval Officer, by William Lynch, set at daybreak on a tropic island bay. Poems, tales, and essays crowd the table: Unequal Marriages, The Icebergs, Doctor Sian Seng, Western Recollections, and a piece on the plantation of General Taylor.

A history of the costume of men, a wild birds of America piece, and short verses fill the middle pages. The back of the number holds a review of new books and the Editor's Table, where the magazine spoke in its own voice. One steel plate, Why Don't He Come, fronts the issue as its picture.
53957-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-4-a:
Graham's Magazine for April 1849, volume thirty four, number four, is a number of the Philadelphia monthly. Graham's was among the best known American magazines of its day. Tales, poems, essays, and reviews fill the number, with fashion plates and views. A bridge and church of Saint Isaac and a Mormon temple at Nauvoo stand among the pictures.

The lead piece is The Poet Lí, a fragment from the Chinese by Mrs Caroline H Butler. Lí, called the Exiled Immortal for his learning, is shown by the lake of Tai-hoo with his mother. The contents add a naval tale, a gipsy queen, and a history of the costume of men. A piece on Jenny Lind, the Swedish singer then famous, joins the Editor's Table and the review of new books.
53960-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-5-m:
Graham Magazine volume thirty-four, number five, came out at Philadelphia in May 1849. A fashion plate from Paris heads the number, with dress, flower, and lace shops named in French. Contents mix tales, poems, an ode, costume history, wild birds of America, and fifty suggestions, plus an editor table and book reviews.

Angele Hull leads with Mr and Mrs John Johnson Jones, a tale of everyday life. The Jones pair are common folk with one bar: they long to be fashionable, and money at last bursts the charmed gates for them. Mrs Jones rises on frothy suppers and baited guests. The satire grants that money gives wit to fools and beauty to beasts in a land that out democrats democracy. Tales, verse, and plates show a prime American parlour monthly.
53963-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxiv-no-6-j:
Graham Magazine was a famed monthly of tales and verse from Philadelphia. The copy here is book 34, part 6, for June 1849. A plate of Paris dress wear fronts the issue. A second plate, cut for the sheet, shows the star of the night.

W Gilmore Simms leads with The Picture of Judgment, a tale of old tombs in Italy. That tale tells of a cave found by a man named Manzi in 1833. Its stone chests held a noble clan, plus guests of a strange race. Verse, thoughts, and short tales fill the rest of the issue. Themes run from the birth place of the artist Benjamin West to wild birds of the land. Notes on new books and a page from the chair close the month.
54009-metropolitan-subway-and-elevated-s:
A transit bulletin fills this item: Metropolitan Subway and Elevated Systems, presented as bulletin number forty-nine by the Electric Railway Historical Society, priced at a dollar and a half. Its first section treats the Boston Elevated Railway rapid transit system, and opens with the shape of the whole network.

Boston's transport, the bulletin says, joins rapid transit and surface lines under one fare, with transfers for a continuous ride. The system runs to more than five hundred miles of line, of which thirty-seven miles are subway and elevated track. It serves a district of over ninety square miles and more than a million people. Early lines, the Tremont Street subway among them, date to 1901, with later growth to Forest Hills, Cambridge, Everett, and East Boston.
55362-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-1-ju:
Graham's Magazine for July 1849 is the first number of the thirty fifth volume of a famed Philadelphia monthly of letters and art. Steel engravings and music came with the issue. The contents page sorts its goods into fiction, essays, and articles on one side, and poetry, music, and fashion on the other.

The lead piece is a life of Major General Stephen Watts Kearny, the soldier of the Mexican War. Tales fill the rest: True Unto Death, The Foundling, The Widow of Nain, and Cross Purposes. Big names crowd the masthead as past helpers, from Bryant and Cooper to Longfellow and Lowell. Poems on miners, emigrants' daughters, and a tulip tree give the number its softer side.
55372-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-2-au:
Graham Magazine for August 1849, volume thirty five number two, is a Philadelphia monthly of fiction and verse. A full table of contents lists its tales, sketches, and articles for the number. The Curtain Lifted leads the fiction side of the issue. Indian Legend of the Star and Lily and Jasper St Aubyn follow in that list.

Sketches of Life in Our Village and Olden Times add prose of a lighter kind. Two Hours of Doom and The Captive of York promise darker tales for readers. Poetry fills a second list, with legends, sonnets, and songs in the mix. Watouska, a legend of the Oneidas, heads that verse section of the number. An Editor Table and a review of new books close the monthly in the usual form.
55380-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-3-se:
The September 1849 number of Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-five, number three, mixes fiction, essays, poetry, music, and fashion from Philadelphia. Its fiction and articles include General Training by Alfred Street, Jasper St Aubyn, Sketches of Life in Our Village, and Jessie Lincoln.

A legend piece gives the introduction of death and the origin of medicine worship among the Ogibwas. Love Tests of Halloween, Colored Birds with The Bullfinch, A Traveler's Story, The Two Paths, and Wild-Birds of America fill out the prose. The verse runs from To the Lily of the Valley and The Spanish Maiden to The Angel's Visit and Woman's Heart, a sonnet. General Training opens by ranking the village summer: the Fourth of July, general training day, and camp meeting.
55383-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-4-oc:
Graham's Magazine, volume thirty five, number four, is the issue for October 1849. The Philadelphia monthly mixed tales, poems, music, and fashion plates. An engraving named The Baggage Waggon opens the number. The contents list a dozen tales and a full page of verse.

The lead tale, A Year and a Day, comes from Caroline Butler. It opens on a poor Philadelphia author worn down by want. His wife is dead, and his young daughter sews to keep the home. A rich old man, thought a miser, passes their window each day. Other pieces treat an engraver's daughter and a recreant missionary. The editor's table discourses on lasting fame. Graham's was among the best loved American monthlies of its day.
55388-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-5-no:
Graham's Magazine, volume 35, number 5, is the Philadelphia issue of November 1849. A table of contents divides fiction and articles from poetry, music, and fashion. An engraving titled Happy as a King was made for the magazine.

The fiction list opens with a serial by Henry William Herbert, Jasper St. Aubyn, or The Course of Passion, continued from page 213. Its hero loved Theresa Allan with all the love he could bestow, yet chose evil for his good and rushed into deceit. Men at Home, A Year and a Day, Major Anspach, Homewood, The Battle of Trenton, and The Life Insurance follow among the articles. The Balize and Wild Birds of America come with them. The poetry pages offer The Broken Household, The Fear of Death, Bunker Hill at Midnight, and The Seminoles' Last Look. An editor's table and reviews of new books close the number.
55396-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxv-no-6-de:
The December 1849 number of Graham's Magazine, volume thirty-five, number six, printed at Philadelphia, mixes fiction, poetry, music, and fashion. Its prose includes The Conscript by Joseph Chandler, A Case of Gold Fever, The Death of Cleopatra, and a Mas-Sa-Sanga legend of western Canada called The Two Cousins. An Editor's Table and reviews of new books close the prose side.

The number opens with The Conscript, subtitled The Foundation of Morals. The Widow Berien's daughter Louise has kept her promise for two years: she will marry Adolph, but not until her mother consents or withdraws her opposition. The girl presses her mother to speak plainly and say what secret reason stands against the match. Verse in the number includes To My Steed, Summer's Night, and The Undivided Heart.
57601-democracy-in-france-january-1849:
Democracy in France, January 1849, is François Guizot's pamphlet on the state of his country after the revolution of 1848. John Murray of London published this fourth edition in 1849. Guizot, a historian and former minister, insists that nothing in the pages bears the impress of his personal situation while such events pass before his eyes.

His charge stands in one phrase: the evil at the root of all France's evils is the idolatry of democracy. It undermines, he argues, her governments and her liberties, her dignity and her happiness. He wrote after Louis Napoléon Bonaparte's election to the presidency and says the words would stand unchanged had General Cavaignac won instead. The pamphlet is a leading document of French liberal conservatism at mid-century.
58237-motion-pictures-1940-1949:
Motion Pictures, 1940 to 1949 is the cumulative catalog of copyright entries for films, issued in 1953 by the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress. The volume sold for $10 from the Register of Copyrights in Washington. Its main list runs to page 503, followed by an index and a series list. A summary counts the decade's registrations by class.

Class L, motion-picture photoplays, holds 7,122 entries. Class M, motion pictures other than photoplays, holds 11,645, for a total of 18,767. Class M takes in many animated cartoons and newsreels, and nontheatrical films as well. Each entry gives the title, the claimant, the copyright date, and the registration number, with more detail where it was to hand. The catalog is a reference shelf book for film scholars and rights searchers.
59748-devils-tower-national-monument-wyo:
A guide to Devils Tower National Monument in Wyoming came from the United States Department of the Interior in 1949. The National Park Service issued it under director Newton Drury. Devils Tower was the first national monument made, set up by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1906 under the Antiquities Act. The Sioux knew the rock as Mateo Tepee, meaning Grizzly Bears' Lodge.

The guide gives its size: it rises 1,280 feet from the river bed and 865 feet from its base, by the Belle Fourche River. Its base spans about 1,000 feet, its top 275 feet, with an acre and a half of growth on the summit. A part on the rock's birth grants that men of science do not agree on how it formed. All grant it was once molten rock forced up from deep in the earth.
59817-blue-ridge-parkway-virginia-and-no:
Blue Ridge Parkway, Virginia and North Carolina is a National Park Service booklet of 1949. It names the Secretary of the Interior, Krug, and the Park Service director, Drury, on its title page. The Parkway, it says, is a unit of the National Park System, owned by the people and run for them by the Park Service.

The contents give the four seasons, what to do and where, and mile posts and entrances. The road is then described by sections, from Shenandoah National Park to Roanoke, on to the North Carolina line and Linville River, and so to the Great Smoky Mountains. Regulations remind drivers that the Parkway is for passenger cars, and rangers are presented as helpers as well as enforcers.
67182-a-history-of-epidemic-pestilences-:
A History of Epidemic Pestilences is a medical history by Edward Bascome, a doctor of medicine, published in London in eighteen fifty one. Its span runs from the earliest ages, long before the birth of Christ, to eighteen forty eight, as the title states. Researches into the nature, causes, and prevention of plagues fill out the title's promise. A verse motto holds that the very air is big with death.

The book is dedicated to the Earl of Shaftesbury and to Doctor John Conolly, both named on the dedication page. Plague, cholera, fever, and other mass killers are traced age by age. Bascome writes before germ theory had won, when air, water, and land were blamed for secret venom.
71572-the-gold-seekers-of-49:
Kimball Webster wrote this narrative, The Gold Seekers of 49. It is a personal account of the overland trail, and of adventures in California and Oregon from 1849 to 1854. Manchester, New Hampshire, printed it in 1917. An introduction and life of the author by George Waldo Browne stand at the front, with pictures by Frank Holland and others.

Browne tells how the book came to be. Webster, a New England farm boy who had worked in granite quarries, caught the gold fever in April 1849, a little over twenty years old. Methodical by habit, he kept a journal of the whole crossing and of his years as a miner in California and a surveyor in Oregon. Webster died while the book was in the making, and it is dedicated to his daughters.
8603-notes-and-queries-number-01-novembe:
Notes and Queries began on Saturday, November 3, 1849, as a threepenny weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists to ask and answer questions. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of it. The first number prefers to show rather than promise, offering a specimen of the exchanges its prospectus had described, and leaving future numbers to prove the idea.

Inside, readers pose puzzles about books, words, customs, and family history, and other readers reply with evidence from libraries and parish records. The journal grew into a long-lived institution of British literary scholarship. This opening issue is a small treasure for historians of reading, showing how, before search engines, curious people built knowledge together, one printed query at a time.
anthem-pg1249:
Ayn Rand's novella is told by a young man known only by his council-given name, Equality 7-2521, in a city where the word I has been forgotten. Men live, work, and sleep in groups, and the Council of Vocations chooses each person's trade. Writing alone is a crime, and this journal is written in secret.

Working as a street sweeper, he finds a hidden tunnel from the old Unmentionable Times and teaches himself the lost power of light. His discoveries, and his love for a woman in the fields, drive him to flee the city. In the forest he finds books, and in them a single sacred word. The fable states Rand's case for the free individual.
arxiv-2412-00949:
Nicholas Lenzen, Amogh Raut, and Andrew Melnik present a study from twenty twenty-four on game agents in Minecraft that take goals as sound. A past agent, STEVE-1, follows goals coded as latent marks from text or sight. The team adds ears: a map from sound marks to the same goal space. That map is learned with no change to the agent's core.

They build a sound and video model for Minecraft and a prior net that turns sound into goal marks. The sound led agent plays at a par with the text and sight led ones. The team weighs what each sense gains and loses as a goal channel. Code and the sound model are open.
arxiv-2412-01149:
Joseph McGovern computes generating series for counting indices attached to compact Calabi-Yau threefolds, assuming these indices have a modular character. His examples are all quotient spaces. They include a Z7 quotient of Rødland's pfaffian threefold, a Z5 quotient of the Hosono-Takagi double quintic symmetroid, a Z3 quotient of the bicubic, and a Z5 quotient of the quintic. For each case he works out Gopakumar-Vafa invariants up to the highest genus that the boundary data allow.

For the quintic quotient alone, enough invariants emerge to give one real test of the modularity assumption. McGovern also treats five multiparameter examples in which computing a single index fixes the rest. He proposes a change to an earlier formula so that it takes torsion into account, since the examples work only because their intersection and Chern numbers stay small. An appendix discusses quotient threefolds and their Wall data.
arxiv-2412-01349:
Bobomurat Ahmedov and co-authors catalog small ripples in a teleparallel gravity theory. Their 2024 paper covers the BDLS theory, the teleparallel twin of Horndeski gravity. To test how structure forms in the cosmos, both the smooth background and its ripples must be understood. Prior work exists, but a full gauge-by-gauge account was missing.

They review every gauge choice for scalar, vector, and tensor ripples on a cosmic background, up to second order. The catalog gathers results that observers and coders can plug into existing tools. Teleparallel gravity swaps curvature for torsion as the engine of gravity's effects. A clean perturbation reference helps compare this family with standard gravity. The authors hope the survey eases uptake of the theory.
arxiv-2412-01749:
Reho and co-authors compute, from first principles, how superconductivity leaks into a lead telluride and lead layered device in a 2024 paper. Such semiconductor-superconductor hybrids are candidate platforms for Majorana zero modes, the building blocks proposed for topological quantum computing.

Solving quantum equations for both the normal and superconducting states, the team resolved an induced energy gap on the semiconductor side. Mixing between the layers softens that gap. The pairing strength varies with direction, a needed trait for unconventional superconductivity, and its reach was mapped in space. Yet a sizable energy barrier at the interface blocks the zero modes that simple models predict. The results temper hopes for this material pair.
arxiv-2412-01949:
Mateusz Stolarski and co-authors refine how machine learning picks the people most likely to spread something through a network. Marketers, health officials, and platform designers all want those key nodes, and trained models already beat classic centrality scores. The weak point is labeling: knowing a node's true influence means simulating cascades, and bucketing those results badly wastes the signal.

Their Smart Bins scheme slices simulation outcomes more cleverly, and they prove its edge over older labeling. The trained models then predict not just a node's reach but other traits of the spread it starts. Tests across networks of varied kinds and sizes show the method generalizing well. The authors frame careful labels, not fancier nets, as the frontier.
arxiv-2412-02349:
Marco Casagrande and Daniele Antonioli present CTRAPS, a set of protocol-level attacks on FIDO2 security keys, in a 2024 paper. FIDO2 is the open standard behind passkeys and hardware login keys, and its device protocol had never had its application interface audited. The authors found two attack families hiding in that layer.

Client impersonation attacks exploit the lack of client checks to tamper with keys, including zero-click deletion of stored passkeys. Confusion attacks trick devices and users into running unwanted commands while believing they run legitimate ones. Eleven attacks worked on six popular authenticators and ten major services. The team disclosed the flaws responsibly and proposes eight backward-compatible fixes.
arxiv-2412-02749:
Sven Põder and co-authors train deep learning to spot dark matter clumps by their wake in stars in a 2024 paper. Small dark subhalos inside the Milky Way are hard to see directly. As one plows through a star field, it leaves a wake that betrays its mass.

They simulated clumps moving through star and dark matter backgrounds matched to one distance from the galactic center. Networks learned to tell whether a clump was present and to guess its mass. Detection held up down to fairly small clumps and transferred to other distances. Star overdensity and velocity spread were the most telling features for the search.
arxiv-2412-03149:
Chuandi Zhang and co-authors study magnetic transitions in a crystal with a triangular atom layout in a 2024 paper. The compound holds manganese atoms with high spin on a triangular lattice that resists simple magnetic order. Related cobalt and nickel compounds show exotic quantum states, and this manganese version acts as their classical counterpart.

Magnet and heat measurements on powder samples showed two magnetic transitions in a row, just above one degree above absolute zero. Neutron diffraction at very low temperature revealed the ground state: manganese moments ordered in a Y-like pattern across two planes. Between the two transitions the pattern seems to shift to a simpler form held by heat-driven effects. The sequence matches theory for such triangular magnets.
arxiv-2412-03249:
Wenjie Sun and co-authors use machine learning to speed up optimal qubit layout for quantum circuits, in work from 2024. Mapping a logical circuit onto real hardware is slow when done by exact solvers. Redundant search steps eat most of that time.

Their method, MLQM, prunes the global search space using prior knowledge and learned cues. A data scheme grows the training set by rearranging gates and qubits, fixing sample scarcity. Local search is pruned too, through a solver setting that adapts on the fly. Together the cuts raise solution speed while keeping layouts optimal. Faster mapping matters as circuits outgrow hand tuning.
arxiv-2412-03549:
Chao Duan and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, a theory that predicts when soap-like molecules suddenly cluster into micelles. That threshold, the critical micelle concentration, governs detergents, drug carriers, and cosmetics. Designers need it as a function of molecule shape and water conditions.

Their self-consistent field theory unifies the threshold, micelle structure, and formation pathway in one frame. Long-range electric forces are handled exactly, so charged and uncharged surfactants both fit. Salt effects emerge naturally. Tests on three common surfactant families matched expectations across a wide span of thresholds. A predictive theory turns surfactant design from trial batches toward calculation.
arxiv-2412-03649:
Kempski and co-authors tie two space puzzles to one cause in a 2024 paper. Cosmic rays spread through the galaxy at rates that hint at patchy magnetic sheets. Radio waves from far quasars also show rare extreme scattering events, blamed on thin sheets in space gas. The sheets blamed for the radio events match the size tied to cosmic ray motion.

The team shows that sheet shapes and fill rates drawn from quasar data explain the ray spread with no free knobs. They then list tests that new radio arrays can run. Echoes in pulsar signals and burst events could back or break the model. Lensed quasars and event timing offer more checks.
arxiv-2412-04449:
Zhang and five colleagues present p-MoD in twenty twenty-four, an efficient design for multimodal language models. Such models handle text and images together but cost a lot to train and run. Most of their computation goes to processing vast numbers of vision tokens. The Mixture of Depths idea lets each layer process only key tokens.

Applying that idea to multimodal models raises stability and data problems. The authors add a gated weight normalization and a symmetric token reweighting scheme. Vision tokens grow more redundant in deeper layers, they observe. A progressive decay schedule thus cuts the kept token share layer by layer. Tests on fifteen benchmarks matched or beat baseline models. Inference used about half the compute and cache of the baselines.
arxiv-2412-04649:
Simone Borelli, Francesco Giovinazzo, Francesco Grella, and Giorgio Cannata present a robot arm controller that dodges obstacles with partial sensing, in two thousand twenty-four. Their arm carries arrays of distance sensors on only some links. Safe work beside people, though, needs the whole body to move away from sudden hazards.

The method turns sensor readings into a sparse cloud of points around the robot. It then finds the closest pair of points between that cloud and each arm link. A top-priority motion task moves the whole body away, even at links with no sensors. Tests in still and moving scenes matched established methods, with a wider safety margin in places.
arxiv-2412-05149:
Michael Hu and co-authors published a report in 2024 on the second BabyLM Challenge, a contest for training language models on little data. Human learners need far less text than models do, and the contest tries to close that gap. Entrants train on a fixed budget of at most one hundred million words. This year added better text sets and an image-and-text set.

Thirty-one entries were scored on grammar, question answering, and other skills across three tracks. A hybrid model design beat the other approaches overall. No entry beat the baselines on the image track. Follow-up checks tied more compute to better scores and found the best entries changed data, goals, and design together.
arxiv-2412-05249:
Daniel Harman and co-authors lay the math base for a scheme that hides a slow message inside a normal network stream. Their 2024 paper calls the method Ghost Modulation. It rides on cross-technology links, where one kind of gear talks through another's signals, and it needs only a software update to run.

Such a channel is lopsided: packets drop and delays blur the timing, which makes the math tricky. The authors write out models for the signal and the channel, then give a rule for reading the message that follows best-guess logic. They add a method to find the packets and lock onto their timing, backed by simulations. Known short error-correcting codes are then applied, with error rates reported.
arxiv-2412-05349:
Ilyasse Lamrani, Hanaa Zitane, and Delfim Torres present a 2024 mathematics paper on control of fractional systems with tempering. Fractional equations remember their past, which suits materials with memory. Tempering softens that memory at long times. Two questions matter: can inputs steer the system anywhere, and can outputs reveal its full state?

The authors first solve the system class with a Laplace transform method. They then give exact conditions for controllability and observability in terms of two Gramian matrices, the standard tests in control theory. Kalman-style rank criteria make the checks easy. Two classic chaotic circuit models, the Chua circuit and the Chua-Hartley oscillator, serve as worked examples of the theory.
arxiv-2412-05449:
Raphael Shu and four co-authors test how teams of AI agents can work as one in business settings. One agent can solve a great deal, but hard tasks with many parts call for a crew. How crews should pass work and messages, and how to grade them, is still unsettled. Their 2024 report grades a new collaboration framework on tasks drawn from three business fields. The task set is shared with the report.

Two modes are put to the test. In coordination mode, agents talk in parallel and point to shared payloads by name. In routing mode, messages are passed on with no central hand. Coordination reached 90 percent success on set goals. Crews beat single agents by up to 70 percent on those grades. Named payloads lifted code-heavy tasks by 23 percent, and routing cut wait times.
arxiv-2412-05649:
Shourya Verma and co-authors rebuild and extend a neural model that predicts computer network performance, in a 2024 paper. Queuing theory and packet simulators struggle with today's large, varied networks. RouteNet-Fermi instead uses a graph neural network that reads the network's layout and traffic to forecast performance. The students re-implemented it and added new memory cell types.

Alongside the original gated recurrent units, they built versions using long short-term memory cells and plain recurrent cells inside the graph network. Comparing the variants clarifies how the choice of memory cell shapes accuracy in this setting. The authors present the result as a flexible testbed for future work on learning-based network modeling.
arxiv-2412-05749:
Namrata Das and co-authors compare, in a 2024 paper, how transformer models of different sizes and shapes perform at writing computer code on their own. Automated code generation promises relief from slow manual programming, and most attention has gone to giant language models. The authors ask a narrower question: how does the transformer's own architecture, its depth and complexity, affect its coding skill? Their system generates C++ solutions from problem statements.

The study tests models across problems from basic arithmetic to heavy computation. Robustness is judged by how well each architecture handles that rising difficulty. The authors frame the work as guidance for builders who must trade computing cost against coding reliability. Rather than chasing the largest model, they map where added complexity actually pays off for code generation tasks.
arxiv-2412-05849: Yichen Qin, Christian Sevenheck, and Peter Spacek compute in a 2024 math study a set of numbers called irregular Hodge numbers. The numbers belong to a family of connections built by Frenkel and Gross on a punctured line. The family covers almost simple groups and their representations. As a payoff, the new values prove a conjecture by Katzarkov, Kontsevich, and Pantev. That conjecture concerns mirror Landau-Ginzburg models of minuscule homogeneous spaces.
arxiv-2412-06549:
Angie Nataly Melo Castillo and co-authors tackle hidden pedestrians in road scenes in a 2024 paper. Self-driving cars must spot people on foot, yet people partly or fully hidden behind objects remain hard to detect, even for strong current systems. Human drivers use scene context to guess where a hidden person may be, and the team aimed to copy that skill.

They built OccluRoads, a data set of real and virtual road scenes with hidden pedestrians, all labeled with rich context notes. Their pipeline joins a knowledge graph, graph embeddings, and Bayesian reasoning to predict whether a hidden person is present. It reached a strong score and beat standard machine learning models by up to 42 percent.
arxiv-2412-06849:
Haotong Yang and co-authors fuse graph neural nets with large language models in one deep build, in a paper from 2024. Past fusions lean one way: text models swallow graphs as tokens and lose form, or graph models squash text into fixed vectors and lose sense.

Their build threads graph message passing straight into transformer layers, so text and form are read at once. A cross focus step reads full node and edge text with no squash. Twin heads let the language side write freely while the graph side calls in one pass. Scores hit top marks on key graph sets.
arxiv-2412-06949:
Ahmad Bin Rabiah, Nafis Sadeq, and Julian McAuley boost in 2024 chat-based recommendation by fusing talk signals with user-item history. Chat recommenders often lack the pattern data that sharpens picks. A new data set links Reddit talk to a large movie rating bank to fill that gap.

Their language model frame aligns chat picks with history-based embeddings. Gains reach double digits on hit rate and ranking quality scores. The frame beats talk-only, history-only, and plain language model rivals. Richer item knowledge, the authors argue, is the missing half of chat recommendation.
arxiv-2412-07049:
Zizhao Hu, Xiaolin Zhou, and Mohammad Rostami test a simpler form of attention inside vision transformers. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-four. Vision transformers sort images by weighing how parts of an image relate to each other. The usual design builds both the query and the key afresh for each input. The authors ask whether the key can stay fixed instead.

Their tests show that a fixed key can match or even beat the standard design. Placed inside a Metaformer backbone, the fixed-key block also works well as a middle stage. It blends the strengths of plain convolution and self-attention. The result hints that attention can be cut from two steps to one with no loss.
arxiv-2412-07449:
Zhi-Xiang Jin and three co-authors develop a basis-independent account of quantum coherence, in work from 2024. Coherence is usually measured against a chosen basis, which makes the amount seem basis-bound. For sets of states that stay unchanged under any unitary change, that limit can be lifted, and the maximally mixed state serves as the incoherent reference.

The authors set out how the basis-independent and basis-dependent views relate. They then show uses of the new view, including links among coherence, entanglement and quantum discord in multipartite systems, all framed through relative entropy. Readers get a cleaner way to talk about coherence where no basis is preferred.
arxiv-2412-07749:
Soumi Haldar and co-authors present a 2024 chemistry paper on why simulated molecular magnets relax too slowly on paper. Single-molecule magnets could store data at the molecular scale, but warmth shakes their lattices and the shaking erases the stored spin. Simulations of that spin-phonon relaxation often miss the measured rates by wide margins.

The standard simulation treats only a small active space of electrons. The authors test, for the first time systematically, what happens when correlation beyond that space is added, with two post-CASSCF methods. Cobalt and dysprosium magnets served as the case studies across temperatures. The richer treatments brought predictions to quantitative agreement with experiment. The paper tells modelers the cheap shortcut was the problem.
arxiv-2412-07949:
Frank Wang, writing solo, presents a 2024 calculation in general relativity. Near a heavy body such as Earth, space and time are curved. A local observer, though, can always set up coordinates in which physics looks flat and simple. Wang gives an explicit transformation between the standard Schwarzschild coordinates for a spherical mass and such local inertial coordinates. He then shows what the change of view reveals about light.

As a demonstration, he follows a photon fired sideways near Earth's surface. In local terms the light traces a parabola, much like a thrown stone. Its downward bend, though, comes out about three times larger than the bend a slow Newtonian particle would show. The example gives a clean local picture of how gravity bends light, a classic test of Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2412-08149:
Han and eight co-authors fixed a flaw in twenty twenty-four in bridge tools that fill in lost parts of images. Those tools march all pixels on one noise plan, but real fix steps run out of sync across pixels. High-detail pixels get short-changed by the shared plan, they argue.

Their tool first guesses the image slope map in the lost zone. Sharp zones then get earlier, gentler noise steps than flat zones. That pixel-wise plan lets fix steps lean on each other in time. On real sets it beat top past tools, with clean-image scores up by three to fourteen percent.
arxiv-2412-08249:
Three authors, L-R Gounis, A Kehagias, and A Riotto, show that spinning black holes refuse to be tidally stretched, at every order, in a 2024 paper. A body's Love numbers measure how it deforms under an external gravitational pull. For black holes in four dimensions the static values keep turning out to be zero, a fact that seems too clean to be accident.

Working in the Ernst formalism with Weyl coordinates, the team analyzed the full nonlinear deformation of a Kerr black hole in an external tidal field. The static Love numbers vanish at all orders of the field's strength, extending earlier results for non-spinning holes. The vanishing traces to hidden nonlinear symmetries of the system. The work explains the robustness rather than merely recording it.
arxiv-2412-08549:
Pascal Epple, Igor Shilov, Bozhidar Stevanoski, and Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye ask whether watermarked songs can be traced inside a music generator in two thousand twenty-four. AI music tools learn from vast stores of human work, much of it under copyright. If training songs carry hidden marks, the model's output may betray their use.

Two models were trained side by side, one on marked songs and one on clean ones, and their outputs compared. Marks that ears cannot hear still shifted what the model made. The size of the shift hinged on the marking method and on how much marked data was in the mix. The team also tested how well a top marking method resists removal tricks.
arxiv-2412-09449:
Suddhasattwa Brahma and co-authors present a 2024 theory paper on early universe cosmology in string theory. The setting is a heterotic string model with two moving domain walls. The authors build a duality chain to study late-time behavior. Reduced to four dimensions, the theory surprises them. It breaks no energy condition, so no bounce or ekpyrotic phase appears. Instead a passing de Sitter phase shows up: a stretch of accelerated expansion.

The phase stays inside the trans-Planckian bound, a key sanity limit. The team then builds an axion cosmology on it, with a time-varying axion coupling. Cosmologists get a string-based route to a de Sitter stretch that dodges known traps. Transient expansion phases matter because our own universe seems to sit in one. A model that yields it without breaking core rules is a notable catch.
arxiv-2412-10049:
Hu and co-authors propose SuperMark, a watermarking method for images that needs no training yet resists tampering. Watermarks protect ownership as AI images mix with real ones, but trained methods struggle to balance clarity and toughness. Their 2024 framework hides the mark inside random noise, then uses a pretrained upscaling diffusion model to turn that noise into the final image.

To read the mark, the image is run backward to the noisy start and the mark is recovered. The backward step's stability gives toughness, the team argues. Tests reached about 99.5 percent correct extraction under standard distortions and about 89 percent under adaptive attacks, with image quality matching rival methods. The scheme transfers across datasets, models, and sizes.
arxiv-2412-10149:
Glowing carbon radicals could power brighter screens and quantum bits, but their excited states defy the usual simulation tools. Jingkun Shen and six co-authors take a data driven shortcut in 2024. They gather the largest database yet of radical shapes and spectra. Then they teach a fast semiempirical model its best parameters directly from experiment. The training needs far less data than machine learning usually demands.

The tuned model predicts excitation energies several times more accurately than the same method with handbook parameters. Four freshly made radicals tested it blind, and it held up. The authors offer the model as a screening engine for radical based electronics. Sparse data, spent wisely, can stand in for heavy theory.
arxiv-2412-10249:
Alessandro Perelli, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Matthias Ehrhardt sketch images mid solver in a 2024 paper. Inverse imaging problems like CT involve huge images and data. Each solver step that touches the full image costs dearly. Stochastic methods already subsample the data side to save time.

Their algorithm, ImaSk, sketches the image side instead. Each iteration works on a randomly chosen resolution of the image. A saddle point view turns it into a gradient method with stored past gradients. For linear models with strong regularization, they prove linear convergence. CT simulations show the method reaches the target solution faster. More resolution levels cut the computing time further. The idea ports stochastic savings from data space into image space.
arxiv-2412-10449:
Romulo Santos and Jorge Sales apply advanced analysis tools to turbulent flow in a 2024 paper. Turbulence moves energy from large swirls to small ones, where it dissipates as heat. The authors model that flow with special operators and split the energy by place and by scale.

Using microlocal methods, which track how waves behave at fine scales, they derive a formula for the dissipation rate. They show it matches a known form in both spatial and spectral regions. The work links abstract operator theory to a concrete question in fluid physics: where turbulence spends its energy.
arxiv-2412-10649:
Christopher Tralie and three co-authors show in 2024 that hidden echoes can tag music made by AI tools. They hide a faint echo in training sounds, so soft that listeners cannot hear it. Later, they check if the echo shows up in sounds the model creates.

The team tried three kinds of audio models, and all of them passed the echo into their output. A single echo worked best, but longer spread-out echo patterns could carry more data. The mark even survived fine-tuning, mixing, and pitch shifts used in training. The authors say this old watermark trick could help prove where a model's training data came from, a live issue for rights and licensing.
arxiv-2412-10749:
Zhangbin Li and co-authors present a method that helps AI answer questions about videos with sound, in a 2024 paper. To answer well, the model must find the object that makes the sound and follow it through the clip. Guessing wrong there leads to wrong answers, so tracking the right patches of the image is the core problem.

Their method tracks image patches in three passes run side by side. One pass follows patches with strong motion, one follows patches that match the sound, and a third keeps only patches tied to the question. Graph networks carry the tracking within each short segment, and the three streams merge to form the answer. On standard test sets the method matched or beat recent rivals, even some trained on far more data.
arxiv-2412-10949:
Florian Kammüller, a solo author, extends a formal framework for security engineering with a way to prove that secret data do not leak, in a paper from 2024. The framework is built inside the Isabelle proof tool and models insiders and infrastructure. The paper's head title frames it as part two of security engineering in that framework.

The new part adds information flow security. Kammüller uses a notion called a shadow, drawn from the work of Morgan, to stand for what an observer at a lower level could see. He proves the shadow view matches the classic notion of noninterference inside the framework. That match yields conditions under which refining a design keeps it secure, solving a known paradox. A flight radar system serves as the running example.
arxiv-2412-11649:
Lecture notes from a 2024 workshop at the Institute for Advanced Study explain how gravity emerges from scattering math, in a paper edited from talks by five lecturers. Scattering amplitudes describe how particles bounce off each other. The notes show that classical gravity hides inside those quantum formulas.

A hydrogen atom example sets up how different motion regimes reveal bound and unbound behavior. Familiar results of general relativity, such as the delay of light near the Sun and Mercury's orbital drift, fall out of the amplitude view. Later sections apply worldline methods to black holes, gravitational waveforms, and three-body problems in astrophysics. The notes open a fast-growing field to students who know quantum theory but not the amplitude toolkit.
arxiv-2412-11949:
Tobias Rohe and co-authors test, in a 2024 paper, drone imaging with deep learning to count coconut palm trees on a Ghanaian farm. The farm had lost track of its trees across several planting phases. Knowing the tree count drives yield forecasts and farm planning, but counting by hand is slow and error prone.

Drone footage was captured in September 2022. A real time object detector, YOLO, was trained to spot palm crowns in the images. Real examples were scarce, so the team generated synthetic images to bulk up training. They assessed the detector inside a semi automated counting framework. They also tried accuracy boosting tricks, and weighed the system's practical value for farmers. Automating the count could turn a dreaded chore into a routine flight, with numbers a manager can plan around.
arxiv-2412-12249:
Roark Habegger and Ellen Zweibel ask what changes when a tenth of each supernova's energy starts out as cosmic rays rather than heat and motion. Explosions stir the gas between stars and can launch galactic winds. Their 2024 simulations of a layered gas patch run two versions of the same setup, identical except for that energy split.

The cosmic ray version drove a faster, hotter, and heavier outflow long after the blasts. Both runs formed cold clouds holding over half the mass, through two instabilities working together. One instability also produced very heavy wind loading with few explosions. Cosmic ray pressure drifted apart from gas density, cutting the share of ray energy lost as heat. Resolving the magnetic field finely proved essential to that result.
arxiv-2412-12649:
Robert Aufschläger and three co-authors build, in 2024 work, a text-aware veil for name-like fields in data tables. Veiling such fields needs ladders of broader terms, oft picked by hand at whim. Their line reads each value's sense from learned text codes, then groups close values rung by rung, which grows the ladder on its own.

Thirteen text codes, open and paid, were tried with two group ways. On a known adult data set the grown ladders beat hand ones for later use, most at low veil grades. More veil picks thus come to hand, and the shared data keep more worth. The code is public.
arxiv-2412-13049:
Joshua Groen and co-authors present TIMESAFE, a guard system for timing attacks on 5G fronthaul links in 2024. Modern cell networks split base station parts, and the fronthaul link between them needs exact timing. New packet standards carry that timing well but guard it poorly.

The team shows spoofing and replay attacks against the timing protocol in action. One spoof made a production-ready private 5G base station fail within two seconds, needing manual restart. Their machine learning monitor spots such attacks with over 97.5 percent accuracy. The work presses security into a layer built mainly for performance.
arxiv-2412-13249:
Oscar Arandes and Emil Bergholtz explore a chain of driven resonators as a quantum sensor, asking where its sensitivity truly comes from. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Open quantum systems can react sharply to tiny nudges, which tempts sensor designers. The chain here follows the squeezed Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a classic with distinct bulk phases.

The pair compare setups that differ in bulk topology and in the modes at the chain's ends. They test sensing of both plain shifts and the skin effect, where waves pile at one edge. Their study goes past tiny nudges to swings of any size. Tuning matters: the best settings boost the quantum edge without demanding fragile fine-tuning. The authors stress that practical sensors must avoid knife-edge regimes. The work maps where this platform can really deliver.
arxiv-2412-13749:
Xin Su and Zhuoran Zheng wrote a 2024 paper on merging photos taken at distinct light levels into one rich image. Phone shots keep growing in size, and old merge methods are too slow for real time use on small devices. Users also want a say in how the final image looks.

Their method leans on a color lookup grid that can grade huge images at speed. Merging shots at mixed light levels is unsure work, and that doubt strains the grid. A teacher and student network pair models that doubt to keep the grid robust. An implicit function adds an edit mode so users can tune results to the scene. Tests showed the method ranks high on both speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2412-13849:
Can Wang and co-authors present a physics paper from 2024 on reading quantum bits. In a superconductor-based quantum computer, gates are fast and sharp, but reading the bit lags behind. The strong signal used to probe the bit can also knock it out of its state.

The team designed a new layout that links the bit and its reader along the length axis. The layout kills off stray cross links that cause errors. It also adds a bend to the reader's response that trims two error kinds. In tests, reads were right 99.8 percent of the time in about two hundred nanoseconds, with no first-stage amplifier. After removing setup errors, pure read accuracy topped 99.9 percent. The design fits setups that read many bits at once.
arxiv-2412-14249:
Eve Dones, Quentin Henry, and Laura Bernard add tidal effects to gravitational wave templates in a 2024 paper. When two neutron stars or similar bodies orbit, each raises tides on the other, and those tides leave fingerprints in the emitted waves. Accurate templates must include them to read the signal correctly.

The authors compute the full waveform amplitude with adiabatic tidal effects up to a stated post-Newtonian order. They decompose the wave into modes tied to spin-weighted spherical harmonics, built from radiative multipole moments. Such precision helps observatories infer the stiffness of neutron star matter from real events.
arxiv-2412-14549:
Barak Budnick, Ofer Biham, and Eytan Katzav analyze networks that grow by attachment yet also lose nodes at random. Their 2024 paper defines the PARD model: at each step a new node links preferentially to well connected nodes, or a random node is deleted. A single parameter captures whether growth or shrinkage wins overall.

Using a master equation and computer simulations, the authors map the steady distribution of node degrees on both sides. When the network shrinks overall, the degree distribution settles with an exponential tail. When it grows, the tail follows a power law instead. The switch between them is a phase transition at the balance point. Such models fit real networks whose members also leave, from online platforms to citation graphs.
arxiv-2412-14749:
Adel Rahman and Leonard Susskind study vector bosons in de Sitter space in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Their setting is the static patch, the region one observer can see in an expanding universe. The field is a massive vector boson described by the Proca action. They argue its true physical mass differs from the mass written in the Lagrangian.

The physical mass gains an extra term tied to the size of the de Sitter space. That shift has a striking consequence. The theory may stay well-defined even where the naive mass looks tachyonic, or unstable. They identify special features at the edge of stability, a specific mass value. Fixing a static patch also breaks the full symmetry of de Sitter space. That break explains why their modes need not fit the usual symmetry classes.
arxiv-2412-14849:
Hongling Xu, Yice Zhang, Qianlong Wang, and Ruifeng Xu build a data synthesis framework for few-shot aspect-based sentiment analysis, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Large language models can generate training samples where data is scarce. Earlier augmentation methods modified existing samples and lacked diversity. In-context learning approaches suffered labels that strayed from task requirements.

Their dual-stream framework synthesizes data from two complementary directions. One stream is key-point-driven; the other works from instances. Together they produce diverse, high-quality sentiment samples in low-resource settings. A label refinement module then cleans up the synthetic labels. Extensive experiments show the method beating previous few-shot solutions. It also outperforms other language-model data generation methods tested. The work targets sentiment tasks where annotated examples are few.
arxiv-2412-15149:
Xin-Yi Liu, Yue-Liang Wu, and Zhen Fang study the QCD phase transition with holographic models. Their 2024 arXiv paper compares two gravity-based model systems. One system adds a scalar field to the standard setup. Both models are tested against results from lattice QCD. The team then uses the models to describe neutron stars.

Both models matched lattice behavior well. The scalar system showed a first-order phase transition in the pure gauge sector. That matches what Yang-Mills theory predicts. For neutron stars, the team added leptons to keep electric charge balanced. They computed the cold equation of state and mass-radius links. The scalar system described star traits that fit current observations. Tidal deformability was also checked.
arxiv-2412-15249:
Shubham Agarwal and seven co-authors ask whether today's large language models can help write literature reviews, the survey sections that summarize prior work in a field. Their paper came out in 2024. Reviews are essential but slow to write, especially as publication volume grows.

They split the task in two: finding the relevant papers from a query abstract, then drafting the review from what was found. For retrieval, the model first extracts keywords, searches an external database, and then re-ranks the hits. Re-ranking doubled recall compared with naive search, and it exposed the model's reasons. For writing, the model first plans an outline, then drafts section by section. Their tests suggest models can assist reviews well when the job is decomposed this way. They release their evaluation protocol for future models.
arxiv-2412-15349:
Pratham Singla, Ayush Singh, Adesh Gupta, and Shivank Garg propose a planning framework that mixes city-wide optimization with neighborhood voices, in a 2024 paper. Fast-growing cities struggle to balance grand infrastructure needs against local wishes. Most methods choose one side: top-down optimization or bottom-up community planning. Their hybrid runs in two tiers. First a solver lays out basic infrastructure for the whole city region.

Then four software agents, each speaking for a sub-region, propose changes tuned to local demographics. A master planner weighs and merges the proposals into one coherent plan. The team tested the framework on a new dataset of maps from three fast-urbanizing Indian cities. Results showed finer, more balanced development than either approach alone, while the city still functioned as a whole. The authors offer the design for planners in rapidly developing regions.
arxiv-2412-15749:
Li and Xie overturn a common assumption about dark matter: that clashes involving many particles at once are too rare to matter. That holds for ordinary thermal dark matter, but not when the particle slows down while still far hotter than its own mass. Their 2024 paper works through one such case, where ultralight wave-like dark matter destroys itself into pairs of light particles.

Each clash then seeds more light, producing a runaway growth the authors call photon proliferation in the young universe. Applied to the light temperature after neutrinos split off, the effect tightens limits on the dark matter coupling by several orders of magnitude. The authors say the lesson extends to other particles and forces.
arxiv-2412-15849:
Hanchun Jiang and Toshiya Namikawa study how doubt in the cosmos's second dawn affects our power to bound the waves sent out by the first burst of growth. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

That dawn, when the first stars lit gas anew, leaves a large-scale mark in the glow left from the hot early cosmos. Sky-wide probes will read that mark to test the old waves. The team asks what goes wrong if the true past of that dawn has a unlike shape from the smooth form used to fit the data. With a probe like a planned space scope, they find the bounds stay much the same. The result calms a fear for such tests.
arxiv-2412-15949:
Wei-jie Fu, Jan Pawlowski, Robert Pisarski, Fabian Rennecke, Rui Wen, and Shi Yin wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies the moat regime of dense quark matter, where meson links wobble in space in a wave-like way.

The team looks at how pions act in real time at set heat and density. They show the moat comes from particle-hole-like ripples near the Fermi surface. Those ripples plant a peak in the pion's spectral shape at nonzero space-like momentum. That peak reads as a new quasi-particle, which they name the moaton. Their frame also tests if the even chiral phase can hold against a wavy condensate. At the densities eyed, such a phase looks highly unlikely.
arxiv-2412-16149:
Sangmin Choi, Alok Laddha, and Andrea Puhm wrote this 2024 theoretical physics paper on a hidden symmetry of electromagnetism. Earlier work tied a universal rule about very soft photons to an endless set of phase rotations acting on matter at the edge of spacetime. Each rotation carries a conserved charge.

Here the team extend those charges to all orders in the coupling strength. They prove that keeping the charges conserved is exactly the classical rule for soft photon emission found by others in 2019. They also widen the matching memory formulas from particles to full matter fields. The result completes a three-way link among symmetry, conservation, and observable effects, known as an infrared triangle.
arxiv-2412-16249:
Guozhong Zheng and co-authors asked in 2024 why people act fairly when they split money, even though classic theory says they should grab what they can. In lab games, one player offers a split and the other can accept or reject it, leaving both with nothing.

The team let computer players learn from rewards, with each player keeping score for both roles in the game. Fair offers grew on their own when players valued past play and future gains. Deals were more likely to succeed as offers rose, matching lab results with people. The pattern held under other role setups and in a grid of players. Fairness, they argue, needs no outside cause.
arxiv-2412-16649:
Smashing a fast particle into a nucleus and knocking out a single nucleon lets physicists read the nucleus's inner structure. Yoshida and Tanaka review this quasi-free knockout method in the era of exotic radioactive beams. New detectors, such as the MINOS system in the SEASTAR project, have sharpened what the reactions reveal. The review covers both the basic idea and fresh results.

Recent work extends the method to low-energy knockouts and to knocking out alpha particles, tight clusters of four nucleons. Whether such clusters form inside nuclei, and how universally, is a live question. The authors introduce a framework, CDCCIA, that builds two-nucleon correlations into the reaction theory. That step is needed to connect cluster properties with what experiments measure, including reactions that eject several nucleons at once. Future projects will target heavier noble clusters too.
arxiv-2412-16849:
Yuxiang Zhang and five co-authors share a 2024 technical report on tuning reasoning models for expert fields. Big models that think step by step do well on broad tasks, but expert work needs training data that is scarce and lacks the reasoning steps themselves. The team tries to copy a new tuning style from a top AI lab, using only a small set of expert examples.

Their system, OpenRFT, stretches those few examples three ways. It makes new questions from old ones, writes out fake reasoning paths for a model to learn from, and uses few-shot prompts at test time. On a science knowledge test, the tuned model gained clear ground with just one hundred examples per task. Code, data, and models are shared in public.
arxiv-2412-17849:
Jungpil Shin and co-authors detect Parkinson's disease from handwriting motion in a 2024 paper. The disease stiffens movement and slows the hand, leaving traces in writing. Most past systems averaged features over a whole writing task, which can wash out fine changes and direction cues.

Their method mines the first and last tenth of each task for new dynamic features, 65 in all, and merges them with 23 known ones. Layered statistics then sharpen the set, and a floating search keeps only the most telling features. The aim is a detector with better accuracy, stability, and sensitivity than whole task averages give.
arxiv-2412-17949:
Where two ribbons of graphene meet, a trapped electronic state can sit at the junction, protected by topology from ordinary disturbance. Hazem Abdelsalam and co-authors classify those states across a wide family of ribbon shapes in a 2024 paper, including shapes chemists have already made. They then ask what the trapped states are good for.

Their answer is sensing and chemistry rather than computing. A modeled double junction reacts strongly to a common pollutant gas molecule settling nearby, its transport shifting in a readable way. The authors argue the pinpoint nature of junction states makes them fine probes, opening a route they call topological chemistry.
arxiv-2412-18149:
Xiao Guo, Manh Tran, Jiaxin Cheng, and Xiaoming Liu wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on making face images of a specific person from text. A user gives one reference photo and a written prompt, and the model should draw that same face doing or wearing what the text says.

Older methods either need fresh tuning for each person or drift away from the prompt.
