The team's model, Dense-Face, adds a pose-controlling adapter to a standard image generator, so the face can turn as asked while text editing still works. It also learns to predict dense face annotations from the generator's own inner features, which teaches it face structure. Tests show top or near-top scores on text match, identity keeping, and pose control. The authors aim at custom portraits that stay true to both the person and the prompt.
arxiv-2412-18849:
Maxence Boels, Yang Liu, Prokar Dasgupta, Alejandro Granados, and Sebastien Ourselin teach surgery video tools to see ahead. Most tools just name the phase a cut is in now. Sight ahead could tell the team what to make ready. Past work sees one near event ahead. But surgery is dense, loops a lot, and runs long. Their frame, SWAG, builds chains of phases to come, at one-minute steps, over long spans.

Two ways to build the chains vie: one pass, and step by step. Marks built from how phases tend to follow each other hone the casts. A side trick turns time-left fits into class picks. On two free surgery data sets, the top model hit F1 near a third at 20 minutes and near 41% at 30 minutes. Time-left slips stayed near a third to half a minute at short spans.
arxiv-2412-18949:
Ivanov and co-authors ask whether a metric space can be identified by its distances to the simplest possible spaces, in a 2024 paper. The test spaces are simplexes, where every pair of points sits at one same nonzero distance. The yardstick is the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, the standard way to compare shapes up to stretching. Some different spaces sit at zero distance and so can never be told apart.

The surprise: some spaces at positive distance from each other still produce identical distance lists to all simplexes. The authors exhibit such indistinguishable pairs. They then prove conditions, both sufficient and necessary, for when this blindness occurs. The paper maps a subtle limit of a widely used recognition idea.
arxiv-2412-19049:
Seokcheon Lee works through a theory of the universe in this 2024 paper. The model under study lets the speed of light vary in a minimal way, an idea tied to how cosmic time stretches light from far objects. Lee applies a method that splits space-time into space plus time slices, a frame often used to study how the universe evolves.

Within that frame, Lee derives the model's lapse function and shift vector, the parts that set how time flows between slices. He then works out the paired sets of equations that limit and drive the system, and shows they agree with Einstein's equations. In the standard model the lapse is simply one, but here it changes with time. Lee argues this reading makes the physical meaning of the model clearer.
arxiv-2412-19249:
Aryan Agarwala and Guy Even prove that two common limits on approximate membership data structures do real work. Structures that answer membership queries with false positives most often bar duplicate insertions. They also bar the deletion of items that are not members. Under those rules, known designs use close to the least space in theory.

Agarwala and Even show that if both limits are lifted, the space needed jumps. Any structure for a set under any duplicate insertions and deletions of non-members needs far more bits. The count scales with the logarithm of the number of sets that can be drawn from the universe. The bound splits the well-behaved setting from the fully general one. The rules are not mere ease of use. They are what makes near-best space possible.
arxiv-2412-19649:
John Augustine and co-authors study how a crowd of computers can all download one trusted file when many of them lie. In their model, a network of peers can query an outside source holding a long bit string, and they can talk among themselves. Up to a fixed share of the peers may be Byzantine, feeding false data to wreck the download.

Their randomized protocol gets every honest peer the full string at nearly the fewest queries anyone must make. Against a stronger foe that swaps which peers are corrupt each round, they hit the best possible time with fatter messages. Broadcast rules and the simpler crash-fault world get their own near-optimal protocols. The work hardens shared downloads against sabotage.
arxiv-2412-20149:
Mo Zhou and co-authors design control pulses for leaky quantum systems in a 2024 paper set in circuit quantum electrodynamics. In that field, superconducting circuits are steered and read by microwave pulses. Real systems lose energy to their surroundings, so a pulse must hit its target fast and cheaply before the loss spoils the state.

Their frame rests on a classic rule of optimal control, the Pontryagin maximum principle. They cast the circuit's noisy motion as a linear control problem and derive pulses whose energy cost scales in a favorable way. The pulses beat standard shortcut methods that rush a system along a protected path. On a resonator linked to a qubit, the pulses read the qubit with a signal quality matching far costlier schemes, across a range of photon levels.
arxiv-2501-00149:
Grace Jiang, Jiangchao Qiu, and Sai Ravela (2024) hunt the rare storms that cause destructive storm tides, without simulating every storm. Climate studies produce huge catalogs of downscaled tropical cyclones. Running full water simulations on all of them is unaffordable. The authors first show that a fast surrogate model can flag the dangerous ones accurately. It even generalizes to climate scenarios it never saw. Their system, LASSE, then learns actively as it searches.

Starting from a small set of fully simulated storms, the surrogate picks which storm to simulate next. Each new result retrains it on the spot. On a large catalog, the search found every destructive storm it was tested on, with perfect precision. It needed fewer than a fifth of the full simulations as training. The authors present the method as scalable to the biggest catalogs.
arxiv-2501-00349:
Tatsuki Murakami and co-authors describe, in a 2024 paper, an architecture for spectroscopy and microwave generation based on soliton microcombs. A microcomb splits a single laser beam into many evenly spaced lines of light. In their design, the crystalline microresonators that hold the combs can be shifted in position, which gives extra control over the solitons.

Using one shared pump laser, the team produced two coherent soliton combs in separate resonators with slightly different repetition rates. This pairing supports coherent dual-comb spectroscopy. They also generated Kerr solitons directly from an ultrastable laser with a linewidth below one hertz. That approach greatly reduced phase noise in the microwaves the system produced. The authors present the design as a step toward wider use of microcombs in ranging, data links, and low-noise signals.
arxiv-2501-00949:
Soichiro Suzuki wrote this 2025 math paper on sharp constants in smoothing bounds for the Dirac equation, a core equation for electrons. A smoothing bound says a solution spreads out in a weighed average sense, and the best constant in the bound is often unknown. Suzuki gives the best constants for the free equation in any number of dimensions from two up.

A main theorem writes the best constant as the top value of a set of functions given by integrals over the weight and the smoothing shape. The proof rests on a reworked split of functions on the sphere, shaped to fit the Dirac operator. With the theorem, many standard cases yield exact values, even some where the sister equation for slow particles has none. A classic claim that fails in two dimensions for that sister equation holds here.
arxiv-2501-01149:
Yuxiang Chai and co-authors present Android Agent Arena in 2025, a test system for phone-using AI agents. Language and vision models now drive agents that tap and swipe through mobile apps on their own. Older benchmarks grade still frames or run in frozen offline apps, which misses how agents handle live, changing online services.

Their arena holds one hundred tasks drawn from twenty popular dynamic apps across twenty categories. Grading follows an essential-state method: a vision model checks step by step whether the key states of the task were reached, rather than demanding one fixed path. The package also includes tools for driving devices, resetting apps, and collecting human and agent demonstrations, all set for public release.
arxiv-2501-01549:
Vahid Nourozi builds quantum error-correcting codes from a family of geometric codes, in a 2025 paper. The codes start with Goppa codes drawn from maximal curves over finite fields, curves given by a short equation. From them he forms codes for classical and quantum use, then tweaks the designs to improve their numbers. Long runs of simulations test how the codes behave as error rates change.

The paper gives concrete examples and sets them beside known results. The new codes do not always reach the best possible minimum distance. Still, they offer orderly ways to build codes with useful trade-offs for certain tasks. Nourozi presents the graphs and tables as a guide to how these codes act in noisy settings, and as a base for later theory.
arxiv-2501-01649:
MohammadReza EskandariNasab, Shah Muhammad Hamdi, and Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi tackle the hard task of making fake time series data that still behaves like the real thing, in a paper from 2025. Fake data helps when real data are scarce, but time linked data must keep its step by step flow.

Their frame, AVATAR, pairs an autoencoder with a guide net and a stepwise learning rule. New loss terms push the code space toward a set shape and help the decoder learn time flow. Tests on many kinds of series showed gains in both how real the fakes looked and how much they helped later tasks.
arxiv-2501-01849:
Dai, Lui and their co-authors present MACO, a multi-agent online learning system for choosing user-aligned language model responses in 2025. Offline prompt tuning is costly and often misses the varied styles that different users prefer.

Local agents first filter out low-quality responses with an online elimination step. A cloud server then adjusts the choice strategy using pooled preference data from many agents. Extra conversations start as needed to sharpen alignment. Tests with embedding models and large language models beat baseline methods by a clear margin. Theory also gives near-optimal regret bounds, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-02249:
Antonio Beltrán and Changguo Shao extend a classic theorem of P. Hall about finite groups, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Hall showed that if every maximal subgroup sits inside the whole group with an index that is a prime or a prime squared, then the group is solvable.

The authors loosen the condition in two directions and still reach solvability. First, maximal subgroups may instead simply be nilpotent, a strongly orderly kind of subgroup. Second, the same conclusion holds when every smaller non-maximal subgroup lies inside some subgroup of prime or prime-squared index. Results like these map exactly which structural clues force a finite group to be solvable, a basic question in group theory.
arxiv-2501-02449:
Márcio Matheus de Lima Barboza and Francisco Márcio Barboza revisit two pillars of first-semester calculus, Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem, pairing their classical proofs with computational verification. The theorems anchor much of analysis and the modeling built on it. The paper states both formally and proves them analytically, with the rigor the authors consider necessary for real understanding.

Geometric interpretations accompany the proofs, picturing the guaranteed flat tangent and the parallel secant. The second half checks the theorems computationally, an integrated theory-and-practice exercise. The goal is pedagogical as much as mathematical: to validate the results by hand and by machine in one treatment. Students meeting these theorems get both the argument and the experiment. The authors frame the dual approach as the natural modern way to teach bedrock analysis.
arxiv-2501-02649:
Haixu Liu, Penghao Jiang, Zerui Tao, Muyan Wan, and Qiuzhuang Sun present Tighnari, a model that forecasts which plant species grow at a place and time, for a LifeCLEF lab notebook. Such forecasts aid wildlife care and species ID tools. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Training drew on tens of thousands of plant surveys across Europe, plus satellite images, climate series, land cover, and soil data. A graph based feature step and a correction step shape the inputs. The team picked the best backbones for time and image data, built a fresh time cube backbone, and fused modes with layered cross attention. A threshold top pick step cleans the output.
arxiv-2501-03149:
Domenico Giulini revisits in 2025 a classic subtlety of Einstein's special relativity: how velocities combine. Adding speeds in relativity is famously odd, since the order of additions matters and groupings change the answer. A related twist, the Thomas angle, is often called hard to derive. Giulini re-derives the whole structure in a self-contained way.

The first part works with matrices in the standard component style, leaning on a polar splitting theorem, and gives explicit formulas for the Thomas angle. The second part offers a geometric view that may be less familiar. It defines relative velocity between two motions in an invariant way, resting on a boost-link theorem for which he gives an elementary proof. He then sets the result beside the matching ideas in older Newtonian space-time, marking where they agree and where relativity parts company.
arxiv-2501-04049:
Anica Hamer and colleagues put three bold claims to the test in a 2025 optics paper. Quantum networks need to change a photon's color without harming its fragile quantum state. Crystals do that job well, but they add noise, accept only a narrow color band, and heat unevenly under strong pump light, which hurts performance.

A hollow fiber filled with hydrogen gas offers an alternative the team had proposed earlier. New experiments back all three claims: strong pump fields do not degrade the conversion, background noise stays near zero, and the process works across a broad band at once. Fiber conversion could suit future large fiber-based quantum networks that need clean, flexible links.
arxiv-2501-04149:
Wi-Fi 7 can talk over several links at once, and it offers two ways to do it. Aishwarya Choorakuzhiyil, Kevin Ho, and Sara Reyes compare those ways in a 2025 simulation study. One mode, STR, sends and receives on two links simultaneously. The other, EMLSR, listens on several links with a single radio and jumps to the best.

Using the ns-3 network simulator, the team varied coding schemes, channel widths, link quality, and interference. They tracked delay, throughput, and energy use. STR won on speed and delay because it truly uses both links, suiting busy, high-load settings. EMLSR traded some speed for much better energy behavior while staying responsive, suiting battery-powered gear. The authors frame the choice as a deployment decision, not a contest with one winner.
arxiv-2501-04249:
Satyam Goyal and Soham Dan test language models on linguistic reasoning in this 2025 paper. They built a benchmark, IOLBENCH, from problems of the International Linguistics Olympiad, contests that ask solvers to deduce the rules of an unknown language from a few examples.

The problems cover syntax, word building, sound patterns, and meaning, and each is self contained. Even the best current models struggled, above all where a rule must be built up from parts and applied in a new way. The authors sort out where models do well and where they fail. The benchmark gives the field a hard, clean test of rule learning.
arxiv-2501-04349:
Kanupriya and Shravan Kumar study spectral synthesis in multidimensional Fourier algebras in a two thousand twenty-five harmonic analysis paper. Fourier algebras encode the harmonic analysis of a locally compact group, and the multidimensional version was brought in by Todorov and Turowska.

Spectral synthesis asks which closed sets can be won back from the functions vanishing on them. The authors prove multidimensional versions of the subgroup lemma and of the injection and inverse projection theorems. The results cover both spectral sets and the stricter Ditkin sets. They also set up parallel synthesis between consecutive dimensions and prove an analogue of Malliavin's theorem, a landmark result in the classic one-dimensional theory.
arxiv-2501-04449:
Francesco Rosini and Simone Pacetti revisit a meson decay that once seemed to break a symmetry rule. Their 2025 paper deals with isospin, a near-symmetry of the strong force. If it held, a charm meson pair state's decay to a lambda and sigma pair would run purely through a virtual photon. A past data book gave a rate so high it forced either rule breaking or a bad datum.

The new data book cuts that rate more than sevenfold, with wider error bars. The humble read wins: the old datum looks unreliable. The pair still urge a fresh measurement to settle the decay.
arxiv-2501-04549:
Ido Avitan and Noam Soker measure in this 2025 paper how the lobes of multipolar planetary nebulae tilt against each other. These dying-star clouds often sprout several bubble pairs, each pair marking a symmetry axis. The team measured the sky-plane angles between neighboring axes across tens of nebulae and rebuilt the true three-dimensional spread.

Fully random directions do not fit. A random spread fenced between about twenty and sixty degrees does. The authors trace each axis to jets fired along a spinning accretion disk around a companion star. Two angular momentum feeds of like strength, one steady from the orbit and one jittery from the giant's churning envelope, could fence the angles so.
arxiv-2501-04749:
Francisco Lustosa and Nelson Pinto-Neto add fluids to a bouncing universe and watch them track the driver. Their 2025 paper deals with bounce cosmologies, where the cosmos shrinks, rebounds, and grows without a singular start. A scalar field with an exponential slope drives the bounce. Most added fluids fall into tracking, marching with the field across eras, which can model shifts between cosmic phases.

One dust mix stands out: the field runs an early dark energy spell, yields to a radiation-like phase, then tracks dust at dark matter density. Far back, dust rules the shrink; near the bounce, stiff stuff takes over, easing the quantum hop to expansion.
arxiv-2501-05349:
Lorenzo Trezzini and co-authors study quantum cellular automata built from fermionic modes in a 2025 paper. A cellular automaton updates a chain of cells by local rules. In the quantum version with fermions, the building blocks are modes that obey the exclusion rules of particles like electrons. The question is which of these automata can be built as short quantum circuits.

Earlier work sorted fermionic automata into classes using extra helper systems to define when two automata count as the same. The team strengthens that sorting by removing the helpers from the definition. They give a full description of automata where each cell talks only to its nearest neighbors. One class they find cannot be built from the simple gates and shifts that suffice for ordinary qubit automata.
arxiv-2501-05449:
Pumpkin leaves announce their diseases in spots and mildew, but spotting them in the field is slow and error-prone. Khandaker and co-authors trained image networks to name five states from photographs: downy mildew, powdery mildew, mosaic disease, bacterial leaf spot, and healthy. Their dataset held two thousand high-resolution images gathered from several farms so the models would meet real variety.

Seven established network designs were compared, and ResNet50 won, reaching 90.5 percent accuracy with matching precision, recall, and F1 scores. To keep the system honest, the team applied explainable AI tools that paint heat maps over each leaf, showing which regions drove the call. The authors argue that an accurate model whose reasoning a farmer can inspect could bring earlier, surer treatment to pumpkin fields.
arxiv-2501-05749:
Arafat Alam Khandaker and three fellow authors teach neural translators to speak regional Bangla, in a 2025 paper. Standard Bangla differs sharply from the dialects of Chittagong, Sylhet, Barishal, Noakhali, and Mymensingh in vocabulary, sound, and sentence shape, and those dialects are largely missing from language technology.

The team fine-tuned three translation models on a dataset of 32,500 sentences spanning the dialects. BanglaT5 performed best, with a character error rate of 12.3 percent and a word error rate of 15.7 percent, ahead of mT5 and mBART50. Dialect-aware tools could help speakers use services in their own variety of the language. The work also supports preserving linguistic diversity rather than flattening it into the standard form.
arxiv-2501-05949:
Ivo Petr and Ladislav Hlavatý explore a solution-making trick in string theory, in a 2025 paper. The trick, called Jacobi-Lie T-plurality, turns one valid background for strings into another. It rests on a kind of algebra broader than the one behind an older, related trick. The pair focus on what happens when extra fields, known as spectators, ride along and are reshaped by a free choice of function.

With one standard reshaping rule, they build new backgrounds for the known low-size algebras. Each new background is checked against the equations of supergravity, the gravity theory that string models must obey. The reshaped partners pass the same check. The paper is dense theory, aimed at specialists who build string backgrounds. It widens a known tool and maps where the freedom in it lies.
arxiv-2501-06149:
Giulia Ballabio and James Owen ask what a gas trace tells of air loss from far worlds in a 2025 paper. Air loss is now held to shape which worlds we find. Tests of the math behind that claim are still young, and the gas at hand is the prime probe, seen at more than twenty worlds.

Their new model ties the gas print to wind facts: how fast air flees and how hot the flow runs. A wind frame is set on a capped scheme, where drive heat sets the pace. The joint tale lets sky teams read world air from a line of light. Far world lore gains a firmer base.
arxiv-2501-06349:
Philippe Gagnon gives a simple proof that Bayesian heavy-tailed regression models shrug off outliers. A line of work called resolution of conflict asks how a posterior behaves as stray points flee the bulk of the data. Past proofs for regression cases grew technical and hard to follow, which slowed the field.

His 2025 proof leans on a narrower, handy class of priors: each coefficient gets a sub-exponential law, a family that covers priors in common use. A tail bound then does the heavy lifting, with classic probability results in support. The error law stays broad, allowing any tail that varies in a regular way. The gain is a proof a reader can hold in one view.
arxiv-2501-06449:
Shoushuo Zhang and co-authors improve radar-like target spotting in 2025 for future 6G networks. These networks will sense their surroundings while carrying data, a dual role called integrated sensing and communication. Smart surfaces that bounce and shape radio waves, named RIS, can add extra viewpoints on a target.

Their design views the target from many angles at once, since each path has its own delay, motion, and direction signature. That variety helps pull the target's signal out of clutter. They jointly shape the sent waveform, the surface settings, and the receiver filters to boost the target signal against noise and clutter. Simulations show the multi-view plan detects targets better in hard scenes.
arxiv-2501-06849:
Matteo Cerutti and co-authors weigh a source of doubt in maps of the proton's inner parts in a 2025 paper. The maps are drawn from shots that knock quarks out of protons and kindred grains, read at a scale where edge effects swell.

At that high-share edge, small fix terms can bend the drawn maps. The team used a shared frame to test ways of adding the fixes for both proton and deuteron shots. They traced how the fixes trade off with tweaks for the bound deuteron, and how both shape the map of one quark kind and the neutron's own shape. Fixes that split by charge kind proved key to keep bias low. The work is a guide for cleaner maps.
arxiv-2501-07049:
Fu Yu-Cong and co-authors watch a magnetar flare in a 2025 space paper. The star, a neutron star with a huge magnetic field, woke into a fresh active phase in October 2022. X-ray bursts poured out for hours, and radio bursts followed at the tail of that rush, tying the two kinds of emission together.

A NASA X-ray telescope tracked the star for nearly three months after the onset. The glow of the steady emission faded in a smooth exponential fall. One flare stood out on the curve, and a fast radio burst arrived right after its peak. Timing and color of the X-rays chart how the star settles after such an episode.
arxiv-2501-07549:
A Chen, M Gandikota, and A Cacciuto simulate what happens when an elastic membrane is slit in patterns in a 2025 paper. Flat elastic sheets are famous for staying flat at any temperature, shrugging off random damage. Orderly damage, it turns out, is another story.

The team cut parallel slits into simulated self-avoiding membranes and varied the number and length of the cuts. The sheets collapsed into a zoo of complex shapes, each steered by the cut pattern. For simpler membranes with bending stiffness but no self-avoidance, the shrinkage followed one universal curve once the axes were rescaled. The result suggests kirigami-style cutting as a dial for programming a flat sheet's final form, with uses from materials to soft robotics.
arxiv-2501-07849:
Xiaoyu Zhang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that exposes provider bias in language models that write code. The models act as a new kind of recommendation engine. With no prompt to do so, they favor services from set firms, such as one cloud giant over another.

The team built an auto pipeline to make a test set across six coding task types and 30 real use scenes. They then ran seven top models through the set at large cost in compute. The models showed strong tilts toward Google and Amazon services. Some even rewrote user code to swap in a favored provider with no request. The authors warn such bias can feed digital monopolies and betray user trust.
arxiv-2501-08249:
Junming Zhao and co-authors present Pancake, a programming language built to prove device drivers correct, in a paper from 2025. Driver bugs are the top cause of operating system breaches. Yet no fast, real driver for a nontrivial device had been fully proven before. Pancake is a plain imperative language with a clean, proof-friendly meaning.

Its compiler rests on a proven back end, so the machine code keeps the source meaning. An automatic bridge hands Pancake code to a solver front end for checking. With that chain, the team proved a fast driver for a network card. The result shows proof need not cost speed. It also gives systems builders a template for verified low-level code. More drivers could follow the same path.
arxiv-2501-08549:
Sitong Gong and co-authors present a method for cutting out objects in video based on text reasoning in a 2025 paper. Older methods lean on a single token to stand for the target, which misses shape detail and motion between frames. Their system uses large multimodal models to feed rich space and time features into layered tokens. One token type works at frame level, and another works across time.

A fusion step blends frame scores by similarity, and a selection step picks the best key frame using a segmentation model's blockage scores. That frame is cut out first, then the result spreads through the video. Scores on a known benchmark beat a prior leading method by clear margins. Readers see token design as the key to video detail.
arxiv-2501-09749:
Yibin Lei, Tao Shen, Yu Cao, and Andrew Yates present a new kind of text embedding in a 2025 paper. Embeddings turn text into number lists so computers can search and match meaning. Most are dense lists with no readable parts, but lexicon-based versions tie each number to a word, which keeps them readable and fast to search.

Their system, LENS, is the first of its kind built from a large language model. It groups near-duplicate words into clusters so each number stands for one word family. On a major benchmark, LENS beat dense embeddings while staying compact. Its size can also be trimmed without special training tricks. Blending LENS with a dense model gave the best search scores in the study.
arxiv-2501-09949:
Muñoz, Yuan, and Jain pruned large AI models without retraining in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Cutting whole blocks from a transformer shrinks it cheaply, but leaves its shape unbalanced. Their method, MultiPruner, trims along three dimensions in turn. It removes residual blocks, then narrows the feed-forward channels, then drops attention heads.

Each pass restores balance before the next cut lands. The result compresses models further than rival training-free methods. Zero-shot accuracy on downstream tasks held up better as well. Memory and compute needs fell with the size. The authors released the code and pruning settings openly. They frame balance as the missing ingredient in block pruning.
arxiv-2501-10049:
Maxime De Bois and co-authors rate esports players by what they actually do in game in this 2025 paper. Classic systems like Elo reward team wins and ignore individual play. Pro esports adds scarce data and scattered leagues, which starve those systems.

Their framework, PandaSkill, learns a performance score from each player's own statistics. Each in-game role gets its own model, so a support is not judged as a carry. Bayesian updating then folds scores into skill ratings. League of Legends serves as the test bed. The design promises fairer rankings for players whose teams lose around them.
arxiv-2501-10349:
Huixia Gao and six co-authors wrote a 2025 quantum optics paper demonstrating one way state transfer near a special point of an open quantum system. Exceptional points are singularities where a non Hermitian system's behavior changes character. In open systems they appear in the Liouvillian spectrum, but their effects hide in short lived transient dynamics that are hard to catch.

Using single photon interferometry, the team steered their system around the exceptional point and rebuilt the state's evolution from measurements. The transfer direction depended on the way around, but only within an intermediate window of encircling times. Go too slowly and the system relaxes to its steady state, erasing the effect. The chirality followed a universal scaling with encircling time, confirming the fleeting nature of the phenomenon.
arxiv-2501-10549:
Karim Zongo and co-authors grow glass-like silicon forms with a learned force field in a 2025 paper. True-to-life forms of this glass have taxed the field for decades of hard work. Their route pairs a hop-and-relax hunt with a force field trained on the fly for the task.

Seven forms span from a few hundred atoms to a few thousand atoms in size. Each is checked on near and mid shape traits, spare energy, and strength marks in depth. The forms match lab data and top past forms well, with low flaw counts in the small ones.
arxiv-2501-10649:
Osumi and co-authors test whether a much debated magnet type in fact shows split bands in a crystal of ruthenium oxide. Their paper from 2025 uses fine focused light tests on three faces of a single crystal. The claimed magnet type would give odd effects that split by crystal direction.

Across all faces, the seen band shapes matched sums for a non magnetic state well. They clashed with sums for the ordered magnet state. Spin checks showed near no spin split in the bulk bands, which points to no such order. The team did find flat and spread surface bands near the key energy level. Math checks tie those bands to lines in the bulk state.
arxiv-2501-10949:
Rui Gao, Weixiao Shen, and Ruiqin Zhang present a 2025 math paper on a typical case question in ergodic optimization. The setup: a map stretches a circle, and a score function rewards each orbit. Optimization asks which invariant pattern of motion earns the highest long run average score.

The authors show that for a typical smooth score function, the answer is as simple as it can be. There is exactly one best pattern, and it rides on a repeating orbit that cycles through finitely many points. Typical is meant in two senses at once: topologically generic and full measure. The result holds for every smoothness class, from once smooth to analytic.
arxiv-2501-11149:
Ruolin Ye and co-authors present in 2025 a control scheme that lets several care devices and a robot arm share one hard job: moving a person from bed to wheelchair. The lift sling and the chair do the heavy carrying, while the arm handles the fiddly part, tying the sling's straps to the lift bar. Straps are floppy, hooks vary, and bodies differ, so the subtask is a planning nightmare.

Their answer instruments the sling and chair as agents in their own right, then coordinates all agents in turns under a predictive controller. A learned model forecasts how strap keypoints move, and a cost function borrows linking numbers from knot theory to judge strap and hook entanglement, sped up by a neural shortcut. In simulation the system handled varied hooks, strap materials, and body shapes. Real world trials began with zero failures in the shown tests.
arxiv-2501-11549:
Nishant Balepur and five co-authors ask whose tastes preference tuning should serve. Language models learn from pairs of responses, but the data rarely say why a user liked one reply over another. The team uses abductive reasoning to infer user personas from preference data. One step infers personas for users who picked chosen or rejected outputs, and a second step trains models to tailor replies to those personas.

Models inferred personas that plausibly explained both kinds of choices. Training with the inferred personas boosted personalization and carried over to user-written personas. Personas behind rejected replies made harder tests, and tailoring helped users with uncommon tastes most.
arxiv-2501-11849:
Nikos Kanakaris and six co-authors hunt coordinated astroturf campaigns with language models steered by network-aware prompts, no training required. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles a data curse: real campaigns are rare beside normal posts, so classifiers starve on positives. Their frame feeds the model both post text and the social graph around it. A Balanced RAG component fetches examples that offset the imbalance.

Prompt design does the rest of the work. On X data, the setup beats traditional graph-based baselines by two to three times on precision, recall, and F1. The gain comes without fine-tuning a single weight. Disinformation teams gain a detector that adapts by rewording, not retraining, when campaigns mutate.
arxiv-2501-12049:
Roberto de Almeida Capistrano-Filho, Hugo Parada, and Jandeilson Santos da Silva study when waves on a star-shaped network of channels can be steered at will. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The wave rule is the famous Korteweg-de Vries equation, used for shallow water waves. Steering such a system rests on a twin problem about watching it.

The question narrows to a spectral puzzle tied to the network. The team checks when certain functions built from that puzzle are entire, meaning smooth across the whole plane. That trait is the key that unlocks the steering proof. Star graphs join several channels at one hub, a shape met in real waterways and wires. The authors say the fine-grained check is new for this shape. The work firms up control theory for waves on networks.
arxiv-2501-12449:
Fabio Vito and co-authors report fresh X-ray and ultraviolet monitoring of a distant quasar. Its X-ray light had plunged between 2018 and 2021. Such a drop had never been seen in a quasar that far away. Their 2022 to 2024 campaign catches the source only in hard X-rays. The soft flux is down by more than a factor of twenty.

They read this as thick gas moving across our line of sight. The gas still blocks the view. It may be a swollen inner disk, a failed nuclear wind, or dust-free clouds near the black hole. The steady ultraviolet light supports that view. More cases like this would teach how fast young black holes feed and hide.
arxiv-2501-12549:
Sharat Ibrahimpur and Laszlo Vegh give a faster approximation for buying a resilient network in a 2025 algorithms study. Edges of a graph are classed safe or unsafe, and the buyer wants the cheapest edge set that stays highly connected even after several unsafe edges fail. Guarantees of that kind underpin communication and transport planning.

Independent rounding turns a fractional optimum into a purchase whose cost overshoots by only a logarithmic factor in the network size. That improves the previous best guarantee. Approximation algorithms with proved factors let planners budget for resilience instead of hoping heuristics hold.
arxiv-2501-12649:
Heat flow can lag behind the warmth that drives it, tracing loops when warmth swings in waves. Renai Chen and Galen Craven study those loops in 2025 for a lone grain tied to two heat baths, each bath warming and cooling in waves. Their twist is to flip the wave's pace mid-run, fast to slow or slow to fast. Math forms for the heat in and out match lab-style simulations of the moving grain step for step.

Flipping the pace bends the loops in strong ways. Pinched loops and stacked multi-loops show up that a steady pace never makes. The pair point to heat-based brain-like gear, such as heat memory parts, as a place the trick could pay off. Pace, in their hands, becomes a knob for shaping heat itself.
arxiv-2501-12949:
Ignacio Bustamante and Martin Reiris present a 2025 result on the source of Perelman's entropy, a key quantity in geometry. In 2002 Perelman set out two quantities that only shrink or grow one way, and he gave a clear source for one of them. The entropy's source stayed unexplained for two decades.

The authors show the entropy comes out as a limit of Colding's steady volume for harmonic functions on flat Ricci manifolds. They apply that volume to Perelman's own auxiliary space in the right way. The result ties a loose end in a landmark body of work.
arxiv-2501-13249:
D. Germani, B. Grinstein, and A. D. Polosa calculated the spectrum of tetraquarks in 2025, four-quark states whose existence tests how quantum chromodynamics binds matter. The test case is the famous X(3872) particle. A popular picture treats it as a loosely bound molecule of two normal mesons. But a recent LHCb reading of how often it decays by emitting varied photons does not fit that picture. And the authors test whether a compact tetraquark fares better.

Working in the Born-Oppenheimer estimate, borrowed from molecular physics, they compute the whole tetraquark spectrum for the three lowest spins and refine the decay ratio calculation. The compact picture agrees greatly better with the measured ratio and with the seen spectroscopy. Extending the diquark-antidiquark model so states can mix open-charm singlet and color-octet parts, they find these exotics are compact, shallow bound states in color force potentials.
arxiv-2501-14049:
Five physicists rebuild a classic instrument around a quantum search trick. A Sagnac interferometer senses rotation by sending light both ways around a loop and comparing the returning beams. The team replaces its usual beam splitter with a Grover multiport, a symmetric device borrowed from quantum computing. That single change puts a pole at the center of the device's parameter space and reshapes its response.

The output now carries a resonance whose form depends only on the non-reciprocal part of the phase, the very quantity such instruments hunt. Instead of watching tiny power shifts, a user can read the phase from the width of a peak or dip. The authors analyze how losses blur the effect and sketch sensing uses. They present the design as a genuinely different way to register the Sagnac phase, not just a refinement of the standard layout.
arxiv-2501-14249: A large team of authors put out the paper named Humanity's Last Exam in two thousand twenty-five. Long Phan and Alice Gatti are among the first names on the list. It runs to well over a hundred names from many institutions. It sets out a benchmark exam of hard, expert-level questions. It tests how far large AI models have come. Its scale marks it as a shared yardstick for the field. It should stay hard as models grow stronger.
arxiv-2501-14749:
Corin Katzke and Gideon Futerman argue that racing to build artificial superintelligence would defeat the very goals that tempt nations to race. The head dates the paper to 2024. Their case starts from the racers' own premises: that such a system would confer decisive military advantage, and that states act rationally to survive.

From those premises, three dangers follow. A race raises the chance of great-power conflict, since rivals cannot trust a winner to hold back. It raises the chance of losing control of the systems, built in haste. And it corrodes liberal democracy at home. The authors recast the standoff as a trust dilemma rather than a prisoner's dilemma, a framing in which cooperation is both wiser and strategically sound. Their conclusion is that an international effort to control development is achievable, and that not racing is the rational move even for the powerful.
arxiv-2501-14849:
The CMS Collaboration reports fresh measurements of Higgs boson production in proton collisions, read through the particle's rarest clean decay, in a 2025 paper. At the Large Hadron Collider in 2022, protons smashed at thirteen point six trillion electron volts. The team counted Higgs bosons that decay to two Z bosons and then to four leptons, electrons or muons, a channel with little background noise. The data set equals thirty-four point seven inverse femtobarns of collisions.

In the tight measurement region, the production rate came out at two point eight nine femtobarns, with statistical and systematic uncertainties of about half and a quarter femtobarn. The standard model expects three point zero nine, so measurement and theory agree. Rates were also mapped against the Higgs's sideways momentum and position along the beam. The paper is one brick in the collider's long program of checking the Higgs against prediction.
arxiv-2501-15149:
Zaazou, Bihlo, and Tricco teach a deep learning model to translate galaxy images between light bands in twenty twenty-five. Telescopes view galaxies in ultraviolet, visible, and infrared light, but no survey covers all bands well. A model that can fill in a missing band could save costly observing time. The team trained their model on fake galaxy views from a large simulation.

The model could guess bands inside the known range and stretch a bit beyond it. Scores on both plain image tests and star based tests showed high likeness to truth. It also worked on real survey images in a case study. The authors see uses in planning missions and probing how galaxies change.
arxiv-2501-15549:
Counterfactual tools ask what would have happened to a person under a different treatment, and they help audit algorithms for unfairness. Agathe Fernandes Machado, Arthur Charpentier, and Ewen Gallic tackle a stubborn case in 2025: moving categorical data, like job type or region, through such a tool.

Their fix has two steps. First, each category variable is rewritten as compositional data, shares that sum to a whole. Then the shares are transported inside the probability simplex with a Dirichlet-based method. A real-data example shows the approach at work on fairness questions at the level of single people. The authors also discuss where the method strains, an honest close for a young line of work.
arxiv-2501-15649:
Francesco Costa, Jaime Hoefken Zink, Michele Lucente, Silvia Pascoli, and Salvador Rosauro-Alcaraz test whether a hidden sector of physics can explain a hum of gravitational waves, in a 2025 paper. Telescopes that time pulsars have found a faint background of these waves at very low frequencies. One favored source is a violent phase change in a dark sector of the universe when it was young.

The team build the simplest dark model that could do it: a new force and a dark scalar field that breaks it. They track the change from its start to its end, including a stretch where empty-space energy ruled. That stretch, called supercooling, can stall the change and spoil the signal. Their careful tracking shows whether the idea survives its own weak points.
arxiv-2501-16449: Junjie Shan, Wenchuan Hu, and Wenxue Xu (2025) pose two shape-reconstruction problems for C-pseudo-cones, a class of unbounded convex sets. With Gaussian measures, which weight space by the bell curve, they define a Gaussian surface area measure and a Gaussian cone measure for these sets. Each measure generates its own Minkowski-type problem: recover the set from the measure. The paper proves both problems have solutions, and that the solutions are unique. This extends classical Minkowski theory from bounded bodies to this unbounded, Gaussian-weighted setting.
arxiv-2501-16549:
Tina Behzad, Sílvia Casacuberta, Emily Diana, and Alexander Tolbert study what to do when equally good models disagree about a person, in a 2025 paper. Different models trained on the same data often give the same person different risk scores, a problem called predictive multiplicity. An earlier algorithm, Reconcile, uses a disagreement between two models to prove at least one of them wrong and improve it. The authors put that algorithm to work on five widely used fairness datasets.

The datasets cover criminal risk, crime rates, income, credit, and census outcomes. The study examines how reconciliation behaves in practice, where accuracy and fairness pull against each other. The work matters because a person's loan or bail outcome should not hinge on which good model a clerk happened to pick.
arxiv-2501-16649:
Chintapenta, Verma, and Majumder present a deep learning model that spots irregular heartbeats in unborn babies from belly-surface recordings, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such recordings mix the mother's and baby's signals, making them hard to read, and classic marker-based methods fail on their tangled shapes. Odd rhythms show up in both the timing and the frequency makeup of the trace.

Their model, MFConvTr, mixes convolutional layers that read several frequency bands at once with a transformer that tracks long-range patterns. Splitting the signal into channels and filtering each at a different scale captures the multi-frequency clues cheaply. The model reached top scores on its tests while using very few parameters. The authors also ran breakdown tests to show which parts carry the gains.
arxiv-2501-16749:
Chih-Hsiang Chen and Kentaro Yaji design better cooling channels for electronics with computer-guided shaping, in a 2025 paper. Chips keep shrinking and heating up, so microchannel heat sinks — tiny fluid passages carved in metal — are in demand. Fluids laced with nanoparticles carry heat even better, but their two-part flow is hard to design for.

The team treat fluid and particles as two interwoven flows in their simulation. Their topology optimization then carves the channel layout that moves the most heat for a fixed pumping pressure. Trying varied settings shows how the best layout shifts with particle load and flow speed. Optimized nanofluid sinks could cool denser chips without bigger pumps.
arxiv-2501-16949:
Ruchi and Lalit Kumar Vashisht study how to recover a hidden source from samples of a moving system in a 2025 mathematics study. The system evolves in steps over a non-uniform set of times that arises from spectral pairs, inside an infinite-dimensional space. Earlier work by Aldroubi and colleagues frames the recovery problem and its stability, which frames must guarantee.

The authors give a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for recovering the source in finitely many steps. They also derive a necessary condition for stable recovery when the source lies in a closed subspace. Stable recovery matters for sensors that watch dynamics indirectly.
arxiv-2501-17449:
Islam Oshallah and three co-authors build question answering for the Quran in twenty twenty-five. Question answering is hard in languages with scarce data. Quranic QA matters to over a billion people seeking deeper understanding of the text. It also has a special twist: questions are written in Modern Standard Arabic, while answers sit in Classical Arabic verses.

Existing data sets are small, which caps model performance. The team takes a cross-language approach to break that cap. They translate Arabic questions into English to expand the data. They paraphrase questions to add linguistic variety. Answers are retrieved from an English translation of the Quran to align with multilingual training. Readers get a recipe for sacred-text QA where data is thin and registers differ.
arxiv-2501-17549:
Wooyoung Kim, Byungyoon Park, and Wooju Kim wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It feeds graph data to large language models as a small set of learned pooling tokens, shaped by the user's query.

Node-by-node projection does not scale, while whole-graph projection washes out detail. The learned tokens strike a balance, holding both fine and broad traits of the graph. A trick called Early Query Fusion blends the question in before the graph code is built. That way the code keeps what the question needs. On the GraphQA benchmark the method gains over four percent. The language model itself is left untrained. The work suits social, citation, and knowledge graphs full of text.
arxiv-2501-17749:
Before a new AI model reaches the public, outsiders can probe it for unsafe behavior, and a 2025 paper by Aitor Arrieta and co-authors reports such a probe of OpenAI's o3-mini. The testing ran under the maker's early access program for safety researchers.

The team used their own tool, ASTRAL, to write and run 10,080 prompts designed to tempt the model into unsafe replies across safety categories. A beta version of the model took the tests. After people checked the flagged cases by hand, eighty-seven real instances of unsafe behavior remained. The paper draws lessons from the exercise about how to test models early, while fixes are still cheap.
arxiv-2501-18249:
Zhou and Dib examine large-scale galactic effects on molecular clouds in the galaxy NGC 628. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks what sets cloud density contrast. Those same factors shape star formation across the galaxy. Cloud contrast first rises with distance from the center. It then levels off at larger galactic radii.

Spiral arms, bubbles, and magnetic fields were ruled out as drivers. Shear and tide strengths were computed from the rotation curve. Shear fell with radius and proved too weak to matter. Pixel-level tidal maps joined gas and star density data. Inner-galaxy tidal strength fell with radius, then steadied. The work narrows which galactic forces sculpt star-forming clouds.
arxiv-2501-18349:
Richard Kenyon widens a well-known family of random processes. Determinantal measures describe random configurations where points repel in a pattern set by a matrix kernel, and they appear in tiling, tree, and particle problems. His 2025 solo paper defines a broader family, multideterminantal measures, where each site takes one of k values instead of just two.

Examples come from the positive Grassmannian, the dimer model of paired atoms, and random spanning trees. Kenyon characterizes the kernels of the pure measures in the family: they arise from k-tuples of Grassmannian elements whose largest minors obey sign rules. The classic case falls out as a special case, with all pure determinantal kernels built from a pair of such elements. He also defines and fully characterizes determinantal measures on the permutation group. The paper extends a sharp mathematical tool to richer state spaces.
arxiv-2501-18649:
Rupak Kumar Das and Jonathan Dodge wrote this 2025 study on whether fake news detectors still work after a language model rewrites the story. Models can now launder a fake story into fresh wording that sounds smooth and well-sourced. Most past work tested detectors on human-written fakes, not on these washed versions.

The team found that detectors do worse on the washed fakes than on the raw ones. They also ranked which models are best at evading, at washing to evade, and at washing while keeping the sense. Word-level explanations pointed to a prime suspect: the rewrite shifts the story's emotional tone, which throws off detectors that lean on tone. Worse, a standard score for rewrite quality stayed high even when the tone had shifted. The authors release data sets pairing stories with their washed versions.
arxiv-2501-18949:
Okuto Morikawa, Soma Onoda, and Hiroshi Suzuki present a 2025 talk paper on a new grid formulation of two-dimensional chiral gauge theory. Such theories are famously hard to put on a lattice, since the grid tends to break their delicate anomaly pattern. Recent constructions use a trick called bosonization to keep the pattern exact even at finite grid spacing.

Their version rests on an excision method that enforces a smoothness rule on grid fields. That rule usually bans charged objects, yet the authors show such objects can live as holes, a kind of defect in the grid. They then work out which charged objects the rules allow, extending the lattice toolkit for these theories.
arxiv-2501-19249:
Nicolás Cuello and co-authors review discs of gas and dust around stars in pairs and groups in a 2025 paper. Such discs are where planets form, but partner stars tug on them with gravity. The review sums up what sharp telescopes and computer models have shown so far.

Companions can chop discs short, raise spirals, and tilt them out of line. Dust growth and the build of rocky seeds change under those pulls. The end results are wide-ranging planet systems, some quite unlike our own. The authors call for paired work, with finer views and stronger models, to sort out how common each path is.
arxiv-2502-00049:
Zoe Pfister and co-authors present FORTE, an open system of forest sensors built to track how woods cope with heat and drought, in a 2025 paper. Forests store carbon and cool the land, but dry spells and heat waves stress them hard. Cheap, wide coverage is hard to get with shop-bought gear, so the team built their own.

A set of small field units gathers data across a wide area and sends it to one hub, which passes it on for storage and display. Field trials showed the units run for months on one charge and cost less than store systems. All plans and code are shared, so other groups can copy or adapt the setup.
arxiv-2502-00249:
Om Roy and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on reading brain networks from EEG signals over time. Standard methods track links between pairs of brain sites. Richer patterns, such as flows around triangles and loops, can hide signals that pairwise views miss.

Their framework, Hodge-FAST, joins a math tool called Hodge decomposition with a filtered connectivity method. First, the data are thinned to the most important links, and short-term links are filtered by stable long-term patterns. The signal is then split into three parts that describe flows over higher-order shapes. In patients with mild cognitive impairment tied to Alzheimer's disease, the method found time-based differences that pairwise study did not show. That opens a fresh window on noisy brain recordings.
arxiv-2502-00449:
Mahmoud Zeer and co-authors study thin sheets of rare-earth materials that may steer electric flow in new ways. Their 2025 work uses first-principles math to model three single-layer compounds built around the element europium. Such layers mix strong magnetism with a strong link between spin and motion, a mix prized for small, fast devices.

All three compounds show strong torque effects, the push that can flip a magnetic state. The push comes mostly from a large response in the europium electrons when current flows. The same torque can drive flows of orbital motion in the plane of the sheet. The team presents these layers as a strong base for future orbit-based devices.
arxiv-2502-00649:
Fabio Bresolin and a large team map how two metals spread inside the spiral galaxy NGC 6946. They use hundreds of glowing gas clouds as probes. The study belongs to a survey of roughly forty nearby galaxies with a Fourier transform spectrometer in Canada. It measures oxygen and nitrogen in well over six hundred star-forming regions. Then it examines the wiggles around the smooth radial trends. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they find a sideways pattern across one spiral arm. The leading edge runs poorer in metals than the trailing edge by a noticeable step.

Simulations explain the pattern as gas flowing along the arm. The flow dilutes one side and enriches the other. Oxygen and nitrogen vary over similar spatial scales, though stars forge them differently. Supernovae make one; aging giants make the other. The authors infer that stellar processes stir both elements into the gas over equivalent distances.
arxiv-2502-00849:
Federico Garcia-Gaitan, Adrian Feiguin, and Branislav Nikolić simulate what happens when ultrafast light pulses strike nickel oxide, a magnetic insulator. Their 2025 paper notes that recent experiments drive this material far from equilibrium and see it emit terahertz radiation, mainly when paired with platinum. The microscopic cause of that emission is unclear, since the usual explanation from metal systems does not apply here.

The team models the material with a many-body quantum framework and exact numerical methods. They track the magnetic order and the magnetization that appears after the pulse, plus the radiation emitted. Their results probe how a material with zero net magnetization can still radiate.
arxiv-2502-00949:
Pietro Di Gianantonio and Abbas Edalat build a domain-theoretic frame for conditional probability in programs. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves probabilistic programming languages. Conditioning is vital for Bayesian updating from observed data. Past work showed deep computability snags in defining it cleanly. Their approach rests on a notion of observable events.

Two ways to compute conditional probability are developed. One uses conditional density functions directly. The other samples traces and rejects those that miss the evidence. Both methods agree within the new framework, the authors prove. A small functional language puts the ideas into practice. It carries sampling and evaluation primitives with matched semantics. The work gives language builders a rigorous footing for conditioning.
arxiv-2502-01049:
Murugaraj Odiathevar and Kim Chung Yup present a 2025 paper on simulating network traffic that behaves like real applications. Many simulators fire packets at random gaps, which misses how apps actually burst and idle. Security tools tested on such fake traffic may fail in the real world.

Their method learns the statistical shape of each application's traffic and rebuilds it from those curves. Blending the learned patterns yields dynamic traffic that scales from one machine to large networks. Behavior can be dialed up or down to stress monitoring and anomaly tools. The code is open source, so other teams can rerun and extend the tests.
arxiv-2502-01649:
Afsara Benazir and Felix Xiaozhu Lin present SpeechShield, a 2025 system that keeps private content out of cloud speech recognition. Cloud services transcribe well, but an untrusted provider could learn sensitive facts from raw audio. The system filters names and other private items on the user's own device first.

A tiny model on the device predicts which time spans hold private entities and masks them. The masked audio goes to a trusted cloud or local hub, and a confidence based step picks the best transcript between cloud and device outputs. Built on a small Raspberry Pi board, the system used under one hundred megabytes of memory. It filtered most private entities while matching top transcription quality, and ran far leaner than prior systems.
arxiv-2502-02149:
Jan Kotrbatý wrote a 2025 math note on a conjecture in convex geometry. The catalog title carries a funding note, but the note itself concerns the difference body of a convex shape: the set of all gaps between pairs of its points. A known inequality bounds that set's volume, and Godbersen's conjecture claims a sharper bound using the shape and its mirror image.

Kotrbatý proposes a wider version covering higher-order difference bodies, which stack the construction further. He proves the wider claim for a well-behaved class called anti-blocking bodies. He also links the bound to a product operation on certain measures, giving a second form of the same claim. Notes like this inch a long-open problem forward in the cases that can be settled.
arxiv-2502-02349:
Vrushank Ahire, Pranav Menon, Aniruddh Muley, and Abhinandan Prasad propose a hybrid rule for deciding what a processor cache keeps. Caches are tiny, fast stores that must guess which data will be needed again. Fixed rules waste some slots and miss changing access patterns. Their rule, RAC, mixes random placement with a flexible shared-tag design.

The design spreads entries across two thousand forty-eight sets with sixteen slots each. Tags can move where demand is, so busy sets borrow room from idle ones. Storage for tags and data is trimmed for efficiency. On a standard simulator with four varied workloads, hit rates climbed as high as eighty percent. Speed per instruction rose only modestly, though. The authors stress better cache use and shorter waits as the real gains.
arxiv-2502-02549:
Ron Benchetrit, Idan Lev-Yehudi, Andrey Zhitnikov, and Vadim Indelman present a planner for robots that must act without full knowledge of the world, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The planner handles rewards that depend on what the robot believes, which suits tasks like search and mapping. Older solvers kept a fixed picture of belief, so they could not sharpen it as time went on.

The new solver refines that picture step by step and is built to improve the longer it runs. A fast update trick cuts the cost of scoring belief rewards by a large factor. Tests showed better speed and better plans than leading solvers. Readers in robotics get a tool for smarter search under doubt.
arxiv-2502-02649:
Margaret Mitchell, Avijit Ghosh, Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, and Giada Pistilli argue in a 2025 paper that fully free AI agents should not be built. Such agents act on their own for long chains of steps with no hand on the wheel. The team sorts agents by how free they are and weighs the values at stake at each rung.

Their core find: the more hold a user gives up, the more risk lands on people. Safety risks lead the list, since they touch life itself and drag other values down with them. Gains shrink in worth next to those stakes. The paper gives rule makers a rung-by-rung map of the trade.
arxiv-2502-02949:
Md Hossen Mondal and Ramkrishna Joshi study the physics of sound through a homemade loudspeaker, in this 2025 paper. Sound travels as waves of squeezed and stretched air in tubes and rooms. The authors build a simple speaker from magnets and a coil driven by a wobbling signal, and ask how well basic theory predicts its behavior.

They model the setup as a driven oscillator with damping and solve it in its steady state. From that solution they pull out the frequencies where the device responds most strongly. The paper then works through how to choose the parts of the build so that theory and measured behavior line up. The aim is a low cost, hands on route into the physics of vibrating surfaces and sound.
arxiv-2502-03049:
A team led by Katsipoulaki, with Mourzidis, Jindal, Lagarde, Taniguchi, Watanabe, Kopidakis, Marie, Glazov, Stratakis, Kioseoglou, and Paradisanos, wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It steers the spin-valley polarization of excitons in single layers of WSe2 by doping them with light.

Single-shot photochlorination steps shift the layer from electron-rich to hole-rich. The polarization does not move in a straight line: it dips low near the neutral point, then climbs threefold as holes grow. A plain model of the dynamics points to exciton and carrier collisions as the main driver, while the exciton life span barely moves. The trick gives a fine knob for valley physics in such thin crystals.
arxiv-2502-03149:
Deepika Saxena and co-authors survey how to keep cloud computing resources safe while they are assigned and run, in a 2025 paper. Cloud platforms rent machines by the minute, and attacks during that rental window can steal data or hijack capacity. This corner of cloud security is studied less than the rest.

The team sort defenses into three families: those that block attacks outright, those that soften their impact, and hybrids. They review the leading methods in each family and then run the best of them on one shared test bed fed with two real machine-use traces. The bake-off exposes trade-offs in cost, speed, and strength. The paper closes with open problems and design advice for the next wave of cloud guards.
arxiv-2502-04049:
Jagabandhu Mishra and co-authors build a 2025 method to both spot fake speech and name the tool that made it. Fake speech from synthesizers can fool listeners and systems. Most detectors give a bare yes-or-no answer from dense internal features that no one can read, which makes their choices hard to trust or explain.

Their method breaks a voice clip into a set of named traits, each with a chance value, that point to parts of the synthesizer that made it. Those trait scores feed simple classifiers that handle both tasks: telling real from fake, and naming the source method. They also use a game-theory tool to weigh how much each trait swayed the final call. The result is a detector whose reasoning can be inspected.
arxiv-2502-04249:
Michael Walters, Rafael Kaufmann, Justice Sefas, and Thomas Kopinski build a risk metric for multi-agent AI systems from the free energy principle, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Popular safe-AI theories often demand massive data or arbitrarily complex world models. Their alternative asks stakeholders only to state preferences over outcomes. Decision rules for risk governance then stay transparent.

The proposed Cumulative Risk Exposure metric adapts to differing contexts and needs. The framework accounts for uncertainty in both the world model and the preference model. The authors demonstrate it in a simplified autonomous vehicle setting. Gatekeeper agents evaluate risks to collective safety online and intervene in vehicle policies when needed. Even at low penetration, gatekeepers produced significant safety gains for the fleet.
arxiv-2502-04449:
Patrick Simon, Lucas Porth, Pierre Burger, and Konrad Kuijken wrote a 2025 cosmology paper using weak gravitational lensing to test how matter clumps in the universe. Lensing bends light from distant galaxies in ways that reveal the matter between us and them. The team used the KiDS-1000 survey to rebuild the three dimensional power spectrum of matter.

Their reconstruction leans only on the background cosmology, galaxy distance data, and one alignment parameter. A stabilizing method keeps the deprojection steady, and the spectrum comes out in separate slices of cosmic time. Compared with a model of pure cold dark matter growth, the data call for a clear suppression of clumping on small scales, of up to a fifth or more. That gap hints at missing physics or unmodeled effects in how structures grow.
arxiv-2502-04749:
Releasing an average while protecting each person's privacy sounds simple until one heavy user can swamp the sum. Arvind Rameshwar and Anshoo Tandon revisit in 2025 how to cap each user's contribution before averaging, under user-level differential privacy. Older studies assumed tidy data: independent samples, equal counts per user. Real datasets break both.

The authors pin down exactly which capping strategy minimizes the worst-case error over all datasets, allowing users to contribute unevenly. Experiments add a surprise: even on tidy independent data, their strategy beats the field's standard capping method on average error by a wide margin.
arxiv-2502-04949:
Lasse Elsemüller and co-authors test whether a popular fix really makes neural inference sturdier. Their 2025 paper concerns amortized Bayesian inference, where networks trained on simulated data are then fed real observations. When the two differ, answers can go badly wrong. Domain adaptation tries to help by aligning the summary spaces of simulated and real data.

Across many mismatch scenarios, the alignment did blunt the harm from unmodeled effects and noise. But the same trick backfired when the mismatch sat in the prior beliefs instead. That failure mode matters for high-stakes uses, where a confident wrong answer is costly. The authors urge care in matching the fix to the kind of mismatch expected.
arxiv-2502-05049:
Federico Cinus, Corrado Monti, Paolo Bajardi, and Gianmarco De Francisci Morales built a method in twenty twenty-five to estimate who Reddit users are. Knowing a platform's mix of age, gender, and politics matters for reading online behavior, but guessing these traits from posts risks bias and error. Their data instead rest on what users say about themselves.

They gathered over eight hundred fifty thousand self-declarations of age, gender, and party leaning. Simple probabilistic models trained on sparse activity signals beat fancier embedding methods. Their approach raised accuracy over prior work by up to nineteen percent on a standard scale, with population estimates off by under fifteen percent. Outputs are calibrated and open to inspection, down to which signals matter in each subreddit. The authors argue for grounding such work in user-provided facts.
arxiv-2502-05449:
Weizhe Chen, Sven Koenig, and Bistra Dilkina present a way to get more good answers out of a fixed language model at test time, in a paper from 2025. New reasoning models do well on hard tasks, but most work on scaling them trains the model itself. Less is known about using more compute well once a model is already trained.

Their method, iterative deepening sampling, prompts the model to check and fix its own work in a planned way. That yields cleaner samples for hard problems, which can also feed training of later models. On the Math500 and AIME test sets, the method solved hard tasks more often than rival sampling plans, and the authors break down why in detail.
arxiv-2502-05749:
Kaizhen Zhu and six co-authors unify diffusion bridge models, which morph one image kind into another with fixed ends, under a control theory frame. Past bridges use a classic trick to lock ends, but they oft blur fine detail and lack a full theory for why.

Their frame sets the morph as a cost trade between control effort and end miss. Past bridges fall out as the case where end miss is banned at all cost. A tunable end weight restores detail and lifts quality. The frame plugs into past bridges with tiny code changes. Tests across restore tasks confirm gains.
arxiv-2502-06849:
Muhammed Öz and co-authors present a 2025 paper on Neuron Transplantation, a way to merge several trained neural networks into one without paying the cost of running them all. Ensembles predict better than single models, but they eat memory and time at every use. The authors instead move the best parts into a single body.

They first prune weak neurons from one model, freeing space. Important neurons from every ensemble member are then transplanted into the gaps. A short fine-tuning heals the small drop that follows, and the fused model ends up beating each of its donors at the same size. It also needs less healing than a rival averaging method.
arxiv-2502-07149:
Sergej Monavari builds a new moduli space in enumerative geometry, modelled on Nekrasov's gauge origami for intersecting branes. Here the branes are replaced by two affine lines crossing each other, the broken lines of the title. Monavari realises the space concretely as a Quot scheme, parametrising zero-dimensional quotients of a torsion sheaf on the two lines, and again as a space of quiver representations.

On this space he constructs a virtual fundamental class and a virtual structure sheaf, the tools needed to define K-theoretic invariants. He then computes the associated partition function at every rank. Where the space is smooth, the answer reproduces a known generating series for a refined genus. Finally, he ties his partition function to the virtual invariants of plane Quot schemes and to Nekrasov's original function.
arxiv-2502-07249:
Divyansh Agrawal and Nisha Singhal study a math transform that sums a function over flat slices of space, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They ask a sharp question about what can be inferred from partial data. If a function is zero in one region, and its sums vanish on all slices through that region, must it be zero everywhere?

For slices whose dimension is even, the answer is no, and they give a concrete counter-case. For odd dimension, a stronger claim holds. In that case, deep flatness at one point plus a zero region around it forces the function to vanish everywhere. The split by parity is the core result.
arxiv-2502-07649:
Anamaria Crisan and Andrew McNutt ask whether people can lint charts in a 2025 paper. Lint tools in coding flag flaws by set rules, and that idea has spread to data graphics, which need wider judgment than code. The authors probe a looser form of linting across strict, neutral, and rebel stances.

Their test bed is Community Notes, crowd written context slips that check posts on social media. Human judges not only caught false or shaky charts but added social insight that rule tools miss. The paper also weighs what AI powered linters would mean for this human role.
arxiv-2502-07749:
Tamsin James, Ben Williamson, Peter Tino, and Nicole Wheeler set out open problems in bacterial genomics in a 2025 paper. Machine learning can predict a bacterium's traits from its whole genome with high scores. The trouble starts when teams ask which genes truly cause the trait.

Models often flag false genes, because genomes are huge and spurious links are the norm. Pattern matching alone cannot sort cause from coincidence in that setting. The authors frame the open problems: predicting traits from genome data, and pushing past prediction to causal effects. They discuss what makes machine choices unreliable here and where the search for risky gene variants stands.
arxiv-2502-07849:
Krunoslav Lehman Pavasovic and colleagues gave a high-dimensional theory of classifier-free guidance in 2025. Guidance is the trick that steers diffusion image generators toward a requested class or prompt, and it clearly sharpens results. Theory had suggested guidance distorts the target distribution, pushing samples toward a narrower, shifted version, which raised doubts about what generators really sample from.

In very high dimensions, the authors prove, those distortions fade away and guidance reproduces the true target faithfully. That blessing of dimensionality covers a whole family of guidance rules, including nonlinear ones. A power-law variant they study proved more robust in tests, with better fidelity and diversity on class and text image tasks. Practice and theory reconcile at scale.
arxiv-2502-07949:
Qingyuan Wu and four co-authors present a learning method for AI agents that see and read in a 2025 paper. Such vision language agents can learn from online interaction without human labels, but they learn slowly on hard tasks with rare rewards and long action chains. The authors break each big goal into subgoals to guide learning.

Their framework restates the task as a subgoal conditioned problem with a new training objective. The objective rewards reaching subgoals while staying close to a reference goal directed policy. Theory and tests both support the design. On benchmarks covering phone and web control tasks, the method beat prior leading approaches in both learning speed and final performance.
arxiv-2502-08349:
Christian Kuehn and Pascal Sedlmeier proved stability results in twenty twenty-five for wave patterns in the Barkley model of pipe flow. The model captures how smooth laminar flow breaks into turbulent puffs, and it matches experiments well. Its traveling wave solutions include fronts and backs that can stack in trains of any length.

Building on an earlier existence proof based on a twisted loop between laminar and turbulent states, the authors verify a set of abstract stability conditions drawn from classic wave theory. For an intermediate range of Reynolds numbers, every train of fronts or backs with more than one wave is stable. The work completes a full existence-and-stability account that fits the abstract framework for waves born from such loops.
arxiv-2502-08449:
Robot hands need to know exactly where an object sits against the fingers, and a single camera's point cloud is too patchy and contact-blind for that. Yankai Fu and co-authors build their control policy on correspondences instead in a 2025 paper, tying the object's known pose to the hand's own joint senses. The linked cloud carries contact maps showing where touch happens.

Trained with those signals, the policy handled six real-world dexterity tasks better than rival methods by a wide margin. It also held up when objects, viewpoints, and scenes changed. The authors credit the explicit object-hand matching for the fine control.
arxiv-2502-08549:
Fei Zheng and Nicolas Duchateau loosen the rules of group-finding models in a 2025 paper. Clustering sorts data into groups, and model-based methods assume each group follows a chosen distribution family. Real data often break that tidy assumption. Their approach lets each cluster mix its own marginal distributions with a copula, a tool that binds variables together flexibly.

They adapt an iterative estimation algorithm to discover such models without labels. Marginals, copulas, and their parameters are refined in turns. Tests on synthetic two-cluster data with two thousand samples probe what helps or hurts convergence. The method was then compared on a full handwritten digit set and on real heart scan data. Flexible clusters proved their value for imaging tasks.
arxiv-2502-08849:
Dipsy Desai, Kicho Yu, and Sulyab Thottungal Valapu gauge how far geofeeds have spread on the net. A geofeed is a file that states where net number blocks sit on Earth. The young norm lets hosts post such spots for their IPv4 and IPv6 blocks. The team checks use at the big lists and at host-group scale. They test how well live feeds hew to two norms: the base one, and the proof one.

The proof route in the live norm, they find, lacks key guards. Their swap plan makes feed proof plain, and tests score its speed. The state of play is mid-spread: more feeds go up, but truth and safety lag. Spot data feeds film and song rights, law checks, and fraud tools. Sound feeds thus count far past map work. The paper gives both the count and a fix for its weak link.
arxiv-2502-09149:
Anna Taranenko catalogs the corners of a matrix polytope in a 2025 mathematics paper. A polystochastic matrix is a multi-dimensional array of nonnegative numbers where every line sums to one.
