All such arrays of a given size form a convex shape whose corner points, the vertices, are the building blocks of the whole set.

For two small shapes, the author lists every vertex, correcting an earlier published enumeration. New constructions then build vertices for larger cases from smaller ones using multidimensional matrix products. Symmetric vertices with large support are also produced for one family in all higher dimensions. The results belong to combinatorics and convex geometry, where the famous Birkhoff polytope is the two-dimensional ancestor of this family. Complete vertex lists are rare and valuable: they let others test conjectures on the whole family.
arxiv-2502-09249:
Aleksandrs Belovs and Stacey Jeffery give space-efficient quantum error reduction without log factors in a 2025 paper. A bounded-error algorithm can be run again and again, with a majority vote, to shrink the chance of a wrong answer. That classic trick costs a factor that grows with the log of the target error.

Transducers, a newer model of quantum computation, allow a trick akin to purification that cuts error at constant cost. The team show how that gain can be pulled back to plain quantum algorithms while keeping the space bill low. The log factor that majority voting pays is avoided. The result sharpens what repeated runs must cost.
arxiv-2502-09549:
Kyungchan Lim and five co-authors trace the full life of phishing domains in a 2025 study. Phishing sites steal logins and payment data, and blocklists react only after harm starts. The team argues the real choke point is domain registration, the moment a fake site's name is born.

They followed close to seven hundred thousand phishing domains over thirty-nine months, from sign-up to takedown. Two thirds were registered for the crime itself, often with cheap name endings that copy a brand's name under a different ending than the real firm uses. Detection speed barely improved for such domains, and sites stayed reachable for days after being flagged. The authors map where the system leaks and where faster action could cut the harm.
arxiv-2502-09849:
Gambetti and co-authors survey how explainable AI for medical decision support is judged by the humans meant to trust it. They gathered thirty-one human-centered evaluations and sorted them by explanation method, study design, and adoption barrier. The field leans heavily on after-the-fact, model-free explainers such as SHAP and Grad-CAM, over eighty percent of studies.

Clinician samples were tiny, under twenty-five in most studies. Explanations usually raised trust and confidence, yet often raised mental workload too and clashed with how doctors actually reason. The authors propose a stakeholder-first framework, blending social and technical lenses, to steer explainers toward tools clinics can truly use.
arxiv-2502-10249:
Danilo Monteiro Ribeiro studies burnout and instability among software developers in a 2025 paper. Software work changes all the time, and developers feel that churn as instability. Burnout, a state of exhaustion and cynicism, harms health and output, and drives staff out. Whether felt churn feeds burnout had not been tested.

A survey drew 411 developers, who rated both their burnout and the churn they felt. That churn came in three flavors: team, technology, and task. Both key signs rose clearly with all three kinds of churn. A sense of professional efficacy dipped only weakly with team and technology churn, and not with task churn. Exhaustion was the most common symptom, and task churn the most felt. The results give bosses concrete levers for healthier teams.
arxiv-2502-10449:
Ajinkya Gaikwad and co-authors study two hard graph problems in their largest-smallest form. One asks for the biggest set of nodes whose removal splits two named nodes, where no smaller set inside it would do. The other asks for the biggest such set whose removal leaves a graph that splits in two parts.

Both tasks are judged by a size limit, and the team shows each can be solved by an algorithm whose slow part depends only on that limit. The first result settles a question left open in 2019. Their proof leans on a known meta-result that trims the graphs down to a tough core case, a route that was not clear at first.
arxiv-2502-10549:
Francesco Amoroso and co-authors present a 2025 proof in number theory, written in French, of a conjecture by Schinzel. The claim concerns how a certain kind of curved set can meet a one dimensional torus. The set sits inside powers of the multiplicative group. Such unlikely meetings of algebraic sets are a classic type of question.

The proof rests on a geometric form of Bézout's theorem and on lower bounds for height developed by other named scholars. Unlike earlier work, the result is explicit: it depends on the height and degree of the set in question. The authors note that the approach was inspired by a similar statement about products of elliptic curves, proved by another team whose method they adapted.
arxiv-2502-10649:
Patrick Schelling, Antonio Martinez Margolles, and Logan Echazabal study how heat moves in a single layer of hexagonal boron nitride in a 2025 paper. At short scales and low heat, heat can travel as a wave, a behavior called second sound, rather than spreading by slow diffusion. Standard conductivity values then fail to predict what happens.

Using atom level simulations, they compute response functions that describe heat flow over time beyond the diffusion picture. Their results suggest second sound should be visible at a scale near one hundred nanometers in cold conditions. At warmer levels the flow still departs strongly from diffusion based forecasts, they find.
arxiv-2502-10749:
Zehua Liu, Han Wu, and Yuxuan Yao lead a team merging fine-tuned language models by estimating their task vectors at low rank, no base model required. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Merging blends specialist models into one without further training. Interference between specialists is the usual failure mode.

The team noticed task vectors concentrate their energy in a few dominant directions. A low-rank estimate therefore keeps the signal and drops much of the clash. They cast merging as an optimization problem built on that estimate. Wide experiments showed less interference and better preservation of each skill. The method advances merging benchmarks without touching training data. Not needing the base model widens where it can be applied. The authors frame low rank as the natural geometry of fine-tuning. That idea may guide merging theory generally.
arxiv-2502-11249:
Bërdëllima extends a classic calculus lemma to infinite-dimensional spaces in this 2025 math paper. Hadamard's lemma says a smooth function near a point can be split into its value there plus a sum of smooth parts, one per direction. The classic form lives in finite-dimensional space.

Bërdëllima proves the same split works in a separable Hilbert space, a space with endless dimensions but a countable base. The paper states the finite case first, then carries it over. Such splits are basic tools for studying smooth maps. The result gives analysts one more classic tool in the big-space setting.
arxiv-2502-11649:
Amin Qasmi and co-authors stage a game where language model agents fight over public opinion in a 2025 paper. The setup borrows from social psychology, with bias toward friendly views, tight budgets, and fines for spreading falsehoods. Agents spend resources to sway a population or debunk rivals.

Strong bias toward in-group views tightened camps and deepened overall splits. Weak bias left views scattered, with little movement at all. Heavy spending on debunking won early ground but drained funds and faded fast. The game shows how rules and budgets, not just message craft, steer belief wars online.
arxiv-2502-11849:
Charles Elbar and Andrea Poiatti wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on an equation that models how two phases of a material separate. The anisotropic Cahn-Hilliard equation tracks that split, but here one phase barely diffuses at all. Its double-well potential also varies from place to place across the domain.

The authors first prove that weak solutions to the equation exist. Then they study what happens as the width of the border between phases shrinks to zero. In that sharp interface limit, and with an energy condition in place, the solutions settle into a weighted anisotropic Hele-Shaw flow. That flow is a simpler model of motion through a narrow gap. The paper adds computer simulations that show how the direction-dependent traits change the patterns the equation makes.
arxiv-2502-12349:
Amyloid deposits signal several diseases, but the standard dye test for them is judged by eye and can mislead. Owen Lailey and co-authors present a dye-free measuring method in a 2025 paper. Congo red staining under polarized light is the classic check, yet the dye binds other structures and shows stray colors. Their method reads the fibrils' own light-bending signal with numbers instead of impressions.

Four tissue types were measured, from belly fat to gut and thyroid samples. The aim is a quantitative call that different labs can repeat. Misdiagnosis risk from dye quirks is the problem being solved. The authors frame the method as an upgrade to polarized microscopy practice.
arxiv-2502-12749:
Rajat Adak, Saraswati Girish Nanoti, and Prafullkumar Tale revisit token sliding on chordal graphs in a 2025 paper. Tokens sit on a graph's corners, no two adjacent. A move slides one token along an edge to a free corner. The question is whether any layout of a set size can be reached from any other by such slides.

For interval graphs the answer can be computed fast; for split graphs the question is NP-hard. Chordal graphs sit between the two, and their case was left open by the earlier work. The team take up that gap, and weigh where the chordal case falls on the line between easy and hard.
arxiv-2502-12849:
Gianluca Guglielmo and Marc Masana present a 2025 paper on teaching neural networks to flag inputs unlike anything they were trained on. Such out-of-distribution detection keeps models from making unsafe calls on strange data. Most methods read only the final layer's output, ignoring the rich signals in middle layers.

The pair shows that middle layers carry useful warning signs of their own. They train the network with a contrastive loss that shapes those layers, then merge several layers into one combined response. Tests across many data sets show detection improves when middle layers join in. The work argues that a network's depth is a resource for safety, not just for accuracy.
arxiv-2502-13049:
Paul Boniol, Donato Tiano, Angela Bonifati, and Themis Palpanas present a new way to group time series data in a 2025 paper. Grouping such data is hard, and most tools show users little more than a center line for each group. That leaves people unsure why items were placed together.

Their method, called k-Graph, turns short pieces of each series into a graph, which shows links between the pieces. It builds several graphs from pieces of different lengths, so users need not pick a length in advance, and uneven series can still be used. In tests, the method grouped data more truly than leading rivals. It also gave clear reasons for each group, which the authors stress as the main gain for real users.
arxiv-2502-13249:
Alfredo Braunstein and co-authors overturn a comfort belief in Bayesian inference: that knowing exactly how data were made keeps the answer landscape simple. Their 2025 paper finds the feared fracture, replica symmetry breaking, even under those ideal Nishimori conditions. When the landscape fractures, many standard approximations fail.

The counterexample is a patient-zero hunt in a fast-spreading epidemic on a graph. The team tests a cavity method's steady solution and finds it unstable toward the fractured phase. Correlated disorder, baked into epidemic models, is the likely culprit. The result warns that even perfectly specified epidemic inference can hide a fractured posterior. Mean-field and sampling tools may then mislead without warning.
arxiv-2502-13449:
Dongki Kim, Wonbin Lee, and Sung Ju Hwang present a 2025 paper on a language model built to understand molecules in depth. Knowing molecules is key to knowing living things and to finding new drugs. Past models could shift between tasks, but they often read molecular features poorly.

The new model, called Mol-LLaMA, is trained on data types that cover the core features of molecules. The data aim at the skills needed to reason about structure and behavior. A special module blends input from several molecule encoders, each strong in a different way. Tests reported by the authors show gains in grasp and in the model's power to explain its answers.
arxiv-2502-13849:
Hou, Tang, and Toh tackle in twenty twenty-five a class of hard optimisation problems used to relax mixed yes-no quadratic programs. These relaxed problems carry huge numbers of constraints and variables, which makes them slow to solve at scale. Their method bets that good solutions have low rank, a compact hidden structure, and builds that bet into an augmented Lagrangian scheme on curved spaces.

A key rewrite turns most awkward squared constraints into simpler straight ones after the low-rank split. They also show a hard projection step can be recast as an easy convex problem under mild conditions. Tests confirmed the speed gains. The method also fits general problems of the same family, serving as a prototype solver.
arxiv-2502-14049: Christine Breiner and Ben Dees study the bad points of energy minimizing maps into branching spaces, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The target spaces include complexes that model tree-like buildings. At bad points the map fails to be smooth, and those points group into layers by type. The authors sort those layers in a natural way and prove they can be measured in a well behaved way. Their result extends classic facts to a far rougher setting.
arxiv-2502-14449:
Robert Helling wrote this physics paper in 2025 on Bohmian mechanics, a view of quantum theory in which particles follow real paths steered by a wave. The view is said to match all tests of standard quantum theory. Helling tests that claim with a setup built on the GHZ state, a linked state of three parts. Here the qubits are read as positions in space.

He finds a clash: for links between positions at unlike times, the path view gives answers that standard theory does not. The clash turns on the fact that such positions cannot be jointly fixed. To erase the gap, the path view would need an added account of how the wave collapses when watched. The paper thus marks a spot where the two views split, at least in their plain forms.
arxiv-2502-14749:
Aikaterini Gkogkou, Guido Mazzuca, and Kenneth T-R McLaughlin study what happens to a wave made of many solitons as their number grows without bound. Their setting is the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, a standard model for wave packets in optics and fluids. They examine multi-soliton solutions whose spectral data pile up on two bounded horizontal segments of the complex plane, with the associated constants kept away from zero.

In that limit they prove the solution settles, on bounded regions of space and time, into a fast-oscillating elliptic wave traveling at a constant speed: a soliton gas condensate. They then add an extra soliton component and rigorously confirm predictions from the kinetic theory of soliton gases in this deterministic setting. The work differs from earlier analyses where the constants shrank with the number of solitons.
arxiv-2502-14949:
Ahmed Heakl and co-authors (2025) release KITAB-Bench, a test set for machines that read Arabic documents. Arabic text recognition lags far behind English: the script is cursive, runs right to left, and varies richly by style and calligraphy. Yet document AI pipelines increasingly depend on OCR to feed retrieval systems, and Arabic archives are huge. The benchmark gathers 8,809 samples across nine major domains and thirty-six subdomains.

The samples cover handwriting, structured tables, and twenty-one kinds of charts used in business reporting, not just clean printed prose. The authors ran modern vision-language models, including GPT-4o and Gemini, through the set. Their findings show where today's best systems stumble on Arabic, from joined letters to dense tables. A shared, hard benchmark is what a field needs to improve in public, and Arabic OCR has lacked one until now.
arxiv-2502-15149:
Yung Kim and seven co-authors steer the band structure of electric circuits by changing their edges, in this 2025 paper. The circuits mimic non-Hermitian physics, where energy is not conserved and wave patterns hug boundaries. Such systems are described by a generalized Brillouin zone, a loop of complex momenta that replaces the usual band picture.

By tuning the boundary part of their circuit lattice, the team split that zone into several separate loops holding both fading and growing waves. That differs from the single skin-effect pattern seen before. Sliding the boundary settings deformed the loops until the topology flipped, a phase change driven by the edge rather than the bulk. The authors say this extreme edge sensitivity could be harnessed for sensors and switches built from ordinary circuit parts.
arxiv-2502-15249:
John Campbell widened a set of famous formulas for the reciprocal of pi squared in a 2025 math paper. The formulas, due to Guillera, are fast-shrinking number series built with a classic proof method. Campbell adds three free parameters to them, stretching each formula into a family.

His proof leans on a speed-up method built from a known algorithm and an old series of Dougall. The new families keep the same fast shrink rates as the first formulas. From them he builds fresh rational series of a mixed type that were not known before. The work shows how one striking formula can seed a whole shelf of kin. Such series matter for high-precision computing and for the theory of special functions.
arxiv-2502-15349:
Feiyang Chen and co-authors build a workshop where attention, the engine of modern language models, can be tuned for any chip, in a 2025 paper. Attention variants multiply faster than hand-tuned code can follow, and each new processor demands fresh optimization. Their framework, AttentionEngine, breaks the computation into swappable blocks and searches the tuning space on its own.

Speedups reached tenfold on setups older tools could not handle. The code is open source, from a Microsoft team. For labs squeezed between model ambition and hardware sprawl, an automatic tuner turns weeks of specialist work into a framework call.
arxiv-2502-16049:
Data that change over time carry shapes within shapes, and Tamal Dey and Shreyas Samaga build a topological lens for watching them evolve. Their framework, quasi zigzag persistence, fuses two established tools: one that tracks features across several scales at once, and one that follows features through a sequence of snapshots. The result is a stable signature that records both the static form and its dynamics.

An algorithm computes the signature efficiently. Bolted onto machine learning models, it sharpened sleep-stage detection from brain recordings, a task where the pattern itself is the diagnosis. The authors present the method as a general instrument for time-varying data, from physiology to finance, wherever evolving shape carries the signal.
arxiv-2502-16149:
Ashok Kumar, Hemangi Madhusudan Shah, and Bankteshwar Tiwari work out the fine geometry of the Funk-Finsler metric in this 2025 paper. The metric lives in spaces of constant curvature: the flat Euclidean case, the spherical case, and the hyperbolic case. The authors set out to compute its main curvature quantities exactly.

They derive the metric's S-curvature, Riemann curvature, Ricci curvature, and flag curvature in each of the three settings. The S-curvature turns out to sit at one sharp constant value in flat space, bounded above by that value in hyperbolic space, and bounded below by it in spherical space. The flag curvature follows the same pattern around its own constant, with the direction of the bound flipping by setting. The results pin down how this asymmetric geometry bends in each kind of space.
arxiv-2502-16249:
Arshia Afzal and co-authors open a new direction in 2025 for fast sequence models that read in both directions. Linear attention models train quickly and infer cheaply, but they were built for one-way tasks like text generation. Tasks such as classification need context from both sides, and no unified way existed to extend the fast models there.

Their framework, named LION in the paper, restates the three core forms of the causal models in bidirectional shape and proves they match. Three example models with different decay styles show the recipe works broadly. On standard two-way tasks the models matched or beat classic attention models while training faster and inferring more cheaply than state-space rivals.
arxiv-2502-16349:
Bouy and co-authors hunt for planets that drift alone in space, with no star to orbit. Such free floaters, some as light as giant planets, form a key clue to how stars and planets are born. Their 2025 search uses early images from the Euclid space telescope, aimed at a young star nursery in Taurus. Old ground images, taken over more than twenty years, add motion data.

Fifteen point sources moved and shone like nursery members. Six were already known as dim, cool objects. Nine are new, with types that may run from cool stars down to near-planetary masses as low as one or two Jupiters. The authors say follow-up checks must confirm them. Scaled to the whole nursery, the count hints at dozens more.
arxiv-2502-16449:
Haoran Su's 2025 dissertation speeds emergency vehicles through crowded city streets using multi-agent reinforcement learning. In New York City, medical response times rose sharply over a decade, and much of the delay comes from travel itself.

Three projects make up the work. One joins vehicle routing with traffic light pre-emption and cut emergency travel time by over forty percent. A second clears lanes in mixed human and self-driving traffic, cutting times by forty percent. A third mapped fairness across boroughs, finding delays tied to sparse signals in one and congestion in another. Fixes include better station placement and intersection design.
arxiv-2502-16649:
Zehra Sen and Stefanie Sonner studied in 2025 the long-term behavior of equations that model biofilm growth, a slime layer made by microbes. Such equations are of porous-medium type, with spots where they break down or move very unevenly. The work is set in a bounded region with fixed zero values at the edge.

Under broad terms, a global attractor is shown to exist, meaning all solutions are drawn to one set over time. With smoother solutions and a sign rule near the breakdown spots, a stronger attractor follows. That in turn shows the global attractor has finite fractal size. Results extend to paired systems where a second spread equation joins the first, as in biofilm models.
arxiv-2502-17049:
Heart attacks are forecast from clinic numbers, yet the air outside the clinic also loads the heart. Xin Zhang and co-authors build a prediction system that reads both in this 2025 paper. Their framework, TabulaTime, fuses patient records with streams of air pollution data, the kind of time series older risk scores throw away.

A custom module combs the pollution stream for patterns at a cost that grows only linearly, and attention weights expose which mixes of body and air drove each forecast. Against strong standard learners the system improved accuracy by more than twenty percent, and pollution data alone carried much of the gain. The authors target the acute coronary syndromes, the sudden heart events where hours of warning change outcomes, and argue environment belongs inside the risk chart.
arxiv-2502-17149:
Bertrand Meyer and Reto Weber rebuild the basics of programming as a small piece of mathematics, in a 2025 paper. Their theory, called PRISM, starts from plain set theory and assumes nothing: every property is proved. One concept covers both programs and their specifications, built from a single relation and a single set.

Three operations, choice, composition, and restriction, do all the work. From them the authors derive the classic laws of programming as theorems, and a simple subset relation defines correctness, specialization, and refinement. Dozens of theorems about programs follow. All of them were checked by machine with the Isabelle proof tool, and the proofs sit in a public repository.
arxiv-2502-17349:
Minyeong Hwang and four co-authors design molecular linkers that are both varied and chemically valid. Linkers join fragments in lead optimization and PROTAC design. Models that ignore fragment 3D poses sample widely but break rules, while pose-aware models stay valid yet narrow. HybridLinker needs no extra training to bridge the two.

A pretrained pose-free model proposes bonding topologies, and a diffusion posterior sampling step, LinkerDPS, steers a pose-aware model with them. An energy-style function ties topology to point clouds. The hybrid beat baselines on validity and diversity in both basic design and applied drug tasks.
arxiv-2502-17649:
Yuhao Wang and co-authors show, in a 2025 optics paper, how two protected light states living at separate interfaces can merge and reshape the light they shed. Such interface states are prized for their toughness, and here they sit in a gain medium that feeds them energy. Bringing the interfaces closer couples the states into a bonded pair and an anti-bonded pair.

The bonded mode glows dimly and evenly in all directions, while its partner glows brightly in a tight beam. Changing the gap between the interfaces tunes the energy split, the quality factor, and the beam shape all at once. The authors pitch the pair as a design platform for beam shaping, nonlinear optics, and quantum devices.
arxiv-2502-18149:
Nasrin Altafi and co-authors open a study of a special algebra family and its dual generator. Their 2025 paper concerns Artinian Gorenstein algebras whose Macaulay dual generator is a binomial. Such algebras sit at a crossroads of algebra and geometry. The team asks which classic traits these algebras hold.

In codimension three, every such algebra has the strong Lefschetz property, a prized symmetry of its structure. Each can be built by doubling a fitting zero-dimensional scheme in the plane. The authors also pin down exactly when these algebras are complete intersections. For general codimension, they give conditions that force the weaker Lefschetz property. Those conditions are shown to be sharp, so the results close the question neatly.
arxiv-2502-18349:
Meredith Shea studies a tiling model from statistical mechanics in this two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. The Aztec diamond dimer model places domino-like pairs on a lattice region, with weights that vary periodically. Recent work clarified its statistics under general periodic weights. Shea defines a variant that breaks periodicity in one direction by stitching together two different two-periodic weightings, and computes its correlation kernel.

The computation extends methods of Berggren and Duits, using the Eynard-Mehta theorem and a Wiener-Hopf factorization. From a form of the kernel suited to asymptotic analysis, she derives local behavior in the model's different macroscopic regions. The leading-order local statistics agree with the ordinary two-periodic model, as expected. The sub-leading terms, however, are changed by the seam between the two weightings, which is the paper's main finding.
arxiv-2502-18949:
Moritz Winterott and Samir Lounis propose a new way to read swirling magnetic patterns inside materials, in a 2025 paper. These three-dimensional spin textures could store data in future devices, but spotting them is hard. Tools that sense the stray magnetic field fail for a class of magnets whose field cancels out. The authors use scattering theory to show the textures carry a hidden electric charge pattern instead.

That charge arises when neighboring magnetic moments point in mixed directions and electrons scatter among them. It leaves marks in phase images made by electron holography, a microscope method. The team computed how much each known and new effect adds to those images under varied settings. Their results open a path to finding textures that older methods miss.
arxiv-2502-19049:
Many natural and social systems are part clockwork, part dice roll, and stochastic differential equations are their native language. Learning such an equation from one noisy recording usually demands prior guesses or bespoke training. Patrick Seifner and co-authors pretrain a foundation model, FIM-SDE, on a library of example paths so it can read off the drift and dice terms of a new system on sight.

From double-well dynamics to stock, oil, and wind records, the pretrained model matched specialists trained per dataset, and a brief fine-tune put it ahead of all of them. One general reader for noisy dynamics could speed up modeling across the sciences.
arxiv-2502-19249:
Michael Hu and co-authors study how training on formal languages shapes language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Formal languages are rule-built toy languages, simpler than natural speech. Earlier work showed that a first phase on such languages can help models learn real language later.

The team asks which features of the toy language carry the benefit. They argue two conditions matter: the toy language should mirror the dependency structures of natural language, and it should stay within the model's computing limits. Experiments support the first condition strongly and the second modestly. Strikingly, the pre-phase cut the needed natural language data by about a third. Attention patterns learned early stayed important later.
arxiv-2502-19449:
Ugwumadu and co-authors study effects of galactic irradiation on heat and electron flow in tungsten in a 2025 paper. Radiation damage at the atomic scale is a lasting puzzle for materials in space and reactors.

Using a site-projected heat method, the team models bulk tungsten and twin grain boundaries with missing-atom defects. A standard displacement model sets the damage level. Heat maps after cascades show how conductivity varies by place. A second method gauges electron flow changes from vacancies and boundaries. Charge transport proves strongly defect-dependent. The findings aid design of radiation-tough materials and tiny heat and electron devices for space use.
arxiv-2502-19649:
Jan Wehner and co-authors survey representation engineering for large language models in a paper from 2025. The approach steers a model by editing its inner activations, not its inputs or weights. That promises control that is clear, cheap in data, and flexible.

The survey is the first full map of the young field. It sorts methods into a three-step pipeline: find the right internal pattern, turn it into a usable handle, then apply control. Uses range from honesty to safety and style. Strengths and limits are weighed against prompting and fine-tuning. Open problems include clashes between concepts and weak theory. The taxonomy gives new researchers a shared map of the terrain.
arxiv-2502-19749:
Jinhao Pan and co-authors present a 2025 benchmark for social bias in language models that hides in plain sight. Models learn bias from their training text. Term based tests miss much of it now, since models have learned to dodge blunt biased replies while subtler forms persist.

Their benchmark, DBB, wraps bias concepts inside natural real world scenes with soft framing. Six top models were scored on the set. The models looked clean on term level tests yet still backed biased claims in the nuanced scenes. Data, code, and results are shared in a public archive. The work urges bias checks that probe meaning, not just word pairs.
arxiv-2502-20049:
Suffa and co-authors push fluid simulation to huge scales in this 2025 computing paper. Their method lets solid objects move through a simulated fluid on a regular grid, with cells partly filled by solid where the two meet. The hard parts are mapping complex shapes onto the grid cheaply and keeping the physics right.

Their mapping is both accurate and efficient, and the solver code is generated automatically for both normal and graphics processors, reaching most of each chip's peak speed. The coupling adds only modest cost. A spinning rotor test used up to 4.3 billion grid cells and scaled well across tens of thousands of processor cores on two supercomputers.
arxiv-2502-20349:
Wilka Carvalho and Andrew Lampinen argue that cognitive science should study people in richer, more natural settings, in this 2025 paper. Lab tasks are tidy, but real behavior is messy and wide-ranging. Theories built only on tidy tasks may fail to explain how minds work in daily life.

The authors review work from brain science, mind science, and artificial intelligence. Natural tasks often stir different behavior and brain processes than stripped-down ones. Models trained on natural data also learn in new ways. The pair urge the field to join these strands, using modern AI tools to build theories that hold up across the full range of human behavior.
arxiv-2502-20949: Luigi Montoro, Luigi Muglia, and Berardino Sciunzi prove a symmetry result for a class of partial differential equations in a 2025 paper. The setting is a half space with zero boundary values, and the equation mixes a p-Laplacian drive with a singular term that blows up near zero and a general reaction term. Using prior bounds and the moving plane method, the trio show every positive solution rises steadily as one moves away from the boundary, square to it. The result is a theory step for singular elliptic problems.
arxiv-2502-21049:
Jingru Fu and co-authors present a framework that simulates how an individual brain will age, in work from 2025. Predicting a person's future brain scans is hard because ageing and disease follow shared patterns yet each brain differs. Generative models can make realistic average templates, but they miss personal variation over time.

Their framework learns population ageing paths with a generative network, then adapts those paths to one person using a parallel transport method from geometry. Because the simulation warps the original scan smoothly, the anatomy stays consistent by design. Tests used scans from a public dataset covering Alzheimer's disease and healthy ageing. Starting from a single baseline scan, the system produced realistic three-dimensional scan sequences. It could also model the shift from normal ageing into disease.
arxiv-2503-00049:
Judging the mood of a video takes more than reading faces; a slumped posture, a bleak backdrop, or a tense action can carry the feeling. Jiamin Luo and co-authors set a new task in a 2025 paper that asks systems to find a video's sentiment, locate where it sits, and say what drives it. Their setup uses both the plain scene cues and the hidden ones.

Their model mixes specialist parts that take turns by scene type, with a causal block that lifts the hidden cues above the plain ones. On new test sets built for plain and hidden cues, the model beat leading video language systems by wide margins. The authors argue that mood in video is a whole-scene property, and systems that read only faces will keep missing it.
arxiv-2503-00149:
Mengzhu Chen, Isabella Pedraza Pineros, Arvind Satyanarayan, and Jonathan Zong build a tactile chart tool in a 2025 paper. Tactile charts let blind and low vision readers feel data, but they are hard to design. New designers face dense guidelines, and experts face slow, scattered workflows. Interviews with expert designers shape the tool.

Tactile Vega-Lite extends a known chart grammar with tactile defaults drawn from those guidelines. New users get compliant charts fast, and experts can override any default. A study with twelve creators shows faster cycles, more consistency, and automatic braille and spacing work, the authors report. Expert critique adds new design lessons.
arxiv-2503-00349:
Anne-Men Huijzer and co-authors prove convergence for learning in resistor networks in a 2025 paper. Energy-based learning offers an alternative to backpropagation for training. Such methods suit analog hardware that learns in place.

Rigorous convergence theory for these methods has been missing. The team studies contrastive learning on a network of adjustable resistors. All elements are linear, which keeps the math tractable. The method turns out to equal projected gradient descent on a convex function. Convergence then holds for a stated range of step sizes. A stochastic version inherits the guarantee as well. Readers get a first firm footing for analog learning theory.
arxiv-2503-00549:
Yuan Liao, Xinjie Ma, Andreas Neuhierl, and Linda Schilling ask, in a 2025 paper, how sure we should be of a neural network's stock return forecast. Machine learning in asset pricing usually hands over a single number, with no error bar. Investors then treat shaky and solid forecasts alike.

The team shows that network forecasts share the same large-sample behavior as classic nonparametric estimates. That link yields a closed-form standard error for each forecast, plus a workable bootstrap when the formula is awkward. Feeding these error bars into a cautious portfolio rule gives a principled reason to shrink bold bets. In tests, the approach improved out-of-sample results. Honest uncertainty, the authors argue, is part of the forecast, not a footnote.
arxiv-2503-00749:
Vyacheslav Futorny and Santanu Tantubay work on the representation theory of Hamiltonian Lie algebras in a 2025 math paper. Lie algebras are systems that track symmetry, and a representation turns their abstract rules into concrete linear maps. The pair study a known tool, the Shen-Larsson functor, which builds modules for one algebra from modules for a related symplectic algebra. Their question is whether the tool keeps modules simple, in the sense of having no smaller pieces inside.

The answer is yes, apart from a finite set of special cases. The simple modules they obtain are of cuspidal type, and their weight counts match the size of the starting module. The result extends what was known for other Cartan type algebras to the Hamiltonian case, which had been left open.
arxiv-2503-00949:
Francisco Marín Sola generalized in 2025 a classic inequality about the shadows of convex bodies, one of the cornerstone results of affine geometry. The inequality links a body's volume to the volumes of its projections, and it holds no matter how the body is stretched.

A recent extension replaced the projection direction with a whole small convex body and added a power parameter. Marín Sola pushes that version further, letting the underlying measure be any rotationally symmetric one with a mild concavity property. For the simplest power, he also builds empirical versions of the inequality, inspired by a fresh reading of the original result as a statement about random samples. The work widens a deep tool of geometry.
arxiv-2503-01349:
Kurt Girstmair revisits a set of numbers Hecke introduced in work on Eisenstein series, which Hecke called rational but cumbersome to compute. His 2025 paper shows these numbers are less mysterious than they look. They are essentially generators of certain number fields tied to roots of unity. The name comes from how they arise: inverting a matrix built from better known cotangent numbers.

For a wide class of cases, those where the index is square free, the paper gives a fairly closed form. The numbers appear as blends of roots of unity with rational weights. A second formula uses generalized Bernoulli numbers and Gauss sums. The work connects a historical aside in Hecke's writing to standard objects in algebraic number theory. It replaces case by case computation with structure.
arxiv-2503-01649:
Cheng-Cheng Yu and co-authors present a scheme to catch a damaging error in neutral atom quantum computers, in a 2025 paper. Atoms can leak out of their working states during two-qubit gates, above all through decay of excited Rydberg states. Such leaks spread into linked errors and weaken error correction.

Their protocol swaps helper and data atoms in line, so leakage can be handled without extra atom species or extra helpers. Two decoders are built for unlike detection powers. When leakage and loss can be seen, as in one atom type, their located decoder reached a high error threshold and beat standard error models. When only loss can be seen, a second decoder targets the worst linked faults and matched standard performance. The authors offer the scheme for real atom machines.
arxiv-2503-01749: Eris Rocha Walchek constructs big generalized Heegner classes in a 2025 paper in pure number theory. Heegner classes are special cohomology classes tied to modular forms, and they feed deep conjectures about elliptic curves. Working on the quaternionic side, the paper interpolates those classes p-adically along a Coleman family, a continuous family of finite-slope forms. A single big class then specializes to the classes of each member. The construction follows the approach introduced by Jetchev, Loeffler, and Zerbes for the classical case.
arxiv-2503-02249:
Changhe Chen and colleagues ask whether large language models can learn how to design soft robots, in a paper released in twenty twenty-five. Designing such robots mixes materials, mechanics, and control, and often depends on trial and error. The authors built a test set using a simulator that creates soft robot challenges. The tasks cover moving across the ground, handling objects, and balancing. Models must link a plain task description to choices about body shape and materials.

Tested models showed they could pick up useful design patterns, but they often missed small differences between designs that perform quite differently. The authors also show that model choices can serve as a starting point for a real design search. They offer the test set to help other researchers compare models on equal terms.
arxiv-2503-02349:
Yajun Liu and Beth Andrews develop in 2025 a method to spot sudden change in a special kind of time series as data arrive. Their series hold shares that must sum in a set way, depend on their own past over many steps, and react to outside inputs. A running detector for such series could flag shifts in fields from health to transport safety.

First they prove that their generalized model settles into a steady, well behaved pattern under stated conditions. Their detector itself is nonparametric, meaning it leans on few assumptions about where a change comes from, and its power grows to full with enough starting data. As a case, they fit monthly rates of alcohol linked car crashes over a decade, with drink prices as the outside input. The method cleanly found the known change point in that series.
arxiv-2503-02949:
Elena Cáceres, Brian Kent, and Harita Balaji unify two analogy programs between gravity and electromagnetism in a 2025 paper. Both programs turn certain spacetime shapes into electromagnetic potentials. One, gravito-electromagnetism, compares tidal forces across the theories. The other, the double copy, builds gravity solutions from electromagnetic ones in reverse. The authors show the resulting potentials usually match the spacetime's own symmetry vectors.

Those vectors, called Killing vectors, were long known to behave like electromagnetic potentials. Using them, the team links two forms of the double copy without leaning on special coordinates. They spell out the hidden assumptions in one form and the role symmetry vectors play. A key claim: matching tidal tensors across theories needs the same source rules as the double copy. Special spacetimes with an extra symmetry tensor make the correspondence vivid. The paper gathers these threads into one perspective.
arxiv-2503-03149:
YiQiu Guo and seven co-authors present DSVD, a 2025 decoding method that helps large language models catch their own errors while writing. Models often state false facts with confidence, and checking only after the full answer costs time. DSVD checks the text as it forms. One part grades the draft continuously, in parallel with writing. Another part rolls back to the error point and rewrites just that stretch when a problem appears.

Across five benchmarks, the method raised truthfulness in question answering and factual accuracy in scored summaries. It also stacked well with older faithful-decoding methods, lifting them further. The authors argue that live self-checking is a practical route to more trustworthy models, since it needs no separate verifier model and fits real deployment.
arxiv-2503-03649:
Andrei Ermolaev and seven colleagues simulate a learning machine made of light traveling through optical fiber, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In an extreme learning machine, only the final readout is trained, while the middle layer scrambles inputs in rich, fixed ways.

Here the scrambling comes from the fiber itself, as pulses spread and mix under nonlinear and dispersive effects. The team models the process with a generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation. They test it on the standard handwritten digit task and vary how the data is encoded, read out, and noised. Accuracy topped ninety-one percent in one dispersion regime and ninety-three percent in the other. A key finding is a built-in penalty: quantum noise on the input pulses caps how well the machine can do. The study maps where such photonic learners can shine and where physics holds them back.
arxiv-2503-04249:
Junhao Shi and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a flaw in training strong AI models with weak teachers. The setup, called weak-to-strong generalization, uses a weak supervisor to steer a stronger model. In theory, the strong model should rise above its teacher. In practice, it often just copies the teacher's errors, a failure called overfitting.

Simply removing wrong labels is not a clean fix, since it thins out hard questions. The authors propose a two-stage framework that improves both the quality of the guidance signals and the quality of the questions. Tests on three families of large language models and two math benchmarks showed clear gains. On some models, the method reached full recovery of the strong model's own ceiling. The work speaks to the core problem of guiding systems smarter than their overseers.
arxiv-2503-04349:
Steinacker and co-authors compare in 2025 two ways to design bike networks that hold up well as conditions change. Good bike networks lift cycling, but growth over long horizons is hard to plan. Network effects and shifts in travel choice make the task complex.

One path uses direct welfare optimization, the other a simple network heuristic. Both were tried on plans for cycle superhighways in Copenhagen. The complex models gave better welfare, but only by small margins. They also proved more fragile when inputs were off. The result is a warning that fancy long term plans can rest on shaky ground, despite high benefit to cost ratios.
arxiv-2503-04549:
Lucien Ng and five co-authors present a cheaper way to run a setup ritual that many privacy proofs depend on, in a 2025 paper. Certain zero-knowledge proofs need a public string, called Powers of Tau, built from secret randomness. If that secret leaks, anyone can forge proofs. Volunteers add randomness one by one in public ceremonies, but earlier blockchain designs charged each helper many costly on-chain operations.

Their system, Lite-PoT, cuts that cost in two ways. A fraud-proof scheme drops the pricey checks to a flat few per helper, letting ceremonies reach far larger sizes than before. A second trick bundles many helpers' additions into one update, sharing the cost among them. Tests showed about a sixteen-fold reach over past on-chain designs. The authors aim to make joining a ceremony cheap enough that decentralization actually happens.
arxiv-2503-04749:
Noel Portillo surveys digital transformation in the petrochemical industry in a 2025 paper. Plants run on century-old foundations while facing safety, environmental, and cost pressure. Internet-of-things devices promise relief, yet adoption crawls across the sector.

Trade secrecy, thin research budgets, doubts about new tools, and decision-maker resistance all brake the change. The paper reviews recent industry research spending and catalogs current Industry 4.0 pilots and implementations. Challenges and openings are weighed side by side. The analysis aims to give sector leaders a realistic map of where connected sensing can pay off first.
arxiv-2503-05249:
En-Jui Chang constructs a family of quantum error codes in a 2025 paper that resist a shared drift error. All qubits in a device drift together under their own physics, and that joint drift can damage stored data more than random single errors. Long storage makes the joint drift the main threat, as in trapped ion systems.

Chang builds codes that hold a fixed total excitation, which blocks the joint drift by design. The codes keep a high data rate while still fixing small errors. The smallest code stores one logical qubit in eight physical ones. It roughly doubles the data rate of the best past code of this type and lifts its error threshold about four fold.
arxiv-2503-05749:
Petropoulos and a large team of co-authors compile an encyclopedia-style guide in 2025 to operations and supply chain management. The field keeps evolving as firms face tangled problems across industries, from factory floors to global shipping. Their article gathers the strategies, tools, methods, and best practices that mark the field's current edge.

Settings where these ideas have been put to work are covered too, sector by sector. The piece is built for non-linear reading, the authors say: a reference to dip into, not a story to finish. Readers in view range from scholars and students to working managers. A single first port of call can save a newcomer weeks of hunting through a scattered field.
arxiv-2503-05849:
Nikolaj Kühne Jakobsen builds the first tool support for a software modeling language in this 2025 thesis. The language, Conceptual, describes system behavior as self-contained, reusable units called concepts. Good early abstractions predict good software, but modeling well is hard.

The thesis pins down the language's syntax and meaning, building on earlier work. It then maps Conceptual models into Alloy, a language with strong automatic analysis tools. A simple compiler performs that mapping, letting developers reason about their models. Case studies show the language's range in practice. The compiler even caught faulty specifications published in the literature, and an editor plug-in rounds out the tooling.
arxiv-2503-05949:
Maggio and Carlone introduced a mapping method in twenty twenty-five that lets robots build three-dimensional maps labeled by meaning, ready for whatever task is at hand. A robot may need the scene split into chairs and tables for one job, or into safe and unsafe zones for another.

Their system, Bayesian Fields, builds the scene from soft three-dimensional blobs. Instead of fixing object boundaries in advance, it clusters the blobs according to the current task. When several camera views label the same spot, it merges the labels with a proper probability update rather than a plain average. That respects how the underlying vision-language model actually behaves. The result is a detailed map that uses little memory and yields clean object shapes on demand. The code is open source. The authors argue task-shaped maps beat one-size maps for real robots.
arxiv-2503-06249:
Ulrich Haisch studies how an anomalous gluon interaction would change Higgs boson production at colliders. The process in view is Higgs production via gluon-gluon fusion. The extra effect comes from the triple-gluon operator in the Standard Model effective field theory, known as SMEFT. Haisch carries the calculation to two loops.

The analysis covers matching and running within the SMEFT, the core steps of renormalization group improved perturbation theory. Haisch presents the work as a blueprint for such calculations beyond leading order. Readers get a full map of the subtleties that arise when effective field theory methods meet precision collider physics.
arxiv-2503-06549:
Zhigang Bao and colleagues prove a decorrelation transition in the Wigner minor process. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies eigenvalues of a large Wigner matrix and all its minors. The top eigenvalues of the full matrix and its nearest minor track each other closely. That link weakens as minors shrink further. A critical regime was known for the Gaussian unitary case.

Forrester and Nagao had derived an explicit joint correlation formula there. Bao and colleagues prove the same formula holds in full generality. Their proof covers the Wigner minor process beyond the Gaussian case. They also give a complete analysis above and below the transition. Eigenvector overlaps are treated alongside eigenvalues. The decorrelation transition is thus proven in full.
arxiv-2503-06649:
Matteo Buzzegoli, Kirill Tuchin, and Nandagopal Vijayakumar cheapen a radiation calculation that heavy-ion physics needs. Charged fermions spiraling in a strong magnetic field inside a rotating medium shine with synchrotron light. The exact formula exists but costs heavy computation, a problem when the medium is the quark-gluon plasma born in collider crashes.

Their quasi-classical WKB approximation tracks the exact result closely at a tiny slice of the numerical cost. The derivation handles rotation and the magnetic field together, the realistic case for plasma fireballs that spin as they burn. The shortcut should let modelers include this radiation channel in simulations that previously skipped it as too dear.
arxiv-2503-06849: A large international team, including K Abe, reports in a 2025 paper the first differential measurement of a rare neutrino reaction. When a neutrino strikes matter in a neutral-current event, it can knock out a single positively charged pion. The cross section for that process had not before been mapped in detail across the range of outcomes. Such maps test the models used to read neutrino experiments, and they help separate true signals from look-alike events in detectors.
arxiv-2503-07449:
Donát Takács and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on the piston effect in fluids near their critical point. There, a fluid is both gas and liquid at once in a sense. A sudden heat jolt sends a pressure pulse through it, a thermoacoustic quirk. Models of the effect need codes that are fast and free of fake waves.

Their code splits the field into parts that reverse and parts that do not. That split parts the sums into a wave form and a heat form, each with its own time step plan. The grid is staggered in space and time and runs in full explicit steps. They then run the piston case on the new code.
arxiv-2503-07549:
Lisa Johanna Schumacher, Mauricio Bustamante, Matteo Agostini, Foteini Oikonomou, and Elisa Resconi look past the first triumphs of neutrino astronomy. IceCube, the lone giant neutrino telescope, has named its first cosmic sources, two active galaxies. But it catches few particles and sees only part of the sky at once.

The authors forecast a joint network, PLEnuM, pooling new telescopes rising worldwide over the next two decades. Together the fleet could catch up to thirty times more neutrinos and watch the whole sky without pause. Shared analysis should speed source discovery, in some cases by decades. Fainter sources anywhere overhead come into reach, with tens of new finds plausible.
arxiv-2503-07849:
Sander Beckers offers a new definition of actual causation in a 2025 paper. The question is as old as philosophy: given everything that happened, which earlier event truly caused the outcome?

The definition builds on Beckers' own nondeterministic causal models, a broader version of the standard framework. Rather than resting on gut calls about examples, it grows from the job causation does in sharing and learning causal models. Steps along the way generalize counterfactual dependence and simplify model structure. The final verdicts match his earlier definition almost everywhere. The gain, he argues, is a principled base instead of a pile of intuitions.
arxiv-2503-08049:
Nadarasar Bahavan and co-authors teach deep nets to say 'new kind' when a shot fits no class they know. Closed nets force each shot into a known bin, a risk in safe-first fields. Their 2025 way, SphOR, shapes the eye's space first and fits the judge last. Class marks are set square to each other so kinds stand far apart. Shots are then held on a ball skin as bell blends.

Shake tricks ride the train to blunt false faith. Open-set craft past this pair-fit the eye and judge as one, so the eye bent odd for new kinds. Stock sight builds, built for broad tasks, bent no less. A space shaped for the open task can flag new kinds clean, they hold.
arxiv-2503-08149:
Sonaldeep Halder, Kartikey Anand, and Rahul Maitra use a generative learning model to build lean trial wavefunctions for quantum chemistry. Quantum computers can, in principle, compute a molecule's energy exactly, but the trial state, or ansatz, must stay shallow for today's noisy machines. Their 2025 method lets a Restricted Boltzmann Machine pick what matters.

The model trains on rough, low-rank pieces of an approximate wavefunction. It then predicts which high-rank pieces carry the real weight in the ground state. Those pieces are split back down, screened by a perturbation test, and built into a compact ansatz. Bayesian tuning keeps the learning cheap on little data. No extra measurements are needed after training. The aim is accurate molecular energies on near-term hardware.
arxiv-2503-08649: Marta Calanchi and Massimo Grossi study a degenerate Poisson problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. The equation models diffusion where the conductivity fades near the boundary of a smooth bounded domain, at a rate set by distance to the edge and an exponent below one. They describe how the solution behaves near the boundary and discuss its regularity properties, that is, how smooth the solution can be expected to be under a continuous source term.
arxiv-2503-09249:
Retrieval-augmented summarization writes a summary with example summaries in hand, and the examples' lengths quietly steer the result. The authors of this study argue that length diversity among examples has been overlooked, and they build it into the retrieval step.

Their algorithm, DL-MMR, scores candidate examples by relevance to the query and by the spread of their target lengths, so the pool covers short and long models of the answer. Unlike the standard relevance method, it never compares examples against each other, which slashes the computing cost of building the pool by orders of magnitude and saves memory by a similar factor. Experiments showed summaries as informative as the standard method's, now with length under control.
arxiv-2503-09349:
Simon Geirnaert and co-authors model how the accuracy of a brain-based listening decoder changes with the length of the time window used, published in 2025. Such decoders use brain signals to tell which of several speakers a listener is attending to. A core trade-off links window length to accuracy: shorter windows react faster but judge less reliably.

Usually, that trade-off curve is mapped by testing many window lengths, which is costly. Their method models the curve from labeled correlations at a single window length. After a standard transform, the correlations for attended and unattended speech are modeled as normal distributions. Tests on two decoder types, one linear and one a deep network, showed low modeling error. Most true accuracies fell inside the estimated confidence ranges.
arxiv-2503-09549:
Fabio Cassini and Chiara Segala present a 2025 study of the turnpike effect in control problems where many agents interact and noise shakes the system. The turnpike effect says that the best long-run plan spends most of its time near one steady state, like a highway between two cities. Earlier proofs covered calm, deterministic systems. The authors show the effect survives in discrete time with random noise, under the right conditions on stability and control.

Stiff systems, whose parts move at very different speeds, are handled with exponential integrators, a time-stepping method that copes with stiffness. Computer tests confirmed the theory. The exponential method beat standard explicit schemes, and the turnpike control stayed effective under noise. The work extends a planning shortcut to realistic, uncertain swarms.
arxiv-2503-09749:
Yuan and Bowyer built a new test in twenty twenty-five that tells if two eye photos come from the same kind of twin. The iris is the colored ring in the eye, and its marks are used to check who a person is. Folks once thought left and right iris marks were as unlike as those of strangers.

Their twin-net tool learns from pairs of photos and sorts them as twin-type or not. It trains on real twin pairs, same-person pairs, and pairs of strangers. Both the iris marks and the skin and lids near the eye help the tool decide. Its scores beat the scores past work found for human judges.
arxiv-2503-09949:
Yuanxin Liu and six co-authors ask whether big AI models can judge AI-made videos in a 2025 paper. Video generators improve monthly, and scoring their output by hand does not scale. Older automatic scores were built for other jobs or trained narrowly on one trait.

The team built a benchmark of generated videos with human preference labels across fifteen traits, from realism to motion quality. They then tested eighteen large models that see and read. The best models still trail human judges, but they clearly beat the older specialized scorers. The largest models did best. The paper also probes which design choices matter most when a model is used as a judge. The findings support one generalist judge over many narrow ones, while marking how far the approach still has to go.
arxiv-2503-10449: Rolf Schneider gives a new proof for a measure transport problem in this short 2025 math paper. The problem is the Gauss image problem for pseudo-cones, a question about moving a measure on a sphere from one pattern to another. Schneider solves it with a special case of Kantorovich duality, a classic tool for transport problems. The note is brief and proof-focused, aimed at readers in geometry who know the Gauss image setting.
arxiv-2503-10549:
Youngjin Kwon and Xiao Zhang build MASQUE in this 2025 paper, a text-guided makeup generator that shields faces from recognition systems. Face recognition now sits inside government and business services, and misuse worries are growing. Makeup-based defenses are popular, but older ones mostly impersonate a chosen identity, which dodges poorly and invites abuse. They also smear artifacts across the whole face.

MASQUE uses a diffusion model steered by the user's own text prompt, so the makeup stays local and personal. It needs no outside identity: a pairwise trick compares two shots of the same person to guide the attack. Tests on open models and commercial services showed stronger dodging than all baselines. Image quality and prompt flexibility also improved, and the effect survived image transforms.
arxiv-2503-10849:
Thévenet and five co-authors showed that water turns into a superacid deep inside planets in twenty twenty-five. At crushing pressure and heat, the chemistry of water shapes the insides of planets and the deep carbon cycle. Tests had found hydrocarbons in hot, ionized water turning into heavy hydrocarbons and nanodiamonds. No clear path explained the change.

The team ran quantum simulations of molecules, with boosted sampling and machine-learned force laws. They watched hot, squeezed water ionize into a bath like a superacid. That bath adds protons to hydrocarbons, making short-lived five-way carbonium ions. These forms shed hydrogen and yield reactive carbocations. The carbocations grow chains that end as nanodiamonds. Pressure also shifts charge in methane, feeding the same web. The authors claim the first proof of a superacid water regime. It ties the odd changes seen in tests into one story.
arxiv-2503-11149:
Michael Brannan, Daniel Gromada, Junichiro Matsuda, Adam Skalski, and Mateusz Wasilewski prove a quantum version of a classic graph theorem in a paper from 2025. Frucht's theorem says every finite group is the symmetry group of some graph. The quantum version replaces groups and graphs with their quantum counterparts. The authors first build several quantum Cayley graphs for a given quantum group.

They then give a systematic way to merge those graphs into one with exactly the right symmetries. They also show the dual of any non-abelian finite group is quantum rigid, meaning a Cayley graph exists whose symmetries are exactly that dual. The result anchors quantum symmetry theory.
arxiv-2503-11249:
Optimal transport measures how costly it is to reshape one distribution into another, and slicing tricks make that cost cheap to compute in high dimensions. A team of authors extended those tricks in 2025 to data that live on a sphere, such as directions or points on Earth. Their method projects spherical data onto tree-shaped structures on the sphere instead of flat lines, keeping more of the data's shape.

From a new spherical Radon transform they derive closed formulas for the transport cost, giving a distance they call STSW. Theory in the paper shows the distance is well defined and does not depend on how the sphere is rotated. Experiments on gradient flows and self-supervised learning test the metric against recent rivals.
arxiv-2503-11549:
Ahmadreza Jeddi and co-authors speed up vision models by pruning tokens in a 2025 paper. Vision transformers process images as token sets, and attention costs grow steeply with count. Their method, SAINT, drops look-alike tokens using similarity graphs, with no retraining, and adapts how much to prune at each layer.

The authors map a three-stage life of tokens inside transformers and prune hardest early. For image models, throughput doubled with under one percent accuracy loss. For vision-language models, tokens fell by seventy-five percent with small quality cost. Readers get a unified speedup for both model families.
arxiv-2503-12349:
Jianzhu Yao and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 benchmarking how well language models plan strategically and reason socially. Social strategy is harder than solo puzzles, since success depends on reading partners and rivals. Their benchmark, SPIN-Bench, mixes classic planning tasks, competitive board games, cooperative card games, and negotiation scenes in one frame. An arena lets agents play these settings out.

The team varies action spaces, state complexity, and agent counts to stress different skills. Today's models handle fact recall and short plans decently. They stumble on deep multi-step reasoning over big state spaces and on coordination under uncertainty. The authors offer the bench to spur work on multi-agent planning and human-AI teaming.
arxiv-2503-12549:
Alexander Koebler, Ralf Gross, Florian Buettner, and Ingo Thon help robots grasp hidden objects in two thousand twenty-five. Flexible factories need robots to grip items in random poses. Parts often hide each other or sit behind structures. Missing depth data then breaks grasp point math.

Their autoencoder based inpainting rebuilds the missing point cloud parts. Robust object matching can then compute grip points as usual. The method plugs into a live industrial grasping system. Far fewer objects get discarded by the process now. Real world occlusion, not just lab cases, is the target.
arxiv-2503-12649:
Hao Chen and four co-authors scale up the merging of trained models in a 2025 paper. Merging several fine-tuned models into one multi-skill model avoids costly joint training. Older merging recipes assume tidy in-house models and break down as the pool of candidates grows.

Their method recasts merging as a constrained optimization problem. A classic Frank-Wolfe routine repeatedly picks the single most useful model from the pool. Each pick triggers a small local merge that improves the combined objective. The objective encodes the behavior the final model should show. Candidate models themselves mark out the space of allowed solutions. The design suits the messy open ecosystem, where models arrive with partial documentation and varied origins.
arxiv-2503-12849: Ankur Pandey, Nijjwal Karak, and Debarati Mondal connect two ways of calling a set negligibly small in function spaces whose growth rule varies from point to point. One is Sobolev capacity, defined through the energy of functions covering the set. The other is a generalized Hausdorff measure built from a gauge function. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they prove that sets of zero capacity also have zero generalized Hausdorff measure, for suitable gauges, in both variable-exponent Sobolev spaces and a class of Musielak-Orlicz-Sobolev spaces.
arxiv-2503-13049:
Stikuts and co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on making a dragged particle lock into fractional speeds. Shapiro steps are plateaus where a driven system holds its velocity steady while the driving force grows, long known for particles crossing wavy landscapes, but only at whole-number speeds. The team drive one colloidal particle across an optical landscape whose shape and rhythm they can sculpt.

In the non-sinusoidal, time-modulated landscape, fractional steps appear beside the integer ones. Tracking the single particle reveals the microscopic dance behind each kind of lock-in. Tuning the shape of the landscape and the driving protocol moves and widens the steps at will. The authors present the setup as a flexible bench for studying synchronization in soft matter, one particle at a time.
arxiv-2503-13249:
Ziming Li and co-authors report tests of a prototype veto tank for a neutrino observatory in a 2025 paper. The observatory, TAO, will sit about thirty meters from a reactor core in Taishan, China, and measure its antineutrinos with record sharpness. Around its central detector sits a water tank that must veto, or flag, stray particles that could fake a signal.

The tank holds a thick shell of pure water watched by hundreds of small light sensors, sharing electronics with its big sister experiment, JUNO. The prototype departs from the usual cyclic design, as its title states. The team checks how the water Cherenkov light system performs with those sensors and electronics, including a software trigger that decides what counts as an event. Long stability runs round out the test.
arxiv-2503-13349:
Otger Ballester and a large team of co-authors lay out, in a 2025 preprint, the technical design of a laser radar for watching the sky over a gamma-ray observatory. Cherenkov telescopes read gamma rays through air showers, so air quality bends their data. The pathfinder Barcelona Raman LIDAR will monitor the air above the northern site of the Cherenkov Telescope Array. It pairs a steerable 1.8-meter mirror with a pulsed laser firing ultraviolet and green light. Two elastic and Raman channels read how aerosols scatter and absorb that light.

The instrument is rebuilt on a retired telescope frame. Parts include a coaxial laser path, a near-range system, a liquid light guide, and a custom polychromator. A year of tests at the mountain site checked stability and semi-remote running. The design leads to the final observatory LIDAR. Real-time air data should keep the gamma-ray science accurate.
arxiv-2503-13649:
Antonios Valamontes and Ioannis Adamopoulos ask whether future observatories could ever catch a white hole in the act in a 2025 paper. White holes are the time-reversed twins of black holes, allowed by the equations yet never seen. The authors build a computing framework to judge detectability before anyone claims a sighting.

Two data streams feed the test. A space antenna, LISA, would supply the polarization of a background hum of gravitational waves. A ground experiment, CMB-S4, would supply polarization patterns in the cosmic microwave background. Monte Carlo simulations generate candidate signals, Bayesian inference weighs them against noise, and signal-to-noise estimates deliver the verdict on feasibility. The framework is a rehearsal: it prices the evidence a real claim would need, in two independent sky channels.
arxiv-2503-13949:
Bao-Yun Dong, Yanhua Zhou, Wei Wang, and Tao Wang build a tunable version of a classic light-matter model using Rydberg atoms in a cavity. The Dicke model couples a crowd of two-level atoms to light, and its anisotropic form lets the counter-rotating coupling terms vary against the rotating ones. Those terms matter, but in natural setups their ratio is fixed. The team's trick is to drive the system with a pumping laser that pulses in a set rhythm.

The pulsing reshapes the effective coupling, sliding the ratio anywhere from zero to infinity. Strong attractions between the Rydberg atoms come along for free, pushing the model into the strongly correlated regime. As a demonstration, the authors show the tuning helps prepare target quantum states gently and reliably. They offer the setup as a platform for quantum simulation and many-body studies.
arxiv-2503-14649:
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, pairs a language model with searches of an outside knowledge base to give more reliable answers. Wenqi Jiang and co-authors tackled the cost of serving such systems in 2025. RAG comes in many variants whose workloads differ sharply, so a server tuned for one variant can waste resources on another.

The team first define a structured description, RAGSchema, that captures the range of RAG designs. Profiling several workloads then showed large performance gaps between them. Their optimizer, RAGO, adjusts the serving setup to each workload's shape. In tests it doubled throughput per chip and cut the wait for the first token by over half.
arxiv-2503-14749:
Sophia Hager and three co-authors teach language models to say how sure they are, honestly, in this 2025 paper. People increasingly ask AI chatbots factual questions. A useful answer should carry a sense of its own reliability, but today's models state confidence that does not match their actual error rates. They may sound certain while being wrong a third of the time.

The authors focus on semantic confidence: how likely the answer's meaning is right, regardless of the exact wording. Their procedure, uncertainty distillation, first estimates a model's uncertainty on practice questions, then maps those estimates onto true probabilities using held-out data. The model is fine-tuned on examples that speak their calibrated confidence aloud. After training, the stated confidences tracked observed error rates well. The work matters for any setting where a user must decide whether to act on an AI's answer.
arxiv-2503-14849:
Zhuoyi Yang and Ian Harris adapt a large language model to spot bad log lines in a 2025 paper. System logs record events, and odd lines can warn of failures or attacks. Their model first learns the rhythm of normal logs from big data sets. It then learns to predict the next line in a healthy sequence.

A reward based round of training sharpens its eye for odd lines. The model judges new lines by how poorly they fit the learned rhythm. Tests on three classic log sets beat prior best methods. The setup needs no hand labeled attack examples to get started.
arxiv-2503-15149:
Zhaoxiang Shen and four co-authors train a machine learning stand-in for a costly physics calculation, in a 2025 paper. Many-body dispersion forces are the subtle attractions that hold liquids and soft matter together, and computing them exactly is slow. Polymer melts need those forces described well, which blocks large simulations. The team builds a surrogate model on a trimmed neural network that keeps only the most relevant atomic links.

The model was checked on melts of polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyvinyl chloride. It predicted the forces with high accuracy and held up on new structures. A fast surrogate lets researchers run melt simulations at sizes and lengths that the exact method cannot reach, which serves plastics design and recycling research.
arxiv-2503-16849:
Longsen Gao and co-authors design a controller that can safely free a stuck solar panel on a space station. Their 2025 paper treats the task as a robot arm job in orbit. The jammed panel sits on a hinge whose traits change over time, and the station must not be harmed.

Their method learns the hinge's traits on the fly, within safe bounds, while it plans each move. The cost it weighs blends two drives: probing the system to shrink doubt, and acting well once the traits are known. The team tests the plan in computer runs of the freeing task and in lab trials, both in free fall and on the ground. It beats rival schemes on how well it learns the traits and how well it steers.
arxiv-2503-17049:
Giulia Cavalleri and Alain Miranville study best control of a brain tumor growth model that joins lactate use, spring like tissue traits, and tissue harm. Control here means picking drug doses that steer the tumor best. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The model links a spread equation for tumor cell density with one for lactate, a force balance for tissue shift, and a rule for harm growth. Two controls stand for chemo and a lactate targeted drug. The authors set a cost score for care, prove that best controls exist, and show how the state shifts when controls shift. They end with a first order rule that any best care plan must meet.
arxiv-2503-17149:
Guchuan Li, Sarah Petersen, and Elizabeth Tatum lift a classic splitting result, in a 2025 preprint, into the equivariant world of stable homotopy theory. In the nineteen eighties, Mahowald and Kane broke a certain product of spectra into simpler pieces. That split powered much progress on the stable homotopy groups of spheres. The present paper works with the real form of connective K-theory, which carries an action of a two-element group. The authors build the matching split for the cooperations algebra at the level of spectra, not just algebra.

They describe the split pieces as equivariant Adams covers. A parallel split for ordinary cohomology with its equivariant upgrade is recorded too. Along the way they compute the full operations and cooperations algebras for both theories. Such computations are the raw fuel for spectral sequence work. Specialists gain a sharper tool for periodic phenomena in equivariant homotopy.
arxiv-2503-17349:
Jianing Qi, Jiawei Liu, Hao Tang, and Zhigang Zhu present a 2025 paper on a weak spot in models that join vision and language. Such models name and describe objects well, but often reason poorly about where things sit in space. The authors ask why, since the models do carry data about token order and image layout.

Their checks found an imbalance: image tokens carry much larger values than text tokens, which drowns out the model's sense of order. Three new tools measure how much a model leans on order and how attention splits across inputs. Targeted fixes based on the checks restored order sense as predicted. The work shows how probing a model can guide sound repairs.
arxiv-2503-17549:
