Andrzej Rostworowski goes back to a classic numerical relativity test: whether ripples in empty spacetime can focus and collapse into a black hole. The result from the early 1990s by Abrahams and Evans has led to decades of attempts to verify it. The threshold behavior is a trap for numeric work. The work reports first steps toward a check of his own.

Rostworowski sets up Einstein's equations for a vacuum, axisymmetric spacetime with vanishing twist in spherical-polar coordinates. A linear version of the system is derived alongside the full one. The author finds concrete blocks to stable evolution exactly at the collapse threshold, where the key physics lives. The work is openly a first step, aimed at a setup that can survive the critical regime.
arxiv-2503-17849:
Masroor Bashir and co-authors scan a mass map of the sky for spots that break the mold in a 2025 paper. The map, from a high dry scope, bends light from the dawn glow to weigh all stuff in its path.

Shape counts of three kinds were read patch by patch and set by side of mock maps from the reign law. A stitched score asked if a flaw stays firm across cuts and grain grades. The whole sky and each half read clean by that score. Small patches told a mixed tale: a few read off, most near a famed cold spot of the dawn glow. No patch was shared with a past space map's flaws, which pins those on noise. The authors urge a fresh look with deep field reads.
arxiv-2503-18049:
Matthäus Schulik and co-authors model how moons of young giant planets can lose their air. Their 2025 paper deals with satellites heated above their normal temperature by light from the planet. Low gravity makes such moons prone to heavy loss of gas into space.

The team finds that some gases, such as ammonia and methane, can form layers that trap heat under planet light. Those hot profiles drive escape at rates well above simple model estimates. A moon can lose most of its air this way unless its interior cools fast. Escape rates also rank by gas type, since upper layers decouple by heat. The result helps explain why some moons may be bare while others keep thick air.
arxiv-2503-18449: Oscar Kivinen, Alexei Oblomkov, and Dimitri Wyss present a 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry, on invariants of a plane curve singularity. Using motivic integration over symmetric powers of a deformed curve, they study two kinds of discriminant integrals. One recovers the motivic classes of the principal Hilbert schemes of points on the curve. The other gives the plethystic exponential of the motivic Igusa zeta function, a result that also holds in higher dimensions. Combined with work of Gorsky and Némethi, the integrals gain an interpretation through knot Floer homology.
arxiv-2503-18549:
Xiaolong Yin and co-authors build a training ground for AI that designs 3D parts step by step, in a 2025 paper. CAD models are built from sketches plus steps like pushing, spinning, and cutting shapes. Past methods covered sketches and simple steps, but not spinning. That left many real shapes out of reach.

Their gym sits on a real CAD engine. An agent proposes one command at a time. The gym builds the shape so far and feeds it back to the agent. Rewards reflect how close the shape is to the target. Training in the loop lets the agent learn long command chains. Support for the spin step widens the range of parts the agent can design.
arxiv-2503-18649:
Jin and Zhou build in 2025 a Ginzburg-Landau theory for triple Q magnetic orders on hexagonal lattices. The head title frames the work as a phenomenological theory of these states. Models with two and three spin components are covered through symmetry allowed terms in the free energy.

Full phase diagrams emerge from competing interaction parameters. Single, double, and triple Q states each carry their own symmetry breaking patterns and collective excitations. Real materials such as a sodium cobalt telluride show the same interplay of frustration and multiple ordering vectors. The frame links microscopic couplings to observable traits, a tool for predicting new phases in frustrated magnets.
arxiv-2503-18749:
Continued fractions of power series over finite fields behave in ways number theorists are still mapping. Erez Nesharim, Uri Shapira, and Noy Soffer Aranov study what happens to probability measures built from shifts of a quadratic Laurent series, as they move on a space of lattices. Earlier work showed some of the mass escapes to infinity, and a conjecture predicted all of it would.

The authors disprove the conjecture using one concrete case: the series over the two-element field whose coefficients follow the Thue-Morse sequence, a famous self-similar pattern. Their proof rests on explicit symmetries they found in its number wall, a combinatorial picture of the series. The paper appears in 2025.
arxiv-2503-18849:
Ivan Chuprov and co-authors use in 2025 physics informed neural networks to backtrack a pollution plume to its source. The math runs advection and diffusion in reverse: from where contamination is measured, infer where it leaked. Such inverse problems are touchy, and the weather refuses to sit still, with weak and strong winds and sometimes several sources at once.

Their networks learn with the governing equations written into the training, so guesses must respect how pollutants actually spread. Many architectures and settings were compared, and accuracy hinged sharply on those choices, a dependence the authors map into concrete recommendations. Tests included real world data with realistic atmospheric variability. Source locations came out with high accuracy across the scenarios tried. The authors present tuned physics informed networks as a stable tool for environmental monitoring, where finding the leak fast decides how much land and water can still be saved.
arxiv-2503-19549:
Zubair Shaban, Nazreen Shah, and Ranjitha Prasad tackle, in a 2025 paper, the messy reality of training AI models across many phones and sensors at once. In federated learning, devices train locally and send updates to a server, keeping raw data private. Sending updates over the air, all at once, is fast. But real wireless channels add noise, signals fade, and devices differ in data and stamina, which can wreck convergence.

Their framework, RoCo-FL, builds the mess into the math. Local updates are treated as deliberately inexact, within structured limits that act like a stabilizer. The team proves the method still converges for the hard, non-convex objectives used in practice. On three image and handwriting datasets, it beat rival methods in accuracy and stability, especially when slow stragglers joined. The authors frame noise-proof design as a condition for real-world deployment.
arxiv-2503-19749:
Pavan Uttarkar and co-authors hunted for a polarization effect in one-off fast radio bursts, in a 2025 paper. Fast radio bursts are bright, brief flashes from deep space whose source is still debated. Some repeating bursts lose their polarization as their waves cross a messy magnetic cloud near the source. That loss can map the cloud. One-off bursts are harder to check because most telescopes catch them in a narrow band.

The team searched twelve one-off bursts caught by the ASKAP array in Australia. One burst showed strong loss of polarization, the first firm case for a one-off burst from this array. A second showed a hint of the same effect. They also checked that the strong case had no steady radio glow beside it. The pattern fits a shared origin for repeating and one-off bursts, with one-off sources the older kin.
arxiv-2503-19849:
Anthony Sulak and Olga Turanova study a math model of tissue growing in a setting where the food and space vary from place to place. Their 2025 paper uses a porous-medium equation, where the tissue spreads like a fluid through a sponge. As the model's pressure law steepens, the tissue should act more like a packed, unsqueezable mass.

The authors prove that, in that stiff limit, the model's answers settle onto those of a free-boundary problem of Hele-Shaw type. In such a problem a sharp edge splits the grown tissue from the empty space. To pass to the limit they first pin down bounds: one on the slope of the pressure, and one of a classic form that caps how fast pressure can fall.
arxiv-2503-19949:
Zuev, Salmagambetova, Djakov, and Utkin review automated analysis of video-EEG in epilepsy in a 2025 paper. Epilepsy is often diagnosed with EEG and long video-EEG monitoring. Reading these recordings by hand takes a great deal of time.

The review covers recent machine learning tools for finding and predicting seizures from EEG and video. It notes barriers such as varied seizure signs, unclear labels, and few shared multimodal data sets. The authors also propose a new pipeline that uses concept-based learning to estimate treatment effects from video-EEG data. They frame it as a path for future work.
arxiv-2503-20049:
Gabriel Bo, Justin Gu, and Christopher Sun present a 2025 project paper on reading disease signs from blood cell genes. Blood diseases arise across a family tree of cells, from stem-like progenitors down to mature types. The team asked whether a model trained on progenitors could capture signals that carry through the whole tree.

An autoencoder compressed over twenty thousand gene measures from progenitor cells into a compact code. That code held enough signal to classify disease states in both progenitors and their mature descendants. Three classifier designs were tested on the codes, topping ninety-five percent accuracy on multi-class tasks. A zero-shot test, applying the progenitor model to mature cells unseen in training, also scored well.
arxiv-2503-20149:
Estimating a treatment's true effect is hard when hundreds of instruments and controls crowd the data. Xiduo Chen and co-authors proposed in 2025 a ridge-based instrumental variables method built for exactly that high-dimensional tangle.

Their two-step design first splits the data and runs a ridge regression, then projects with a ridge-style matrix before a simple final regression. The scheme removes estimation bias whether or not the true model is sparse. They prove consistency and normal limiting behavior, and supply a matching variance estimate for practical testing. Simulations show the method beating sparsity-based rivals, and an application revisits schooling's effect on earnings.
arxiv-2503-20249:
Local projections are a popular way to trace how an economy responds over time to a shock. Masahiro Tanaka tackles a weakness of Bayesian versions of the method in this 2025 paper: they lack a true likelihood, so stand-in versions can give poorly calibrated beliefs. His fix builds a quasi-likelihood from a moment-based criterion, in the style of Laplace-type estimators.

The method avoids strict assumptions about the data's distribution while keeping inferences well calibrated. It also yields credible bands that hold across all horizons at once, which matters when the whole response path is the object of interest. The same frame extends naturally to instrumental variable settings, where shocks are isolated with outside instruments. Computer simulations back the approach.
arxiv-2503-20449:
Laura Gardini and co-authors analyze jagged one-dimensional maps whose pieces are straight lines sharing one fixed point. Their paper appeared in 2025. Such piecewise maps appear in economics, engineering, and ecology. The team shows their motion can be read through the well-known piecewise linear circle map. Away from the shared fixed point, bounded behavior narrows to two options: stiff cycles that are not hyperbolic, or quasiperiodic orbits that densely fill line segments, and both can coexist.

A financial market model illustrates the theory. Its price paths look chaotic at a glance, with irregular swings that suggest randomness. The analysis proves they are quasiperiodic instead, following a hidden regular order. The authors say the distinction matters before anyone labels market motion as chaos.
arxiv-2503-20949:
Bjorn Larsen and co-authors present a fast way to build joint pulsar timing data sets, in a 2025 paper. Pulsar timing arrays watch spinning neutron stars for the faint stretch of nanohertz gravitational waves. Combining decades of data from many telescopes takes years, which shuts out fresh observations. Their Lite method picks the best available data set for each pulsar by a figure of merit, instead of waiting for a full merge.

Tested on the second international data release, the Lite version still detected the shared red noise signal. Its strength estimate ran a bit high, likely from single-pulsar systematics. The full data set remained better at resolving the telltale correlation pattern between pulsars. A halfway subset taken early in merging matched the full set surprisingly well. The authors offer Lite as a route to quick, preliminary wave limits.
arxiv-2503-21149:
When light drives a material in a repeating cycle, it can push charge and spin currents in new ways. Naoya Arakawa and Kenji Yonemitsu established in 2025 which symmetry rules those currents must obey, extending a classic set of rules called the Onsager reciprocal relations. They focus on sideways currents in a steady state created by a pump light field, for round, linear, and two-color light.

The sideways charge and spin conductivities obey the reciprocal relations in all cases studied, but the dominant terms depend on the light's polarization. Computer calculations backed the arguments. One caution follows: the charge signal cannot always be read as the classic anomalous Hall effect, while the spin signal can be read as a spin Hall effect.
arxiv-2503-21249:
Yufei Bo and Meixia Tao design a joint code for sending matched images from two senders over wireless links, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each sender holds one of a pair of linked images, such as two views of one scene. Each codes and sends its own image, and the receiver rebuilds both.

Older learned methods pick up the link between the images only by feel from data. The new design states the link in plain math through a shared chance model of the coded forms. That model sets how many symbols each sender may spend. At the receiver, each rebuilt image helps restore the other, and a shift block lines the codes up for best use of their link. One loss trains the whole chain, and tests show crisper rebuilds for the bits spent.
arxiv-2503-21749:
Shitian Zhao and a team of co-authors build a suite for text in images in twenty twenty-five. Image generators often garble the words they are asked to render. Prompt richness and rendering fidelity pull against each other. Their suite, LeX-Art, attacks the problem from the data side.

A synthesis pipeline built on Deepseek-R1 curates a data set of ten thousand images. Each is high-resolution, refined for aesthetics, and rich in rendered text. A prompt enrichment model, LeX-Enhancer, strengthens weak prompts. Two text-to-image models trained on the data reach state-of-the-art text rendering. A new benchmark, LeX-Bench, grades fidelity, aesthetics, and alignment. A new metric measures text accuracy more robustly than edit distance alone.
arxiv-2503-21849:
Zsofia Talyigas, Francesco Paparella, Bastien Mallein, and Emmanuel Schertzer ask whether evolution selects the fittest or merely the luckiest in a 2025 mathematical biology study. Selection judges phenotypes, the traits an organism shows, and chance events blur the link between a good genotype and reproductive success. The authors model that blur and its long-run consequences.

Their analysis shows a Goodhart-like effect emerging inside evolution itself: once a trait becomes the target of selection, luck in expressing it can swamp the underlying quality. The result reframes how biologists should read adaptation, since winners may owe their place partly to fortune.
arxiv-2503-22449:
Ahmad Biniaz and five co-authors bound how many points a region must hold before it contains small sets of every color, in a paper from 2025. Coloring tuples of points rather than single points is a fresh twist on classic polychromatic problems. Hypergraphs supply the general language.

For points in the plane with disks as regions, pairs can be colored so any disk with at least about 3.7 to the power k points holds pairs of all k colors. For abstract hypergraphs of bounded complexity, similar exponential bounds hold. They also prove deep tuples exist inside big hypergraphs and relate tuple coloring thresholds to ordinary vertex coloring ones.
arxiv-2503-22549:
Anja Beck, Michele Atzeni, and Eluned Smith extract decay amplitudes from B meson data without a fixed model. Such decays, nicknamed electroweak penguins, can hint at new physics. Amplitudes vary with the masses of the decay products in a smooth way. Past fits forced those shapes into set forms, which can bias the hunt.

Their trick rewrites the angular decay rate so a sPlot method can run on the angles. Weight functions then pull out each wave's size as a smooth curve. Fake data with both S and P waves check the method's power. The curves come out unbiased and can face theory head-on. Hadron shape factors, above all in the S wave, stand to gain.
arxiv-2503-22749:
Kanishka Ranaweera and co-authors add adaptive clipping to private few-shot learning to protect its accuracy. Their 2025 paper works where two scarcities meet: few labeled examples, and a formal privacy guarantee that usually costs model quality. Clipping, which caps how much any one example can sway training, is where much of that cost is decided.

Their method adjusts the clipping threshold as training proceeds instead of fixing it once. It fits several private meta-learning algorithms that learn how to learn from small data. Dynamic control limits how much sensitive information leaks while curbing overfitting on tiny sets. Tests show better generalization under the same privacy promise. Privacy tools that forget less could serve medicine and other fields where data are both scarce and sensitive.
arxiv-2503-22849:
Alberto Padoan and Jeremy Coulson define distances between linear system behaviors over finite time spans. Behavioral theory describes systems by their allowed signal sets. Comparing such sets across different sizes needs care.

Their distances ignore coordinate choices, rotations, and reorderings. Models of unlike dimensions can still be compared fairly. The measures blend model complexity with fit in one principled scale. That blend solves a long-standing puzzle in the theory. Modeling becomes a search for the closest unfalsified model. Their best model class is named and characterized fully. A time series anomaly task shows the metrics at work. Finer resolution beat older distances on that task.
arxiv-2503-23149:
Chenglong Ma and co-authors set a new task for medical AI: imagine how a chest scan would look if a disease progressed, and explain the change in words. Silent image predictions leave doctors unable to check the reasoning. Their dataset pairs repeat scans with what-if prompts and written interpretations of the expected changes.

Their model, ProgEmu, generates the future image and its explanation in one autoregressive stream. It beat rivals at matching the stated progression. The authors see uses in decision support and in training clinicians to foresee disease courses.
arxiv-2503-23549:
Van Higgs and Doug Pickrell wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five on a round version of a classic quantum system. The classic system is the harmonic oscillator, a particle held by a spring-like pull. In flat space it splits into separate one-way motions and can be solved with standard raising and lowering tools.

The spherical version does not split that way, which makes it harder. The two-dimensional case turns out to be the critical one. For it, the authors compute the full set of energy levels and a key counting function called the partition function. They note the system may matter for chiral models in two-dimensional field theory.
arxiv-2503-23849:
Jiachen Jiang and ten co-authors study X-ray spectra of a fast-feeding class of active galaxies beyond the local universe, in a paper from 2025. These galaxies host small black holes feeding near their limit. Almost all prior X-ray work covered only nearby cases, unlike other galaxy classes studied far away.

They analyze fourteen such galaxies at moderate distance from a new all-sky X-ray catalog, matched to optical survey data. Their X-ray brightness fits the expected link to ultraviolet light. Most spectra are very steep, and one hints at strong soft excess emission. Matching feeding rates to optical values needs a large correction whose standard basis may not hold here.
arxiv-2503-24349:
Shafin, Rabbi, Hasan, and Zibran studied release speed and security in the Maven software ecosystem in twenty twenty-five. Modern apps rest on chains of libraries, and how often each library releases shapes both freshness and risk. The team traced ten thousand Maven artifacts across more than two hundred thousand releases and one point seven million dependencies.

Faster-releasing artifacts spent far less time outdated. They also carried fewer known vulnerabilities, the CVEs tracked in security databases, in their dependency chains. The link was a strong negative correlation in both cases. The authors argue that quicker release cycles are a practical security strategy, not just a convenience. Their findings speak to developers, maintainers, and the people who run shared software ecosystems.
arxiv-2504-00249:
Five researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on neural networks that solve physics problems and can adapt to new conditions. Standard physics-informed networks learn one solution for one set of boundary conditions, so a change at the edge forces retraining. The authors want a network that, once trained, answers for any boundary setup.

Their network learns the shape of a wave decomposition rather than one fixed solution. Training uses a spread of randomly chosen boundary conditions. On a test system of two linked oscillators, the trained network predicted solutions for new conditions correctly. The trick cuts the ratio between training effort and later use.
arxiv-2504-00349:
Thomas Bailie and co-authors add a memory buffer to layered graph networks for forecasting in a 2025 paper. Such networks read time series at several scales, fine for weather maps, but moving information between scales loses detail. Their model, HiGFlow, stores what each scale has seen in a flexible memory.

Theory shows the memory keeps new feature maps from over-smoothing and sharpens the network's pattern tests. In benchmarks the model beat strong rivals, including transformer systems, cutting average forecast error by about six percent on two standard measures. Code is public. The work targets forecasting tasks where coarse and fine patterns both matter, from weather to traffic.
arxiv-2504-00649:
Rui-Hao Bi, Wei Liu, and Wenjie Dou present a universal way to compute moments of correlation functions for exact quantum dynamics in open systems. Their 2025 paper extends recent work on memory kernel coupling theory.

Their method works for arbitrary system-bath coupling that can be written as a polynomial in the bath coordinate. They show that recursive commutators of a system operator obey a universal hierarchy. With that structure, higher-order moments come from evaluating system and bath expectations apart. Bath values come from derivatives of a generating function. They apply the method to the dipole autocorrelation function for the spin-boson model, with linear and quadratic coupling.
arxiv-2504-00749:
Machado and co-authors studied in 2025 what happens to quantum vortices when the interactions inside a spinning superfluid suddenly change. Their system is a two-dimensional rotating Bose-Einstein condensate, modeled with an exact many-body method. By tuning interaction strength against rotation speed, they prepared states with one or several vortices. Then came the quench: an abrupt jump in interaction.

Single vortices broke apart and then fully revived, reassembling their starting pattern. Pairs and triples showed near-revivals, echoing the original state without perfect return. Many-vortex systems tipped into chaotic many-body motion. Between sat a regime of distorted vortices and fragmented density clouds. The authors call the revival pattern a universal response to such quenches. Results like these guide cold-atom experiments that simulate quantum fluids.
arxiv-2504-00849:
Sunjung Kang, Vishrant Tripathi, and Christopher Brinton study remote tracking systems in a 2025 paper. Such systems must keep a live view fresh while also rebuilding past paths accurately later. Freshness alone, measured by the age of information, misses that second goal. With a finite buffer, a system must choose which packets to keep or drop.

They compare three policies: keep old, keep fresh, and their own policy that drops packets based on gaps between arrivals. Keeping the freshest data minimizes age but not rebuilding error. Their policy adjusts retention using generation times and balances both goals. Analysis and simulation of queue behavior back the comparison.
arxiv-2504-00949:
Bernat Capdevila and four colleagues present a model-independent way to analyze a rare B meson decay without binning the data. The four-body decay's dynamics depend on two invariant masses, and standard analyses either bin in those masses or assume a model for the amplitudes. Their moments-based method extracts continuous observables unbinned in both variables.

The approach needs no statistical fit, avoiding bias and poor uncertainty estimates with small samples. The team gives Standard Model predictions for the unbinned observables and derives new geometrical bounds on their values. They study zero-crossing points of key observables as new physics contributions vary. The method can also test the amplitude models that experimental analyses rely on.
arxiv-2504-01449:
Zaipeng Duan, Xuzhong Hu, Pei An, and Jie Ma add image made virtual points to laser point clouds, in work from 2025. Laser scans grow sparse at range, which hides small and mid range objects from scene parsers. Photos can spawn dense virtual points, but those points bring noise and heavy compute load.

A filter keeps only useful fake points by density and distance to real points. A robust encoder then reads image space to cut noise weight in features. Fine steps boost sparse shape traits through local point and voxel grouping. Tests on two large driving sets lifted scene scores with few added points. Gains centred on mid range targets that laser alone reads poorly.
arxiv-2504-01649:
Nuno Crokidakis models a siege with differential equations in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Siege of Syracuse, from two hundred fourteen to two hundred twelve BC, ended with Rome taking the city despite strong defenses and Archimedes' war machines. The model tracks how fast Syracuse's stores drained, how its people fell, and how long the Roman army held out. Strategy and supply enter as settings that steer how these amounts change.

The study finds a sharp line for how strong Syracuse's defenses had to be. Above it, the city holds off the attack in the model; below it, collapse comes. Since history records the fall, the author holds that the defense strength sat below that line. Tests vary siege length, supply limits, and defense strength to show which points mattered. It shows math modeling can shape claims about old battles, not just retell them.
arxiv-2504-01749:
A team including Niklas Hansen and Jakub Copak reports a method for placing nanodiamonds with DNA origami in a 2025 paper. Color centers in nanodiamonds are useful for quantum sensing and information work. Their use has been held back by hard placement and coupling problems.

The authors attach DNA to nanodiamonds in a stable way, then assemble them with gold nanoparticles on DNA origami. By setting the gap between particles, they tune how the diamond centers emit light. At short gaps, the fastest decay path rose about tenfold. The work points to plasmon-driven effects that can shape emission for quantum photonic and sensing uses.
arxiv-2504-01849:
Rohin Shah and a large team of co-authors set out a technical plan for keeping future general-purpose AI safe and secure. Their paper appeared in 2025. They sort the risks into misuse, misalignment, mistakes, and structural harms, then focus on the first two, where engineering can bite. For misuse, the plan is to spot dangerous capabilities early and wall them off with security, access limits, monitoring, and built-in safeguards.

For misalignment, they propose two lines of defense. The first builds an aligned model through stronger oversight and robust training. The second assumes failure and contains harm through system-level monitoring and access control. Interpretability and uncertainty tools feed both. The authors frame the approach as defense in depth for systems whose power is still growing.
arxiv-2504-01949:
Tristan Fauvel and four co-authors compare Bayesian methods for borrowing treatment effects across trials, in a simulation study from 2025. When a new trial cannot recruit enough patients, borrowing results from related studies can help. Borrowing whole treatment effects, not just control data, is less understood, so the team simulated six trial settings with varied endpoints.

They varied trial size and how far the borrowed effect drifted from the truth. At matched error rates, power gains over a plain analysis were usually small, and some adaptive methods lost more. Borrowing cut estimation error when effects agreed but hurt coverage as drift grew. Matched prior designs balanced gains and robustness best.
arxiv-2504-02049:
Robots, drones, and smart sensors must coordinate without a central boss, and Tyler Hanks and co-authors give that coordination one mathematical language in a 2025 paper. Their language is the cellular sheaf, a structure that decorates a network graph with data spaces and translation rules between neighbors.

On top of it they define a standard form, the nonlinear homological program: a sheaf, energy functions on the links, and convex goals at each node. Consensus, formation keeping, and flocking, usually three separate crafts, all fit the form, even mixed in one heterogeneous team. A distributed algorithm built from the alternating direction method of multipliers solves the programs locally, node by node. Simulations show the machinery working. The pitch is unification: many coordination problems, one solver.
arxiv-2504-02249:
Sungwoo Kang studies stock price prediction in Korean markets in this 2025 paper, based on the head byline. Most past work leans on crafted technical indicators drawn from price data. Kang asks whether a deep model fed only raw price and volume data can do as well.

Data covered Korean stocks from 2006 to 2024. Labels were built with a triple barrier method, marking whether price first hit an upper, lower, or time limit. With tuned settings, a recurrent network matched the performance of a strong classic model that used indicators. Using the full price and volume record beat using closing price alone. Window and model size interacted, with one pairing giving the best results.
arxiv-2504-02449:
Sergey Shpectorov and Tianxiao Zhao close a decades-old question in graph theory by proving a certain graph cannot exist. Strongly regular graphs are networks where every counting rule about neighbors comes out constant. One long-unresolved parameter set describes a graph on eighty-five vertices where each vertex has fourteen neighbors, with three shared neighbors for adjacent pairs and two for non-adjacent pairs.

The authors first use the catalogue of small cubic graphs to restrict what the neighborhood of any vertex could look like. Then they list every possible neighborhood around a largest three-clique and test each against the counting rules and against geometric embedding conditions. Every case ends in contradiction. The empty result matters because feasible parameter sets that no graph realizes are as informative as new graphs: they mark the true borders of the theory.
arxiv-2504-02649:
Mahmoud Khabou, Edward Cohen, and Almut Veraart wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a model for counts that repeat in time with a seasonal beat, where past counts can sway the present across a web of linked series.

The model is a Poisson autoregression with many series, a seasonal cycle, and memory that may stretch far back. The authors prove the process settles into a steady seasonal state, and bound how fast it gets there. They then give a fast Markov stand-in and prove its fitted values hold up as data grows. A test on weekly rotavirus case counts in Berlin beats the prior PNAR model at forecasting.
arxiv-2504-02749:
Sohaib Alam, Jun Zen, and Thomas Scruby find a fault-tolerant measurement schedule for the Bacon-Shor quantum error-correcting code through a coloring game, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The schedule has period four and covers spacetime with constant-weight detectors.

Earlier approaches leaned on code concatenation to reach a noise threshold. Here the schedule emerges as the solution to a coloring game played on a square grid. Under a uniform circuit-level noise model, simulations show a threshold near zero point three percent when decoding with minimum weight perfect matching. The authors conjecture a decoder tailored to the scheme could push the threshold higher, making the code more practical.
arxiv-2504-03149:
Ruben Otxoa and co-authors lay spin bits on a six side grid with spin free fat dots as the links, in a paper from 2025. Spin bits in chip stone hold their state long and build with stock chip craft, a strong base for scale. Fat dots with no spin take volt calls and pass grip twixt bits at speed.

The team runs a known fault code on the grid in sim. Gate flaw gates sit at a set line past which the code wins. At near pure gates, each mind bit costs a few thousand flesh bits and a chip of palm size could host ten thousand mind bits. Counts make the grid a scale path.
arxiv-2504-03449:
Michele Botti and Lorenzo Mascotto prove a family of inequalities for functions that jump between mesh cells in a 2025 paper. Modern simulation methods chop a domain into many-sided cells and let the solution behave separately in each. Analysis of such methods needs Sobolev-Poincare inequalities: bounds that tie a function's size to its slope, cell by cell, over very general meshes.

Their result covers shape-regular meshes of polygons and polyhedra in any dimension, including plain triangles and grids as special cases. The constants in the bounds depend openly on the geometry, so users can see the price of a bad mesh. Key tools are new trace inequalities and stable ways to undo the divergence operator under mixed boundary conditions. The estimates serve error analysis for nonconforming methods on nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2504-03549:
Kumar and Rajesh analyse in twenty twenty-five the splash thrown off when energy hits the edge of a one-dimensional uneven gas. The gas thins out with distance by a power rule, and the blast sits at its border with empty space. Energy input flings fast spatters into the vacuum, and the gas left behind loses energy by a power law over time.

The pair solved the flow equations exactly with a self-similar method, finding the decay exponent for each thinning rate. Computer simulations of colliding particles matched the exact answers. Knowing the exponents also fixed how density, speed, and temperature evolve in space and time. The work gives a clean benchmark for blast physics in graded media.
arxiv-2504-03749:
Jeremy Morlier, Mathieu Leonardon, and Vincent Gripon tested a plain trick in 2025 to shrink vision models: feed them smaller images. Most ways to lighten a model cut its parts, round its numbers, or distill it into a small twin. Input size had been little explored as a shrink tool. The team cut image size step by step and watched the effect on two tasks, sorting and scene labeling, and on two model families.

On standard test sets, smaller inputs kept scores near the top while cutting memory and compute by a large share. The authors say the trick can sit beside the classic tools rather than swap them out. They frame it as a sound new path for teams that must run vision on tight gear.
arxiv-2504-03849:
Valerii Chuiko, Giovanni Da Rosa, and Paul Ayers predict molecule energies with deep learning, in two thousand twenty-five. Their input is not the molecule's shape, but its one- and two-electron integrals, a compact record of its electronic structure. The descriptor they build stays unchanged when the molecule moves, turns, or is reframed.

An attention-based network learns from that descriptor and keeps a key property: energy scales cleanly with system size. Training on small, few-electron systems can thus guide calls on larger ones. They test the method on hydrogen clusters, a hard case where electrons are strongly linked. Results beat geometry-based learning models on accuracy, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-04049:
Tian-Xiao He wrote a 2025 paper on multiple Riordan arrays, a class of number grids with set rules for their rows. The paper is the first in a planned sequence on this topic. Riordan arrays link to counting problems, and the multiple form extends the classic case to richer sets.

He describes the arrays by a lead sequence and a set of further sequences that fix their shape. The paper then defines a group built from these arrays, plus some of its subgroups. Shortened forms of the arrays are set out as well, along with a study of when those forms keep a trait called total positivity.
arxiv-2504-04149:
Wei and six colleagues build a light amplifier on a chip with a mirror designed by computer search in twenty twenty-five. The amplifier is a channel in lithium niobate glass, spiked with the metal erbium. Such amplifiers boost weak light signals in fiber networks. At the channel's end they placed a tiny mirror shaped by an inverse design search.

The mirror bounced light back through the channel for a second pass of gain. Net gain rose by a large margin over a twin device with no mirror. The design also removed the need to pump light in from both ends. The team says the trick can pack stronger amplifiers into dense photonic chips.
arxiv-2504-04649:
Jingtao Lin and Jingtao Shi prove a maximum principle for a hard control problem in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A decision maker steers a system tracked only through noisy observations, while caring about risk. Random jumps, tangled forward-backward dynamics, and non-round control sets make the problem thorny.

The team first recasts it as a full-information problem with a special generator. New variation techniques handle the way costs blow up with risk. The result is a global principle that any optimal control must obey. They apply it to risk-sensitive investing under a factor model. A filtering chapter derives a corrected equation for tracking the hidden state amid jumps and linked noise.
arxiv-2504-04849:
Speech is movement: the tongue and lips trace fast, complex paths that map onto the sounds of language. Sam Kirkham, a solo author, set out in 2025 to discover the motion laws behind those gestures from data. A sparse equation-finding method searched recordings of tongue and lip movement for simple formulas that fit.

A basic spring-like model, of second order, fit most gestures well. About a third of cases, though, needed a nonlinear force to match the data. That split supports the idea that a self-running nonlinear equation governs how speech organs move. Kirkham closes by mapping what data-driven discovery still cannot do, and where it may next find the rules behind language and behavior.
arxiv-2504-04949:
Linwei Zhai and co-authors build L3AC, a light neural codec that squeezes audio with a single quantizer, in a paper from 2025. Neural codecs turn sound into compact codes that generative models can use. Leading designs lean on heavy networks and stacks of quantizers, which limits their use on small devices.

L3AC pairs one quantizer with lean folded networks and small transformer blocks. A new block, TConv, tracks sound changes at several time scales at once. In tests across many data sets, the codec matched or beat top rivals at rebuilding sound. It did so with about a tenth of the compute cost. The single-code design also makes it easy to reuse in later tasks.
arxiv-2504-05249:
Wenzhao Tang and co-authors present Texture2LoD3, a 2025 method that rebuilds detailed building models from street panoramas. City models at the finest detail level need watertight shapes, tagged facades, and few polygons. Hand building them is slow, and plain photo meshes break those rules.

Their trick leans on the rough building models cities already have. Each flat face of a rough model becomes a target for flattening the matching panorama view. Running segmentation on those flat, true-scale textures keeps the model's clean geometry while adding facade detail. On their new ReLoD3 test set, facade segmentation accuracy rose by 11 percent. The pipeline could spread detailed city models widely, aiding solar estimates and driving simulators alike.
arxiv-2504-05349:
Eugen Barbulescu, Antonio Alexoaie, and Lucian Busoniu present a 2025 computing paper on pruning neural networks. Pruning cuts weights to make a network faster and lighter at run time. Most methods chase scores on benchmarks and leave the pruning process itself poorly understood.

Their method, Hyperflux, treats pruning as a system that evolves in a continuous way. Two forces drive it: flux, the response of the loss gradient when a weight is removed, and pressure, a global push toward cutting weights. That model makes behavior readable at both the single-weight and whole-network levels. A new pressure schedule targets a chosen sparsity with care. Tests on standard image sets with several known networks gave competitive results.
arxiv-2504-05749:
Zoltán György, András Pályi, and Gábor Széchenyi probe the limits of a maths tool for spin qubits in a 2025 paper. Spin qubits store information in the spin of a single electron or hole in a semiconductor chip. The g-tensor method predicts how gate voltages drive such a qubit, but it had only been tested on the simplest driving setups.

The team checks three harder cases, with one or two gates and with one or two driving tones. In two of the cases, the method still works, and they give formulas for the drive speed and a known frequency shift. In the third case, two gates with two tones, the method breaks down. Three extra parameters are needed there, as their worked example of a round quantum dot shows.
arxiv-2504-05949:
Haripada Roy, writing alone in a 2025 paper, proves a sharp form of Hardy's inequality for a half-space inside the Heisenberg group. Hardy inequalities bound a weighted average of a function by a measure of how much it varies, and sharp forms name the best possible constant. The Heisenberg group is a curved space that models certain kinds of motion and vision problems.

Roy's version holds with no limits on its parameters, widening a joint earlier result that needed such limits. Here the variation term is taken over the whole space rather than just the half-space. The best constant is worked out for the main range of cases, closing a gap in the theory.
arxiv-2504-06349:
Lorenzo Bertassi and co-authors propose a new test for pairs of giant black holes in a 2025 paper. Two such black holes bound close together should make their shared gas glow in shifting ways. Orbital motion boosts the light aimed at us, like a lighthouse beam sweeping past. The surrounding gas then re-emits that light in broad spectral lines.

The team model how a disc of this gas answers the sweeping beam. The blue and red sides of the lines answer half an orbit out of step with each other. A single black hole with pulsing brightness cannot mimic that pattern. The lag split offers a fresh signature for hunting true black hole pairs in survey data.
arxiv-2504-06749:
Mélina Poulain and ten co-authors report the first direct sighting of star clusters merging at the heart of dwarf galaxies. Their 2025 paper uses sharp Hubble images of five dwarf galaxies whose centers look complex, with several nuclei and tidal tails. Dense nuclear star clusters sit at the centers of most galaxies, and two rival stories explain their birth: local star birth from gas, or clusters that drift in and merge.

Simulations of moving clusters reproduced the odd centers well, backing the drift-and-merge reading. The event is quick, under 100 million years, and rarely caught, which may explain why none had been seen before. Population studies say merging rules in dwarf galaxies while local birth rules in giants. Large sharp surveys could now map each step of the process.
arxiv-2504-06849:
Johannes Lang and co-authors present a faster way to simulate glassy systems that never settle, in a 2025 paper. When a glass is quenched, it ages: it keeps changing on time scales that grow with its own age. It never reaches a steady state. That endless drift makes the math costly, with effort growing as the cube of the time span.

Their method stores the system's response curves on a two-dimensional grid and fills gaps by smart interpolation. The cost then grows more slowly than the time span itself. They ran it on a classic spin glass model and reached times a thousand times longer than before. At those spans, a sharp change point showed up between glasses that forget their past well and those that do not. Oddly, the change traits vary with the setup rather than staying fixed.
arxiv-2504-06949:
Zhixuan Lin and co-authors prune wasted work inside a transformer that forgets, in a 2025 paper. The model type adds a forget gate to attention, and many heads forget so fast that they lean on nearby words only. Far links then cost computing time for near zero gain.

Their method drops those decayed links on the fly, with a threshold that proves the dropped weights are trivial. In training runs, attention cost fell by about seventy percent across model sizes. End to end training sped up as well, more so for long texts. Scores did not drop. Code is shared in public for teams that train such models.
arxiv-2504-07049:
Kristian Stølevik Olsen and co-authors show in 2025 how to harvest work from forces that never settle. Tiny noisy systems, like beads in optical traps, can be steered to extract work, and control theory cuts the cost. Yet the timing pattern of restless forces itself holds untapped value, the team argues.

They give exact formulas for the best steering protocol and its work yield for any driving force and duration. A general bound in the slow limit depends only on coarse, time-averaged traits of the force. The best protocols often act as information engines, measuring the start state to cash in on the force pattern. Examples include periodic driving and active matter.
arxiv-2504-07349:
Donglin Sui and Mohammad Deghat steer a drone to circle a target it cannot see directly in a 2025 paper. Bearing only measures give direction, not distance, to the hidden target. A new estimator pins the target spot within a preset time chosen in advance. A controller then guides the craft onto a ring around that spot.

Math proofs cover the full loop of estimation and control errors. The design skips explicit signal differentiation, which cuts noise gain. Simulations and real drone flights both back the claims. Set time convergence beats the usual wait and hope pattern. Search and watch missions gain a firm timing promise.
arxiv-2504-07849:
Francesca Dilisante, Pablo Valganon, David Soriano-Panos, and Jesus Gomez-Gardenes present 2025 work on infections picked up while people travel between places. Models of linked local groups tend to count spread that takes place inside each place alone. Spread during the trip itself, on shared transport, is left out of most such models.

The team extends a known movement model so that agents can catch the disease in transit as they move and return. Adding that route lowers the bar for an outbreak to take off by a marked amount. It also spreads the path of the outbreak across places, most of all in the early stage. Local control that looks sound on paper may thus fall short in fact.
arxiv-2504-07949:
Kefan Chen and co-authors build lifelike avatars whose hands can touch their faces, in work from 2025. Hands drive how a person acts and feels in a scene, yet most head and hand avatars skip the touch. That gap shows in calls, games, and virtual worlds, where a hand on a cheek should wrinkle skin and cast shade.

Their model, InteractAvatar, pairs a hand template with 3D Gaussian splats, soft blobs that render with photo flair. A tune step tracks pose-based shifts, such as folds and shade as joints bend. A touch module then shapes how hand and face press and slide. Tests on fresh views and on pose swaps, even across faces, held fine detail. The tool can play back new poses with the same touch feel.
arxiv-2504-08049:
Angelina Ibarra and Joshua Peeples adapt an anomaly hunting method for radar images that see through clouds and darkness. Synthetic aperture radar pictures look grainy and strange, so spotting the odd patch takes care. The base method, PaDiM, scores each patch by how far it sits from learned normal patterns, but that score has no ceiling.

Their variant swaps in the adaptive cosine estimator, which judges by angle instead of distance. Scores now live inside fixed bounds, making thresholds easier to set and compare. The pair test the change across several radar data sets, scoring hits at both whole-image and pixel level. Code is public.
arxiv-2504-08149:
Danielle Sullivan-Pao, Nicole Tian, and Pooya Khorrami present LoRAX, a system that learns to name which AI generator made an image, and keeps learning as new generators appear. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Attribution guards media trust by tracing synthetic pictures to their source model. Old models fade as new generators launch, and retraining from scratch is impractical.

LoRAX adds a tiny, cheap feature extractor for each new task. Each extractor is trained with a low-rank adapter, using a sliver of the base model's parameters. The extractors stack without erasing old skills. On a continual deepfake detection bench, LoRAX matched or beat top rivals in every setting. It did so with a fraction of the trainable parameters of full methods. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2504-08249:
Damola Ajeyemi and two colleagues speed up safety checks for systems run by barrier-function controllers, in a 2025 paper. Such controllers keep a system inside a safe set, but they can also cause odd behavior like runaway paths or false resting points.

Checking where the system can reach is a good audit, yet the controller solves an optimization at each step, which slows the math. The authors swap in a trained neural network that mimics the controller. A monotone embedding then bounds the network's outputs with standard tools. One run of the embedding yields a safe over-estimate of all reachable states. Closeness results tie the stand-in back to the true controller.
arxiv-2504-08349:
Victor Barroso-Nascimento, Ekaterina Piotrovskaya, and Elaine Pimentel work on the meaning of proofs in a logic of resources. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Linear logic is careful about how often each fact may be used, unlike standard logic. That care makes it useful for describing programs and processes.

Meaning in this logic is often given by sets of contexts or by spaces built from proofs. The authors take a third route based on proof theory itself. They extend a method that defines meaning through what can be proved from a base of facts. Past work had done this for a one-sided form of the logic. This paper carries it to the classical, two-sided form, for a large fragment of it.
arxiv-2504-08449:
Jian Wang, Rishabh Dabral, Diogo Luvizon, and co-authors present a framework for tracking human motion from wearable devices in this 2025 paper. Headsets, smart glasses, phones, and watches each give different signals, and those signals come and go. The goal is one system that captures and describes body motion from any mix of them.

Their method, called Ego4o, turns sensor readings, camera views from the wearer's side, and optional written motion notes into a shared code. A decoder then rebuilds the motion from that code. When no written notes exist, a large multi-modal model can draft them, and those drafts in turn sharpen the tracking. Tests showed the system holds up when inputs drop out and improves when more signals combine. The authors see it serving virtual and augmented reality, where body tracking must work on consumer gear.
arxiv-2504-08549:
Chong-Ye Chen and co-authors present a holographic study of spontaneous vectorization in a 2025 paper. The model extends scalarization ideas to vector fields in the space around an anti-de Sitter black brane.

A tachyonic instability, driven by the vector field effective mass, moves the system to a vectorized phase. That phase holds lower free energy past a critical temperature and coupling. A striking find is a screened volume law for entanglement entropy. Entropy scales with region size through a screened density set by a geometric surface outside the horizon. Entropy also moves non-monotonically with temperature. The work opens new entanglement patterns in holographic systems.
arxiv-2504-08649:
Charamaras and co-authors find vast sum sets in dense parts of swap groups. A swap group here is a count-able set where sums swap free. Two group traits frame the work: a thin twin set and a thin twin map. The team sets low bounds on how dense a part must be. Past that bound, the part holds a sum set of a set form. The form sums two picks from one vast set B in the group.

A shift t may lead the sum set in one of the two forms. Both group traits prove a must for the claims to hold. The team also marks which spread chains let the claim run. Their low bounds prove best in a strong sense in the work. No less dense part can dodge the sum set by their proof.
arxiv-2504-08849:
Mallika Mainali and Rosina Weber explore cognitive attributes in financial choices in two thousand twenty-five. Such traits shape how people take in facts, weigh options, and decide. AI that aims to think like humans must count these traits. Past alignment work stressed values and skipped the traits that set people apart.

The pair first survey the literature on these traits. They then set five rules for what counts as such a trait. Last they sort a set of traits tied to finance choices. The three parts form a base for AI that mirrors human choice. Finance is a high stakes test ground for that aim.
arxiv-2504-09049:
Adrianna Romanowski, Pedro Valois, and Kazuhiro Fukui test whether language models can spot the funny lines in stand-up comedy. They propose a humor detection metric with three scoring options: fuzzy string matching, sentence embedding similarity, and subspace similarity. Models received transcripts under various prompts and had to extract the humorous quotes.

Leading models, including ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, scored at most fifty-one percent regardless of prompt engineering. Human evaluators scored forty-one percent on the same task, so the models actually won. Agreement varied widely for both groups. The authors read the result as evidence of humor's subjectivity and the difficulty of mining punchlines from live performance transcripts.
arxiv-2504-09249:
Aniket Pal and co-authors built a test set in 2025 for how well AI can read and search handwritten study notes. Notes mix equations, sketches, and loose handwriting, which breaks tools built for printed pages. Their benchmark, NoTeS-Bank, gathers hard notes from many fields.

Two tasks anchor the set: answer questions with boxed proof from the notes, and first guess the field, then fetch the right page and answer. Scoring covers ranking quality, recall, box overlap, and answer match. Top vision-language models and search tools were run against the set, and their transcription and reasoning gaps showed plainly. The authors offer the benchmark as a stiff new yardstick for document AI. It pushes tools toward the messy notes students really keep.
arxiv-2504-09449:
Sorting a million data points into families is slow work for classic algorithms, and Trung Ha, Joonas Nattila, and Jordy Davelaar built a faster sorter in a 2025 paper. Their open-source package, aweSOM, trains self-organizing maps, grids that learn to fold data into clusters, on graphics processors as well as ordinary chips.

A second module stacks several runs of the map and merges their verdicts, so clusters rest on repeated evidence rather than one lucky layout. Against the older Python tools it descends from, the package ran ten to a hundred times faster and used far less memory. It scales toward a hundred million points with many features each. The authors pitch it at astronomers and other scientists whose datasets have outgrown the proof-of-concept tools the field started with.
arxiv-2504-09649:
Bruno Souza and co-authors add galaxy mergers to a universe model with a fractal spread of galaxies, in a 2025 paper. The base model is an uneven cosmos that starts with a shared big bang. Its galaxies sit in two stacked fractal patterns with set dimensions.

The authors let merger gain follow a decaying power law with distance in time. They solve the model for small merger rates and test which settings stay sound. Patterns drawn from recent surveys fit for a range of merger strengths and starting scales. The results show mergers can join such a cosmos without breaking it. The work speaks to critics of the standard smooth model.
arxiv-2504-09749:
Agnese Barbensi and co-authors search by computer for band links between low-crossing knots. The work dates to 2025. Bands join knots in ways that can keep or flip their twist sense. The team uses grid sketches to run the search at scale.

Their work sharpens a known table of band gaps a lot. They found two new gap-one pairs with fewer than seven crossings. One pair is a twist-flip match for a knot with seven crossings. In all they set thirty-three new gap-one pairs for knots up to eight crossings. An added note builds a proof for twist-flip bands in a whole knot family.
arxiv-2504-10049:
Théo Gigant, Camille Guinaudeau, and Frédéric Dufaux ask how best to feed a slideshow to an AI summarizer. Modern vision-language models can take text, images, mixed pages, or even the full video of a talk, and each choice changes cost and quality.

Through careful comparisons, they find that pulling the slides out of the video beats handing over the raw recording. The best results came from weaving slides and the speaker's transcript together in order, preserving the structure of the talk. They also map how to spend a fixed input budget wisely for text-heavy decks. The study closes with reflections on how the two channels interact and how models could handle such documents better.
arxiv-2504-10149:
Michal Danilowski, Soumyajit Chatterjee, and Abhirup Ghosh present a 2025 paper benchmarking a trick that phones and edge devices badly need. Models deployed in the wild meet data unlike their training set and lose accuracy; test-time adaptation retunes them on the fly without labels. Most research, though, assumes server-grade conditions.

Their benchmark, BoTTA, stresses methods with what devices actually face: few test samples, few categories, varied shifts, and overlapping shifts in one sample. Many recent methods stumbled on small data or unseen categories. One method more than doubled accuracy with five hundred twelve samples at modest memory cost on a Raspberry Pi. The authors recommend adapting periodically, not continuously, and report resource use alongside accuracy.
arxiv-2504-10449:
Long reasoning chains run faster on a leaner architecture in Junxiong Wang and co-authors' 2025 paper. Standard transformers pay steep memory and time costs as chains grow, since attention scales badly. Their M1 model swaps in a hybrid design built on the Mamba sequence architecture.

Skills were distilled from strong reasoning models, then sharpened with reinforcement learning. On hard math contest sets, M1 matches top distilled rivals of like size and beats earlier lean models. Generation ran over three times faster than a tuned transformer engine of the same size. Cheaper test-time reasoning could widen access to strong math help and cut serving costs for labs.
arxiv-2504-11049:
Giovannetti, Lloyd, and Maccone present a quantum algorithm that estimates the determinant of a matrix. The method rests on quantum spectral sampling, which reads off information from a matrix's eigenvalues. It estimates the logarithm of the determinant for positive sparse matrices.

The running time grows only with the logarithm of the matrix size, far faster than earlier methods that grew in direct proportion to it. The same approach estimates any sum built from a function of the eigenvalues. Examples include the partition function of a physical system and the entropy of a density matrix. The authors frame the result as a broad speedup for eigenvalue-based quantities.
arxiv-2504-11149:
Alejandro Luque-Cerpa, David Orellana-Martín, and Miguel Á Gutiérrez-Naranjo apply a formal computing model to disaster relief. Their 2025 paper starts from a real problem: after quakes, storms, or refugee crises, aid groups compete for funds while help is duplicated in some places and missing in others.

The authors frame relief as a shared equilibrium problem where each group's best plan depends on what others do. They then show that membrane computing, a model based on cell-like compartments, can capture that problem. A family of such systems computes the balance points for relief work. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 serves as the test case. The paper speaks to both computing theory and planners who want aid efforts that fit together.
arxiv-2504-11249:
Luke Evans and co-authors show that cryo-electron microscopy images hide a simple inner structure in a 2025 paper. Cryo-EM photographs frozen molecules from many angles, and neural methods now infer molecular shapes from learned internal representations. What those representations look like geometrically was unclear.

The team applied manifold learning to representations of the hemagglutinin protein, from both simulated and real data. The high-dimensional codes turned out to lie on smooth, low-dimensional surfaces. Simulated data covered the real data's surface well. Reading the surface's main directions linked them to physical parameters of the molecule. A simple hidden geometry strengthens trust in these inference tools and may guide better ones.
arxiv-2504-11349:
Yang and co-authors review in 2025 how AI methods rebuild 3D medical images from radiology scans. Clear 3D images aid diagnosis, but scans cost time and expose patients to radiation. AI promises sharper rebuilds with less scan time and lower dose.

The review sorts methods into four families by how they encode the target image. Those are grid forms, basis expansions, basic shape units, and neural implicit forms. Links among the families are drawn, with radiance field methods set as a subtype of the last group. Shared test sets and scoring metrics are summed up. The authors close with open problems and likely next steps for the field.
arxiv-2504-11449:
Fabio Apruzzi, Francesco Bedogna, and Salvo Mancani build symmetry theories for a class of gapless models, in work from 2025. Some quantum systems have symmetries that act on sheets or lines rather than whole volumes. Those subsystem symmetries break the usual rules of relativity, so new tools are needed.

The authors build a bulk theory whose edges produce the target models. Gapped and symmetry-breaking edge choices yield dual forms of the same physics. Their sandwich method covers several known models, from plaquette to cube types. Hidden self-duality shows up as a defect where phases meet. The framework gives a recipe for free theories that realize such symmetries in a nonlinear way.
arxiv-2504-11649:
Alan Panuco Linan, Daniela Perez, Carlos Luna, and Gustavo Romero test gauges of the pull force's own heat count. The work came out in 2025. They check if the gauges heed the second law when a black hole shifts form. The thought that heat count ties to pull itself has some weight. Still, each gauge must match the known Hawking-Bekenstein count at a hole's rim.

The test case is a shift of form. A plain Schwarzschild hole eats a charged test speck. It then turns into a charged Reissner-Nordstrom hole. The team also runs the shift in reverse. They check two gauges of the count. One is built from the Weyl form. One is built from the Bel-Robinson form. Both pass the second law test. The fine points hinge on if the shift can be run back or not.
arxiv-2504-11949:
Jie Wang, Chen Ye Gan, Caoqi Wei, Jiangtao Wen, and Yuxing Han wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It matches features across videos by motion alone, a tack the authors call Flow Intelligence.

Classic matchers read how a scene looks, and break on noise, shift, or a change of sensor kind. This method pulls motion marks from pixel blocks across frames and pairs those marks between clips. Motion is by nature free of shift, turn, and scale woes, and it needs no training data at all. Tests show it beats look-based rivals in the hard cases where they fail. Uses run from robots to scans.
arxiv-2504-12149:
Zi-Zhao Zhang, Rong Li, and Bo-Chao Liu study charmonium like mesons in a 2025 physics paper. These heavy particles contain a charm quark and antiquark, and some states do not fit the conventional picture. A diabatic approach can describe ordinary and exotic states in one framework.

Using a more realistic potential with spin dependent forces, they compute the spectrum below a set energy. Masses align well with experimental data. They also give the probability that each state is a simple quark pair versus a meson pair. Several famous states show significant molecular components, and two states are matched to expected conventional levels.
arxiv-2504-12549:
Iris Ma and co-authors present a 2025 paper on how much text language models memorize from books. The team asked whether a whole book could be pulled back out of a trained model. They fed the model the first chunk of a book and let it write on, step by step, from what it retained.

With that method, one famous children's book was rebuilt with very high likeness, and parts of other books came back well. Books that are widely read, and thus likely repeated in training, came back best. The team also found that safety tuning barely changes the effect. The work tests the limits of current guards.
arxiv-2504-12749:
Weijia Li, Guanglei Chu, Jiong Chen, and three co-authors set a check in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Logical anomalies are not scratches or dents. They are wrong links: too many objects, wrong counts, or set-ups that can not be. Past detectors bolt on reasoning modules. That hurts their use and clarity. The team sets out Reasoning Logical Anomaly Detection as a task. Systems must find flaws and explain them. They put forth LAD-Reasoner.

The reasoner is a multimodal model on a three-billion-parameter vision-language backbone. It is trained in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning builds grasp. Group relative policy optimization sharpens detection and reasoning. Rewards back how exact the output is and its shape. No hand-written data is used. On the MVTec LOCO data set, it matched a seventy-two-billion-parameter sibling on accuracy and F1, with shorter reasons.
arxiv-2504-12849:
Phung Lai and co-authors present FedX, a 2025 system for federated learning on fleets of small internet of things devices. Federated learning trains one shared model across many devices without moving their private data. The catch is hardware: phones and sensors vary wildly in power, and full models are too heavy for the weakest.

FedX splits the global model into sub networks of different sizes. A weak device gets a smaller slice, but with more bits kept per weight, so its accuracy stays up. A strong device takes a bigger slice at coarser precision. The server does the quantization work, sparing the devices. Each device trains only what it can afford, and the pieces still combine into one model. Balancing utility against overhead this way lets health trackers and asset sensors join training that would otherwise exclude them.
arxiv-2504-13049:
Wenmin Zhao, Ana Solaguren-Beascoa, and colleagues join two kinds of foundation models for single-cell biology in a 2025 study. One model family reads DNA sequence, while another reads single-cell measurements. Each alone misses what the other sees, and gene regulation depends on both sequence and cell context.

Dynamic token adaptation bridges the two, translating DNA embeddings into the token space of the single-cell model. Training an adapter on that bridge lets the combined system predict regulation in varied genetic settings. The authors probe how DNA changes ripple into the learned regulatory networks. The method is general, with the single-cell case as the worked example.
arxiv-2504-13149:
Matt Schmittle and co-authors teach off-road robots to aim far beyond the small map they can sense. A robot in unknown country sees only a local patch; past that lies fog, and treating all fog alike leads it into bad terrain or off course. Their Long Range Navigator learns a middle representation instead: from camera views it predicts which far frontiers are worth heading for, then scores them against the goal.

The system trains on unlabeled first-person video alone, which makes it cheap to scale and move between machines. In field trials on a quadruped robot and a large vehicle, adding the navigator cut the times humans had to step in and sped up decisions. The authors argue that picking good directions, not building giant maps, is the right long-range skill.
arxiv-2504-13249:
Hunters of new particles at colliders usually look for a bump in one clean channel, and anything stranger slips past. Liam Brennan and co-authors widen the net with a topology they call di-object plus X: a resonance decaying to two ordinary particles, produced alongside extra, unusual activity in the same collision. That extra activity, read through new variables built from the geometry of the collision's phase space, becomes the anomaly detector's evidence. Techniques first honed on di-jet searches carry over to these event-level features.

On benchmark signals ending in tau pairs or muon pairs plus X, the method reached discovery-level significance where a standard bump hunt saw nothing. The authors offer it as a way to catch new physics that does not announce itself politely.
arxiv-2504-13549:
Fonio, Sagaut, Budinski, and Lahtinen present an adaptive lattice gas algorithm in a 2025 paper, with both classical and quantum versions. Lattice gas methods are used to simulate nonlinear systems. They include cellular automata and the lattice Boltzmann method.

Starting from a one-dimensional integer lattice gas, the authors carry out only a fraction of the possible collisions. Those fractions are adapted so results match the lattice Boltzmann method. They then build a quantum version with a linear collision operator. It uses measurement and reinitialization steps. The paper notes cases where many time steps can be run. The work links a classic simulation family to quantum computing.
arxiv-2504-13749:
Lion Frangoulis, Zahra Khatibi, Lorenzo Mariano, and Alessandro Lunghi speed up the hunt for magnetic molecules in this 2025 paper. Designing compounds with target traits usually takes years of back-and-forth between theory and lab work. Single-molecule magnets show the cost: big gains came slowly and at great expense.

The team's pipeline mixes three tools. Genetic search breeds new candidate structures from old ones, machine learning screens them cheaply, and accurate quantum calculations check the best ones. The system can invent fresh building blocks rather than only reuse known ones. As a test, it produced new cobalt compounds with record magnetic traits in a small fraction of the usual time.
arxiv-2504-13849:
Puneet Jain wrote this 2025 review of research on making immersive technology usable by disabled people. Extended reality, or XR, mixes virtual and layered digital worlds. Cheap headsets have spread fast, yet many designs shut out users with disabilities. A leading conference on accessible computing, ASSETS, has drawn a wave of work on that gap.

From about fifteen hundred papers sent to the conference between 2019 and 2023, Jain found 26 focused on XR for disability. Sorting them revealed six main focus areas, which the review examines one by one. It also maps the methods used, from user studies to built prototypes, and tracks how the field grew year by year. The review gives new researchers a clear entry point.
arxiv-2504-14049:
Haruhisa Iijima asks what sets the brightness of open corona regions on the Sun in a 2025 paper. Coronal holes are dark patches tied to open magnetic fields. The textbook view says open regions are dark by nature. Three-dimensional simulations with radiation and magnetics test that view.

Open regions in the model shine about as bright as quiet regions. Energy fed in from churning surface magnetism sets the brightness, not corona dissipation quirks. Fake telescope maps show standard brightness cuts can miss open regions, above all at low resolution. Real satellite maps back the claim. Field extrapolation settings sway results too. The open flux problem may stem from such misses.
arxiv-2504-14449:
Sridharan and co-authors present an imaging strategy in two thousand twenty-five for a next-generation radio telescope array, the ngVLA. The facility spans a wide frequency range with sharp sensitivity and resolution, opening new discovery space. Its science goals demand images with very high dynamic range, the contrast between bright and faint features.

The baseline plan leans on the array's own sensitivity. Frequent self-calibration, where the instrument corrects itself using the sky signal, counters air-driven delays on short timescales. Pointing self-calibration fixes aim errors. Using these tricks routinely can simplify several subsystems and improve reliability. In some cases the approach may even reach the thermal noise limit. The paper lays out the reasoning and shows examples in parallel.
arxiv-2504-14649:
Eugene Tang KangJie and four co-authors survey what older adults want from lessons about artificial intelligence. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Most past work on AI teaching looks at students and children. This team asked one hundred three adults aged fifty and up about their drive. They also asked about struggles and how these adults like to learn.

The adults said learning about AI matters to them. They want its benefits and hope to avoid its risks. They also see it as needed for the years ahead. Many found the topic hard to grasp and did not know where to start. Above all, they favored learning by doing, with hands-on practice. The authors close with design ideas to build AI lessons that fit older learners.
arxiv-2504-14849:
Zongrui Pei, Junqi Yin, and Jiaxin Zhang review what language models can do for materials science, in this 2025 perspective. Chatbots trained on text have swept the field, and the authors ask how far they can help find and design new materials, above all greener ones. The paper surveys progress so far and the ways language tools can join with other methods.

Three deep topics anchor the discussion. First come the limits of today's models and what they mean for lab use. Next, a fully automated discovery pipeline. Last, drafting tools that fuse existing knowledge into designs for sustainable materials.
arxiv-2504-15149:
Chen Su and co-authors build a machine learning route to cosmology from the universe's emptiest places in this 2025 paper. Cosmic voids bend light, and that bending carries clues about matter and gravity. The trouble is that no tidy formula predicts the signal, so classic analysis stalls.

Their framework learns from simulations instead. A forward pipeline grows fake universes across many settings, complete with the messy link between galaxies and their dark matter homes. A neural estimator then studies the mock data until it can read real void lensing backward, returning the odds for two key cosmic parameters. Tests on held-out settings showed honest answers: the estimates landed on the truth with error bars of the right size. The authors offer the method as the first step toward running void lensing on real survey data.
arxiv-2504-15949:
Firas Ben Ramdhane and three co-authors map the rules that make non-linear cell grids act in clean ways. In such a grid, one local rule is used at each cell, all at once. Three traits shape much of what the grid can do. Does each state have a prior state? Can the rule run in reverse? Does it permute in each axis?

The paper shows how these traits — surjectivity, reversibility, and permutivity — push on and bound each other. It gives tests for when a rule is permutive in one sense or in both. Worked cases show where each claim holds and where it stops. Non-linear rules lack the neat tools that settle such points for linear rules. The authors fill that gap. They make clear which acts non-linear grids can and cannot do.
arxiv-2504-16049:
Ashutosh Dwibedi and co-authors compute flow traits of spinning nuclear matter in a 2025 paper. Heavy ion crashes create matter that spins, and spin signals show up in particle patterns. The team studies how spin alters shear flow and electric flow in hot matter. Two models frame the work, a gas of hadrons and a quark model.

Spin splits flow into parts along, across, and sideways to the spin axis. Heat curves for those parts dip in a valley shape. Spin trims the size of flow ratios versus still matter. A sideways electric flow appears even with no net baryon load. The results help read spin signals from real crashes.
arxiv-2504-16649:
Pei Lin and co-authors build a robot hand that picks up paper using touch sensing in 2025. Thin, floppy items like paper defeat most robot hands. Seeing them is hard, and grip plans are scarce. Their hand carries fine touch sensors on many fingers. Slips are sensed live and grip force is tuned to stop them.

Grip moves come from a learned policy trained on staged pinching motions. Tests covered paper of varied stock, thickness, and stiffness. The system succeeded in near nine of ten tries. The authors claim a first for touch based paper grasping with a nimble hand. Helper robots for daily tasks are the target use.
arxiv-2504-16849:
Axel Brandenburg and co-authors ask whether a rotation-driven instability can run inside the Sun's near-surface shear layer. Their 2025 paper simulates mean-field dynamos in rotating, shearing boxes. The magnetorotational instability needs the field strong enough and the shear of the right sign.

Above a threshold shear the instability did switch on for negative shear. Like the classic omega effect, it wound up toroidal field. Oddly, the work flowed from field to motion: magnetic energy paid for strong kinetic churning. For the real Sun, the authors judge the turbulent diffusion too strong. The instability likely stays off, leaving the standard effect in charge.
arxiv-2504-17749:
