Steven Wilson and Sina Khanmohammadi present a neural network that predicts the strength of links between layers of a network. Their 2025 paper tackles multilayer graphs, where the same nodes connect in several layers and links carry weights, not just yes-or-no ties. Weight prediction is harder than plain link prediction and has had less study. Their method, MSGCN, spreads node data across layers while keeping the shape of the graph.

Tests on networks with known cross-layer links show strong and steady accuracy across many structures. The team also tried the method on the London transport network, where it predicted passenger loads between stations that lack a direct link. The work gives planners a tool for flows in layered systems.
arxiv-2504-17949:
Ruichen Xu and co-authors study how move schemes affect the performance of simulated annealing. Their paper deals with a key design choice for this method: how to make each new move.

They join theory with tests on move settings, such as how many bits move and how far, under varied temperature schedules and system sizes. Tests used the Lennard-Jones problem and another benchmark. Moving exactly one particle chosen at random per step gave the most efficient result. Acceptance rates and convergence were studied. Partial updates can beat full moves in high-dimension settings, a handy guideline for users.
arxiv-2504-18149:
Some quantum states that capture strong interactions between particles are easy to write down but hard to load onto a quantum computer. Han Xu, Kazuhiro Seki, and Seiji Yunoki tackle one such state, the Gutzwiller wave function, for fermions with a threefold symmetry, in this 2025 paper. Their hybrid scheme splits the loading task between quantum hardware and a classical computer.

One route prepares the state by measuring helper qubits and keeping the lucky runs; they chart how often luck strikes as the state's key parameter varies. A second route uses smart sampling to compute energies instead. Tests on a trapped-ion machine for a two-site model matched exact answers well. The work maps a path toward simulating strongly interacting matter.
arxiv-2504-18449:
Yoseph Berhanu Alebachew and Chris Brown plan an experiment on bias in code review in a 2025 paper. Reviewers can favor or dismiss code for reasons beyond its quality. Such bias often acts without the reviewer's own awareness. Watching where reviewers look may expose early warning patterns.

Eye tracking will map focus spots as reviewers read code screens. Sequence models will then hunt patterns tied to biased outcomes. The team expects alerts on suspect reviews to cut needless pushback. Fairer reviews could also widen who thrives in software teams overall. The work will track gaze in a controlled test setting.
arxiv-2504-18649:
Andrei Tonkikh, Balaji Arun, Zhuolun Xiang, Zekun Li, and Alexander Spiegelman presented a replication protocol in 2025 that stays fast under attack. Systems that must agree despite faulty or hostile members face a trade-off: cautious designs are slow on good days, eager designs collapse under small attacks.

Their protocol, Raptr, merges both styles through a new prefix consensus step. In a test spread across regions with one hundred copies, it reached two hundred sixty thousand transactions per second with sub-second delay on good runs. Delay stayed low even at high load. Under network faults, including a one percent message drop rate, performance barely slipped. The design aims for near-optimal delay with graceful decline.
arxiv-2504-18949:
Ruy de Queiroz traces a thread in Wittgenstein's work from note books to late books and past them. The work dates to 2025. The thread ties sense, use, and what flows from a claim. Open web files of the full Nachlass made the hunt sharp.

He takes that thread as base for a game-form sense frame for the tongue of logic claims. Key bits from print and draft works build the case. So do bits from sense staff who back a split view of proofs and sense. The shift at stake runs from signs read off a state of things to signs in use. Follows of claims, cast as moves in tongue, sit at its core.
arxiv-2504-19449:
Zhenyu Zhang and co-authors present R-Sparse, a training free way to cut activation cost in large language models in a 2025 paper. Big models are costly at run time, above all on edge devices. Using only a sparse subset of activations can cut compute and memory traffic, but many methods fail on modern activation types or need heavy retraining.

Two observations drive the design. Within one linear layer, the non sparse part of the input acts like a few bias terms, and the full computation can be approximated by mixing input channels with weight singular values. Replacing the linear layers on that basis reaches high sparsity in advanced models without retraining.
arxiv-2504-20149:
Resch, Benka, Bauer, and Pfleiderer report magnetic order in single crystals of a rare earth compound, ErB2, at low temperatures. They grew the crystals with a floating zone method and probed them in several ways. Their 2025 paper brings the measures together to pin down how the magnetism sets in.

Below about 14 kelvin, the erbium moments settle into ferromagnetic order through a smooth phase change. The moments strongly prefer to lie in the flat plane of the crystal, a trait that appears well above the ordering point. A field in the plane aligns them with ease and little lag. A field along the hard axis barely moves them until a sharp flip near 12 tesla.
arxiv-2504-20449:
Naoto Nakatsuji and his four co-authors, publishing in 2025, map the electronic landscape of a three-layer crystal sandwich with a twist. Each layer of the material WSe2 is rotated slightly against its neighbors. The misalignment prints two overlapping moiré patterns, like two window screens overlaid. The team models how the atoms settle and what energy bands result, for the two natural twist styles.

The middle layer feels both patterns at once, doubling the depth of the energy landscape. In the helical twist style, the settling creates domains where the combined pattern forms a Kagome lattice, famous for hosting flat energy bands. In the alternating style, deep triangular wells appear instead. A modest electric field can flip which layer holds the electrons at the band edge. The authors present trilayers as a wider design space than the much-studied bilayers.
arxiv-2504-20549: Evgeny Feigin wrote a paper from 2025 on an algebraic form of a known geometric equality about symmetry spaces. The original claim, since proved, says two spaces of sections have the same size. Feigin recasts both sides as sizes of algebraic modules named for Demazure, then builds an explicit bridge between them. The bridge works in type A only, but covers a far wider class of cases than the geometric claim.
arxiv-2504-20649:
Sreeraj Rajindran Nair, Benjamin Southwell, and Christopher Ferrie bring short-time processing to quantum signals in a 2025 paper. Sound and image tools often work on data in short overlapping chunks, which keeps costs down for streams and huge files. Quantum versions of the Fourier transform exist, but no one had built the chunked variant. Their short-time quantum Fourier transform fills that gap.

A new overlap-add method stitches the chunks back together using a permutation gate. The paper shows filtering done in the quantum Fourier domain, with the filter held in a quantum register or in a block-encoded gate. Practical details get attention too: offsets, skipped frames, an overlap-save variant, and scaling that drifts as windows change. The work ports a workhorse signal technique into the quantum setting.
arxiv-2504-20849:
Anum Afzal, Alexandre Mercier, and Florian Matthes study machine-made ad text for the music trade, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Shops want text made from data, but plain methods tend to repeat the same phrases again and again. A set of near-twin ads is of little use, so range matters as much as quality.

The authors test several large language models, with fine-tuning and with few-shot or zero-shot prompts. They set a base line for text that is both good and varied. They also add a new score, JaccDiv, that gauges how much a set of texts spreads out. The lessons reach past music, to any field where the same kind of text is made at scale.
arxiv-2504-21049:
Sneha Baskota trains a deep network to sort web addresses into four risk classes in a paper from 2025. Phishing pages steal credentials and money, and older detectors miss new attack types. The model reads an address as a sequence of characters. A bidirectional memory network then judges context from both directions. Classes cover benign, phishing, defacement, and malware addresses.

Training used more than six hundred fifty thousand labeled addresses. The system reached ninety-seven percent accuracy overall. The author reports clear gains over traditional techniques. False positives, a pain point for older systems, were a design target throughout. The paper is a compact applied study in security machine learning.
arxiv-2504-21449:
Denis Grebenkov studies imperfect reactions driven by diffusion onto 3D targets in a 2025 math paper. A diffusing particle may not react at once when it hits the target, which changes how much material flows onto it. Grebenkov uses a spectral method based on a special set of functions tied to the target surface.

In that frame, the steady cloud of particles and the total flow take forms set by surface eigenvalues, which give the key length scales of the target. Using donut shaped and paired ball coordinates, he solves the problem for a torus and for two balls. A simple two term formula for the flow is given and checked. Uses in chemical physics are discussed.
arxiv-2504-21649:
Dahal and Hymas show that separate regions of spacetime share quantum entanglement in twenty twenty-five. The vacuum of a quantum field is not empty of correlations. They demonstrate entanglement between the future and left Rindler wedges of flat spacetime. The past and right wedges are likewise entangled.

That pattern underlies the Unruh effect, where acceleration creates particles. The authors propose extracting the entanglement with two simple detectors. The detectors sit in the past and right wedges. Tuning their frequencies in step with time transfers the entanglement to them. Teleportation through the vacuum might then be possible. They suggest current superconducting qubit technology could implement the protocol.
arxiv-2505-00049:
Language models now sit for personality tests, and Wenhan Dong and co-authors survey the young science of measuring machine psychology in this 2025 paper. Six dimensions organize the field. They span the tests borrowed from human psychology, data sets built for models, and scores for consistency and stability. They also cover the findings so far, plus the arts of simulating personalities and whole behaviors.

Some models do show stable personality-like patterns under a fixed prompting style. Yet scores swing with task and wording, and tools built for humans fit awkwardly on systems that can play any role on request. The authors catalogue the mismatches honestly and sketch what sturdier measurement would take. The survey is aimed at researchers who want the humanizing of AI to rest on evidence rather than vibes.
arxiv-2505-00449:
Bart Jacobs and Justus Fasse verify shared memory code in this 2025 paper. Their target is the core of Rust's atomic reference counting, a scheme that frees shared data when the last user lets go. Relaxed memory rules, which let processors reorder accesses, make such code hard to prove correct.

Their modular approach suits programs built from relaxed atomic accesses and fences. They argue it is sound under the C20 memory model when paired with a simple static analysis, admitting one open sub-problem. Under a slightly strengthened model that bans out of thin air values, the approach stands alone, with no analysis and no assumptions. They define step by step semantics, prove them sound, and plug into existing concurrency logics.
arxiv-2505-00649:
Marco Braga, Pranav Kasela, Alessandro Raganato, and Gabriella Pasi adapt search rankers to new domains by adding and subtracting model weights. Language models re-rank documents well until vocabulary and style shift under them. Task arithmetic merges models trained on different tasks through simple weight operations. No extra fine-tuning is required.

The team synthesizes diverse task and domain knowledge into a single retriever this way. Experiments span scientific, biomedical, and multilingual collections. Re-ranking quality rose by up to eighteen percent on one standard measure and fifteen on another. Both gains came at zero-shot, on tasks the merged model never trained for. The analysis also maps where the trick strains. Code is public. For search teams facing a new domain with no labeled data, weight arithmetic offers a cheap first adaptation.
arxiv-2505-00749:
A team of authors sets out an open system for AI agents to work together in a 2025 paper. Firms now deploy many narrow agents that must cross firm and tool lines to finish joint tasks. Without shared rules, those agents cannot talk, plan, or pay each other in a trusted way.

The system, Coral Protocol, gives agents a shared language and a neutral base. It sets standard message forms, a way to run joint tasks step by step, and a means to form trusted teams on the fly. The authors stress that the base stays open and vendor neutral. They pitch it as a base layer for a coming internet of agents.
arxiv-2505-00949:
A large team at NVIDIA presents a family of reasoning language models in a 2025 technical report. The models, named Llama-Nemotron, aim to think step by step without wasting effort. Long chains of thought raise cost and slow replies. The team tunes the models to switch deep reasoning on for hard tasks and off for easy ones.

The report describes how the models were trained and tested across math, code, and science tasks. Careful data mixing and staged training kept quality high while trimming size and compute. The models are released for other builders to use and study. Efficient reasoning matters because these models are now used at huge scale every day.
arxiv-2505-01049:
Nishant Jain, Xunpeng Huang, Yian Ma, and Tong Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It puts multi-step consistency models on firm theory ground, a class of fast generators that rival diffusion models.

Consistency models map a noisy input to any point on the reverse path, so samples come in a few steps. The authors prove a tight bound on the gap to the true spread, reached in a step count that grows only with the log of size over error. A like bound holds when the data are rough, with a step count that grows with dimension. They also show the models can be learned well with small steps, in both smooth and rough cases. The rough-case rates lead the field.
arxiv-2505-01149:
Kimberly Shen and co-authors model the tug of war between forest and savanna. In the tropics, the two may be rival stable states of the same land. Fire holds savanna open, while thick forest shades fire out. The team builds a spatial model where seeds spread, fires jump, and plants regrow, all with random timing.

Their model's bistability comes from repeat fires that keep tree cover low. Where forest packs dense, fires fail to spread and cover stays high. A smoothed version of the model also shows two states, but its short term paths drift from the spatial one. The gap between fast fire and slow growth proves key.
arxiv-2505-01249:
Christopher Williams studies how the brain joins many glances into one view of a scene. His twenty twenty-five paper models each fixation as a sharp center with a blurry edge, like the human fovea. The retinal change from full scene to glance is written as a linear down-sampling.

That linear form allows exact inference for hidden scene variables in factor models. It also turns where to look next into a design problem with a clear best answer. The rule picks the glance that should gain the most information. Tests on face photos and handwritten digits show the models work. Readers see a tidy math frame for active vision.
arxiv-2505-01449:
Jiayu Wang, Aws Albarghouthi, and Frederic Sala forecast which way to adapt a language model before paying for the trial in this 2025 paper. Fine-tuning and in-context tricks each shine in different settings, and picking wrong burns compute. Their framework, COSMOS, predicts both score and cost for each candidate plan.

Two predictors do the work. Small proxy models fed with embeddings guess fine-tuning outcomes, while scaling laws fitted on few samples forecast retrieval-based in-context learning. Across eight benchmarks the framework's predictions tracked reality closely. The savings were large: about ninety-three percent less compute on average, and near ninety-nine percent in the heaviest cases. The authors argue that choosing an adaptation strategy should start with a forecast, not a fleet of trial runs, and that deployment budgets can shrink without giving up quality.
arxiv-2505-01649:
Ali Ovgun and Reggie Pantig derive new black hole solutions in 2025 for models with dark photons. Dark photons may carry a hidden force tied to dark matter. From the force law between fermions, the pair works out fixes to the classic Schwarzschild shape, some tied to spin.

The fixes shift the horizon, heat, light ring, and shadow of the hole, most strongly at short range. A mass term damps the shifts with distance in an exponential way. Higher-order magnetic terms add spin-linked bends near the horizon. The results set up tests through wave astronomy and hole imaging.
arxiv-2505-01749:
Qi Song and co-authors present in 2025 a unified way to hide secret data inside other data using implicit neural networks. Classic hiding tools need a fresh design for each data type, which limits their reach. The new method stores both secret and cover data in the neurons of one network.

A private key shared by sender and receiver marks where secret data sits in the network. A key-based pick rule places data in the right spots for storage and recall. Tests span images, video, sound, and three-dimensional forms, all handled by the same frame. Broad success hints at wide use for safe and private data exchange.
arxiv-2505-01849:
Bandyopadhyay and a co-author applied Markov models to Twenty20 cricket chases in a 2025 paper. In a chase, the second team must reach a set target with balls and wickets running out. A past gauge, the Pressure Index, scores how hard that squeeze feels ball by ball.

Higher-order Markov models track how each ball's outcome leans on the last few, not just the last one. Joined with the pressure gauge, they chart how a chase tips toward win or loss. Teams can read the charts to pick when to attack and when to hold. The work turns raw score feeds into chase plans.
arxiv-2505-02349:
Hakam Alomari, Christopher Vendome, and Hilal Gyawali introduce srcVul, a tool for finding and patching vulnerable code clones. Copying code is common in software development, but clones propagate vulnerabilities across every copied segment. Fixing one copy leaves the others exposed.

The tool combines program slicing with locality-sensitive hashing. It first builds a database of vulnerability-related slices from known vulnerable programs and their patches, indexing each slice's structural characteristics as a vector. When scanning a target program, it matches slicing vectors against the database and recommends a patch when it finds a similarity. Evaluated against three state-of-the-art detectors, srcVul reached ninety-one percent precision and seventy-five percent recall on established vulnerability databases and open-source repositories. The authors argue the approach scales while staying precise. For security teams, it offers a way to hunt down every copy of a known flaw, not just the original.
arxiv-2505-02549:
Yongxiang Li and co-authors tackle person matching across normal and heat-sensing cameras in a 2025 paper. The task, called person re-identification, must match the same person in day images and night thermal images without hand-labeled training data. The gap between the two image types makes the job hard.

Common methods group images by computer and trust the group labels, but those labels carry errors that pile up as training goes on. The authors build a learning scheme that expects label noise and resists it, guarding against overfitting and drift. Their method aims for steadier matching where no labels exist at all. Surveillance and search teams get a more robust tool for cross-camera tracking.
arxiv-2505-02749:
Tin Nguyen and six co-authors ask how courts might judge AI tools that predict repeat crime, in a 2025 paper. Tech and legal fields have built separate ideas of fairness. That split makes it hard to turn tech measures into lasting policy. The problem is sharpest for high-stakes tools used in courts.

The team searched legal sources for signs of tech fairness ideas. Main tech criteria could be linked to rights such as due process and equal protection. Laws, though, tend to adopt only some criteria and can clash with each other. The authors build a new frame that joins court scrutiny levels with tech criteria. They test the frame against rules in Europe, China, and India as well. The aim is shared ground for policy and design.
arxiv-2505-03049:
Thirty-four hackathon teams spent a weekend pointing large language models at chemistry and materials problems, and Yoel Zimmermann and co-authors catalog what they built. The projects span the full research cycle: they predict molecular traits, design new materials, automate lab work, manage data, draft papers, and mine past papers for new ideas.

Patterns emerged across the projects. Models handled low-data problems better than expected, with added reasoning switched on. They served as quick test-build platforms as much as tools that predict. The review is candid about weak points too: trust in the outputs, clear logic, and results others can repeat all lag behind raw power. The authors frame the set as a snapshot of a field mid-change.
arxiv-2505-03149:
Joseph Kettelkamp and co-authors present a way to rebuild heart images from free-breathing, ungated MRI scans. Their 2025 method shows each motion phase as a warped copy of one still template image. A low-rank model captures the whole family of warps in compact form. Each warp comes from flowing along a smooth velocity field between the template phase and the target phase.

The template and the motion model are learned straight from the raw scanner data, with no labels or outside training set. Because the motion model is tightly constrained, the recovery beats current motion-resolved and motion-compensated methods. The tests use free-breathing three-dimensional cine scans of the heart.
arxiv-2505-03249:
Owen Moulding and a large team report multilayer crystal field states in a cerium compound in two thousand twenty-five. Crystal field states set how f electrons act in such solids. In the local view those states stay locked on one site. Polarized Raman spectra of CeCoSi break that simple picture.

More excitations show than the local model allows for. The team reads that as entanglement of states across cerium layers. Spin, orbital, and sublattice traits join in that composite. Such mixing could seed new quantum orders past this one case. Any system with local but not global symmetry loss may host them.
arxiv-2505-03349:
Scheduling random jobs on parallel machines admits a near perfect scheme when the job sizes come in few flavors, prove Antonios Antoniadis and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Each job's length is a coin flip between short and long, and the goal is to minimize the average finishing time in expectation.

The key move reshapes any optimal policy into a stratified one that decides only at set moments, at negligible cost. Two traps, keeping the new policy informed and stopping delays from piling up, are disarmed in turn. Dynamic programming then finds the best stratified policy. A looser version gives a strong guarantee for the general case.
arxiv-2505-03749:
Cut a triangle by its longest side, again and again, and the angles of the shards could in drift run wild. Amalia Adlerteg and Linus Carlsson bound that drift in 2025 for a three-way cut. Their method splits the longest side in thirds and joins the cuts to the far corner, then repeats on each shard. The work is drawn from Adlerteg's thesis work.

For a general start, the top angle of any later shard stays under a fixed multiple of the start's top angle, part proved and part shown by number runs. Two clean starts, the equal-sided and the right isoceles, earn full two-sided bounds. Mesh builders need such bounds: shard angles gone wild spoil the sums that ride on the mesh.
arxiv-2505-04149:
Omer Avci proves, in a 2025 number theory paper, that the torsion points of an elliptic curve stop growing in a certain tower of number fields. Torsion points are the finitely many points on the curve that return to the start after repeated addition, and they form a tidy group.

Starting from a curve over the rational numbers and a square-root number field, the tower adds layer upon layer of p-power roots of unity style extensions. For primes above five, Avci shows the torsion group over the whole tower equals the one over the base field. That equality lets him list every group that can occur, borrowing the known list for square-root fields.
arxiv-2505-04349:
Harsh Patil measures the size of a group pair using relative cohomological dimension, a count of how many steps a certain algebraic resolution needs. His setting is a relatively hyperbolic pair: a group that behaves hyperbolically except around a chosen peripheral subgroup. He proves the relative dimension is always finite when the group has no torsion.

He also shows the number survives quasi-isometries, changes that distort distances only mildly, provided the peripheral subgroup is unconstricted and built from finitely many pieces at every level. As a by-product, his methods compute the dimension outright in a range of cases.
arxiv-2505-04749:
Pavel Gvozdevsky extends a classic rigidity theorem for algebraic groups from fields to rings in a 2025 paper. The Borel-Tits theorem sorts maps between simple groups over fields into tidy types. Such maps spring from ground field maps plus group scheme maps. Gvozdevsky asks whether that tidy story survives over general rings.

For a class of adjoint group schemes with rich root data, it does. Abstract isomorphisms between point groups split into ring maps and scheme maps as in the field case. Mild side conditions keep the proof on track. The result widens a cornerstone of algebraic group theory. Rigidity, it turns out, is not a luxury of fields alone.
arxiv-2505-05149:
Mansour Naslcheraghi and Gunes Karabulut-Kurt present a 2025 scheme to analyse the web that links ground stations and satellite groups for space awareness. Keeping watch over all actors in space needs a network that stays aware at all times. When objects can be seen and steered rests on real orbits, which tangle the web in ways a static view misses.

Their scheme treats the time pattern of each satellite, its temporal spectrum, as the key design element. It folds in real dynamics to map how the ground-space web is built, which stations sit alone, and which rule the web. Sims of the full system measure how each satellite's time pattern shapes links within and between constellations. The counts show how ground stations and groups act on each other in practice.
arxiv-2505-05449:
Ryan Plestid and Mark Wise tackle a bookkeeping problem in particle theory in a 2025 paper on reactions with atoms and nuclei. When light or electrons bounce off a bound system, small corrections can depend on the inner build of that system. The math uses functions that must obey strict symmetry rules, yet common shortcuts hide or break those rules mid-calculation.

The authors lay out a way to write those functions so the symmetry stays visible when the target is heavy and barely recoils. In that form, shortcuts can be taken without breaking the rules. The same form also pulls out the largest terms that dominate the outcome. They work through electron scattering from nuclei in detail to show the method in action.
arxiv-2505-05549:
Vishnu Jejjala and co-authors train neural networks to recognize the symmetry type of special math functions that count black hole states, in a 2025 paper. Modular and related forms generate the numbers of quantum black hole microstates. Given only a truncated list of a form's Fourier coefficients, the networks had to guess its modular weight, a key label.

Feed-forward networks learned the task well for negative-weight forms, including the exact forms used in black hole counting formulas. Positive weights and tangled mixes of theta functions proved harder. The authors call the study a proof of concept: learning machines can spot how data organizes itself under modular symmetry. They see a path toward automated checks for hidden symmetries in quantum gravity.
arxiv-2505-05649: Paweł Pietrzycki studies a class of operators on spaces of analytic functions in this 2025 math paper. He looks at spaces where multiplying by a fixed function shifts the input, and where that shift can be undone from the left. Under natural conditions, the undoing map turns out to be a Cowen-Douglas operator, a well-studied class with rich structure. Pietrzycki then asks how extending functions beyond their first domain, from a subspace left fixed by the operator, relates to the spectrum of the operator restricted to that subspace.
arxiv-2505-05949:
Max Glockner and colleagues built a question-answering benchmark out of invented news in a 2025 paper. Retrieval benchmarks rot quickly: questions that once forced a model to look facts up become answerable from memory as newer models train on fresher data. NeoQA sidesteps the rot by generating fictional news events, entities, timelines, and articles, so no correct answer can exist in any model's training data.

Questions must then be answered purely from retrieved evidence, and only when that evidence suffices. Variants include missing and misleading details to test caution. The authors found models often miss subtle mismatches between question and evidence and rush to answer on thin support. Controlled fiction gives retrieval research a stable yardstick.
arxiv-2505-06349:
A compact dead galaxy from the early universe spins fast and holds little dark matter, Robert Pascalau and co-authors report in a 2025 paper. Space telescope surveys found many massive quiet galaxies earlier than models can explain. Deep spectra of one such galaxy, seen as it was when the universe was young, resolve its stars' motions across its face.

The galaxy packs huge mass into a tiny span yet rotates vigorously. Its dark matter share runs low beside its stars. Such relics likely formed in a furious early burst that burned gas into stars with rare efficiency. Their existence pressures galaxy formation theory to speed up.
arxiv-2505-06649:
Dimitris Korobilis studies how central bank rate shocks spread through the United States economy, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. He builds a large Bayesian model that tracks many series at once and treats shocks as hidden factors. The design keeps the math fast even as the data set grows, and it lets policy effects shift over time.

Shocks are picked out with high-speed market surprises plus sign rules on the results. The method held up across many model choices. A key result is that the Federal Reserve sway over single consumer prices shifted a lot in the high price-rise years from two thousand twenty-two to two thousand twenty-four. Readers get new detail on how policy reaches prices.
arxiv-2505-06749:
Yuan and Zhou present a 2025 paper on bringing cooperative self-driving to ordinary cars through cheap dash-cams and open software. Connected-vehicle systems usually demand pricey sensors and units that lock into one brand. Their kit leans on mass-market edge devices drivers already can buy. Light vehicle-to-everything links run over LTE and WiFi instead of dedicated radios.

Standards alignment keeps the kit compatible with planned infrastructure. The team targets public gains first, such as smoother traffic flow management at scale. Feasibility tests check whether the low-cost links carry data fast enough for cooperation. The pitch is autonomy's safety benefits without a luxury price tag or a new car.
arxiv-2505-06849:
Subramani and Bartscher pair learn tools with slim sums for a heat twin of a lamp sink. Twin tools mock real gear live and guess its next states. Their twin tracks a car head lamp heat sink in the work. Flow sums give a base of true heat paths for the sink. Slim forms, built by mode splits, hold those paths at low cost. Learn tools then pick the best slim form for each new state.

Four learn tools take the pick task in the test runs. Tree, near-peer, curve, and nerve tools all get a shot. The nerve tool wins with a mean miss of 54.240. Guess and true marks sit close in the count checks. The frame scales, reads plain, and suits car heat work. It backs firm builds and care that plans in front.
arxiv-2505-07149:
Heqing Ren and co-authors shield image models from attacks that probe whether a photo was in the training set, in a 2025 paper. Membership inference is a quiet privacy threat. It can expose whose data trained a medical or personal model. Federated learning lowers some risks but does not stop such probes.

Their defense, AugMixCloak, transforms query images before they reach the model. Augmentation blends plus a compression step fuse away telltale details. A hashing stage first spots queries that copy training images. Two stages together blunt the attack's signal. Model accuracy for honest users is the key constraint. Privacy engineers gain a practical, model-agnostic cloak. The method suits services that answer outside queries.
arxiv-2505-07349:
Badhan Kumar Das and co-authors present a transformer model that classifies brain bleeding from MRI scans taken in two planes, in a 2025 paper. Scans vary in contrast and orientation, which makes the task hard for neural networks. Resampling images to one fixed plane can lose information.

Their model uses two encoders, one for top-view scans and one for side-view scans, and joins them with cross-attention. A marker vector tells the model when a contrast is missing. Tests on a real clinical data set support the design. The work aims to help clinicians spot bleeding reliably despite varied scan setups.
arxiv-2505-07549:
Melchior Wirth proves a link between two ways of measuring how fast quantum systems settle in a 2025 mathematics paper. Quantum Markov semigroups describe systems that evolve and lose information to their surroundings over time. A key question is how quickly their entropy gap to the steady state shrinks.

Wirth shows that shrink at a steady exponential rate exactly when a known inequality, the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality, holds. The proof covers a broad class of algebras used for infinite quantum systems. He also extends a practical criterion for checking the inequality to a symmetric class of such evolutions. Results of this kind underpin error bounds for quantum devices and algorithms.
arxiv-2505-07649:
Dominique Fourdrinier, William Strawderman, and Martin Wells construct special estimators in a 2025 paper. Their target is the mean of a multi-dimensional bell-shaped distribution, judged by squared error. Bayes minimax estimators are prized because they are admissible like Bayesian rules yet carry the cautious risk guarantees of frequentist ones. Building them has been a live problem.

The authors show such estimators can be built through integral transforms, using two classic transforms, as long as the prior is chosen with the right spherical shape. Several worked examples show the method in action. The paper is technical and aimed at mathematical statisticians.
arxiv-2505-07849:
Revanth Gangi Reddy and nine co-authors present SweRank, in a 2025 preprint, a fast way to find the code behind a bug report. Given a plain-language issue, developers must locate the files and functions to change. That hunt eats time on every project. AI agent systems can do it, but they are slow, pricey, and often closed. Classic ranking models are cheap but trip on the wordy, failure-focused style of issue text. SweRank pairs a retriever with a reranker trained for this exact job.

To train it, the team built SweLoc, a large dataset from public GitHub projects. It pairs real issue reports with the code edits that fixed them. On two standard test sets, SweRank topped both older rankers and costly agent systems. The dataset also lifted other retrievers and rerankers when they trained on it. The authors offer both as resources for cheaper, open issue localization.
arxiv-2505-07949:
Alan Junzhe Zhou and co-authors show how a correction model adds ordinary matter effects to dark-matter-only cosmos simulations, in a 2025 paper. The catalog names one author, but the byline lists a full team. Fine maps of warped light from distant galaxies carry rich data, yet gas and stars bend those maps in ways dark matter alone cannot predict. The correction model shifts matter in the base runs to mimic those effects.

The three-setting model fit a wide battery of map statistics at once. The set ran from basic pair counts to wave-based and moment measures. Fits held within two percent across scales and depth slices for a survey-like setup. The test used a leading hydro simulation suite as ground truth. The authors say this clears the way for light-warp studies using the full, non-bell-shaped data in small-scale maps.
arxiv-2505-08049:
Prakhar Godara, a solo author writing in 2025, asks whether apparent learning biases are real. Studies of a two-choice gambling task claim people overweight good news and seek confirming proof. Godara shows those patterns can arise even with perfectly fair updating.

When fair Bayesian updating is cast as a learning rule, its step sizes shrink over time but stay even. Fitting a standard model with uneven step sizes then falsely recovers both biases. Master equations show the two accounts give the same behavior signs. New test designs are proposed to tell true bias from this artifact.
arxiv-2505-08549: Jitender Singh generalizes in 2025 a classic test for when a polynomial cannot be split into factors. The proof uses Newton polygons, shapes that encode root size data for polynomials over valued domains. A key factorization result comes first, and the new splitting tests follow from it as direct cases, with the Dumas test among them.
arxiv-2505-08649:
Particle physics allows more than the one Higgs boson already found, and Miralles and co-authors ask whether a lighter extra scalar could still be hiding. Their 2025 paper works inside the aligned two-Higgs-doublet model, a framework that adds a second Higgs doublet while keeping flavor physics calm by aligning its couplings.

The team ran global fits with a Bayesian tool across every layout where at least one added scalar, neutral or charged, sits below the known Higgs mass. The fits weigh theory rules against precision electroweak data, flavor measurements, Higgs results, and direct searches at past and present colliders. Each layout's surviving room is mapped. The exercise tells experimentalists where a light scalar can still live in this model family, and which measurements would close the remaining gaps.
arxiv-2505-09049:
Madhur Mehta asks how lumpy the universe's most compact objects can be when gravity itself is modified, in a 2025 essay. Exotic compact objects, star-like things denser than neutron stars but short of black holes, are test beds for theories that add higher-curvature terms to Einstein's gravity.

Working through two such theories, the essay derives how the compactness ceiling shifts. The corrections scale with the coupling strength divided by powers of the would-be horizon size. In some real systems, observations suggest the shifts could be large enough to notice. The essay, honored in a gravitation essay contest, frames compactness as a clean dial for spotting modified gravity.
arxiv-2505-09149:
Ichiro Oda presents a fully covariant quantization of quadratic gravity in this 2025 paper. Quadratic gravity adds higher-derivative terms to Einstein's theory, which may help quantize gravity. The challenge is doing so while respecting general coordinate invariance at every step.

Working in the de Donder gauge with BRST symmetry, Oda computes the equal-time commutation relations in detail. The relations between the metric and its time derivatives vanish identically. He then reads off the theory's physical content: a massless graviton, a massive scalar, and a massive ghost. The ghost makes the theory non-unitary as it stands. Oda closes by discussing whether confining the ghost could restore a unitary scattering matrix.
arxiv-2505-09349:
Ilnura Usmanova and Kfir Yehuda Levy design a learning method that optimizes a system while never breaking its safety limit. Safe optimization fits robots and self-driving tasks, where trials themselves must stay inside the fence. Older methods burn many samples or scale badly as dimensions grow.

Their primal-dual method tunes two step sizes with unusual care. The dual steps breathe with the constraint's state, while primal moves stay leashed so both sequences remain safe at every step. The team proves a convergence speed that beats the best known rates for this setting. To their knowledge, it is the first primal-dual scheme with safe updates throughout. Simulations back the math, and the design extends to several constraints. Safe learning could thus run longer in the real world without a human hovering.
arxiv-2505-09549:
Susarla and co-authors report long-term timing of seven ecliptic pulsars watched with the Irish arm of the LOFAR radio array. Pulsars near the ecliptic plane feel the solar wind at full strength, and low radio tones magnify that touch. The data span two to three years of steady watching.

Their 2025 paper gives arrival times, timing solutions, and dispersion measure tracks for each pulsar. Dispersion, the delay laid on the signal by free electrons, swings with each pulsar's height above the ecliptic, a clean solar wind signature. Pulse widths widen with tone for some stars and hold for others. The set feeds both solar wind science and the wider pulsar timing game.
arxiv-2505-09649:
Abisha Thapa Magar and Anup Shakya built a next-word tool in a 2025 project paper. Guessing the next word is a core task for language software, but the best tools today are huge nets trained with vast data and costly machines. The pair asked whether a leaner design could still do the job well.

Their design joins a graph net with a memory net. The graph part codes the sense of the words so far, and the memory part uses that code to pick the next word. They trained it on a Wikipedia text set with modest gear. The project shows a graph-based route to word guessing that small teams can afford to try.
arxiv-2505-10149:
Mirai Ikebuchi extends a counting argument about axioms to higher-order logic in a 2025 paper. Familiar theories, like that of groups, can often be stated with far fewer axioms than first written down. For first-order theories, a homology-based method already gives hard lower bounds on how few axioms can suffice, by turning the theory into algebraic objects.

Ikebuchi carries the method into the typed lambda calculus with product and unit types, where equations run between lambda terms rather than simple symbols. Homology groups are defined for such a theory, and the count of its independent cycles yields a floor on the number of equations any presentation must contain. The result gives logicians a new measuring tool for higher-order systems.
arxiv-2505-10349:
Ye Zheng and co-authors propose a private way to count how often values occur in this 2025 paper. In local differential privacy, each person scrambles their own data before sending it. That protects people from an untrusted collector, but it can blur the counts.

Their method, Joint Randomized Response, pairs people into groups of two. The pair scrambles their binary data together, and group membership stays hidden. The team proves the privacy level matches the classic single-person method. In tests on real and made-up data, counts were far more exact in most cases. Gains reached up to two orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2505-10449:
Martin Rodriguez-Vega, Terry Loring, and Alexander Cerjan present a condensed matter paper, published in 2025, on tracking a material's topological identity as its shape changes dimension. Topological invariants are usually defined for one fixed dimension, leaving no language for what happens when a flat island of material is stretched into a chain. The authors build that language using real space markers computed locally.

Their test bed is a lattice of magnetic atoms on a superconductor, reshaped from a round island toward a one dimensional chain. The markers follow the topology through the reshaping and also grade how well it survives disorder. The authors offer the framework as a design tool, for instance to find the thinnest slab that still behaves as a three dimensional topological material.
arxiv-2505-10549:
Zachary Bare and seven co-authors hunt for new battery materials by computer screening, then make one in the lab. Their twenty twenty-five paper targets Wadsley-Roth niobates, a family prized for fast lithium storage. Fewer than thirty such structures were known, which limits the search for better or cheaper mixes.

The team swapped elements into ten known templates, across forty-eight elements, and tested thousands of candidates with quantum calculations. Over a thousand looked stable enough to exist. They then synthesized one predicted mix and confirmed its structure by X-ray. The new material stored charge fast and beat a recent benchmark of the family.
arxiv-2505-10649:
Xianrui Li, Yufei Cui, Jun Li, and Antoni B Chan improve learning from whole-slide medical images in a 2025 paper. A single tissue slide is huge, so models learn from bags of small patches and weigh which patches matter. Hospitals keep gaining new cases, but retraining from scratch each time is costly, and naive updates make models forget.

The authors found that forgetting in such models sits mainly in the attention layers that weigh patches. They counter it two ways: a teaching loss that preserves old attention habits, and a memory pool of past patch bags for rehearsal. The pair should let diagnostic models grow with new data safely.
arxiv-2505-10749:
Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Zhisheng Tang, and Mayank Kejriwal propose, in a 2025 paper, planning for grid world tasks by having a large language model write the agent's policy as code. Classic planning leans on search or reinforcement learning. Code, by contrast, is readable, editable, and reusable across similar tasks.

Their framework, called iterative programmatic planning, has the model output programs that map states to action sequences. Several prompting styles are tried: direct code writing, refinement guided by pseudocode, and a curriculum that builds up difficulty. A feedback loop then revises the code based on how it scored. Six leading models were tested on two hard benchmarks, a grid reasoning suite and a mini grid suite. The iterative approach beat direct code writing by wide margins, and set a new best result on one benchmark.
arxiv-2505-10949:
Chenhui Xu, Dancheng Liu, Amir Nassereldine and Jinjun Xiong argue that arithmetic precision, not bad minima, causes physics-informed neural network failures, in their 2025 arXiv paper. These networks solve differential equations, yet often the physics loss falls while the true error stays large. The standard story blames local optima behind steep barriers.

The authors show the real culprit: in standard thirty-two-bit arithmetic, the optimizer's convergence test triggers too early and freezes the network in a failure phase. Switching to sixty-four-bit precision lets plain networks solve the equations cleanly. Training follows three stages whose boundaries shift with precision, reframing reliability as an arithmetic question.
arxiv-2505-11649:
Chu and four colleagues study how people bond with AI companion chatbots in twenty twenty-five. The bots offer steady empathy and praise, which can feel like closeness. Over seventeen thousand user shared chats from Reddit forums were analyzed. The team tracked how feeling flows between user and bot.

The bots mirror user mood and pump up good feelings. That held even when users shared explicit or rule breaking content. Such mirroring may drive the intimacy illusion the title names. An anonymized data set of charged chats is released for study. The authors urge treating social bots as high risk for tender users.
arxiv-2505-11749:
Jiahao Yu and co-authors filled missing data by hiding its pattern in two thousand twenty-five. Real datasets often have gaps from failed sensors or skipped answers. Good filling should erase clues about where gaps were. If gaps remain predictable, the data still leak their pattern. The team targets the shared information between data and gap mask. Lowering it step by step drives their method.

Each round shrinks a divergence between joint and separate patterns. The best filling solves a flow equation they derive. Standard flow training gives that velocity field. Older filling methods appear as rough special cases. Tests on synthetic and real data were extensive. The framing unifies a scattered field of techniques. Cleaner imputation helps every downstream model.
arxiv-2505-11949: Hossein Larki and Najmeh Rajabzadeh-Hasiri extend a symmetry idea from graphs to a broader class called ultragraphs. Their 2025 paper defines what it means for a group to act on an ultragraph in a self-similar way, generalizing a notion due to Exel and Pardo. To each such action they attach a C*-algebra, an object blending algebra with analysis. They study those algebras through two models, one built from an inverse semigroup and one from a tight groupoid.
arxiv-2505-12049:
Mehran Shakerinava, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, and Adam Oberman widen how smart agents weigh goals in a 2025 paper. Most agents chase one score. But some wants cannot be traded: a first goal may outrank a second at any cost, like safety over speed.

Old lore showed that dropping one smooth rule lets worth be a ranked list, not a lone score. The team finds a plain, handy test for when a lone score fails and a two-part score is forced. They then map such scores in full, for two parts and for any count, in step-by-step choice tasks. Agent builders gain a firm base for ranked aims.
arxiv-2505-12149:
Physics-guided neural nets learn fast under natural gradient steps, but each step costs heavy compute. Andrés Guzmán-Cordero, Felix Dangel, Gil Goldshlager, and Marius Zeinhofer cut that cost in a 2025 paper. Three tricks stack in their method.

A matrix identity shrinks the core solve by a wide margin. A borrowed subsampling scheme adds momentum-like speed. Random sketches trim work further when batches run large. In tests, the stack reached the same error up to 75 times faster. Random tricks helped most early on in small problems. The team maps where each trick pays off.
arxiv-2505-12549:
Maggio, Lim, and Carlone present VGGT-SLAM, a system that builds dense 3D maps from ordinary video using only uncalibrated monocular cameras. It builds on a feed-forward reconstruction method that turns short video clips into local maps, then stitches those submaps together. Earlier systems aligned submaps with simple transforms covering shift, rotation, and scale. The authors show this is not enough for uncalibrated cameras, because the true scene can then only be recovered up to a projective transform with 15 degrees of freedom.

Their fix is to align submaps by optimizing over that full family of transforms, while also respecting loop closures when the camera revisits a place. In extensive tests, the system produced better maps over long videos that the base method cannot handle alone, since its memory demands grow too large. The work extends feed-forward reconstruction to practical, longer mapping runs.
arxiv-2505-12849:
Ben Liu and Zhen Qin speed up a state of the art image generator called TarFlow, in this 2025 paper. The model marries transformer blocks with a flow method and tops several benchmarks. Its weakness is sampling: the step by step design forces slow, sequential drawing of each image.

The authors recast sampling as an iteration problem and attack it with a blended solver method. They first rank blocks by how fast each settles and score how good a starting guess each receives. Difficult blocks then get more iterations and careful starts, while easy ones finish quickly. Across four model variants the trick sped sampling up to about five times. Image quality scores did not slip. Code and trained models are public.
arxiv-2505-13249:
Le Vu Anh, Dinh Duc Nha Nguyen, and Phi Long Nguyen present a 2025 study on a hidden flaw in large language models. Test data can leak into the data a model trains on, which makes test scores look better than they are. Past tools for spotting such leaks have been weak or slow. The team set out to build a faster and surer check.

Their method, called RN-F, reads faint leftover patterns in the model's own signals to flag leaked items. It needs one pass, uses no gradient work, and adds no extra math load. The method works across models and needs no change to the model itself. On several models and leaked data sets, RN-F beat the best prior tools, with gains of up to 10.5 percent on detection scores. The work gives testers a light way to guard the honesty of model scores.
arxiv-2505-13449:
Maram Albalwe, Blair Archibald, and Michele Sevegnani extend a graph-based modeling method so it can handle real-time systems, in a 2025 paper. The method, built on bigraphs, describes systems that change both in space and in links, like a person in a room or phones in contact.

Until now the method had no sense of time. The authors add digital clocks drawn from several viewpoints, so a model can show time passing between actions. Their setup lets each state offer a choice: let time pass, or act now. They built the approach in an existing toolkit and tested it on examples, including cloud system requests. The work opens the method to deadlines and timed behavior.
arxiv-2505-13649:
Ayrton da Cruz Pereira do Nascimento, Henrique Boschi-Filho, and Jorge Noronha work out proton structure functions from a holographic gravity model, in a paper from 2025. Such maps show how a fast probe sees the parts inside a proton.

Their frame extends past holographic work to models where a scalar field shapes the bulk space. The chosen field form matches known lattice results for glueball mass and hot pure gauge heat traits. With the scene set, probe fields yield the two structure functions. One of them matched lab data well at large momentum share, and the proton mass came out right.
arxiv-2505-13749:
Yousef Shakiba, Henry Sinclair-Banks, and Georg Zetzsche study where the border lies between easy and hard problems in systems with a single counter. Their 2025 paper starts from two classic tasks. Reachability asks if an exact state can be hit. Coverability asks if a state at or above a target can be hit. The first is known to be hard, the second much easier.

They place both tasks in a broader frame set by a Presburger formula that links target and reached state. For three kinds of systems, they prove a sharp split. Each formula makes the problem either hard in the NP-complete sense or solvable in a low circuit class. They also show which side a formula falls on can be decided.
arxiv-2505-14049:
Gao and co-authors build a medical image classifier whose decisions read as plain logical rules built from named concepts. Concept-based models promise explanations doctors can audit, but soft concept scores can smuggle stray information, and most give only case-by-case reasons. Their 2025 framework learns yes-no concepts from images, then layers logic over them to extract rules.

The rules explain both single cases and the model's global behavior. On two medical imaging tasks, the model matched rival accuracy while generalizing far better to data from new sources. The authors release their code. They present rule-based reading as a safety feature for clinical AI.
arxiv-2505-14449:
Yi-Cheng Lin, Huang-Cheng Chou, and Hung-yi Lee tackle subgroup bias in speech emotion recognition in a 2025 methods paper. Systems that read emotion from voice can perform unevenly across demographic groups, raising fairness concerns. Fixing that bias usually needs explicit demographic labels, which are hard to obtain because of privacy rules and user reluctance.

Their method infers rough group structure without such labels. A module uses pseudo-labels from a pretrained model plus unsupervised clustering with k-means to spot hidden subgroups in the data. Experiments show the pseudo-labels help reduce performance gaps between groups. Fairer emotion tools matter as voice AI spreads into hiring, health care, and customer service.
arxiv-2505-14549:
Dzung Pham and co-authors test in 2025 whether large language models can spot human names well enough for privacy work. Privacy tools lean on models to find and hide personal data, and names are a core type. Names that sound like common words can fool the models even in short texts.

The team built a test set of more than twelve thousand real but ambiguous names in many short clips. Across twelve top models, recall for those names fell by twenty to forty percent versus clearer names. Trap texts that mix data with commands made the miss rate far worse in one work tool. The gap raises fairness fears for privacy cover.
arxiv-2505-14649:
Dubicki and co-authors study tiny magnetic whirlpools called skyrmions, and how they stack in layered films, in a 2025 paper. A skyrmion is a stable swirl of atomic spins that could store bits in future low-power devices. The team looks at stacks of ultrathin magnetic layers, where a skyrmion in one layer feels the stray field of its neighbors. That coupling can hold the stack together.

Starting from the standard model of micromagnetism, the authors boil the energy down to a simpler form. For many layers, the whole system reduces to one skyrmion per layer, each set by its place, size, and twist angle. They prove that lowest-energy states exist for fixed spots. For the two-layer case they solve the puzzle fully: the winners are two whirlpools with opposed in-plane spins, held by their own stray fields.
arxiv-2505-14749:
Ding-fang Zeng presents a 2025 physics paper on the complementarity of gravitational collapse, the second in a series. The catalog title differs, but the text itself develops an exact one body method, called XOB, for two body gravity problems such as merging black holes.

Zeng shows that the method, expanded for weak fields and low speeds, matches the standard post Newtonian series to all orders for the conservative part of the motion. With a modulated formula, it yields merger waveforms that agree closely with large numerical simulations. Zeng argues the match supports inner structure in black holes.
arxiv-2505-14949:
Zach Yarbrough and co-authors build PINCH, a tool that sorts noise glitches from real signals in LIGO gravitational wave data. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses triggers from matched-filter search pipelines. Short noise bursts can mimic waves and muddy the hunt for real events.

Support vector machines were trained on triggers from quiet times to learn the look of plain noise. Each trained model then scores unclear triggers by how noise-like they seem. Scores above a set line mark a trigger as glitch-made. The method ran on both LIGO sites for the second half of the third observing run. Cleaner trigger lists help astronomers trust candidate waves.
arxiv-2505-15249:
Yerin Hwang and five co-authors ask whether doctored images can fool the vision-language models now used to grade text-to-image output. These model judges are popular for scoring how well a picture matches its prompt. Their reliability on the visual side had barely been tested.

The team defines several image-induced biases and adds them to FRAME, a new benchmark built with varied score distributions across domains. Every tested judge inflated scores for manipulated images, in every domain. Stacking multiple biases made the effect stronger, and pairwise judging was fooled too. Prompt-based defenses did not remove the bias. The authors call for sturdier model judges before evaluation pipelines lean on them further.
arxiv-2505-15449:
Arisa and three co-authors study how a step like electric potential controls quantum phases in a one dimensional Hubbard chain. The Hubbard model captures electrons that move along a chain and repel when they share a site. At half filling, the chain can act as an insulator, a metal, or a band insulator.

By tracking tunneling energy, charge and spin gaps, and entanglement between chain halves, the team maps all three phases. In the metal phase both gaps close, and local pair counts and entanglement wobble in a near periodic pattern as the potential steps grow. Added spin polarization shrinks the metal region. The work shows electric steps as a knob for phase control.
arxiv-2505-15749:
Pritthijit Biswas and Jaya Iyer write, in 2025 work, a note on special zones inside a space of stable bundles over a curve. The zones in view collect bundles that own at least two free-standing global parts. Such zones are a classic topic in the study of curves and their linked spaces.

For a typical curve and a fixed twist of set size, the pair study the zone for rank-two bundles. At low curve genus they show the zone has strong traits tied to ratios of shapes. At genus three it is stably of that kind, at four it is a step weaker, and from five up it is linked by chains of special curves. They also show some low counting groups of a linked surface are empty.
arxiv-2505-16049:
Dongyoung Park and Gaby Dagher model cyber defence as a game in which attacker and defender both pursue their own payoffs, rather than a zero-sum fight. Their framework spells out payoff functions built from the chance and cost of each exploit, the value of network nodes, and the cost of planting honeypots. Solving the game yields Nash equilibria — strategy pairs neither side wants to leave — that guide both attack and defence choices.

Simulations confirm that the model sharpens network security. Cheap, likely attacks such as phishing and social engineering draw attackers most, so defences should meet them first. Adding more nodes spreads an attacker's effort thin and improves the defender's outcome. The authors present the model as a practical tool for allocating security resources, one that scales as networks grow and keeps the costs of defence in view.
arxiv-2505-16149:
Zirui Pang and co-authors clean the answer keys of famous image classification tests using vision-language models, in a 2025 paper. Benchmark sets like ImageNet and CIFAR still carry wrong labels, and many images actually show several classes while listing one. Those missing labels quietly corrupt model rankings. The team's framework, REVEAL, combines several vision-language models with automated and crowd label-checking tools. It flags suspect labels, pools the predictions, and filters by confidence and consensus.

Human verifiers confirmed the fixes across six benchmark test sets, bringing labels much closer to human judgment. The framework outputs soft labels with likelihoods rather than blunt verdicts. An analysis of the models involved surfaces ten observations about their strengths and blind spots. The authors argue fair evaluation starts with honest test data.
arxiv-2505-16449:
Gianmarco Del Sarto, Matthias Hieber, and Tarek Zöchling analyze a climate model with noisy boundaries. Their 2025 paper couples an energy balance model to geophysical flow equations. The link runs through a dynamic boundary condition, with and without random noise. Such models mimic how surface energy and ocean motion interact.

The team proves the full system is well-posed in a strong global sense. The proof covers the plain deterministic case for large starting data. It also covers the noisy case in a standard function space. Well-posedness means solutions exist, are unique, and behave stably. That groundwork lets later studies trust simulations built on the model.
arxiv-2505-16649:
Zhichao Zhu and co-authors rework the Forward-Forward learning rule, a training method that skips backpropagation. Each layer learns from a goodness score instead of a global error signal. Old scores just add up squared activations. They ignore how neurons vary together. Noise, in this scheme, is usually a nuisance.

The new score uses the effective dimensionality of a layer's response. The rule squeezes that spread for noisy copies of one input and stretches it across different inputs. No hand-made negative examples are needed. Scores rival other non-backprop methods. Noise turns into a helper here, aiding generalization. The authors pitch the method for brain-like chips where randomness comes free.
arxiv-2505-16849:
Böckling, Paulheim, and Iana introduced a simple method in twenty twenty-five for grounding language model answers in a knowledge graph. Models often invent facts or rely on stale memory, and fetching facts from a structured graph can fix that, but many fetching schemes are heavy and brittle.

Their method, Walk&Retrieve, wanders the graph along short paths from the question's key terms. It then turns what it finds into plain sentences, building a small text the model can read before answering. No training on special data is needed, so the method adapts at once when the graph changes. Despite its simplicity, it matched or beat more complex systems on answer accuracy and cut made-up facts. It also answered faster and scaled to large graphs. The authors offer it as a strong, light baseline for future work.
arxiv-2505-17149:
Qin Chen and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how well large language models can forecast from data. Forecasting guides choices in fields from health to trade. Models shine at talk and code, yet skill at forecasts from real data was untested. The team built a test set, named PredictiQ, to fill that gap.

The set holds over a thousand queries drawn from dozens of real data sets in eight fields. Their checks weigh text insight, code craft, and how well the two line up. Twelve known models took the test. All faced steep hurdles in this kind of work. The team shares the test in public for later use.
arxiv-2505-17349:
David Porlles and Wei Chen trace the Meissner effect, the expulsion of magnetic fields by superconductors, to the quantum geometry of momentum space. Their paper appeared in 2025. Recent work defines a quantum metric from how filled states overlap at neighboring momenta. For superconductors with several bands and mixed pairing, the team shows the superfluid weight, the stiffness behind the Meissner effect, equals a weighted sum of that metric's parts.

Summing the metric also gives the spread of the state's localized wave packets, a stability marker for superconductivity. Their marker can be drawn site by site on a lattice, even with disorder included. In test cases, the diamagnetic current turned turbulent around impurities, and the field penetration depth grew, matching experiments.
arxiv-2505-17449:
Inpyo Song and Jangwon Lee build a fast system that warns of traffic accidents before they happen, in a paper from 2025. Early warning is vital for safe self-driving, but most methods use heavy extra modules that slow them down. Real-time use needs both speed and accuracy.

Their system reuses features already computed by a single object detector, skipping extra extraction steps. A new training loss forces attention onto objects linked to the coming crash over irrelevant ones. On two standard benchmarks it ran several times faster than rivals, at dozens of frames per second. Accuracy still reached top levels, and warnings stayed explainable.
arxiv-2505-17749:
Ghada Sokar and Pablo Samuel Castro wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on why deep reinforcement learning agents trained on raw pixels fail to scale. Larger networks often perform worse in such settings, and the cause was unclear. Earlier fixes patched the issue indirectly through new designs or training tricks.

The authors trace the problem to one junction: where the image encoder, a stack of layers that read the pixels, hands its output to the dense layers that decide actions. They call this junction the bottleneck. Their analysis shows earlier remedies were all easing pressure at that same point. They propose global average pooling as a simple, direct fix for the bottleneck. The method avoids the complexity of the earlier workarounds.
arxiv-2505-17849:
Daniel VandenHeuvel and Sheehan Olver developed in 2025 an efficient finite element method for equations whose solutions are smooth in pieces, with wrap-around boundary rules. Their basis uses orthogonal polynomials defined on arcs of a circle. Operators built from this basis stay banded and cheap, whatever the mesh or degree.

The basis also spans the basic modes of constant-coefficient operators, which helps time-stepping problems run smoothly. Links between convergence and where the solution can be extended into the complex plane are drawn. Several example equations show the behavior in practice. The authors offer the basis as a strong swap for Fourier or integrated Legendre bases where jumps occur.
arxiv-2505-17949:
Mieke Wessel and Svenja zur Verth write, in twenty twenty-five, a math paper on counting solutions to a quadratic equation with restricted variables. A quadratic form is an expression built from squared terms and cross terms. They study a non-singular form, meaning a well-behaved one, with many mixed terms. They fix a target integer and ask how many weighted solutions land on it. The weights come from a chosen sequence, which limits which variables count.

Their tool is the circle method, a classic way to count number theory solutions by splitting an integral into parts. They give conditions on both the weights and the form that let the method work. Only solutions up to a set height are counted.
arxiv-2505-18049:
Gaole Dai and co-authors build a vision system inspired by how the human eye splits its sensing work. Their 2025 paper notes that cone cells handle color while rod cells track motion and light change. Modern cameras echo that split: normal cameras capture color, while spike cameras record rapid brightness changes.

Their system, SpikeGen, feeds both streams into a generative model that works in a compressed latent space. The team test it on several joint tasks: sharpening blurred images and video, rebuilding dense frames from spike streams, and synthesizing new views of fast scenes. Experiments show the split design handles these tasks well. Borrowing the eye's division of labor may help machines see fast, messy scenes more reliably.
arxiv-2505-18149:
Giving a language model more time to think usually means generating many long attempts, which costs tokens and patience. Aradhye Agarwal, Ayan Sengupta, and Tanmoy Chakraborty notice a pattern in 2025: for reasoning tasks, short traces are far more likely to be right than long ones. Their method, First Finish Search, starts several independent attempts at once. It simply returns the first one that finishes. No extra training is needed.

On hard math contest sets, the method lifted one model's accuracy to 82 percent, a gain of 15 points, close to a leading commercial system. The theory explains when stopping early helps and when it can mislead. The authors argue that simple test-time tricks still hold untapped power.
arxiv-2505-18549:
Judging whether an AI tutor's reply actually helps a student takes more than one score. Baraa Hikal and three co-authors enter a 2025 shared task on grading tutor responses along four lines: spotting the student's mistake, locating it, giving guidance, and suggesting a doable next step. Their system fine-tunes one language model for all four tracks through a single training pipeline.

At judging time, they add a twist: an ensemble step that listens for disagreement among model votes, which improves coverage of rare labels. The system placed first in Providing Guidance, third in Actionability, and fourth in both mistake tracks. The authors present the work as evidence that disagreement-aware tuning makes educational judging sturdier.
arxiv-2505-18849:
Mohamed Aly Bouke builds a theory of random fractals in this 2025 paper. Classical iterated function systems stamp out self-similar shapes by repeating fixed maps, and his generalization makes the maps both nonlinear and random, which he calls RNIFS.

He proves that stable fractal attractors exist for such systems, using contraction conditions and Lyapunov style criteria. Simulations across many functions and random schemes then measured the shapes that emerge, with box counting giving dimensions between 1.4 and 1.89. A case study against the classic Sierpiński triangle shows the random version keeping the global shape while adding inner detail. The work aims at modeling rich natural fractals.
arxiv-2505-19149:
Shuyu Wang and four co-authors present an image editing system guided by a large multimodal model in this 2025 paper. Such models read both text and images, but past editing tools used mainly their text side. That leaves edits imprecise when instructions are vague or scenes are complex.

Their system, MIND-Edit, pairs the large model with an image generator. One strategy rewrites unclear user instructions using the model's reasoning. A second strategy lets the model's visual grasp form guiding signals for the edit itself. Joint training lets the two strategies reinforce each other. In tests, the system beat leading editing tools on both scores and visual quality. The gains were clearest in hard, complex scenes.
arxiv-2505-19249:
Mir Sazzat Hossain and co-authors share a new data set in 2025 for sorting bent radio galaxies by image. Bent galaxies shoot out curved jets of radio waves as they move through gas in galaxy clusters. Their bent shape tells scholars about the gas and about how clusters grow and change.

Few shared data sets exist for this task, so progress has been slow. The new set, called RGC-Bent, sorts galaxies into narrow-angle tail and wide-angle tail kinds. It comes from a known radio survey and ships with clear prep steps. The team tested top deep learning models on it, from classic image nets to transformer forms. A model called ConvNeXT scored best on both kinds. The set and scores are shared to speed work in the field.
arxiv-2505-19649:
Santiago Radi proves a set of first-of-their-kind facts about a group built from a simple polynomial rule. Iterated monodromy groups arise by tracking how a polynomial's solutions branch as inputs loop around. Radi studies the group for the polynomial whose rule adds the imaginary unit after squaring. He shows this group is just-infinite, meaning every proper quotient of it is finite. He also shows it branches regularly over its own copies.

The third finding is negative: the group lacks the congruence subgroup property, a tidiness condition many such groups enjoy. Together these give the first known example of a polynomial's group with all three traits at once. Radi adds detail on three kernels that measure how far the group sits from that tidiness condition. The work sharpens the map of what these groups can look like.
arxiv-2505-19949:
What makes a training example teach a language model to reason? Siqi Kou and co-authors answer with influence functions. The tool traces a model's skill back to the individual examples, sequences, and tokens it trained on. Their attribution study covers chains of thought for math and coding problems. Such chains are the usual fuel for sharpening reasoning after training.

The findings cross domains in surprising ways. Hard math examples improve both math and code reasoning. Easy code tasks help coding most. Simply reweighting a dataset by flipping these difficulty preferences doubled one benchmark score and lifted another. Zooming in further, exploratory moves inside a solution help everywhere. But math leans on plain-language logic connectors while code leans on structural syntax.
arxiv-2505-20049:
Hongsong Wang, Ao Sun, Jie Gui, and Liang Wang teach computers to learn new hand gestures without forgetting old ones, in a paper published in 2025. Most gesture systems handle a fixed set, but real uses keep adding signs. Saving old training videos may be barred by privacy or storage, so the system must learn from what it already knows.

Their framework invents stand-in features for old gestures from stored class summaries, then mixes them with real data for new gestures. A replay step keeps the classifier's weights aligned with old class centers, and a trimmed loss limits distortion from the fake features. A final retraining balances old and new. Tests on two public gesture datasets showed strong retention. The method suits sign language and control systems that grow over time.
arxiv-2505-20849:
Rosendahl and Kirkeby present a 2025 framework for checking data flow inside custom hardware designs. Chips built on programmable arrays speed up heavy computing, but their parallel layout is hard to design well. Data must move between parts at the right time and rate. The framework studies that traffic without running the chip, a static check done from the design text.

The check maps how parts of the datapath talk to each other. Those maps show jams, dead ends, and waste that a designer can fix early. Static checks cost far less than building and testing a flawed chip. The authors aim the tool at design and tuning stages of hardware work. Clear views of data traffic are a base need for fast, sound accelerators.
arxiv-2505-20949:
Andrea Giovanni Nuzzolese, writing alone in 2025, presents PyRML, a Python library for building knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs weave mixed data into linked facts for many fields. Mapping languages like RML state how to turn tables into graph form. Python users lacked a native way to write and run those mappings.

PyRML supports the core of RML inside plain Python code. Mappings can be authored, run, and tested in one place. It plugs into Pandas for data and RDFlib for graph handling. Workflows stay modular and open to inspection. Shared, repeatable mappings help teams trust their graphs. The library lowers the entry bar for careful data integration.
arxiv-2505-21249:
Mohamed Benzaghta and co-authors propose data-driven ways in 2025 to manage handovers in cellular networks. As networks grow denser and users move at varied speeds, fixed handover settings often fail. Settings that are too slow cause dropped links, while fast ones cause wasteful back-and-forth switches.

One approach tunes handover settings with a smart search method. The other lets a learning agent pick the serving cell from live network data. Both beat standard benchmark settings in a real-world scenario modeled with ray tracing. Transfer learning helps both adapt to new user speeds, including drone users.
arxiv-2505-21549:
