Neutrino masses are another target, since the standard model leaves them unexplained. The team seeks one set of new particles, near the weak scale, that can do both jobs.

Their setup adds one extra Higgs doublet, one charged scalar particle, and one right-handed neutrino to the standard cast. Neutrino masses arise from three known routes working together, a seesaw step plus two loop effects. Careful alignment of the Higgs fields keeps flavor-changing effects small, which is the danger in such models. The authors show the setup can also fit the Cabibbo angle puzzle and the W boson mass gap.
arxiv-2506-23049:
Leander Melroy Maben and co-authors introduce AURA in 2025, an open-source voice assistant that can act, not just chat. Speech systems have advanced fast, yet no open system offered full speech-to-speech talk over several turns with tool use and step-by-step reasoning. AURA joins open speech recognition, speech synthesis, and language models in one pipeline.

The assistant books calendar events, looks up contacts, searches the web, and sends email, and new tools plug in through plain prompts. On standard voice benchmarks it beat all open-weight rivals on one knowledge test, nearly matching a leading closed system, and scored well on a chat quality test. Human judges gave it ninety percent success on complex multi-turn speech tasks.
arxiv-2506-23249:
Maria Fernando and Mallikarjunaiah present a phase-field framework for slow shear cracking in elastic materials, in a 2025 paper. Phase-field models smear a crack into a damage zone, which makes hard fracture problems computable.

Their version unites two upgrades: the mesh refines itself around the damage zone as the run proceeds, and the stored energy follows a nonlinear law for modern materials. A modified energy balance yields two linked equations for motion and damage. Standard elements solve them on the adapting mesh. Four key parameters are tuned by careful limit analysis. Results show robust convergence with better use of computing effort than fixed meshes.
arxiv-2506-23349:
Naggita and LaChance argue that the scores used to price and select training data can quietly mislead. Data valuation methods rate how much each data point helps a model. Buyers in data markets might pay by those scores, so fairness matters.

Testing nine datasets and six valuation methods, the authors show simple preprocessing choices swing the scores wildly. Selecting data by score can deepen class imbalance. Data from underrepresented groups tends to be undervalued. They propose Data Valuation Cards, standard reports that disclose how scores were produced. Wider disclosure, they argue, would curb misuse and build trust in data markets.
arxiv-2506-23549:
Huai-Chih Wang and co-authors teach AI agents to coordinate with partners they have never met. Working with strangers is hard for multi-agent systems: training against diverse partners helps, but adaptation to a truly new partner is slow, and fine-tuning costs too many interactions. Their framework, CooT, uses in-context learning instead. Trained on recordings of agents with strong behavior preferences, it infers a partner's intent from a short history of play and aligns its own actions, with no parameter updates.

On two benchmarks, a cooking game and a football game, CooT beat population-based training, fine-tuning, and meta-learning rivals. Human judges also preferred it as a collaborator. Stress tests showed it adapts quickly and stays stable when a partner suddenly changes style. The authors aim the method at human-AI teamwork, where habits are unknown and retraining is costly.
arxiv-2506-24049:
Kévin Le Balc'h, Jingrui Niu, and Chenmin Sun revisit a basic question in control theory: from which regions can one observe a quantum particle's state on a donut-shaped surface? For the plain Schrödinger equation, any open patch, however small, suffices. Adding a magnetic field changes the story.

The authors study operators that combine electric and magnetic effects on the two-dimensional torus. They prove a geometric condition that is both sufficient and nearly necessary for observability, meaning some regions work and others provably cannot. The condition folds the magnetic potential into the geometry of paths across the surface. It can also be restated as a control condition on the magnetic field itself. The result closes a gap left by the classical theory, where magnetism was an afterthought.
arxiv-2507-00049:
Feiyang Kang and six co-authors present a method to shrink training data for object detection in a 2025 paper. Huge data sets hold much redundancy, yet cutting data blindly can drop rare, vital cases. Older pruning methods either ignore the task or cost too much to run at scale.

Their method first clusters the data and prunes by density, then uses a small proxy model to compare losses on kept versus cut items in each cluster. That feedback tightens or loosens the cut for each cluster on its own. On three large driving and photo benchmarks, the method kept near full accuracy while cutting a fifth of the data.
arxiv-2507-00249:
Nikhil Kumar, a solo author, models how social learning networks form themselves in a 2025 paper. In social learning, people update beliefs by watching others, so who listens to whom shapes what everyone ends up thinking. Usually the network is taken as given. Here, agents choose both how sharp a signal to buy and which aspect of the world to learn about, and those choices build the network itself.

Under a fixed network, each agent's best signal sharpness grows slower than their influence, and private choice falls short of the social best by a factor tied to group size. Under a flexible network, distance between agents sets how much weight they give each other. Agents pick topics in a way that tends to spread influence evenly, which the author identifies as the ideal shape.
arxiv-2507-00349:
Lü, You, and Zhao (2025) introduce a broad family of infinite-dimensional Lie superalgebras and settle their basic structure. A Lie superalgebra mixes ordinary symmetry rules with sign rules borrowed from physics. The family built here twists the known affine-Virasoro type. The twist uses a chosen derivation and a finite-order symmetry that commute. The class is wide. It contains many named algebras at once, from twisted Heisenberg-Virasoro algebras to the W-algebra W(2,2) and the N=1 BMS superalgebra.

The authors determine the universal central extension of the new algebras. That is the standard way of adding the central terms physics applications need. They then classify the well-behaved modules over them, cuspidal ones first, through a weighting method. Then they classify all simple modules with finite-dimensional weight spaces. The results gather many findings from math and physics into one frame, and add new examples.
arxiv-2507-00449:
Zhihao Zhan and co-authors analyze in 2025 why state-space models falter on very long texts. These models promise fast handling of long sequences, unlike the dominant attention design whose cost grows steeply. Yet they struggle to recall distant facts, and the usual test task, recalling one key without context, is too simple to show why.

The team defines a harder joint recall task where the right value depends on context. They prove state-space models cannot solve it in fast time, then blend them with sparse attention that can. A hashing-based version tuned for language beat state-space baselines on both made-up and real long-text benchmarks.
arxiv-2507-00549:
Vijay Yadav and co-authors simulate how two tiny particles interact when a charged polymer floats between them in a 2025 paper. Charged polymers let engineers tune the surface charge of nanoparticles, a skill at the heart of many nanotech designs. The polymer here carries the opposite charge to the particles, so it is drawn to their surfaces.

A subtlety drives the study: particle charge is not fixed. It shifts with acidity, salt, and chain length, an effect called charge regulation. Their hybrid simulation lets charge adjust as the system runs, and they compare it with runs where charge is frozen. Regulation pulled more polymer onto the surfaces. With frozen charge, the polymer instead bridged the gap between particles across a wide range of spacings. The contrast matters for anyone designing particle assemblies.
arxiv-2507-00649:
Wittmer, Cavallo, and Johner simulate flat, self-assembled polymer chains that can break and rejoin. Their 2025 paper deals with equilibrium polymers in two dimensions, built from hard disks linked in lines with no branches, rings, or crossings. Even-width chains are known to pack into compact shapes with fractal edges when long and dense. The team asks if chains of mixed length, set by a finite break cost, share that fate.

They do: the same universal exponents rule both kinds. Length spread follows a known distribution, and mean length grows with break cost and density at set rates. Scattering from the mixed chains shows the same fractal edge as even chains, the team reports.
arxiv-2507-01249:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations published a 2025 paper reporting a search for a hypothetical particle in decays of B mesons. Axion-like particles are candidates in theories that extend the Standard Model, possibly tied to dark matter. If they exist with the right properties, a B meson could decay into a kaon plus the new particle, which would then turn into two photons. That signature is what the search targets.

The data come from electron-positron collisions recorded by the Belle detector, analyzed with its successor collaboration. Physicists sifted the collisions for the telltale kaon-and-two-photon pattern above noise. Searches of this kind either find the particle or fence off where it could still hide, narrowing the masses and coupling strengths allowed. The paper adds a checked corner in the hunt for physics beyond the particle list.
arxiv-2507-01349:
Hitoshi Suda and co-authors built a song set in 2025 in the style of Japanese idol groups. Idol songs pack many voices, thick backing, and loud, dense mixes. Singers swap solo lines and group parts in a set form. Those traits make the songs a hard test bed for music software that must split singers, part out sources, or read chords. Pro composers were hired to write fifteen fresh tracks in that style.

The set ships the full mixes plus the split parts: clean voice tracks, split backing stems, and chord notes. Checks showed its range stands near that of real idol songs. The team ran known music tools on it to show where they strain. The corpus is aimed at fair tests in a hard corner of pop.
arxiv-2507-01449:
Tianyu Liu and co-authors speed up text generation by guessing ahead. In speculative decoding, draft tokens are proposed and the model checks several at once. Retrieval-based versions fetch drafts from a reference text instead of running a small model, but they often fail to find a match. The model's output scores for the last token hint at the next token and the one after. LogitSpec uses that hint twice over.

It first speculates the next-next token, then retrieves references matching the next and next-next tokens, widening the pool of drafts. The method needs no training and plugs into existing inference frameworks. On benchmarks it reached up to two and a half times speedup, with more accepted tokens per step. The authors release the code. The trick is a reminder that model outputs carry more information than the next word.
arxiv-2507-01549:
Jacob Elford and Timothy Davis lead a team checking whether dense gas line ratios can flag an active galactic nucleus, by comparing them against the classic optical verdict. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A tight link between dense gas and star formation anchors galaxy studies. Some claim the same lines betray a feeding black hole.

Five nearby unobscured nuclei were observed with a submillimeter array for three dense gas lines. Three targets yielded the needed detections. Even with the nucleus's influence, the galaxies obeyed the known gas-star formation relation. Optical spectra gave the standard excitation classification for comparison. Where both verdicts existed, submillimeter and optical agreed overall. The authors infer that nuclei excite dense molecular gas and thin ionized gas together. A new diagnostic survives its first cross-check. The survey's reference data set grows in value.
arxiv-2507-01649:
Yoav Gelberg and co-authors present GradMetaNet, a network built to learn from the gradients of other networks, in a 2025 paper. Gradients carry rich signals for tuning, pruning, and studying models. Most tools that learn from gradients use generic designs. Those designs ignore the special structure gradients have.

GradMetaNet follows three guiding ideas from the start. Its design respects the symmetry that swapping neurons leaves a network unchanged. It reads sets of gradients from many data points to capture curvature. It also stays efficient enough for real use. The authors argue this principled design widens where gradient learning can help. Tasks from model editing to faster training stand to benefit.
arxiv-2507-02049:
Abhishek Banerjee, Manuel Buen-Abad, and Anson Hook study axions that are lighter than their couplings would suggest. Their 2025 paper starts from a multi-copy symmetry model of the axion. A small added link between the Higgs field and a reheating field breaks that symmetry just a touch.

That small break opens a large part of the light axion plane to study. It also removes a fine-tuning flaw of the base model and explains why only our sector was reheated after inflation. Heat effects then force one of two fates on the axion's starting angle. It is pinned near a set value, or it is shuffled at random. The authors frame the odds in gambling terms.
arxiv-2507-02549:
Yue Wu builds a controller that steadies a nonlinear system by a deadline the user picks, in this 2025 paper. Model-based control needs exact models, while pure data methods lack safety proofs. Wu's framework joins both: a data method first lifts the system into a high-dimensional linear model, called a Koopman model, and measures its error bound. A new adaptive backstepping design then works on that model.

The design dodges the complexity blow-up that plagues classic backstepping. Tests on the classic Van der Pol oscillator show the states settling near zero within the chosen time, from any start. All signals stay bounded. The author presents the pairing as a way to keep data-driven flexibility with proof-grade rigor for safety-critical control.
arxiv-2507-02649:
Sunder Ram Krishnan extends a key idea from compressed sensing to heavier-tailed randomness, in a 2025 math paper. Compressed sensing recovers sparse signals from few measures when its matrix acts almost like a rotation on sparse vectors. That behavior is the restricted isometry property. Krishnan defines a looser cousin of it, suited to stable laws with exponent below one, whose wild tails break the classic property.

He derives a lower bound on how many measurements the new property needs. The proof joins a concentration bound for fractional moments of stable variables with a covering bound for sparse balls in the matching norm. The count reflects the slow, polynomial grip such tails allow. Krishnan notes the result supports a wider view in the field: for such data, sparse recovery may need tools beyond the classic isometry framework.
arxiv-2507-02749:
Hamza Boumaza and David Langlois study how neutron stars ring when nudged sideways, under a modified gravity theory, in a research paper from 2025. The theory adds a scalar field with higher-order terms while avoiding known instabilities. Star shapes under the theory were computed in earlier work.

The authors derive the equations for axial wobbles of such stars. They then compute the ringing tones, the quasi-normal modes, for several theory settings and matter recipes. Both tone pitch and fade time shift away from standard gravity's values. They also test how the tones track star compactness, probing whether the usual universal links survive the modification.
arxiv-2507-02849:
Talath, Govindaraja, Divyamani, and three colleagues demonstrate a leaner way to reconstruct quantum states in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Quantum state tomography normally needs many measurement settings; for three qubits the conventional Pauli approach uses sixty-three. Their scheme needs only seventeen settings for full three-qubit tomography. They ran it on IBM's one hundred twenty-seven qubit open-access processor in Osaka, preparing the entangled three-qubit W state.

They also implemented a two-qubit protocol with seven settings to reconstruct two-qubit marginals of the W state. Theory says any two of a three-qubit pure state's two-qubit reductions determine most such states uniquely. Strikingly, the W state rebuilt from its marginals had consistently higher fidelity than the one from full tomography. The authors present this as proof of principle that subsystem-based tomography is not just cheaper but practically better on today's noisy hardware.
arxiv-2507-02949:
Vipula Rawte and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how faithfully language models use the sources they are given. Retrieval-augmented generation feeds a model outside facts to improve accuracy. Yet models often ignore or distort those facts, so answers drift from the evidence.

The team defines a score, Entity-Context Divergence, that measures how much retrieved facts survive into the answer. They call a model's skill at keeping facts its RAG-ability. Tests across current models show that skill is low in most of them. Their framework, RADIANT, extends a preference training method to teach models to align answers with retrieved evidence. It trains the model on pairs that reward faithful use of entities in context. The work gives builders both a yardstick and a training fix.
arxiv-2507-03049:
A bot that must tell why it acts owes each hearer a tale at their own depth, and that depth grows as the pair live as one. Ferran Gebellí and co-authors build a tale frame for the long haul in a 2025 study. A mind stock of what the hearer knows is kept and fed back, so tales can cite old lore as known.

Three builds of the frame, all word mill borne, are tried in two posts: a ward watch bot and a cook help bot. The win build drafts the tale whole, then trims it to the hearer's stock. It cuts depth just when the stock holds kin lore, and no more. The frame's aim is trust that lasts past the first meet.
arxiv-2507-03149:
Six authors, listed by first name in the record, study how accent strength shows up in the movements of speech in 2025. A strong accent means a speaker's sounds stray far from a standard pattern. The team wanted a measure based on how the tongue and lips actually move, not just how speech sounds.

They scored accent by comparing what speakers said with dictionary forms, sound by sound. A learned tool then guessed the hidden mouth movements behind the recordings. In read speech from American and British speakers, tongue position split the two groups best. The sounds most affected were the r-like vowels and low back vowels. The work aids tools that analyze accents on their own.
arxiv-2507-03749:
Nicolas Tessore and Alex Hall argue that shot noise in galaxy clustering maps is not noise at all. Their twenty twenty-five paper reworks a standard correction in cosmology. When points sample a field, pairs of a point with itself add a fixed term to the power spectrum.

That term, they show, cannot take the off-values often blamed on sampling quirks. Odd values instead signal real small-scale clustering or its lack. In simulations, how tracers are drawn from the field creates exactly those shifts. The cleanup matters: mislabeling signal as noise biases the cosmic measures that galaxy surveys exist to deliver, from dark energy to the growth of structure.
arxiv-2507-04349:
Jaeseok Jeong and co-authors present a way to add feeling to machine-made speech in this 2025 paper. Their system, TTS-CtrlNet, builds on a text-to-speech model that turns written words into spoken voice. Unlike older tools, it lets emotion shift over the course of a single spoken line.

The method borrows a trick from image software: keep the base model frozen and train a copy to handle the new control signal. That way the voice keeps its natural sound and its skill at copying a new speaker. The team shares design choices that made the control work well. Tests show the speech matches target feelings more closely than prior systems.
arxiv-2507-04549: Matilde Maccan studies symmetry groups of flag varieties in a 2025 math paper. These varieties are quotients of a semisimple group by a parabolic subgroup. Here the field has positive characteristic and the subgroup may be non-reduced. The paper works out the group scheme structure of the neutral component of their automorphism group. The result extends a classic theorem of Demazure on such groups. It shows the theorem holds for flag varieties in this broader setting.
arxiv-2507-04649:
Tuan Dang and Manfred Huber give a mobile work robot a human-like way to remember space, in this 2025 paper. Standard robot navigation builds one global map from sensor data, but such maps can drift out of consistency and fail in new places. Learning-based methods, meanwhile, cost heavy computation and generalize poorly.

Their hybrid map copies a human trick: hold local surroundings in short-term frames, then stitch those frames into a global sketch. Each local frame mixes raw position data with learned features, blending geometry and recognition. The frames join a topological map, written as a graph of places and links, and a tree-based planner uses both layers to route. Tests on public datasets and in their lab showed effective navigation. The code is public, and the authors pitch the design for collaborative robots in changing workplaces.
arxiv-2507-04749:
Chengyu Wang and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, a framework to rebuild three-dimensional shapes and their materials from photos taken from many angles. The core problem, inverse rendering, is to untangle shape, surface material, and lighting from flat images. Their method, MatDecompSDF, trains three neural parts jointly. One represents shape as a signed distance field, which gives the distance to the surface at each point. One predicts material traits such as base color, roughness, and metal content. One models the unknown scene lighting.

A rendering layer that follows physics links these parts back to the input photos, so training can proceed end to end. Extra rules enforce smooth materials and valid shape fields. Tests on synthetic and real data beat prior methods, and outputs can be edited and relit.
arxiv-2507-04849:
Manal Alsairafi, Nikolaos Dimitrakopoulos, and Malgorzata Worek compare decay models for four-top-quark events in a 2025 paper. Such events at the Large Hadron Collider are rare and rich in spin clues. How the decays are modeled can shift what the data seem to say.

One route keeps full higher-order fixes in both making and decay, with spin links intact. The other leans on shower tools with near spin links. The team test both at a set collider energy, across total and split rates. Extra decay fixes inside the shower tools are also weighed. The read guides how future four-top studies should treat decays.
arxiv-2507-05049:
Rodolphe Abou Assali introduces a biharmonic Steklov problem with Neumann type boundary conditions for differential forms. Steklov problems link interior equations to data on the boundary and yield spectra that encode shape. The author shows the new problem is well posed, so solutions exist and behave in a stable way.

A discrete spectrum is proved, with variational formulas that characterize each eigenvalue. Estimates of Kuttler and Sigillito type relate the new eigenvalues to those of the Steklov, Dirichlet, and Neumann problems. A comparison with the biharmonic Steklov problem under Dirichlet conditions is also given. The work extends spectral theory for higher order problems on forms, a setting with uses in geometry and physics.
arxiv-2507-05149:
Tom Hickling and co-authors present a 2025 paper on optimizing turbulent flows, the chaotic swirling found in engines and airflows. Engineers care about long-run averages, such as mean drag or heat flow, rather than any single instant. Standard gradient methods fail here, because the flow's chaos makes their gradients blow up over time.

Their online gradient flow method updates the design as the simulation runs, instead of waiting for a finished run. The approach scales to the huge grids that real turbulence needs. It suits tasks such as shaping parts, steering flows, and tuning model closures. The paper lays out the method and why it stays stable where older tools diverge.
arxiv-2507-05449:
Random clouds of points drawn from a bell curve have a tidy theory of splitting, built in a 2025 paper by Moshe J White. A Radon partition divides a point set into two groups whose convex hulls overlap, a basic fact of geometry with deep uses.

White packages all such splits of a set into one object, a Radon polytope whose faces are exactly the partitions. For points drawn at random from a Gaussian, he derives formulas for the chance that a given split is a Radon partition. The formulas lean on conic kinematic integrals and intrinsic volumes, and close fully in some cases. The frame may shed new light on open problems such as a relaxed form of Tverberg's conjecture.
arxiv-2507-05549:
Khatiwada and four colleagues weigh the ethics of AI made art in twenty twenty-five. Image generators now flood creative fields, and public doubt is rising. Their study walks through five trouble spots. Each gets a history, a cause, and a set of views.

The spots are carbon emissions, false media, copyright breach, star likeness misuse, and artist job loss. Their research ties the tools to real harm in each area. Fixes are proposed case by case. The core claim is that the field needs proper laws and rules. Without them, the same harms will keep scaling, they argue.
arxiv-2507-05649:
Kaixiang Zhao and co-authors present in 2025 DESIGN, a framework for running graph neural networks on encrypted data without huge slowdowns. Fully homomorphic encryption lets servers compute on sealed data, but graph models under it are usually too slow for real time use. Their insight is that input graphs carry much redundancy that uniform processing wastes effort on every node.

The server scores node importance from encrypted degree data, then prunes unimportant parts of the graph. It also varies activation complexity by node importance. Tests show large speedups over prior encrypted methods with competitive accuracy. Code is public for secure graph analytics work.
arxiv-2507-05949:
Damianos Michaelides, Simon Bate, and Marion Chatfield describe a software package for the R language in a 2025 paper. The package, called hassediagrams, helps researchers map the structure of an experiment before they model its data. Getting that structure wrong can lead to the wrong model and misleading results.

The tool works out the layout structure of a design and draws it as a Hasse diagram. It then folds in how items were randomized, which yields a second, restricted structure that can also be drawn. The terms in that structure tell the analyst which terms belong in the model. The authors say this steady route keeps model choice consistent across studies.
arxiv-2507-06549:
Shan Shen and co-authors predict stray electric effects in memory chips in 2025, before the chip is laid out. Custom memory blocks fill modern systems, yet stray capacitance shifts how they behave once drawn, forcing costly redesign rounds. The team asks if those strays can be forecast from the early circuit plan alone.

Their two-stage model pairs a graph network that sorts the wires with plain networks that guess each value. Tricks handle the flood of dull inner wires and pull in the circuit's block structure. On four real memory designs, error fell by up to nineteen times against the best past model, they report. Early simulation sped up nearly six hundred-fold. Forecasts that good could let designers fix problems while changes are still cheap.
arxiv-2507-06649:
Quantum circuits too big for today's machines can be cut into smaller pieces, run separately, and stitched back together. Friedrich Wagner and co-authors apply that trick to a sampling job: drawing candidate solutions from a trained optimization circuit called QAOA. Cutting distorts the results, broadening the spread of answers and shifting it toward worse ones. The team attacks the distortion by choosing cut points with integer programming, keeping the number of cuts as small as possible.

Cutting also shrinks each piece, which reduces the noise that corrupts real quantum hardware. In experiments on actual quantum processors, the trade favored cutting for large circuits: the noise saved outweighed the distortion added. Small circuits gained less, since their noise was already low. The authors read this as evidence that optimized cutting can stretch problem size and tame noise on near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2507-07049:
Pinak Banerjee works out gauge potentials on the M5 brane in a twisted cohomotopy frame. His twenty twenty-five paper sits in M-theory, where a single M5 brane carries rich field content. Flux densities alone do not give the full picture; potentials and their gauge shifts need a global form.

The work assumes the four-flux of M-theory is quantized in four-cohomotopy, a non-abelian cohomology theory. The three-flux on the brane sits in a twisted three-dimensional version. Twists from background gravity and orbifold placements are now included. Empty concordances of charged fluxes yield the classic potentials, and doubled ones yield gauge shifts. The math tightens a program in high-energy theory.
arxiv-2507-07149:
Renyuan Liu and co-authors present a 2025 framework for training neural networks right on phones and edge devices. Training on the device saves privacy and cuts cloud cost, but memory is tight. The stored values from each layer eat most of that memory, and squeezing them without loss of accuracy is hard.

Their framework, DAF, attacks the snags at the system level. It pairs chip aware math steps with joint chip and graphics packing to shrink the stored values on the fly. A smart paging scheme moves data in and out to cut wasted memory gaps. The authors report large memory savings with training kept fast, which opens on device training to more apps.
arxiv-2507-07249:
Jae Dong Noh, Aleksander Lasek, Jade LeSchack and Nicole Yunger Halpern wrote a 2025 paper on a classic relation in thermal physics for quantum systems with a spin symmetry. The relation must hold to prove how systems respond when pushed from balance. Single energy states of some quantum systems were lately shown to obey it. A spin symmetry clashes with the standard story of how such systems settle, though.

Using a newer version of that story, the team derives the relation for the symmetric case. The small-size correction is normal in some settings but can grow larger in others. Tests on a short spin chain backed the normal case.
arxiv-2507-07349:
Haodong Tian and co-authors build a new frame for instrumental variable analysis when effects bend rather than run straight. Such tools use a third factor, like a gene variant, to tease out cause when hidden factors blur direct study. Older methods for bent effects either lack power or can mislead, the authors argue.

Their frame sorts people into strata and reads the effect shape with few added assumptions. It can also pinpoint thresholds where an effect turns on. In simulations, it beat rival methods when the instrument was weak and recovered true effect shapes well. Applied to UK Biobank data, it found a level of alcohol intake past which blood pressure clearly rises, matching medical guidance.
arxiv-2507-07449: Takuma Byakuno proves an embedding theorem in metric geometry in this two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. The Gromov-Hausdorff space collects all compact metric spaces, with a distance measuring how nearly isometric two spaces are. Starting from a convergent series with positive terms, he takes for each term the spaces whose diameter stays below it. He proves the supremum-metric product of these subspaces embeds isometrically into the Gromov-Hausdorff space itself, a self-similarity result about the space of spaces.
arxiv-2507-07549:
A team of twelve radio astronomers maps a faint glow at the core of the galaxy cluster Abell 3558. The cluster sits in the heart of the Shapley Supercluster, a huge swarm of clusters. Faint wide glows in cluster cores are called mini-halos, lit by fast particles in hot gas. Fresh low-band radio data from two arrays let the team redraw the glow shape and tie it to X-ray maps of the gas.

The glow proved wider than past maps showed, with a new arm that spans a long stretch to the north. Its full span now stands far past the past mark. Glow shape tracks the X-ray gas marks, cold fronts and all, in a tight match. The glow tone is steep, and its tie to gas glow bends with wave band. Class rules for such glows get a fresh test here.
arxiv-2507-07749:
Alexander Zuyev and Victoria Grushkovska design a controller that steers a system toward a moving target curve without needing a model of the system, in a 2025 paper. The method, extremum seeking, wiggles the controls and reads the cost, which here is the gap between the system's state and the target curve. Such curves arise as best paths in a class of chemical reaction problems, where the goal is to maximize the average product over a set time.

The pair build the controller so the system traces a path near any given reference curve. They test it on a model of a chemical reaction that heats as it runs. Computer runs show the tracking errors staying small. The paper adds control theory for a case where the target moves and the model is unknown, a common bind in process engineering.
arxiv-2507-07949:
Sizhen Bian and co-authors shrank activity-recognition models for wearables in this 2025 paper. A watch or band must spot walking, sitting, and other actions on tiny hardware, so the model must be small yet accurate. Their design, TinierHAR, mixes slim convolutions with memory units and a time-averaging step. Across fourteen public data sets, it kept the average accuracy of bigger rivals.

Against its predecessor it used 2.7 times fewer parameters and 6.4 times fewer operations; against a classic deep model the savings ran far larger. The team also ran the first careful part-by-part study across all three models, showing what each piece contributes. They close with design rules for future tiny recognizers and release everything for others to benchmark.
arxiv-2507-08149:
Valerie Chen and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how more self-directed coding tools change the way programmers work. Many past studies cover chat helpers or code completion tools. Far fewer test agents that write files and run code on their own, and those tests lean on fixed benchmarks. The team ran a controlled study with users of a leading helper tool.

Agents helped in ways beyond the simpler helpers, at times finishing tasks users may not have managed alone. They also cut the effort needed to finish tasks. Still, users did not always grasp what the agent had done, which the authors flag as a barrier to wider use. The paper draws lessons for tool design and study methods.
arxiv-2507-08249:
Bill Marino and Ari Juels present a 2025 position paper on a new risk in artificial intelligence. Interest is growing in letting AI agents hold cryptocurrency and use smart contracts on their own. The authors argue that this step could open wholly new kinds of AI harm, not just faster versions of old ones. Money that moves on its own, with no human in the loop, changes what a rogue agent can do.

The paper first sets out the traits of crypto systems that make the pairing risky. It then lays out three new harm paths in detail, in what the authors call a first taxonomy of its kind. Traits such as instant, final payments and code-run deals leave little room to undo damage. The authors close with a call for more study of guards and limits, and offer first ideas as a start.
arxiv-2507-09049:
App reviews hide useful complaints about privacy and security inside a flood of everyday feedback. Aakash Sorathiya and Gouri Ginde present CMER, a method that mines those ethics-related reviews without hand-labeled training data. It pairs a language inference model, fed with domain-tuned test statements, with a large language model that does the final sorting.

The team tests the pipeline on more than 382,000 reviews of mobile investment apps. They compare several inference models and three language models, then combine the best of each. The combined system found 2,178 privacy and security reviews that a keyword search had missed. Those reviews can be turned into concrete requirements for app teams. The authors show the approach scales to a problem where ethical language is rare and specialized.
arxiv-2507-09349:
Ramos, Moriggi, and Machado present a paper from twenty twenty-five on dynamical entropy in high-energy nuclear collisions. The entropy notion extends earlier work on proton collisions to heavy ions. It can estimate the starting entropy density of the fireball. A gluon distribution function supplies the key probability input. Realistic models are built with scaling behavior and a classic collision approach. Normalization and scaling make the entropy nearly independent of nucleus size. Results are given as entropy density across rapidity.

The work ties entropy estimates to measurable gluon structure. It offers a bridge between theory and collision data. Heavy-ion programs gain a new diagnostic from the frame.
arxiv-2507-09749:
Beau Leighton-Trudel develops, in a 2025 paper, a test for when shared information between distant parts of a quantum chain can act like a distance. The recipe builds a number from mutual information, the amount two sites reveal about each other, and asks whether it obeys the triangle rule that real distances must follow. The test is tuned so a standard decay pattern gives back ordinary distance.

Under broad conditions, the author proves that slow, power-law decay of mutual information yields distance-like behavior, while fast exponential decay breaks it. An exact solution of the transverse-field Ising chain checks the claim. At the chain's critical point the decay sits near the benchmark power and the triangle defect stays harmless. In gapped phases the defect turns strongly positive, marking the failure of distance.
arxiv-2507-09949:
Kabir and co-authors sort job postings into a ranked category tree in a 2025 paper. Online job boards must tag each post well to power search, matching, and market studies. Job titles shift fast and blur across fields, so plain text sorting falls short. The team builds a model that learns jobs and industry classes in one shared space.

The model blends the standard job class system used in the United States with a house taxonomy from a job board. Graph links between like jobs ride along with the tree structure. That blend helps with cold starts, where a brand-new job type has no past examples. On a large postings set, the model beat past methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2507-10049:
Yao Ma and Yong-Liang Ma study what scalar mesons are made of and how that makeup changes dense matter, in a 2025 physics paper. Mesons with spin zero come in several flavors, and their internal mix is disputed. The authors extend a linear sigma model with baryons. They add flavor structures built from antisymmetric tensors of the chiral groups. They tune the model to reproduce nuclear matter at its normal saturation density, while keeping known vacuum facts.

With those anchors, the model predicts a plateau in the symmetry energy at middle densities. That feature is needed to match both a famous neutron star merger signal and lab data on lead nuclei. Neutron star structures are then computed for several parameter sets. The work links a particle's inner recipe to the size of the densest objects in the universe.
arxiv-2507-10349:
Zhiyuan Zhao and co-authors present, in a 2025 forecasting paper, a transformer model built to predict demand peaks across many future weeks at once. Retailers need such forecasts for buying and stocking, and holiday or promotion peaks are the hardest and the most costly to miss. Their model leans on context known ahead of time, like sale events.

A new attention scheme aligns each future week with the context that shapes it, inside both the reading and the writing halves of the model. On two large in-house retail data sets, peak accuracy rose by up to thirty percent. Overall accuracy stayed level with the best rivals. The authors aim the tool at smoother shopping during big events.
arxiv-2507-10449:
Han and four co-authors built a question-answering dataset for coral reefs in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Reef photos hold vital health clues, but reading them takes expert eyes. Vision-language models could let anyone query reef images, if trained on the right data. No large dataset existed for that purpose.

CoralVQA gathers nearly thirteen thousand real reef images from three oceans and sixty-seven coral genera. Over two hundred seventy-seven thousand question-answer pairs probe ecology and health. Marine biologists helped build a semi-automatic labeling pipeline for quality. Benchmarks of leading models exposed clear weaknesses in reef reasoning. The authors offer the set as a foundation for conservation tools.
arxiv-2507-10749:
Benjamin Stoler and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a way to generate dangerous driving scenarios for self-driving cars, grounded in real crashes. The scenarios that matter most for safety are exactly those missing from normal driving logs. Pure invention risks unrealistic tests.

Their framework first learns a behavior representation from large driving logs by contrastive training. A small crash-rich dataset, labeled roughly from video, fine-tunes that representation toward accident behavior. The result selects attacker trajectories that are both risky and believable. Plugged into two earlier generation pipelines, it upgrades their realism. Training and grading self-driving systems on crash-shaped danger could close a blind spot in road safety testing.
arxiv-2507-10949:
Andrew Newman leads a team of fourteen in a 2025 study of the cosmic web when the universe was young. Two tools can map that web: counts of bright galaxies, and shadows cast by gas between galaxies in quasar light. The team checked whether the two maps tell the same story.

Survey maps of the same vast volume let them pair gas absorption with galaxy density street by street. A simple model fit the pairing well. A few spots broke the pattern: strong gas shadows with no galaxy crowd, hinting at clusters whose galaxies are too dim for the usual surveys to catch.
arxiv-2507-11049:
Dahyun Lee and co-authors bring journalistic method into AI stance detection for news in this 2025 paper. Stance detection labels what position a text takes on a topic. Such labels can widen the views that news recommenders show readers.

Past work stuck to short posts and a few rich languages. The team build the first Korean data set for stance at the level of full articles. It holds about two thousand labeled news pieces. Their agentic method uses in-context learning guided by reporting practice. Viewpoint-aware feeds could soften filter bubbles and polarization. The data set also opens Korean media research to wider study. Newsrooms could use the labels to audit their own balance.
arxiv-2507-11249:
Ruohai Guo, Jiang Zhu, Xing Jiang and Fengzhong Qu wrote a 2025 paper on estimating a linear model when the measurement matrix itself is random. Past work covered the case where that matrix has full rank on average. The fitting problem was known to be nearly convex, with a fast split-based method. This work widens the ground a lot.

The authors allow the average matrix to fall short of full rank. They prove the fitting problem is fully convex, with strong duality. In the underfilled case, matrix randomness can even help estimation at times. A single fast method handles both cases. Computer runs back the claims.
arxiv-2507-11649:
Daniel Commey, Benjamin Appiah, Griffith Klogo, and Garth Crosby set out, in 2025 work, a private way to grade shared learning systems. In such systems, many sites train one model together without pooling raw data. Grading still leaks facts, since shared scores can hint at what each site holds.

Their plan uses proofs that show a claim is true while hiding the facts behind it. Each site proves its own loss score sits below a set line, and shares no raw score. The team built the full plan with no outside tools and tried it on two data sets, one of hand-drawn digits and one of body moves. They weigh the plan by its cost in time, data sent, and ease of checking.
arxiv-2507-12049:
Manuel Barusco and co-authors release a software library in a 2025 paper on visual anomaly detection. Spotting defects or oddities in images usually means learning from normal examples only, since anomalous ones are rare, and researchers lacked one tidy toolkit for the many methods in play.

MoViAD bundles state-of-the-art detection models, trainers, datasets, and evaluation tools in a modular design. It covers continual learning, semi-supervised and few-shot setups, and noisy data. For real deployment it adds edge and Internet-of-Things support, with model compression and quantization for small devices. Profiling tools help users weigh accuracy against running cost.
arxiv-2507-12149:
David Ziemkiewicz and Sylwia Zielińska-Raczyńska weigh a way to swell faint light leaps in a cuprous oxide crystal in a 2025 paper. The leaps in view are of a shy kind, four-fold in form, from states that ride high in the crystal. Plain light takes them weak.

A tiny gold or silver craft at the crystal's face can lend its own wave to the leap. The pair writes the math of that lend. They add a mean-field way to sum it for large states. They grade crafts of gold, silver, and copper kin for the swell each can give. The work is a map for bench tests to come.
arxiv-2507-12449:
Camera-only self-driving stacks can dodge obstacles on a budget, and a research team led by Van-Hoang-Anh Phan tested one on a campus, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their stack spots objects with a fast detector and gauges distance with a depth-guessing model. A classic path rule then steers the car.

Depth models were compared head to head for truth, speed, and toughness in real scenes. Trials ran across varied campus setups with mixed obstacles. The stack handled them well, the team reports. The work backs a low-cost path to safer campus and yard vehicles, where lidar rigs price out.
arxiv-2507-12649:
Three authors led by Christine van Stiphoudt grade new smart grid data models in three phases while they are still on the bench. Grid talk grows as homes and cars join the power web, and new models must phrase that talk. A flaw in a model can stall flex power deals once live. Past checks split: word reviews here, live fit tests there, with no one path that weds both.

Their method runs plain trait reviews and live system tests in one three-step flow. It fits both word models and data models at each build stage. A trait list for grade marks comes with the flow for team use. Early flaw finds cut fix costs for grid code teams.
arxiv-2507-13049:
Frédéric Jean and two co-authors compare in 2025 rival notions of pliability for horizontal vectors in Carnot groups. Carnot groups are the tangent worlds of sub-Riemannian geometry, where motion is allowed only along certain directions. Several definitions of non-rigid vectors have been proposed lately, driven by questions about monotone sets and Whitney extension.

The note lines the definitions up side by side and tests which imply which. A linked question is whether the multiexponential map, which sends control data to reachable points, is open. Clarifying the web of definitions keeps later theorems from resting on look-alike but unequal concepts, a quiet kind of progress that geometry depends on.
arxiv-2507-13349:
Adam Smercina leads a team reading the life story of a wispy galaxy being torn by its giant neighbor. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. F8D1 is an ultra-diffuse satellite of the M81 galaxy. It is among the nearest of its kind beyond the Local Group. Tides are visibly disrupting it. Deep Hubble images resolve its individual stars.

Two deep fields cover the center and a spot along its long axis. Eight shallower fields trace the rest. Star formation histories are computed field by field. Those histories reveal what made the galaxy so diffuse. Tidal processing, bursty feedback, and spin are rival explanations. The evidence weighs them for this one clear case.
arxiv-2507-13449:
Star bursts will soon rain at a rate no crew can eye: a new sky eye may log a million a year. Reynolds, Gagliano, and Villar free a hunt tool for that rain in a 2025 study. The tool seeks like bursts for any new burst, by its light curve's shape and by its home star town's tint.

Tints are wiped of dust ere the match. Users set how many kin to fetch, and how hard burst shape weighs next to home tint. Chance runs guard the match when marks are thin. The pack ships with a stock of twenty thousand burst marks and walk through guides. One in a million odd balls is the aimed catch.
arxiv-2507-13549:
Jim O'Connor and three co-authors train racing controllers in a game in twenty twenty-five. The game is Xpilot-AI, which now has a new racing mode. Its physics includes inertia, friction, and gravity, making driving a hard control task. The team used NEAT, a method that evolves both the shape and the weights of neural networks.

The racing mode allows flexible track designs and tests many agents in parallel. That makes it fast to improve controllers over generations. Evolved controllers cut lap times by up to about a third compared with their starting point. They also learned sound racing tactics, such as better lines through corners. Readers see neuroevolution produce skill from scratch in a tough physics setting.
arxiv-2507-13849:
Airton Deppman models in this 2025 paper how the layered shape of human social life breeds both agreement and inequality. Social circles nest fractally: about five close supporters, then widening rings up to roughly 150 regular contacts. Deppman builds socioeconomic exchanges on such a scaling network and studies how consensus forms inside it.

Using a generalized calculus suited to the scaling, the model yields heavy-tailed outcome distributions of the kind seen in real wealth data. The tails, he argues, are not accidents of policy or talent but children of the network's own geometry. The same ladder that spreads news and tools also concentrates their rewards. Chat apps ride the same layered web.
arxiv-2507-14049:
Paweł Budzianowski and co-authors present EdgeVLA in 2025, a leaner design for robot control models that see, read, and act. Big models of this kind can guide many robot tasks, but they run too slowly on small robots with tight power and memory. The team wanted real-time speed without losing skill.

Their first change drops the step-by-step guessing of the robot hand's target spot, which sped up responses about sevenfold. Their second change swaps the big language core for a small one, which trained just as well in early tests. The result matched a leading open model in training behavior while using far less memory. The team released the model and code for others to build on.
arxiv-2507-14349:
Anthony Badea, Austin Baty, and a large team measure the shape of particle collisions using archived data in a 2025 particle physics analysis note. Thrust shows how pencil-like or spherical the debris of an electron-positron annihilation is, a classic probe of the strong force. The data were recorded decades ago by a detector at the European laboratory's former collider, at the energy of the Z boson peak.

Using archives again with modern methods squeezes new precision from old collisions. Event shape measurements test quantum chromodynamics calculations and help tune the simulations every collider study depends on.
arxiv-2507-14649:
Minsuh Joo and Hyunsoo Cho present a way to tell when a large language model is likely making things up, in a 2025 paper. Such false but smooth answers are called hallucinations, and they pose a real risk when people trust the output. Their method, Cleanse, scores how unsure a model is by looking at its hidden internal states as it writes.

The trick is grouping. The method clusters those hidden states and checks how much of the overall sameness sits inside each cluster. Tight, coherent clusters suggest a firm answer. A scattered pattern warns of a shaky one. The team tested the score on four public models and two question-answering sets. It flagged false answers well. The authors offer the method as a guard rail for safer use of chatbots.
arxiv-2507-14749:
Wai Keen Vong and Brenden M. Lake tested whether a computer model can learn words from the kind of input a small child actually receives. A child learns language from limited daily experience, while large models train on enormous datasets. An earlier study trained a network on sixty-one hours of video and speech from one child's head camera and found it could link words to the things they name. The open question was whether that success depended on that one child.

The pair used automatic transcription across the full SAYCam collection, over five hundred hours from three children, and trained networks on each child's data. Models learned word meanings that carried across videos, children, and image sets, though each child's input left its own pattern in what was learned.
arxiv-2507-14849:
Yifei Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of a trade-off in training smaller language models to reason. Copying the long reasoning chains of a top model can lift a small model's reasoning sharply. What that heavy diet does to the model's other skills, such as finding and using facts inside a long document, was largely unexplored.

The team tested a family of open models distilled from a leading reasoning system across long-context tasks. These tasks matter for search-augmented systems that must pull the right facts from long inputs and reason over them. Their checks bridge two skills often studied apart: step-by-step reasoning and long-context understanding.
arxiv-2507-14949:
Philippe Balbiani and Olivier Gasquet settled the complexity in twenty twenty-five of deciding satisfiability for a bimodal logic combining transitivity with weak density. Modal logics extend reasoning about necessity and possibility; adding axioms changes how hard it is to test whether a formula can be true somewhere. The authors' prior work introduced windows as a device for polynomial algorithms in a related logic.

After revisiting the folklore bimodal K4 case, they show windows, mixed with standard bimodal algorithms, decide the transitive weak-density case in polynomial space. Both satisfiability and validity come out PSPACE-complete. The paper is a technical completeness result: it pins this logic's difficulty exactly and showcases the windows method as a reusable proof technology.
arxiv-2507-15049:
Andrés Navarro, Carlos de Quinto, and José Alberto Hernández present a drone built to think beyond its pilot's sight, in a 2025 paper. Drones are becoming flying nodes in future networks, expected to sense and decide on the spot. Their budget quadcopter joins 5G links, onboard edge computing, and large language models. A panoramic camera feeds recognition software, while an operator can step into the view through virtual reality.

Field tests confirmed low-delay video processing and sturdy 5G connections. The language model layer distilled raw footage into actionable insights for decision makers. Trial missions covered emergency response, infrastructure inspection, and environmental watching. The authors argue the mix of edge AI and connected models gives small drones outsized awareness. They offer the platform as a low-cost template for autonomous aerial intelligence.
arxiv-2507-15249:
Yanbing Zhang, Zhe Wang, Qin Zhou, and Mengping Yang present FreeCus, a way to put a chosen subject into new AI images with no training at all, in a paper from 2025. Custom image tools usually fine-tune per subject or train a special encoder on huge data. Those costs limit real use. Modern diffusion transformers, the authors argue, already hold the needed skill, untapped.

Three tricks unlock it. An attention-sharing step preserves the subject's layout while leaving room to edit. A reworked feature-shift analysis sharpens fine detail capture. A multimodal language model enriches the meaning fed to the generator. Tests matched or beat trained rivals at keeping identity across scenes. The method also plugs into inpainting and control pipelines as they stand.
arxiv-2507-15549:
René Sitters speeds up near-optimal planning for delivery vans that can only carry so much. The capacitated vehicle routing problem asks how a fleet should serve scattered customers without overloading any van. For points in the flat plane, the best known fast approximation schemes were still slow in a precise technical sense.

The new scheme runs in quasi-polynomial time, a middle ground far faster than the previous champions for this problem. The route there goes through a reduction: any capacitated instance becomes an uncapacitated puzzle about drawing a fixed number of paths between two points through every customer. A fast scheme for that puzzle is the engine of the result. The author notes that a truly polynomial scheme for the path puzzle would likely lift the whole problem with it.
arxiv-2507-15749:
Steve Howell and co-authors report likely catching Betelgeuse's long-suspected companion star on camera at last, in a 2025 paper. Betelgeuse, the red supergiant in Orion, pulses and dims on a roughly six-year rhythm that its own throbbing cannot explain. Speed and position data also hinted at a smaller orbiting partner. The team used speckle imaging on the eight-meter Gemini North telescope in 2020 and 2024.

In 2020, mid-dimming, the partner should have hidden behind the star, and none appeared. In 2024, days after the predicted widest split, a faint point showed at the expected spot and angle, about six brightness steps dimmer than Betelgeuse. The signal is weak, one and a half times the noise, so the team calls it probable, not proven. If real, the companion neatly explains the giant's long rhythm.
arxiv-2507-15949:
Claims that particle colliders can test the deepest rules of quantum physics are challenged in a 2025 paper by Steven A. Abel and co-authors. Recent work has proposed collider tests of Bell's inequality and of entanglement, using top quarks, tau pairs, or Higgs boson decays.

The authors argue that none of these proposals can do what is claimed. Colliders measure only the momenta of the final particles, and those values can all be read at once. Using a known construction, they build a local hidden variable theory that copies the data exactly. That theory obeys Bell's limits by design, so no collider setup of this kind can break them. The paper urges care in how such results are described.
arxiv-2507-16149:
Sabine Münch and Stephen Raach give an exact solver for picking the best set of items under a weight limit, in a paper from 2025. Each added item helps, but with shrinking extra gain, and the total weight must fit a budget. The problem is hard in the strict sense, yet many users need the true best set, not a near miss.

Their method searches branch by branch and prunes paths that cannot win, with several speed tricks added. They test it on made-up cases for three classic problems and on cases from real data. It beats the best known solvers and a leading commercial tool on their tests.
arxiv-2507-16249:
Srivatsan Krishnan and co-authors use many learning agents to map neural networks onto chips, in a 2025 paper. Mapping decides where each part of a network runs, and it shapes speed and energy use. The space of choices is vast, and single agent search wastes many trials.

Their team of agents splits the search, and a clustering step gives like choices to the same agent. That keeps parallel training from stepping on itself. Trials showed the method needs far fewer samples than a single agent to reach a good map. Delays and energy delay scores fell by large factors at equal sample counts. The work targets accelerator design.
arxiv-2507-16549:
Antoine Glicenstein and four co-authors measure subradiant dynamics in a cold cloud of ytterbium atoms with space and time resolution. Subradiance is a collective effect where excited atoms hold energy far longer than single atoms would. A depletion imaging method exploits the internal level structure of alkaline earth like atoms to map excited state population directly.

Both population maps and scattered light intensity track the decay of subradiant modes over time. The two measures agree well with each other. Simulations of two level atom ensembles match the data in a quantitative way. The work gives a direct view of how collective modes store and release light in dense cold ensembles, a topic of interest for quantum optics.
arxiv-2507-16849:
Yi-Shan Chu and Hsuan-Cheng Wei improve how satellite images are segmented after disasters, when maps of the damaged area are needed fast and labeled examples are few. Their work supports an emergency mapping product run by Taiwan's space agency. They start from a handful of hand-labeled regions and widen them with a statistical confidence method, creating a larger, weakly labeled training set.

A vision transformer model then learns from combined imagery of two satellite systems, with several decoder designs and staged training losses. Two cases test the pipeline: the 2022 drought at China's Poyang Lake and the 2023 wildfire on Rhodes. The refined maps came out smoother and more consistent with high-resolution reference products. The authors offer the method for rapid mapping when ground truth is scarce.
arxiv-2507-16949:
Mojtaba Shirozhan, Fabien Quéré, and Subhendu Kahaly show in 2025 how to make single flashes of extreme ultraviolet light lasting mere attoseconds. Bouncing light off a mirror racing near light speed squeezes it into such bursts, useful for filming electrons in motion. The mirror here is a sheet of electrons blasted off a thin foil by a laser.

Earlier setups often made ragged trains of pulses instead of one clean flash. Shaping the drive laser's waveform coaxed the foil into forming a single tidy electron sheet. Tuning the delay between lasers then controlled the flash's strength, length, and color spread, pointing to compact tunable sources.
arxiv-2507-17049:
Pablo Valle and co-authors argue that judging robots only by whether the task got done misses most of what matters, in this 2025 paper. Robots that see, understand speech, and act are spreading into real work. Success rates say nothing about how gracefully a task was done or how sure the robot was. The authors adapt eight uncertainty measures and five quality measures to robotic manipulation by such systems.

A large study then tests whether those measures actually catch shaky or sloppy performance across many trials and robots. Nine evaluation angles get compared. Trustworthy deployment needs dashboards, not pass-fail stamps, and this work supplies candidate dials. It also warns where popular metrics flatter the machines they grade.
arxiv-2507-17449:
Albin Márffy and co-authors report a 2025 study of a thin magnetic material made of manganese, bismuth, and tellurium. Thin layers of the material can in theory show a rare Hall effect with no outside magnet. In practice that state is hard to see, and the team probes why.

Tests of resistance in the cold state pointed to a plain, non conducting state, likely tied to flaws in the layers. A strong magnet field brought out a different state with the rare traits. Pressing the layers with fluid pressure shrank the plain gap. The result hints that less flaw driven harm may let the rare state show more often.
arxiv-2507-18249:
Cyber ranges let power grid defenders practice against attacks without risking the real grid, but building one by hand is slow and costly. Muhammad Roomi and co-authors present a 2025 framework that generates such ranges on its own.

The team first defines a modeling language for smart grids, written in a format both people and machines can read. The language folds in standard configuration files used by real grid equipment. A tool chain then reads a model and builds a working cyber range from it. Models can be shared and rebuilt elsewhere, unlike one-off custom ranges. The authors aim to close the gap between lab research and live grid defense training.
arxiv-2507-18349:
Huan Yuan and co-authors report, in a 2025 physics study, a lab test of how defects form when a material crosses a special phase change. A classic frame, named for Kibble and Zurek, says how many defects a fast change should leave behind. It was built for plain phase changes, though. Whether it holds for changes in a band's topology, a deep trait of the wave states, was not clear from past tests.

The team used cold atoms in a lattice made of light, where a key dial can be swept fast. They read the spin wave states to rebuild the count of excitations, the defects in this set-up. That count grew with sweep speed in a power-law form. The form fits the classic frame well. The work opens lab study of this rule for topology changes.
arxiv-2507-18549:
Steven Frank shows that learning algorithms and natural selection obey one shared law, in his 2025 arXiv paper. The Price equation, an evolutionary bookkeeping identity, partitions any change into parts. Applied to a system's parameters, it yields what he calls a force-metric-bias law with four ingredients.

A force term pushes parameters uphill on performance. A metric term rescales steps by inverse curvature. A bias term adds momentum or shifts the frame. A noise term enables exploration. Natural selection, Bayesian updating, Newton's method, gradient descent and the Adam optimizer all fall out as special cases. Fisher information and related quantities appear naturally, giving algorithm design a common foundation.
arxiv-2507-18949:
Yongjie Li, Ruilin Nong, Jianan Liu, and Lucas Evans present a framework for adaptive learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models can tailor study paths to each student. Their system uses model-powered analytics on live learning data to shape a personal curriculum.

The framework keeps assessing each learner and adjusts pathways and resource picks to match progress. Teaching strategies shift with the data, keeping material relevant and engaging. Trials across varied school settings showed clear gains in engagement and knowledge retention. The authors argue the approach can move standard teaching toward a more student-centered model.
arxiv-2507-19449:
Qi Xiao and co-authors demonstrate the first steady vacuum ultraviolet laser for a nuclear clock in a paper from 2025. The clock would tick on a jump inside the thorium-229 nucleus. That jump needs light at about 148 nanometers, deep in the ultraviolet.

Pulsed lasers had reached the line, but a steady, narrow beam is needed to control nuclei. The team made the light by mixing waves in cadmium vapor. The source gives a steady beam with a very narrow line width. Its color can be tuned across a broad range. Power is small but enough for spectroscopy. A steady source brings a working nuclear clock closer.
arxiv-2507-19549:
Nadeen Fathallah, Daniel Hernandez, and Steffen Staab present AccessGuru in 2025, a system that finds and fixes web accessibility faults in page code. Most web pages break accessibility rules, shutting out users with disabilities. Fixing them by hand takes expert time. The team first sorts faults into three kinds: syntax, meaning, and layout. Their system pairs existing checkers with large language models to spot faults of all three kinds.

Corrections follow prompts shaped by the fault kind. On a new benchmark of real faults, the system cut violation scores by up to eighty-four percent. Prior methods reached at most half that. The work aims to lower the cost of an inclusive web.
arxiv-2507-20249:
Giulia D'Agostino and Chung-Chi Chen ask whether professionalism in expert questions can be measured from the words alone. Their 2025 paper studies financial analyst questions, a high stakes setting where how a question is built matters. A new annotation scheme scores structural and pragmatic features such as prefaces, discourse regulators, and request types.

Two datasets were built, one of human and model generated questions rated for perceived professionalism, one labeled by origin. The same features tracked both human judgments and who wrote the question. A classifier using only these readable features beat strong baselines at spotting expert written questions. The authors call professionalism a learnable, transferable construct.
arxiv-2507-20449:
Noor and co-authors build a network for matching researchers with collaborators, based on what people write about rather than whom they cite. Their topic-based network uses a topic model with a science-tuned language model to link researchers across fields by shared interests. A distortion worries them: prolific authors publish across many topics, so their minor interests drown under their main ones and the network misses links.

Their fix is cloning. Each author's publications are clustered by topic, and every cluster becomes its own node, letting one person belong to several communities at once. Judged on the resulting groups, the cloned network produced more meaningful communities than the plain one. It also surfaced a wider range of possible collaborations, which the authors offer as the practical payoff for interdisciplinary teams.
arxiv-2507-20549:
Song-Bo Zhang and Lun-Hui Hu find a mixed pairing state in chiral magnets in a 2025 physics paper. The setting is a chiral antiferromagnet, a magnet whose spins twist in a set swirl. The team study its spin texture on a kagome lattice, a net of linked triangles. Two electron types live in the system: one plain and one Dirac-like.

When a plain superconductor sits next to the magnet, the texture spawns pairs of both main kinds at once. Opposite-spin singlet pairs and same-spin triplet pairs form side by side, each with net motion. The triplet pairs spring from the spin swirl itself, with no net magnet pull or spin-orbit force. A phase gap between the two pair kinds can be tuned by joint angle. Tests with Josephson joints could spot the state through swings and phase flips.
arxiv-2507-20649:
Shmuel Gurvitz and Dmitri Sokolovski define tunneling time for electrons through driven barriers, in work from 2025. How long an electron spends inside a barrier is a long argued physics question. Leads with finite bandwidth add their own delays, muddying any direct time read.

A wobbling barrier driven by a steady field links wobble strength to current delay. In the slow drive limit, simple formulas give the time dependent current directly. Subtracting lead delay from total delay isolates the true barrier dwell time. That dwell time always shrinks to zero for wide or high barriers. Optical experiment data match the derived times well in their checks.
arxiv-2507-20849:
Yilun Qiu and co-authors personalize large language model output by comparing users with each other in a 2025 paper. Most personalization leans on a user's own history alone. Yet how a user differs from peers who liked similar things carries strong signals. Writing those differences into text prompts, though, often fails to capture them well.

Their framework works in the model's hidden space instead. It builds soft prompts from the gap between a user's embedding and peers' embeddings. A sparse filter then keeps only features relevant to the task before feeding them into a frozen model. On review-writing tests, the method beat baselines across several measures. The authors share their code for others to try.
arxiv-2507-20949:
Hamada and Loges present a 2025 physics paper proving that six-dimensional supergravity models form a finite family once all anomaly rules apply. Local anomaly freedom alone leaves endless model choices. Adding global anomaly freedom changes the game. The pair boil the rules down to a giant linear program and study its dual with standard tools.

A universal cap falls out: at most 3,003 tensor multiplets in any consistent model. Finiteness of the whole landscape follows from that bound. One extreme model saturates the cap with a huge repeated gauge group, oddly echoing a known F-theory champion. The paper turns an open sea of models into a countable shore.
arxiv-2507-21049:
Zedong Wang, Siyuan Li, and Dan Xu rebalance multi task learning at the representation level in a 2025 paper. One network learning many tasks can suffer when tasks fight. Standard fixes rescale losses or massage gradients in the optimizer. The shared representation space, where tasks actually meet, was largely left alone.

Their method, Rep-MTL, scores how salient each task is inside that shared space. Entropy penalties steer those saliencies away from domination. Sample wise alignment across tasks encourages sharing of useful features. The goal shifts from pure conflict removal to protecting each task's training. Four benchmarks covering task and domain shifts tested the idea. Even with plain equal loss weighting, gains were competitive. Power law checks confirmed better balance among tasks.
arxiv-2507-21349:
Amirmohammad Shamaei and co-authors use a patient's earlier brain scans to rebuild new ones faster, in a 2025 paper. MRI is a mainstay of brain care, but long scan times raise costs and tire patients. A previous scan of the same person carries much of the needed detail. Earlier methods aligned that old scan with slow classic tools. Their pipeline pairs a first reconstruction network with a learned alignment model and a transformer that polishes the result.

They tested it on 2,808 images from 18 people, speeding scans by factors of five to twenty. The method beat rivals on quality scores at every speed. Brain segmentation run on the rebuilt images also matched reference results more closely. Total rebuild time fell sharply against classic alignment, which the authors say suits live clinical use.
arxiv-2507-21449:
Rohan Hitchcock and Jesse Hoogland propose a benchmark for local sampling in neural networks in a 2025 paper. Network loss landscapes have flat, degenerate regions, and common sampling algorithms carry global guarantees that rest on shaky assumptions there. The authors argue evaluation should shift from the whole posterior to local regions. Their benchmark tests how faithfully samplers reproduce local posterior shape, and it scales to very large models.

Several popular algorithms were compared on it. A preconditioned variant of Langevin sampling represented local geometry best. The authors note global guarantees are still missing, but useful local information can be extracted even in huge models.
arxiv-2507-21749:
Veerababu Dharanalakota, Ashwin Raikar, and Prasanta Ghosh present a dynamic learning rate scheduler in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The learning rate strongly shapes neural network training, yet it is usually fixed in advance. Complex problems often need the rate to adapt as training unfolds.

Their scheduler adjusts the rate from the loss values seen during training itself. They test it on physics-informed neural networks and on image classification with plain and convolutional networks. In these tests, the scheduler sped up training and made it more stable. The authors pitch it as a simple fix for a common tuning headache. Adapting the rate to the loss curve replaces guesswork with feedback.
arxiv-2507-22049:
Logan Cross, Nick Haber, and Daniel Yamins test AI social simulations in a 2025 paper. Language model agents can now act out human social scenes, but trust in their behavior needs proof. The team validate their setup in two stages using classic social dilemma studies. First they find which mental parts agents need to copy known human results.

Both persona based differences and theory of mind proved essential for matching third party punishment, where bystanders punish unfair acts. With that architecture locked, the team ran fresh conditions the human studies never tried. The recipe offers a path from mere imitation to prediction, the step that would make agent simulations a real research tool.
arxiv-2507-22349:
Han and co-authors shrink neural networks for phones and edge devices by trimming unneeded bits from each layer's weights. Mixed precision, giving each layer its own bit count, beats a single setting but is hard to tune. Their 2025 method, MSQ, rounds and clamps weights so the lowest bits can be trained smoothly, then pressures those bits toward zero so whole bits can drop away.

A curvature measure lets the method cut several bits at once, which speeds training. In tests, trainable parameters fell up to eightfold and training time by up to eighty-six percent against earlier bit-level methods. Accuracy and compression stayed competitive. The authors pitch the method for teams training lean models on limited hardware.
arxiv-2507-22649:
Sarah Anderson and co-authors trace where two meteorite kinds were born in this 2025 paper. CM and CI meteorites are among the most primitive space rocks known. Simulations of young giant planets growing and drifting show their parent bodies came from far apart zones.

CM parents formed near Saturn's birthplace, while CI parents came from beyond Uranus. The two kinds reached the asteroid belt at different times, the team shows. Comet-like bodies arrived with the CI group. Only the CM group, they add, could have fed water to the rocky planets. The timing also pins where the small grains inside CM rocks formed.
arxiv-2507-22749:
Luca Biferale and co-authors release a large data set on how pollution spreads in churning air, in a 2025 paper. Finding a leak or smoke source from a few sensor hits is hard, since gusts scatter the traces. The team built clean test data that search methods can be graded against.

The data come from direct simulations of full three dimensional flow. They track hundreds of millions of tracer particles released from five point sources, with and without a mean wind. Each record holds a particle path and the local flow speed along it. The set also gives smoothed density maps for quick tests of source finding methods.
arxiv-2507-22849:
Andrew Campbell, Anna Scaglione, and Sean Peisert design a way for a network of agents to find shared patterns in data none of them fully sees, in a 2025 paper. Each agent holds only some rows of the data table, and there is no central collector. Their method runs a private version of the power method, the classic route to the top patterns, across the network.

Agents pass along only partial summaries of the current estimate, and rely on random starts plus tuned noise to meet a formal privacy guarantee.
