The authors prove both the privacy level and how fast it settles, with network shape built into the rates. On real data it beat naive local private methods, above all at middle privacy settings.
arxiv-2507-22949:
Jingwei Sun, Zeyu Xia, and Wei Zhang analyze a numerical scheme for a coupled flow and phase system, in a 2025 paper. The system models fluids with two mixed parts that can separate. Their scheme uses helper variables to keep the math stable. It splits the coupled parts so each can be solved apart.

Only simple, fixed-form solvers are needed at each step, the authors note. The scheme is stable for a rewritten total energy, whatever step size is used. The authors derive error bounds for both the phase and the flow parts. Those bounds reach the best rate expected for this kind of method. Space is handled on a staggered grid, and time by a two-step method. The analysis supports use of the scheme in fluid simulations.
arxiv-2507-23049:
Shih-Yu Chang published a research paper in 2025 extending a mathematical tool for tracking how operators change when perturbed, into the harder world of continuous spectra. Many of them in quantum theory and geometry have smeared-out spectra and no tidy basis, and the non-self-adjoint ones are unstable to analyze. Multiple operator integrals organize such questions.

Chang builds the generalized theory for them. It covers their algebraic rules, continuity, size bounds, and a perturbation formula that extends classic results. As an application, a spectral shift formula of Krein type is derived and pushed to arbitrary accuracy orders. The framework is meant to serve spectral theory, operator algebras, and noncommutative geometry alike.
arxiv-2507-23249:
Shankhadeep Mondal and Ram Mohapatra bring graph theory to bear in this 2025 paper on keeping data safe when pieces go missing. Frames, redundant signal codes, shrug off erasures during transmission, and each frame pairs with a dual that rebuilds the signal. The question is which pairs lose least when one or two pieces vanish.

Using the spectral radius and operator norm as error yardsticks, the authors give conditions for the best pairs under one and two erasures. A tight frame grown from a connected graph, with its standard dual, proves best for a single loss. They also compute error sizes for graph frames directly. Radio and storage codes share the same need.
arxiv-2507-23449:
Shervin Rahimzadeh Arashloo presents a method for spotting odd patterns in streams of data that change over time, in a paper from 2025. The catalog title differs from the title printed in the text; the text's version names signature-kernel one-class learning. The method learns what normal data looks like and flags what strays. Older tools compare data point by point and miss the shape of the whole path.

His method reads each series as a path, using a kernel built for that view. It also adds a penalty that respects how normal data clusters in space. The math keeps the same form as the base method, so old solvers still run. Tests on five known benchmark sets place the method near the top of the field. It also handles unevenly spaced samples, which real sensors often produce.
arxiv-2508-00349:
Yuga Kanaya and Kenjiro Takazawa study popular matchings in a 2025 mathematics paper. A popular matching pairs people or items by preference in a way that would win a majority vote against any rival pairing. Checking popularity directly takes far too long, so researchers use two kinds of shortcuts to test it.

One shortcut describes the graph structure of such matchings, tailored to each problem variant. The other uses best weight matchings and works the same way for all variants. The authors prove each shortcut can be derived from the other, for three variants of the problem. Their proofs give a unified view, rather than relying on both describing the same matchings.
arxiv-2508-00549:
Daniel Wolf and six co-authors showed in 2025 that leading vision-language models cannot tell left from right in medical scans. Judging where body parts sit relative to each other is basic to clinical reading. The team tested GPT-4o, Llama 3.2, Pixtral and JanusPro on such questions, and every model failed the task. Adding drawn markers, letters or colors onto the images helped only modestly.

Scores on medical images stayed far below those on everyday photos. The models seemed to answer from stored anatomy knowledge rather than from the picture in front of them. That habit produces confident, wrong conclusions. The authors released a benchmark dataset, MIRP, to measure this skill systematically. They frame relative position reading as a gate skill that clinical AI must pass before wider use.
arxiv-2508-00749:
Johanna Grahl and co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, whether a program-analysis trick can map how software models change. Teams that build systems from parts and connectors need to know when an edit alters behavior. Their tool runs a model symbolically, tracking both the path taken and the concrete values, down to states visited and the rules that fired. An upgraded code generator gathers all that at run time.

Candidate runs are judged on speed, smallness, and how fully they cover the behavior. The verdict is mixed: the method shows real promise for spotting meaning-level differences between model versions. But it strains as systems grow, and the authors flag scale as the wall to break before the approach serves big industrial models.
arxiv-2508-01049:
Nicholas Corrado and Josiah Hanna tackled a quiet flaw in 2025 in how teams of learning agents train. Each agent learns from its own stream of play, and the joint stream can drift from what the team plan says it should be. That drift warps the slope each agent climbs. The result can be a poor joint plan even when each agent's own slope points the right way on average.

Their fix, called CoSER, steers play from the center toward joint moves that the stream has under-sampled. Across a range of team games, it cut joint sampling error faster than plain play. Agents trained on that stream reached the best joint plan more often. The authors pitch it as a trust boost for team learning.
arxiv-2508-01149:
Yufeng Wu and Dennis Hong built a tiny four-leg robot with no loose wires at all. The work dates to 2025. The robot is about the size and weight of a smart phone. It is shared as an open design for research and school use.

The bot walks for over an hour on one charge and can survive drops from a meter high. Its parts cost about three hundred dollars and can be made on home-grade printers or bought from web shops. One person can build it in under an hour on average. With plain control rules, it walks fast for its size, turns fast, jumps, and climbs mild slopes.
arxiv-2508-01449:
Mohamed Belfkir, Mohamed Amin Loualidi, and Salah Nasri use machine learning to sharpen a search for double Higgs boson events, in a paper from 2025. The target decay leaves two bottom quarks and two photons, a rare and faint signal at the Large Hadron Collider's current energy. The team trained two classifiers on simulated events: a boosted tree model and a graph neural network that uses event geometry.

The graph model beat the tree model clearly. It tightened the expected upper limit on double Higgs production by about twenty-eight percent. Both beat the latest published experimental results on limits and on the Higgs self-coupling constraint, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-01749:
Runkai Zheng and co-authors improve how noise is used in privacy-preserving dataset distillation, published in 2025. Machine learning models rely on large data sets that often hold sensitive information. Differential privacy can generate synthetic data with a set leakage budget, but it needs much data to match models trained on the original.

Dataset distillation instead creates a compact synthetic set that trains models efficiently. Current private distillation methods, though, waste private information: they sample and optimize in a synchronized way, and rely on noisy signals from randomly started networks. The new framework separates sampling from optimization for better convergence. It also matches signals in an informative subspace to blunt the effect of privacy noise. On a standard image set, it gained a clear margin at a set size.
arxiv-2508-01949:
Nasir Sohail, Aftab Shah, and Kristo Väljako study a question in abstract algebra in a 2025 paper. Semigroups are sets with a rule for combining pairs of items. Some semigroups sit inside richer ones that also allow undoing moves. Whether a given ample semigroup fits that way is known to be undecidable in general.

The authors narrow the question to special classes of ample semigroups. For those classes, they give answers on when the embedding works. They seek fits that keep all three operations of the host intact. Examples in the paper split the left and right versions of the ample property. Some semigroups hold one side but not the other. The work maps parts of a boundary that no general method can cross.
arxiv-2508-02249:
Stefan Kuhlmann and Robert Weismantel prove a threshold rule for finding the shortest vector in a lattice under the infinity norm, in a 2025 paper. A lattice here is the set of all whole-number mixes of a matrix's columns. Their result says that once the matrix has at least as many columns as a certain determinant bound, a shortest nonzero vector always has infinity norm one. That tidy structure yields an algorithm whose cost stays manageable when the bound is small.

The rule also sharpens results in integer optimization: for a system of inequalities with whole-number right sides, some optimal whole-number solution sits on a face of dimension below that same bound.
arxiv-2508-02449:
Zhibing Zhang and Qian Zu proved Liouville-type theorems for a complex fluid system in two thousand twenty-five. The equations describe magneto-micropolar fluids, which carry magnetic fields and tiny rotating particles. Liouville theorems say that under set growth limits, the only steady solution is the trivial one.

Using an iteration method, the special structure of the equations, and new mixes of interpolation tools, they prove such results when solution size grows slowly on ring-shaped regions. An energy method plus careful analysis of a linked equation then relaxes the limits by logarithmic factors. The loosest limit falls on angular velocity, which may grow at any polynomial rate in their result.
arxiv-2508-02749:
Road crews plan repairs from forecasts of how pavement will decay, and most forecasts treat each road stretch as if it stood alone. Lu Gao, Ke Yu, and Pan Lu argue the network matters in a 2025 paper. A stretch's neighbors share traffic, weather, and ground, so their decay should rhyme.

The team feeds a graph neural network the road map itself, letting each stretch learn from its neighbors' state. Their test bed is a Texas data set with over half a million pavement readings, one of the largest in the field. Models that used the network layout beat those that ignored it. For agencies that must stretch repair budgets, sharper decay forecasts mean fixing the right mile at the right time.
arxiv-2508-02949:
Jakub Karnowski and Przemysław Szufel wrote a 2025 paper on oligarchic economies, with Ukraine as the case in point. There, a few rich owners rule key sectors and join mines, mills, and power plants under one roof. They also grip key networks, which blocks rivals and locks in waste.

Past work praised the gains of breaking such rule, but proof by model was scarce. The authors build a computer model where firms with mixed skills trade inside a value chain. Some firms sit under oligarch grip and some do not. Runs of the model score how distinct break-up plans change total output growth. Results show the best plan depends on where the oligarch sits in the chain. At times the fix is raw access; at times it is grip on deals.
arxiv-2508-03049:
Jun Zhang, Chao Yi, Mingxi Ma, Mengling He, and Chao Wang tackle sharper hyperspectral images, a key task in remote sensing. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five notes that these images have a huge number of spectral bands. That size makes methods that mix low-rank and smooth priors hard to apply head-on.

Their method, called JLRST, works on a smaller subspace form of the image instead. It checks gradients of grouped coefficient tensors in all three modes to use spectral links and shared patterns. A log-based norm cuts bias from the standard tensor norm. In tests, the method beat top model-based rivals on both speed and accuracy.
arxiv-2508-03249:
Pritha Paul and Chris Clarkson draw pictures of how relativity bends the apparent shapes of cosmic structures, in this 2025 paper. Astronomers map galaxies by redshift, and motion along the line of sight squashes round clusters into ellipsoids, a famous distortion. On the largest scales, subtler effects from the Doppler shift and from gravity's own redshift join in.

Those higher order effects break the symmetry of the squashing, turning spheres into egg or bean like forms. The authors work out how over dense regions, clusters and superclusters with matter falling in, and under dense voids with matter flowing out, should look once the full relativistic treatment is applied. The pictures matter practically: stacking voids to measure them assumes they stay radially symmetric, and they do not.
arxiv-2508-03349:
Sanath Kotturshettar, Pedro Costa, and Rene Pecnik test whether a pillar of weather science, Monin-Obukhov similarity theory, holds inside a closed channel. The theory describes turbulence over open ground in stable air. A channel's walls confine the flow and shrink its eddies, which may break the theory's assumptions. The team ran detailed simulations across strengths of flow and stability.

One ratio rules the answer: the channel's half-height divided by the Obukhov length, a measure of stability. Where that ratio falls decides which scaling law the average wind profile obeys. The authors give a formula to estimate the ratio straight from the control settings of a simulation or duct. Their rebuilt profiles matched the simulations well and predicted wall friction accurately, a number engineers need for pressure losses in stratified flows.
arxiv-2508-03749:
Fiorista and five co-authors counted platform crowds from security cameras in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Transit agencies need live crowding estimates, but fare data and staff reports are blunt tools. The team tested three computer vision routes on station footage from Washington's metro. Over six hundred hours of privacy-protected video fed the study.

One route detects and counts each person with modern object detectors. A second classifies the whole scene's crowd level with a vision transformer. A third segments the image and converts areas into counts with a depth-aware regression. The authors report that vision alone can support real-time estimates. Timely estimates, in turn, could trigger crowding relief before platforms jam.
arxiv-2508-03849: Xiaolu Zhang and co-authors report what elementary teachers first thought about teaching quantum topics in this 2025 study. Eleven teachers joined a funded project to build their own quantum knowledge and make classroom materials for young students. The teachers began with limited knowledge of the subject themselves. Even so, they voiced excitement about bringing the ideas to their classes, and they believed early contact with quantum concepts would open future doors for their students.
arxiv-2508-04049:
Jiayi He and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 on generating sign language videos that separate motion from the signer. Producing natural signing under exact meaning control is hard, and past systems need piles of footage per signer. Their method stores each sign once as pose, gesture, and mesh data with no identity attached. A second stage stitches retrieved signs into smooth motion paths.

A renderer then dresses the motion in any chosen person's appearance. Tests show the split is not just workable but helpful, giving high quality plus free choice of signer. The authors call motion a portable choreography layer that different bodies can perform.
arxiv-2508-04149:
Xuan Qi, Rongwu Xu, and Zhijing Jin wrote this AI paper in 2025 on training language models to match human taste. Preference data, pairs where one answer beats another, drive that training, but such data are dear. Worse, no good method picked which pairs teach most. The team propose a difficulty test drawn from the training method itself: pairs whose hidden reward gap is small are the hard, telling cases.

Training on those hard pairs beat five strong rival pickers across data sets and tasks. Just ten percent of the original data sufficed for the win. The authors frame the pick as principled, not a hunch, since it reads the model's own reward math. They offer it as a way to align models well when data budgets are tight.
arxiv-2508-04249:
Pramod Kamal Kharel and eight co-authors built a quantum-optics style simulator for studying how the infant universe made particles and entanglement, in this 2025 arXiv paper. During inflation, stretching space squeezed quantum fields, creating particles and linking their states. Exact math runs out quickly in such problems, so a faithful simulator is valuable.

Their framework uses Gaussian states and circuit-like steps that mirror optical squeezers. Starting from the standard empty state, they evolve it through a two-mode squeezer across many cosmic settings. Two entanglement measures from the simulator matched analytic bounds in both speeding and slowing universes. The team also shows how added thermal noise dulls both measures. The tools aim to make early-universe quantum effects easier to explore.
arxiv-2508-04349:
Hongze Tan and co-authors shape rewards by token in language models in a 2025 paper. Training by reward lifts reasoning, but common methods give one score to a whole reply. Each word in a good or bad reply thus gets the same credit.

Their fix weighs each word by its entropy, a gauge of how unsure the model was. One method scores per word, one per full reply chain. The word level method steers the model to better paths. The chain level method proved more stable on long chains of thought. Fine grained credit may sharpen reasoning with less waste.
arxiv-2508-04549:
Underwater video is murky, moving, and full of animals that blend into reefs, so captioning it automatically is hard. Quang-Trung Truong and co-authors release MSC, a dataset built to teach machines marine video. Each clip comes with three partners: the footage, a written caption, and masks that outline the animals frame by frame.

Their captioning pipeline works in two stages, and it splits clips where the scene's main animals change, which enriches what the captions can say. The triplets let models learn to ground words in the right animal rather than guessing from the whole scene. The authors position the set as a benchmark for marine video understanding and generation alike. Both data and code are released for other researchers.
arxiv-2508-04849:
Yifan Su, Rishi Veerapaneni, and Jiaoyang Li loosened the execution constraints on warehouse robot fleets in a 2025 paper. Multi-agent path finding plans hit-free routes for many robots, but real robots run late, and a plan tied to exact timesteps breaks under delay. Time-based plan graphs fix this by replacing clock times with ordering dependencies between agents. Bidirectional versions relax some dependencies into pairs that can be traversed in either order, letting delayed robots recover gracefully.

The authors' method, BTPG-max, finds more of those flexible pairs than prior methods and is provably locally maximal: no further pair can be added to its output. In practice the extra bidirectional edges improve anytime actions and robustness to delays, making fleets less brittle when reality intrudes on the plan.
arxiv-2508-05149:
Seraphina Fong, Marco Matassoni, and Alessio Brutti ask how much speech data a data-poor AI needs to hear words right. Top speech models shine in rich languages, yet most languages of the world have thin data. Their 2025 study uses a frame where a light bridge links a speech reader to a language model. It grades two multilingual language models on known speech test sets.

First, the team counts the data volume it takes to tie a strong speech-only tool. That volume is steep, which backs the fear that thin languages start far back. Next, bridges first trained on rich languages cut the pain a lot, most of all when the new set is tiny. Languages with one bridge or many both helped. The readings give a scale for low-data speech work.
arxiv-2508-05649:
The authors present in 2025 an AI-guided system that improves product search by modeling how shoppers reformulate queries over a session. Note that the head byline and the catalog list differ slightly, so team framing is used. Standard rewrite tools treat each query pair alone, missing the step-by-step drift of intent that real browsing shows in large interaction logs.

They mine structured query sequences from eBay logs to reconstruct those journeys. Language models then generate diverse, intent-keeping alternatives beyond what collaborative filtering finds. The rewrites can feed related-search links and themed carousels. Tests showed measurable gains in conversion and engagement.
arxiv-2508-05949:
Jialin Yang and five co-authors surveyed carbon-aware task scheduling in twenty twenty-five. Their field is container orchestration systems such as Kubernetes. Cloud data centers now use vast energy. Language model training and deployment made them grow fast. They emit a lot of carbon in turn. When and where jobs run is one lever operators can in fact control.

The review sorts current Kubernetes scheduling strategies into two families. One is hardware-centric and one is software-centric. It tags each with its sustainability goal. It groups them by algorithm too. On that base the authors set out a comprehensive taxonomy for cloud scheduling research. It is centered on environmental sustainability. They close with new trends and open challenges. The survey aims to guide the design of schedulers that treat carbon as a first-class constraint for next-generation cloud systems.
arxiv-2508-06149: Cho and Cheong present a study from twenty twenty-five on steering the character of chat models with prompts. Their method writes the five classic character traits as numbers inside a plain prompt, with no extra model training. Tests on trait display, chat writing, and mimicry of human traits show clear, distinct traits across models. Short prompts and mild trait levels worked best, and the authors call it a lean route to character-aware chat agents.
arxiv-2508-06449:
Jindrich Zapletal offers a new geometric way to build the Solovay model, a classic setting in set theory. The paper lays out the model's axioms through geometry rather than through the forcing machinery usually used to construct it. That shift matters, because forcing proofs can be long and technical, and the geometric view promises a cleaner path to the same ground.

With that framing, Zapletal gives short, forcing-free proofs of the model's classical results. The same framing also serves as a tool for developing the theory of balanced forcing in purely geometric terms. The work opens a series on independence relations inside this model, relations that record which statements the model leaves open rather than deciding.
arxiv-2508-06649:
Daniel Wang and co-authors test large language models in a 2025 study for two kinds of bias. One kind links traits to a group by habit, such as a faith or a party. The other kind shows in skewed mixes of people in text the models write, far from real-world shares.

The team asked four advanced models to write profiles of people and then checked the links that emerged. All four models showed both kinds of bias toward many groups. Such skew can mislead readers who trust model output about users. The study gives builders a clear way to measure the harm.
arxiv-2508-06749:
Brenda Cervantes-Vergara and ten co-authors place a sensitive particle detector near the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Their device, MOSKITA, is a skipper-CCD set about 33 meters from the collision point to catch low-energy leftovers of high-energy collisions. Data came from beam-on and beam-off periods in 2024. The set covered proton-proton and lead-lead running.

Event rates were reported in a model-independent way across two ionization bands. No clear beam-linked signal appeared in the low-energy band for either collision type. The high-energy band showed a slight rate rise after lead-lead collisions. Low-energy results set limits on the mass and millicharge of hypothetical millicharged particles.
arxiv-2508-06849:
Sanjana Gautam, Mohit Chandra, and their co-authors argue that AI design should start from lived experience. Their 2025 paper notes that personal history shapes how people judge an AI system's safety, trust, and ease of use. Past work taught models to copy human preferences or sorted harms into lists, but rarely studied lived experience itself in a systematic way.

Their framework weaves experience into design and testing across the whole build cycle. It draws on philosophy of experience, human centered design, and studies of human AI interaction, plus work from psychology, education, health care, and social policy. A taxonomy of experience types anchors the proposal. The goal is systems that grasp the backward looking, emotional, and context bound sides of human thought.
arxiv-2508-06949:
Arya Tanmay Gupta presents a dissertation on parallel algorithms that need no synchronization in a 2025 paper. The catalog record gives the creator only as the word By, while the text byline names Gupta. Multiprocessor systems keep growing, and locking steps cost time and resources.

Proving that a lock-free algorithm still settles to the right answer used to require mapping the whole global state graph, an exponential chore. Gupta's theory cuts that work down: it is enough to show each node's local state graph forms a partial order. The dissertation builds lock-free algorithms for several problems and re-certifies known ones. Experiments showed faster convergence than scheduled runs. The result lowers the proof burden for asynchronous computing.
arxiv-2508-07449:
Gunnar Peng, Ehud Yariv, and Ory Schnitzer study how a fluid slides over a surface cut with thin, liquid-filled grooves. Their 2025 paper looks at flow driven by shear, where the grooves hold a second fluid that is far less thick than the one above. They focus on the hard case where that inner fluid is close to having no thickness at all.

Simple guesses say slip should grow very fast in this limit, but the authors show it grows more slowly. The drag is set by a tiny layer near the tips of the ridges between grooves. They give formulas for shallow and deeper grooves, and their results match computer solutions well. The work corrects earlier estimates used for such surfaces.
arxiv-2508-07549:
Sophie Crisp, Ryland Goldman, Arif Ismail, and Spencer Gessner present start-to-end simulations of a compact, linac-based positron source. Their 2025 paper deals with slow positrons, which are key for studying material surfaces but hard to produce with low emittance and high brightness.

Fast positron sources have broad energy and angular spread. Moderators can turn fast positrons into slow, mono-energetic ones, but their efficiency is usually very low. Slowing the fast beam with a linac first can raise that efficiency a lot. Their simulations use G4beamline to model a 100 MeV electron beam on a tungsten target, focused by an adiabatic matching device and then decelerated.
arxiv-2508-07949:
Christiane Quesne presents a 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics, on a matrix Hamiltonian with rotational symmetry in any dimension. Quesne introduces a spin-extended version of the so(d+1,1) algebra and shows it frames the system neatly. Extra operators complete a basis for one of the algebra's representations.

Inside that frame, the constants of motion of the system in one representation fall out with little effort. Quesne then carries them into the Schrödinger picture, including a Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector with spin. The paper derives that vector and its properties inside the wider algebraic setting, which may aid other symmetric quantum systems.
arxiv-2508-08249:
Bodas, Harigaya, Inomata, Terada, and Wang present a paper from twenty twenty-five on gravitational waves from a rotating axion field. Axions are hypothetical light particles tied to dark matter ideas. A brief early-universe spin-up of such a field can source strong ripples. The ripples would form a background hum across the sky. Axion fluctuations grow beyond the horizon during that epoch. The resulting wave background carries a marked directional unevenness. That unevenness is a signature fingerprint of the scenario.

The brief epoch dodges strict limits on large-scale ripples. The authors check which detectors could see the signal. Both strength and unevenness may be reachable, they find. The work links particle theory to future sky surveys.
arxiv-2508-08349:
Kamal Choudhary, a solo author, presents an AI model that reads crystal structures from X-ray patterns in a 2025 paper. Working out atomic structure from a powder diffraction pattern is a classic hard problem in materials science, often needing expert effort. The model is a generative transformer, similar in spirit to language models.

It was trained on thousands of known structures and their simulated diffraction patterns. The model was tested with no chemical hints, with a list of elements, and with a full chemical formula. Accuracy rose sharply when chemical information was supplied. Training was fast and simple, the author notes. The tool could speed data driven discovery of new materials.
arxiv-2508-08549:
A team of researchers builds one segmentation framework for three hard medical imaging settings in a paper from 2025. The head title and byline, which add a sixth author, differ from the catalog, and the description follows the head with team framing. Labels are scarce, and scanners differ between hospitals, so models trained in one place falter elsewhere. Their network uses one student taught by two different teachers. The teachers produce varied yet reliable pseudo-labels for unlabeled scans.

Label propagation then spreads voxel-level information inside each image. Strong augmentation at two scales adds global and local knowledge. Across five benchmark data sets and three task types, the framework beat leading methods. The authors pitch it as a generic answer to label scarcity.
arxiv-2508-08649:
Jakub Šmíd, Pavel Přibáň, and Pavel Král published this study in 2025. It tests language models on aspect-based sentiment analysis. That task asks not just whether a text is positive, but how it judges each aspect it names. Plain large models lag behind small tuned models on this compound task. The team asked what happens when the large models themselves get fine-tuned for it.

They tuned LLaMA-based models and tested them on four tasks across eight English data sets. One tuned model, based on Orca 2, beat the prior best results on every task. Yet all models did poorly when asked to work cold, with no or few examples. The paper ends with an error study showing where even the tuned models still stumble.
arxiv-2508-08749:
Yuan Qiu and Ke Yi published a research paper in 2025 on clustering data points while keeping each person's data private. The popular DBSCAN method groups points by crowding, but private versions that print each point's group label, the pair argue, leak or garble too much to be useful. They propose printing the spans of the clusters instead.

On that new target they build a private clustering method that runs in straight-line time and meets a sandwich quality promise in any fixed dimension count. They also prove no method can do much better. A fast private histogram sits inside the method as a reusable part. Tests on fake and real data backed the design.
arxiv-2508-09149:
Car networks that wait for trouble lose to trouble that moves at road speed. Seyed Hossein Ahmadpanah, writing solo in 2025, builds a manager that thinks ahead. A twin of the network, fed on forecasts of traffic, motion, and signal strength, shows the near future. A big language model sits on top as the planner, reading the twin's tale and placing work before the crunch.

The planner also takes orders in plain speech: favor the ambulance lanes today, save power tonight. It bends its aim to match, a trick set-rule systems cannot do. In trials the frame beat both set-rule and learning rivals on scale, grit in wild swings, and fit to new aims. Ahmadpanah frames words as the new control panel for car nets.
arxiv-2508-09349:
Cathy Speed and Ahmed Metwally propose a hybrid method for reaching expert consensus that pairs a generative AI with small panels of senior specialists, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Consensus methods matter where evidence is tangled or thin, but classic Delphi studies burden panelists, flatten nuance, and move slowly.

Their framework, HAH-Delphi, weaves a large AI model into the Delphi rounds under structured facilitation. The AI helps digest a fragmented evidence base and draft context-rich material, while the human experts keep judgment and final say. The authors test the model in three phases: replaying a past study, running a live comparison, and deploying it in a real case. The goal is consensus that keeps conditional detail instead of averaging it away. The study speaks to guideline work in medicine and other complex fields drowning in unfiltered public information.
arxiv-2508-09449:
Jiaqi Yan and seven co-authors make reference-based photo enhancement practical by fetching the references automatically, in a 2025 paper. Classic methods need a hand-picked sharp partner photo. Real users rarely have one ready. Their system retrieves look-alike high-quality images from a category database. A phone shot at a zoo can thus borrow detail from stored animal photos.

A new benchmark built from Flickr photos tests the setup. Each category carries its own reference pool. Their network pairs a semantic retriever with a diffusion generator. Conditioning on retrieved content guides the rebuild. Scores and realism both beat plain upscaling baselines. Textures looked more convincing in side-by-side checks. The authors frame retrieval as the bridge to real deployment. Museums and zoos are the showcase settings.
arxiv-2508-09749:
Qiong Li and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, two feeding black holes caught side by side when the universe was young. Theory says such pairs should be vanishingly rare at early times. Using the Webb telescope's camera and spectrograph, the team found two active galactic nuclei about ten thousand light-years apart, at a redshift of 5.4. It is among the highest-redshift pairs ever confirmed by spectra. Emission-line tests backed the identification.

A ground-based instrument then revealed a glowing cloud of hydrogen spanning over seventy thousand light-years around the pair. It is among the largest such clouds known at that era. The system sits in a crowded neighborhood, possibly the heart of a forming cluster. Counting pairs suggests they are commoner than theory expects. The authors offer the find as a laboratory for how black hole pairs stir the gas around them.
arxiv-2508-09849:
Jan Phillipp Albrecht, Jose Godinho, Christina Hubers, and Deborah Schmidt present software for measuring regions inside three-dimensional X-ray scans in a 2025 study. Computed tomography reveals the internal microstructure of rocks and materials, but turning voxels into trustworthy numbers usually means running a fixed pipeline over the whole volume. Beam hardening and partial volume effects corrupt that uniform treatment in places.

Interactive quantification lets an analyst adapt the analysis region by region while keeping measurements reproducible. Materials scientists studying pores, grains, and cracks gain numbers they can defend, rather than artifacts of an automatic threshold.
arxiv-2508-10449:
Dhruv Dosi and co-authors build a tool that spots service key marks on power plans. The work dates to 2025. Old floor plans oft live just as scanned sheets. With no machine-read form, large reads turn slow and fault prone for build teams.

The team made a tagged set of forty-five scanned power plans. It holds near two and a half thousand marks in more than thirty classes. Past trained spot models were set on the set in a fair frame. The best model hit a strong mean score. Their light tool then finds, names, and counts the marks in real time. Its output feeds cost and care flows.
arxiv-2508-10649:
Debvrat Varshney and co-authors forecast land cover change with a generative diffusion model in this 2025 paper. Impervious surfaces such as roads and roofs heat land, speed runoff, and cut groundwater recharge. Earth system models need future land cover as an input, but forecasting it has lagged behind weather and water forecasts.

Their approach treats the forecast as a data synthesis task. A diffusion model learns from historical maps and side data across the whole continental United States. It then generates plausible future imperviousness maps a decade ahead. Results are compared with a baseline that assumes no change. The paper lists traits a generative model needs for this job. Feasibility tests support the new paradigm for land planning.
arxiv-2508-10849:
Metin Ozturk, Maryam Salamatmoghadasi, and Halim Yanikomeroglu add sky layers to phone nets to save power, in a study from 2025. Base stations eat much power, so firms switch some off when load is low. Land nets alone can lack room or reach when cells sleep.

Their plan shifts users across tiers: land towers, drones, high craft, and satellites, a first for the last of these. Shifts weigh delay, so no user is parked on a slow tier by rote. AI tools squeeze data and smooth hand-offs in the plan. A worked case showed big power cuts and glad users. The team frames the tier mix as a path to green 6G nets that still feel fast.
arxiv-2508-11249:
Asela Hevapathige, Asiri Wijesinghe, and Ahad Zehmakan wrote a paper from 2025 on graph neural networks that spread information the way opinions move through a crowd. Diffusion-based graph networks borrow from physics, but most assume the spread is uniform and still. That limits them on varied graphs, caps their depth, and leaves their long-run behavior murky. The team builds a framework that unifies several opinion dynamics models into one trainable diffusion rule.

Each node gets its own behavior, and neighborhood influence shifts over time, so the spread adapts to the graph's local shape. Deep stacks stay efficient and readable. The authors prove the framework can settle into many different end states, covering diverse convergence patterns. On node labeling and influence estimation tests, it beat leading graph networks. They pitch opinion dynamics as a principled engine for graph learning.
arxiv-2508-11749:
Tudor Dimofte, Wenjun Niu, and Victor Py study in 2025 line operators in three-dimensional holomorphic quantum field theories. Such theories include twisted versions of supersymmetric models. Line operators and their fusion rules encode deep structure, but their representation theory needed development for these settings in a systematic mathematical form.

They argue lines correspond to modules over an algebra Koszul-dual to bulk local operators. A non-renormalization result lets quantum corrections to fusion be summed exactly in many theories. They propose axioms for the full structure, named a dg-shifted Yangian. Gauge theory examples confirm the picture, with explicit computations of both sides.
arxiv-2508-11849:
A robot brain built on a lean sequence model learns to walk by sight, Yinuo Wang and Gavin Tao present in a 2025 paper. Their controller fuses body senses with depth images into compact tokens. Stacked Mamba layers scan those tokens in near-linear time, keeping memory small and long-range links intact.

Training runs end to end with a standard policy method, under shuffled terrain and looks plus a rising obstacle density. Tests pit it against rivals in cluttered, uneven worlds with still and moving hazards. Fast sequence math could put capable walking controllers on cheaper robot hardware.
arxiv-2508-12049:
Sergiu Klainerman and Xuecheng Wang prove how fast waves die down in materials that treat directions unequally. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In such non-isotropic media, wave speed depends on the heading. Sharp decay bounds are the first step to proving that small waves stay tame forever.

The striking point is what the bounds rest on. They need only how the system interacts with one special scaling field. From those bounds, the pair give two short proofs of global regularity. Those cover systems with cubic nonlinear terms in three space dimensions. Simpler proofs of such results are prized, since the classic ones are long. The authors hope the method will crack the harder case of biaxial crystals. There, light bends in two distinct ways.
arxiv-2508-12149:
Haochen You and Baojing Liu present MOVER, a way to align text, video, and sound in one shared space for search across types. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. Pair-wise drills work well for two types but scale poorly to three or more. They can also leave the shared space with weak shape and sense.

MOVER pairs a soft match rule drawn from transport math with a shape rule that shrinks the bulk of the point cloud. The shape rule, called GAVE, keeps groups tight and well spread by sense. Tests on text, video, and sound search beat top past methods in both raw and tuned runs. New type mixes also held up well.
arxiv-2508-12349:
Junyi Ma and co-authors present in 2025 a tool that spots the exact frames where a hand touches or leaves an object in first-person video. Such timing matters for virtual reality and for teaching robots by watching people. Older tools need masks or fixed lists of actions, which limits their use.

Their tool, called EgoLoc, picks smart sample frames from hand motion and asks a vision-language model to judge contact and parting. Feedback loops then refine the call. It needs no training labels for each scene. Tests on public data and new benchmarks show it lands the key moments well across varied clips.
arxiv-2508-12549:
Atasi Panda, Harsh Sharma, Anand Louis, and Prajakta Nimbhorkar tackle fair assignment of items to platforms when groups need balanced shares, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Each item has a value on each platform, and each platform pays a curved cost that grows as it takes more items or more from one group. Hard caps are replaced by soft cost penalties.

The goal is the cheapest assignment that still hits a set total value. A fast method with proof-backed error bounds uses linear programming and flow tools. A special case with equal values gets an exact method, while the broad case with overlapping groups is shown to be hard. Readers get flexible fairness with clear limits.
arxiv-2508-12949:
Gökhan Torun argues that a fairer way of squaring up quantum bases gives better measures of quantum resources. Turning skewed bases into orthogonal ones is routine, but the standard Gram-Schmidt route depends on ordering and can distort the physics. The symmetric Löwdin method treats every vector alike and stays closest to the original set.

From it he defines probabilistic weights that never go negative, unlike an older rival scheme. The weights support clean measures of coherence and superposition, plus entropy-based gauges of how spread out a state is. Tests confirm the symmetric route preserves resource character better.
arxiv-2508-13049:
Tejas Chaudhari and four co-authors present XR-NPE, a neural processing engine for extended reality in two thousand twenty-five. XR gear must run perception tasks on tight power and area. Their engine is a mixed precision SIMD design for those loads. It is the first to support FP4 and several Posit formats.

Layer adaptive methods pair with quantization aware training to hold accuracy. A rebuilt multiply circuit cuts dark silicon in the compute array. Selective power gating trims energy use further in the design. Chip runs show strong gains in area, power, and arithmetic intensity. FPGA tests beat rival accelerators on efficiency as well.
arxiv-2508-13149:
Kyung-Su Kim wrote this 2025 physics paper on exchange interactions in a Wigner crystal placed in a magnetic field. A Wigner crystal forms when electrons in two dimensions settle into a regular lattice. Its magnetism comes from exchange moves, in which several particles swap places by tunneling.

Kim uses a semi-classical expansion suited to wide particle spacing. With only a magnetic field, the swaps arise from many-particle tunneling along complex paths. To first order in the field, each exchange constant gains an Aharonov-Bohm phase along the zero-field path. With Berry curvature present as well, the tunneling must be traced in a mixed position and momentum space. Each constant then gains a Berry phase too. When both effects act at once, the two phases combine, and the paper works out how.
arxiv-2508-13749:
Mohammad Taha Shah, Sabrina Khurshid, and Gourab Ghatak took on a risk-tuned choice task in 2025. In a bandit task, a learner pulls one of many arms and learns from the payoffs. Most bandit work chases total payoff. Their aim is the Sharpe ratio, a score that weighs mean payoff against its swing. That aim is a fraction, so mean and swing must be learned as one.

Their method samples from a paired belief over mean and spread for each arm. One sampling rule serves all risk tastes, unlike past mean-swing forms. They prove a tight bound on lost ground over time and a match bound that no method can beat. Tests on made-up bandits showed the method ahead of past risk-aware rivals.
arxiv-2508-14149:
Eleonora Giovannetti examines in a 2025 paper what a quantum bounce means across three formalisms of quantum cosmology. The classic idea pictures a collapsing universe branch scattering into an expanding one. That picture gives a quantum account of the semiclassical big bounce proposal.

Mean values and spread of the volume operator back the proposal in the Wheeler DeWitt frame. Grounding checks hold for the simple isotropic case in that frame. In the Dirac approach, the same idea describes Kasner shifts in uneven Bianchi models instead. The author frames quantum scattering, borrowed from particle physics, as one model for many settings. Behavior reads scalar like or fermion like depending on how unevenness enters.
arxiv-2508-14249:
Matthias Hetzenberger, Georg Moser, and Florian Zuleger teach a typed programming framework to reason about the expected cost of programs that flip coins, in a 2025 paper. Probabilistic programs are everywhere, yet proving how long they run on average lags far behind proving them correct. Their tool is a refinement-typed probability monad inside Liquid Haskell, a language whose types carry checkable claims. Random behavior is encoded in the types themselves.

An automated solver then discharges many cost claims with little human annotation. Four case studies test the range: meldable heaps and the coupon collector run nearly automatically, while randomized quicksort and zip trees mix automation with interactive proof. The zip tree result is the first formal check of its expected runtime. The authors pitch the monad as a bridge between programming practice and proof.
arxiv-2508-14349:
Sean Fletcher and co-authors release a cell image data set for studying a chemotherapy drug, in a 2025 paper. Taxol is widely used against cancer, and its cell-level effects matter for care and research. Lab checks of those effects need costly gear, skill, and prep time. No public image set existed for automating the check with deep learning, so the team built one.

The images show rat glioma cells dosed with Taxol at several strengths. Their baseline model pairs a known image network with attention blocks that sharpen key features. A neighbor-based classifier then reads the learned image codes to name the dose level. The authors frame the model as a benchmark, not a final tool. Both the data set and code are public for other groups to beat.
arxiv-2508-14549:
Florian Oberender shows in 2025 that a workhorse algorithm for reading quantum states can settle on the wrong answer. Maximum likelihood iteration is prized for being simple and for seeming to converge to a sound density matrix. Oberender constructs cases where the iteration stops at spurious fixed points that are not the true solution.

To guard against the trap, he gives a check based on first-order optimality conditions that tells whether a result is truly the desired one. He also generalizes the algorithm and proves it matches factorized gradient descent, tying the method to a wider family of optimization tools.
arxiv-2508-14949:
Patricia Amado-Caballero and co-authors use explainable AI to find what sets coughs of different lung diseases apart. Their 2025 paper starts from cough recordings turned into spectrograms, images of sound over time. A neural network classifies them, but its reasons are hidden. Occlusion maps show which parts of the image drive each decision. The team then analyzes those highlighted regions closely.

Weighting the spectra by the maps revealed real differences between disease groups. Coughs from chronic obstructive disease varied more in the key regions. Raw spectrograms, by contrast, showed no clear group differences. Several spectral features were extracted from the highlighted zones. The authors argue the method makes cough analysis more interpretable. It could sharpen diagnosis by pointing to disease specific sound signatures rather than overall patterns.
arxiv-2508-15249:
Alaul Islam, Fairouz Grioui, Raimund Dachselt, and Petra Isenberg present a 2025 workshop study of data displays on smart wristbands that wrap the whole wrist. Which part of the band you can see depends on your arm's posture, so one layout cannot fit all moments. With no such product on the market yet, the team ran a paper-based ideation workshop across four scenarios: office work, leisurely walks, cycling, and driving.

Participants designed layouts per posture and data type. A strong preference emerged for responsive designs that adapt as the arm moves. The authors map how spatial layout and chart choice should shift with posture. They offer the results as design groundwork for a coming device class. Supplemental material is posted openly.
arxiv-2508-15449:
A model that has learned harmful facts can be told to forget, but most forgetting is a lid, not a purge. Chengcan Wu and four co-authors aim for the purge in 2025 with a one-way warp of the model's inner space. Their method bends the hidden states of set layers through a projection that cannot be run backward. Harmful traces fall off the far side of the bend; sound knowledge rides through.

Past ways, which push against the bad data in training, leave the traces in place, and a short re-teach can wake them. The warp held up under such re-teach attacks in the team's tests. It also kept the model's plain skill near whole. The team claim the top marks so far on the twin test of forgetting well and keeping well.
arxiv-2508-15649:
Zhong Guo and Prabir Barooah publish a simulation model of a central chilled water plant, built for training learning-based controllers, in a 2025 paper. Such plants, bundles of chillers, cooling towers, coils, and cold storage, eat a large share of building energy. Controllers that learn by trial need a model that stays sane when trials wander outside normal operation.

Existing component models can output nonsense beyond their comfort zone. The authors refit the components through constrained optimization so that every heat exchanger's capacity is respected whatever inputs arrive. The assembled plant model then holds valid across a much wider range, which is exactly what learning controllers need for safe exploration. The model is public in a common simulation environment. A closed-loop control simulation illustrates its use.
arxiv-2508-15749:
Antonio Galvao and Gabriel Montes-Rojas introduce a new framework for quantile regression with many outcomes at once in this 2025 paper. Quantile methods study the spread of results, not just the average. Past multi-outcome versions used angles, vectors, or link models. This one builds straight from the joint chance structure of the outcomes.

The method builds multi-outcome quantile curves from a chain of single-outcome fits, each one conditioned on the last. That chain keeps the meaning of the curves clear and makes fitting flexible. The authors prove the large-sample traits of their estimator and test it in simulations, where it held up well across varied link patterns. As a real case, they track how exchange rate moves passed into prices in Argentina from 2004 to 2024.
arxiv-2508-15849:
Ziyu Wang, Elahe Khatibi, and Amir Rahmani build a question-answering system for medicine that reasons in causal steps. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Language models often answer medical questions with shallow guesses or made-up facts. Fetching source text helps, but plain similarity search can pull the wrong evidence for a diagnosis task.

Their system searches for documents that match the causal chain behind a case, not just its keywords. It then prompts the model to reason step by step along that chain, like a clinician would. Tests on three medical question sets beat plain retrieval systems by up to about ten percent. Gains over tuned medical systems were also clear. The design improves accuracy and makes the reasoning easier to inspect.
arxiv-2508-16149:
Jongmin Lee and Sungkyu Jung study how to name the center of a spread of points when the space itself is curved. On flat ground, a mean does that job, but curved spaces need care. Their 2025 work widens the toolkit to a broad class of loss rules, not just the squared gap used for the classic mean.

The pair set mild terms on the loss rule and on the spread of points. Under those terms, they prove a center of this kind both exists and is the only one. The proof covers centers for the true spread and for samples drawn from it. Their frame unites past results on when such centers are unique. It also gives a base for sturdy location work in curved data spaces.
arxiv-2508-16549:
Anjeza Krakulli and a co-author give the fuzzy notion of a set's complement a firm topological meaning in this 2025 paper. In fuzzy topology, sets come in shades, and the standard complement is defined by algebra alone. That breaks the familiar rule that the complement of an open set is closed, leaving the theory internally at odds.

The authors attach an ordinary topological space to every fuzzy one. On that space they build its fundamental groupoid, the structure recording paths and loops, dressed with a topology of its own. Through that lens they characterize when fuzzy complementation behaves as topology says it should. The construction turns a definitional mismatch into a checkable geometric property, and it imports the tools of algebraic topology into a field that began with graded truth values.
arxiv-2508-16649:
Juan Barandiaran and Martin Rivas wrote a 2025 paper on a classical picture of the electron like Dirac particle meeting a light wave packet. In their model the particle has structure: a charge centre circles a mass centre. They integrate the motion numerically for a particle starting at rest, and share the notebook.

Whatever the charge sign, the wave hands over momentum, energy, and spin. The mass centre ends up drifting along the wave's travel direction. Spin change splits into two parts, from torque about the mass centre and from work along its path. Wave settings and starting spin steer the outcome, which they map case by case.
arxiv-2508-16749:
Victor-Louis De Gusseme led a large team reporting a robot cloth competition in a 2025 paper. Robots struggle with cloth, and the field lacked shared benchmarks to compare methods fairly. Their contest, run at a major robotics meeting, focused on one task: choosing where to grasp cloth so a robot can unfold it in the air. Eleven teams took part with varied methods.

The public dataset holds hundreds of real unfolding attempts across dozens of garments, including the contest trials. Hand-built methods did surprisingly well, and there was a clear trade-off between grasp success and coverage. Contest results also differed sharply from earlier lab reports, stressing outside testing.
arxiv-2508-16849:
Lihao Zhang, Zongtan Li, and Haijian Sun build a new way in 2025 to map wireless channels in space. Next-era networks need big antenna arrays and exact maps of how signals travel. Old maps, from rules, ray tracing, or field tests, trade off sharpness, speed, and scale.

Their method rebuilds travel paths from sparse loss readings alone. Flat gaussian patches form the scene shape in a first stage, tuned for radio work. A second stage fits how radio energy spreads, with a loss rule that uses many views. The team reports sharper rebuilds at lower training cost than past light-field methods. A cheap, sharp channel map could help place antennas and predict dead zones before a network is built.
arxiv-2508-17549: David Eppstein proves a drawing theorem for plane graphs in this 2025 mathematics paper. Take any plane graph and any smooth convex curve that is not a straight line. Eppstein shows the graph can always be drawn with straight edges so that the curve crosses every face of the drawing. No face escapes the curve: each region, including the outer one, is stabbed by it. The result joins graph drawing with a stabbing property from geometry, and the proof works for every such graph and curve at once.
arxiv-2508-17849:
Jingyi Liao and co-authors fix, in a 2025 paper, a skew in how smart picks feed object find training. Box tags are dear, so smart picks choose the best boxes to tag by hand. The rest get fake tags from the model. Early models do well just on the big classes, so fake tags flood with them. Small classes starve, and the end model leans. Their fix picks more small-class boxes for hand tags, to even the full set. A soft fake-tag path, tuned to the task, lifts fake tag truth as well.

On set bench sets, the pair hit top marks for this work. Tag cost drops while find skill holds, the team shows.
arxiv-2508-18149:
Sarah Winkler extends reactive synthesis to richer logics in a 2025 paper. Synthesis builds a controller that provably meets a temporal specification against any environment moves. Her setting lets rules compare values across time steps, a lookback feature earlier tools mostly banned.

That freedom makes the problem undecidable in general, so the procedure may not always halt. Still, it is sound, and complete whenever a bounded-length winning strategy exists. For several useful fragments it becomes a true decision procedure, recovering known results and adding new ones. Readers get a wider synthesis frontier with honest limits.
arxiv-2508-18549:
Maike Züfle and co-authors present a 2025 paper on grading machine translation. Most scores for such work look at one source sentence and one translated version, then give a grade. People, by contrast, often judge a version by setting it next to other versions of the same text. The authors build two new scores that copy that habit.

One score, called COMET-polycand, grades a version with help from other versions of the same sentence. The other, COMET-polyic, draws on translations of like texts and the grades people gave them. Adding just one extra version lifted the match with human grades by a clear margin. More added versions helped further, and the team has shared its models in public.
arxiv-2508-18649:
Nanxi Li, Zhengyue Zhao, and Chaowei Xiao presented PRISM in 2025, a framework that aligns vision-language models for safety through structured reasoning. Current guards often over-block harmless requests or align too shallowly to catch complex threats that need real thought. PRISM takes a slower, deliberate approach modeled on careful human reasoning.

Its pipeline reasons in four stages, one per category of multimodal safety violation. A training method builds better reasoning traces with tree search and then refines them by preference optimization. Tests on two jailbreak benchmarks showed large drops in attack success, with robustness gains reported. The head byline adds two more authors beyond the catalog list, so the work is framed as a team effort. Readers get a guard that shows its reasoning, stage by stage.
arxiv-2508-18849:
Bo Peng and Michele Pizzochero design ribbons of carbon fullerene cages that carry a chain of atomic magnets along one edge, in a 2025 paper. Adding extra C60 cages to one side of a Janus fullerene nanoribbon creates an odd bond count, leaving one unpaired electron and a quantized magnetic moment in an otherwise nonmagnetic strip.

Lined up, those spin-half cages settle into an antiferromagnetic ground state, neighbors pointing oppositely, and the pattern survives changes in the ribbon's detailed structure. Against graphene ribbons, the fullerene route may be easier to build with atomic precision. The authors propose the strips as a platform for scalable spin devices and for exploring many-body quantum phases.
arxiv-2508-18949:
Wenyin Zhou and co-authors reframed a molecule-building method in 2025 around energy, the score that says how natural a shape is. Tools that dream up molecular shapes serve drug docking, protein folding, and design. Flow matching, which morphs random shapes into real ones step by step, is a leading approach.

Their view learns a single map that carries a random layout toward a true structure, guided by energy ideas. The setup links to two neat traits: applying the map twice changes little, and results stay stable. It also echoes the polish step used by a famous folding tool. On docking and backbone-building tests, the method beat recent flow and diffusion rivals on the same budget. The authors call the energy lens both sound in theory and strong in practice.
arxiv-2508-19149:
Claudio Battiloro and co-authors build the first theory of algorithmic collective action when several groups push on one system at once, in work from twenty twenty-five. Users can steer learning systems by coordinating their shared data. Real movements, though, splinter into multiple collectives with overlapping goals. Earlier theory handled only a single collective at a time. The new framework studies signal planting in classifiers.

Collectives of different sizes aim at chosen target classes. Goal alignment between groups shapes how much each achieves. Size interplay decides whether allies help or hinder each other. Quantitative results replace hunches about multi-group dynamics. Earlier experiments find their missing theoretical explanation here. User-side steering gains a realistic, multi-actor foundation.
arxiv-2508-19449:
Software crashes flood development teams with duplicate reports of the same bug. Mamun, Uddin, Xia, and Zhang build dedupT, a system that sorts crash reports by reading their stack traces, the lists of function calls recorded when a program fails. Older methods compare traces as plain text or judge each frame alone, missing how the frames fit together.

Their method first adapts a pretrained language model to the special language of stack traces. A small ranking network then uses those rich representations to order likely duplicates. On four public datasets, dedupT beat both deep learning rivals and classic methods at ranking duplicates and spotting truly new crashes. Ranking quality rose by more than fifteen percent over the best learning baseline. The authors say the tool can cut the manual triage work that slows bug fixing.
arxiv-2508-19549:
Sukdev Mahapatra maps how low craft fall from their paths as thin air drags on them, with a plain math model, in a paper from 2025. Low paths serve talk, guide, and Earth watch work, yet drag eats their span in ways owners must call in advance. Air grade shifts with height and sun mood, which bends the fall pace.

The model ties drag rules and air curves to craft mass, face size, and height to read the fall clock. Tall, light craft with broad faces fall fast, while low mass craft ride longer. Reads are set next to space agency models and past print for scale. True air grade proves the hinge term. The guide serves fleet plans in a sky that grows more full.
arxiv-2508-19949:
Sauri builds estimators for quantities derived from trawl processes, a family of continuous-time random processes used for data with memory, in a 2025 paper. A trawl process is fully described by one curve, its trawl function, but researchers often need nonlinear summaries of that curve over finite or infinite horizons.

His nonparametric estimators target exactly such summaries, built from samples taken either densely over a fixed window or across a long span. The first estimator is consistent and turns Gaussian in the limit no matter how strong the process's memory is. The second behaves the same under a growth condition on the test function. The results also yield a test for time dependence that memory cannot distort.
arxiv-2508-20049:
Ivan Martinez-Berumen, Pereg-Barnea, and Coish published this physics paper in 2025. It shows how rhythmically shaking a magnetic material can create protected channels for waves along its edges. The waves are magnons, ripples of the spins inside a magnet.

Their model is a square grid of spins with a twist force, called the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, that is wobbled in time. The wobble can flip the material into a topological phase, where edge modes appear that resist scattering. These edge waves mix single magnons with bound pairs, a richer blend than usual. By shifting the relative timing of the wobble along the two grid directions, the team can steer which way the edge waves run. Such control could matter for future magnon circuits that carry signals without charge.
arxiv-2508-20249:
Charles Gauthier offers a new way to test a classic model of how people value future rewards, in a solo 2025 paper. The model, exponential discounting, says each added delay cuts value by a steady share. Departures from it are common, but measuring how far a person departs, without assuming a set utility shape, is hard.

Gauthier derives a representation of the model that yields a measure of efficiency for such departures. The approach uses revealed preference, reading choices rather than asking about them, and it allows wide differences between people. Scanner data from shop checkouts, tracked over time, illustrate the method. The results give insight into where departures from steady discounting come from. The work is aimed at economists who study saving, spending, and self-control over time.
arxiv-2508-20549:
Weihai Zhi, Jiayan Guo, and Shangyang Li present MedGR2, a framework for medical reasoning with vision-language models, in a 2025 paper. Medical AI is held back by a lack of high-quality labeled data from experts. Fine-tuning on small sets often fails on new tasks, and reward-based learning lacks good reward signals.

Their system grows a data generator and a reward model together, so each improves the other. The cycle creates fresh multi-modal medical data for training. Models trained on that data beat baselines trained on large human-made sets. A compact model rivaled far larger ones. The authors frame the shift as moving from data scarcity to data generation.
arxiv-2508-20649:
Angan Mukherjee and Victor Zavala argue for weaving physical laws into machine learning for chemical engineering, in a 2025 perspective paper. Pure data models can fit plant records yet fail outside them, while pure physics models miss real-world mess. Physics-constrained learning mixes the two for reliability and sense. The approach has proven itself elsewhere, but chemical plants pose special snags.

The authors list the hard parts: deciding how much physics to embed, fusing it with learning without breaking either, scaling to huge datasets and simulators, and knowing how unsure a prediction is. They survey recent progress and point to prizes worth chasing: closed-loop design of experiments, live control of running plants, and processes that span many scales at once. The piece is a roadmap for a field mid-merger.
arxiv-2508-20949:
Christopher Jackson, writing alone in 2025, makes a flexible kind of disease progression model practical for the first time. Multi-state models track patients moving between health states, but the usual version assumes the risk of moving does not depend on how long a patient has sat in a state. Real illness often breaks that rule, and past fixes were narrow or lacked software.

Jackson's trick rewrites the waiting time in each state as a chain of hidden phases, which turns the model into a hidden Markov model that standard tools can fit. A moment-matching step keeps the chain short by mimicking simple waiting shapes such as the gamma or Weibull forms. The method ships in a new R package called msmbayes, which fits such models by Bayesian or likelihood methods. Tests by simulation check out, and a study of thinking decline shows the workflow.
arxiv-2508-21049:
Ramazan Bahrami and Ramin Yahyapour did relation extraction from single sentences in 2025 with capsule networks and dynamic routing. The task is to read a sentence and name the relation between its entities, a core step in building knowledge from text. Their method lets capsule groups vote and reroute until they agree on a reading.

The approach beat the state of the art on four standard data sets named in the study. On a larger, similar set drawn from Wikidata it did poorly, and the team traced part of that gap to noisy labels in the data. They link the wins to re-representation, a brain-inspired change of representation at comparison time that sharpens matching. Readers get both a strong method and a diagnosis of where benchmark noise can fake a failure.
arxiv-2508-21449:
Niklas Jansen, Jonas Gösgens, and Hector Geffner teach a planner's action model from partial traces, in a 2025 paper. Planning systems need formal action descriptions, but real logs rarely show everything an action touches.

Their test case is the sliding-tile puzzle, where traces show tile positions but not the blank square, and actions are bare direction words. The authors define a variant of the STRIPS language that allows hidden action arguments, pinned down by queries over the state. Their learning algorithm builds those queries step by step for each action. They prove the learner correct and complete, then test it on traces from known planning domains to show it scales.
arxiv-2508-21549:
Liding Zhang and co-authors make robot path planning faster by guessing smartly before a route exists. Popular sampling planners narrow their search once they find a first path, but until then they wander the whole space, which wastes time. Their planner, MIT*, builds an estimated search region from prior cost guesses, so the hunt starts focused.

An adaptive sampler shifts strategy as the search unfolds, and a sparse collision check speeds a lazy backward search. In tests spanning four to sixteen dimensions, the planner beat established single-query rivals on path cost, computing time, and success in tight spaces. It also ran real robot manipulation tasks. The authors present it as a practical step for robots that must plan quickly in cramped, high-dimensional worlds.
arxiv-2508-21649:
Joseph Feest, Hélène Ruffieux, Camilla Lingjærde, and Xiaoyue Xi wrote a 2025 statistics paper on estimating networks from biomedical data when samples differ. Most network analyses assume every sample shares one dependence structure. In mixed disease settings that assumption can mislead, since gene links shift with disease stage.

Their method, NExON-Bayes, builds sample level ordered traits, like stage, into a joint Gaussian graphical model. It extends a spike and slab framework so the trait can reshape the network, and it learns how much each trait matters. A tailored variational algorithm keeps the fitting fast enough for high dimensional omic data. In simulations, the method beat both the plain graphical model and other covariate aware rivals at recovering the true network.
arxiv-2508-21749:
Mathias Weller and Norbert Zeh ask how much extra wiring a network needs to hold many family trees at once in a 2025 paper. In evolution studies, a network can display several trees by adding reticulations, cross-links between branches. Shared structure lets trees share parts of the network.

They show that some sets of trees share almost no usable structure. For a modest number of trees, any network displaying them needs nearly the naive maximum of cross-links. For more trees, the needed count matches the known ceiling for displaying all trees, up to constant factors. Simple counting arguments drive the proofs, which extend to unrooted networks as well.
arxiv-2509-00749:
Sangyu Han, with two co-authors, Yearim Kim and Nojun Kwak, questions how sparse autoencoder features in vision models are usually explained. Interpreters inspect patches where a feature's activation is highest, but self-attention mixes information across the whole image, so an active patch may merely co-occur with the true cause.

Han and his co-authors propose Causal Feature Explanation, which uses Effective Receptive Field maps and input-attribution methods to find patches that causally drive each activation. Across CLIP-ViT features, these maps often diverge from naive activation maps, revealing hidden context needs, such as a roaring face feature requiring eyes and nose together. Patch insertion tests confirm the causal patches recover or suppress activations better.
arxiv-2509-00849:
Shaina Raza leads five authors in total, with Maximus Powers, Partha Pratim Saha, Mahveen Raza, and Rizwan Qureshi, in testing whether prompting can reduce stereotypes in text-to-image models for occupations. Such models are powerful creative tools but risk amplifying harmful social biases in who they depict.

They build a pilot benchmark covering five roles: chief executive, nurse, software engineer, teacher, and athlete. Five leading models, closed and open, receive neutral prompts and fairness-aware prompts designed to encourage demographic diversity. Outputs are annotated for gender and race. Prompting shifts representation substantially, but effects vary by model: some diversify well, others overcorrect into unrealistic uniformity, and some barely respond.
arxiv-2509-01049:
Jiaji Zhang, with two co-authors, introduces a neural approach to non-Markovian quantum state diffusion. That framework models open quantum systems with wavefunctions. The environment retains memory in such systems. Standard machine learning merely approximates wavefunctions or mean values. Their operator-based approach aims for broader use and clearer meaning.

An operator construction algorithm uses a neural network as a generator. It rebuilds the stochastic time evolution operator from many trajectories. The method is benchmarked on the spin-boson model. Diverse spectral densities are covered in those tests. Accuracy is shown across those cases in the paper. The operator also proves useful for absorption spectra. It can rebuild reduced density matrices at long timescales as well.
arxiv-2509-01349:
Tuning the settings of stochastic gradient descent is often guided by trial and error. This method is the workhorse of machine learning. Chanju Park, Biagio Lucini, and Gert Aarts argue that a network's phase diagram can supply better intuition. Each phase shows a distinct pattern. The singular values of the weight matrices move in their own way in each phase.

The team borrows from disordered systems in physics. Learned features map to soft spins. The starting weight variance acts as disorder strength. Temperature is set by the ratio of learning rate to batch size. Three phases appear as training proceeds. A Langevin equation tracks the descent process. It shows how the singular values evolve in each phase. The picture links physics to training choices for multilayer networks.
arxiv-2509-01449:
Gravitational wave detectors such as LIGO listen for ripples in spacetime with laser interferometers of extreme precision. Anna C. Green, with twelve co-authors, examines how tiny optical defects, distortions at the nanoscale, can limit those cosmic-scale observations. Future detectors, the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, aim for still greater sensitivity, so the defect question grows sharper.

The work relies on Finesse, the community's leading interferometer simulation tool, which models optical, quantum, and mechanical effects together. The team explores how defects warp the laser light's shape and cap detector performance, and presents recent advances in modeling those effects. Their aim is practical: guide the design of next-generation optics so that flaws measured in billionths of a meter do not blind instruments built to hear the universe.
arxiv-2509-01549:
Recommender systems must refresh their suggestions as new data pour in and tastes shift, yet recomputing from scratch is slow. Viacheslav Yusupov, Maxim Rakhuba, and Evgeny Frolov present a fast warm start method for a scalable graph-based recommender called UltraGCN. Warm starting updates the old model instead of rebuilding it.

Their linear approach adapts a low-rank approximation, a compact stand-in for a large matrix, to the graph model. The method delivers fresh recommendations up to thirty times faster than conventional updates, with gains in recommendation quality rather than losses. Tests on large catalogue data sets show the approach scales well. Yusupov and the co-authors aim to keep recommendations relevant in systems where data volume and user preferences change constantly.
arxiv-2509-01749:
Yangyadatta Tripathy and Barjeev Tyagi build a full math model of a hybrid microgrid, a small power network that mixes direct and alternating current parts. The model joins converters, which change power from one form to another, with their controls and loads. Inputs come from sources like solar cells, batteries, or fuel cells at a steady direct voltage. Filters smooth the output before it reaches the lines.

Each converter type is modeled with its own states and inputs, then three of each are combined. Network and load models complete the hybrid system. Tests of the model eigenvalues, which flag stable or unstable modes, guide a controller design. Placing those values by feedback steadies the grid.
arxiv-2509-01849:
Shayne Waldron gives a basic classification of finite reflection groups that use quaternions in two dimensions. Quaternions extend complex numbers with three imaginary parts, and reflection groups are symmetry sets built from mirror like maps. His tool is a reflection system, a lean setup that captures the group data. Past classifications turn out to be incomplete under his check.

Waldron lists all groups of this rank two type with clean presentations, meaning short rule sets that generate each group. He finds four groups of the same order and reflection count that are not the same group. One of those four was unknown before. The simpler route may help extend the theory to higher ranks.
arxiv-2509-01949:
