To address this gap, the team focused on a challenging cross-cultural encoding-decoding task beyond machine translation: foreign newcomers requesting Chinese names from Chinese users. They examined how people collectively built a digital Babel Tower through encoding strategies. The team collected and analyzed over seventy thousand RedNote comments using a creative human-in-the-loop method with large language models. That work derives a systematic framework covering cross-cultural information encoding strategies, how they combine and layer to complicate decoding, and how they connect to engagement measures.
arxiv-2602-18649:
Yongzhong Xu studies grokking networks. His 2026 paper notes grokking, the sudden shift from memory to generalization after training, tied to low-dimensional structure. Yet network weights live in high-dimensional spaces: how can low-dimensional learning yield solutions resisting compression?

He trains shared-trunk Transformers with heads for addition, multiplication, and a quadratic task modulo ninety-seven, across three sizes and five decay settings. Comparing per-matrix SVD, joint cross-matrix SVD, plus trajectory PCA, he finds grokking paths confined to a two-to-six-dimensional subspace, while single matrices stay full-rank. Rebuilding from three to five trajectory components recovers over ninety-five percent of final accuracy, while both SVD methods fail below full rank. Yet static decompositions capturing most spectral energy still wreck task structure. The result supports a holographic encoding principle: grokked solutions are low-rank globally in learning directions but locally full-rank in parameters.
arxiv-2602-18949:
Energy time series such as solar irradiance, wind speed, and electrical load repeat daily and seasonally. Stationary models and simple carry-over cannot capture their changing statistics. Cyril Voyant, with five co-authors, introduces closed-form forecasting rules for cyclostationary processes in 2026.

The rules extend carry-over through a closed-form coefficient built from local correlation between the current observation and its phase-aligned lag. That construction preserves periodic variance and covariance. It also cuts effective degrees of freedom through symmetry. The result is a training-free closed-form limit of carry-over under periodic non-stationarity. Tests on synthetic signals and real renewable energy data show consistent gains over classical carry-over, above all at multi-hour horizons. The framework offers a physically readable, minimal baseline that gives the same result each time. Symmetry does the work here. That keeps the method simple and clear.
arxiv-2602-19049:
Long chains of thought raise accuracy, but they cost dearly at inference time. Yinhan He, with seven co-authors, rethinks token-efficient post-training in 2026. Existing reward-shaping methods control effort only at sequence level. They cannot steer effort token by token.

The authors propose IAPO, an information-theoretic frame. It assigns each token an advantage from its conditional mutual information with the final answer. Informative steps gain weight. Low-utility exploration gets suppressed. Theory shows verbosity can fall monotonically without harming correctness. Tests show accuracy rises while reasoning length falls by over a third. IAPO beats existing token-efficient methods across reasoning datasets. Information-aware shaping thus offers a general path to cheaper reasoning.
arxiv-2602-19149:
Image generators can be tricked into unacceptable content. Gurjot Singh, with four co-authors, adds a post-generation safeguard in 2026 called ReVision. Prompt filtering and safety-aware training can both be bypassed. They also often degrade output quality. A guard that acts after making, without touching the generator, avoids those costs.

It analyses generated images and edits unsafe concepts selectively. Earlier post-hoc editors localise imprecisely, limiting use in multi-concept scenes. A vision-language-model-assisted spatial gating mechanism fixes that, enabling instance-consistent, integrity-preserving edits. A benchmark of hundreds of images spans single- and multi-concept cases mixed with benign concepts. Alignment toward safe prompts improves, background distortion falls sharply, and nudity detections vanish. External benchmarks and a human study confirm the gains.
arxiv-2602-19449:
Large vision-language models translate images into representations for reasoning, but their vision encoders often stumble on domain-specific tasks like medical diagnosis or fine-grained classification. Jason Wu and nine co-authors note that representation errors then cascade through the language model into wrong answers. Existing adaptation methods tune the projector between encoder and language model, keeping the two components coupled.

The team introduces CRAFT (Codebook RegulAted Fine-Tuning), a lightweight way to tune the encoder with a discrete codebook anchoring visual representations to a stable token space. Nothing else in the model changes, so domain adaptation no longer needs re-alignment whenever the encoder changes. The adapted encoder can then boost vision-language models with different language models behind them.
arxiv-2602-19649:
Compression size can jump after edits, and Lempel-Ziv 77 is a classic test case. Gabriel Bathie and three co-authors study LZ77 sensitivity under many substitutions, building on Akagi, Funakoshi, and Inenaga's 2023 result that one edit at most doubles compressed size. The naive k-edit bound is a factor of 2 to the k, and the authors had guessed the true factor was about k.

Surprisingly, sensitivity stays constant, with k entering only as a linear additive term. A string within Hamming distance k has LZ77 size at most 3 times the original plus 4k. The bound is nearly tight, with examples reaching 3 times plus k, times one minus epsilon. A trichotomy refines the factor 3 by compressibility. The factor runs up to about 3 when the compressed size is small, and 2 in the middle range. It falls to 1 when large, in contrast to LZ78's one-bit catastrophe.
arxiv-2602-19849:
The asteroid Apophis will pass near Earth in 2029, and understanding where such bodies come from puts that passage in context. A 2026 arXiv paper by M. Brož and six co-authors analyzes possible source populations for Apophis-like bodies, above all the Flora family, whose composition matches LL chondrite meteorites.

Simulating the Flora family over roughly a billion years, the team finds Apophis-like orbits unusually persistent in near-Earth space, so at least one such body is typically present. Encounter probabilities vary over time with sharp peaks, and Apophis itself sits in an unremarkable range. Such persistence also favours temporary capture as Earth co-orbitals. While Apophis poses no threat in the next few centuries, similar objects carry roughly a one-in-five lifetime chance of Earth impact, ending otherwise by solar approach or planetary impact.
arxiv-2602-19949:
Light can carry particle-like singularities in phase and polarization, lines of darkness that weave threads through three-dimensional space. A 2026 arXiv paper by Danilo Gomes Pires and four co-authors asks how those structures behave in complex, turbulent media, where their stability has been debated.

Known for half a century from work on dislocations in wave trains, these singularities are the building blocks of many optical topologies. The authors run complementary numerical and experimental studies with atmospheric turbulence as the test case, finding agreement and equivalent dynamics. Their key finding is that vortices of polarization and of phase act alike in one-sided turbulent channels. The work clarifies open questions and matters for imaging, communication, sensing, and information transfer in noisy settings.
arxiv-2602-20549:
Picking a prior is central to solving ill-posed imaging inverse problems, since a prior that clashes with the data brings heavy bias. Frederic Wang and Katherine L. Bouman note that Bayesian model choice needs the model evidence for each candidate prior, yet computing that evidence under a diffusion prior is intractable. Most current estimators need many density checks or an exact clean score. The paper proposes DiME, a new estimator built for this gap.

DiME estimates the evidence by integrating over time slices of posterior sampling runs. It reuses the many mid-run samples that reverse diffusion sampling already yields. It needs only a handful of posterior samples, about twenty, for an exact estimate. Tests show it matches exactly computable evidence, picks the right diffusion prior, and spots prior misfit in hard non-linear inverse problems, including a real black hole imaging case.
arxiv-2602-20849:
Field theories gain power when their parameters obey stable relations, and a new class of transformations promises exactly that. Bohdan Grzadkowski and Odd Magne Ogreid study GOOFy transformations in this 2026 arXiv paper. These transformations act on bosonic and fermionic fields while leaving the Lagrangian density unchanged, using a generalized charge conjugation applied in a non-consistent way.

Requiring the kinetic terms to stay invariant fixes the form of the transformed fields, which yields a systematic recipe for GOOFy-invariant models. The resulting parameter relations stay fixed under renormalization-group running through two and three loops. The Standard Model fails the GOOFy test as a viable electroweak theory, but the two-Higgs-doublet model may pass it, giving a concrete example beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2602-21149:
Chaos in many-body systems is gauged by the largest Lyapunov rate, but broad limits on its size are poorly known. Swetamber Das sets direct Hamiltonian-own upper bounds in this 2026 arXiv paper for classic systems with local links. The bounds come from split-second steadiness rules, told through mass scales and link-energy bend.

Two classes emerge: non-breakable bounds set by worst-case bend and mass, and ergodic ceilings that keep spectral facts about group modes and finite-size effects. For a 1D rotor chain, the ergodic ceiling takes closed form and marks a motion off-limits zone, backed in numbers. In the heat limit it nears a mass ceiling free of heat and link strength, setting a least time span for losing start rules.
arxiv-2602-21249:
Data quality lacks a shared meaning, and old-object data lacks quality grading at all. Markus Matoni, Arno Kesper, and Gabriele Taentzer address both gaps in this 2026 arXiv paper. They define quality facets cut to telling facts about old-object items, grounded in a deep study of facets in use and shown with domain cases.

The meaning is then tested in trials against a curated set of real-world data-quality problems from the old-object domain. That trial backs the meaning, yielding a full account of data quality for this domain. Readers get facets built for old-object accounts plus proof they work on actual problems, not just theory wish lists.
arxiv-2602-21349:
Super-Earth spacings look mostly featureless except for excesses of planet pairs sitting slightly wide of first-order resonances. Sam Hadden and Yanqin Wu extend the breaking-the-chains model to explain both features in this 2026 arXiv paper. After disk migration settles super-Earths into resonant chains, scattering a planetesimal population holding only a few percent of system mass reorganizes them remarkably.

Scattering rattles chains by repelling adjacent pairs wide of their resonances. Some chains stay rattled but intact, forming the observed excesses wide of resonances. In other systems the rattling seeds later instabilities that break chains entirely. If individual planetesimals weigh around a Pluto mass, instabilities can onset tens or hundreds of millions of years after birth, explaining the disappearance of near-resonant pairs on that timescale.
arxiv-2602-21449:
Van-Chung Luu and three co-authors propose a semi-gridless variational Bayes method for channel estimation in extremely large MIMO systems. Huge antenna arrays and high-frequency operation promise faster, lower-latency sixth-generation links. But they push communication into the near field, where spherical wavefronts replace planar ones and old estimators falter.

The team rewrites the near-field channel model for uniform linear and planar arrays into separate direction-of-arrival and distance parts. Directions are estimated gridlessly with a von Mises distribution, while distance uses a coarse-to-fine grid search. Their semi-gridless variational Bayes algorithm then reconstructs channels with efficient update rules. Simulations show improved near-field reconstruction accuracy and stronger estimation for both direction and distance components.
arxiv-2602-21749:
Social bot hunting guards the health of online information. Graph neural network tools face severe class skew from the high cost of making bots, plus network noise from bots that mimic humans and forge false links. Longlong Zhang and five co-authors propose RABot, a multi-level graph-boosting design that tackles both problems at once. A local-aware extra-sampling plan blends rare-class vectors within local subgraphs, steadying the cutoff when data are scarce.

At the same time, a reinforcement-learning-driven edge filter combines similarity-based edge features with adaptive threshold tuning to cut spurious interactions during message passing, yielding a cleaner topology. Tests on three real-world benchmarks and four graph backbones show RABot beating state-of-the-art baselines. Since its augmentation and filtering modules sit apart from the underlying architecture, RABot plugs into existing pipelines with minimal overhead.
arxiv-2602-22149:
Heart disease kills nearly twenty million people a year, and the Framingham Risk Score is among the most widely used tools for predicting who is at risk. Emannuel L. de A. Bezerra and five co-authors note its blind spot: it never explains why a patient lands in a risk category, or what would lower that risk. They build a logic-based explainer that fills that gap.

Grounded in first-order logic and explainable-AI principles, the explainer finds a minimal set of patient attributes sufficient to justify a given classification. It also sketches actionable scenarios, showing which changeable factors would drop a patient to a lower risk band. Tested across tens of thousands of input combinations, it turns a trusted black-box score into advice a clinician can act on.
arxiv-2602-22449:
Cyberbullying wounds social and mental health, yet most detectors assume each comment carries a single type of abuse. Mirza Raquib and five co-authors note reality is messier: one comment can mix threats, hate speech, and harassment. Multi-label detection is therefore essential, but it has drawn little attention in low-resource languages like Bangla, where robust pretrained models are scarce.

Transformers grasp context but can miss sequential dependencies, while LSTM models track sequence but lack semantic depth. The team fuses context-aware BanglaBERT with a two-layer stacked LSTM, aiming for a generalized model with moderate accuracy. For Bangla content moderation, the fusion offers a practical multi-label detector where single-label tools fall short.
arxiv-2602-22649:
Woojae Hong and five co-authors built an open-source desktop tool for labelling medical scans by hand, with machine help. Voxel-level labels are vital for testing imaging algorithms, yet manual labelling of 3D scans is slow and costly. Past tools also handled slices one by one, with no unified workflow.

Interactive Medical-SAM2 GUI runs locally inside the Napari viewer and treats a 3D volume as a stack of slices. Box or point prompts start a mask, which then spreads through the stack with Medical-SAM2. Users work through cases in one folder, refine with point prompts, and export per-object volumes and 3D renders, with geometry kept intact. It is meant for research labelling only.
arxiv-2602-22749:
Shijie Dong and three co-authors prove sharp decay estimates for a weak null wave system, a simplified stand-in for the Einstein vacuum equations. For small-data solutions, they bound the gap between the solution and its leading term by faster-decaying lower-order terms in retarded time, the difference between time and radius.

The estimates are shown sharp for a generic class of fast-decaying small initial data, meaning no better general rate exists. Two striking consequences follow. One component's energy admits a lower bound that generically grows without limit as time runs to infinity, a blow-up at infinity. That same component also shows an energy cascade flowing from high to low frequencies.
arxiv-2602-23149:
Isabella Alvarenga and one co-author study two one-dimensional versions of the contact process, a model of how a population spreads or dies out across a line of sites. In the contact-and-barrier version, the population lives to the right of a barrier that moves at random. In the multitype version, two species compete for the same space, starting on opposite sides of the origin.

The authors prove that both models form tight, well-defined boundary lines between occupied and empty ground, or between the two species. After shifting by a fixed speed, the boundary position follows a bell-curve law. The proofs rest on a renewal method built from a new patchwork construction, which assembles each process from space-time pieces over random-length time spans.
arxiv-2602-23349:
Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz and three co-authors introduce FlashOptim, a suite of optimizations that cuts memory for neural network training by over half per parameter. Standard mixed-precision training stores many bytes per parameter: the parameter itself, its gradient, and one or more optimizer state values, typically four bytes each. Training even a 7-billion-parameter model can thus be impractical with under 100 GB of accelerator memory.

Two techniques drive the savings. Better master weight splitting exploits a tight bound on its quantization error. Companding functions greatly reduce error in 8-bit optimizer state quantization. Together with 16-bit gradients, they cut AdamW memory from 16 bytes to 7 bytes per parameter, or 5 bytes with gradient release, and shrink checkpoints by more than half. Tests on SGD, AdamW, and Lion show no measurable quality loss on standard vision and language benchmarks, including Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-23549:
Xinyi Zhang studies how a boundary shapes the bulk of two half-space models: exponential last passage percolation and the log-gamma polymer. For each, she proves convergence of rescaled last passage time and free energy to the directed landscape. The window sits at distance f(n) times n to the two-thirds from the boundary. Boundary attraction stays weaker than f(n) times n to the minus one-third.

That condition is sharp: any strength of that order changes the limit for large time gaps. For exponential last passage percolation, a phase transition appears in point-to-point passage time as attraction varies. As attraction grows, fluctuations shift from a bulk KPZ regime to a boundary Gaussian regime. A critical window is ruled by the positive part of a shifted Gaussian. The limit there pits a Gaussian boundary part against a bulk part that vanishes under Gaussian scaling.
arxiv-2602-23849:
Jordi De Jonghe and Alexander J. B. Russell study how to start unstable fluid and plasma simulations so they reach the nonlinear stage faster. The 2026 paper tests initializing with linear eigenmodes, the natural wave patterns of an equilibrium, instead of random velocity noise.

Using the MPI-AMRVAC code and eigenmodes computed with Legolas, the authors simulate a sheared fluid interface, a Harris current sheet, and a sheared plasma interface. Starting from a superposition that includes the fastest-growing mode cuts the time spent in the linear stage sharply, in the best case by an order of magnitude, versus noise or analytic perturbations. Which extra modes are included also shapes later nonlinear evolution, for instance by speeding symmetry breaking. Coupling spectral codes to fluid codes thus saves real compute time.
arxiv-2602-24049:
Avigdor Veksler and three co-authors present an automated algorithm for designing island divertors for stellarators, the exhaust structures that must handle extreme heat loads within material limits. The 2026 paper needs only two user-chosen starting points on the island separatrix, a simplicity that lets the team, in a fixed magnetic equilibrium, explore the divertor parameter space.

Heat loads are estimated with a field-line diffusion model, and divertor solutions that meet heat requirements while capturing a high power fraction are found by parameter scan and Bayesian optimization. Optimization matches the scan's performance at a fraction of the compute cost. Resulting divertors satisfy heat requirements across varied cross-field diffusivities, and scans over islands show that low-elongation islands are easiest to satisfy. The simple parameterization supports further physics and optimization studies of stellarator exhaust. In short, the design holds up under heat.
arxiv-2602-24249:
Jamie Lee and eight co-authors study how adolescents envision AI's role in health management, a perspective prior research has largely missed by focusing on providers, caregivers, and adult patients. The 2026 paper uses design fiction and co-design workshops with adolescents aged fourteen to seventeen, set in the context of a family celiac diagnosis.

Three envisioned roles emerge: enhancing health understanding and help-seeking, supporting family health management, and providing guidance while respecting autonomy. Trust proves nuanced, and views divide on support from health AI. Overall, adolescents see AI's value as moving them from efficiency to meaning, creating time for valued activities. The authors argue that future health AI should encourage adolescent autonomy and reflection while supporting activities, rather than merely speeding up health tasks.
arxiv-2603-00049: Huang presents BiJEPA, a two-way joint embedding predictive architecture that forces cycle-steady prediction between data segments. Standard JEPA predicts one way only, from context to target, missing signal in the reverse link. A norm rule on vectors tames the instability of symmetric prediction and stops code blow-up. Tests on fake cyclic signals, chaotic Lorenz paths and image data show BiJEPA settles stably without collapse. It captures chaotic semantic structure and learns robust time and space codes for generation and generalisation.
arxiv-2603-00149: Li and colleagues present ReMD, a physics-true diffusion system for fluid super-resolution that fixes residuals across scales with a multigrid design. Each reverse step couples data fit with light physics cues, then fixes the residual across scales using a multi-wavelet basis that captures both large structures and fine vortical detail. The coarse-to-fine design speeds convergence and preserves fine structures without equations. Across atmospheric and oceanic tests it improves accuracy and spectral fidelity, cuts divergence, and matches diffusion baselines with far fewer sampling steps.
arxiv-2603-00249: Tamhane and colleagues present Hubble images of ionised filaments in group galaxy NGC 5044, with widths of 50 to 120 parsecs, scaling inversely with pressure. Hubble, ALMA and MUSE data yield densities and magnetic fields, with equipartition fields falling from about 40 microgauss centrally to about 20 at 5 kiloparsecs, two to three times weaker than clusters. Stability would need stronger radial fields, and ultraviolet imaging finds no star formation. The galaxy holds an ionised gas core inside its Bondi radius, linked to filaments, suggesting inflow toward the black hole.
arxiv-2603-00349: Yang and five colleagues study how teams of language model agents work together, arguing that final task success alone hides where joint work breaks down. Their COOP framework ties high level team conduct to visible progress in the task setting and sets checkable joint requirements, so failures can be traced over time. A repair tool built on it forecasts requirement failures from group plans and opens focused channels for fixes. Trials in two settings show gains in success and requirement keeping, at the price of added choice and message load.
arxiv-2603-00449: Deen and Lam hunt for earlier sightings of asteroid 2024 YR4, a former Torino Scale 3 object with a possible lunar impact in 2032. Searching 2016 survey images with a matched filter tuned to its predicted look, they identify candidate precoveries that sharpen approach distance uncertainty more than three hundred fold. If confirmed, the refined orbit rules out a 2032 lunar impact and eases planetary defence work. The candidates should be easy to check during the asteroid's 2028 Earth approach.
arxiv-2603-00749: Campbell and Jansen show that standard network meta-analysis biases non collapsible effect measures toward the null when studies enrol heterogeneous populations. Using binary outcomes and the non collapsible odds ratio, they demonstrate the bias even when effect modifiers do not differ across studies, because baseline risks still vary. The common treatment effect assumption therefore fails under mixed populations with different baseline risks. Their bookend approach splits mixed population studies into two homogeneous parts and weights them, correcting the bias.
arxiv-2603-01149: Boyer and Majumdar solve a model of a sluggish walker whose diffusion slows with distance from the origin. The walker resets to places it visited before, favoring familiar ground. At late times its typical displacement grows ultra-slowly, as a power of log time, and its position law tends to a scaling form. For any positive exponent the scaling shape is bimodal with a dip at zero and non-Gaussian tails. Generalized moments in one dimension follow exactly and link to the constant-diffusion model.
arxiv-2603-01449:
Restoring a clean image from an MRI scan often uses models that mix facts from across the whole picture. Xiangjian Hou, Chao Qin, Chang Ni, and colleagues ask in 2026 when that wide mixing truly helps. MRI jobs differ a lot, so a design that helps one job may add little to the next.

The group built a fair test bed with a small local model and a wider variant beside top global models. For fast scans and for sharper images, the small local model held its own against global rivals. For noise removal with uneven noise, global models did best, since they can judge how trust in each spot varies. The lesson is to match the model to the scan task and its physics.
arxiv-2603-01549:
Robots that take orders in words and act on what they see often miss how the world moves when they act. Jisoo Kim, Jungbin Cho, Sanghyeok Chu, and colleagues add that missing sense in this 2026 work. Their method, Pri4R, trains vision-language-action models with extra four-dimensional facts not used at run time.

During training, a light extra head predicts how points in space will move in three dimensions. Robot features feed that head, so the shared code learns how scenes shift under actions. At run time the model reverts to its plain form, with no extra inputs or cost. Tests in simulation and on real robots show clear gains on hard handling tasks. Extra checks confirm that point-track training is what teaches the action-world link.
arxiv-2603-01649:
Alvaro Pernas and Ricardo Puebla shape single photons so quantum network nodes can swap information despite mismatched tones. Their 2026 work sits in superconducting waveguide networks, where nodes pass single light particles along guides. When nodes ring at different frequencies, direct exchange fails and the network cannot scale.

The pair derive the controls needed to shape a photon at any chosen offset from its natural tone. That shaping allows on-demand, precise exchange between nodes that do not resonate with each other. They map which control settings suit common photon shapes and which suit real lab setups. Simulations support high-fidelity transfer between distant, off-tone nodes. A simple extension of the same controls also creates remote entanglement, a linked state shared across the network.
arxiv-2603-01949:
Cristiana Diaconu, Miles Cranmer, Richard Turner, and colleagues turn fixed physics simulators into probabilistic ones without retraining. Their 2026 work starts from a gap: learned PDE simulators predict one outcome, yet many real systems are chaotic and uncertain. Training probabilistic models from scratch wastes the strong deterministic models already built.

Retrofitting fine-tunes a pre-trained model with a proper scoring rule for distributions, called CRPS. The same recipe applies across unlike backbones with minimal code changes. On single-system models, rollout scores and error measures improve by wide margins over matched deterministic tuning. A PDE foundation model retrofitted on a target data set shows the same pattern at larger scale. The result says probabilistic physics modeling can be an upgrade, not a rebuild.
arxiv-2603-02049:
Yisu Zhang, Chenjie Cao, Tengfei Wang, and colleagues link camera-guided video generation with 3D scene reconstruction. Their 2026 framework, WorldStereo, attacks a split: generated videos look great, yet rebuilding consistent 3D scenes from them fails. Camera control is loose and content shifts between viewpoints in raw generator output.

Two geometric memory modules bridge the gap inside the generation process itself. A global memory injects coarse structure through point clouds updated as generation proceeds, enabling precise camera control. A spatial-stereo memory constrains attention with 3D correspondence, so fine details stay consistent across views. The control branch design stays efficient by reusing a distilled video backbone without joint training. Benchmarks for camera-guided generation and reconstruction both favor the approach, from single and panoramic inputs alike.
arxiv-2603-02149:
Namhoon Kim, Narges Moeini, Justin Romberg, and Sara Fridovich-Keil present a cleaning method for noisy 3D scans in this 2026 paper. Many scans, from medical CT to electron imaging, suffer heavy noise. Their method, 3D Field of Junctions, fits each small block of a volume with joined wedge shapes. Wedges meet at sharp edges, so real structure is kept, not blurred.

No training data is needed, which avoids the risk of invented detail. Nearby blocks are pushed to agree, so the full volume stays coherent. Tests covered low-dose CT, electron tomography, and laser point clouds in bad weather. In each case the method beat a mix of classic and neural rivals. It can also plug into wider scan repair tasks.
arxiv-2603-03549:
Edoardo Gargiulo and Efe A Ok settle when order-preserving maps can be extended without stretching them further. Extending a Lipschitz map, one that never stretches distances by more than a fixed factor, from a subset to a whole space is a classic problem. Their 2026 paper adds two demands at once: the map must stay order-preserving, and its values live in a Hadamard poset, a curved ordered space.

In one dimension the extension always exists. In two or more dimensions, with only weak conditions on the target space, a universal extension exists exactly when the domain's order is trivial, meaning no real ordering at all. Hilbert posets satisfy the conditions, so the result covers them directly. One corollary stings: there is no order-respecting generalization of Kirszbraun's classic extension theorem.
arxiv-2603-03849:
Yao Ma computes what neutron stars are made of inside a chiral model of nuclear matter, and finds a tension worth chasing. His 2026 analysis uses an extended linear sigma model in mean-field approximation, where baryon and meson masses arise from spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking. Several couplings between mesons and nucleons steer the results, and one newcomer, the delta meson, reshapes the symmetry energy in a decisive way.

The delta produces a plateau in symmetry energy at intermediate densities. That plateau reconciles two stubborn measurements at once: the neutron skin thickness of lead-208 and the tidal deformability of a typical neutron star. An explicit symmetry-breaking term then links to the pion-nucleon sigma term. Matching astrophysical limits demands that term be negative, stiffer stars and larger maximum masses, against its positive vacuum value. The mismatch hints how model parameters must run with density.
arxiv-2603-03949: Yu Takiguchi and Koji Nemoto propose an SIS competition model for opposing rumors, for instance fake news versus its corrections. The simple model links rumor spread with opinion change: rumors shift opinions, and opinions in turn fix infection rates. The authors work out every steady state analytically with its stability, uncovering a novel coexistence mechanism. Coexistence means belief in one rumor paradoxically aids spread of the opposing rumor, so a lower infection rate can actually enhance a rumor spread.
arxiv-2603-04149: Zenari and others explain timescale diversity in recurrent circuits through topology. They present a random recurrent network with adjustable degree variety, deriving a mean-field theory with degree-conditioned motion. The theory shows partial weight symmetry plus degree variety creates a non-Markovian memory term as self-coupling. Stability criteria show degree variety drops the critical gain and confines unstable modes to hubs, and slow hub neurons integrate slow inputs. The mouse connectome explains wide single-neuron timescale ranges and their positive link to in-degree.
arxiv-2603-04349: Zemskova and colleagues pick keyframes for long egocentric video questions. More frames slow multimodal models and cut accuracy, so frame choice is key. FocusGraph finds query clips with a light Scene-Graph selector reading compact graph captions. Keyframes then come from an offline program evolved sparse flow method with no learned parameters at inference. It leads on FindingDory and HourVideo while cutting question time cost.
arxiv-2603-04549: Zhang and colleagues control what language model agents remember with Adaptive Memory Admission Control. Agents lean on long term memory for multi-session reasoning, yet current systems barely govern retention, hoarding stale or hallucinated facts or relying on opaque, costly policies. A-MAC treats admission as a structured choice, scoring content type prior, temporal recency, semantic novelty, factual confidence, and future utility. Lightweight rules extract features, one model assisted assessment judges utility, and cross-validated optimization learns adaptive policies, reaching F1 of 0.583 on LoCoMo with latency down 31 percent.
arxiv-2603-05049: Frans van Die and Vincent Desjacques study dynamical dark energy's effects on cosmic structure growth using a two-fluid model. The method lets the dark energy formula of state cross the phantom divide smoothly, matching DESI results. Dynamical dark energy supports sound-wave-like perturbations, inducing scale dependence in matter swing growth and halo bias. For cluster halos, the scale-dependent bias amplitude rivals that from massless neutrinos in ΛCDM. A guess for two-tracer power spectrum plus bispectrum analysis finds bispectrum information key to detecting this dependence.
arxiv-2603-05249: Zi-Jie Chen and team improve control of open quantum systems to be both robust and optimal, where imperfections like setting uncertainty and decoherence degrade test platforms. Most prior control targets arbitrary unitaries in closed systems, but their raised algorithm suppresses imperfections and noise with notably better scalability for open systems. Test validation in a superconducting quantum circuit shows it beating the usual closed-system counterpart at ultra-low infidelity, with the same hardness scaling and a modest prefactor lift. The work advances quantum optimal control toward real quantum technologies.
arxiv-2603-05349: Jérôme Leblanc and team present hybrid Liouvillian recursion for Green's functions on a quantum computer. From a ground state circuit, the algorithm makes local and inter-site Green's functions. They show it on a superconducting four-site Hubbard processor. Computed Green's functions feed the Galitskii-Migdal formula, beating Hamiltonian expectation for energy figures. Results show exponential settling and polynomial hardness in Green's-function accuracy. Results also show toughness to noise and preparation inaccuracies.
arxiv-2603-05749: Srivastava and team look into mid-air drop-bit collisions at ratio three. Forecast models of spray-drying and pickup need knowing collisions. Wetness and density changes show outcome works and offset's role. Density decides swallowing versus surface stay. High wetness cuts splitting in glancing collisions. The changed working Weber number with density and wetness maps results. Joined with past results, edges collapse at constant size ratio and Ohnesorge number. At a given offset, size-ratio and Ohnesorge changes alter the key splitting Weber number through shape and viscous drag.
arxiv-2603-06149: Turino and his team set out PQC-LEO, a benchmarking suite that automates tests of post quantum cryptographic algorithms across x86 and ARM chips. Quantum computing puts current public key cryptography at risk through Shor's algorithm, and while NIST has standardised several post quantum schemes, hard adoption problems remain. A proof of concept run shows the suite works and backs research into adoption. One clear find is that higher security builds lose more speed on ARM than on x86.
arxiv-2603-06749: Kube and colleagues survey robotic foundation models for industrial control and test how ready they really are. The survey maps the model landscape and distills industrial needs, from collaborative platforms and mixed sensing to edge limits and safety-critical operation, into interdependent implications. Those become an assessment frame with a large catalogue of concrete criteria. Evaluating hundreds of manipulation-capable models shows limited, uneven maturity: even top models meet only a fraction of criteria, with narrow peaks rather than broad coverage.
arxiv-2603-07049: Biswas and colleagues build a fix for gaps in power grid sensor data. When shared links fail, whole groups of sensors can go dark at once, so past fixes that use only the readings on hand miss the cause. Their plan groups sensors in even sets and picks routes so few sensors in one set share one path. A low-rank fill-in step then rebuilds the lost readings, and tests show the route-aware plan beats plain fill-in when links fail.
arxiv-2603-07749: Santos and colleagues study how mixed teams shape AI systems building, using four AI teams at a large software company in Brazil and Portugal. From Grounded Theory and 25 talks with workers across varied projects, they find six key roles for mixed teams. They diversify viewpoints for bias spotting, bring empathy to AI building, address unfair treatment, and support open shared choices. Mixed teams also safeguard against bias and grow broadened thinking. The findings highlight varied viewpoints and offer tips for weaving fairness into software building habits.
arxiv-2603-07849: Welch revisits a claim that major tropical storms grew more common relative to all storms from 1979 to 2017. Splitting the ratio by storm class, he finds the trend was driven mainly by fewer weak storms, not more strong ones. Weak-storm counts fell by about a sixth between halves. Extending the record through 2023 changes the picture: strong storms now rise too, so the sign of fiercer storms rests on both fewer weak and more strong cases.
arxiv-2603-07949: Zheng and colleagues cut inference costs for vision-language-action models by splitting work between edge devices and the cloud. Environment-oriented partitioning breaks under visual noise, and current edge-cloud splits ignore step-wise redundancy in embodied motion, disrupting the physical continuity of movement. Their RAPID framework addresses both faults with a redundancy-aware, compatibility-optimal partitioning scheme built for diverse vision-language-action models. Experiments report speedups of up to about 1.7 times with only a few percent of overhead, easing edge-device pressure while meeting real-time needs.
arxiv-2603-08049: Chandio and colleagues examine how YouTube production and consumption dynamics shape extreme ideologies, a link prior work has left understudied by focusing mainly on user behavior and recommendations. They combine one year of watch history with two waves of ideological surveys from 1,100 participants in the United States. From that record they identify users whose views shifted markedly toward extremes and compare what those users produced and consumed with the rest. The study traces how the interplay between supply and viewing, not either side alone, relates to ideological change.
arxiv-2603-08249: Pol and colleagues bootstrap audiovisual speech recognition for languages with zero audiovisual resources, using synthetic visual data as the only visual supervision. AV recognition combines acoustic and visual cues to improve transcription under hard conditions, but most under-resourced ones lack labeled video corpora for training. For Catalan, where no real AV data exist for training, the authors synthesize over 700 hours of talking-head video and fine-tune a pre-trained AV-HuBERT model. On a Catalan benchmark it nears state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv-2603-08349: Kostrzewa and colleagues present a new method for making plausible counterfactuals for time series sorting. The approach performs gradient-based optimization straight in the input space. To enforce realism, the method joins soft-DTW matching with k-nearest neighbors from the target class, pushing new ones to adopt a lifelike time-based structure. The overall goal is a multi-faceted loss function weighing key traits.
arxiv-2603-08849: Jiayin Zhi and colleagues ask when language-model help helps or harms critical thinking. In a 393-person test, models were offered early, throughout, late, or never, under short or ample time. Help from the start lifted scores under pressure but hurt with ample time, while starting alone showed the mirror pattern, making timing central to human-model teamwork.
arxiv-2603-08949: João Barretto-Bittar and colleagues diffuse error signals through a network for temporal credit assignment. Biological learning assigns credit over time despite sparse, imprecise feedback, often via neuromodulators acting across space and time. Their mechanism spreads the credit signal locally, so neurons learn without direct feedback, and it improves learning on three benchmark tasks with recurrent spiking networks and sparse feedback links.
arxiv-2603-09049: Zhanlin Liu and colleagues offer EPOCH, a shared engineering protocol for repeated system tuning. Existing methods run task-specific loops rather than one shared protocol for baselines and tracked self-gains. EPOCH splits work into baseline building and repeated self-gains, structures each round into role-set planning, building, and review stages, and runs work through standard commands and round-level tracking.
arxiv-2603-09149: Kunyu Tan and Mingjian Liang present RTFDNet, a three-branch network for RGB-thermal segmentation that stays robust when sensor signals partly go missing. Older methods stress balance between the two modes yet degrade badly under such loss. Their design unifies fusion and decoupling in one encoder-decoder, with gated channel exchange and light spatial attention sharing cues. Two regularization terms keep unimodal paths strong without harming the fused stream, allowing efficient standalone inference.
arxiv-2603-09249: Jincenzi Wu and colleagues aim at human-like social reasoning in language models, which often lean on surface patterns instead of grasping social cues. They build ToMBench-Hard, an adversarial benchmark of training cases that resist shortcut answers. Their Social-R1 framework then supervises the full reasoning path with rewards for structure, logical integrity, and information density. A small model trained this way surpasses much larger rivals and generalizes across eight diverse benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-09349: Xiong Zhang and colleagues identify a feature mismatch pattern behind domain shift in graph anomaly detection, which they name Anomaly Disassortativity. Anomalous nodes, from fake news to malicious transactions, look very different across domains, so cross-domain detectors generalize poorly. Building on their model of this pattern, they introduce a graph foundation model that adapts at test time after a single training phase. Across fourteen real-world graphs it reaches state-of-the-art detection accuracy.
arxiv-2603-09649: Guoqing Liu and colleagues directly observe the melting of a classical continuous spacetime crystal, in a table-top experiment using macroscopic active granular disks. A spacetime crystal holds periodic order in both space and time; theirs forms a 2D triangular lattice that rotates as one rigid body and lasts almost a day. Tuning the disk packing fraction reveals a three-stage melting with a spatially hexatic phase and coexistence regions. Spatial and temporal orders melt separately: defects proliferate to kill the first, a distinct route takes the second.
arxiv-2603-09949: Jones and Yang study duality operators on spin chains and on anyon chains, with a fusion category symmetry in the background. They set out how such an operator is fixed by data from a quantum cellular automaton on the symmetric part of the algebra. That automaton also gives a bimodule category, and the operators form a simplex whose extreme points match its simple objects. For models built on tensor product spaces, the team shows the outer symmetry must end up weakly integral in the infrared.
arxiv-2603-10549: Mohammed Salah and co-authors bring models that read both images and words to defect hunting in carbon fiber composites, using heat imaging. Training detectors the usual way needs costly, slow datasets of inspection sequences. Their framework skips that: encoders already trained on natural images, plus a light adapter, give zero-shot finding of hidden defects and where they sit. On 25 sequences with impacts at varied energies, the adapter beat classic reduction methods on signal quality, with strong detection overlap.
arxiv-2603-11249: Karim Ben Hicham and coauthors present DISCOMAX, a differentiable algorithm for thermodynamic phase equilibria. It keeps learned models true to physics in training and inference. Learning from equilibrium data is hard, since equilibria arise from an extremum principle. The method lists feasible phase states. It joins them with a masked softmax in the backward pass. It sends the true equilibrium forward. On binary liquid-liquid data, it beats surrogate-based methods. It works for other equilibrium data too.
arxiv-2603-11449: Wang and co-authors prove sharp integral mean estimates for (α,β)-harmonic functions on the unit disk. Such bounds say how large these functions and their partial derivatives can grow on average. The proofs use a Poisson-type kernel and hypergeometric function forms tied to boundary data. The team also draws out coefficient estimates from the main bounds. Their Hardy space-type results extend classic inequalities for harmonic and α-harmonic functions to this wider two-parameter family.
arxiv-2603-11749: Krestnikov asks why language models trained on clashing data still lean toward correct answers. His tests use small transformers, 3.5M to 86M parameters, on math problems shown with right and wrong solutions. When errors are random, accuracy climbs from 65 to 85 percent with model size. When errors follow one coherent false rule system, accuracy falls to chance. A second false rule, oddly, restores most of the truth bias. He proposes a Compression-Consistency Principle: training favors the most compressible answer cluster, not truth itself.
arxiv-2603-11949: Ding and co-authors introduce delayed backdoor attacks, which split a backdoor's trigger from its firing in time. Classic backdoors fire the instant a trigger appears, which barred everyday words as triggers. Their prototype, DND, hides a small stateful module that counts exposure and waits for a set threshold. Only then does the attack break out, after a quiet latency phase. On four NLP benchmarks, DND keeps clean accuracy at 94% or better while dormant. Once awake, its attack success nears 99%, they report.
arxiv-2603-12049: Bauer, Gusel, and Scoccola put multiparameter persistence modules on firm ground. They study q-tame modules under the interleaving distance. That space turns out to be metrically complete in their results. Each object also splits into indecomposable parts in an essentially unique way. Two objects sit at distance zero exactly when they are isomorphic. Many module categories used before appear inside this one as full subcategories, which marks it as a natural home for the field.
arxiv-2603-12249: Chen, Zhao, Wang, Han, Patwardhan, and Cohan build SciMDR, a training set for scientific document reasoning across modes. Dataset builders face a trade-off among scale, faithfulness, and realism in such data. Their synthesize-and-reground frame works in two stages to ease that trade-off. Claim-centric synthesis first makes faithful QA pairs on focused segments of papers. Programmatic regrounding then embeds those pairs into full-document tasks with realistic complexity. Models fine-tuned on the 300K pairs improve on several scientific QA benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-12349: Basu and Chakraborty score AI-guided discovery picks with a budget-sensitive score whose proofs were machine-checked. Labs must choose which candidates deserve costly tests, with no principled score to compare strategies. Their BSDS metric penalizes false discoveries and excess abstention at each budget level. Twenty theorems behind it were checked with the Lean 4 proof assistant. A drug case study pits 39 proposers on HIV data. A simple random forest greedy method beat every LLM setup, which added no marginal value.
arxiv-2603-12449: Gregory and co-authors introduce FloeNet, a mass-conserving emulator of global sea ice that generalizes across climates. The model learns from the GFDL SIS2 sea ice model in training runs. It emulates six-hour budget tendencies for ice and snow growth, melt, and advection. Training used a reanalysis-forced ice-ocean run, with tests on pre-industrial and rising CO2 climates. FloeNet beat a non-conservative rival on mean state, trends, and year-to-year variability in both poles. Its thermodynamic versus dynamic response also stays physically readable.
arxiv-2603-12749: Zheng Gao and co-authors design a semantic watermark for images from diffusion models that can localize tampering. Watermarks in the starting noise can be forged by inversion and regeneration attacks. Global semantic binding helps, yet stays weak against coherent local edits. Their SLICE splits semantics into subject, environment, action, and detail factors. Each factor is anchored to a distinct region of the starting noise. Tests beat prior methods against strong regeneration attacks while keeping image quality.
arxiv-2603-13549: Nils E. Strand, Siyao Yang, Yuehaw Khoo, and Aaron R. Dinner introduce TT-Metadynamics for high-dimensional free energy exploration. Enhanced sampling methods grow prohibitively costly beyond a few collective variables, since bias storage grows exponentially. Their method periodically compresses the sum of Gaussian bias functions into a low-rank tensor train representation. That keeps memory use efficient and stops bias evaluation cost from growing with simulation time. A sketching algorithm builds the tensor train with linear scaling in the number of variables.
arxiv-2603-13649: Marcos Piotto and co-authors present Linnaeus, a system that classifies autonomous systems on the Internet. Such systems play diverse roles, from community backbones to hyperscale content providers and submarine-cable operators. Taxonomies based on network data alone fail to capture how these systems differ in role and operation. Linnaeus adds rich non-network features to topology and BGP data, and uses domain-adapted LLMs with classic machine learning. Its taxonomy has two levels and allows multi-label assignments for hybrid roles. On nearly 2,000 labeled systems it scored well.
arxiv-2603-13849: Ruffenach introduces EVE, a neuron that carries its own probability distribution instead of a single number. Each unit has an explicit prior, a learned posterior, and its own regularization term. The study varies the neuron's inner dimension, from one up to larger latent spaces, and tracks how its working regime changes. Two added axes, local capacity control and a time-based extension, are also tested. Diagnostics show some inner variables can be measured and link to downstream behavior in forecasting and tabular tasks.
arxiv-2603-14349: Pan and co-authors present OMIT, a network for matching images with text through optimal partial transport. Cross-modal matching must score how well a caption fits a picture, fast and well. OMIT uses a cross-modal mover's distance over fine image and text fragments, sped by Sinkhorn iterations. Partial matching trims stray fragments that would otherwise muddy the score. Tests on Flickr30K and MS-COCO show top results against rival methods. Visual checks further explain how the matching behaves.
arxiv-2603-14549: Pathak and Han prune visual tokens to speed up large vision-language models. High-resolution image tokens carry quadratic cost, a key bottleneck. Past pruning leans on raw attention scores and misses token overlap. A flaw named attention shift also skews those scores. Their ASAP method fixes the shift with a dynamic two-way soft mask. A weighted merge step then folds alike tokens into dense patches. ASAP keeps 99.02% of LLaVA-NeXT-7B scores while cutting FLOPs by about 80%, they report.
arxiv-2603-14949: He and Salm deform special harmonic forms by perturbing the ambient metric. Their objects are Z/2-harmonic 1-forms with k-nondegenerate singular behavior. Metric wiggles shift the local expansion coefficients of such forms. For a natural degenerate class, a tuned metric shift exists. Under it, the form deforms to a nearby non-degenerate one. A quantitative Nash-Moser argument closes the existence proof. Deformation theory for singular harmonic forms gains firm ground. The result links metric choice to form regularity.
arxiv-2603-15049: Ortiz and co-authors predict stellar occultations by the dwarf planet Haumea and its ring through 2030. Haumea spins fast, has a stretched three-axis shape, and hosts a slow ring. The team flags eleven useful events for stars down to Gaia magnitude 21. They study the 4 May 2026 event in most detail. Its shadow path should span 2224 kilometers, give or take 30. Speckle imaging also found a faint companion star that will be occulted too.
arxiv-2603-15349: Colombo and co-authors study the resolvent equations for harmonic and bi-harmonic calculi in dimension five. These calculi grow out of the S-spectrum and a mapping theorem for slice hyperholomorphic functions. Their resolvent operators come from reshaped Cauchy kernels, so the equations differ from the classical ones. The authors derive both resolvent equations in this setting. They also obtain the matching product rules and Riesz projectors for the two calculi.
arxiv-2603-15449: Wang and co-authors chart how steep-spectrum radio-loud active galactic nuclei evolve across cosmic time. Their beaming-minimized sample holds 4,555 sources out to redshift near four, drawn from XXL, VLA-COSMOS, and other surveys. A luminosity-and-density evolution model fits the radio luminosity function. Luminosity growth rises toward cosmic noon, then flattens, while density falls with redshift. The same model family that fits star-forming galaxies also fits these nuclei. In kinetic form, black hole growth tracks the cosmic star formation history.
arxiv-2603-15649: Catak and co-authors secure federated learning for 6G tasks with quantum key distribution. Clients train local models for channel estimation and radar sensing. A BB84-style protocol plus pairwise masking hides each client's raw updates. The server merges masked updates without seeing plain parameters. Tests report an NMSE of 0.216 for channel estimation. Radar sensing reached 92.1 percent accuracy with 0.72 mIoU. With an eavesdropper present, error rates rose and all rounds aborted as designed.
arxiv-2603-15749: Delucchi and co-authors offer a practical test for BL Lac host galaxy type. Jets in BL Lac objects outshine their host galaxies at most wavelengths. Hosts are thus rarely studied, and their shape stays a guess. The team built realistic fake BL Lac spectra for both host types. They ran the spectra through the public QSFit tool. Two QSFit runs per source yield one sorting parameter. The split works when jets stay below a stated gamma-ray power. Two galaxy types still blur the call, they note.
arxiv-2603-15949: Sijan and co-authors benchmark language models on Bangladeshi social language skills. Fluency alone misses hierarchy, kinship, and custom cues in Bangla talk. BanglaSocialBench holds 1,719 cases checked by native speakers. Three domains cover address terms, kinship reasoning, and social customs. Twelve current models took the test with no examples given. Errors cluster in set patterns rather than random slips. Models overuse formal address and miss valid pronoun options. Kinship terms blur across religious lines in model answers. Downward elder-to-younger address draws the worst mistakes.
arxiv-2603-16049: Rocha and Dias port the Rodeo spectral filter onto multi-level qudits. Qudits extend qubits with more levels per carrier. Higher ancilla levels run several control steps at once. Their Rodeo form uses a general d-level ancilla qudit. A Rodeo kernel, a two-frequency interferometer, does the energy filtering. A microcanonical variant reads entropy from a single energy sweep. Tests on Ising chains use ancilla sizes three, four, and five. The qutrit build cut fluctuations by 18 percent against qubits.
arxiv-2603-16249: Nguyen and co-authors classify white blood cells under extreme class imbalance. Rare cell types matter for leukemia screening, but deep models favor common classes. Their hybrid system adds several fixes. A Pix2Pix module cleans image artifacts. A Swin Transformer ensemble with contrastive embeddings learns robust features. A final step uses cell shape cues to rescue odd cases. On WBCBench 2026, the method reached a Macro-F1 of 0.77139.
arxiv-2603-16849: Rigotti, Thumiger, and Frick present GIST, a graph neural operator built to respect gauge invariance. Spectral encodings capture mesh geometry, but exact versions cost cubic time and break gauge symmetry through solver artifacts. GIST instead uses pairwise inner products of cheap approximate spectral embeddings. The authors prove these products estimate an exactly gauge-invariant kernel, at linear cost. They also bound the mismatch when a model moves across mesh resolutions. On mesh benchmarks with up to 750,000 nodes, GIST sets new state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2603-17149: Jaudou and co-authors demonstrate one time pad encryption with keys drawn from pools of synthetic DNA. The one time pad gives perfect secrecy, but needs a shared random key as long as the message, used once. Their primitive duplicates random DNA molecules to install the same entropy source at two distant sites. Local sequencing turns the molecules into a shared binary mask. They ran the protocol between Tokyo and Paris, generating a mask of about 400 megabits. Copy number statistics add resistance to interference.
arxiv-2603-17249: Efstratiou, Russo, and Luceri map how science news flows between social media and news outlets, using COVID-19 as the case. They analyze 1.24 million tweets and 211,000 news articles that cite pandemic science papers. The most influential accounts were mostly individuals with medical or research credentials. They also find a coordinated network that amplifies a small set of credentialed experts with contrarian, anti consensus views. Papers pushed by these actors overlap heavily with news coverage. Notably, outlets often covered studies only after social media superspreaders had highlighted them.
arxiv-2603-17549: Yu, Liu, Zheng, and Yang tackle a hard inverse problem in epidemic tracking. Case counts alone do not pin down how fast a disease spreads over time. Their CIRL framework learns a map from past case patterns and time cues to hidden reproduction numbers. A renewal equation keeps the outputs in line with known disease dynamics. Tests on synthetic outbreaks plus SARS and COVID-19 data held up well, they report.
arxiv-2603-17649: Petersson and Thakur ask when Freudenthal algebras are homogeneous. These algebras match Jordan algebras of degree three that stay simple under field extensions. Homogeneity means every Jordan isotope of the algebra looks the same. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for that trait. The first Tits construction of cubic Jordan algebras carries much of the link. A local form of that construction plus a local-global rule rounds out the study.
arxiv-2603-17949: Shelah develops homogeneous iterated forcing along a linear order of steps. The forcings keep old sequences of ordinals intact and collapse no cardinals. His focus falls on steps with small support, a chain condition, and strategic completeness. Such setups carry many automorphisms of the index order itself. The tools serve models where sets behave like Borel sets modulo a chosen ideal. He also revisits saccharinity, a trait that can rule out stray new reals.
arxiv-2603-18149: Campbell and co-authors analyze extreme rainfall in the eastern United States with a geometric framework. The work answers the EVA 2025 Data Challenge using a large climate model ensemble. Three target quantities cover spatial extent and duration of extreme rain, each needing extrapolation. A spatial geometric model plus a sampling step keeps time information for duration estimates. Topography and season effects are included, and diagnostics support the model fit.
arxiv-2603-18349: Jose, Nair, and Greenstadt analyze persuasive political content on Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform for AI agents. LLM classifiers, checked against expert labels, flag propaganda across 673,127 posts and 879,606 comments. Propaganda forms 1% of all posts but 42% of political content. Just 4% of agents made 51% of these posts, clustered in five communities. Comments show limited power to amplify the propaganda, they find.
arxiv-2603-18449: Zhao and co-authors present Cross-Model Neuron Transfer for reusing safety functions across large language models. Open-source models already carry varied safety-related functions that are costly to rebuild. CNT moves a minimal neuron subset from a donor model into a target model. The neuron-level move supports adding or deleting a function in a modular way. Across seven models and three tasks, performance loss stayed under 1% for most models.
arxiv-2603-18649: Yu and co-authors present Click-to-Ask, an AI helper for live shopping streams. An offline module turns mixed product data into structured records. It also drafts compliant sales copy before the show. During the stream, sellers click viewer questions to trigger answers. Replies draw on the structured records plus a memory of the live event. On TikTok stream frames, question recognition reaches 0.913 accuracy. Response quality scores 0.876. The system cuts prep time and speeds replies to viewers during broadcasts.
arxiv-2603-18849: Herlyng and Shadden map coherent flow structures in brain ventricles. Cerebrospinal fluid moves on many scales, in space and in time. Snapshots alone make unsteady transport hard to read. Finite-time Lyapunov exponent fields give a time-integrated view instead. Models cover adult human and embryonic zebrafish ventricles built from imaging data. Human flow mixes heart pulsation, fluid secretion, and beating cilia. Ridges in the exponent fields mark coherent structures that match lab findings. Full Navier-Stokes runs resolve fine transport traits that Stokes flow misses.
arxiv-2603-18949: Othmane and co-authors remove heart signal noise from womb contraction readings. The readings track labor but pick up the mother's heart pulses as stray signals. Their method uses algebraic tools that estimate slopes without a fixed model. The setup keeps the true signal shape away from heart pulse spots. It also damps slow drift and mains hum. Pulses are sorted across channels, then subtracted with no extra heart lead. Early tests on two healthy volunteers match a standard template method.
arxiv-2603-19649: Huang and co-authors present PolicySim, a sandbox that simulates social platforms with language model agents. Platform policies like recommendation and filtering can deepen echo chambers. Testing them live finds risks only after harm is done. PolicySim models users and platform moves as a two-way dynamic. A user agent module is fine-tuned for platform-specific realism. An adaptive intervention module uses a contextual bandit with message passing. Experiments show faithful simulation at micro and macro levels. The sandbox supports proactive policy tuning before launch.
arxiv-2603-19749: Ma, Ming, and Zhao study bialgebra structures built on Reynolds Leibniz algebras of any weight. A Reynolds Leibniz algebra pairs a Leibniz algebra with a weighted Reynolds operator. The authors give matching descriptions of these bialgebras in two ways. They use matched pairs and Manin triples. Next they check when Yang-Baxter solutions fit with Reynolds operators. That fit defines triangular Reynolds Leibniz bialgebras. Last, they classify all two-dimensional triangular cases.
arxiv-2603-19849: Scantamburlo and co-authors propose a simple signal that separates human dialogue from text written by large language models. They map each text to theme scores with the Empath lexicon tool. Their semantic delta is the gap between the two strongest theme scores. Model-written texts show higher deltas, meaning themes stay more tightly focused. Human dialogue spreads themes more evenly. A Welch t-test confirms the gap across varied human corpora. The cheap, zero-shot metric is meant to support, not replace, other detectors.
arxiv-2603-20049: Long and co-authors model how heat and stress gradients compete to move hydrogen in metals. A temperature gradient drives hydrogen by thermomigration, a less studied effect. Stress gradients drive a better known form of migration. Their framework joins both effects through an effective chemical potential. It runs inside a finite element code. Case studies cover iron and nickel heat exchangers and zirconium fuel cladding. Thermomigration often wins in heat-carrying parts, even with large thermal stresses. Near sharp stress peaks, stress-driven flow takes over instead.
arxiv-2603-20549: Biswas and Lin ask whether audience engagement shapes how legislators talk across party lines. Prior work stresses how elites shape mass opinion instead. They study over 1.1 million cross-party interactions on Twitter/X. The data cover U.S. state legislators and their audiences in 2020-2021. Democrats gained modest engagement; Republicans often faced penalties. After visible cross-party exchanges, legislators engaged again more often. Their rhetoric also shifted toward causal reasoning and positive emotion. Engagement thus seems to reinforce constructive cross-party communication.
arxiv-2603-20649: Lian and co-authors prove global results for a class of dispersive wave equations with weak damping. The class covers the Camassa-Holm equation and the hyperelastic rod wave equation. They show energy conserving weak solutions exist for all time. The proof works in a time weighted H1 space. Two more results give strong solutions for all time. One covers small initial data, the other sign changing data. Their work recovers and extends many known results for these models.
arxiv-2603-20749: Citro and Palitta give BoostConv, an accelerator for nonlinear fixed point iterations, a firm theory base. The method had shown strong results in past uses. It could even reach unstable fixed points that plain iteration misses. Still, no full proof of convergence existed until now. Their work states a robust form of the algorithm. They prove convergence under clear sufficient terms. Tests span a linear case, a small benchmark, and a large Navier-Stokes flow.
arxiv-2603-21349: Savage and Madill test whether video transformers can detect respiratory distress from video. Clinicians spot early signs of breathing decline by sight, which opens a window for earlier care. They filmed healthy volunteers recovering after hard exercise. Early clips show more shortness of breath, which creates a temporal ordering task. A ViViT encoder with Lie relative encodings and motion guided masking, plus an embedding comparison strategy, reaches an F1 score of zero point eight one. The results suggest modern video transformers can read subtle changes in breathing mechanics.
arxiv-2603-21449: Meyerovitch and Young study the covering radius of shift spaces, a quantity tied to sending data over noisy channels. They focus on sofic shifts, which are described by labeled graphs. Their main result shows that the covering radius of a primitive sofic shift is always a rational number. They also describe an algorithm that computes the exact value from a labeled graph presentation of the shift. The work settles basic questions about how tractable this quantity is.
arxiv-2603-21549: Salimi and co-authors fix a weak spot in Bayesian fitting of ordinary differential equation models: measurement error whose size changes over time. Standard practice assumes constant error variance, which can badly skew parameter estimates when the real error varies. Their two-step framework first fits a heteroscedastic Gaussian process to estimate the time-varying error. Bayesian inference then uses that error curve inside the likelihood. In simulations and two real applications, the approach gave more reliable estimates and predictive uncertainty than constant-error models.
arxiv-2603-21949: Biernacka and co-authors implement strong call-by-need, a lazy evaluation style that also fully normalizes terms. No earlier system was both simple and fast. Their RKNL abstract machine came automatically from a higher-order evaluator using memothunks for sharing. A standard tool turned the evaluator into a machine description, short and clear. The team proves the machine extends the lazy Krivine machine for weak call-by-need. It also tracks normal-order evaluation with bilinear overhead, linear in both reductions and input size.
arxiv-2603-22049: Thom proves a growth bound for 1-cocycles tied to group representations on Banach spaces. The group G is finitely generated, and its representation is uniformly bounded and of c0 type. Thom shows any 1-cocycle for that action grows slower than the word length of group elements. In other words, its growth is sublinear. As a corollary, he obtains the same statement for Hilbert spaces. That version covers strongly mixing unitary representations.
arxiv-2603-22249: Murrugarra-Llerena and co-authors release EgoGroups, a benchmark for spotting social groups in first-person video. Group detection finds people who interact as a unit, like friends. Older benchmarks lean on surveillance footage and few scene types. EgoGroups instead spans 65 countries. It covers low, medium, and high crowd levels under four weather and time conditions. The data carries dense labels for people and groups, plus place metadata. Tests show vision-language models beat supervised baselines in zero-shot use. Crowd density and cultural region shift the scores.
arxiv-2603-22349: Di proposes PFSR, a federated recommender that personalizes sequences for each user. Sequential recommendation in consumer electronics leans on user behavior models. Most carry quadratic compute cost, which blocks real-time use. They also adapt poorly to each user's own needs. PFSR adds an Associative Mamba Block that reads user profiles from a global view. It lifts prediction speed at the same time. A Variable Response Mechanism fine-tunes settings per user. A Dynamic Magnitude Loss keeps more local personal detail through training.
arxiv-2603-22449: Carrón and co-authors test whether the cosmic microwave background's hemispheric power asymmetry reaches beyond raw variance. They measure shape and topology statistics on local patches of the Planck SMICA map. Fits to those measures yield local estimates of variance, gradient variance, and fit quality. They confirm the known variance dipole at high significance. They also report a separate dipole in gradient variance, plus mild spatial change in fit quality. All three dipoles point toward the same sky region.
arxiv-2603-22549: Jangir and Ahmed study how frequency chirps reshape electron-positron pair creation in strong electric fields. They use the Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner formalism to track the pairs in real time. Chirps strongly alter the momentum patterns of the created pairs. In two-color setups, where a weak field assists a strong one, large chirps can lift the total yield by orders of magnitude. Chirping the weak field alone captures nearly the whole gain. As chirp strength grows, the yield also stops caring much about field polarization.
arxiv-2603-22649: Ivezić and co-authors compare self-supervised learning methods for medical images. Such methods learn from unlabeled data, but the best choice varies by domain. The team tests joint embedding methods against predictive variants on ultrasound and histopathology images. Where key signal sits in a small area, view-invariant methods work best. Where signal spans the whole image, as in liver ultrasound, predictive methods win. Expert clinicians checked the value of the learned features. The authors offer rules for matching method to image type.
arxiv-2603-22849: Ma and co-authors trace the heat stability of platinum oxides to mechanics. These oxides are key catalysts, but heat limits their use. A structural shift can raise their resilience by several hundred kelvin. Before the shift, an over-tight lattice builds local self-stress via a moiré pattern. That stress cuts heat endurance. After the shift, the network turns flexible, with balanced freedoms and constraints. The new moiré superlattice relaxes elastic energy. The authors offer network connectivity as a design rule for harsh settings.
arxiv-2603-23149: Pappa and co-authors present DILLO, a fast steering layer for safety-critical agents. World models can foresee action outcomes, but visual simulation is slow. Their claim: a policy's latent state plus planned actions already hold enough signal. A vision-language teacher labels offline trajectories with outcome text. A language model student then learns to predict those outcomes from latent data alone. At run time the path is text-only, running many times faster. Tests on MetaWorld and LIBERO show better episode success from the steering.
arxiv-2603-23249: Zhou and four co-authors present WeCAN, a learning system for scheduling task graphs on mixed hardware. Such graphs drive query plans, data pipelines, and compiler workloads that fight over limited pools. WeCAN scores task-pool pairs in one pass, then builds a schedule in one shot. A weighted cross-attention encoder weighs which tasks fit which pools. The team studies why list-scheduling maps leave an optimality gap. Their skip-extended map widens the orders and closes it. Tests on TPC-H queries and compiler graphs beat baselines.
arxiv-2603-23749: Ndzomga studies how to benchmark AI agents without paying for full test suites. Agent scores depend on the scaffold around the model, so results shift across setups. Across eight benchmarks, 33 scaffolds, and over 70 model setups, rank order stays stable even when exact scores drift. Ndzomga proposes testing new agents only on tasks with past pass rates of 30 to 70 percent. This cuts task counts by 44 to 70 percent while keeping rankings close to full runs.
arxiv-2603-23849: Antony and co-authors present VILLA, a system that pulls virus mutation facts from scientific papers with language models. Good ground-truth datasets are scarce, and past extraction work leaned on short, neat text. VILLA uses multi-step retrieval to handle open-ended extraction. The team built a test set of 629 mutations in ten influenza A proteins from 239 papers. VILLA beats plain retrieval and other agent tools on this task, they report. The work targets virology, a field past studies largely ignored.
arxiv-2603-24249: Ngeow and co-authors measure the distance to the Carina dwarf spheroidal galaxy with pulsating stars. They gather near-infrared time-series data in J, H, and K bands with the Magellan telescope. The sample holds 43 RR Lyrae stars, 11 anomalous Cepheids, and 102 dwarf Cepheids. RR Lyrae stars give a distance of 103.7 kiloparsecs, with small stated errors. Dwarf Cepheid relations agree well with that value. Anomalous Cepheids give a smaller distance, which hints that their period-luminosity relation depends on metallicity.
arxiv-2603-24749: Shatwell and co-authors present TIGeR, a unified framework for retrieval across time, images, and place. Forensic tasks often need an image from the same place as a query but at a chosen target time. TIGeR supports single and multi-modality queries in one form. It performs geo-localisation, time-of-capture prediction, and geo-time-aware retrieval with that same form. A curation pipeline produced 4.5 million training triplets and 86,000 evaluation triplets. Experiments show TIGeR beats strong baselines while preserving location identity through large changes.
arxiv-2603-24849: Papadopoulos and co-authors use eye-tracking to study preference in pairwise AI image choice. Preference learning relies on human pairwise judgments, yet the process behind them is little understood. Thirty participants did 1,800 trials while their gaze was recorded. The gaze cascade effect replicates: gaze shifts toward the chosen image about one second before the decision. Gaze features predict the binary choice with 68 percent accuracy. Transitions between images also separate confident from uncertain decisions, with low-confidence trials showing more switches per second.
arxiv-2603-24949: Sinclair introduces an operator construction on finite geometric lattices. A nonassociative diamond product on the lattice basis yields creation operators indexed by atoms and a self-adjoint Hamiltonian. The Hamiltonian changes rank by at most one. On the rank-radial subspace it is therefore a Jacobi matrix. In this way, lattices directly produce finite orthogonal polynomial systems. The Jacobi coefficients have closed formulas. Boolean lattices give the centred Krawtchouk matrix, and projective spaces give q-forms matching the q-Hahn family, with no symmetry assumed.
arxiv-2603-25049: Wan and co-authors study the fine rings of light that circle a spinning black hole in a magnetic field. The setting is Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson spacetime. They track photon paths under a weak field and focus on unstable round orbits. Three numbers describe each ring: radial squeeze, angle advance, and time delay. The team maps how spin, field strength, and viewer tilt change those numbers. They also work out higher-order images near the critical curve. The field reshapes the paths, leaving marks that future images could read.
