Their system, ConTex, reformulates the job as learning one shared intervention strategy that can produce a counterfactual for any new input at once. The intervention function is split into where to act and how to act. That structure yields counterfactuals which are more valid and sparser than instance-wise ones, at a small fraction of the cost. The split also reveals which features matter for each target, adding a forward-looking view of model behavior.
arxiv-2606-18149:
Radfar maps exactly how little data a physics-informed neural network needs to recover a river's friction from its flow, in a 2026 benchmarking study. The Manning friction coefficient drives shallow water models used in flood work, and inverse PINNs can estimate it by blending sparse observations with the governing equations. How sparse and how noisy those observations can get before recovery fails was not systematically known.

Two test channels anchor the study, a one-dimensional analytic case and a two-dimensional sloped channel with a curved bed. Radfar varies observation count, noise level, and which variables are observed, recovering friction jointly with the flow field in a two-phase fit. The two-dimensional case proves robust. It lands within a few percent of the true friction given at least ten depth and velocity observations at moderate noise. The full grid charts the failure frontier.
arxiv-2606-18249:
Peng and colleagues unify image understanding and image generation inside one autoregressive model, in a 2026 paper. Unified multimodal models promise a system that can look at a picture, make one, and edit it, all in a shared context where it reads its own creations without re-encoding them. The hard part is representation: understanding wants high-level meaning, while generation wants fine visual detail, and one tokenizer must serve both.

Their model, UniAR, rests on a unified visual tokenizer that maps both jobs into the same semantic space. Bitwise visual tokens enlarge capacity at modest cost, multi-level features add expressiveness, and a parallel bitwise prediction scheme speeds decoding. The system generates high-fidelity images with strong instruction following and text rendering, alongside versatile editing. The authors argue the tokenizer, more than any other choice, is what makes unification work.
arxiv-2606-18749:
Le Gia proposes a way to find anomalies in 3D medical scans without any training, in a 2026 medical imaging paper. Zero-shot anomaly detection suits clinical practice. There, scanners, protocols, and patient populations shift, and annotated examples of pathologies may not exist. But most existing methods work on single 2D images.

The framework CS3F slices each volume along anatomical axes. It encodes the slices with a frozen 2D vision transformer, and pools neighboring slice features into volumetric tokens. Anomalies are scored by cross-subject mutual similarity: tokens with no close analogue in other subjects score high. A coarse-to-fine tokenization counters the dulling of lesion signals by depth pooling. Evaluated on brain MRI covering metastases, glioma, and stroke, and validated on lung CT, the results show 2D models can localize anomalies. The payoff of fine tokenization depends strongly on lesion contrast and modality.
arxiv-2606-18849:
Kizhuprakkat and a large DESI team present a catalog of eighty-nine thousand K-giant stars, used to dissect the Milky Way's distant stellar halo, in a 2026 astronomy paper. The halo spans twelve to about one hundred kiloparsecs from the galactic center. It is a fossil record of accreted galaxies. Its chemo-dynamical structure sorts stars from debris of eaten systems.

Applying the HDBSCAN clustering algorithm to the stars' motion, the team found five prominent substructures: Aleph, the Sagittarius stream, the Gaia Sausage-Enceladus merger remnant, Cetus-Palca, and the Orphan-Chenab stream. The stars in no substructure, the residual halo, proved telling. Samples with strongly prograde and strongly retrograde motion share similar, bimodal metallicity distributions, unlike either merger's. The low-angular-momentum residual looks like the Sausage-Enceladus distribution, even at much lower binding energy. That constrains how that merger filled the halo.
arxiv-2606-19249:
Kapil and colleagues introduce the Transformer Geometry Observatory in 2026, a set of experiments on the geometry of vision transformers. Vision transformers are widely used, but how their internal dimensions and spectra evolve in training is far less studied. The first observatory study focuses on spectral geometry. It evaluates models on ImageNet-100 with a battery of measures for rank, entropy, flatness, and anisotropy of internal states.

Results show a steady rise in dimensional use across training. Anisotropy falls, spectral entropy rises, and eigenspectra grow flatter over time. That pattern runs against the common intuition that training concentrates information into a few dominant directions. Instead, variance spreads progressively across dimensions. The effect is strongest in the final classification token, which shows the highest effective rank and lowest anisotropy in the network.
arxiv-2606-19549:
Lin Tang and five colleagues ask in 2026 whether merged model adapters will keep their skills, before training ends. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, trains cheap add-on updates that give one base model many special skills. Merging two adapters is cheap, but strong solo adapters can clash badly once combined.

Tang's team define mergeability as how much single-task skill survives a merge. Signals from the first few percent of training forecast that outcome well. Key signs are how updates and gradients align across tasks, and how much they disturb shared internal features. Their tool, MergeProbe, turns those signs into retention estimates for pairs and sets. It then advises a direct merge, reweighting, pruning, or routing instead. On a five-domain benchmark, MergeProbe posts the best average and worst-case retention. Checking early turns merging into a measured choice.
arxiv-2606-19749:
Dang Nguyen, Wanqing Hao, Yanai Elazar, and Chenhao Tan benchmark AI systems that review research papers in 2026. Agentic review tools promise relief for strained peer review, yet no one knew how to grade them. Two open-source systems, one proprietary system, and a zero-shot baseline face the tests.

Six language models, from frontier to efficient tiers, power the systems in turn. One test checks whether AI reviews track paper quality signals like citations and acceptance calls. Every system beats chance at pairwise ranking, with the best pairing reaching eighty-three percent. A second test hides planted errors of four kinds inside papers across eight fields. The strongest setup catches about seventy-two percent of those errors. Pooling detections across all six models lifts recall to eighty-three percent, since models catch unlike flaws. A public deployment study finds users voting positive, with false alarms the chief complaint.
arxiv-2606-19849:
Yang Tan and five colleagues push streaming video language models past one hundred frames per second in 2026. Streaming systems must ingest video nonstop while answering queries with low delay. Speeding single modules says little about whether the whole pipeline keeps up.

ViCoStream treats inference as one coordinated pipeline of stages. Visual preprocessing, encoding, token dropping, and model prefilling all share the schedule. Chunk-wise execution and CUDA-stream overlap keep stages busy in parallel. Visual token control and bounded attention cap per-chunk cost. Query-side retrieval bounds memory growth over long streams. A bottleneck migration study shows how chunk size and token retention trade speed against accuracy. On one A100 card the system hits one hundred thirty-four frames per second. First-token delay stays under fifty milliseconds with accuracy near full-history baselines.
arxiv-2606-19949:
Ruoxuan Yang and Chuan Li offer a semi-automatic fix for broken skeletons of tube-like structures in 2026. Extracting centre lines from 3D scans of blood vessels, roots, or neural wiring often leaves false links between nearby branches and gaps where data is missing. Hand repair is slow and fiddly. Their method starts from just two points chosen by the user, a source and a target, and proposes the connecting path.

Component-wise spanning trees carry the path steadily within each piece, while a filtered Delaunay graph bridges gaps and ambiguous junctions. Candidate steps are scored by direction smoothness, closeness, component match, and progress toward the target. A C++ viewer built on Libigl shows the repairs on brain vessel data, clearing typical crossing and dotted artefacts. Interactive cleanup of this kind can unblock measurement and flow studies.
arxiv-2606-20149:
Lucas Norder, Ata Keşkekler, and Richard Norte demonstrate the largest lightsails yet pushed measurably by laser light. Their 2026 paper concerns laser-driven sails, ultralight craft that ride radiation pressure from a beam instead of carrying fuel. A working sail must combine tiny mass, a wide area, and survival under brutal optical power, a trio no earlier test had achieved in one structure. The team made silicon nitride membranes nanometers thick yet millimeters wide, patterned with billions of holes.

Resonant modes let these films reflect 99 percent of incoming light despite their thinness. Their flexibility turned radiation pressure into displacements of up to 1.75 micrometers, fifty thousand times larger than earlier lightsail responses. The membranes also kept reflecting well under laser intensities like sunlight at the Sun's surface. Beyond propulsion, the structures form a testbed for high-power nanophotonics and directed-energy systems.
arxiv-2606-20549:
Sha Yi and five colleagues generate robot hand designs directly from human demonstrations. Their 2026 paper tackles robot morphology learning, which lags control learning because searching design and control together is a huge combinatorial problem.

Instead of learning a complex controller for each candidate design, the framework uses one simple control policy before and after fabrication: matching fingertip positions through inverse kinematics. Over 4 million frames of human fingertip motion from everyday manipulation drive the design optimization. Candidate hands are scored by how well the shared policy can replay human motion. Design generation becomes data-driven, with control held deliberately dumb.
arxiv-2606-20649:
Leonard Wossnig simulates a post-automation economy to find which fiscal instrument can reach the durable surplus AI creates. His 2026 paper builds an agent-based, stock-flow-consistent model where production uses an endogenous nested-CES technology. Wealth concentration is microfounded through heterogeneous, persistent returns to wealth.

The model separates two channels: a competitive return on reproducible robotic capital, and a mobile, foreign-held intellectual-property rent earned by AI. Taxation and capital mobility respond behaviorally inside the simulation. The central result is that the durable surplus is the foreign-held AI rent. Policy for the automation age must aim at the rent, not just at robots.
arxiv-2606-20949:
S Avraham and eight colleagues report fluctuations in 2026 at an oxide interface with incipient polar order, reported with initials in the hosted byline. Finding hidden local order at buried interfaces is a central challenge for quantum materials. Second-order electrical responses can reveal symmetry breaking that linear transport misses. The team uses a potassium tantalate interface with strong spin-orbit coupling.

Second-harmonic resistivity shows large, repeatable fluctuations. They persist even in large devices. They appear across all studied surface orientations. The authors propose that local breaks in structure drive the patterns. A nascent polar state, pinned near the impurity layer at the interface, is the suggested source. Such signals turn an electrical measurement into a probe of nanoscale order. That could guide design of oxide devices that use interface physics for new functions.
arxiv-2606-21049:
Ilya Chevyrev and Emilio Ferrucci investigate locality of rough path lifts in 2026, asking whether a lift over an interval depends only on the path inside that interval. Rough path theory lifts a path by adding its iterated integral data. Every sufficiently regular path admits such a lift. Locality would make lifts easy to glue and compute. Their results, however, are largely negative in the deterministic setting.

No local, homogeneous lift can be defined on Hölder paths at the roughest regularity levels. No Lévy area can be both bounded and local under stated assumptions. The boundedness demand is shown to be sharp: dropping it allows a construction. On the stochastic side, local lifts of fractional Brownian motion are classified. Impossibility results are useful guardrails. They stop researchers from hunting for definitions that cannot exist, and point to the extra data a workable theory must carry.
arxiv-2606-21249:
Cengizhan Bayram tests a sharp hypothesis in 2026 about retrieval heads, the attention heads that copy facts from earlier text in a transformer model. Rotary position embeddings rotate query and key vectors at rates set by a base value, theta. Critics suspect that rotation either stops retrieval heads from forming or weakens them as theta grows. Bayram checks this across four open 7 to 8 billion parameter models from two attention families.

Masking the 87 detected retrieval heads collapses needle-in-a-haystack accuracy from perfect to zero, while masking random heads changes nothing, so the heads are causally vital. Yet higher theta does not mean fewer heads, and the effect of theta on recall flips sign between model families. No universal RoPE law survives; architecture, data, or tokenizer choices must drive the differences.
arxiv-2606-21449:
Giacomo Maletto lays foundations in 2026 for a version of Hilbert's sixteenth problem about how algebraic curves can arrange themselves on a surface. The classic problem asks which patterns of ovals a plane curve can form; Maletto generalizes to arrangements of several curves meeting transversely on a compact real surface. He encodes the topological type of an added curve with a combinatorial triple built from intersection numbers, Dyck words, and rooted trees.

With that encoding, topological types correspond exactly to combinatorial objects, turning geometry into data that software can enumerate. Applying Bezout-type obstructions, Viro patchworking, and a new Julia library called NWT, he fully classifies arrangements of three lines with a cubic curve. Arrangements of three lines with a quartic get a partial classification, marking the frontier for larger cases.
arxiv-2606-21749:
Omprakash Chakraborty, Leo Fillioux, Ismail Ben Ayed, and Jose Dolz fix a trust problem in deep learning in 2026. Networks state confidences that do not match their real accuracy, usually erring toward cockiness. The standard remedy, temperature scaling, rescales all logits by one global factor. But miscalibration is lumpy: the worst gaps sit in different confidence ranges depending on the setting, and one temperature cannot chase them all.

Their Quantile-Adaptive Temperature Scaling maps each prediction to its confidence quantile and lets temperature vary monotonically along that axis, leaving well-calibrated high-confidence predictions nearly alone. The design ties neatly to a reshaped calibration-error objective. Across datasets and model families, class imbalance, and distribution shifts, QaTS beats other post-hoc methods, without changing any prediction, only the honesty of what it claims.
arxiv-2606-21849:
Xiang, Bai, and Ma describe a quantum limit cycle in 2026, a self-sustaining oscillation in an open quantum system kept alive by steady energy dissipation. Limit cycles are familiar in classical chemistry and biology, but building one from quantum parts requires feedback that links the system's order to its own control settings. Their design couples an absorbing-state phase transition with exactly such a feedback loop.

The resulting cycle repeatedly crosses tipping points, the thresholds where the state flips, rather than crossing once and settling. Near each crossing, dynamical susceptibility and long-range correlations spike, then fade until the next pass, making the crossings act as built-in early-warning signals. Each transition also brings a sharp rise in the energy dissipation rate, so entropy production grows in steps over time. The authors present the cycle as a route to engineered fluctuations in driven quantum systems.
arxiv-2606-22649:
Francesco Di Salvo, Sebastian Doerrich, and Christian Ledig improve out-of-distribution detection for medical images in this 2026 paper. Foundation models describe medical scans richly, but they falter when patients, devices, or scanning conditions shift. Flagging unfamiliar inputs matters before such models are deployed safely.

The authors argue reconstruction-based detectors were held back by scoring, not by reconstruction quality. The usual score, a plain residual norm, flattens the error structure and suppresses exactly the deviations that matter. Their method, MaRS, learns the normal data manifold with a lightweight autoencoder, then measures deviation by a Mahalanobis distance on the residuals, which accounts for variance in each direction. The detector needs no labels and works post hoc on frozen models. Across three imaging modalities and several shift types, MaRS beat confidence, distance, and reconstruction baselines.
arxiv-2606-22749:
Yuchuan Ding, Linfei Li, Lin Zhang, and Ying Shen address a resolution problem in computer vision in this 2026 paper. Vision foundation models output coarse feature maps, because they process images in patches. Tasks needing pixel-level detail suffer. Existing upsampling methods either blur what the features mean or need heavy retraining for each new model.

Their method, RaysUp, rebuilds high-resolution feature maps in a ray domain shaped by geometry, not by plain two-dimensional interpolation. It encodes directional guidance, uses cross-attention that works at any output resolution, and adds a ray positional encoding built from Plücker coordinates, which describe lines in space. A final attention step pools nearby features while respecting geometry. Across dense prediction tasks, RaysUp matched the best reported accuracy with only sixteen percent of the parameters of AnyUp, and ran about seven times faster.
arxiv-2606-22849:
Chatchai Promsiri and three colleagues extend the thermodynamics of conformal field theories in this 2026 paper. A standing problem is how to interpret changes in the central charge, a number measuring a theory's degrees of freedom. The authors build a new central-charge Rényi entropy using the Casini-Huerta-Myers map, which relates entanglement in a field theory to thermal physics on a curved space.

Their construction works in an ensemble holding charge, volume, and a central charge potential fixed. They show the new entropy satisfies all four fundamental Rényi inequalities, so it behaves as a genuine Rényi measure should. It captures entanglement averaged over an ensemble of holographic theories with fluctuating degrees of freedom. For near-extremal configurations, residual entropy comes from the central charge sector rather than heat. A mass gap sets a characteristic temperature and a special Rényi index separating two regimes.
arxiv-2606-23149:
Ram Massas and Michael Margaliot study when a wobbling input beats a steady one in a 2026 control theory paper. A system shows a positive gain of entrainment when a periodic input yields a larger average output than a constant input with the same mean. Purely linear systems gain nothing this way. The authors ask what changes when the system stays linear inside but reads its output through a static nonlinear map. The answer turns on a mismatch between the average output along the wobbling orbit and the output at the averaged resting point.

Massas and Margaliot derive a second-order formula showing the output map's curvature sets the leading effect. When the output is convex on the reachable directions, the gain is never negative for any periodic input. Concavity flips the sign. They also read the gain as an average divergence between the orbit and the averaged rest point.
arxiv-2606-23449:
Shanhui Zhao and colleagues present AOHP, an open-source operating system harness for AI agents, in a 2026 paper. Agents now call tools, extract information, and manage memory across applications on a user's behalf. Conventional operating systems were designed around applications, not agents, and offer little native support for them. Running agents on such systems brings overhead and safety risks. Agent-native operating systems are an emerging idea, but researchers lacked an open testbed for exploring the architectural pieces such systems need. AOHP aims to be that testbed, targeting personalized, efficient, and secure interaction.

Zhao and colleagues build the harness at the operating system level and release the source code openly. The design explores what primitives an agent-mediated system should expose directly, instead of bolting agents onto application-centric workflows. The authors position AOHP as shared infrastructure for the research community to test agent-native designs.
arxiv-2606-23549:
El Gantouh and Mahinzaeim analyze systems made of two parts that influence each other only through their boundaries, in a 2026 paper on applied mathematics. Each subsystem evolves on its own, while boundary conditions pass information between them. The systems are positive, meaning quantities that start nonnegative, such as counts or concentrations, stay that way. The key questions are whether solutions exist and behave well, and whether they settle down over time.

Working in a general semigroup framework, the mathematics of time evolution, the authors derive simple tests on the boundary coupling operators. Passing them guarantees the coupled system is well-posed, with solutions that exist, are unique, and depend sensibly on starting values. Spectral criteria, conditions on the system's characteristic values, then guarantee exponential stability, so disturbances fade at a steady rate. Feedback theory and perturbation methods support the framework, and examples show it in action.
arxiv-2606-23649:
Teng and colleagues present a new radio survey of molecular gas in sixty two nearby galaxies, in a 2026 paper on galaxy evolution. Galaxies form stars from cold molecular gas, and the star forming main sequence links each galaxy's star formation rate to its mass. Galaxies below that sequence are quenching, meaning star birth is shutting down. Whether gas runs out or stops forming stars efficiently is an open question.

Using the Green Bank Telescope, the survey maps carbon monoxide emission, a tracer of molecular gas, for galaxies chosen from the CALIFA optical survey. Combining both datasets yields gas masses, star formation rates, and chemical abundances. The median gas depletion time rises steeply toward red galaxies. Crucially, quenched galaxies can hold gas reservoirs like star forming ones; they simply form stars from it far less efficiently.
arxiv-2606-23749:
Zhang presents an open source Python package for simulating how axion dark matter would move atomic spins, in a 2026 paper on particle physics software. Axions are hypothetical light particles proposed to solve a symmetry puzzle in the strong force, and they are also candidates for dark matter. An axion field can act on spins like a faint magnetic field that is not really there, called a pseudomagnetic field. Resonance experiments hunt for the tiny spin motions it should cause.

The package, axionbloch, solves the Bloch equations, the standard rules for spin evolution, for ordinary and exotic interactions. Its simulations produce the signal signatures searches are designed around. The author calibrates the simulations against theoretical expectations to verify their accuracy. The package is publicly available with documentation and example scripts covering varied axion models and experimental setups.
arxiv-2606-23949:
Tang, Chen, and Ying compress high dimensional probability tables into a compact non negative format, in a 2026 paper on numerical methods. A distribution over many variables is a table with one entry per combination. Storing it grows explosively as variables are added. The hierarchical Tucker format fights this by factoring the table along a tree. Plain versions can assign negative probabilities, which are meaningless. The non negative variant forbids that, and fitting it is the hard part.

The method runs in two stages. First, an interpolation step builds a plain hierarchical Tucker approximation. Then a second stage refits that output against a non negative ansatz, using a tailored second order method. Both stages scale linearly in the number of variables, so the scheme reaches genuinely high dimensions. Experiments confirm success on varied probability tables, serving variational inference and density estimation.
arxiv-2606-24149:
Liu and colleagues solve an optics problem that blocks the next set of gravitational-wave detectors. Detectors steady their long arm cavities with an auxiliary stabilisation laser, before the delicate science measurement starts. Planned upgrades use new mirror coatings of AlGaAs and GaAs crystal. Those coatings absorb too much of the green light the current scheme relies on. So the scheme fails on the new mirrors.

A multi-wavelength replacement starts from an infrared auxiliary beam. Its wavelength sits safely outside the coating's absorption bands. Tripling its frequency yields green light that phase-locks to the science laser through its own second harmonic, which ties both lasers together. In a tabletop test, Liu's team shows stable control of cavity detuning and a robust shift into locked operation, by steering the auxiliary laser. The 2026 test confirms the scheme can bring future coated detectors onto resonance in a controlled way.
arxiv-2606-24449:
Alansari and colleagues fix how a leading video tracker remembers, arguing its memory writes are where tracking dies. SAM2-based trackers store past masks, typically selecting them by confidence alone. Under occlusion, rapid motion, and distractors, confident but wrong masks get written into memory, and the tracker drifts. Their 2026 module, SENTRY, is a training free, plug and play refine before write layer that validates each candidate update before committing it.

Multiple segmentation hypotheses per frame are aggregated, backtracked into short tracklets, and checked with neighbour aware, cycle consistent matching against recent trajectories. Masks that are temporally and geometrically consistent are favoured. The base architecture stays untouched; only the write policy changes. Plugged into five strong baselines, SENTRY brings consistent gains on nine benchmarks. New zero shot state of the art results land on several major tracking suites. It runs at practical speeds, adding well under a gigabyte of memory.
arxiv-2606-24649:
Wang and colleagues split three-dimensional scene understanding between two cooperating agents. One decides where to look. The other writes down what it sees. Zero shot 3D work has been recast as video keyframe reading for multimodal models. Fixed videos offer finite viewpoints, though, and leave three-dimensional structure implicit. Their 2026 framework attacks both limits with a closed loop between the two agents.

The Perception Agent summarises the scene into a structured cognitive map, documenting object attributes under consistent instance IDs across viewpoints. The Planning Agent reads that map, decides which query relevant viewpoints are missing, and adds critical views. Perception feedback filters mismatched candidates, and steers the next round of viewpoint planning. Iterating until candidates are resolved, the pair assembles split views into one coherent scene model. Wang's team presents collaborative thinking, rather than a bigger single model, as the route past the viewpoint bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-24849:
Zixuan Li and twelve colleagues improve how multimodal language models follow the structure of a text prompt when generating images. Models often render appearance well but break the prompt's structure. Object counts, spatial relations, attribute bindings, and rough layouts get lost. The authors blame a single conditioning stream that entangles planning with rendering. Their method, IV-CoT, splits visual queries into two cascades. Structural queries first build a latent visual plan. Semantic queries then render appearance on top of that plan.

Training only sketch supervision guides the structural queries toward real structure. No sketches are needed when the model runs. The whole reasoning happens implicitly in one forward pass. Results on the GenEval and T2I-CompBench benchmarks beat prior approaches. Visualisations show the two query types playing complementary roles. Li and colleagues argue this separation is what structure aware generation was missing.
arxiv-2606-25149:
Systems that act before being asked are spreading fast, from lighting that adapts to activity to robots that plan ahead. Nima Zargham and four colleagues, writing for a Graphics Interface 2026 workshop, argue that proactivity itself is still loosely defined and unevenly used across research and practice.

Simple reminders and recommendation tools are routinely labelled proactive. Their mechanisms and aims differ sharply from systems that take real initiative. Design and evaluation methods, built for reactive interaction, miss what makes proactive behaviour hard: timing, appropriateness, user control, transparency, and trust. The workshop gathers researchers and practitioners across human computer interaction and AI to give the concept a firmer footing. On shared terms, proactive systems can then be designed, compared, and judged.
arxiv-2606-25249:
Search engines often recheck a fast first pass with a slow, careful ranking model, even for easy questions. Ata Cinar Genc, Emir Kaan Korukluoglu, and James Allan argue in 2026 that the heavy step should be spent only where it helps. Their framework scores each query with a utility function and routes it to one of three paths: plain keyword search, a light neural reranker, or a heavy one. A trained classifier learns the routing from limited labelled data.

Measured against always using the heavy reranker, the routed system cut median response time dramatically, in some tests by more than fifty times. Ranking quality stayed close, ranging from somewhat lower to slightly better depending on the dataset. Oracle tests show even larger gains are possible if routing improves, though learning the router well proved difficult.
arxiv-2606-25449:
A chatbot that remembers a wrong fact but forgets the evidence behind it can be worse than one that remembers nothing. Alex Kwon names that failure brittle memory in 2026 and builds an evaluation for it. A conversation drifts and the memory is compressed to a fixed budget. Then a correction arrives. Can the model recover the true answer, scored exactly against ground truth with no judge model involved? Eight models face paired memory conditions under matched budgets.

Lossy memory was never better than empty memory, and clearly worse for models inclined to answer rather than abstain. One simple policy repaired much of the damage: keep the source that lets an answer be recomputed, and drop the stored conclusion instead. The failure also compounded across repeated memory cycles and showed up in three deployed memory systems and real dialogue data.
arxiv-2606-25649:
Shift invariant subspaces of the Hardy space, the analytic function spaces on the disk, are each generated by one inner function. Rounak Biswas and Srijan Sarkar ask in 2026 when the projections onto two such subspaces essentially commute, meaning their commutator is compact, a small error in operator terms. Halmos' classical two projections theorem supplies the machinery. The answer comes as local conditions on the two generating inner functions, checkable piece by piece rather than globally.

Pairs whose commutator is not merely compact but finite rank receive their own characterisation. Essential commutativity links to Fredholmness of the projection pair in the sense of Avron, Seiler, and Simon, tying the question to index theory. Applications sharpen known tests for when truncated Toeplitz operators are compact, and reframe compactness of certain contractions through model theory. Several characterisations on the polydisc close the work, where several variables complicate every picture.
arxiv-2606-25949:
Ehsan Zabardast, Bhuwan Paudel, and Javier Gonzalez-Huerta report an industrial case study of a software product built from 267 microservices. Microservice designs promise that each service evolves independently, yet in large systems dependencies often pile up around a few services. The team combined three kinds of dependency evidence, compile-time links, run-time calls, and task dependencies, and checked their reading repeatedly with the engineers who run the system.

A recurring shape emerged from the network maps. A dense core of dependency magnets sits at the centre, wrapped by a transition zone of services increasingly entangled with the core, then an outer region of lightly connected services. Naming the pattern the dependency black hole, Zabardast and colleagues map its parts onto an accretion disk, an event horizon, and a singularity, and state three hypotheses about how such concentration grows.
arxiv-2606-26049:
Matteo D'Achille and Christoph Thäle compute face statistics for Poisson-Voronoi tessellations in hyperbolic space. A Voronoi tessellation carves space into cells around random seed points. Each cell holds the spots closest to its seed. Hyperbolic space curves negatively, which changes the geometry throughout. Earlier exact results covered only dimensions two and three, in work by Isokawa.

Formulas now cover every dimension and every face size. The authors determine the volume densities of faces of each dimension for any positive seed intensity. A new formula of Blaschke-Petkantschin type, in hyperbolic space, does the heavy lifting. The ideal tessellation, reached as intensity shrinks toward zero, gets closed forms too. All face volume densities and typical face volumes come out explicitly there. The results extend a classical strand of stochastic geometry into curved space.
arxiv-2606-26249:
D. Trevascus and the GRAVITY+ Collaboration chase a maybe-planet in the PDS 70 system. That young star hosts two confirmed protoplanets, a rare pair still forming inside their birth disk. A third point of light has appeared repeatedly, deeper in the system. It could be a third inner planet. It could also be a dust clump riding the disk's rotation, a common impostor in this field. Earlier data could not separate the two stories.

New interferometer observations fail to find the source again. VLTI/GRAVITY+ combines large telescopes into one sharper eye, and the point source is absent at the expected spot. Absence argues for the dust clump reading: a planet should persist and move predictably. The campaign doubles as a methods demonstration. Angular resolving power of this class can vet candidate protoplanets against disk features, a filter the field badly needs as candidate lists grow.
arxiv-2606-26449:
Mohammad Faizan and Dalal Alharthi question a comforting habit of retrieval-augmented systems. Such systems answer questions using documents they fetch first. They often print citations beside the answer. But a citation does not prove that source shaped the answer. Their framework, ProvenAI, splits transparency into three layers. Each layer can be measured on its own. The layers cover answer correctness, citation quality, and real document influence.

ProvenAI runs a seven-stage pipeline over the HotpotQA distractor benchmark. That benchmark requires joining facts across documents. It covers more than seven thousand questions. The questions draw on a corpus of about half a million passages. Answers reached an accuracy a little above half. Citation quality scored higher. One worked example exposed the gap the authors name. A perfectly cited source had only weak influence. Meanwhile, seven uncited sources measurably shifted the answer.
arxiv-2606-26549:
Ao Hu and nine colleagues present PMDformer, a transformer model for long-term time series forecasting. Forecasting far ahead matters for energy, finance, and traffic planning. Transformer models often chop series into patches, short segments treated as units. Comparing patch shapes across variables is hard because scales differ. A tall patch and a short patch can share the same shape.

Their patch-mean decoupling subtracts each patch's average before comparison. Shape information then stands apart from level, so attention compares true shapes. Two attention modules complete the design. One restores the removed trend when producing output. The other limits cross-variable attention to the most relevant recent segments, avoiding stale correlations. Wide experiments show PMDformer beating leading rivals on stability and accuracy, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-26649:
Adam Mondl, Matthew Maisel, and John H. Brock automate the writing of enforceable AI agent policies. High-stakes agents need rules that provably bind them. Classifier guardrails offer no formal guarantees. Hand-coded symbolic rules cannot cover real policy documents. Their pipeline translates agent prompts, tool descriptions, and plain-language policy texts into formally checked policies in the Cedar policy language.

A generator-critic loop does the translation. A language model drafts policies. A hard critic checks syntax, schema fit, contradictions, and emptiness. A soft critic, another model acting as judge, scores meaning alignment against a rubric. Drafts must pass both before an external engine enforces them at run time. On the MedAgentBench medical benchmark, the automatic policies covered much more of the source specification than earlier hand-coded enforcement.
arxiv-2606-26849:
Ke Chen and five colleagues present LFNet, a network for finding the most eye-catching object in an image, whatever sensors supplied it. Salient object detection must segment that object cleanly. Two model families dominate, convolutional networks and state space models. The authors show the two have opposite spectral biases: each prefers different frequency content in its features. Their strengths are complementary.

Liquid fusion merges the two streams dynamically. The design borrows from liquid neural networks, whose internal states evolve continuously. One backbone's features act as the evolving state; the other's act as an incoming stimulus. A gating mechanism blends them based on content. The fused features then drive the segmentation. The authors report gains toward a general detector that works across single-sensor and multi-sensor scenes.
arxiv-2606-27049:
Goh and Taylor extend their two-field model of dark energy, the unknown driver behind the speeding expansion of the universe. Their quintom framework uses two scalar fields so the energy's pressure-to-density ratio can cross a key boundary. It moves from phantom behaviour, below that boundary, to quintessence behaviour above it over cosmic time. Attention now turns to small ripples, called perturbations, and how they shape large-scale cosmic structure in 2026 analysis.

Linear ripple equations for the model are derived step by step. Ripples in this model suppress the matter power spectrum, a measure of clumping across scales, in familiar ways. They also boost the late-time Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect, a faint imprint left on ancient microwave light by evolving gravity wells. Fitting sky surveys, microwave data, and supernova records leaves the model slightly favoured over a standard rival formula.
arxiv-2606-27149:
Arregui and colleagues examine how scattered moderation shapes Mastodon, the social network split across thousands of self-governed servers. The team builds a signed, directed, time-changing network from one year of records. Follows form positive links, while daily block actions form negative ones. Big questions follow: does constant local blocking destabilise the whole, and how does news then spread in this analysis of 2026?

Despite nonstop moderation, the structure stays strikingly stable over the year. Link patterns and degree shapes persist, and averaged transitions settle near Markovian balance over middle time scales. A marked split appears between instances that mostly ban and those mostly banned. Information starting in the banning minority spreads more efficiently, inside and outward. Flow in the reverse direction stays fragile. Echo chambers emerge even in a globally balanced network, and stricter spread rules strengthen them.
arxiv-2606-27449:
Aggarwal argues that the standard Transformer wastes capacity by giving every layer the same number of attention heads. Splitting the hidden dimension equally forces early heads to work in narrow subspaces, too cramped for complex local patterns. The Prism Transformer replaces the uniform layout with a progressive head schedule: head count rises with depth. Early layers use few, wide heads for local composition. In the 2026 machine learning paper, deep layers use many, narrow heads that decompose patterns into specialised features.

The reshuffle is parameter-neutral and compute-neutral, keeping identical weight matrices and operation budgets. Across three model scales, from roughly one hundred million to three quarters of a billion parameters, validation loss drops consistently. Zero-shot benchmark scores improve on commonsense and reasoning suites. Non-uniform allocation unlocks capacity that was already paid for. Architecture, not scale, was the bottleneck. The schedule invites rethinking other uniform design habits.
arxiv-2606-27749:
Devadatta Hegde proves a special case of Franke's theorem directly in 2026. The setting is level one spherical automorphic forms on the upper half-plane. The claim is clean. Every such form is a cusp form plus a combination of Laurent coefficients of the standard Eisenstein series. Franke's general theorem says far more. It spans automorphic forms on any reductive group, built from Eisenstein series induced from cuspidal forms on Levi subgroups.

The general proof is heavy machinery. It invokes Langlands' construction of the discrete automorphic spectrum. Hegde's proof avoids that entirely. It rests on basic analytic properties of automorphic forms. Green's identity does the key work. The simplest instance of the theorem is thereby verified by elementary means. Readers get a self-contained entry point into a deep circle of ideas in the Langlands programme.
arxiv-2606-27949:
Scientific simulations chase ever higher accuracy. The cost is longer runs and heavy power use. Gülçin Gedik, Robert Schöne, and Roman Iakymchuk test mixed-precision computing in 2026 as a remedy. Mixed precision uses cheaper number formats where full precision is not needed. Two solver benchmarks serve as case studies, the Reactor Simulator and LULESH.

Both benchmarks improved. For the Reactor Simulator, time-to-solution and energy-to-solution each fell by about thirty percent, with accuracy intact. For LULESH, time improved by up to thirty percent. Energy fell by up to twenty-five percent in the main results, with savings up to thirty-seven percent reported in the conclusion. Selectively lowering precision in key kernels drove the gains. Tuning proved inherently application-specific. The authors flag two open challenges, narrowing the search space and automating the implementation. Wider application studies are planned.
arxiv-2606-28349:
Zeju Li, Ziyang Zheng, Yizhou Zhou, and Qiang Xu built HMARS, a memory system that helps language models reason over very long material. Standard retrieval fetches a few text chunks and can discard the decisive evidence before reasoning even starts, especially when relevance only becomes clear in wider context.

HMARS instead manages long contexts like organized memory. Sub-agents guard bounded regions, mid-level agents coordinate regional context for each query, and a frontier model reasons over the evidence pages they return. The team built two diagnostic benchmarks stressing evidence breadth and how relevance depends on context. Across long-document and multi-turn tasks, HMARS beat retrieval, reranking, full-context, graph-based, and agentic rivals. Analysis showed the wins came from gathering the needed evidence more completely.
arxiv-2606-28549:
Zachariah Addison, writing alone, presents a topological index for a class of magnets that momentum-space tools miss. The Chern number usually classifies insulating phases by how electrons wind through momentum space. Addison defines a position space counterpart for chiral magnetic systems, systems whose magnetism twists in a handed way.

A nonzero position space index guarantees protected states living inside the energy gap, localized at the edges of potential barriers in momentum space. The effective field theory behind these insulators reveals a fixed, quantized link between the transverse forces that move quanta around momentum space. Skyrmion phases, where spins swirl in tiny vortices, carry nonzero values, and the index extends the classical skyrmion winding number. Curiously, a seeming barrier prevents a system from carrying both kinds of topology at once.
arxiv-2606-28649:
Nima Dorzhiev, writing alone, attacks robots through their senses. Language-model-controlled robots built on the ROS 2 framework take instructions from what they see and hear, so a malicious sign, a spoken phrase, or faked sensor data might hijack behavior. Dorzhiev's RIPA study is, to his knowledge, the first systematic multi-channel test of such sensory prompt injection.

Across one hundred runs per variant and five models from four families, vulnerability proved model-specific rather than size-driven. One seventy-billion-parameter model fell to every variant, while smaller models shrugged off direct overrides. The smallest matched the large model's weakness. A hybrid semantic firewall stopped all known patterns yet let about a tenth of obfuscated attacks through. A third channel, poisoning the robot's LiDAR-derived picture of its surroundings, succeeded completely on one major model.
arxiv-2606-28749:
Hossain studies how undergraduate students lean on large language models, the AI chat tools many now use while writing essays. His study ran at a public university that serves many minority students, and it draws on 382 survey responses, 14 interviews and hundreds of written answers. Earlier tools judged reliance only by how often students used AI, which he argues misses what students actually contribute themselves.

Four kinds of reliance emerged from the data. Strategic users, about a third of the group, used AI most thoughtfully, while a small dependent group, about 4.5 percent, leaned on it heavily. Oddly, the strategic group scored lowest on standard measures, which Hossain reads as a flaw in those measures. He also found about 13 percent of students refuse AI for ethical reasons, a group current frameworks ignore.
arxiv-2606-28849:
Sandor and Yang study how the number of ways to write a whole number as an ordered sum grows for a special set of allowed parts. The set contains zero and every positive integer whose base-four expansion starts with one or two. Its representation function counts ordered sums of a fixed length using only parts from that set. Shallit had shown the three-part count rises strictly, disproving a 2002 conjecture of Dombi.

Extending that line, the pair prove that for every sum length of three or more, the step-by-step increase grows like a polynomial in the target number. Matching upper and lower bounds pin down that growth rate. They also build a large set, filling almost all natural numbers in density, whose representation counts rise strictly at every length. That construction answers a problem Dombi posed in 2002, and further open problems are listed.
arxiv-2606-29149:
Yang, Bi, Wang and Yin simulate how compact stellar systems, tight clusters of stars, evolve inside halos of ultralight dark matter. Such clusters are used to constrain the dark matter particle's mass, because wave interference in ultralight dark matter heats clusters and expands them, potentially clashing with observations. The team's earlier work showed internal two-body relaxation among stars also matters and had been overlooked.

Here they vary three more influences: metallicity, the Milky Way's tidal field, and particle mass. Metal-richer systems proved more resistant to disruption. The Milky Way's tides, by altering how clusters orbit inside their halos, significantly affected stability. Heating grew stronger with particle mass when the system is much smaller than the dark matter's wavelength scale, opposite to the reverse regime. Existing constraints from systems like ultrafaint dwarf galaxies may need careful revision.
arxiv-2606-29249:
Navinder Singh, writing from Bathinda, looks back at forty years of work on high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. Cuprates are copper oxide materials that carry current with no resistance far above absolute zero. The core puzzle is the mechanism, the process that makes this happen. One idea, gaining ground since a 2015 consensus paper, is that the effect grows out of repulsive forces between electrons, forces that push them apart.

Singh sets out three main schools of thought and weighs the evidence for each. He also discusses the hard tests the repulsive idea still faces. A 2022 experiment on Anderson's super-exchange mechanism, an early proposal for how magnetic forces pair electrons, gets close attention. He closes with an updated list of Anderson's dogmas: facts drawn from many experiments that any good theory must fit. That list has grown since 2000, as new shared findings have come in.
arxiv-2606-29349:
Kim and two colleagues reconstruct the full vibration of a structure from only a few sensors. Virtual sensing matters for structural health monitoring, where knowing displacement and force everywhere, from sparse measurements, is a basic challenge. They formulate the task as optimisation constrained by the elastodynamic equation, the physics law of elastic motion: the unknown force distribution is the variable, and full-field displacement and force are recovered together.

Gradients come from reverse-mode automatic differentiation through the physics solver, and an L-BFGS optimiser iterates to the best state. The pipeline pairs an offline finite element stage with an online GPU stage. On three test cases of rising complexity, a cantilever plate, an elbow pipe and a reactor pressure vessel, the method beat modal expansion everywhere. It cut displacement errors by factors of two to seventeen. GPU acceleration gave up to a sixty-five fold speedup over CPU.
arxiv-2606-29449:
Hopkins works toward a KKL theorem for high-dimensional expanders, extending a classic result from the analysis of Boolean functions. The original KKL theorem describes low-influence functions on the hypercube, functions where no single input bit matters much. Analogues beyond the cube now support breakthroughs in several areas, yet expansion demands have kept the versions narrow.

Hopkins introduces a local-to-global method for studying low-influence functions on simplicial complexes, the higher-dimensional cousins of graphs. If every link of a complex satisfies a KKL theorem, he proves, then the whole complex does too. Building on work by Gotlib and Kaufman, he also proves a weaker dimension-dependent version for complexes with any nontrivial two-sided expansion. Applications include the first-ever characterization of non-expanding functions on dense clique complexes, plus a small-set expansion theorem for the Ramanujan complexes introduced by Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne.
arxiv-2606-29549:
Esrafilian and Ali-Akbari study how motion changes holographic entanglement entropy in a charged plasma. Holography here is a duality that describes a hot quantum system through gravity in a higher-dimensional space. The entropy measures how strongly two regions are quantum-linked. Their plasma also carries a nonzero chemical potential, which tracks how much the system favours adding charge.

Sufficiently high velocity raises the entropy, especially when that potential is larger. At high temperature and high velocity together, that dependence almost disappears, as thermal effects dominate over charge-density effects. At near-light speeds, the entropy grows very rapidly with velocity. Velocity becomes the dominant parameter, and it largely suppresses the thermal and chemical contributions alike. The study maps how three competing influences trade off inside this strongly coupled plasma.
arxiv-2606-29649:
Hua and West investigate a moderation loophole: harmful text drawn as ASCII art, pictures built from typed characters, can slip past vision-language models used as content filters. Such jailbreak attacks encode banned words visually. The authors ask how image resolution affects whether models detect the harmful content.

They generate ASCII art images at ten resolution scales across eight character construction modes. Modes range from dense block characters to word-embedded designs. Eight state-of-the-art vision-language models are evaluated on English and Chinese corpora. Detection rates decline sharply once resolution passes certain thresholds. The thresholds recur across models, modes, and languages. Word-based modes prove the most resistant to detection at every resolution. The authors call this a systematic vulnerability in vision-language moderation and argue for resolution-aware evaluation standards.
arxiv-2606-30149:
Annamalai Shanmugaraj, Roland Haas, Erik Schnetter, and Sofie Koksbang simulate gravitational waves passing through dark matter halos. Standard treatments use geometric optics, treating waves like rays. That view fails when structures match the wave's own length scale. The team evolves waves numerically through spherical astrophysical structures. Weak and strong gravity regimes are both covered.

Their scheme evolves the full Einstein equations for the waves. Gaussian, NFW, and Burkert density profiles serve as lenses. Scattering depends strongly on how the lens potential is distributed, not just its mass. With wavelength set below the Schwarzschild radius, diffraction effects stand out. Through the Gaussian density, waves do not follow null geodesics. That holds in both weak and strong gravity settings. For the Burkert profile, the wavefront's convexity flips on exit. Future detectors might read halo structure from such signals.
arxiv-2606-30549:
Jessica Hutchison and eight colleagues measure whether students actually think about the code an AI writes for them. AI completion tools suggest code that students accept with one keystroke. Accepting blindly short-circuits the reflection learning needs. Their tool, Clover, logs every interaction with suggestions. It also inserts attention checks during programming tasks. Those checks probe whether students are thinking as they work. A taxonomy of behavior metrics organizes the measurements.

Interaction patterns were compared against attention check performance. Task performance entered the analysis as well. Students who accepted suggestions more often scored worse on checks. Higher tab-accept rates tracked lower engagement. Longer dwell time before deciding pointed the other way. It was associated with higher attention check scores. The authors discuss using such process data in teaching. Attention checks might support reflection during AI-assisted programming. The findings give instructors measurable signals instead of impressions.
arxiv-2606-30649:
Nolan Coffey, Faithful Odoi, Makenzie Johnson and Nasir Eisty test whether watching an AI negotiator's private reasoning can catch it lying. Agents increasingly negotiate and transact for users, so pipelines need runtime checks that stated intentions match real behaviour. The team staged used-car sales talks: a seller agent privately knew of a hidden defect, while a buyer agent had only public market data.

A third agent monitored the seller's chain-of-thought, its written step-by-step reasoning, against its messages, and warned the buyer on spotting concealment. Monitoring raised the buyer's walk-away rate across model pairings. Yet a stubborn intelligence gap appeared: weaker buyers often could not turn a warning into a fair counter-offer, and still accepted exploitative deals after being alerted. Sellers who knew they were watched changed tactics, but concealment persisted. The authors read the results as promise plus clear limits for light oversight.
arxiv-2606-30949:
Yang Zou, Zijian Ding, Yizhou Sun and Jason Cong automate the tedious rewrite that turns ordinary software into code a chip-design tool can synthesise. High-Level Synthesis builds hardware from C-like code, but real-world programs use constructs the tools reject, and fixing them by hand can take experts days. AgRefactor is a multi-agent workflow in which language-model agents perform the refactoring. A self-evolving memory stores factual and strategic lessons from earlier tasks and retrieves them for new ones. Automated refactoring tools are mixed in, so cheap mechanical edits do not burn model calls.

On 9 of 11 challenging real-world benchmarks, each 5 to 10 times longer than prior work's hardest cases, AgRefactor matched or beat both the best automated tool and a strong model-based baseline. Further agent-driven optimisation gave a 6.51 times geometric-mean speedup over the leading pragma tuning tool.
arxiv-2606-31049:
Berra-Montiel, Molgado, and Santacruz apply phase space quantization to two classic models of an uneven early universe. The Taub and Kantowski-Sachs models are homogeneous but anisotropic: space expands at different rates in different directions. The usual route, the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, hits factor ordering ambiguities. Different orderings of the same formula give different physics.

The authors use deformation quantization instead. It rests on the Weyl map and the Moyal star product. They build explicit Wigner distributions for both models. A split of the Hamiltonian constraint tames the convergence problems that often plague the star product. From the diagonal Wigner distributions, they recover the standard wave functions exactly. The results come out in terms of modified Bessel functions. That ties the phase space picture back to standard quantum cosmology.
arxiv-2606-31249:
Guo and eight colleagues report a winning system for few-shot hidden emotion recognition, reading feelings people conceal in long videos. Their XInsight Lab entry took first place in Track 3 of an EI-MIGA-IJCAI challenge. Weak emotional clues are sparse in long footage, so the system fuses many feature sources.

Skeleton motion, facial Blendshapes, vision foundation features, video features, and semantic priors all feed the model. A cross-attention design uses still pose as the query and small motion changes as keys, which strips out body shape and identity bias. Multiple instance learning pooling then picks out brief emotional moments. The team also show that large vision models can collapse on micro-motion tasks and fake general skill through shortcut learning.
arxiv-2606-31749:
Naik and Sreekanth model how a hot, dense quark-gluon plasma moves toward chemical equilibrium while it expands. Quark-gluon plasma forms in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Its particle mix starts out of balance, with gluons ahead and quarks undersaturated. The authors use conformal Gubser flow, an expanding-flow solution with transverse motion built in.

Fugacity parameters track the chemical imbalance, and master rate equations evolve them alongside the expansion. Both finite baryon density and transverse expansion delay equilibration, leaving quarks lagging gluons longer. Total thermal photon output drops in this scenario, yet early high-momentum photon production rises. The time structure of emission rates may give experiments a visible signature of the equilibration process.
arxiv-2606-31849:
Sonaniskar and three colleagues give the Rubin Observatory a fast way to estimate stress in its giant primary-tertiary mirror. The M1M3 mirror is an 8.4-metre borosilicate optic held by 156 pneumatic actuators. Full finite-element runs are too slow for real-time safety checks on every correction, yet the irreplaceable glass must never be overstressed.

Their method precomputes unit stress fields for the first 20 natural bending modes with NASTRAN. Because stress follows strain, combined-mode peak stress is predicted by a root-sum-square blend of the unit fields. Validation against full NASTRAN simulations for mixed corrections, including astigmatism, coma and spherical modes, agrees within a few percent. Operations can now check stress margins almost instantly.
arxiv-2606-31949:
Cirici and Horel construct algebraic models for the homotopy type of configuration spaces of certain algebraic varieties. Configuration spaces record the possible positions of distinct points on a variety, and their homotopy type is a long-standing object of study in algebraic topology. The varieties treated here are of Tate type, and the models capture tame information that reflects the ℓ-adic homotopy type.

Weights in étale cohomology supply the main tool for building the models from algebraic data. The same machinery also gives models for more general arrangement complements, both in the tame sense and over the rational numbers. Such models let topologists compute with spaces that are otherwise accessible only abstractly. The results connect arithmetic geometry with the classical theory of configuration spaces.
arxiv-2608-00349:
Lin and co-authors measure the differential limb coupling effect with the PARVI spectrograph. New extreme-precision radial velocity instruments use single-mode fibers and adaptive optics. They hunt tiny stellar Doppler shifts from orbiting planets. Target stars are partly resolved at the diffraction limit, though. Red- and blue-shifted disk sides then couple into the spectrograph unequally.

That coupling, DLC, can add error near a metre per second for nearby target stars. Their observing strategy aims to produce shifts of hundreds of metres per second. They executed that plan with the diffraction-limited PARVI instrument. Data also characterize PARVI's tip-tilt guide camera and its performance. Analysis of the derived velocities is under way. The RVs are deeply entangled with other instrumental effects, they note. Mitigation for HISPEC is the end goal.
azoth-et-ignis-das-ist-das-wahre-element:
Herman Fictuld published this German hermetic treatise in 1749, under a Latin title meaning azoth and fire. Its subject is the true elementary water and fire, the Mercurius philosophorum, presented as the one necessary thing among the first principles of the philosopher's stone. A second title joins it: Aureum Vellus, the golden fleece, its origin and its exalted state.

Fictuld promises lovers of hermetic philosophy the prima materia itself, with its practice opened and expressed. He defends the old speech of poets and philosophers as their rightful inheritance, kept by younger writers in due succession. The hosted scan, from an old Fraktur printing, reads very roughly in machine form. Even so, the book shows eighteenth-century German alchemy arguing in its own terms: azoth, fire, and the one matter.
bronte-shirley-1849:
Charlotte Brontë published Shirley in 1849, her ambitious condition-of-England novel of the mills. The tale is set in Yorkshire against the Luddite risings of 1811 to 1812. It was the first major industrial novel by a woman in English letters of the time.

Mill owner Robert Moore brings new machines as starving weavers plot to smash them at night. Shirley Keeldar, a brisk heiress, and meek Caroline Helstone view his world from two sides. Caroline pines in a parsonage while Shirley runs her estate and teases her old tutor. A shooting, a mad dog's bite, and two weddings close the social panorama of Yorkshire. Brontë wrote it in grief, as her brother and sisters died around her.
buddhist-mahayana-texts-sbe-49:
E. B. Cowell, F. Max Muller, and J. Takakusu translated the Buddhist Mahayana Texts of 1894. The volume closed the Sacred Books of the East series as number forty-nine. Key Mahayana scriptures of the Greater Vehicle appear in English here.

The Larger and Smaller Sukhavati texts describe Amitayus and his Pure Land. The Vajracchedika, or Diamond Sutra, teaches emptiness in sharp dialogues. Other pieces include the Heart Sutra tradition's core ideas in early form. These scriptures shaped the Buddhism of China, Japan, and Tibet profoundly. Muller edited the whole Sacred Books series and contributed translations himself. The volume gives East Asian Buddhism in its own sublime words.
castro-de-iusta-haereticorum-punitione-1:
Alfonso de Castro, a Spanish Franciscan theologian, published De Iusta Haereticorum Punitione in 1549. The Latin title means on the just punishment of heretics. Castro advised Spanish rulers at a time when Spain's church courts pursued Protestant and other accused heretics.

Three books weigh what heresy is, which penalties the law allows, and how rulers and judges should act. Castro argued for firm punishment but also set limits and urged care in proof. He drew on scripture, church law, and past cases to build his rules. The work is a key source for how learned churchmen defended persecution in law, and why they thought mercy toward heresy was a public danger.
catalogue-of-a-large-and-splendid-librar:
Cooley and Keese, auctioneers at 191 Broadway in New York, issued a sale catalogue in 1849. It covered the remaining library of Judge Furman, a noted book collector. The sale was set for the evenings of May 15 and 16. Rare works on American history, the arts, alchemy, Shakespeare, and the drama head the bill, together with old coins and medals.

Numbered lots run from travel and history to fairy legends, geology, and lives of naturalists, each with its binding and format briefly noted. Some lots carry a short remark, as on a curious work on hieroglyphics. A long Shakespeare group and engraved plates close the list. The scan's lettering is rough in places, but titles and order stay readable.
cia-0000009449:
Three American prisoners of war were sighted in An Xuyen province, an October 1972 CIA report states. An Xuyen, at South Vietnam's southern tip, was deep Viet Cong country in the Mekong Delta. Prisoners held that far south lived far from the known northern camps.

Southern sightings mattered because the Delta's camps were small, mobile, and rarely photographed. A confirmed trio added names and a place to the southern prisoner map. Officials cross-checked the report against men known missing in the south. The file shows the search reaching the map's bottom edge, where information was scarcest.
cia-0000009649:
Three American prisoners, identified with the US 25th Division, were sighted in a January 1972 report from a Cambodian place the title cuts short at Komp. The 25th Division fought in South Vietnam's III Corps region, near the Cambodian border. Prisoners taken there could be marched across that border.

Cross-border captivity hid men in sanctuaries American forces could rarely reach. A sighting naming their division gave officials a strong check against unit loss records. The report shows the war's geography spilling past Vietnam's edge. It also gives three ground soldiers a dated trace inside Cambodia's camps.
cia-0000009749:
Inside Cambodia stood a Viet Cong prisoner of war camp, described in a November 1969 CIA report. Viet Cong sanctuaries across the border held supplies, hospitals, and prisoners beyond South Vietnam's reach. American forces would strike those sanctuaries the following spring.

A camp in Cambodia proved captivity already crossed borders years before that strike. Prisoners held there vanished from both countries' open records. Reports like this one were often the only sign of their location. The file adds a Cambodian site to the prison map at an early date, when the border war was still officially secret.
cia-0000009849:
Unidentified American prisoners were observed in Sam Neua and in Hanoi in 1965, an item filed in April 1971 recalls. Sam Neua is the main town of Houa Phan province in Laos; Hanoi needs no placing. Two capitals of captivity appear in one backward-looking report.

Retrospective reports helped fill the early years, when record keeping lagged the fighting. A witness recalling 1965 in 1971 could still add faces and places to thin files. Memory fades and shifts, so analysts handled such recall with care. This file preserves it as filed, an attempt to recover the prison story's first chapter.
cia-0000012249:
Five years after the Berlin Wall split Germany, a CIA paper from January 1966 takes stock of East Germany's outlook. Walter Ulbricht's communist regime ruled the smaller German state under Soviet protection. The Wall had stopped the flood of refugees westward, and with it the regime's worst crisis.

The paper weighs the regime's stability and finds it resting on concrete and Soviet backing. It also looks at the economy and at East Berlin's drive to be treated as a real state. The study captures a workers' state that endured by force, judged coolly by the other side.
cia-0000014749: Anatoliy Antonovich Yatskov, also named Yakovlev, fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1973. The title calls him Julius Rosenberg's handler. It also notes his mention in the Rosenberg case record. A handler file still active in 1973 shows how long the atomic spy case kept generating paper, twenty years after the trial.
cia-0000022649: Two downed American pilots may have died in Thanh Hoa Province, North Vietnam, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. The word possible marks the doubt honestly in the title itself. Thanh Hoa held the famous bridge that American planes attacked for years. Uncertain deaths were the hardest entries, leaving families between hope and grief with no firm word either way.
cia-0000036849:
A Hanoi correspondent's dispatch in English, written for Prensa, fills a CIA record dated October 4, 1967. Its subject is the capture of American pilot McCain over North Vietnam. The dispatch is one of several in the files that follow the same capture.

Inside, the story is told as Hanoi wanted foreign readers to hear it. Comparing such dispatches lets readers see how one event was shaped for export. The file adds a further layer to the record of McCain's first days in captivity. Read beside the other dispatches, it shows the same story being shaped for different audiences abroad.
cia-0000042349:
The theory of scientific socialism should be developed in practice, argues an item in a CIA record dated August 1, 1988. Scientific socialism was the Soviet system's name for its ruling doctrine. By 1988 that doctrine was under strain across the socialist world.

Inside, the item defends and develops the theory in the approved terms. American analysts collected such pieces to gauge the health of Soviet thought. The file shows ideology being argued over near the system's end. Within a few years the doctrine defended here would lose its state. That state had carried the theory, by law and by force, for seven long decades.
cia-0000045249:
Rivera y Damas spoke on Talavera and on the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1985. The archbishop joined two hard matters in one public appearance. His counsel carried weight with the government and the country alike.

Inside, his words on the affair and the kidnapping are preserved. A prelate who speaks on politics in wartime chooses his ground carefully. Talavera's case and the president's daughter were both tests of law. The file holds the archbishop treating them together, as questions of justice in a country where justice was the scarcest good of all.
cia-0000049149: The National Police's role in investigating the murders of six Jesuit priests is the subject of a CIA item from 1990. The priests had been killed at their university residence the previous November, by soldiers. Police work on a military crime was doubted from the start, and this item preserves how that role was described.
cia-0000049249: Explosions at the Central American University in El Salvador fill a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. The university, run by Jesuits, stood at the war's moral center, and bombs there were messages as much as attacks. That same year, its rector and five brother priests were murdered on its grounds.
cia-0000102949: Good performance of Soyuzzoloto during the nineteen seventies, plus origin and development of an unnamed subject, form declassified CIA document 0000102949, dated August 6, 1984. The heading joins two numbered topics. Readers find a short gold-trust performance record, a change of subject from labor to mining inside the same Soviet cluster of filings.
cia-0000108049: Corrective Labor Camp at Volzhskiy, Rsfsr is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108049, dated August 1, 1986. The title places one corrective labor camp at Volzhskiy, in the RSFSR. RSFSR is the heading's short form for the Russian republic in full. The brief record is a single camp item, filed in the summer of 1986 as released there.
cia-0000112349: Copilot's Brother Speaks on Guilin Air Disaster is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112349, dated November 5, 1992. The title gives a speaker by relation: the copilot's brother, on the Guilin air disaster. His name is not given in the heading itself. The brief record is a family statement item, filed in the autumn of 1992 as released.
cia-0000115549: PLO: Impact of the Lebanese Incursion is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000115549, dated October 1, 1987. The heading measures an impact: what a Lebanese incursion did to the PLO. PLO shortens Palestine Liberation Organization at the front of the title. The brief record is an impact assessment item from the autumn of 1987 as released in the files.
cia-0000117849: Untitled re: to Assistant Secretary of State Edwin a. Martin from Minister Ca is the heading, cut off mid-name, on declassified CIA document 0000117849, dated February 5, 1962. The catalog marks the file untitled, then describes a message to Edwin A. Martin. Its sender, a minister, breaks off at Ca in the heading. The brief record preserves the partial sender name exactly as released.
cia-0000118649: Situation Report As of 1900 Hours Local Time, 22 March 1968 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000118649, dated February 5, 1968. The title times its report to 7 p.m. on March 22, weeks after the file's own February date. That ordering stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is an hour-timed war report item from 1968.
cia-0000126949: From January 1991, a CIA Terrorism Review surveys anti-American terrorism in Latin America. With the Cold War ending, the region's guerrilla groups were losing their outside sponsors. The review takes stock of the threat as it stood at the start of the new decade. A 1991 survey of anti-American violence doubled as a Cold War closing inventory, sorting which dangers would outlive the rivalry that had funded so many of them.
cia-0000132449:
The Soviet Union and the Cuban revolution are assessed together in a CIA document dated January 4, 1960. The large question behind it was how far Moscow would go in backing Castro. Analysts had to judge Soviet intent from speeches, trade talks, and visits.

In time the answer reached as far as nuclear missiles placed on the island. The document was written long before that crisis, when the commitment was still forming. For readers, it preserves an early agency judgment on the partnership. Comparing its caution with later events shows how fast the relationship deepened during 1960 and after.
cia-0000132649: A Cuban attempt to hide an arms buy in Europe fills a CIA item dated May 3, 1960. Arms dealers in Europe asked fewer hard questions than sellers in the United States. Havana was masking its search for weapons behind cover stories and middlemen. The short item lays out the attempt and how analysts said they had spotted it.
cia-0000132749:
January 4, 1961 was the first full day after the United States cut diplomatic ties with Cuba, and the CIA marked it with this briefing. The break, made on January 3, ended formal relations between the two governments. The paper records the island as that new reality began.

Several Cuba briefings share this date, and together they form the agency's post-break baseline: what Cuba looked like once embassies closed and confrontation stood alone. Months later came the Bay of Pigs, planned in the shadow of this rupture. The declassified text was freed years later through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000134249: Cuban developments fill item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series, dated July 5, 1960. By that summer the phrase needed no further gloss for regular readers of the series. The numbered run kept the Cuba watch in order week by week. The short item brings the developments up to date as analysts recorded them at the start of July.
cia-0000136149: With a date of 4 April 1954, a CIA cable in the open files deals with a request that ODACID weigh the Central American situation. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136249: The CIA cable from 5 May 1954 deals with Instruction 10 for broadcast, the series running past eight with no beats skipped, in a file now declassified. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136349: Withdrawal plans for the stations called SHERWOOD and SAHARA are laid out in this June 1954 LINCOLN cable, to be executed when directed. SHERWOOD will terminate all radio circuits except one, switch to reserve crypto pads when ordered, and send named personnel out immediately, while others stay briefly to liquidate equipment. Cryptographic material is to be destroyed. The cable is the PBSUCCESS operation planning its own disappearance.
cia-0000136949: Radio facilities have one primary job, this May 1954 cable states. That job is handling PBSUCCESS traffic. SKILLET's help to another office is limited. Emergency help, including evacuation planning, is set out elsewhere. Other help is allowed if it does not interfere. The station should explain this to SKILLET. Willingness exists, but the priority load is heavy. Only limited assistance is possible. Other offices' requests should stay at a bare minimum. Crystals for evacuation planning will be pouched.
cia-0000139449: Project SUN STREAK, the United States government's remote viewing effort of the 1980s, is the program behind document 0000139449, dated 1988.
