Four global heart rhythm societies joined to set out best practice. An expert group reviewed the literature and voted on each recommendation. The document updates and replaces the 2009 consensus on this topic. Each point comes in a short knowledge-byte form with support text. Later sections give a practical outline of the procedure. New tools, methods, and big trial results shape the guidance.
europmc-pmc8494649:
Yao and co-authors build a gene and epigenome atlas of the mouse primary motor cortex. This region runs movement and is conserved across mammals. Single-cell methods can give molecular signatures for its many cell types. Merging such data into one account was the hard part.

The team made gene and epigenome profiles for over 500,000 single cells. New math methods joined the data types and checked that cell types held up. The atlas holds over 56 neuronal cell types that replicate across methods. It also notes a layer-4-like excitatory group unusual for motor cortex. Thousands of shared marker genes and control elements came out of the merge.
europmc-pmc8774049:
Zhao and co-authors compare how the Omicron and Delta variants of SARS-CoV-2 grow and enter cells. Omicron carries more than 50 mutations, many tied to spread or immune escape. The team grew both variants in lab cell lines with high levels of the entry enzyme TMPRSS2. Head-to-head growth races were also run.

Omicron grew more slowly than Delta in those cells. In a lung cell line, it grew poorly while Delta thrived. Drugs that block the TMPRSS2 route stopped Delta but not Omicron. Drugs that block the internal entry route stopped both. Omicron also fused cells more weakly than Delta.
europmc-pmc8887649:
Sekhon, Cartwright, and Francis build a questionnaire that measures how acceptable a health intervention feels. Acceptability shapes whether treatments get used at all. A framework names seven parts of it. They include burden, ethical fit, and how well the point of the intervention makes sense. The team wanted one generic tool for any intervention. They built it through a five-step validation method.

The item pool began with 138 candidate questions. Most were cut or rewritten to cover the seven constructs. Two disease-specific versions came first. Feedback from stakeholders refined the wording. A generic version followed. Think-aloud tests used the COVID-19 vaccine as the test case. Twenty participants tried prospective and retrospective versions. Most items read clearly. Three constructs still caused some confusion. The authors report those honestly.
europmc-pmc8942849:
Halfmann and co-authors test Omicron infection and disease in mice and hamsters. Rodent models are the proving ground for countermeasures. A national program network ran the experiments together. Several Omicron isolates were used. Both normal animals and human-ACE2 transgenic animals were infected. Earlier variants served as the comparison. Infection levels, weight loss, and lung damage were tracked.

Omicron infected the animals less strongly. Weight loss stayed limited. Viral burden in upper and lower airways ran lower. Hamsters showed the same pattern. Lung infection and tissue damage were milder than with older isolates. Other variants of concern caused worse disease. The authors call Omicron attenuated in rodents. That matched early human clinical impressions. The results support using these models for Omicron countermeasures. They also hint the variant's biology truly shifted.
europmc-pmc8976049:
Dong and Zhang present STAGATE, a method that finds spatial domains in tissue from gene expression maps. New spatial transcriptomics tools keep gene data tied to place. Reading which spots form one domain is the challenge. Boundaries are where simpler methods blur. STAGATE uses a graph attention auto-encoder. It learns compact codes for each spot. Spatial position and gene profile feed in together. An attention step weighs each neighbor's likeness. That helps most at domain edges.

An optional module adds prior cell type groupings. The team validated the method across platforms. Resolutions and tissue types varied widely. Domain calls improved substantially over rivals. The method also denoised data while keeping patterns. Stacked tissue sections could be joined. Batch effects between sections shrank. Three-dimensional domains emerged from the rebuilt tissue. The authors offer it as general software.
europmc-pmc9279149:
Becker and co-authors chart how colon tissue changes as polyps turn into colorectal cancer. They profiled single-cell chromatin access and gene activity in 48 polyps, 27 normal tissues, and 6 cancers. Samples came from patients with and without inherited APC mutations. Each sample gave data from 1,000 to 10,000 cells.

A large share of polyp and cancer cells showed a stem-like state. These cells form a continuum of change from healthy tissue to cancer. Advanced polyps gained regulatory T cells and a pre-cancer fibroblast type. Cancers showed exhausted T cells and new fibroblast states. DNA methylation changes ran opposite to access changes along the path. The map offers markers for staging polyps by risk.
europmc-pmc9421549:
Borges and co-authors give a systematic review of reviews on infodemics and health misinformation. An infodemic is a flood of mixed true and false health claims during a crisis. The team searched five databases on 6 May 2022 for prior systematic reviews. Quality checks used the AMSTAR 2 and GRADE tools.

The search found 31 systematic reviews on the topic. Health misinformation on social media ranged from 0.2% to 28.8% of content. Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, and Instagram spread it fastest. Harms include wrong readings of evidence and more vaccine hesitancy. Mental health and health budgets also suffer. The authors call for joint action across sectors. Laws, awareness drives, and better digital literacy all play a part.
europmc-pmc9511749:
Kuo and co-authors ask whether mitochondrial oxidative stress in tumors is foe or friend. Reactive oxygen species build up when cell metabolism runs hot. Mitochondria are the main source of that stress. Balance between stress and cleanup is vital for cell survival.

In cancer cells, mitochondrial stress feeds tumor growth. It aids spread, new blood vessels, and immune escape. The same stress shapes other cells in the tumor setting. M2 macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells all bend under it. The review gathers work on both sides of that line. It then weighs plans to tune the stress level. Pairing such plans with immunotherapy is the key proposal. Past attempts lacked a shared base, the authors note. Their survey aims to give the combo work firmer ground.
europmc-pmc9524349:
Mishra and co-authors run cross-ancestry genome-wide studies of stroke to guide drug finds and risk scores. Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Past gene hunts leaned hard on European ancestry samples. That bias left other groups poorly served.

The meta-analyses covered 110,182 stroke patients and 1,503,898 controls. Five ancestries took part, with 33% non-European shares. Signals appeared at 89 independent loci, of which 61 were new. A follow-up set of 89,084 more cases confirmed most primary loci. Effect sizes lined up well across ancestries. Gene work pointed to candidates such as SH3PXD2A and FURIN. Drug target leads included F11, KLKB1, and PROC. An integrative polygenic score predicted ischemic stroke across groups. It added signal beyond standard clinical risk factors.
europmc-pmc9627549:
Vidal-Itriago and co-authors assess microglia diversity and what it means for the central nervous system. Microglia arrive from mesodermal stock before birth. They settle in the brain and renew themselves for life. Their share runs from 5 to 12% of cells in brain tissue.

Shape is the striking trait of these cells. They reshape their arms and bodies with each new cue. Forms range from fine branched shapes to round amoeba-like ones. Old views read shape as a simple rest or alarm switch. New work shows a far richer range of forms and jobs. The review links each form class to the work it does. Microglia ties with neurons get close attention. Many shape and function links are still unmapped, they note. The authors close with the tools and questions that may map them.
europmc-pmc9636149:
Min and Lee review molecular targeted therapy for cancer treatment and where it heads next. Such therapy began with approvals in the late 1990s. Small molecules and antibodies block signals that tumors need. The approach now anchors precision care for many cancers.

Targeted drugs often beat classic chemotherapy on balance. They hit cancer cells harder and spare patients many side effects. The review sorts agents by class and target kinase. Receptor kinase blockers lead the tour of drug types. EGFR, ALK, and MET blockers each get treatment. Drugs against BCR-ABL, BTK, and JAK follow in turn. RAS pathway and cell cycle drugs are also covered. Drug resistance is the chief flaw of the whole approach. The authors sum up plans to beat that resistance. Toxic effects and their handling close the account.
europmc-pmc9883449:
Chen and co-authors study how SOCS2 affects radiation response in hepatocellular carcinoma. Radioresistance is a main cause of radiotherapy failure in this liver cancer. Screening by RNA sequencing flagged SOCS2 as a candidate marker of response. The team then tested its role in cells and animals.

High SOCS2 levels raised radiation sensitivity in tumors. They also raised ferroptosis, an iron-linked form of cell death. SOCS2 bound the transporter SLC7A11 and marked it for breakdown by ubiquitination. Loss of SLC7A11 then drove lipid damage and cell death. Tumor tissues showed opposite patterns for the two proteins. The authors propose SOCS2 as a target to improve radiotherapy outcomes.
fielding-tom-jones-1749:
Henry Fielding published The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling in 1749, and it stands among the first great English novels. Fielding, a magistrate and playwright turned novelist, called it a comic epic in prose. Its plan is vast, balanced, and full of life.

Tom, a good-hearted foundling raised by Squire Allworthy, is turned out for scrapes and seeming baseness. His road to London crosses rogues, soldiers, inn brawls, and the lovely Sophia Western, while the prim villain Blifil schemes at home. Fielding's voice, wise and laughing, guides it all. The novel helped fix the form of English fiction itself.
frus-1861-d149:
From Paris on 29 August 1861, William Dayton closed the month with a report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 149 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton closed August with word from a Paris grown used to the war. The crisis mood had cooled into a watchful calm. His letter shows the French file settling into the long routine that would mark the rest of the year. A watchful calm in Paris was worth an army corps to the Union that autumn. Good value in a calm report is a theme the autumn file repeats with cause.
frus-1861-d249:
A dispatch dated 28 August 1861 carried word from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 249 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d49:
Writing to London on 3 June 1861, William H. Seward directed Charles Francis Adams on the summer's work. The letter is document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June orders from Seward pressed Adams to watch British shipyards and ports. Southern agents were already seeking ships and arms in Britain. The letter shows the contest moving to docks and yards, where quiet work by consuls and envoys could stop a warship before it sailed. Southern agents in London worked through ship brokers, which made the yards a front of the war. Quiet work in the yards saved more Union ships than any note could.
frus-1862-d149:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, sent word to Charles Francis Adams in London on 23 September 1862. Adams held the post of American minister to Britain. Their exchange is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, where this letter appears as Document 149.

The day before, Lincoln had made public his plan to free enslaved people in the rebel states. British leaders now had to weigh a war that was openly about slavery as well as union. Regular dispatches let Seward steer his envoy's talks in London while British opinion took shape in the proclamation's first days. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d249:
Dated 23 January 1862, Document 249 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, in the section given to France.

Late January found the allied move on Mexico under way and the American war entering its second calendar year. Seward kept Dayton on a short, steady leash of written orders, since a cable across the Atlantic did not yet exist. Letters like this one carried both policy and tone: firm on the war, careful not to provoke Paris. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d349:
On 11 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, in a letter printed as Document 349 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The catalog title gives the name as Merrier.

Seward wrote in the heart of the Trent crisis, when his handling of foreign envoys was being tested daily. France's minister mattered because Paris often moved in step with London on American questions. A letter to Mercier in that week was both business and signal: Washington meant to deal fairly with France while the British storm blew. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d449:
On 6 August 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Baron Friedrich von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. The note is Document 449 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote a fortnight after the Union defeat at Bull Run, when foreign ministers were recalculating the war's likely length. Gerolt, Prussia's veteran envoy, was a channel to one of Europe's friendlier courts. Notes of this kind kept resident ministers supplied with the government's view and handled the steady business between the two states. The letter is part of the 1861 foundation of the Prussian file, laid down while the war's shape was still unclear to everyone.
frus-1862-d49:
A State Department letter of 16 April 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 49 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d549:
On 30 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Roest van Limburg. It is Document 549 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward closed September with the Dutch file in good order, answering the minister's late-month notes in his prompt fashion. The emancipation order was now a week old, and its effects were beginning to reach the legations. Between the United States and the Netherlands the practical questions stayed what they had been: ships, trade, and the rules of neutrality. The note is a routine piece made interesting by its moment. Its writer knew the routine itself was a form of reassurance. Friendly powers took comfort from it.
frus-1862-d649:
On 24 May 1862, Robert H. Pruyn wrote from his post in Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 649 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn had lately succeeded Townsend Harris, the first American minister sent to Japan.

Letters from the Japan legation dealt with trade, the safety of Americans there, and the mood of the shogun's court. Pruyn's report is one of those working papers, not a speech or a treaty. It earns its place because the full run of such letters is the best record we have. It shows how the two lands dealt with each other in the 1860s.
frus-1863p1-d149:
The legation sent three letters on 9 April 1863; this one, from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, opens the set. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 149 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day in mid-April shows the post still at full stretch after the raider's seizure. Adams covered the yards, the law, and the talk of the town in his split sheets. This one opens the set of 9 April. The run of his April mail is a close record of the ship fight's turn, kept by the man who fought it from the legation.
frus-1863p1-d249:
An instruction dated 24 July 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 249 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d349:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 3 January 1863. It appears as document 349 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d449:
A letter of 6 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 449 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d49:
Stephen R. Mallory wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 26 October 1862. Mallory was the Confederate secretary of the navy; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 49 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The navy office's stake in London was ships. Southern buyers in Britain were having warships built in its yards, and Mason stood watch over that work. Mallory's letter belongs to that file, the sea side of the South's push abroad. Printed in the Union's record, it pairs with the Adams letters in the same volume, where the other side fought to stop those very ships.
frus-1863p1-d549:
The date 5 June 1863 heads a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d649:
The 26 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d149: Roosevelt wrote to King Farouk of Egypt on November 20, 1943, on the eve of the Cairo Conference in the king's capital. The letter is Document 149 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A courteous letter to a host king was standard summit manners, and Egypt's young king ruled the land where the leaders were about to meet. The record names the two men and the date. The text is printed in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d249:
The calls paid on President Roosevelt at Cairo on the afternoon of 22 November 1943 are covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No records of these conversations have been found, and the editors draw their account from the President's Log and from Admiral Leahy's diary.

Leahy records tea at Kirk Villa with the President, Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, Madame Chiang, General Marshall, and Harry Hopkins. Churchill's visit, the note says, presumably took place apart from the Chiangs' call. Nothing in the surviving evidence suggests that weighty problems were discussed at either visit, and the editors judge both to have been courtesy calls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d349:
Elmer Davis, director of the Office of War Information, sent Brendan Bracken, the British minister of information, a secret priority protest from Washington on 30 November 1943. Its subject is a Reuters dispatch from Lisbon that had given away the Cairo Conference a day before the official announcement.

Davis concedes that Reuters is a private firm beyond British government control, yet the dispatch was passed by British censorship for radio abroad while kept out of British papers. He lists the harms. First came a perilous breach of security. Then lost political value, since Germany and Japan could blanket the world with their own version first. Last came the fury of American reporters who had kept extraordinary secrecy. He calls the leak the worst of many such incidents and warns it could become a grave obstacle to Anglo-American understanding.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d449:
From December 5, 1943 comes this further agreed record of a United States-United Kingdom meeting at the Second Cairo Conference. Both delegations approved the wording, which makes agreed minutes one of the firmest kinds of evidence in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The conference was then in its final stretch.

Readers find the joint account of what the two governments put on record that day, while the military chiefs met in parallel and the Tehran pledges awaited detailed plans. Set beside the British and American minutes of the same date, this text lets a reader test one side's memory against the other's. That cross-checking is how sound summit history gets built.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d49: Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on October 21, 1943, from the Moscow Conference. His letter is Document 49 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull had traveled to Moscow for the first three-power meeting of foreign ministers, a trip few had expected the aging secretary to make. The record names the parties and the date. What Hull reported home must be read in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d549:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on January 19, 1944, in the continuing exchange between the department and the traveling summit's home base. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

By mid-January the questions flowing between Hull and Roosevelt included the follow-up to Tehran's pledges and the building of a postwar organization, Hull's great project. The Secretary's health and influence were both waning that year, but his channel to the President remained busy. For readers, the message shows routine at the top of wartime government: regular, formal, and carrying real decisions inside its courtesies.
frus-1944-quebec-d149:
General Wilson expanded his theater review for the War Department on September 8, 1944, in telegram Naf 774. The Dragoon transfer to Eisenhower was in hand, so the message concentrates on Italy and the Balkans. In Italy, Alexander's offensive had been running since August 26, and Wilson weighed two futures for Kesselring's army.

If the Fifth Army's coming offensive hammered the Germans before they could withdraw in order, Wilson foresaw decisive results and pursuit toward the Ljubljana Gap and Brenner Pass. If demolitions and bad weather covered an orderly retreat, only the Lombardy Plain could be cleared that year. In the Balkans he expected German forces trapped south of the Danube, and a small force stood ready to occupy Athens.
frus-1944-quebec-d249: An editors' note records a preparation that went unused. On September 13, 1944, Hull sent Roosevelt a memorandum on the shipment of arms to Ethiopia, so the president would be ready if Churchill raised the question at Quebec. The memorandum's text is printed in the 1944 Foreign Relations volume on Africa. No indication has been found that the subject was actually discussed by Roosevelt and Churchill at the conference.
frus-1944-quebec-d49:
Roosevelt replied to War Shipping Administrator Emory Land on September 2, 1944. The reply came the day after Land's message. The exchange appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

A presidential answer within a day shows urgent shipping business. Such business could not wait in a queue. Land's agency fed every theater and ally. Its allocations shaped what the Quebec Conference could promise. For readers, the pair brings a binding subject into view. Hulls and cargo space rarely draw attention. Without them, no strategy agreed in Canada could move. Not one division would have sailed.
frus-1945-50-intel-d149:
Dated 7 May 1946, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) to the President’s Chief of Staff. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 149, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d249:
A text titled "Report by an Ad Hoc Subcommittee of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee" bears the date 7 November 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 249 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Findings come first in a reader's eye, but the body of a report is where the proof sits, fact by fact. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. Subcommittee reports did the detailed work for the full committee, weighing facts and drafting the choices the main body would vote on.
frus-1945-50-intel-d349:
A memorandum dated 1 July 1948 was prepared for a named reader. The reader was the President of the Discussion at the 14th Meeting of the National Security Council. It is document 349 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d49:
Another paper prepared for the Secretary of State's Staff Committee is dated 26 November 1945. It follows the committee's 168th meeting by six days. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Committees consume papers the way furnaces consume coal, and a second staff paper in a week shows the intelligence question still burning at State. Drafters wrote these papers knowing the secretary's senior men would test every line. Readers can compare this paper with the one prepared on 15 November to see the department's thinking move. That movement, visible across the November run, is the sound of a bureaucracy closing in on its final ask.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d149:
British newspapers were blaming Washington for Mikolajczyk's fall, and Stettinius moved to correct them. His memorandum to the President of 28 November 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It encloses two telegrams, one on the premier's reasons for resigning and one quoting the London press.

A number of British papers, he reports, wrongly lay the resignation to an American refusal to guarantee Poland's frontiers. To counter the stories, the Department issued a statement on 25 November. A frontier guarantee, it said, was not and could not have been an issue. The government's long-standing policy of never guaranteeing set frontiers in Europe was well known, and it stood.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d249:
Roosevelt told Churchill on 4 October 1944 that the Soviet staff would see the allied plan for Japan. These excerpts of his telegram number 626 are printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The editors' note spells out what the plan asked of Russia.

American military men in Moscow, the President writes, will make the Joint Chiefs' statement to Stalin available to the prime minister. That statement set the missions for Soviet forces in a joint war. They were to secure the Trans-Siberian Railroad and the Vladivostok peninsula. Allied air forces would strike Japan from the Maritime Provinces and Kamchatka. Sea lanes between Japan and the mainland would be cut, Japanese forces in Manchuria destroyed, and the port of Petropavlovsk opened for American naval use.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d349:
Radios and newspapers carried this agreed text on February 7, 1945: the Crimean Conference's first word to the world. The release states that the three leaders, with their chiefs of staff and foreign secretaries, are meeting in the Black Sea area. Their aim is to finish the defeat of the common enemy and to build firm foundations for a lasting peace.

Meetings, it says, are going on without pause. The conference opened with military talks, a full review of every European front, and a complete exchange of information. Complete agreement for joint operations in the final phase is claimed. The text tells the public much, while naming neither Yalta nor a single decision.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d449:
Oil equipment stripped from Rumania's fields drives this British memorandum of February 10, 1945. London welcomed word that Soviet authorities had agreed to stop removing equipment from fields where British interests were involved. The Ruat plant, too, would remain in place. But much had already been taken.

If the removed equipment was not returned, London argued, it must count as deliveries on account of reparations. Compensation for the oil companies should be arranged. The Ruat plant should be restored to working order and brought back into production quickly. The memo shows reparations being fought over barrel by barrel, not just in billions.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d49: Roosevelt wrote back to Churchill on 9 January 1945, answering the prime minister on the day his letter came. Document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta preserves the reply, as published by the Office of the Historian. The rapid back-and-forth of that week shows two governments synchronizing their positions before meeting Stalin together in the Crimea.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d149:
President Truman replied to Ambassador Patrick Hurley in China in a top secret telegram dated June 4, 1945. The message is document 149 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hurley had sent frank reports on the military situation in China and on what he saw as the worldwide aims of America's European allies.

Truman thanks him for the candor and says the matters are getting full consideration in American planning. He has no official word that Britain wants command of the Chinese armies, he adds, and sees no gain in changing the present command setup in China. Many of Hurley's questions, he notes, may be taken up at the coming three-power conference. A note lists the questions: Hong Kong's future, trusteeship for Indochina, and support for democratic government in China.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d249:
Ambassador Tarchiani pleaded Italy's colonial case in a memorandum to President Truman dated July 6, 1945. The extract printed here is document 249 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The memorandum sets out the position, wishes, and hopes of the new Italian government.

Italy has willingly abandoned the Fascist dream of empire in East Africa, Tarchiani writes, though she spent more than 36 billion lire building modern systems there. Libya, he argues, is national territory, administered like Italy's home provinces. Eritrea and Somaliland are Italy's oldest colonies, where Italian capital and labor brought civilization, and their people, he claims, favor continued Italian rule. He asks that Italy's rights be recognized in some form that spares her modest African holdings and her national dignity in a moment of distress.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d349:
What the United States meant to achieve in Germany troubled a Central Secretariat paper of July 12, 1945. Marked SC-145, it suggests the Staff Committee send the Secretary a statement of views for the Berlin meeting. The aim was a clearer definition of the government's objective in occupying Germany. A draft by MacLeish is attached.

The draft states the problem bluntly. Signs suggested that no common agreement existed on the American purpose in the occupation. No full definition of purpose could be found in existing papers, and the directives for each phase of the occupation did not rest on one. The paper reached Secretary Byrnes at Babelsberg in revised form.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d449:
London's qualifications on Greek elections fill a British Embassy paper of July 10, 1945, paraphrasing a Foreign Office telegram of July 9. The proposal that invitations to the Soviet and French governments be issued by the Americans and British, not by the Greek government, is not strictly in line with the Varkiza Agreement. It might cause some resentment in Athens.

Nevertheless, the Foreign Office does not regard these objections as too serious. It is prepared to support President Truman's proposal, particularly as time is getting short. But it is strongly opposed to advising the Greek government to hold elections before the plebiscite. That, London argues, is Greek internal politics, to be settled by Greeks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d49:
Stalin confirmed the meeting date once more in a personal and secret message to President Truman on June 3, 1945. It is document 49 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, printed from the Truman Papers. Stalin had received Truman's message of June 1 and replied from Moscow two days later.

The message is only two sentences long. Stalin notes Truman's cable and repeats that he has already written that he agrees to July 15 as an entirely suitable date for the meeting of the three. With Germany defeated, that date set the timetable for the Potsdam Conference, where the Allies would take up the shape of postwar Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d549:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Truman a top secret memo on July 7, 1945. Signed by General George Marshall, it is document 549 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The subject was the sharp shortage of troop ships for the Pacific war.

The chiefs say General MacArthur's needs have grown, and deficits will last through late 1945. Seven captured passenger ships in European ports could carry 37,500 troops in all. The largest is the Europa, rated at 10,000 men. The chiefs urge Truman to ask the prime minister for all seven ships for U.S. troops. A draft letter to Churchill is attached, and the question of who ends up owning the ships is put off.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d649:
Lowell Pinkerton, the consul general at Jerusalem, sent a secret assessment of Palestine on July 10, 1945. It is document 649 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had asked what might follow an adverse British ruling on Jewish immigration.

Pinkerton cites the inspector general of police, who does not expect a general Jewish uprising. Large-scale illegal immigration, though, is predicted, and preparations in the Balkans are already reported. Terror attacks by the Stern group and the Irgun are expected against the British. Many in both the Jewish and Arab communities, he adds, are armed and some are well trained. The largest body, the Hagana, is well disciplined. It would act as a group only on its leaders' orders, if Arabs attacked after terrorist provocation.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1049:
William Clayton cabled Thomas Blaisdell in London on July 29, 1945, about the British decision to halt coal exports. Clayton had learned the War Cabinet adopted the working party's findings in substance. He urges that Britain be pressed hard to change course, and to keep shipping usable coal to Europe at the old rates.

America's own six million ton allocation for Europe will draw fire at home, he warns. Domestic heating shortages loom, and shipping and rail capacity are strained. If British exports stop at the same moment, the outcry will grow. Clayton argues Britain can still spare a quarter million tons a month for European relief, rather than shifting the whole burden to the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1149:
Deputy Prime Minister Mikolajczyk of Poland sent his third memorandum of the day on 24 July 1945. Three formal papers in a single day mark a rare burst of pleading. With the Big Three settling Poland's future in another land, he used every channel open to him.

Mikolajczyk spoke for the part of Poland's government that looked West. His papers asked the summit to hold the line on a free vote and fair borders. This third paper closes the day's set. After it, the summit moved on, and the Polish case rested on what paper could do. The trio survives as the high mark of Warsaw's lobbying.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1249:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Truman on 25 July 1945. The letter came from his last full day at the summit. The next day's count would make Attlee prime minister and send Churchill home, his war leadership at an end.

A direct exchange between the two leaders was the top level of wartime dealing. Churchill's letters to Truman mixed business with the warmth of a shared fight. This one closes the day's pair, matching the president's note to him. Whatever its errand, it passed between partners at the hour their partnership ended, and the record keeps it in that light.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1349:
On 16 July 1945 the acting secretary of state wrote to Norman Armour, the American ambassador in Spain. The message left Washington on the day before the Potsdam Conference opened. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Spain stood apart from the war's endgame, ruled by Franco and watched with suspicion by the victors. An ambassador there needed clear guidance on how far to go with a regime the Allies disliked but had to handle. This instruction shows the department tending a hard post at a busy hour, and it widens the volume's map beyond the summit grounds in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-149:
Dated July 31, 1945, this delegation memorandum came on the last full day of the Potsdam Conference. Staff wrote through the final hours to ready the closing texts. The memo was kept with the American papers and printed in the second Potsdam volume. It carries the mark of the conference's third numbered memorandum set for that date.

Papers from the final day have an end-of-work feel. Options have narrowed to choices. Writers focus on exact words and clear tasks. Readers can feel the nearness of the finish in the memo's direct style. It forms a small but true part of how the settlement got written.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-49:
Thompson's minutes record the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon, with Byrnes in the chair. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The first business was fixing a date for the Council of Foreign Ministers.

Byrnes proposed that the council meet not later than September 1. Molotov asked what day of the week that would be, and Eden answered that it was a Sunday. Molotov said he agreed, and the date was settled in those terms. The talk then turned to the council's composition. Molotov asked if five members were meant, noting that composition would decide what questions the council could take up. Byrnes answered that the first meeting, in London, would be of five. It would formally set up the council and decide its procedure there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d749:
Grew wrote to Byrnes from Washington on July 25, 1945, in document 749. The Acting Secretary kept his chief informed through the conference's second week. His letters mixed news, warnings, and the state of opinion at home. This one entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A deputy's mid-conference letter has a steadying role. It reminds the travelers that a government still runs behind them. Readers see Grew guarding the home front of policy. The document also shows how much the summit depended on trust between two men. Byrnes could bargain freely because Grew held Washington firm.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d849:
Henry Stimson wrote to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945, in document 849. The Secretary of War addressed his cabinet colleague as the Potsdam Conference opened. Stimson's letters that summer carried the war's heaviest questions. This one entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A Stimson letter to Byrnes joined the two departments that owned the peace's making. War and State had to move together or not at all. Readers see that partnership in formal, careful prose. The document opens the conference with the cabinet's senior voice. It reminds readers that Potsdam's table sat inside a government, not above one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d949:
Luther Gulick, an adviser on Pauley's reparations staff, sent him this undated memorandum, filed with the July 29, 1945 papers. It gathers new evidence on Soviet removals from Berlin. Three fresh reports are listed. One covers factory removals in the Russian sector. One covers art removals from the American sector. One covers property of American citizens and neutrals.

The new material reports raw materials, scrap, and cable machinery being taken in the Russian sector, even household sewing machines. Berlin's public art collections had been stored for safety, many in the zoo flak tower. The reports say the distinctive and valuable pieces were picked out and removed.
frus-1964-68v26-d149:
An intelligence memorandum dated October 6, 1965, and numbered OCI No. 2330/65, reports on the upheaval in Indonesia. It is document 149 in Volume XXVI of the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. The memo says the army has countered a leftist coup attempt of October 1. It puts the army, for now, firmly in control. It expects the army to move against the Indonesian Communist Party, but only with care.

The text recounts the kidnapping and murder of six generals by the 30 September Movement. It notes President Sukarno's wish to settle the crisis himself, as a political matter. The memo weighs whether Sukarno will shield the Communists or yield to the army.
gao-gaoreports-b-295449:
In GAO ruling B-295449 and B-295449.2, dated March 2, 2005, Abt Associates Inc. was the protester. The Centers for Disease Control had awarded the National Opinion Research Center a contract to plan and run health-related surveys. Abt attacked the scoring of both technical offers and of the winner's costs. GAO denied the protest. On talks, the firm was not hurt by the flaws alleged. Extra credit on the points raised would still leave its technical offer below the winner's. The winner's cost was also far lower.

On the merits, the firm's first offer lacked detail on key staff skills and consultant availability. Its revised offer still fell short.
gao-gaoreports-b-297849:
TVI Corporation protested an Army award for filter canisters in GAO decision B-297849, dated April 19, 2006. The winner was 3M Canada Company. The goods were C2A1 filter units for gas masks. They are key life safety parts. The firm hit past work marks and a small firm mark. Both marks were scored wrong, it said.

GAO sustained the protest. The firm had sent much past work data. Most was found old or off point. The call said such a case gets an unknown risk mark. The agency gave a mid risk mark in its place. That swap was wrong. The winner's small firm mark was also wrong. It met no test for a neutral mark and gave no real plan.
gao-gaoreports-b-298349:
PAI Corporation protested a NASA award for safety and health work in GAO decision B-298349, dated August 18, 2006. The winner was Consolidated Safety Services. The site was Ames Research Center. Work held job safety, plant hygiene, and medical help. The firm claimed bias. It also hit marks and talks on weak spots.

GAO denied the protest. No proof of bias was in the record. Marks fit the stated tests and were sound. Points the firm said should have been in talks were aired well or were not key flaws. Key flaws are what talks must air. Minor points need not be raised. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298949:
Caddell Construction Company, Inc. protested a Department of State award for a new embassy compound. The site was Djibouti, in eastern Africa. The contract went to American International Contractors (Special Projects), Inc. GAO ruled in B-298949 on January 10, 2007.

A 1986 security law limits such work to United States persons. The agency cleared the winner on a joint venture theory. It treated the firm as linked in fact to its parent. Yet the firm had sworn it was no such venture, formal or in fact. The agency's call clashed with that sworn word. Its clearance could not stand on that base. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-305349:
Public polls by the Social Security Administration are at issue in this GAO decision, B-305349, dated December 20, 2005. The agency hired the Gallup Organization to survey the public. The polls asked what people know of Social Security. They also asked what people know of plans to reform it. Six rounds of polls ran from 1998 through 2004.

The legal question was whether the hire broke 5 U.S.C. section 3107. That law bars the use of funds to hire a publicity expert. GAO held there was no breach. For this work, Gallup was not a publicity expert under the law. The agency's power to run the program also gave it power to poll. The ruling helps agencies judge when survey work stays lawful.
gao-gaoreports-b-306349:
A syndicated newspaper article is the subject of this GAO letter, B-306349, dated September 30, 2005. The Education Department worked through the firm Ketchum, Inc. Ketchum hired the North American Precis Syndicate to write the piece. The piece praised science classes in schools. It ran in many small papers and flyers across the country.

The piece named no role for the department in its writing. GAO's past rulings bar that gap. Work made at the government's call must not hide its source. GAO treated the hidden source as covert propaganda. That broke the ban on such use of funds. The letter adds one more breach to the same contract file.
gao-gaoreports-b-307849:
A fee paid back to a pension agency may not be kept in this GAO decision, B-307849, dated March 1, 2007. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation did study work for a large firm. The work tied to a plea to waive claims under the pension law. The firm paid the agency back for the study cost. The agency asked if it could keep the cash.

GAO held that it could not. The sum was not a gift the agency could take. No law lets the agency charge for this work and keep the fee. Cash got for the government must go to the Treasury. The firm must be told the sum goes there, not to agency funds.
gao-gaoreports-b-400049:
Barnesville Development Corporation lost its protest. GAO decided B-400049 on June 30, 2008. The General Services Administration sought office space in Melbourne, Florida. The space would house a Social Security office. The call set a floor shape rule for the space. The floor could be no more than twice as long as wide. The firm's block broke that shape rule on its face.

GAO denied the protest. The toss of the bid was fair on the call's terms. A layout clause did not waive the shape rule. The two clauses can be read to stand side by side. Terms that can both stand must both be heeded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-249:
Capital Financing, GAO-05-249 of April 8, 2005, weighs a new way to pay for big federal builds. A capital fund, as drawn, would spread a build's cost through yearly budgets. That spread could smooth the spikes that big builds cause. It would keep the rule that full cost is pledged up front. Two test cases, at Agriculture and Interior, ground the study.

GAO shows how such funds would run in real life. It weighs their gains and their snags. It names simpler paths to the same gains, per the title. It closes with points to weigh before any fund is built, drawn from budget experts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-349:
Military Personnel, GAO-05-349 of April 26, 2005, is the mate study on loans that prey on troops. A harsh loan hides its sting in fees, traps, or lies. Such debt can sink a troop's credit and career, and sap a unit's will. The Pentagon holds tools to fight back. Off-limits lists can bar a bad shop from a base. Classes can warn troops off bad deals.

GAO asks how many troops on duty hold such loans. It asks if the tools are used in full, by the Pentagon and by troops. They are not, the title finds. Dormant tools leave the prey path open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1049:
Chesapeake Bay gateways and their grants are audited in GAO-06-1049, a report from September 14, 2006. A 1998 law built a linked network of parks, ports, and museums where the public can reach the bay. The Park Service backs the sites with grants. In 2005, Congress raised doubts about its management. GAO tested how sites are picked, what grants fund, and what fixes are under way.

Headings state the findings. The criteria for picking gateways are not always transparent. They may not be applied in a consistent way. Most grants reviewed funded interpretation of the bay and access to it. Thirty-nine gateways drew multiple grants for those aims. The Park Service has not yet judged whether the grants meet program goals. It has taken steps to manage grants better, GAO found. Oversight and accountability weaknesses remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-149:
Disability claims processing and the offices that handle it are studied in GAO-06-149, dated December 9, 2005. The Veterans Benefits Administration runs compensation and pension claims through a field office network. Senate leaders asked GAO to review efforts to reshape that network. Years of backlogs and uneven service drive the push for change. GAO catalogued the realignment steps taken so far. It then asked whether deeper changes could lift performance further.

The report weighs how work is spread across offices. Some offices carry loads that fit their staff poorly. Moving claims to offices with spare capacity or special skill could speed decisions. GAO tested that logic against the record of past realignments. Any new structure must guard quality as well as speed. The study gives Congress options for a system that veterans judge by how fast and how fairly it answers them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-349:
A Marine vehicle meant to swim to shore and fight on land was in trouble. GAO's May 1, 2006 report, GAO-06-349, reviews the Expeditionary Fighting Vehicle. The vehicle would replace the current amphibious assault craft. It was the Corps' top ground system priority. It took 25.5 percent of the Corps' buying budget for fiscal years 2006 through 2011.

GAO tracked cost, schedule, and performance in design work. It also weighed the causes of the strain and the risks ahead. The title states the core result plainly. The program met hard problems in design demonstration. It faced more risk as it neared production. Readers get a clear early warning on a major weapon buy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-449:
Small, quick satellites were meant to give field commanders space help sooner. Dated March 14, 2006, GAO-06-449 reviews tactical space work at the Defense Department. Commanders had reported shortfalls in space capability despite heavy investment. The department began building TacSats, small satellites made within tight time and cost limits. It also sought small, low-cost launch vehicles for them.

GAO checked results to date for both efforts. It named the challenges they face. It asked whether lessons could inform major space buys. GAO said the department needs a department-wide strategy. Readers get early results on a new approach to space.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-49:
Drone aircraft work best when services can share data, controls, and lessons. In GAO-06-49 (December 13, 2005), GAO reviews unmanned aircraft systems. Such a system joins an aircraft, payloads, and ground controls. Demand from U.S. forces is high and rising. The Defense Department is investing more and often fields systems still in development. Past GAO work warned of interoperability problems that could hurt joint operations.

GAO reviewed how these systems performed in recent joint operations. It judged the soundness of the department's approach to grading joint performance. More effective promotion of interoperability is needed, GAO said. Better performance checks are also needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-649:
Federal foster care and adoption funds are reviewed in GAO-06-649, a GAO report dated June 15, 2006. The programs help states care for children who cannot stay safely at home and support adoptions. Federal spending was estimated to rise from about $6 billion in fiscal year 2003 to $8 billion in fiscal year 2008. Lawmakers worried about how much of that growth came from state administrative costs.

GAO found that spending on administrative costs had grown, but weak data limited analysis of what drove it. State spending shifted with staffing, caseloads, and claiming practices, and the effect on services was unclear. GAO said oversight by the Department of Health and Human Services lacked a strategic, risk-based focus. Stronger oversight would safeguard funds and support states more evenly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-149:
Train wrecks have killed fewer people since 1980, but the accident rate stopped falling a decade ago. GAO examined rail safety oversight in GAO-07-149, issued January 26, 2007. The Federal Railroad Administration writes safety rules and inspects railroads. A wreck in Graniteville, South Carolina, killed 9 people and injured 292. GAO asked how the agency targets its work and judges its own impact.

The agency was aiming its oversight at the top risks, GAO found. Its action plan targets the two main causes of wrecks: human error and bad track. Inspectors now use data models to pick sites likely to have problems. New rules and track inspection vehicles were also in motion. But most steps were not fully in place yet. Their effect on safety would take years to show. GAO said the agency still lacked measures of what its inspections achieve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-49:
New drug output has stalled even as research budgets climb, and GAO-07-49, dated November 17, 2006, asks why. Before a drug reaches market, the Food and Drug Administration must approve a new drug application packed with test data. Hopes ran high that science gains would yield more breakthrough drugs. Yet new molecular entities, drugs with never-marketed ingredients, had gone flat.

GAO studied every one of the 1,264 applications filed from 1993 through 2004. It weighed spending trends against filing and approval counts. It then asked experts what slows the pipeline. They named science hurdles, business calls, patent fights, and rule burdens. Their fix ideas range from better early science to clearer review paths. The report gives Congress a fact base for a debate that mixes health, profit, and risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-549:
Winning the peace after the war is a skill the Pentagon is still building, and GAO-07-549, dated May 31, 2007, grades the effort. Stability and rebuilding missions since the Cold War often run 5 to 8 years. They can cost more lives and money than the combat phase. A 2005 presidential directive told the Defense and State departments to weave stability work into war plans.

GAO reviewed plans at three combatant commands and read the policy stack. The department had a stated approach but thin follow-through. It had not pinned down which skills its forces need for such missions. Measures to judge success were also vague. Joint planning with civilian agencies lagged the directive's call. Lessons from Bosnia, Kosovo, Afghanistan, and Iraq were applied unevenly. GAO urged clear skill lists and firm measures, so the next mission starts from knowledge, not improvisation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-349:
Army Corps of Engineers land records are examined in GAO report GAO-08-349, issued May 9, 2008. The Corps, the fourth largest federal landholder, logs its civil works land in the Real Estate Management Information System (REMIS). GAO tested whether REMIS gave sound data on land disposals from fiscal years 1996 through 2006.

GAO found the disposal data unreliable, as were the records of land held as of September 30, 2006. In two of four districts checked, the same person entered disposal data and checked it, a basic control failure. The system's design also let users pull inconsistent results for the same query. GAO recommended tighter controls, a redesign of the disposal module, clearer guidance, and user training. The Department of Defense agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-49:
With its report GAO-08-49, dated November 16, 2007, GAO turns to Women's Business Centers. The centers train and counsel women who run businesses, with a focus on those facing social and economic disadvantage. In fiscal year 2007, the Small Business Administration funded 99 centers.

Funding for the centers long carried a hard stop: after 10 years, a center was meant to stand on its own. In May 2007, Congress allowed renewable 3-year awards for graduated centers and current ones. Oversight lags, GAO found, since district staff who watch the centers carry many other duties and may lack the right skills. Poor communication left some centers unsure of program rules. GAO also gives guidance to cut overlap with two sister programs, the Small Business Development Center and SCORE programs. The agency gave no comments on the draft.
gdr-constitution-1949:
The German Democratic Republic adopted its first constitution in October 1949, founding East Germany out of the Soviet occupation zone. The text was approved days before the state itself was proclaimed, as Germany split into two rival republics. Its drafters modeled parts of it on the Weimar charter, in the hope of claiming all-German legitimacy.

On paper, the charter promises a democratic republic with free elections, basic rights, and a parliament of the people. In fact, the Socialist Unity Party, backed by Soviet power, ruled without real opposition from the start. The founding law of the workers' and peasants' state thus wore a democratic form over a Leninist reality. A new constitution in 1968 dropped the pretense and named the party's leading role outright. The 1949 text closed the founding act of socialism's forty-year German experiment.
geneva-convention-1-1949:
The first of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protects wounded and sick soldiers in armies on land. Nations redrafted the rules in Geneva after the Second World War, building on a line of agreements going back to 1864. The aim was to make sure that a soldier out of the fight through wounds or sickness is never treated as fair game.

The articles require armies to collect and care for the wounded of both sides, without favor. Medical staff, ambulances, and hospitals are protected, and the red cross emblem marks that protection. Attacking the wounded or those who care for them is forbidden. Nearly every nation on earth has accepted the 1949 conventions.
geneva-convention-2-1949:
The second Geneva Convention of 1949 carries the protection of the wounded to warfare at sea. It adapts the older Hague rules and the land convention to sailors, marines, and others fighting on the water. Two world wars had shown how exposed the wounded and shipwrecked were when ships went down far from help.

Under its articles, the wounded, sick, and shipwrecked at sea must be rescued and cared for by whichever side finds them. Hospital ships are protected from attack and capture, and their crews must be respected. The convention also covers coastal rescue craft and medical aircraft over the sea. Together with its three sister conventions, it forms the core of modern war law.
geneva-convention-3-1949:
Prisoners of war are the subject of the third Geneva Convention of 1949. Written after a war in which prisoners had been starved and murdered in great numbers, it sets firm limits on captors. The text builds on earlier prisoner rules from 1929 that had too often been ignored.

Captured fighters must be treated with respect, given enough food and shelter, and shielded from insults and public display. They may send and receive mail, and the Red Cross may visit their camps. Torture and medical experiments are banned outright. When the fighting ends, prisoners must be sent home without delay, a standard still cited in every modern conflict.
geneva-convention-4-1949:
Civilians in wartime gained their own full shield in the fourth Geneva Convention of 1949. Earlier war law had guarded soldiers and prisoners, while civilians in occupied lands were left with thin protection. The deportations and mass killings of the Second World War made the gap impossible to ignore.

The articles ban murder, torture, hostage-taking, and collective punishment against civilians under an army's control. Forced deportation from occupied land is forbidden, and children, the sick, and the wounded get special care. Occupying powers must keep food and medical supplies flowing to the people under their rule. The convention remains the main legal guard for civilians caught in modern wars.
german-basic-law-1949:
West Germany adopted its Basic Law in May 1949, written by a Parliamentary Council at Bonn. The drafters avoided the word constitution, since the country was divided and the law was meant to be temporary. Its lessons came straight from the Nazi years: never again a republic too weak to defend itself, never again a state above human dignity.

The text opens by declaring human dignity beyond all touch, the clause every other article serves. Power is split between the federation and the states, and the charter arms democracy against its foes, banning parties that seek to destroy it. A powerful constitutional court guards the whole design. The charter of the Federal Republic's economic and moral recovery still governs united Germany today, its temporary name now a badge of permanence.
haddock-somnolism-psycheism-1849:
Joseph Haddock lectured on mesmeric clairvoyance in Somnolism and Psycheism, first printed in 1849. His titles name the states he studies: somnolism, the mesmeric sleep, and psycheism, its mental wonders. Haddock treats clairvoyance as a subject for physiology and philosophy alike. An appendix adds mesmeric and psychical experiments of his circle.

Haddock worked in Bolton, far from London's learned societies. His book gives the movement a provincial English voice of real weight. His case reports rest on sittings with entranced subjects from his own circle. The lectures argue that the soul's powers show themselves in trance. Readers meet mesmerism as small town practice and print. The first edition holds his case entire.
hahnemann-organon-1849:
Samuel Hahnemann was a German doctor who broke with the harsh cures of his day. His Organon of Medicine lays out the scheme he called homeopathy. Charles Dudgeon's English dress of 1849 brought the work to British readers. The book is the root text of the whole school.

Like cures like, Hahnemann holds: a drug that makes a sign in health can cure that sign in the sick. He bids the doctor use the least dose that can still act. Rules for case work and drug tests fill the text. Homeopaths still treat the book as law.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol1-1749:
David Hartley, an English physician, published the first volume of Observations on Man in 1749. The title promises a study of man's frame, his duty, and his hopes. Hartley aimed at nothing less than a full science of the mind built from two simple tools: vibrations in the nerves and the association of ideas.

Volume 1 lays out the theory that all thought grows from linked sensations. Simple impressions join into complex ideas, feelings, and habits through repeated pairing. The scheme made the mind look like a machine of habit, which thrilled some readers and alarmed others. James Mill and later psychologists built on Hartley's foundation, and the book stands as the founding work of association psychology.
hartley-observations-on-man-vol2-1749:
The second volume of Hartley's Observations on Man appeared in 1749 with the first, completing his great system. Hartley was a physician who wanted one theory to cover body, mind, and faith. Volume 1 had set out his psychology of association; the second half puts that psychology to work.

Volume 2 applies the laws of association to religion and morals. Duty, hope, prayer, and the expectation of a life to come are all explained through the linking of ideas and feelings. Hartley, a devout man, meant the system to strengthen faith, not to dissolve it. The result is psychology in the service of religion, unusual for its age. Together the two volumes founded the associationist school that shaped British thought about the mind for a century.
heart-sutra-muller-sbe49:
A few hundred words hold the core of Mahayana Buddhism in the Heart Sutra. The Heart Sutra, in the English rendering of Friedrich Max Müller from 1894, gives that core text in full. Müller's version stood in the Sacred Books of the East, the great Victorian shelf of world faiths.

The sutra says form is emptiness and emptiness is form, and sweeps away each prop the mind would clutch. Monks and lay folk chant it daily from Tibet to Japan. Its end is a mantra that promises passage to the far shore of waking. No Buddhist text so short carries so much weight.
herodian-history-hart-1749:
Herodian lived through the wild years he writes about. His History, finished around 238 CE, tells the Roman Empire from the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 to the rise of Gordian III. J. Hart turned it into English in 1749, and he added an appendix that carries the story on to Constantine.

Eight books hold Commodus on the throne, the year of five emperors, the Severan house, and the chaos of the third century. Herodian writes as a minor official who saw courts at close range. His tale is vivid, moral, and often sharp. For these years he is one of the few full sources that survive.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Volume 7 of In the Fire of the Forge, by Georg Ebers, lets the Ortlieb sisters leave the Town Hall with glad news. Ebers wraps Els and Eva in white head cloths that hide their faces, then lets them watch old Herr Vorchtel cross the square on the arm of the young burgomaster. A city clerk shares a piece of gossip meant to please them both in this volume.

Chapter X reports that Ursula Vorchtel is engaged to the talented young merchant walking with her father. The match will help the old man and his younger son run their large business. Even in deep mourning, Ursula looks out at the world again like a happy girl. Better still, the reproach that spoiled so many hours for the sisters now stands removed. Private relief and a neighbor's engagement close the hearing day on a rare bright note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-mari-ben-e:
Abba Mari ben Eligdor, also called Senior Astruc de Noves, was a noted Talmudist, thinker, and student of physics and the stars. He flourished in the fourteenth century in Salonica, and by 1335 he was already very old. He wrote on the Pentateuch, on Job, on parts of the Talmud, and on science and logic. Only bits of his work survive, and those in manuscript.

His work on Job is a study of why the good suffer, not a plain verse-by-verse reading. In it, Job's four friends stand for four views of evil. One denies evil is real, one looks to reward in the life to come, and one pleads man's ignorance of God's will. The entry counts Abba Mari a loyal student of Maimonides. His book of Refutations against Joseph Caspi has since been lost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aberdeen-scotla: Aberdeen is the chief city of northern Scotland and the capital of Aberdeenshire. Jews, the entry says, have only lately settled in the city. Its one synagogue, at 34 Marischal street, was founded in 1893. Six years later the whole Jewish population came to seventeen families. Of those families, no fewer than twenty-three persons held seats in the synagogue. That small set of facts, drawn from a Jewish year-book of 1899, is the whole of this short city notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abolafio-juan-f: Juan Fernandez Abolafio was a Marano of Seville in the fifteenth century. He worked hard to keep the Inquisition out of Seville in 1480. That effort cost him his life at the stake. He was a learned man who served for years as alcalde de justicia, a criminal judge. He also farmed the royal taxes. The entry rests on two Spanish histories of the Jews in Spain, and gives no birth date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-acre-called-als:
Acre is a city and port of Phenicia. It sits on a point of land at the foot of Mount Carmel. In 1901 it held about 9,800 people, a few of them Jews. Egyptian texts name it about 1500 B.C. as A-ka. Asher claimed the town but could not take it. Sennacherib took Akkú in 701 B.C. and gave it to the king of Sidon.

As a port on a coast with few harbors, Acre held great weight in war. It served as a base in the Maccabean wars. Jonathan the Maccabee was killed there by treachery. Rome made it a colony under Claudius. The Arabs took it in 668. In Crusader days it rose to its peak. It was a seat of the Latin kingdom and of the Knights of St. John, who called it St. Jean d'Acre. Later notes mark its stand against Bonaparte in 1799.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-sar-ha-bira:
Aha Sar ha-Birah, called "Castellan," was a Palestinian amora of the third generation, in the fourth century. He was a contemporary of Tanhum b. Hiyya of Kefar Acco. No ruling or doctrine of his own is recorded in the Talmud. Instead, he reported several Halakot and precedents for others.

His standing seems to have let him help less fortunate fellow Jews. Once, with Tanhum's aid, he ransomed Jewish captives brought to Tiberias. He is also said to have laid Halakot before the sages at Usha twice. Usha, a former seat of the Sanhedrin, still drew learned Jews in his day. The entry notes, though, that the reporter in those cases may have been a tanna of the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akron-ohio-1049:
Akron, Ohio, is the capital of Summit county, forty miles from Cleveland. Jews first settled there in 1850. The Akron Hebrew Congregation, a Reform body, was organized on April 2, 1865. It was incorporated on September 16, 1866, and bought its burial-ground the same day. Its present synagogue was acquired in April 1885 and dedicated that August.

The entry lists the congregation's rabbis and the town's Jewish societies. They include a benevolent Schwesterbund from 1865 and a literary Montefiore Society from 1883. An Orthodox congregation bought a lot for its own synagogue in 1900. Of about 50,000 people in Akron, 225 families were Jewish. Their trades ran from merchant and lawyer to cigarmaker, foundryman, and bookkeeper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-of-mi:
Alexander of Miletus is known as Polyhistor, for the sheer number of his writings. He flourished between 105 and 40 B.C. His subjects ran from geography and history to grammar and philosophy. His book "Upon the Jews" survives only in fragments. Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria preserved them. The work was a string of excerpts from Jewish, Samaritan, and heathen writers on early Jewish history.

The entry calls him a compiler with no taste or judgment. Yet his scrapbook has real value. Whole authors are known to later ages only through his extracts. Among them are the epic poet Philo and the tragedian Ezekiel. Eupolemus, Demetrius, Artapanus, and Aristeas stand in the same debt. Even the anti-Jewish rhetorician Molon survives in his pages. Josephus and Eusebius both drew on the work. Alexander did make plain errors: he wrote that a woman named Moso gave the Jews their Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alkan-alphonse-:
Alphonse Alkan, called Alkan the elder, was a French printer and writer. He was born in Paris in 1809. He died at Neuilly-sur-Seine in 1889. He began as a working printer. He then wrote for trade journals on printing. Later he served as secretary to the Count de Clarac. Clarac kept the Museum of Antiquities at the Louvre.

His books deal with the craft and past of printing. One book treats women who set type in 1794. One gives lives of portrait engravers in France. One tells the past of the Paris book trade. Shorter works take up book foes and book labels. The entry lists his chief books with their years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amado-joshua-ju: Joshua Judah Amado was a Talmudist of Spanish stock. His family had settled at Salonica. He worked early in the nineteenth century. He wrote a book called the Tents of Judah. It came out at Salonica in 1820. The book holds two kinds of matter. One part gives sermons on the Pentateuch. The other part gives legal talks on Maimonides. A short tract and a set of diet laws are added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anacletus-ii-pi:
Anacletus II was an antipope who held Rome for eight years. His true name was Pietro Pierleoni. He stood against Innocent II from 1130 to 1138. His line traced back to a Jewish forebear. That fact drew slurs on him all his life. Voltaire in jest called him the Jewish Pope.

His forebear Baruch grew rich as a lender in Rome. On taking the Christian faith he took the name Benedict. His house rose high at the papal court. Anacletus was picked as pope by one Rome faction. Most of Europe backed his rival in the schism. Rome stood by him to the last, the entry notes. Base tales of theft and worse were spread by his foes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anna-1549: Anna was a daughter of Rabbi Eleazar of Worms. She lived at Erfurt. The entry, only a few lines long, records that Crusaders killed her there as a martyr on December 6, in 1213 or 1214. Her mother, Dolce, and her sister, Bellette, met the same fate. It gives no account of her life beyond her family and her death, and it cites Kayserling's work on Jewish women for the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apollonius-of-t:
Apollonius of Tyana was a Pythagorean philosopher and worker of wonders, born about the year 3 B.C. Some sources, the entry notes, give him a death at only thirty-eight years of age. In Arabic writing his name appears as Balinas or Belenus, a form often mistaken for Pliny.

Arabs called him the Author of Talismans and credited him with a work on the sway of spirit powers over the world of sense. A warning at the end of one translation calls the whole book worthless, copied only to guard readers against strange gods. The entry traces copies of the work in later Jewish libraries and catalogs, and weighs which magical writings truly bear his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arendt-otto-174:
Otto Arendt was a German economist, author, and member of the Prussian Diet, born in Berlin on October 10, 1854. He took his doctorate at Berlin University and entered a literary career with the ultraconservative side of Prussia. He led the cause of bimetalism and protective tariffs, and of policies that kept Prussia's quasi-feudal remains.

So firm was his loyalty, the entry says, that he left his religion, took Christianity, and at times used anti-Semitic phrases. He edited the Deutsche Wochenblatt and wrote many books, from a work on treaty double currency in 1878 to one on the fall of silver in 1899. His handbook of currency policy ran through seventeen editions. His wife Olga taught elocution and wrote tales for the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkelon-1949:
Ashkelon, a city on the southern coast of Palestine, appears in Egyptian texts as Askaruni among the cities rising against Rameses II and Meneptah.
