Beneath those different tools, the authors find a shared aim at the level of the whole task: keeping the body upright and moving safely. The distinction matters for fall prevention and rehabilitation, since training that improves standing still may not transfer to walking. Their analysis gives therapists a cleaner picture of what to train for each.
plos-pone-0356149:
Hao Dun, Maura Sticco-Ivins, Gianni Bonnici, Hannah Beatty, and Benjamin Kopecky wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It presents a surgical technique for transplanting the aorta in mice. Their method uses a single aortotomy, one opening cut in the aorta, in an end-to-side connection.

Mouse aortic transplants are a standard model for studying vessel disease and rejection, but the surgery is delicate and slow. A simpler technique can make experiments more consistent between surgeons and labs. Cardiovascular researchers who run transplant models in mice are the readers who would adopt or test this shortcut.
plos-pone-0356249:
David J. Varricchio and Heath R. Caldwell published a 2026 paleontology paper in PLOS ONE describing the pelvis and hindlimbs of a troodontid dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Two Medicine Formation of Montana. Troodontids, small feathered relatives of birds, are usually known from scraps, so a growth series from embryo to adult is rare. The Flagg Butte material gives an almost full picture of this stretch of the skeleton for the animal they assign, following recent proposals, to Troodon formosus.

Bone shape stayed remarkably consistent across growth: most adult landmarks appear in the young, the real changes being robustness, fusion, and surface texture at predictable stages. Many foot bones showed pathology, a recurring oddity in troodontid samples the authors document rather than hide. Because growth changes so little anatomy, immature specimens elsewhere can be judged taxonomically with more confidence, strengthening study of large North American troodontids.
plos-pone-0356549:
Sydney F. Hope and coauthors published a 2026 animal cognition study in PLOS ONE testing whether Asian elephants can control an impulse, a basic executive skill. Sixteen elephants at Thailand's National Elephant Institute learned to reach around an opaque box to take food from a side opening. Then came a transparent box with tempting front holes, where success meant ignoring visible food straight ahead and reaching around, as before.

The elephants detoured around the see-through box about as well as the opaque one. That may show strong self-control, or the see-through cues may simply have been too weak to tempt them, and the authors hold both readings open. When the box flipped so the learned direction was wrong, hesitation jumped, proof a real habit had to be overridden, and performance recovered quickly across trials. Elephants now join the comparative map of how inhibition evolves.
plos-pone-0357049:
Mariam Adam Al-Hassan, Jodie Bigalky, and Solina Richter set out a protocol, published in 2026. It will map what helps or hinders pregnant women with dangerous blood pressure disorders. The focus is getting care in poorer countries. These disorders are leading killers of mothers and babies. Delays in seeking help are often the difference between a managed case and an emergency.

The team follows established scoping review methods. It has completed searching and screening the literature. It is now extracting findings on barriers and facilitators. These range from cost and distance to beliefs and clinic failures. No results are reported yet. The finished map is meant to show governments and clinics where the path to care breaks down. Fixes can then target the real obstacles.
plos-pone-0358049:
Yi He published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on spotting deepfakes, manipulated images and videos that fool viewers, without needing labeled fakes for training. Most detectors learn from collections of marked forgeries and still miss subtle edits. He's framework, SDDA, trains itself instead, comparing each image in two domains at once: its ordinary appearance and its frequency pattern, which records fine repeating detail.

Two encoders extract features from both views and an alignment step forces them to agree, while four custom measures flag inconsistencies in the learned features. A contrastive objective sharpens the separation between normal and odd patterns, and the author reports the system stayed robust under compression and lighting changes that often defeat detectors. In the reported experiments it beat leading baselines, especially on manipulation types it had never seen. The design aims at an interpretable detector that does not depend on huge labeled fake collections.
plos-pone-0358349:
Bahetibieke Tuohetaerbaike and colleagues charted in 2026 the course of tuberculosis across China and its Central Asian neighbors, looking back to 1990 and forward to 2050. Tuberculosis remains one of the world's great infectious killers, and this region carries a heavy and uneven share of it. The team analyzed trends in the disease burden across more than three decades of data.

They also weigh the drivers behind the trends and project where the burden is heading by mid century under current patterns. Projections like these let health ministries see whether control programs are on pace and where drug resistant disease threatens progress. The regional view matters because tuberculosis crosses the borders that the region's people cross daily.
plos-pone-0358449:
Monika Talarowska-Dublicka, Aleksandra Gapińska, and Maria Finogenow studied the roots of loneliness in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They linked primal emotional systems, the deep drives wired into the brain long before language, to the modern sense of loneliness. Between the two sit early maladaptive schemas, lasting patterns formed in childhood.

The team's model traces how deep emotional wiring can harden into adult isolation through those schemas. That chain suggests where therapy might intervene: not only on lonely behavior, but on the schemas carrying the effect. Loneliness is now treated as a health risk in its own right. Work that maps its inner route gives counselors more than sympathy to offer; it gives them points of leverage.
plos-pone-0358549:
Shengxiang Ma and Wei Jiang published a safety study on subway operations in PLOS ONE in 2026. Subway crashes and failures rarely have a single cause; one fault can trigger the next in a chain. The authors set out to find which risk factors sit at the center of those chains.

Ma and Jiang combined real accident data with network analysis, treating each factor as a node linked to others. The factors with the most and strongest links are the ones worth fixing first, since they feed many kinds of failure. For transit operators, that ranking turns a long list of worries into a short list of priorities for training, checks, and design changes.
plos-pone-0358749:
Lin Qin and four colleagues test a waste based recipe for taming swelling soils, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Expansive soils swell and shrink with the weather, cracking roads and foundations, and the standard cements used to stabilize them are costly and dirty. Their binder, called LSP, mixes lime and sodium silicate into phosphogypsum, an industrial byproduct. Lab samples were then punished with repeated drying and wetting cycles to simulate seasons of abuse.

The treated soil packed denser, needed less water, and swelled far less, with the free swelling measure dropping from well over half to under a third. But the weather cycles bit back: strength fell by about a quarter after fifteen rounds, and water passed through more easily as micro cracks spread. Microscopy credited the improvement mainly to phosphogypsum grains physically filling pores. The study maps both the promise and the expiry date of a greener stabilizer.
plos-pone-0358849:
Rajitra Nawawonganun and two colleagues uncover a paradox for clean air campaigners in Thailand, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They surveyed five hundred fifty-seven parents of primary school children in Khon Kaen, a traffic heavy city in the northeast, during the hot, polluted season of 2025. The question was what drives psychological distress about traffic pollution: the exposure itself, or knowing about it.

Distress was widespread, with about sixty-two percent of parents moderately to highly distressed. The strongest single correlate was awareness itself, in a graded pattern. The more parents knew about air pollution, the more distressed they were. The most aware group carried over four times the odds of the least aware. Using an air quality app also tracked with distress. The authors name the dilemma plainly: education campaigns that raise awareness may raise anxiety too, unless paired with ways to act.
plos-pone-0359349:
Talema Moged Reda leads a team of eight in a 2026 PLOS ONE study mapping damaged land in Ethiopia's Southern Main Ethiopian Rift. Erosion and soil decline there threaten farming, water, and local livelihoods, and hot, salty ground adds stress that is poorly documented. The authors set out to chart where the land is most vulnerable so that limited protection efforts can be aimed well.

They combined satellite imagery from Landsat and Sentinel-2 with rainfall records, elevation data, soil information, and field checks, processed through mapping software and machine learning. Separate layers for erosion, land cover, vegetation health, drought, surface heat, and salt were merged into a single vulnerability map. The result gives planners a picture of which parts of the rift need attention first and where the pressures overlap.
plos-pone-0359549: Nguyen and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on why students say they cheat with AI help. The students were undergraduates reporting their own views. The team weighed five drivers: unclear ethics, what the tools make easy, gaps in school rules, study pressure, and comparing oneself with peers. Knowing which drivers matter most can help universities write clearer rules and fairer tasks.
plos-pone-0360249:
Alexa Keeling and Vijay Daniels published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its subject is the neurological examination, the hands-on set of tests doctors use to check the nervous system. The authors study medical residents, doctors in training, and how confident they feel performing this exam.

Alongside confidence, the study looks at exam avoidance, the habit of skipping parts of the exam or the whole thing. Residents who avoid the neuro exam may miss signs of stroke and other urgent problems. Medical educators can use evidence about confidence and avoidance to fix training where it leaves young doctors unsure.
pmc-10336149:
Zhang, Xiao, Mao, and co-authors review how swelling and immune activity in the brain may help drive diseases that kill nerve cells. Their review covers Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, ALS, and Huntington's disease. Work in these fields once treated brain swelling as a late side effect of damage.

The authors argue the evidence now points the other way as well. Immune activity in the brain can help push the disease forward, not just follow it. That shift matters because it opens new treatment ideas. If swelling helps cause the damage, calming the right immune signals early could slow loss of memory and movement.
pmc-10654649:
Yoshinori Satake, Masashi Izumi, Koji Aso, and Masahiko Ikeuchi link fat pad stiffness to knee pain in a 2023 paper. The fat pad sits below the kneecap in the joint. The patients all had knee osteoarthritis of set grades. The team measured pad stiffness with ultrasound wave speed.

Ninety-seven patients aged 46 to 86 took part. Those with front knee pain had stiffer fat pads. The link held in both simple and adjusted analyses. It did not depend on the joint's wear grade. The authors say a stiffer pad marks the painful state. Ultrasound stiffness checks may help diagnose such pain.
pmc-10655349:
Ni Xiaofeng and six co-authors study the gut microbes of patients with bowel cancer after drug treatment. The treatment often lowers white blood cell counts, a side effect that can turn risky. The team took stool samples from fifty-five patients and fifty-six healthy people. Patients split into groups with low or normal white cell counts, and the team compared their gut mixes.

Gut variety was lower in patients than in healthy people. Fifteen kinds of bacteria set the groups apart. A machine learning model using three kinds of gut bacteria best flagged which patients had low counts. The paper links gut makeup to this treatment side effect.
pmc-10656449:
Emilie Khattignavong and co-authors build, in a 2023 paper, an easy computational way to measure how disordered collagen networks are in disease. Collagen is the body's main structural fiber, and its nanoscale weave shifts in connective tissue disorders. Reading that weave by eye from microscope images is slow and subjective. Their method pairs atomic force microscope images with a Fourier transform, a standard tool that turns patterns into orientation data.

The team tested the approach on skin from mice bred to mimic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Diseased fibers showed murkier edges, altered banding, and less orderly alignment than healthy ones. The transform measured the disorganization and the fibers' direction spread directly, turning pictures into numbers a clinic could use. The authors propose the pipeline as a step toward automated diagnosis of this family of disorders, and a sharper tool for basic collagen research.
pmc-10657349:
Alon Stern and co-authors present a way to read metabolism separately inside a cell's two main workspaces, in a 2023 paper. Cells run chemistry in the cytosol and inside mitochondria, and watching each space on its own has long been a barrier. Studying isolated organelles distorts the picture. Their method works on whole, intact cells fed with traced isotopes.

A computer step splits the isotope patterns into the part belonging to each space, then ties them to flows and amounts with models of metabolism and energy. The split cut uncertainty in flows tenfold and in amounts a thousandfold against older modeling. Across cultured cell lines, one shuttle pathway between the spaces varied widely. The authors expect the tool to serve disease research and bioengineering.
pmc-10659649:
Yanru Deng and co-authors review treatment for diabetes that springs from liver disease. Their 2023 review covers hepatogenous diabetes, a sugar disorder driven by chronic liver damage. It shows up often in cirrhosis and carries a poor outlook, with risks of bleeding and coma.

As the liver worsens, the diabetes deepens, and the pair raise the odds of liver cancer and death. No agreed treatment plan exists for the condition yet. The review gathers recent advances in drugs and care for these patients. It sets them apart from ordinary type 2 diabetes, which has a different root. The authors hope the survey guides a shared strategy.
pmc-10669549:
Sara Pagliarani and co-authors described the female koala reproductive tract in a 2023 anatomy paper. The koala, an iconic Australian marsupial, is now listed as endangered, and breeding programs need a firm map of normal anatomy. The work grew from two efforts: building an artificial insemination program, and defining the tissue changes that chlamydia infection causes in the same organs. Over seventy specimens from wildlife hospitals in southeast Queensland were examined.

The paper details the ovary, oviduct, twin uteri, vaginal complex, and urogenital sinus, in both gross form and under the microscope. Findings are organized by cycle phase: resting, growth, and hormone-active stages. The description gives vets and conservation teams a baseline against which disease changes can be judged.
pmc-10669849:
Purple wheat owes its color to anthocyanins, plant pigments with antioxidant power, and breeders hope the grain can support healthy aging. Daria Mikhailova and co-authors tested bran extracts in 2023 from purple wheat and a near-identical plain line. Chemical analysis confirmed the pigments were present only in the purple bran.

The purple extract quenched free radicals better and protected red blood cell membranes more strongly in lab tests. Both extracts, purple and plain, extended the lifespan of female fruit flies. The authors conclude that the pigments add antioxidant strength, but other bran compounds also help, since the plain extract still protected cells and lengthened fly life. The work supports breeding pigment-rich wheat for health-focused foods.
pmc-10670249:
Rachel Boyd and eight colleagues published a 2023 study of ring chromosomes in blood cancers. A ring chromosome forms when a chromosome's ends fuse into a circle. Rings appear in under 10 percent of patients with hematological malignancies and are linked to poor prognosis, but only small patient groups had been characterized.

The team analyzed chromosomes from more than 13,000 patients at Johns Hopkins Hospital and found 98 with ring chromosomes. Of these, 90 had myeloid cancers and 8 had lymphoid cancers. Targeted DNA sequencing showed the rings are associated with mutations in TP53, a key tumor suppressor gene, and with characteristic patterns of copy number change. The large cohort sharpens the picture of this rare abnormality.
pmc-10671249:
A growth factor best known from metabolism may decide whether a brain withstands Alzheimer's pathology, argue Jonathan Zegarra-Valdivia and co-authors. They focus on insulin-like growth factor I, or IGF-I, which acts on nearly every cascade blamed in the disease, from energy failure to inflammation to protein mishandling. Brains that keep IGF-I signaling strong, they propose, gain resilience.

Weak signaling shows up across the classic risk factors: old age, type 2 diabetes, poor diet, inactivity, stress, and low education. The catch is measurement. Blood or tissue levels alone cannot say whether the signal is truly working, so the authors call for functional tests of IGF-I activity.
pmc-10671449:
Sheiphali Gandhi and five colleagues review the environmental and workplace causes of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This lung disease scars the lungs and grows steadily worse; it mostly strikes older men. The disease is called idiopathic, yet age is its strongest risk factor, and many exposures raise risk further. They include metal dust, wood dust, air pollution, smoking, and diet.

The same factors can trigger acute flare-ups that carry poor outlooks. Recent work stresses inhalation injuries among World Trade Center first responders and military personnel. The review explains how exposures likely interact with genetic susceptibility to start and drive the disease. The authors picked exposures by overall disease burden rather than trying to list them all.
pmc-10672749:
David Hangyasi and seven co-authors report three gum surgery cases using a new magnesium membrane, in a 2023 paper. Deep pockets beside teeth, called intrabony defects, resist regeneration. The membrane's strength let surgeons cut it to fit each defect's shape. A cow-derived bone filler packed the defects beneath it. Three patients with severe gum disease were treated.

Healing ran four to six months. X-rays then confirmed new bone in the defects. Pocket depths shrank by about one and two thirds millimeters on average. Each defect's shape got its own membrane outline. Outcomes looked good in both function and appearance. Magnesium slowly dissolves in the body, sparing a removal surgery. The authors present the cases as proof of concept. Larger trials must confirm the early promise.
pmc-10674249:
Eight researchers led by Elena Formisano ran a trial of a very low-carb, protein-sparing fast in adults with obesity. Half got the liquid formula through a nose tube that feeds the stomach all day. The other half took the same diet by mouth. Forty-four patients were followed for one hundred fifty days.

Weight and waist size fell much the same in both groups. The tube group kept more lean tissue and muscle, and carried less fat, by the end. Their insulin levels were also much lower. The authors say tube feeding of this diet improves body makeup and blood sugar control more than the same diet by mouth.
pmc-10675649:
Laura Jiaxuan Li and co-authors reviewed zeolites in dentistry in a 2023 paper. Zeolites are porous crystal minerals that swap ions readily and stay stable under heat and chemicals. A kin class built with metal links shares the porous frame. Both are gentle on body tissue, which makes them fit for mouth care.

The review covers the main dental forms, such as silver, zinc, calcium, and strontium zeolites, and two kin frames. Uses span fillings, coatings, and germ-fighting adds for dental goods. Their pores can hold and shed helpful ions right where a tooth needs them. The authors chart where proof is strong and where trials are still due.
pmc-10687749:
Armine Asatryan and co-authors set out a risk read of a worm that rides sea fish to Portuguese plates. The worm's young live in fish flesh; raw or half-cooked meals can bring gut pain and rash-prone replies. Spain next door logs rash cases, a sign of live spread in the shared sea yard. Their 2023 plan, run by a Porto sea hub with a Czech mate, picks the Atlantic chub mackerel sold in Portuguese shops as the test host.

Fish are read for worm load by kind and by yard of sale. Load marks then feed a folk risk sum. Hard counts can tell shops and health hands if this fish needs new rules or just known care in the kitchen.
pmc-10688149:
Fulang Wu and colleagues catalogued an oxygen-burst gene family in grasses in 2023. These genes make reactive oxygen species. They help plants handle microbe encounters. Most past work covered broadleaf plants. Grass family knowledge stayed thin before. Seven grass species were analysed together.

More than one hundred genes were found. Evolution links were mapped across species. Maize work then tested fungal partnership roles. Friendly root fungi need these genes. Arbuscule structures develop properly with them. Early partnership steps mattered less here. Fine development control was the key role. Crop symbiosis research gains useful leads.
pmc-10689849:
Xiang and co-authors study how the Sun's outer layer rotates in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. They use daily measures of sunlight at several wavelength bands, plus four kinds of small magnetic features on the Sun. Their aim is to see which features drive changes in the spin of the corona over time.

Using wave-based tools and correlation tests, they find the drivers change with the solar cycle. At solar maximum, one kind of small magnetic element dominates the pattern. In quiet times, two kinds share control, and one grows stronger as activity falls. The authors say this helps explain why past studies disagreed, and why the corona spins faster than the surface below it.
pmc-10690949:
Soundarya Rajapitamahuni, Eun Sun Lyou, Bo Ram Kang, and Tae Kwon Lee wrote a study in twenty twenty-three on Staphylococcus aureus, a common bacterium behind ills from skin boils to sepsis. When iron is scarce, such bacteria send out siderophores, small molecules that grab iron for them. The team asked how life alongside other microbes changes this output.

First they tuned the growth medium, and a glycerol alanine salts medium gave the steadiest output of varied siderophores. Output peaked at neutral pH and at low iron. They then grew the bacterium with other strains and tracked how its output changed. Growth with Pseudomonas aeruginosa wiped the output out, while other partners cut it to one or two kinds. These shifts pushed the bacterium into distinct forms, a sign that microbes act unlike when alone and when in company.
pmc-10692149:
Agustin Perez Santangelo and Guillermo Solovey test what makes people believe political claims, in a 2023 registered report. False news sways votes and acts, and both party loyalty and slow, careful thought are said to guard or expose belief. The team asked 1,353 Argentine adults to judge fact-checked statements by local politicians as true or false, then measured their careful-thinking style and party leanings.

Two findings held firm. Statements that matched a person's politics drew more belief across the board. Careful thinkers also showed more skepticism overall. Two other links, to spotting truth and to party bias, pointed the expected ways but could not be pinned down. The authors urge tests in other settings and formats before drawing morals.
pmc-10693549:
Anna Diez-Villanueva and co-authors hunt for inherited epigenetic marks in family trios in this 2023 paper. Much of the heritability of common disease is still unexplained by gene variants. DNA methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, might pass traits across generations directly. The team read methylation across the whole genome in four healthy families.

Each family held two parents and one child. About 1.5 million sites varied between parents in a pattern fit for inheritance checks. Of those, only 3,488 sites showed no link to any nearby gene variant. Those sites are candidates for true epigenetic inheritance. They sat across the genome, often near promoters, and tended to be fully marked or fully unmarked. The study gives a starting map for follow up work.
pmc-10694149:
Chen Chen and co-authors built a compact light sensor in 2023 that reads polarisation at fine spatial detail. Polarisation analysis serves many optical tasks, but current setups are bulky or split the image across channels, blurring detail. Their design uses a patterned surface with three channels and no interleaving.

A deep neural network turns the surface's output into fast, robust polarisation readings. Both even and uneven polarisation patterns across a scene were measured in tests. The device even told apart two similar-looking glasses. The authors highlight the small size and high resolution, and suggest the approach could seed new designs for optical detection and sensing.
pmc-10694949:
Kejun Liu and six co-authors build a survival predictor for liver cancer from T-cell exhaustion genes, in work from 2023. Worn-out killer T cells are a known feature of this cancer's immune landscape. From exhaustion-linked genes tied to outcome, a six-gene risk score was fitted and checked against patient tissue and cell lines.

Low-risk patients lived clearly longer, and the score held up as an independent predictor beside clinical traits. High-risk tumors lit up immune checkpoint and stress pathways. Silencing three of the model genes in cancer cells slowed their growth and movement in dish tests. A nomogram joining score and clinical data predicted survival with a good fit.
pmc-10695049:
Alexandre de Assis Bueno and co-authors map how ethics is taught in Brazilian public nursing programs, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Program plans for over one hundred active degrees were read in document form. Beyond a set ethics course, ethical themes ran across many subjects.

Care contexts, pharmacology, surgical nursing, and care planning all carried ethics threads. So did topics from palliative care to diversity and mental health. Management and epidemiology joined the list as well. The authors name the core challenge: weaving ethics into every act of caring, teaching, and managing, rather than parking it in one course.
pmc-10695949:
Aleksander Lasek and co-authors design pulse recipes to steer a single electron qubit. The qubit lives in a pair of tiny semiconductor dots. Fast, clean control is hard: stray pulses can kick the electron out of its working states. Their framework searches for pulse trains that turn the qubit any wanted way while staying inside the safe space.

The winning scheme turns the qubit gently yet swiftly, a mix that is hard to strike. Real devices blur pulse edges, so the search counts rise and fall times in. Simulations of a full device confirm the recipes work as drawn. The authors note the logic ports to other qubit types with like gaps.
pmc-10696049:
Toka Hassan, Eman Kandeel, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It turns waste from vegetable oil making into eco-friendly cutting fluids for metalworking, replacing toxic petroleum oils with something renewable and safer.

The team recovered oil from spent bleaching earth, a factory waste, and built a family of emulsifiers on it. Some were charged, some not, some doubled as rust blockers and microbe killers. Mixed emulsifier recipes were blended into cutting fluid formulas at various loadings. Certain mixtures formed stable emulsions where single emulsifiers failed. Two formulas stood out in the reported tests. Spectroscopic checks confirmed the molecules' structures along the way. The authors present the fluids as proof that an industrial waste stream can feed a second industry cleanly, cutting both disposal and drilling into new resources.
pmc-10696749:
Justin Baker and a large team of colleagues set out a plan for a clinical trial on group therapy to prevent suicide among military service members. Their protocol paper, published in twenty twenty-three, notes that suicide harms both health and readiness, and that a shortage of clinicians limits care. The trial compares two group formats given in person at a United States naval medical center. One is a brief cognitive behavioral therapy adapted for groups. The other teaches skills drawn from dialectical behavior therapy.

Participants are active-duty members with recent suicidal thoughts or behavior. They answer electronic questionnaires before treatment, after each session, and at follow-ups months later. The main question is whether the brief therapy is no worse than the skills group at reducing suicidal thinking. The paper describes the design only; results will come when the trial is complete.
pmc-10697049:
Cunte Chen and five co-authors linked faults in a T cell gene to better outcomes in an aggressive leukemia in a 2023 paper. The leukemia strikes T cells early in their growth, and fewer than half of patients survive five years. Sorting patients by risk stays hard because the disease varies so much.

The gene in focus steers T cell growth and activation. Past work tied its low activity to immune failure and poor outcomes in a related blood disease, while blocking it slowed leukemia cells in dishes. The title finding reports that patients carrying faults in this gene had a higher share of killer T cells and fared better clinically. The authors pitch the fault as a marker to refine risk groups and, one day, therapy choice.
pmc-10698149:
Ma and co-authors build a risk score for stomach cancer from a gene family map in a 2023 study. The gene family, Rho GTPases, steers cell movement and growth and shows up in many cancers. Cluster analysis split patients into two subtypes with clear gaps in survival and tumor surroundings. A score built from family genes was tested on outside patient groups.

High scores marked worse outlooks, and the score stood as a lone forecast factor in joint models. In two immunotherapy groups, low scores tracked better drug response. Lab checks confirmed the score's key genes in tissue. The authors offer the score as a guide for prognosis and care choice.
pmc-10698549:
Wright, Cortina-Borja, Knowles, and Urquhart pool global data on how often babies are born with Robin sequence, a jaw development disorder that can block the airway. Care is costly and long term when airway problems are poorly treated. Their 2023 review searched databases for studies on the condition's birth prevalence and was registered in advance.

From 34 studies covering 2,722 cases in 22 countries, pooled prevalence was about 9.5 per 100,000 live births. Estimates varied a lot between studies. Only a third of studies gave a case definition, and definitions differed. Rates trended higher in European groups and lower in registry based studies. The authors call for more data from outside Europe and clearer reporting of ethnicity.
pmc-10698949:
Christian Bode and co-authors review attempts to treat sepsis by steering the host response, in a 2023 paper. Sepsis is the body's own reaction to infection gone wrong, and it kills worldwide. Patients can swing toward too much inflammation, too little immunity, or both at once. Many immune drugs exist, yet trials to push the system either way have failed to save lives.

The likely faults are picking the wrong patients and ignoring the clotting, vessel, and organ damage that runs beside the immune chaos. Sorting patients by their host response type may finally match the right drug to the right person. The review maps current tries and the road to precision care.
pmc-10700249:
Jie Ma, Binghua Zhang, Hao Song, Dongle Wu and Tao Song wrote a 2023 review on the accuracy of digital scans for dental implants taken inside the mouth. Hand-held scanners are replacing molds for implant work. The team gathered studies done in real patients, not lab models. Bias in each study was graded by two reviewers.

Ten studies made the final set. Six checked how true the scans were, with mixed verdicts. Full-arch scans took much less time than classic molds. Prosthetic survival was perfect in the follow-up studies, and bone levels held steady. Scan strategy swayed accuracy a lot, the authors stress.
pmc-10701749:
Chenglong Cao and co-authors report a rare cause of face pain in a case paper from two thousand twenty-three. Trigeminal neuralgia brings severe pain to one side of the face. In this patient, two problems pressed on the nerve at once: a bony growth near the skull base and a loop of blood vessel.

The patient was a man aged forty-six with three years of severe pain on the right side of his face. Scans showed both the growth and the vessel loop. Surgeons removed the growth and freed the nerve from the vessel in one combined operation. He left the hospital without complications and free of pain. The authors urge doctors to consider this rare double cause.
pmc-10701949:
At Israeli rave parties, music and psychedelic drugs meet strict drug laws, and a study asks the people who go how that mix feels. Researchers interviewed regulars who use these drugs about their bodily, emotional, and social experiences. Four themes emerged. Drug policy itself bred insecurity and anxiety at events. Stigma from police and society shadowed the culture.

Negative experiences included hallucinations and disorientation. Positive ones ranged from sharpened senses to stress relief, self-acceptance, and a felt bond with nature. The authors argue that the strict ban, with no harm reduction presence at events, leaves participants less safe, and they point toward policy change.
pmc-10702049:
Zhen Liu and co-authors test in this 2023 study whether a liver hormone in the blood flags blood vessel disease in type 2 diabetes. The hormone, FGF21, helps steer sugar and fat handling and rises under metabolic strain. In 701 diabetic patients and 258 healthy controls, the team measured the hormone and checked neck artery disease and high blood pressure.

Levels ran far higher in patients carrying either condition, and highest when both struck together. The hormone tracked body weight and artery wall thickness, and stood as an independent predictor after standard risks were counted. The authors propose it as a gauge of metabolic load and vessel risk. A blood draw could sort risk at checkups.
pmc-10704649:
Michael Q Nguyen and four co-authors ask patients, not statisticians, whether a popular foot questionnaire asks the right questions after ankle surgery, in this 2023 qualitative study. The Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire scores pain and function well in general foot disorders, but nobody had checked its content validity for ankle fracture patients, a different crowd with different concerns.

Seventeen surgically treated patients, aged 27 to 76 and mostly women, were interviewed between four weeks and eighteen months after their operations. The method was cognitive interviewing: patients thought aloud through each question while researchers probed four steps of answering. Those steps are understanding the item, recalling the experience, judging it, and mapping it onto the offered responses. Where answers stumbled, the instrument, not the patient, is suspect. The study's business is the unglamorous groundwork that decides whether outcome scores deserve the trust trials place in them.
pmc-10704749:
Patrícia Pinheiro de Freitas and co-authors track how food stores that sell fruits and vegetables changed over five years in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. Store audits were done in 2013 and again in 2018 around primary health care health promotion sites. A one-mile zone around each site defined the food environment under study.

After five years, only 35.2 percent of stores were stable: 154 had closed and 155 had opened. Stability was higher in areas with low health vulnerability. In high-vulnerability areas, supermarkets fell in number, while local stores held steadier than specialised fruit and vegetable markets. The authors argue food supply policy must fit local conditions to cut gaps in access.
pmc-10704849:
Peik Gustafsson and co-authors tested whether simple timing tasks can help flag ADHD in children, in work published in 2023. Diagnosis today rests mostly on interviews, which leaves room for doubt. The team compared twenty nine children with ADHD to ninety six peers on three tasks tied to the brain's timing center.

Children with ADHD differed on a visual adaptation task and on finger tapping precision, but not on a blink conditioning task. The same gaps marked a more severe related profile. Tapping precision stood out as cheap, objective, and unbiased. The authors propose finger tapping as a supporting biomarker to sharpen current diagnosis.
pmc-10704949:
Adams and co-authors present a 2023 study comparing hospital experiences of patients with limited English in Australia. Minority patients often report worse care, and language adds its own barrier. A standard patient survey covered three hospitals in one city network over five years. Of 2,291 patients, 490 spoke a language other than English at home.

Surprises emerged in the ratings. The limited-English group scored doctors higher on listening and clear explaining, and rated night quietness better. The same group scored nurses lower on respect and on answering call bells. Overall experience still ran more positive for them. The authors probe why language splits the ward experience in two directions.
pmc-10705149:
Ros and colleagues present imaging methods for birth defects at the neck and chest junction in horses in a 2023 paper. Data on these defects have conflicted, but signs suggest they can matter for health and performance. The study used warmblood horses sent for behavior or performance problems.

The team set out X-ray views that can be done in the field. Almost all horses showed changes to the lower neck vertebrae, and many had rib anomalies such as missing, short, or split first ribs. Grades of defects on the two sides were linked. The new views let vets spot these traits in living horses. A classification system is proposed.
pmc-10707649:
Tang, Liu, and Milner-Bolotin used PISA 2015 data to study collaborative problem solving among students worldwide. The data covered more than 400,000 students in 52 countries and economies. Reports had shown weak skills in solving problems with others, yet few studies looked across countries while respecting the nested structure of the data. The team applied multilevel modeling to link attitudes toward working together, problem-solving scores, and science results.

One attitude helped and one hurt: students who valued relationships scored higher on collaborative problem solving, while those who valued teamwork itself scored lower. Collaborative skill was the strongest single predictor of science achievement among the variables studied. Inquiry-based science teaching showed mixed links depending on the activity. The authors urge schools to build collaborative problem solving into teaching, with care about which inquiry practices they promote. The catalog byline repeats one name three times; the text names three authors.
pmc-10708549:
Vera-Loor and three co-authors tested in twenty twenty-three two green chem routes to turn paper pulp into a finer grade that melts for cloth and films. Mills want such a swap on site with mild chemicals. One route used a peroxide wash at a few base levels.

Peroxide alone did not strip a pulp part, hemicellulose, in full to lift melt skill. A two-step route, with a salt first and peroxide next, did far better. That route cut the stray part and raised the pure share of the pulp. The team weighs shine, thick flow, and use paths for the end pulp.
pmc-10708849:
Emilios Leonidas and co-authors built a fast infrared thermometer in 2023 for measuring heat near room temperature without contact. Contact probes can be slow and drift, but radiation sensors struggle at low heat. Their device uses a special photodiode joined to a fiber cable that carries mid-infrared light. It reads heat in as little as one to five thousandths of a second.

Tests showed it tracking temperatures from about thirty-five to one hundred degrees with noise under half a degree. It matched a standard probe while drilling plastic. The team aims it at jobs like watching motors and batteries and cutting composites. Quick, contact-free reads can catch overheating early.
pmc-10709349:
Liver transplants can be harmed when blood flow returns and iron-driven cell death sweeps the organ. Changbiao Li and co-authors study a protein called Gp78 in that injury in a 2023 paper, using mice bred with the gene removed or boosted in liver cells.

Patients and mice both showed lower Gp78 after flow returned, and lower levels tracked with worse damage. Mice lacking the protein in liver cells suffered less injury and inflammation. Mice with extra protein fared worse. Gene, protein, and chemical scans showed the protein reshapes fat handling so that burn-prone lipids pile up, feeding the iron-driven death through a partner enzyme. Blocking that death route or the partner erased the harm.
pmc-10709549:
Faysal Al-Ghoula, Khushbu Patel, Sam Falde, and four colleagues test whether radiomics tools agree across users in this two thousand twenty-three study. CT lung screening saves lives, but tools that score nodules from scan texture depend on someone first outlining the nodule, a source of variability. Three observers of different training levels, a medical student, a resident, and a radiology fellow, segmented ninety-five malignant nodules from two institutions. Each ran two validated tools, BRODERS and CANARY.

Agreement was strong. Correlation coefficients reached zero point seven seven for nodule volume and zero point nine eight and zero point nine seven for the BRODERS cancer probability and CANARY aggression score. Overlap of the segmentations scored about zero point eight at both centers. The authors conclude both tools are robust to who performs the segmentation, a precondition for using radiomics scores in real screening programs where expert time is scarce.
pmc-10710949:
Yaying Chen and colleagues (2023) studied tiny blood vessel changes in the eyes of patients whose pituitary tumors press on the optic pathways. That pressure damages the nerve fiber layer and eats into the visual field. Using a scan that images retinal blood flow, the team compared 45 eyes from 40 patients with 24 healthy eyes, splitting patients into those with and without temporal field loss.

Eyes with field loss had clearly reduced vessel density around the optic disc, but slightly raised density in a surface layer of the central retina. Eyes without field loss already showed the raised central density. Disc vessel density moved against field damage and along with nerve layer thickness. The authors suggest the early rise in central density could flag patients before field loss begins, while the disc drop marks later damage, making the scan a useful gauge of severity.
pmc-10711849:
Lijie Wang and co-authors set out, in 2023, a protocol for gathering what breast cancer patients say about hormone therapy side effects and the help they want. Such symptoms can bring pain, anxiety, and fear of the cancer returning. Poor support lowers drug adherence, which raises relapse and death risk, so patient needs must be mapped first.

Seven databases plus grey literature were searched for qualitative and mixed-method studies, with no date limit. pmc-10712049:

pmc-10712149:

pmc-10714149:

The authors stress the ease of growing yeast and the fit with long-standing purification recipes. Biochemists gain a steady source for testing how each isoform and its partners behave.
pmc-10714349:
Chemists test a cleaner way to upgrade low-grade gas in a 2023 study led by Świrk and co-authors. pmc-10714649:

One patient had severe scoliosis and needed repeated spinal injections of a therapy drug. Scans in two planes, plus a rocking motion of the probe, located the window between bones. pmc-10715649:
Magdalena Blanz leads a team on early farm life in Hungary. Their study from twenty twenty-three looks at a Stone Age site of the Starcevo culture. It asks how the first farmers kept their stock.

Cattle, goats, sheep, and pigs came to the region then. Crop range shrank as farming spread north from the south. The tests add detail on that shift.
pmc-10716049:

pmc-10716149:

pmc-10716449:

pmc-10717449:
Helena Mansson Sandberg and co-authors ask, in a 2023 study, what drove deep wear in Swedish family doctors in the COVID years. Burnout hit such doctors hard in the plague years. pmc-10718049:
Julia Lignon and seven co-authors report a flea found on a wild opossum in southern Brazil. Their 2023 case report concerns the white-eared opossum, a marsupial that lives close to people. Lab study named it Ctenocephalides felis, the common cat flea. The case shows this flea moves between wild animals, pets, and people. That traffic matters for tracking diseases that fleas can carry.
pmc-10719149:
Cheryl Dyck, Kathryn Isaac, and Leah Edelstein-Keshet present a 2023 paper modeling capsular contracture, the painful tightening of scar tissue around breast implants. The complication can deform the breast after cancer reconstruction or cosmetic surgery. Inflammation from surgical trauma or contamination is suspected of driving it, but the chain of events was untested.

Their math model couples four players: immune cells that arrive at the site, resident fibroblasts, the contractile cells those fibroblasts can turn into, and the collagen they lay down. Simulations show the cell response plus immune recruitment can indeed produce the thick, abnormal scarring seen in patients. The model also suggests which patterns lead to milder outcomes.
pmc-10720649:
Jeanette Zanker and six co-authors test a lab cell line as a stand-in for checking gene therapy strength. The therapy uses a virus to carry a gene for a small signaling protein into nerve cells. The protein must be cut to its mature form to work, which makes lab tests tricky. The cells took up the virus well even at low doses, and better once matured. Only matured cells made and released the finished protein in amounts that rose with dose. The paper backs the matured cells as a sound test bed for such vectors.
pmc-10722149:

Sixty six mutants made far fewer sacs in biofilms, and none made far more. Many hits were genes for swimming parts and for the slime sugars that build the biofilm matrix. pmc-10722949:
Alessandro Passardi and co-authors test inflammatory blood indices as prognostic markers in metastatic colorectal cancer in work from 2023. No validated marker predicts who benefits from the antibody drug bevacizumab, so cheap blood scores are attractive.

The study followed 182 patients on first-line chemotherapy plus the drug, with blood tests at baseline and each cycle. High scores on two indices predicted shorter time without progression and shorter survival. A third index showed no link. Adjusted analysis kept both scores as independent factors. The authors call them easy prognostic tools for treatment planning.
pmc-10723049:
Xue Zhong and co-authors find in 2023 a three-protein team that guards lymphocyte survival and liver balance in mice. One member is a lysosome carrier with no known immune role before this work. Gene changes in it cause low lymphocyte counts, a swollen spleen, and liver harm.

pmc-10725749:
Masahiko Ayaki and Kazuno Negishi study how tear volume and dry eye symptoms shift with the seasons in Japan, in work from twenty twenty-three. Japan's four seasons swing widely in heat and humidity. Those swings may drive the eye surface complaints that clinics see.

Tear volume bottomed out in winter, when air is dry and cool, and ran higher in other seasons. Scores tied to break up time, a second tear test, corneal staining, and felt dryness. The work backs season aware dry eye care.
pmc-10726049:
Athira Nambiar, Harikrishnaa S, and Sharanprasath S apply explainable AI to Indian COVID-19 data in a 2023 study. Hospitals used prediction models during the pandemic to spot patients likely to worsen. Many models, though, were black boxes whose reasoning no one could inspect. That opacity limits trust at the bedside, so the team paired models with explanation tools.

They trained several classifiers, from decision trees to a neural network, to predict severity from symptoms. Two explanation methods then showed which symptoms drove each verdict, in ways any model can use. The tools let doctors check that predictions rest on sensible signs. The study argues such transparency is required before AI triage can be safely routine.
pmc-10728049:
Hyungtae Kim, Ji Su Kim, and Yerl Bo Sung study hip fractures that heal at a tilted angle, in this 2023 paper. Breaks near the top of the thigh bone that stay in place are usually fixed with screws where they sit. When the broken ends heal tilted past a set angle, outcomes worsen. The tilt can also reshape the hip joint so its surfaces grind, wearing the joint out early.

The team split patients by how severe the tilt was after screw fixing. They then tracked how fast joint wear advanced on X-rays in each group. Their aim was to test whether worse tilt means faster wear, as recent advice to correct the tilt assumes. Results can guide surgeons on when to realign such breaks rather than fix them as they lie.
pmc-10729149:
HIV treatment keeps people alive for decades, but the virus and its drugs strain the body's metabolism. Abdurezak Abdela and co-authors checked 518 patients at Ethiopian HIV clinics in 2023 for metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks that feeds heart disease. Two thirds of the group were women, and the average time on treatment was ten years.

Nearly thirty-eight percent met the syndrome's criteria, and about a quarter had abnormal fat distribution. Being over forty-five, female, overweight, or on one of two drug regimens raised the odds independently. Past use of an older drug explained much of the fat problem. The authors urge clinics to screen hearts as carefully as viruses.
pmc-10730249:
A worm infection common in warm regions can, in rare cases, reach the brain or spinal cord and cause grave harm. Rahaf Alanazi and co-authors report such a case in a 2023 paper. Their patient, a woman of forty-four, came to emergency care after fainting and a seizure, a sudden start for a slow parasitic disease.

Scans found a lesion in the front of the brain. Tissue taken from the lesion settled the question: the worm's traces were there, confirming the rare spread. Care for this form of the disease can mix anti-worm drugs, steroids, and surgery, picked by the case. The authors stress that early scans and tissue checks are what catch the diagnosis before deeper harm sets in, above all where the infection is common.
pmc-10733149:
Wei-Lei Wang and co-authors estimate the ocean biological carbon pump in a 2023 study. Surface photosynthesis makes organic carbon that sinks to deeper waters, drawing carbon dioxide from the air. Observation based estimates of that pump strength disagree, and climate models spread widely too.

Using decades of hydrographic data with an inverse model, the team estimate total organic carbon export below the sunlit zone. Only about two thirds reaches one hundred meters, due to rapid breakdown above. Most export lasting beyond a year comes from sinking particles and migrating zooplankton, though mixing of dissolved matter also contributes.
pmc-10735349:
Juan Palavicini and co-authors probe a gene tied to Alzheimer's risk and longevity in a 2023 study. Variants of the gene PLCG2 raise or lower disease risk by version. The gene acts mainly in microglia, the brain's immune cells. Its enzyme splits a membrane lipid into two messengers.

pmc-10735549:

In Alaska Native culture, caring for Elders is a core value, no matter their health. Caregiving can bring stress, isolation, and depression that harm the caregiver's own health. Lewis asks what good caregivers themselves found in the work, alongside the strain.

Interviews with twenty-two Alaska Native caregivers, in rural and urban communities, each ran about an hour. Caregivers spoke of hard duties and of too little education, awareness, and resources, which made the stress worse. As their relative changed with the disease, the blessings took different forms. More time together and shared memories were among them. The study records both sides of the caregiving life.
pmc-10735649:

Exercise cannot cure dementia, but regular activity is one of the behaviors thought to lower risk. The survey covered 328 healthy, Israel-born adults aged 50 and over, recruited online in 2021 and 2022. It measured weekly activity minutes and scored health beliefs with a standard questionnaire.

Participants averaged about 166 minutes of activity a week, yet only 44 percent reached the 150-minute mark often used as a target. In the statistical model, stronger belief that dementia is severe went with less activity, while stronger response to cues to act went with more. Gender and income also mattered. Together the factors explained about 14 percent of the differences between people. The author suggests programs should work on beliefs, above all prompts to act.
pmc-10735749:
Sarah Robbins and co-authors study how diabetes and vaginal microbes together relate to the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, a set of symptoms driven by low estrogen. The authors call for larger studies of this interplay.
pmc-10736149:
Youngmin Cho and co-authors explore in this 2023 study how families stay involved in assisted living, where residents risk falls and lost freedom. Caregivers described coaxing residents to face their health limits, hunting resources, and bracing for problems ahead.

Joint work also mattered: speaking up for needs, joining care and social life, sharing one care plan, and deciding together. Fear of staff pushback and past history shaped how boldly families engaged. The authors argue homes should build real ways to involve families, not treat them as visitors. pmc-10736449:
Jacy Weems, Ellen McCreedy, Grace Wittenberg, and Rosa Baier ask the corporate owners of nursing homes what helped and hurt a national trial run inside their buildings. pmc-10736549:

They watch tapes of sessions and talk with patients, family helpers, and the volunteers who led them. Needs split into setup needs, like a calm room and fit kit, and delivery needs, like tales tuned to each life. Patients grasped new ideas and spoke up well with the right prompts.
pmc-10736849:

One third of that group said long COVID affected their job. Focus groups stressed brain fog, deep fatigue, low mood, and anxiety as core burdens. Partners took on care tasks that cut work time, and many patients cut hours or quit.
pmc-10736949:

Another reads place: imaging that locates gene and protein markers inside intact tissue at fine detail. Special methods capture the cocktail of signals senescent cells secrete. pmc-10737149:
Eric Cerino and co-authors study daily stress and thinking skills in 2023 among older adults in the United States. Feeling in control is tied to healthy aging, but most past work looked at control in general, not control over each day's hassles. The team draws on a national study in which 992 people reported stressors over eight days.

People also took phone tests of planning skill and memory. Feeling in control of arguments went with better planning skill. For memory, the benefit of control over home stress grew with age, helping the oldest adults most. The authors suggest that a sense of control over daily stress may act as a resource for the aging mind.
pmc-10737249:
Di Gessa and Deindl trace free care paths of old folks in England in this twenty twenty-three paper. Free kin care props up old folks' lives as state care lags far back. Snap shots miss how that care grows, fades, or holds cross years.

Inside, six waves of a long age study fed a path-sort run. Five care paths fell out, from no care at all to care all through. Sporadic care, growth paths, and fade paths filled the mid ground. Young wed wives in good health most oft cared all through the span. Sex, cash, home form, and kin form each tied to path sort.
pmc-10737349:

The pair read free text replies to a survey sent out in twenty eighteen. They sorted the fears about aging by group. People who plan to stay, return, or wait each worry in their own way. Readers learn why the hope of care that fits one's culture shapes late life plans for people living abroad.
pmc-10737449:

Six hundred forty-five planning conversations happened, almost all under forty-five minutes. Rolling the program out took staged onboarding, local champions, and tailored support. The findings praise adaptable design and co-created workflows.
pmc-10737549:

Having a local friend tied to more help and comfort from friends, but less from family, and also to more demands from friends. pmc-10737649:

pmc-10737749:
Yochai Shavit, Roi Estlein, Roni Elran-Barak, and Dikla Segel-Karpas wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It looks at how adults of different ages viewed the good and bad sides of their romantic relationships during the first COVID-19 lockdown in Israel.

pmc-10737849:

pmc-10737949:

pmc-10738149:

pmc-10738549:

The outcomes were distress over symptoms, side effects, and satisfaction with health. A sense of control was tested as a buffer between strain and distress. pmc-10738649:

pmc-10738749:

pmc-10738849:

pmc-10738949:

The author says these findings fill a gap, since the topic had barely been studied in Mongolia.
pmc-10740449:

pmc-10740549:

Plant oils have shown anticancer action in lab studies, and interest in adding them to care has grown. Their 2023 narrative review gathers the evidence and weighs its strength.

Several oils slowed cancer cells in lab work, and packaging tricks made them work better. Wrapping oils in solid fat particles, breaking them into fine emulsions, or pairing them with standard drugs each boosted their effect in early studies. The authors stress that human evidence remains thin and that quality and dose vary widely among products. They map the open questions and the delivery systems that future trials should test.
pmc-10740749:
Jan De Waele and co-authors give a care guide in 2023 for a severe belly infection caught in hospital. The illness often follows gut surgery, seeds sepsis in intensive care, and kills at high rates, above all when resistant germs drive it.

The review covers how often it strikes, how to spot it fast with scans and blood marks, and how to pick drugs when resistance runs high. Fungal forms get a full look, with their risk signs and hard diagnosis. Source control, by surgery or drains, anchors care. An open belly option for select cases is flagged for more study.
pmc-10740949:
Eldakhakhny and a large team measure metabolic syndrome in non diabetic Saudi adults in Jeddah in twenty twenty-three. The syndrome bundles waist, pressure, sugar, and fat risks. Over thirteen hundred adults from public clinics gave surveys, measures, and fasting blood. One in six met the syndrome bar.

Age was the strongest predictor, with a best split near thirty-two years. Waist size led the signs in older adults of both sexes. Marriage and smoking raised risk in raw reads. After age and sex fixes, only very high income kept a clear protective link. The authors call for cohort studies to firm the story.
pmc-10741649:
Sherise Rogers, Angel Charles, and Ryan Thomas review harnessing gut microbes against pancreatic cancer in a 2023 paper. This cancer is on track to become the second cancer killer in the United States by 2030. It is usually found late, and survival is dismal.

Immunotherapy transformed many cancers but barely dents this one. The tumor is immunologically cold, walled off from immune cells. Microbes living in and on the body shape that immune climate, the authors argue. Early evidence ties the microbiome to treatment response in this disease. The review maps what is known, then names the studies needed to turn microbes into a lever for therapy.
pmc-10741849:
Arrigo Cicero and co-authors count how many clinic patients might qualify for new drugs that lower lipoprotein(a), a fatty particle tied to heart disease, in a 2023 study. High levels of the particle raise the risk of clogged arteries, and targeted drugs are on the way. The team pool records from about 6,000 Italian outpatients with lipid problems.

Among patients who already had artery disease, about 45 percent had particle levels above the cut-off for the new drugs. Age, standard cholesterol, and the particle itself each predicted who had disease. A further slice of patients sat just below the cut-off, near 5 to 7 percent in primary and secondary prevention groups. The pool of candidates is large, the authors say, even under a strict reading of the rules.
pmc-10742049:
Angelo Luciano and co-authors pair a case report with a review from 2023 on lung cancer that has spread to the brain. Brain spread brings hard symptoms and short survival, and beam treatment can help, yet it can also harm with no gain for some patients.

One case, a patient with a gene change in the tumor, anchors the review. The authors sort through scores and signs that may flag who gains from focused beams versus whole brain beams. Their aim is a better match between treatment and patient, so strong therapy goes to those most likely to gain from it.
pmc-10742449:
Robert Sandlersky and co-authors read satellite images of Mongolian mountain forests through the lens of an unusual thermodynamics, in a 2023 study. The forests face climate pressure, and the team wanted a physics-based way to judge their health.

Nine years of Landsat data fed measures of absorbed sunlight, heat loss, and stored energy, framed by Tsallis statistics. Three working parts of the landscape emerged: water evaporation, heat shedding, and a productivity-linked structural part. Pixel-by-pixel tracking showed forests channel less energy into productivity than alpine meadows, leaving them more exposed to climate change. The authors present the scheme as a resilience gauge for landscapes under stress.
pmc-10742749:
Manon Braat and colleagues ask whether the preventive drugs given around liver radioembolization actually prevent anything, in this study from twenty twenty-three. The treatment seeds radioactive beads into liver tumors. To shield the healthy liver, many centers give a protective drug pair afterward, pentoxifylline and ursodeoxycholic acid, on habit more than evidence.

In their center's seventy patients treated for neuroendocrine or colorectal liver spread, the drugs made no difference. Fifty-one patients who received them fared no better on liver toxicity than the nineteen who did not. What did predict biochemical harm was the radiation dose absorbed by the healthy liver itself. A review of the literature, five hundred thirty-four patients across eight papers, found no consistent advice either. The authors conclude the ritual medication lacks support, and no international guideline backs it.
pmc-10743049: Russo and Mennini wrote in 2023 a short call to arms for health systems worldwide. Their piece responds to the COVID-19 outbreak. The head gives only the opening line. It notes that the outbreak placed strong pressure on health systems in the prior years. It also tested their capacity to withstand stress. No findings or data are shown in the head.
pmc-10743249:
Silia Boukandoul, Farid Zaidi, Carla Santos, and Susana Casal present a 2023 study on frying potatoes in moringa oil. Moringa oil comes from the seeds of a tree grown in warm regions. The team compared it with olive oil and sunflower oil over five days of repeated frying at 180 degrees.

A blend of sunflower and moringa oil was also tested, since pure moringa oil costs more. As frying went on, all oils broke down and healthy fats fell. Potatoes fried in moringa or olive oil kept more of their vitamin C than those fried in sunflower oil. Moringa-fried potatoes also carried lower levels of harmful compounds formed during frying, including acrylamide.
pmc-10743649:
Marcus Rieder and co-authors study numbness after wisdom tooth removal in a 2023 paper. The nerve that serves the lower jaw runs close to the roots of the lower back teeth. Pulling a stuck tooth can bruise it, leaving numb lips or tongue. The team checked how often that happened in one year of cases and how it matched the nerve's path on scans.

Records covered 418 patients and 555 tooth removals in 2019. About six percent had numbness in the first week, and just over one percent still had it after a year. Scan positions of the nerve, whether beside, below, or between the roots, were charted for each case. The map helps surgeons warn patients with real numbers.
pmc-10744249:
Qiuxia Zeng and co-authors catalog a gene family in papaya in a paper whose head dates it to 2023. The genes make channels that move water and small compounds in plants. Those channels aid growth and help plants cope with stress, yet papaya had not been mapped.

The team found 29 such genes and sorted them into five groups. Gene shapes and shared motifs were much alike within groups, with some drift between them. Promoter parts pointed to roles for light, hormones, and stress. Gene activity varied by tissue and by stress, giving a base for later work on fruit and plant growth.
pmc-10744449:
Paula Vigon and co-authors tested how salt water exposure weakens glued joints in carbon composites in a 2023 study. The joints, two carbon fiber laminates bonded with epoxy, were soaked in a saline environment for up to twelve weeks. A standard bending test measured the energy needed to start a shear crack, first under steady load and then under repeated fatigue load. A probability model helped analyze the scatter.

Resistance to peeling apart varied with soak time. The sobering result: the fracture energy a joint can endure forever under fatigue fell to about a fifth of its one time static capacity. The two year test program shows saline exposure and fatigue together erode adhesive joints badly. The authors frame the data as a warning for composite structures in marine service.
pmc-10744949:
Julia Petrović and a large team found a classic quantum effect hiding inside a disordered alloy of five metals. The Kondo effect appears when magnetic atoms scatter electrons in a shared rhythm. Their alloy mixes cerium with four other rare earths in random positions, with cerium levels from barely any to full.

Across all mixes, the effect behaved as if each cerium atom acted alone. That matches metallic glasses, not neat crystal lattices. The team blames the missing regular grid of magnetic atoms, which blocks a shared quantum state. The result widens where physicists expect this loner behavior.
pmc-10745549:
A breath test for lung cancer would spare patients needles and scans, and Zhunan Jia and co-authors put the idea to a clinical test in a 2023 study. Fourteen cancer patients were matched against similar non-cancer controls, with a few tuberculosis patients added. Breath was captured in a standard sampler and read by chromatography.

Thirteen airborne compounds differed between the groups, and a panel of eight separated them respectably in discovery and moderately in validation. The cancer breath ran rich in aldehydes, which the authors trace to an overactive detox enzyme in tumors. They frame breath analysis as promising but not yet clinic-ready.
pmc-10745649:
Yang and co-authors compare sous-vide cooking with standard high-heat cooking for tilapia fillets. They checked muscle structure, texture, fat damage, protein shape, and flavor compounds. Gentle water-bath cooking is prized for even results, but its effects here needed proof.

Sous-vide fillets kept more moisture and showed less protein damage than controls. Their structure stayed tight, with fewer gaps between muscle fibers. Hardness and spring were higher, and fat damage was much lower. Flavor mixes shifted too: some fruity and green notes rose, while harsh compounds fell. The method cut nutrient loss and enriched taste.
pmc-10746449:
Jing Yang and co-authors show how a long non-coding RNA holds back colon cancer by acting as a scaffold. Their 2023 study starts from a cancer database hunt for RNAs that fight tumors. One RNA, named FENDRR, ran low in colon tumor tissue and cells. Raising it in lab cells cut their growth, invasion, and movement, and slowed new vessel growth. Pull-down tests found two proteins that the RNA binds at once.

As a scaffold, the RNA brings an enzyme that tags one of those proteins for disposal, which lowers its level. Gene reads also showed a low-oxygen path dimmed when the RNA rose. Restoring the disposed protein undid the RNA's brake, which backs the chain.
pmc-10747349:
Anna Ziobro and co-authors published this 2023 study on radio tags sewn into textiles. Such tags let garments carry identity chips for tracking and care. Their design splits the sewn antenna from the chip, linking the two through small inductive loops instead of wires. To improve the design, the team first had to learn what drives tag performance.

They built a math model covering each part's impedance, the loops' shared pull, and the voltage reaching the chip. Antenna shape and the tuning circuit both entered the math. The shared pull between loops mattered most above 800 megahertz, where it steered chip voltage strongly. Model results were checked against simulations and bench tests that varied loop spacing. The work gives makers a map of design trade-offs.
pmc-10747649:
Eliza Wolska and co-authors compare two eye drop forms that carry an immune calming drug, in a 2023 study. The drug serves eye care widely, yet market drops hold at most a tenth of a percent and fade fast. The team built an emulsion and a self-mixing oil, each five times stronger.

Fine microscopy mapped the drops' structure, with three dimensional views of each form. Rabbit tests checked eye comfort for the drug forms and for blank carriers. Drug levels were read in the cornea, surface tissue, tears, and inner fluid after repeated dosing. The aim is a stronger drop that lasts longer on the eye.
pmc-10748249:
Stella Roussou and co-authors published a transport safety study in twenty twenty-three modeling how task difficulty and coping capacity combine to set driving risk. The work grew out of the i-DREAMS project, which aims to keep drivers inside a safety tolerance zone with live and post-trip feedback. Human behavior sits at the center of the model.

Eighty drivers in Belgium, Germany, and Portugal took part in naturalistic driving, generating roughly nineteen thousand trips. Statistical models linked road and traffic demands with driver and vehicle resources. Harder tasks came with higher coping capacity, suggesting drivers adapt as demands rise. Comparisons across countries and transport modes round out the picture of everyday risk.
pmc-10748349: Maciej Grzybek and three colleagues wrote an editorial in two thousand twenty-three on new and spreading infections. The piece opens a journal collection on emerging microbes, infections, and spillovers, where germs jump from animals to people. It frames a fast-changing field caught between hard problems and promising new tools. Globalisation and new technology shape both the risks and the responses the field must weigh.
pmc-10749449:
Xavier López and colleagues benchmark cheaper ways of computing the electronic couplings that govern energy and electron transfer between molecules. These couplings decide how fast charges and excitons move, hence how organic electronic materials perform. A rigorous fragment-based configuration interaction method gives trusted values but at high computational cost. Six less demanding techniques promise similar answers faster.

The team compared the approximate methods against the rigorous benchmark on four test systems, including tetracene and benzene-chloride. They covered hole and electron transport couplings, plus local exciton and singlet fission couplings. For charge transport, the approximate schemes predicted the benchmark couplings rather accurately. Exciton transfer and singlet fission couplings proved more difficult to reproduce. Knowing which approximations hold prevents wrong materials predictions at scale.
pmc-10750049:
Yuchao Song and four co-authors asked whether a three-metal nanomaterial harms plants more than its parts alone, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. Such mixed materials are now sold in many products. The test material joined zinc, bismuth, and cobalt oxides, mostly zinc oxide. Lettuce seedlings grew in the material, in zinc oxide alone, and in a plain mix of the three parts.

After three weeks, the mixed material cut root growth and plant weight. The dose that halved growth sat close to the dose for zinc oxide alone, and not far from the plain mix. About two-thirds of the root harm came from zinc ions leaking out of the particles. The authors say the new material's risk is much like that of its parts, which eases how it can be judged.
pmc-10755049:
Florian Postges and co-authors study phase homogeneity in three-part amorphous drug dispersions in a 2023 paper on poorly soluble drugs. Even mixing of polymers in the solid decides how well a drug dissolves and stays dissolved.

Two making routes gave opposite results with the HIV drug efavirenz and two cellulose grades. Hot-melt extrusion gave single-phase blends, while vacuum molding gave split phases. Raman imaging showed drug pooled in cellulose-rich zones of split blends. One cellulose grade mixed more readily due to lower melt thickness. Where phases split, dissolution gains shrank, though grade choice softened the process gap. Formulators get a clear lesson on process control.
pmc-10755849:
Dingyang Chen and co-authors build a cloth electrode that pulls uranium from sea water in a 2023 study. Sea water holds vast uranium, a prize for fuel supply. Their cloth wears a spongy frame laced with grab groups that seize uranyl ions. Spark sites in the frame join the grab work. An AC field drives the pair: grab, then turn the catch to a solid salt form.

Over 24 days in real sea water, the cloth took 12.6 milligrams per gram. No glue or metal sits in the build. Light reads at the molecule level back the grab-and-turn path. The authors pitch flex cloth as a scale path for sea mining.
pmc-10756949:
Chenjun Huang and co-authors issue a Chinese expert consensus on blood tests that help catch liver cancer early, from 2023. Liver cancer is among the most common cancers in the world, and half of new cases arise in China. Finding it early lifts survival a great deal. The statement covers a three-marker blood panel and the GALAD score built from it.

The panel joins two forms of one marker, AFP and AFP-L3, with a third marker, DCP. The GALAD model folds those reads with age and sex into one risk score. The panel of experts, drawn from lab and cancer societies, sets out who should be tested, how labs should run the tests, and how to read the results. The aim is wider, sounder use of the panel for watch lists, early finds, and outlook calls in high-risk care.
pmc-10757149:
Zhimin Gao and co-authors test whether adding an immune drug to standard chemotherapy raises blood side effects in bladder cancer in a 2023 study. The pairing of tislelizumab with gemcitabine and cisplatin is used for urothelial cancer, but its effect on bone marrow suppression was unclear. Records covered 192 patients at one hospital from 2014 to 2022.

After matching, 96 patients in each arm were compared. Low platelet counts of any grade hit 42.7 percent with the added drug against 20.8 percent without it. Age over 70 and the added drug each raised the odds of low platelets about three fold. Low white cells and anemia rates were closer between arms.
pmc-10759849:
Arrani Senthinathan and co-authors chart antibiotic use after spinal cord injury in a 2023 records study. People with such injuries use antibiotics heavily, but outpatient patterns were unmapped. The team linked medical records for 432 Ontario adults from 2013 to 2015 and modeled what drove prescription counts and course lengths.

About six in ten patients received an antibiotic from their family doctor in the period. Urinary tract infections drove about sixty percent of prescriptions, and one drug family, the fluoroquinolones, took about a quarter. Catheter use tripled the expected number of prescriptions. Doctors late in their careers prescribed longer courses than early-career doctors. The patterns point to urine infections as the main target for better prescribing.
pmc-10767549:
Wenfang Xu and co-authors trace how an immune signal helps destroy liver cells in autoimmune hepatitis. The disease, which strikes mostly women, makes the immune system attack the liver. A fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis, where cells burst and spill inflammatory contents, was suspected to play a part. The team focused on the signal IL-17 and a two-protein relay beneath it.

In liver cells, IL-17 raised levels of a sensor protein, IFI16, and boosted its partner STAT3. Cells then showed the bursting death pattern, and extra STAT3 made the damage worse. Blocking IL-17 calmed the pathway in cells and eased liver injury in mice, while forcing STAT3 up did the opposite. The authors name the IL-17 to STAT3 to IFI16 chain as a driver of injury and a drug target.
pmc-10770649:
Ólöf Guðný Geirsdóttir and Anne-Maria Pajari review what is known about protein in the diet for the Nordic Nutrition Recommendations 2023. Protein gives the body key amino acids, nitrogen, and fuel, and it matters most in pregnancy, childhood, and old age, when muscle loss is a risk. Adults in the Nordic and Baltic countries now get about 15 to 19 percent of their energy from protein.

The review weighs how protein needs are measured and finds the main method, nitrogen balance studies, has real limits. It also covers protein quality, food sources, and health effects, which stay hard to separate from other parts of the diet. Because animal protein strains the climate more than plant protein, the authors advise a shift toward more plant-based eating.
pmc-10772349:
Lucas Adams and co-authors characterize antibodies that grip the SARS-CoV-2 spike away from its usual hot spot, and show one protects mice through its tail, in a 2023 study. Most known antibodies target the spike's receptor-binding domain, which mutates freely. This panel aims at the N-terminal domain or other quieter patches. A subset blocks the virus after attachment and coats infected cells thickly.
