One antibody, SARS2-57, protected susceptible mice, but only with its Fc tail intact, meaning it works by summoning immune cleanup rather than neutralizing alone. Its grip site is exactly the patch that emerging variants remodel by deletion. Forced escape experiments grew the same deletion, unless an anti-RBD antibody joined in. The authors argue for cocktails that strike distant sites at once, so the virus cannot dodge with one edit.
pmc-10772549: Yize Li, Xin Ge, and Ru-Rong Ji wrote a short 2023 commentary on a new pain control method. Another team had built a switch that calms nerve cells that sense pain. The switch joins parts of two human receptors to form a channel. A virus delivers the channel into sensory nerves in mice. When a matched drug opens the channel, pain signals fade. The same approach quieted human sensory cells in the lab. The commentators present gene control like this as a promising path to pain relief without standard painkillers.
pmc-10800649:
Zhitao Chen and co-authors link Guangzhou weather to flu waves in children. Their paper, published in 2023 per the head, covers cases from 2019 to 2022 in ages up to seventeen. Weather data came from the provincial service. Models that allow delayed, curved effects traced how temperature, humidity, rain, and sunshine move flu risk.

Cold below thirteen degrees sent risk climbing fast, peaking near six degrees. Humidity raised risk at both low and high ends, in a U shape. Heavy rain beyond a threshold lifted risk sharply, while mid-range sunshine cut it. Effects hit seven-to-twelve-year-olds hardest. Toddlers, oddly, saw lower risk in extremes. The authors say these curves can sharpen flu early-warning systems.
pmc-10808349:
Xiangye Zhao, Xiaoning Li, and Yinghui Xu offer a 2023 review on a cell death pathway that can help or hurt tumors. The pathway, ferroptosis, kills cells through iron-driven damage to their fats. It is not the classic programmed death route. Links to many disorders, tumors among them, have emerged.

The review walks both faces of the pathway in cancer. It can feed tumor growth in some settings and block it in others. Topics include drug targets on the pathway and which cancer cells are prone to this death. Ways to pair it with current treatments are weighed, as is its interplay with the immune attack on tumors. The authors say mastery of this two-faced process is the key to using it in therapy.
pmc-10809149:
Sastry, Vempadapu, and Sivananjiah argue in a paper published in 2023 that the United Nations healthy aging agenda must be tailored to India's own history and traditions. Older Indians were long cared for at home by children. Swift urban growth and youth migration are now reshaping that pattern.

Demand for strong aged care programs is rising with global aging. Many Indian schemes exist but lack full national rollout, due to thin resources and rival priorities. The paper maps how current programs align with the UN agenda. It then weighs blocks and chances for turning policy into ground level care that fits Indian family life.
pmc-10811249:
Tomasz Woznicki and co-authors test whether the beds strawberries grow in can be reused for more than one season. Their study, published in 2023, runs in a plastic tunnel in Norway with a known berry variety. Three beds were tried: coconut fiber, peat, and spruce wood fiber. Each was used fresh, then again for a second and third year. Yield, berry quality, plant shape, and bed chemistry were tracked across the cycles.

Peat and wood fiber gave top yield in year one, with a slight dip on reuse that still matched coconut fiber. Berries from wood fiber tended to taste sweeter, and that bed grew the tallest plants. The authors back wood fiber and reuse as a greener path.
pmc-10822949:
Eleven authors trace milk antibody clones through repeat Covid shots in a 2023 case series. Milk from nursing mothers holds shot-led guard clones, and a mass spec path can read clone by clone. Six donors from a pool of 109 gave milk at 16 time points across two shots.

Each donor grew 89 to 191 shot-led clones, with counts and mix all her own. Most clones, 68 percent, came with shot one and stayed or came back at shot two. Two small sets split off, ones that faded fast and ones born only at shot two, in all donors.
pmc-10825949:
Roberto Baiocco and five co-authors compare young children across family forms in this paper. Debate about same-gender parenting often outruns data. The team studied seventy-six Italian families whose children were born through assisted reproduction. Most were same-gender parent families; the rest had a mother and a father. Children averaged about eight years old.

Parents reported their practices, and children were scored for kindness and for acting-out behavior. Models weighed parenting style while holding age, sex, and income steady. The design asks whether what parents do matters more than family shape. Such evidence informs courts, clinics, and policy. Family psychologists are the readers.
pmc-10828849:
Yahui Yu and co-authors wrote a study, dated 2023 in its text, on how overprotective parenting links to the feelings and acts of children with blood cancer. These children have weak immune systems, so their parents often worry a great deal and step in too much. That worry can shape the child's mood and daily life. The team surveyed parents at three child cancer hospitals in China.

Parents of two hundred and two children filled out forms on the child's feelings, acts, and social life, plus a scale that graded how much they shielded the child. Signs of distress were most common in feelings, then in peer ties. Older age, a longer illness, and more shielding each raised the odds of these problems. A set score on the shielding scale flagged at-risk children well. The team urges staff to help parents ease back.
pmc-10836249:
People exposed to HIV can take preventive drugs afterward, but the course only works if they finish it. Shanshan Liu and four co-authors pooled cohort studies in a 2023 meta-analysis of how well people stick with this post-exposure course and how often side effects drive them to stop.

Across the studies, only about 58 percent of people finished the course as directed. Completion was highest among men who have sex with men, at about 72 percent, and lowest among survivors of sexual assault, at about 42 percent. Side effects were common, reported by about 60 percent, and roughly a third of users stopped because of them. The authors use the gaps to suggest where support programs should focus first.
pmc-10837849:
Ruijing Chen and Jun Chen review a bold treatment idea for metabolic diseases: moving healthy mitochondria, the cell's power stations, into sick cells. Their review appeared in 2023. Faulty mitochondria sit at the heart of many disorders of energy use, from diabetes to fatty liver.

Healthy cells naturally pass mitochondria to injured neighbors, and stem cells can donate them too. Studies show such transfers can restore energy work in damaged tissue. Moving the organelles alone, rather than whole cells, sparks less immune reaction. The review sums up how transfers happen, what they have healed in early studies, and what blocks their use in clinics. The authors see direct mitochondrial therapy as a field worth pushing forward.
pmc-10839049:
Xiaoran Kong, Yatong Zhou, Zhe Li, and Shaohai Wang proposed in 2024 a deep reinforcement learning method that assigns targets and plans paths for a team of drones at once. Both jobs must be solved together in settings with moving obstacles and partial views. They framed the task as a partially observable decision process.

A target assignment network was added to a strong policy algorithm. At each step, the network assigns targets, the policy plans a path for that assignment, and its feedback trains the assignment network in turn. In three-dimensional scenes with many moving obstacles, the system gave complete, well-matched assignments and collision-free paths. It beat prior methods on target completion and adapted better to complex scenes.
pmc-10845649:
Samir and eight co-authors test a heart drug as a brain protector in rats, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Ranolazine, used for angina, also acts in the brain, and the team asked whether it could blunt a chemically induced dementia resembling Alzheimer's disease.

Rats given scopolamine, which disrupts memory, learned a water maze more slowly and showed inflamed, damaged hippocampus tissue. Pre-treatment with ranolazine restored faster learning, raised antioxidant enzyme activity, lowered inflammatory signals, and increased a growth factor that supports neurons. Markers of cell death and abnormal tau fell as well. The results nominate ranolazine for further study as a dementia treatment, though human evidence is far off.
pmc-10849049:
Jingying Wang, Kai Yip Choi, Benjamin Thompson, Henry Ho Lung Chan, and Allen Ming Yan Cheong wrote a pilot study on brain stimulation and sight. The head lists the paper as published in 2023, though the catalog gives 2024. The team tested a weak electric current sent through the scalp, and asked whether where the pads sit changes the effect.

Ten healthy young adults took part in three sessions, with pads in two layouts and one fake session. Each visit gave twenty minutes of the current, and the team measured brain waves from the back of the head before and after. The sight signal fell right after all three sessions, then came back to its starting level. The drop, even after fake treatment, warns against reading too much into small early tests.
pmc-10912849:
Richard Maziarz and co-authors tally what stem cell transplants from donors cost the United States health system. The procedure, allo-HCT, can cure blood cancers but demands years of care. Conditioning, hospital stays, and complications stack the bills. Their 2023 paper takes the payer's view: what insurers actually spend across the whole arc. More than eight thousand such transplants run each year in the country.

World counts top twenty-four thousand a year. Volumes have climbed for decades as the method spread. The team frames cost as a planning problem, not just a price tag. Therapies that shorten hospital time or cut complication rates could save large sums. The paper gives payers and hospitals a shared cost map.
pmc-10920349:
Tingting Li and co-authors report survival and illness among very preterm babies in Shenzhen in a study whose head dates it to 2023. Babies born before thirty-two weeks face high risks, and local outcome data guide care and counseling. The study drew on a network of twenty-five newborn intensive care units across the city.

Of nearly eight hundred babies admitted in 2022, about nine in ten survived. Survival rose steeply with each extra week of pregnancy, from about half at the earliest ages to nearly all at thirty to thirty-one weeks. Two thirds of survivors escaped major complications. Lung disease was the most common serious problem. After adjustments, care factors such as steroids before birth linked to better outcomes.
pmc-11143549:
Bijan Piryaei and Sima Sajadi compare how leading countries work to prevent child drowning, a major killer of young children worldwide. The United States, Australia, and Canada are treated as pioneers in this area. The study reviews their prevention plans and what their drowning reports record.

The three countries use broadly similar measures, such as limiting access to water, teaching water safety, and rescue training, with some gaps by country. The United States reports the widest range of details, from activity and place to supervision and swim skills. The authors suggest Iran set up a central body for prevention and adapt global guidance to local climate and culture.
pmc-11225449:
Godfrey Limungi and co-authors studied tuberculosis treatment in children of a nomadic herding community in Kenya, in a 2023 paper. Child TB stays a major cause of illness and death in poor regions. Moving herder families face extra barriers to steady care. The study ran at Lodwar County Referral Hospital in Turkana.

The team reviewed fifty-nine child records and spoke with eight nurses. Outcomes were counted from the charts. Provider challenges were drawn from deep interviews and grouped by theme. Travel distance, stock gaps, and follow-up loss all surfaced. The findings can shape outreach that fits a moving population.
pmc-11285649:
Kenichiro Sato and co-authors check in a study published in 2023 whether a risk gene for Alzheimer disease also raises other brain side effects in drug trials, even without treatment. The gene variant, APOE e4, is tied to a swelling side effect of new amyloid drugs, which can be confused with stroke events. Knowing its wider effects could sharpen trial safety reads.

Placebo-arm data from twenty-eight trials and 6,313 patients were pooled. Several complaints, from delusions to muscle spasms, were reported more often in carriers. Yet once thinking scores were held equal, none of the gaps stayed firm. The team finds no strong proof of extra non-swelling effects from the gene.
pmc-11532549:
Wang and co-authors show how two proteins, talin and vinculin, join forces to build actin fibers. Focal adhesions anchor cells and must grip actin more firmly to resist force. Talin and vinculin bind at these sites, but whether their pair could start actin growth was unknown.

Testing that pair required rebuilding the steps that switch them on, both mechanical and chemical. The team mixed kinetic assays with re-formed protein systems to watch the process. Together, talin and vinculin triggered actin assembly in these tests. The finding explains how adhesions gain strength when cells pull against their surroundings.
pmc-11532649:
A fifty-four year old Thai woman with Graves disease, an overactive thyroid condition, went to surgery because the disease was pushing on her eyes. Waralee Chatchomchuan and co-authors report what the surgeons found. During the thyroid removal, three lumps that looked like overgrown parathyroid glands were taken out. Under the microscope, most of that tissue was not parathyroid at all. It was hyperplastic thymus tissue, sitting in the neck where it does not belong, mixed with one normal parathyroid gland.

One supposed gland turned out to be a plain lymph node. Her calcium and hormone levels had been normal before surgery, which fit the surprise finding. She needed calcium supplements for six months while her remaining parathyroid recovered. The authors warn that stray thymus tissue in Graves disease can mimic parathyroid overgrowth, and they advise checking blood chemistry before removing such tissue.
pmc-11534349:
A follow-up system built by doctors for doctors is introduced in a 2024 letter by Zhiwen Luo and co-authors. China's hospitals handle huge patient volumes, yet data handling and systematic follow-up lag, above all in sports medicine, where recovery stretches over months.

Existing systems, the authors write, bolt poorly onto clinic routines and were designed without clinician input. Their answer, SportSync Health, streamlines registration, evaluation, and follow-up with quick entry and precise retrieval. Rising sports participation has swollen demand for injury rehab and chronic disease care, making such tools urgent. The letter presents the system as a clinician-first template for data-driven care in busy Chinese hospitals.
pmc-11535549:
Tan and a large team of colleagues list shape-scale gene shifts in Asian genomes in this twenty twenty-four study. Past gene lists lean hard to white roots, which leaves Asian shifts poorly charted. Big shifts in DNA shape can sway traits and ills just as small ones can.

Inside, full gene reads from more than eight thousand folks in Singapore feed the list. The haul holds scores of thousands of shifts, and near two in three are new to science. More than half the Asian-only finds sit in just one of three root groups in the study. Some shifts touch spots that guide drug care, and links to small marks help pin cause in trait hunts.
pmc-11536549:
Kasahara and a team including Teratani and Doi tested a gel in twenty twenty-four that slow-feeds stem cell soup to regrow cut livers in fatty-liver rats. Fatty liver slows regrowth after tumor cuts and raises risk. Stem cell soup holds rich fix goods, and gels can hold and drip it in place.

Rats on a fat diet had part of the liver cut, then gel or blank by a gut vein. Soup rats regrew the rest faster and with more cell marks. Their livers held more fuel stores and showed less cell death. Growth ran by cell swell more than split, they find.
pmc-11536849:
Yongzhou Liang, Ying Liu, Qin Tan, Kaiyu Zhou, Yurong Wu, and Li Yu trace how an anti-aging protein connects to metabolic syndrome, with inflammation as the middleman. Their 2024 study mines a national survey of 13,119 Americans aged 40 to 79 across five cycles. Metabolic syndrome affected nearly 44 percent of the group.

Higher blood levels of the Klotho protein tracked with lower syndrome rates and better component measures. Mediation analysis then asked how much of that link flows through immune-inflammation markers: white cell counts, neutrophil ratios, and composite inflammation indexes. The inflammatory path carried a real share of the association. The authors propose Klotho and its inflammatory shadow as tools for spotting risk early. They also flag the pathway as a possible treatment lever for the syndrome.
pmc-11536949:
Naser Owji and seven co-authors report six cases of a rare eye socket condition caused by mineral oil in tissue, in a 2024 paper. The condition followed sinus surgery in their cases. Oil that seeps into tissue triggers a slow, lumpy reaction. The team also reviewed past cases found in four databases.

Their review sorts knowledge of the condition into clear groups. Those groups cover what the condition is and how it differs from look-alikes. Signs in the clinic and on scans are set out in turn. Lab features under the microscope and treatment options follow. The condition can appear long after surgery, which makes first diagnosis hard. The authors urge eye doctors to keep it in mind for masses near the eyelid. A history of nose or sinus surgery is the key clue.
pmc-11538449:
Luis Contreras-Huerta and co-authors present a 2024 study on how people gather rewards for themselves versus for others. People value their own rewards more, a self-bias. The team tested that bias in a foraging task drawn from animal ecology. Players had to choose when to leave a patch whose rewards faded over time, in settings with varied average rates.

Theory gives a clear rule for the best leaving time. Across two studies, people followed that rule more closely when they foraged for themselves. When they foraged for a stranger, they leaned more on the fading rate in the patch. Traits linked to autism changed the pattern for self-foraging only. The bias may help people gain more.
pmc-11539249:
Karina González, Teresa Eixarch, Laura Nuñez, and Gema Ariceta measure the mental load on parents caring for children with nephropathic cystinosis, in a study from 2024. The disease is severe and lifelong, yet caregiver strain had barely been documented. Standard scales for anxiety, burden, and quality of life were used.

Nine mothers from one center took part; their children averaged about thirteen years old. Six mothers showed anxiety or depression, and four carried severe care burden. General health and health change were the worst-rated life domains. Mothers free of depression and with low burden reported notably better quality of life, and every high-burden mother was anxious or depressed.
pmc-11544449:
Yunmeng Li and six colleagues track sea bacteria across a full year at a Belgian beach, in a twenty twenty-four study. The surf zone at Ostend draws crowds, and its germ mix affects water quality. The team sampled weekly and read full-length gene markers to name the bacteria. They matched the mix against water factors such as temperature, plant pigment, and growth rates.

Seasons shaped the mix far more than human waste inputs did. Spring favored germs tied to sulfur use, while summer favored feeders on organic matter. Fall and winter brought types linked to methanol use and more possibly harmful forms. The study sets a baseline for how beach germs shift with the year.
pmc-11545849:
Antibiotic resistance is pushing researchers back to nature for new germ killers, and algae are a rich hunting ground. Antonio Zuorro and co-authors review the field in 2024, covering the antimicrobial compounds that microalgae and cyanobacteria produce.

The active families include polysaccharides, fatty acids, and phenols, some already effective against drug-resistant bacteria. A mapping of the literature sorted research into five clusters, from resistance itself to water treatment and new drug compounds. The compounds attack germs by blocking protein building and tearing membranes, among other routes. The authors look ahead to scaling algal farming, tuning strains with genetic and metabolic engineering, and turning promising extracts into real treatments.
pmc-11551449:
Annie Curtis, Sze Yen Tan, Anna Boltong, Jennifer Cohen and Nicole Kiss review how childhood cancer treatment affects taste and food liking. Poor nutrition is a risk during treatment and after it, and taste plus food pleasure shape how much a child eats. The review ran two search arms across four databases to June 2022.

Nine taste studies and four food liking studies met the rules. Treatment effects on taste varied widely during care and into survivorship. Children on chemotherapy learned aversions to some foods, and liking for meats and salty foods shifted, while appetite effects also varied. The authors say more work is needed to judge how much these changes matter in clinic.
pmc-11569149:
Nisha Krishnan and six co-authors built a gene activity reference for an Indian Ocean squid, in a 2024 paper. Squids and their kin have large brains and sharp senses for molluscs. Few gene resources exist for this species. The team read gene activity in five tissues: brain, eye, gill, heart, and reproductive organs.

Millions of short reads were pieced together with a standard assembler. The result held just over twenty-six thousand protein-coding sequences. A completeness check found about seventy-two percent of expected genes. Pathway checks showed the squid shares many genes and pathways with higher animals with backbones. The resource enriches the data available for squid studies. It may help work on how this group evolved its brain and senses, the authors suggest.
pmc-11570649:
Krishnasamy Karthik and seven co-authors make a light composite from palm flower waste in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Natural fibers are cheap, light, and break down in nature, unlike synthetic ones. The team drew cellulose from the flowers of the palmyra palm, a waste stream. They used it as a filler in a banana fiber composite with a starch-based matrix. The goal was a strong but green material for light-duty uses.

They characterized the new filler and the finished composite with standard lab tools. Spectroscopy confirmed the cellulose chemistry, and tests gauged strength and behavior. Adding the biofiller improved the composite's properties over the base mix. Such materials could replace plastics in panels and packaging. The study turns farm waste into an engineering input.
pmc-11573649:
Tian Gan and ten co-authors test an idea about the ocean that followed a global ice age more than six hundred million years ago. Their study came out in 2024. The plumeworld idea says a layer of fresh meltwater floated on salty seawater after the ice melted.

The team measured lithium isotopes, a chemical fingerprint, in a rock layer formed at that time along a shore-to-offshore line in South China. The fingerprint weakened with distance from shore, exactly as mixing between meltwater and salty seawater would predict. The pattern also fits weak rock weathering on land during the ice age and stronger reverse weathering on the seafloor. The rise and fall of the meltwater plume matches the time the rock layer took to form.
pmc-11573949:
Yamamoto and six co-authors reported this surgical case in twenty twenty-four. A seventy-six-year-old man arrived with a swollen belly and vomiting. Scans showed his small bowel had telescoped into itself, a blockage called intussusception. The cause turned out to be a lump of pancreas tissue growing in the wrong place, inside the jejunum.

Doctors repaired the bowel with keyhole surgery and removed the affected section. Lab tests showed the misplaced pancreas tissue had turned cancerous. Such cases are rare and hard to catch before surgery, since blockage is often the first sign. Two years later the man showed no sign of the cancer returning. The authors call for more case reports to shape treatment.
pmc-11574049:
Yuying Jin and co-authors select a reliable antibody and build automated counting for a pain-related channel in human skin, in a 2024 paper. The channel, TRPV1, sits in skin nerve fibers and matters for neuropathy and pain. Judging where it lies needs staining methods that truly work on human skin. Data on the specificity and sensitivity of the antibodies in use were lacking, which is the gap addressed.

They screen candidate antibodies from several makers on rat tissue and human skin, then validate the best on cells engineered to express the channel. Final checks run on human skin samples. They also build two automated image analysis routes, one deep-learning based and one machine-learning based. Both count the stained spots along nerve fibers.
pmc-11574449:
Some people carry two or more abnormal blood proteins at once, Saemundur Rognvaldsson and co-authors report in a 2024 screening study. The proteins mark MGUS, a silent state that can precede blood cancer. Iceland's screening program tested more than seventy-five thousand adults over forty.

About one in eleven of those with any abnormal protein had several at once. One protein type, IgM, appeared far more often in the multi-protein group. How such mixed cases progress and how doctors should follow them is poorly known. Population-scale data like this gives clinics a firmer base for follow-up rules instead of guesswork on a rare and puzzling subgroup.
pmc-11575149:
Rongjian Yu and co-authors study the heart's filling phase in long-term cancer survivors, a side of heart function that checks often skip. Survivors face higher risks of heart failure and death, and most screening watches the squeeze, not the refill. Their 2024 study uses a large community cohort with heart scans and cancer histories, covering 5,322 people of whom about eighteen percent were survivors.

About twelve percent of survivors had diastolic dysfunction, much the same share as matched non-survivors. The stepwise pattern was the warning: borderline filling doubled the risk of heart failure, and clear dysfunction more than quadrupled it. Death risk climbed the same way. The pattern held across subgroups and matched the survival curves. The authors urge that refill checks join squeeze checks in the long-term care of cancer survivors.
pmc-11576749:
Reindert Oostveen and co-authors gave a seaweed-based imaging tracer to humans for the first time in a 2024 study. The tracer uses fucoidan, a sugar chain from brown algae that grips P-selectin, a marker that appears on vessel walls and platelets when clots form. Tagged with a radioactive label, it could let scans spot fresh thrombosis early. Ten healthy volunteers received it for safety, spread, and radiation dose measurements.

No drug-related side effects appeared, and the radiation dose was modest. In the lab, the tracer bound human clots, and blocking the target cut that binding. Three patients with fresh leg vein clots were scanned; in one, the tracer lit up exactly at the clot. The authors call the profile favorable while noting the detection signal needs strengthening.
pmc-11576949:
Simona Affinito and co-authors use brain wave reads to probe how early kin of humans used stone tools. The study appeared in 2024. Tool craft drove much of our line's growth, but tool use got less brain care than tool make. Two acts sit in view, hard hits and fine cuts.

Hits with a hand stone were shared with apes and mark the first tool claims. Cuts with a flake are a lone human kin act tied to a known old culture. Both acts lit front and side brain zones. Flake cuts lit those zones more, most in the aim step. The team ties plain brain shifts to fine tool use.
pmc-11577049:
Michele Lemons and co-authors (2024) show that a molecule in the material around cells helps build the tiny spines where synapses form. The molecule is collagen XVIII, known in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans as CLE-1. The team studied spines on the dendrites of the worm's GABAergic neurons, the cells that calm brain activity. In worms lacking the gene, spines were fewer. The collagen was found sitting right beside normal spines, positioned to influence them.

When the gene was switched back on only in those GABAergic neurons, spine numbers partly recovered. That local rescue suggests the neurons themselves deposit the collagen that their own spines need. The extracellular matrix, long treated as mere packing material, here acts as a local instructor of synapse development. The finding adds a remodeling player to the story of how connections are built and kept.
pmc-11577649:
Nasrin Shokrpour, Zeinab Soleymani, and AmirYusef Farahmandi study links between online learning and two kinds of intelligence in nursing students. Their 2024 paper surveys recent entrants at a medical university in Shiraz, Iran. The team ask how electronic learning relates to emotional intelligence and to cultural intelligence.

Over a hundred students completed three questionnaires covering the three topics. Statistical tests found significant ties between emotional intelligence and online learning on one side, and cultural intelligence on the other. Online learning also linked with parts of emotional intelligence. Nurses care for diverse patients and increasingly learn online, so both capacities matter for training. The correlations give educators a reason to build emotional and cultural skills into digital courses.
pmc-11577849:
Qihui Wu and co-authors test a classic herbal formula in mice bred to model Alzheimer's disease, in a 2024 study. The formula, Danggui-Shaoyao-San, has a long history in Chinese medicine. Drugs aimed at amyloid clumps have failed in trials, so the team asked whether the formula works through brain energy use instead.

Treated mice did better on behavior tests, lost fewer neurons, and carried less amyloid. A network study sifted over a thousand herbal parts to 253 core ones. Protein and metabolite maps pointed to energy paths, and lab checks showed the formula tuned a key signal path. That tuning lifted sugar uptake and eased cell power strain.
pmc-11579349:
Saravanan, Haiter Lenin, and co-authors burn lemon peel oil blends in a spark engine with a clad piston crown, in a 2024 study. Peel oil is drawn by steam from thrown peel waste. Blends with fuel at three grades are tried for heat yield and fumes, with scope views of flame birth.

The lean blend beat fuel and rich blends on yield and fumes when bare. Coat on the crown then lifts rich blend yield past bare fuel. Fumes of two harsh kinds fall by a clear edge in that clad rich case. Waste peel may thus serve as a fuel part.
pmc-11580349:
Ahmed Abbas and co-authors present a lab method in 2024 for measuring all five ingredients of a migraine mixture at once with ultraviolet light. The five drugs sit at wildly different doses and their light spectra overlap heavily, which defeats simple tests. Three math models were compared for untangling the spectra. A careful scheme for splitting calibration data avoided biased checks.

One model, a curve-resolution method, recovered each ingredient within a few percent of truth. Its calibration and prediction errors were the smallest of the three. Six sustainability metrics rated the approach green, cheap, and practical. The authors pitch it for quality control of complex drug mixes.
pmc-11580549:
Chun-Zeng Jia weighs, in a 2024 meta-analysis, a hard choice after early bowel cancer is removed through a scope but not fully cured. Doctors must decide whether to send the patient for major follow-up surgery or simply watch closely, and studies have argued both ways.

Jia pooled fifteen studies covering about thirty-five hundred patients. Roughly two thousand had the extra surgery and fifteen hundred were watched. The surgery group lived longer overall and stayed free of recurrence more often, by clear margins. All included studies scored well on a standard quality scale. The balance of evidence favors operating, though each patient's surgical risk still shapes the final call.
pmc-11582349:
Jill Bradshaw and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on what would have helped people with profound and multiple learning needs in the United Kingdom during COVID-19. Little was known about this group, since they are often left out of research. The authors draw on paid and family carers who filled in a survey at four points from late 2020 to late 2022.

Carers said services shrank and had not yet come back to old levels by the third wave. People faced more time alone, worse health, and more signs of stress. The paper also gathers carer views on what support should look like in a future crisis.
pmc-11582449:
Junping Zhou and seven co-workers used sour milk germs to boost taste and health agents in pandan leaves. Pandan is used all through Asia as a food dye and spice. How such germs change it had barely been probed. The 2024 tests used three germ types. Each type soured pandan on its own. The team then gauged traits of the leaf, its guard strength in the body, its scent agents, and its small compounds.

The sour step raised total phenol counts by 13 to 21 percent. Flavonoid counts rose by 33 to 53 percent. Pandan soured with one strain, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, showed the best guard strength. Scent agents such as alpha-ionone rose, and brand new ones showed up too. They took in damascenone and linalool. The work lays a base for soured pandan goods with rich taste and strong health traits.
pmc-11583449:
Jung and nine co-authors tested infection control steps in an intensive care unit for this study from twenty twenty-four. The target was carbapenem-resistant gut bacteria, a hard-to-treat hospital threat. One Seoul unit screened all patients weekly, then added universal gloves-and-gowns precautions plus antiseptic bathing. Rates before and after were compared over nearly three years.

Thirty-five of over one thousand seven hundred patients picked up the bacteria during their stay. The pickup rate dipped slightly but not significantly after the steps began. Colonization by resistant organisms overall did fall. Prior exposure to carbapenem antibiotics and crowded colonization around a patient raised risk. The authors say precautions alone fall short without antibiotic stewardship.
pmc-11584749:
Derek Jones and co-authors present HDBind in a 2024 paper on fast screening of drug candidates. Finding molecules that bind a protein target usually leans on heavy physics calculations or on deep learning models that are hard to speed up in hardware. The team turned to hyperdimensional computing, which encodes data as long binary vectors and learns with simple operations.

They devised graph-based encodings that turn a molecule's structure into such vectors, improving on earlier attempts. On two public benchmark sets the method beat rivals, and it ran on graphics cards and programmable chips with at least ten times better energy use than even a small neural network. The authors argue the approach suits ultra-fast pre-screening of large drug libraries.
pmc-11585049:
Dingwei Ye and co-authors report baseline data from two thousand twenty-four for a large Asian registry of advanced prostate cancer. Prostate cancer is rising across Asia, but its features, treatment, and outcomes in the region were poorly documented. The registry, whose short name is UFO, followed patients at major hospitals in eight Asian countries and regions.

More than three thousand six hundred patients joined between two thousand fifteen and two thousand twenty. Most had cancer that had already spread, while smaller groups had high-risk local disease or a biochemical return without spread. Mean age at diagnosis sat in the late sixties. Quality of life was worst in the metastatic group. Treatment choices followed guidelines and disease progress.
pmc-11585249:
Branislav Kovacech and co-authors re-look at a tau vaccine trial in Alzheimer's disease, zooming in on patients whose blood already showed a strong disease signal. Their analysis appeared in 2024. The vaccine, AADvac1, trains the immune system against the tau protein's binding region, hoping to slow its spread through the brain. The original two-year trial randomized patients with mild disease to six doses then boosters, or to placebo, with safety as the main goal.

This follow-up focused on those positive for plasma p-tau217, a marker of Alzheimer's pathology. In that subgroup the team examined thinking scores, daily living scores, and immune response to the vaccine. The authors say biomarker-selected subgroups may show a vaccine's effect more clearly than the full mixed trial population.
pmc-11585549:
Parkinson's disease harms movement and thinking, yet its roots inside the brain remain unclear. A large team of researchers built a detailed atlas of the disease in 2024 by reading the gene activity of single cell nuclei. They drew on 100 donated brains, cases and healthy controls spanning the full range of disease severity, and covered five brain regions.

Alongside the cell data, they gathered whole-genome data for the same donors. Careful checks kept the data clean, and the finished atlas is posted openly on a public research platform. The authors offer it as a shared tool for finding the molecular roots of Parkinson's and speeding new treatments.
pmc-11585949:
Daisuke Sugiura and colleagues build a low-cost microcontroller system for measuring how crops use water. Their 2024 article addresses the need for higher-throughput ways to find varieties with better water-use efficiency.

The system combines pot weighing, automated water supply, and real-time monitoring over Wi-Fi. It was validated on rice, soybean, and maize under salt, waterlogging, and drought stress. Salt-tolerant rice kept using more water and growing better under salinity than sensitive rice. Waterlogged soybean used less water and grew less. Long experiments revealed efficiency differences between rice varieties and root-shoot changes in drought-stressed maize.
pmc-11587649:
Lara Abou Ammar and a large team explored COVID-19 rapid antigen testing among displaced people in Iraq. Their 2024 paper reports a pilot run by aid groups in four camps. The camps sit in the Kurdistan region of Iraq. The pilot aimed to widen access to testing in displacement settings. It also sought to learn what helps or blocks testing there.

Data covered late 2022 through early 2023. The team judged how well the antigen card test performed in this group. Results were compared by case likelihood, vaccination status, and symptom severity. Participants also shared views on rapid testing for COVID-19 and other diseases. Secondary analysis used de-identified records from the pilot. Findings can guide testing in future outbreaks among displaced groups.
pmc-11587749:
Wang and co-authors set out a trial protocol, published in 2024, to test a bundled approach to feeding stroke patients through tubes. Feeding this way involves many steps, and a lapse in any one can harm the patient. Chinese wards show major shortcomings in this care. Past studies tested single fixes, leaving the value of a whole bundle unproven. The team's bundle joins several proven practices into one routine, applied together. Their trial will roll the bundle out across wards in stages.

The design, called a stepped wedge, lets every ward receive the bundle eventually while still allowing fair comparison. Ten study periods are planned across the wards of eight hospitals. Outcomes will show whether the bundle improves feeding safety and nutrition together. The protocol paper lays out the plan in full before results arrive. That advance record protects the trial from later second-guessing.
pmc-11589749:
Masataka Wada and co-authors probe brain chemistry in depression that resists standard treatment, in a 2024 study. Faults in the glutamate system, a key signaling route, are suspected. The team used magnetic pulses paired with brain-wave reads to gauge that system in the front of the brain.

Sixty patients with resistant depression and thirty healthy adults took part. The pulse test measured a boost effect that mirrors glutamate action in the left prefrontal area. The team then matched brain maps of that activity against gene data from a human brain atlas. Lower activity lined up with lower levels of genes tied to astrocytes, the brain's support cells. The link ties a living brain measure to a cell-level clue in hard-to-treat depression.
pmc-11589849:
Yanan Zhao and six co-authors present EfNST, a new computer method for finding regions in tissue from spatial data, in a 2024 research paper. The data pairs gene activity readings with images of the tissue slice. Such data are vast and noisy, so picking out fine regions is hard.

EfNST uses a scaled image network to learn features at several sizes at once. Tested on six data sets from three platforms, the method beat rival tools on accuracy and ran faster on modest hardware. It picked out small subregions in labelled tissue and found matching marker genes. In unlabelled tissue it still found tiny regions and their gene patterns. The work offers a faster way to map how cells are arranged in tissue.
pmc-11590849:
Stephen Oakley, Samantha Stott, Kerri Gill, and Lyanne Weston test whether built-in body stiffness links rheumatoid arthritis severity to its excess heart disease. Their study came out in 2024. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune joint disease, and patients die early from cardiovascular disease more often than others.

The team measured joint flexibility, artery stiffness, and skin stretch in fifty-eight patients and fifty-seven controls. Joint stiffness tracked with both artery and skin stiffness in the same person. Patients whose joint damage advanced fastest had stiffer joints and arteries, and stiffer skin early in the disease. Since the disease does not attack skin, the authors argue that stiffness is a constitutional trait present from birth. That trait may drive both worse arthritis and worse heart outcomes. Prospective studies are needed to test causality.
pmc-11591149:
A team including Zhuo Yang studies how a giant clam guards its cells against harm from oxygen. The clam lives with tiny algae that make food from light, and that close tie needs a fine balance of cell chemistry. The researchers found a gene switch, TsNfe2l, that turns on defense genes. One gene it controls makes carnosine, a shield against cell harm.

When the switch could not bind to DNA, the shield gene fell quiet and fat damage in the gill rose. The work names a key chain that keeps the clam's cell balance steady.
pmc-11591749: Grażyna Lietzau introduces a special journal issue devoted to the biology of neurodegenerative disorders, in this 2024 editorial. These diseases slowly destroy neurons across the brain and spinal cord, and no cure exists today. That incurability, the editorial argues, makes deeper biological research all the more urgent. The issue was assembled as an open call for studies in the field, spanning mechanisms, models, and candidate treatments.
pmc-11591949:
Stelios Psarras reviews, in twenty twenty-four, how two cell types in the heart shape repair and scarring. The heart heals poorly after injury, and that failure can lead to heart failure. Fibroblasts are cells that build the tissue scaffold. When overactive, they lay down too much collagen, stiffening the heart. That scarring process is called fibrosis. Macrophages are immune cells that can help or harm fibroblasts, depending on their state and subtype.

Psarras argues the pair should be read as a dipole, two poles that shape each other. The influence runs both ways, not just from immune cells to scaffold cells. That two-way talk offers points where treatment might steer repair toward healing and away from scarring.
pmc-11592449:
Bozzola and co-authors review what screen time may do to children's eyes in a 2024 paper. Children now meet phones and tablets earlier and use them longer. The team searched world research on media devices and eye health for ages up to eighteen. They kept 26 studies that fit their rules.

Four risks stood out: early near-sight, full near-sight, digital eye strain, and a sudden inward eye turn. Each risk grew with close, long screen use. The authors call for family teaching on safe screen habits. They also urge doctors to ask about screen time at checkups and when eye trouble appears. Clear talk with parents, they argue, is the first line of defense.
pmc-11594449:
Biancari and co-authors compared two aortic root operations in 2024 for a tearing of the body's main artery, using a European registry of over thirty-seven hundred patients. When the tear reaches the root, surgeons either replace it with a valved tube or rebuild it while sparing the patient's own valve.

Practice varied widely between hospitals. The valved-tube operation was far more common. After matching similar patients, outcomes barely differed, except more dialysis in the tube group. Ten-year death and reoperation rates also matched after adjustment. Both operations proved durable. The authors advise the valve-sparing route when feasible, in experienced hands, since it is the more demanding technique.
pmc-11597149:
Irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease share a grind of gut symptoms, poor sleep, anxiety, and worn-down quality of life. Veronique Traynard and co-authors scoped the evidence in 2024 on add-on therapies that sit beside standard drug care. They gathered current guidelines and trials on diet, activity, talk therapy, and medical nutrition.

The Mediterranean diet, regular physical activity, and cognitive behavioral therapy all earned support as helpful adjuncts. So did selected probiotics, soluble fibers, chitin-glucan, peppermint oil, and targeted micronutrients. The authors say these add-ons can ease lingering symptoms, repair nutrition gaps, and lift daily life, and they frame the review as a toolkit for building personal care plans.
pmc-11597649:
Samuel De La Barrera and co-authors asked in 2024 whether vitamin K levels in blood cause type 1 diabetes. The vitamin helps type 2 diabetes in some studies, but its role in the autoimmune form was unknown. Instead of a feeding trial, the team used genes as natural stand-ins: people born with gene variants that raise vitamin K served as the test group.

Across a very large European diabetes data set, shifts in vitamin K levels did not change diabetes risk. The team also weighed gut microbes, which make some vitamin K, in the same frame. The null result steers diet hopes away from this vitamin for this disease.
pmc-11598449:
Scorpion stings are a real public health burden in warm regions, yet the many venoms and their effects are scattered across the literature. Masoumeh Baradaran and co-authors present ScorpDb in this 2024 paper, a free online database built to gather that knowledge in one place. It catalogs scorpion species along with the peptides and proteins in their venoms and the symptoms stings can cause.

The database starts with the scorpion fauna of Iran, the team's home ground. The authors invite the wider field to add species and venom parts from other regions over time. They aim the resource at toxin experts, spider and scorpion scholars, and drug researchers alike, since venom peptides can also inspire new medicines.
pmc-11599849:
Futagawa leads a team profiling gene variants and symptoms in Japanese neurofibromatosis patients in a 2024 cohort paper. The condition causes tumors and many other features, varying widely by person. Hereditary tumor clinics supplied the cases.

Testing found disease-causing variants in most suspected patients, and a fifth of those variants were new to science. A striking share of adults had malignancies, with breast cancer in a fifth of the women. High blood pressure was also common in adults. Patients with large gene deletions showed stronger skin, bone, and nerve features. The authors urge regular surveillance, above all for cancer and blood pressure. Genetic counseling gains from these local data. Multidisciplinary care is the closing message.
pmc-11600549:
Jiapeng Xu and co-authors published this review in 2024. It updates what is known about flu viruses resisting neuraminidase inhibitor drugs, the class that includes common antivirals. The team gathered worldwide reports of resistant strains and cataloged the gene changes behind them. One change, H274Y, peaked back in 2008 and hit public health hard in places like Japan and the United States.

Resistance arises three ways: changes at the drug's target site, structural blocking, and shifts in protein stability. Global resistance rates for the main flu types sit near one percent and have held steady. Still, stray resistant strains keep appearing. Some pick up extra changes that restore their spread. The authors urge continued watching, careful drug use, and better vaccine coverage, plus fresh antiviral strategies.
pmc-11600649:
Lilian Nuwabaine and co-authors examine the quality of care Kenyan mothers receive in the first two days after giving birth. Good postnatal care guards the lives of mothers and newborns, yet its quality is rarely measured. The team analyzed a 2022 national health survey covering nearly twelve thousand women aged fifteen to forty-nine.

Only about four in ten women got every part of quality care in those first two days. Women who had good care before and during birth were far more likely to get good care after it. Older mothers, phone owners, and cesarean births also fared better. Women in some regions, and those who felt disrespected in hospital, fared worse. The authors call for respectful care and stronger follow-through after birth.
pmc-11600949:
Kaige Ma and co-authors test a sedative drug in Alzheimer's model mice in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The disease involves amyloid buildup, brain inflammation, and nerve cell loss. The drug is known to calm inflammation and protect nerves, but its effect in this disease was unclear.

Mice given amyloid in the brain showed poorer memory and more anxiety-like behavior. Treatment with the drug eased both problems and raised the number of surviving neurons in a key memory area. It also lowered a signaling molecule called CXCL2 and other inflammation markers. Forcing that molecule up, or blocking the drug, removed the benefit. The authors suggest the drug may hold promise for this disease.
pmc-11601949:
The authors show that a fat-ferry protein keeps gut wall power homes in shape, and its loss bares the gut to fire ill. Wall loss and power fail ride with gut fire ills. The ferry hauls a wall fat from the cell's shops to its power homes, where it firms skins and breath. Their 2024 study first finds the ferry's marks low in sick gut sets, with low work marks and harsh ill grain in tow.

In gut skin cells, ferry cuts warp power homes and dim breath. Loss runs on to wall leak in their reads. Guard of the ferry may be a new aim for gut fire care. The work ties a fat path to wall health.
pmc-11603049:
Marburg virus causes a deadly fever with bleeding, and its genome rides inside a coiled protein shell. Luca Zinzula and co-authors mapped that shell with a cold-stage scope method in work from twenty twenty-four. Their map shows a single-layer coil, which differs from an older map that showed a double layer.

The single-layer view brings fresh detail on how the shell parts link and pack the genome. Packing and shell growth are both steps a drug could block, so the new map marks clear targets. The team frames the work as a base for drugs against a virus with no cure yet. Past maps are not wrong, the authors suggest, but this coil form adds a shape drug makers had not seen.
pmc-11603149:
Ilario Baù and co-authors built a tiny molecular machine that runs a chemistry trick in a 2024 paper. Their device is a rotaxane, a ring threaded on an axle, and the ring carries a nitroxide radical, a known catalyst for turning primary alcohols into other compounds with oxygen.

The ring does the oxidizing while a cerium and oxygen pair resets it for the next round. The team reports how the rotaxane was made and proves its makeup with several lab tools, from magnetic resonance scans to voltage tests. They then watched the full cycle run. The work points toward self-running molecular machines powered by clean air-based chemistry.
pmc-11603349:
Yoshiki Sahara and co-authors studied in 2024 how kidney organoids mature, a step needed before they can stand in for real kidneys in drug tests. These lab-grown mini kidneys stay immature, which limits their use. The team tracked single cells over time as the organoids grew.

Cells in the first tube segment matured at uneven rates. Cells that matured fast showed stronger activity in a pathway named for the PPAR alpha receptor. Adding drugs that switch on that pathway and a partner pathway sped maturation. Treated cells took up more protein and grew more sensitive to a known kidney-harming drug. That response is what a good drug-screening tool should show.
pmc-11603649:
Mengqi Liu and Yijin Huang study how quality of life and fear of disease getting worse relate in people with high blood pressure in the lungs, in a 2024 study. Life quality in this group is often poor, and fear may be a key driver. The authors use network analysis to see which parts link most strongly.

They surveyed 255 patients with standard scales for life quality and fear. In the network, the mental side of life quality sat at the center. Fear tied to physical health acted as a bridge to other fears and had the strongest link to family-related fear. The authors suggest care should target that physical fear first, which may protect mental health and overall life quality.
pmc-11603849:
Yuan Tian and co-authors single out an enzyme, peroxidasin, as a driver and warning sign in stomach cancer. This common cancer kills often and lacks good targets. Mining public databases and patient samples, the team found the enzyme far more abundant in tumors than in healthy tissue. High levels marked patients headed for worse outcomes, independently of other factors.

Silencing the enzyme in cancer cells slowed their growth, invasion, and movement. It appears to push cells toward a mobile state and to spur blood-vessel growth, possibly through a major growth pathway. Its levels also tracked drug sensitivity and the mix of immune cells in tumors, hinting it could flag who benefits from immune therapy.
pmc-11603949:
Jin-Da Wang and co-authors survey, in a 2024 study, the eye care workforce in mainland China in 2021. They asked eye clinics at large and mid hospitals in 31 provinces about staff and services. Of 13,400 hospitals, about 74 percent replied, and most of those gave eye care. The count came to 48,652 eye doctors, 64,495 eye nurses, and 14,320 optometrists, who test sight and fit lenses. Per 50,000 people, that is 1.7 doctors, 2.25 nurses, and 0.47 optometrists.

Eye doctor density has reached the world mean, the team finds. Optometrist density sits far below it. Load per doctor also split by place: the mean was about 2,585 patients per doctor. In Shanghai and Zhejiang the load passed 4,000. Tibet was the sole region with under one eye doctor per 50,000 people.
pmc-11604349:
Syarul Arwiz Sahruzaman and Norazian Kamisan report an atypical pulled elbow in a six-month-old girl in work from 2024. Pulled elbow is common in children aged one to four when the forearm is tugged, but it is rare under age one.

The injury happened when the mother rolled the baby and her arm trapped behind her back, with no pull at all. Pain, a still arm, and a pronated position, plus an X-ray ruling out fracture, pointed to the diagnosis. The authors urge doctors to suspect pulled elbow even in infants without a classic pulling story.
pmc-11604949:
Hanzhi Du and colleagues linked heart tracing patterns to lymphoma survival in two thousand twenty-four. This aggressive lymphoma raises heart rhythm risks. Certain wave patterns on heart tracings predict rhythm trouble. Their meaning for lymphoma survival was unknown. Newly diagnosed patients were reviewed retrospectively. Follow-up lasted well over a year typically.

Over a third of patients showed abnormal wave patterns. That group included more men proportionally. Kidney markers also ran higher in that group. Death rates were clearly higher with abnormalities. Two specific wave measures predicted death independently. Other factors for abnormal patterns were modeled too. A simple heart tracing may refine prognosis cheaply.
pmc-11605049:
A team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four on prostate cancer in Sudanese men. The team asked whether diagnosis patterns differ among the country's three major ethnolinguistic groups. Such data are scarce for Sudan and can guide where screening and care are most needed.

Five hundred thirty-two men with biopsy-confirmed cancer took part at six centers. Most, about eighty-four percent, were diagnosed at an advanced stage. The cancer's grade did not differ clearly between groups. One group showed higher levels of a blood marker and younger ages at diagnosis, while another group was mostly over sixty. Matched analysis found one invasion pattern more common in that older group.
pmc-11605249:
Chariya Chap and Sakviseth Bin report newborn chickenpox treated with oral medicine in Cambodia, in work from 2024. The virus can pass from mother to baby around birth, when the baby has no protection. The window of risk runs from five days before to two days after delivery.

Diagnosis rests on the look of the rash and the mother's timing. Standard care in rich settings uses injected drugs and antibody shots. Neither was available in their setting, a gap common in low-resource care. Oral treatment was used instead, and the case tracks how the baby fared. The report offers practical guidance for clinicians facing the same shortages.
pmc-11605549:
Hidenobu Yoshitake and co-authors report, in a conference abstract, a lymphoma that lives inside blood vessels and its rare move into the brain. Their report appeared in 2024. This cancer normally grows only within small vessels and never invades the wall. The team followed cases where brain lymphoma appeared during or after treatment of the vessel form. They stained the tumors for two glue proteins that this cancer characteristically loses.

In ordinary brain lymphoma, both proteins showed strongly around vessels and tumor cells but vanished where cells spread diffusely into brain tissue. The comparison aims to explain how the vessel-bound cancer crosses into the brain. The authors say the adhesion pattern may mark the crossing cases.
pmc-11605749:
A common diabetes drug probably triggered one man's psoriasis, report Simal Qureshi, Sarah Finch, and Michelle Pratt in a 2024 case study. The patient, aged 76, developed the scaly skin disease after starting dapagliflozin, a drug with no classic link to the condition.

Three clues point at the drug: the sudden start, skin samples showing features that fit a drug reaction, and full clearing once the drug stopped. The authors note that drug driven psoriasis has no firm test and can mimic the ordinary kind, from small plaques to whole body redness. They urge doctors to ask about new medicines when skin erupts.
pmc-11605849:
How creative young adults believe they are shapes what they attempt and how they express themselves. Ananya Gupta, Swati Pathak, and Neeraj Panwar explore what sits behind that self-view. They survey 200 young adults, with an average age of about 21, on personality traits, feelings about emotions, and creative self-concept.

A stronger creative self-view went with being open, careful, outgoing, and agreeable. It also went with certain stances toward sadness and fear. When the authors tested which factors predict the self-view, openness explained the largest share, about 27 percent. Neuroticism and attitude toward sadness added small shares of about 2 percent each. The authors suggest that teachers and counselors who know these links can better support creative growth. Personality and emotional attitudes, they argue, are worth attention in programs that build creative confidence.
pmc-11606049:
Kai Liu and colleagues catalogue a cell-wall gene family across the grapevine genome. Their study from twenty twenty-four then tests one gene against salt stress. These LRX genes shape plant growth and stress resistance. Grapevine lacked a full family inventory until now.

Fourteen family members were found and grouped into four branches. Duplication events explained much of the family's expansion. Tissue patterns suggested roles in growth and stress alike. Salt treatment switched several family genes on. One gene, VvLRX7, was characterised in depth functionally. Cell wall proteins mediate how plants sense their surroundings. Breeders gain candidate genes for salt-tolerant vines.
pmc-11606649:
Saiyuri Naicker and six co-authors compare world rules for testing antibiotic stability in this 2024 review. The setting is outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy, where patients get intravenous antibiotics outside hospital. A drug is only usable if it stays stable in the delivery device, and each region tests that differently.

The review found three main problems. Guidance on testing varies widely between regulators, above all on temperature. Some regions have no outpatient specific guidance at all. Only Britain's health service gives dedicated non-regulatory advice for these programs. Uneven rules limit which antibiotics patients can use at home depending on where they live. The authors call for one global testing framework built on agreed criteria and expert practice.
pmc-11607449:
Yang Luo and a large international team compared genomes of tuberculosis patients with genomes of the bacteria infecting them, hunting for interacting pairs. Infection outcomes depend on both sides, yet most genetic studies look at only one. The cohort came from Lima, Peru, and paired samples numbered well over a thousand. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team reports one strong pairing: a variant in a human gene involved in cell membrane rafts tracked with a subgroup of a major bacterial lineage. Tests in infected immune cells supported a real link.

Cells carrying one form of the variant showed stronger interferon responses, while the paired strains carried a mutation changing their chemical balance. In a later cohort gathered during the pandemic, the strain had grown much more common but no longer tracked with the human variant. The authors stress that host, pathogen, and environment jointly shape tuberculosis.
pmc-11607949:
Yan-li Zheng and co-authors measure a stress peptide in heart attack patients. Their 2024 case-control study compares one hundred twenty-eight people with acute myocardial infarction against sixty-two controls, reading blood levels of neuropeptide Y and three related vessel signals.

The heart attack group carried clearly higher neuropeptide Y, alongside higher endothelin and thromboxane and lower levels of a protective vessel enzyme. A cutoff value of the peptide separated patients from controls with fair sensitivity and high specificity. Within the patient group, higher peptide levels tracked with worse artery disease scores and with smoking. The authors suggest the peptide rises with the heart attack process and scales with its severity, making it a candidate marker worth further study.
pmc-11608049:
Phoebe Mbabazi and co-authors count geriatric syndromes among 500 older people living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda, and find women carry more of them, in a 2024 study. Nearly everyone, 94.4 percent, had at least one syndrome at a median age of 64. Frailty, weak physical performance, cognitive impairment, and falls all ran higher in women.

Women averaged 17 percent more syndromes than men after adjustment. Older age, no schooling, underweight, advanced HIV stage, and two or more other chronic diseases also raised the count. The authors urge clinics in sub-Saharan Africa to fold geriatric screening and care into HIV services, with particular attention to women, as this population ages on treatment.
pmc-11608249:
Beatrice Salmaso and co-authors compare the immune landscape of second, metachronous rectal cancers against first tumors, inside the IMMUNOREACT study cohorts. Metachronous cancers arise later in a bowel already treated once, and rectal cases tied to Lynch syndrome are rare enough to leave the biology sketchy. The team stains tumor and healthy tissue for immune markers.

Their 2024 study finds the healthy lining beside second cancers rich in the antigen-presenting HLA-ABC signal, yet the tumors themselves carry fewer CD3 T cells than primary lesions. That split, loud presentation machinery with thin T cell presence, sketches a distinct immune climate for second cancers. The authors argue the difference should steer how surveillance and immunotherapy are planned for these patients.
pmc-11608349:
Mandana Kariminejad and co-authors tune in 2024 an industrial injection moulding process in real time with a Bayesian adaptive design. Short cycle time with no defects is the hard goal in moulding. Classic experiment designs need many runs in a fixed search box, which wastes plant time.

Their method picks each next run from past results, guided by sensor data. A new in-mould sensor read grades shrinkage as parts cool, checked against lab measures. Single and joint tuning chase cycle time and shrinkage at once. The adaptive route is weighed against surface model genetic tools on the same line.
pmc-11608449:
Diarrhea still kills widely in poorer countries, and dirty surroundings may drive more of it than germs alone. Eudora Nwanaforo and four co-authors reviewed the evidence linking pollutant exposure to diarrhea risk in a 2024 systematic review. From nearly 500 papers, eleven met their quality bar, covering pesticides, heavy metals, smoke-related chemicals, microplastics, and preservatives.

Several exposures tracked with more diarrhea: a banned pesticide sprayed before birth, arsenic, cadmium, and microplastics among them. The chemicals may stir gut motion, upset gut microbes, and weaken immune defenses. The authors note big gaps in where studies were done and call for wider, better research on the link.
pmc-11608549:
Xiying He and nine colleagues investigate how a Chinese herbal fever medicine for children reshapes the gut during fever. They compared the granules with ibuprofen in young febrile rats, tracking temperature longer than in earlier work, then sequenced gut microbes and profiled metabolites in colon contents.

The herbal treatment kept fever down longer than ibuprofen. It also nudged the disturbed gut flora back toward normal, boosting two short-chain fatty acid producing species and raising butyric acid levels and its receptor. Anti-inflammatory metabolites rose while fever-linked metabolites and inflammatory signals in the colon fell to normal. The authors attribute part of the medicine's effect to restoring gut microbial balance.
pmc-11608649:
Okano, Nakayama, and Nishizawa test when to drink citrate for clearing lactate after exercise in twenty twenty-four. Citrate drinks are popular and may speed lactate removal from blood. Whether intake before or after exercise works better was unknown. Forty-one healthy male students were assigned to four conditions.

Groups took citric acid before or after exercise, water after, or nothing. All cycled for five minutes on an ergometer. Lactate was measured before exercise and up to thirty minutes after. Overall lactate values and removal rates did not differ significantly among groups. Removal kept rising with citric acid intake regardless of timing. The authors conclude timing mattered little in this small trial.
pmc-11608749:
Nadine Gehrke and co-authors test whether blocking one inflammation signal in liver cells can slow liver cancer tied to fatty liver disease. The signal runs through a receptor called IL-1R1 on the liver cells. Their 2024 mouse study uses animals missing that receptor only in liver cells, given a cancer-causing chemical plus a high-fat, high-sugar diet.

Mice without the receptor grew far fewer and smaller liver tumors than normal littermates. They also stored less liver fat, resisted insulin less, and showed lower levels of markers for cell growth. Fewer suppressive immune cells and killer T cells gathered in their livers. The authors say the receptor helps drive cancer growth in this setting, and that blocking its signal could add to current treatments.
pmc-11610349:
Atte Kallström and co-authors track heart attack trends in Finland across twenty-six years, with a close look at women. Their 2024 study links national hospital and death records for ages thirty-five to seventy-four. Rates had fallen for decades, but hints of a stall prompted the check.

Nearly one hundred ninety thousand non-fatal and seventy-three thousand fatal events were counted. Case rates fell in men and older women, yet the fall slowed in the oldest groups and stopped overall in women. Among women aged thirty-five to fifty-four, rates never moved at all. Death rates and short-term fatality fell in every group. The authors call for stronger prevention aimed at young and middle-aged women.
pmc-11610549:
Na Liu, Lei Wang, Lin Luan, and Huaqing Wang test whether a pneumonia vaccine lowers hospital stays for older adults in China. Their 2024 study covers the 23-valent vaccine against pneumococcal disease. The patients lived in Suzhou City, and the cases were new pneumonia caught outside hospital.

The team compared pneumonia patients with patients who had other chest infections. The pneumonia group had a lower rate of recent vaccination than the control group. After adjusting for other factors, vaccinated adults over sixty had a notably lower risk of hospital care for pneumonia. The effect held for severe cases as well. The findings support wider vaccine use in older adults, a group for whom strong local evidence had been thin.
pmc-11611149:
Researchers weigh the long-term effects of group fishing rights in western Alaska in a 2024 study. Giving catch rights to single fishers can build wealth and spare fish stocks, but it often cuts jobs and widens gaps in fishing towns. The program studied here gave group rights instead to six non-profit groups speaking for 65 small, largely Indigenous coastal villages.

Using survey records on people and households spanning more than twenty-five years, the study compares member villages with nearby ones left out. Member villages pulled ahead on many marks, most clearly on earnings and income, with gains also in schooling and language use. Small village sizes left too little data to tell whether gains grow or fade with time. Still, the authors read the results as proof that group rights can pay off socially.
pmc-11612149:
Louis and a team including Pétré match single asthma symptoms to body traits in five hundred five treated adults in twenty twenty-four. Each of five symptoms was scored for strength on a five point scale. Lung tests and inflammation markers were modeled against them. The symptoms did not move as one block.

Cough tied to smoking, low lung score, and high eosinophils. Breathlessness tied to female sex, high body weight, and low lung score. Wheeze and chest tightness each had their own mix of age, sex, and lung traits. Mucus linked mainly to smoking. The split backs symptom tailored care, they argue.
pmc-11612449:
Li and co-authors present a 2024 study on anchor rods that bend under rock shear in mine and tunnel supports. When rock layers slip, anchors shear and can fail. The team combined bench tests and simulations to watch that bending unfold. They also tracked how stress waves travel through rods bent by different amounts.

Wave energy changed in step with bend degree in a stable pattern. That link grounds a new sound-based test that rates shear damage without digging the rod out. Bench checks showed the test's readings sat close to true measures. The work gives crews a field tool for judging hidden anchor harm before failure strikes.
pmc-11613449:
Zouhair Hanani and co-authors grew advanced ceramic films in two thousand twenty-four. The films blend a lead-based crystal with a touch of samarium. Such crystals can store charge and shift heat under voltage. Bulk versions already show outstanding traits. The team made thin films with a laser deposition method. Thin forms suit compact devices far better.

Samarium doping lifted several traits at once. Charge storage density rose while staying stable with heat. The films survived vast numbers of charge cycles without fatigue. They worked across a wide span from deep cold to strong heat. Heat-pumping and heat-sensing effects proved very large. Those traits suit solid-state cooling and energy storage. The films point toward smaller, tougher electronic parts.
pmc-11613549:
Lena Gerritz and co-authors map how a spin trap behaves in a common lab instrument. Their 2024 paper deals with free radicals, which are active but vanish fast. A trap molecule can catch a radical and form a longer-lived product. Mass tools can then read that product, but its odd ion forms confuse reading.

They made simple mixes of radicals in water and in a solvent, caught with the trap BMPO. A combined liquid and mass method sorted the products. They propose a process that explains the oxidized and reduced ions seen. They also track double products formed when radicals join. A guide based on fragment patterns helps tell ion types apart. The work aims to ease radical hunting.
pmc-11614049:
Jussi Juola, Aarne Hovi, and Miina Rautiainen compare two satellites for forest leaf measures in 2024. A new hyperspectral satellite promises finer tracking of leaf area and canopy cover in northern forests. Whether it truly beats a standard multispectral satellite needed a same-day test.

Field data from thirty-eight boreal plots anchored the comparison. Both sensors' best single-index models scored close. The hyperspectral data, though, offered more strong indexes, and its combined models edged ahead by a few percent. Green, red-edge, and shortwave bands did much of the work. The authors see real, if modest, added value for conifer forests.
pmc-11614549:
Michell Goyal and co-authors study how poor fetal growth in sheep shapes fat cell development. Their 2024 paper notes that growth-restricted females face higher obesity risk later than males. The reasons for that gap are not known. The team made growth restriction by exposing pregnant sheep to high heat.

They took starter fat cells from tissue near the kidney and grew them in the lab. A set of 21 genes changed as the cells matured in most groups and across species. But in male growth-restricted fetuses, six of those genes did not change. That stall may explain their cells' weaker growth into mature fat cells. One gene tied to obesity rose with restriction. The work names targets for later study.
pmc-11615549:
Shu Jing and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper setting out a trial to raise HPV vaccination among young girls in central and western China. The virus can cause cervical cancer, and vaccinating girls aged nine to fourteen prevents it. Free programs exist in some cities, yet cost, supply, and parent hesitancy keep rates low elsewhere.

The planned trial uses a phone mini-program that teaches parents and girls about the vaccine. Its design follows a model that joins information, motivation, and practical skills. Families are assigned by chance to the program or usual care, across several centers. The protocol paper lays out the plan before results exist, so the test of the idea stays honest.
pmc-11615749: A journal cover feature from 2024 presents ReBiA, a robot system built to grow 3D epithelial tissue models in the lab. Tissue models help test drug candidates before human trials, but cost and uneven quality slow their use. Jan Hansmann and co-workers describe a dual-arm robot that runs the lab steps on its own. The system keeps tissue quality steady and lowers cost, supporting wider use of the models and less animal testing. The piece is the cover summary for the full article in the same issue.
pmc-11615949:
Jesus del Amo and co-authors turn a waste stream from foam recycling into new polymers in a 2024 study. Splitting polyurethane foam with glycol leaves a bottom layer rich in isocyanate derived material that had no good use. The team set out to recover its building blocks and spin them into fresh materials.

Water treatment of the layer yielded a diamine and a glycol, which vacuum distillation then purified to near commercial grade. The recovered glycol ran a fresh foam split with results like the commercial stock. The diamine fed synthesis of polyureas and polyamides, with a citrus solvent swapped in for benzene in one route. The work closes a loop in foam recycling.
pmc-11616149:
Shreya Mukherjee and co-authors solve a pump placement puzzle in a teenager with cerebral palsy, in a 2024 case report. Baclofen pumps ease severe muscle stiffness by dripping drug into the spinal fluid. The sixteen-year-old needed his worn-out pump replaced, but his body left no standard route. Severe scoliosis and a nonhealing wound sat beside the old pump, and short bowel syndrome blocked weaning trials.

The team threaded the catheter through a puncture between the top two neck vertebrae, reaching the skull base. The new pump went into a pocket fashioned in the chest. The procedure went smoothly with no complications. The case shows how far creative anatomy can stretch standard therapy.
pmc-11616749:
Yihao Chen and co-authors nominate a transport protein as a biomarker for a rare adrenal cancer in a 2024 study. Adrenocortical carcinoma strikes children and adults alike, with a grim outlook and high death rates. Standard chemotherapy helps inconsistently and brings heavy side effects, so better markers are badly needed.

Profiling tumors across several omics layers, the team found karyopherin subunit alpha 2, a protein that ferries cargo into the cell nucleus, standing out. Its levels track prognosis and may predict who responds to immunotherapy. A marker that does both jobs could steer patients to the right trial early. The study gives this rare cancer a rare gift: a testable lead with clinical uses attached.
pmc-11618349:
Grouping data into clusters is easy; explaining afterward why the groups make sense is the hard part, especially for odd shapes in many dimensions. Tao Zeng and co-authors propose describing each cluster with a handful of boxes in a 2025 paper. Boxes start small to cover a cluster, then merge step by step along a family tree until their shape hugs the cluster well.

A tightening pass then shrinks the boxes for precision. The tree structure finds the right number of boxes on its own and reveals how they relate.
