Tests against older explanation methods showed tighter, more accurate descriptions, which the authors offer for pattern work where people must defend the grouping.
pmc-11618649:
Chronic subdural hematoma, a slow bleed between the brain and its covering, is common in older people and is treated by draining it through a small skull hole. Surgeons disagree on whether washing out the space during drainage helps. The authors gather all randomized trials on the question in a systematic review and meta-analysis, following standard reporting rules. Four trials with 843 patients meet their criteria, and two reviewers extract the data and rate each trial's quality.

Pooling the trials, irrigation cuts recurrence of the bleed compared with no irrigation, with an odds ratio of 0.66. Death rates do not differ between the groups. Complications at first look similar, but a sensitivity analysis that removes the source of disagreement shows fewer complications with irrigation. The authors support washing out the space in practice, while calling for larger, high-quality trials to confirm the finding and check long-term results.
pmc-11618749:
Pin Dong, Kezheng Li, David Rowe, Thomas Krauss, and Yue Wang present a recipe for reading drug levels in blood with infrared light, in a 2024 protocol paper. Clinicians adjust many drugs by measured level, but the standard method is slow, lab-bound mass spectrometry. Infrared spectroscopy is fast and specific, and could shrink to the bedside. Its enemy is background: blood's own fats, proteins, and small molecules drown the drug's signal in the mid-infrared.

Their approach strips that background away step by step, leaving the drug measurable. Using phenytoin, a seizure drug, as the test case, they quantify it in human serum at ten micrograms per milliliter, squarely in the clinical range. The authors note the background-removal trick should serve other sensing methods that fight serum noise, not just infrared ones.
pmc-11619149:
Gum disease can eat into the forked roots of a lower first molar, a defect called furcation involvement that dentists read from 3D cone beam scans. Shishir Shetty and co-authors trained a deep learning model to spot that defect in scan slices in this 2024 early study. They built a set of 600 images, half normal and half with the defect, and held back 85 images for testing.

The model, a ResNet101V2 network, scored 91 percent accuracy on the held-back images, with precision and F1 scores of 0.98 and an area under the curve of 0.98. The authors stress that the study is early and the data set small. A larger study is needed to confirm how well such models work in real clinics.
pmc-11619249:
Deng and eight co-authors test a plant compound against glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, in this two thousand twenty-four study. The compound, ailanthone, has shown antitumor activity elsewhere, but its role in this cancer was untested.

The team found ailanthone slowed tumor cell growth in dishes and in animals by triggering ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, and it crossed into the brain to reach the tumor. It worked by lowering a long non-coding RNA called LINC01956, which otherwise helps the cancer and coaxes nearby macrophages into a tumor-friendly state. Blocking that RNA's pathway weakened signals that help the tumor grow. The chain of effects names several points where future drugs might intervene.
pmc-11619449:
Weiran Shan, Kendrick Zuo, and Zhiyi Zuo report a cancer study, published in 2024, on glioblastoma, a deadly brain tumor. Earlier work showed that a gene regulator called RFX1 can slow the growth, movement, and invasion of these tumor cells. The team searched for existing medicines that raise RFX1 levels, hoping to repurpose drugs already in use for other diseases.

Three blood sugar lowering drugs raised RFX1 in lab grown tumor cells and curbed their growth and spread. Blocking RFX1 removed much of that benefit, tying the effect to the regulator itself. One drug also shrank tumors grown in mouse brains. The authors present RFX1 as a treatment target and these common drugs as candidates worth further study.
pmc-11621149:
Zhi Fu and seven co-authors found that blocking a growth factor can boost a standard drug in a hard type of bowel cancer in a 2024 study. The factor, GDF15, runs high in many cancers and in this bowel type, which is marked by unstable DNA repeats. Its exact role there was unclear.

Levels ran high in patient tissue and in two cell lines of this type. Silencing the factor slowed cell growth. It also made cells more open to the drug, with more cell death. In mice, tumors with the factor silenced shrank more under the drug. The team traced the effect to a cell death path driven by iron and a set of protective proteins. The factor may serve as both a marker and a target.
pmc-11621249:
Lefan Zhuang and co-authors report a rare case of a stem cell product clotting after collection, in a case report from 2024. Stem cell products are gathered by a filtering process that needs blood thinners to keep the lines and the product fluid. Clots during later freezing are known, but clots in a fresh product had not been reported.

The product came from a matched unrelated donor. On arrival, thin white threads of clot floated in the bag. Staff split the product into syringes under sterile care to isolate the clot. Within an hour, the small clots merged into a pink, jelly-like cylinder ringed by serum. The authors suggest adding a blood thinner to the product before such isolation in future cases.
pmc-11621349:
Xiao-Jiao Cui and colleagues test whether simple blood ratios can predict outcomes in severe pneumonia, in a 2024 study. Severe community-acquired pneumonia fills hospitals and kills many patients. Ratios between white cell types and platelets are cheap to get from a routine blood count. The team checked five such ratios against what happened to patients.

The study covered 554 patients treated for the disease. Two ratios, built from neutrophils and basophils against lymphocytes, tracked with death in hospital and shorter survival. A third ratio, built from eosinophils, pointed the other way, toward longer stays but better survival. Several ratios also tracked with admission to intensive care. None stood as a fully independent predictor of death, though. The authors see the ratios as helpful signals to combine with other clinical signs.
pmc-11621649:
Jooyeop Lee and Joon Ho Moon write a commentary in two thousand twenty-four on how heart scarring develops in diabetic heart failure. Heart disease is the top cause of death worldwide, and diabetes raises the risk sharply. Scarring of the heart muscle, called fibrosis, is one path by which diabetes weakens the heart.

The commentary discusses a study that traced a chain of four molecular switches in rat and mouse models. High sugar blocked the first switch, which freed a second to silence a protective third factor. That silencing let scarring proteins build up in the heart. Drugs that act on parts of the chain are already known in diabetes care. The authors argue the chain offers fresh targets for treatment. New drugs with distinct actions could add to current protective options.
pmc-11622449:
Floor Kroese and co-authors follow Dutch vaccine doubters over time to learn what finally moves them. Hesitancy is common, but minds do change, and the reasons matter for the next campaign. Their cohort held over twelve thousand five hundred people who began hesitant or unwilling toward a first COVID-19 shot. Tracking ran from late 2020 to mid 2022, with survival models split into campaign and leftover phases.

By the end, eighty-six percent of the hesitant and thirty-four percent of the unwilling had taken a shot or meant to. Believing the vaccine works was the strongest lever in both phases. Middle-aged adults lagged early, then caught up fastest later. Rules' tightness and local uptake also nudged switchers. The study reads minds in motion, not just snapshots.
pmc-11623449: Brenda Wingfield and Michael Wingfield comment in 2024 on new work about coffee wilt disease. Two outbreaks of the disease have badly hurt coffee growing in Africa. They sum up a PLOS Biology study that points to gene transfer between two fungal species. The transfer, carried by large mobile elements called Starship transposons, may explain why the disease kept emerging again. Readers get a short guide to a finding that links gene movement to real crop loss.
pmc-11623949:
Dezhi Zhao and co-authors show in 2024 that opening tiny channels in bone cells can rescue bone lost to disuse and aging. Loading from movement keeps bone strong, but rest and age blunt that response. The team used an antibody that opens channels called connexin hemichannels in bone cells. They tested it in mice kept off their hind legs and in old mice given leg loading.

The treatment curbed bone loss and cell death during rest. In old mice it boosted bone gain from loading. Open channels released a bone-building factor and lowered a blocking one. The authors see this as a fresh route to treat bone loss, apart from current drug regimens.
pmc-11624549:
Targeted lung cancer drugs called tyrosine kinase inhibitors are taken for long stretches, and their side effects shape daily life in ways clinics may not hear about. Gulikers and co-authors asked patients and their partners directly, in focus groups.

Sixteen patients and twelve partners took part. Patients said side effects were limited and they felt free to raise them with their team, though symptoms they doubted were drug-related sometimes went unmentioned. The researchers also floated therapeutic drug monitoring, adjusting dose by measured blood levels. Patients were open to it in principle, but the idea stirred worry that a lower dose might weaken the treatment. They asked for solid research and frequent check-ups first, a clear condition for winning trust in monitored dosing.
pmc-11624749:
Fiona Hoare and co-authors lay out, in a 2024 protocol, a national study of older Irish adults who reach emergency departments with self-harm or suicidal thoughts. People over sixty-five die by suicide at high rates. Self-harm is the strongest known warning sign, even though its frequency falls with age.

The cohort will gather cases from emergency departments across Ireland. The team aims to chart which traits mark the highest-risk presentations, including attempts of high lethality. Real-life evidence on this group is thin compared with younger cohorts. Knowing who among older presenters is likeliest to die could focus scarce psychiatric follow-up where it saves the most lives.
pmc-11625049:
Takumi Tomoi and co-workers publish an author correction to a study of laser-driven gene expression in moss cells, in a 2024 notice. The original article used infrared laser heating to switch on a gene in single cells and measured the effect with imaging. The correction fixes wording in text and figure captions.

Two captions misstated a phrase about the distribution of a cell type, and one sentence in the main text is replaced with a corrected version. A stray caption sentence that belonged to a supplementary figure was removed. The notice states the article's PDF and web versions have been updated. No results or conclusions are changed.
pmc-11625249:
Takaaki Kamatani, Ryogo Katada, Masataka Watanabe, and Tatsuo Shirota report a rare case of a jaw tumour that spread to the lungs, in a 2024 paper. The tumour type, ameloblastoma, grows in the jaw and seldom spreads. A woman first had a form of it cut from her jaw, with no return at that site.

Twelve years later, scans found more than ten nodules in both lungs. A lung biopsy showed the same tumour pattern, and further tests confirmed the spread. She then took part in a trial of a targeted drug for three years, during which the lung disease stayed stable. The authors warn oral surgeons that this spread can appear more than a decade after surgery that seemed curative. Long follow-up matters even when the jaw stays clear.
pmc-11625749:
Sangavi and five colleagues test a brown seaweed extract against the main tooth decay germ in twenty twenty-four. The germ builds sticky films that shrug off antibiotics. The extract fought the film without killing the germ itself. At top dose it cut film growth by over nine tenths.

Sub killing doses slashed sticking, acid making, and sugar glue output. Surface grip and loose DNA fell as well. Gene checks showed the film and glue genes turned down. Human cheek cells stayed unharmed in safety tests. Three fatty acids in the extract carried much of the punch, the team found.
pmc-11626449:
Andrea Silverj and a large team of co-authors trace West Nile virus lineage one in Italy, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The mosquito-borne virus sickens people, horses, and birds. Italy saw 330 brain cases and thirty-seven deaths in the twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-two season.

The team built a bank of all public virus genomes plus thirty-one new Italian ones. Their tree suggests the lineage first entered Italy from North Africa around nineteen eighty-five. Two distinct strains now circulate in the country. Fresh mutations mark the Italian strains, and the authors urge joint watch across Europe and Africa.
pmc-11626649:
Bacteria of the Streptomyces family make many of our antibiotics, and the recipes sit in gene clusters up to two hundred thousand letters long. Copying a whole cluster into a test host is the bottleneck for discovering new drugs. Kurylenko, Palusczak, Luzhetskyy, and Rebets improve a yeast-based copying method called TAR cloning. Its old weakness was screening: finding the one yeast colony carrying the right cluster took heavy work.

Their upgrade builds selection into the vector, using the yeast killer phenomenon so only colonies with the target cluster thrive. They prove it by capturing the chelocardin cluster, thirty-five thousand letters, and the daptomycin cluster, sixty-seven thousand. Both produced their antibiotics in a new host. The authors say the direct-selection trick can spread to gene clusters from other bacteria, speeding the hunt for natural products.
pmc-11626749:
Fabian Lenhard and co-authors survey how climate worry weighs on daily life. Their 2024 study gathers 1,221 adults in Sweden who say they worry about the climate. Past work hinted that such worry can impair work and social life, but used weak measures of that harm.

Worry that came often was tied to clear impairment on a standard scale. Both the strength and the frequency of worry went with more green behavior, like saving energy. Impairment itself barely changed green behavior. About a third of the most worried group passed the mark for notable impairment. Many in that group said they wanted support. The authors call for help aimed at that group.
pmc-11628949:
Noni Ella Winkler and co-authors report in 2024 on a cholera outbreak in a refugee camp in Ethiopia in 2023, and on failings in the response. The outbreak was confirmed in late August, and 470 cases were treated over about four weeks. Water, sanitation, health, and nutrition conditions in the camp all fell short of minimum standards for emergency aid.

The authors call the shortfall a failure of the humanitarian response. They argue the same pattern is likely in other camps in Ethiopia, where new arrivals strain already thin services. Closing funding gaps for refugee response is presented as an urgent step to prevent a repeat.
pmc-11629549:
Jort J van der Schans and co-authors describe a lab method from 2024 for building better T-cells. Doctors already reshape a patient's own T-cells to attack blood cancers. Adding more than one new trait could help against solid tumors too, but loading several traits at once is hard because virus carriers have limited room.

Their method mixes up to three virus carriers at one time, all made by stable producer cells that were loaded in the same way. The mix puts all three traits into T-cells in one step. Tests showed the single mix beat the usual route of adding one batch after another, giving more complete cells with steadier results. The team offers it as a tool for safer, stronger cell therapies.
pmc-11630049:
Dongdong Luo leads a team on a ring RNA in glioma brain tumors. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with circATP8B4 and its partners. Ring RNAs are often off track in human glioma.

The ring is high in glioma, but its role was unclear. Lab tests showed cutting it slowed tumor cell growth and spread. It also made cells more prone to radiation harm. The ring soaks up a small RNA that would curb a key protein. Mouse tumor tests backed the lab finds in live animals. The chain may offer new cure goals.
pmc-11630849:
Mische Holland, Rachel Rutkowski, and Tera Levin trace the family history of inflammation proteins across primates and rodents, in this 2024 study. The proteins, called caspases, help trigger the body's alarm response to infection. One member has stayed in place across all the species checked. Its kin have had rockier paths, with copies lost or turned into dead genes in some lineages.

The team compared the gene sets of nineteen primates and twenty-one rodents. A second member appears across ape-like primates, while others vanished at varied points. Two of the proteins drive the same alarm pathway, so uneven losses may explain why animal tests mislead human medicine. The paper maps which species truly share our setup and which do not.
pmc-11631049:
Frédéric Thomas and co-authors answer a comment on their cancer evolution paper in a 2024 journal exchange. Their earlier article argued that tumors progress not only by single-cell fitness but by selection for what the tumor as a whole can do. A reader, Dr. Mesut Tez, praised the view and linked it to older ideas about black-box epidemiology and self-organizing systems. The authors reply with thanks and expansion.

They stress the collective adaptability of cancer cell groups, which they frame as group phenotypic composition. Tumors, on this view, act like quick problem-solvers in hostile tissue. The exchange shows a theory being sharpened in public by friendly fire. Such replies help readers see where a new idea agrees with its ancestors.
pmc-11631149:
Zia Ul Mustafa and co-authors present a 2024 survey on child doctors and antibiotic stewardship in Pakistan. Overuse of antibiotics in children feeds drug resistance, and Pakistan's rates are high. The team ran a web survey of 383 paediatricians across all provinces in mid 2023. It probed knowledge, views, readiness, and barriers around hospital stewardship programs.

Only 15 percent had any training on antibiotic use or resistance. Fewer than eight percent worked where a stewardship program functioned. Knowledge was broadly sound, yet only about a quarter thought antibiotics were overused in children. Less experienced doctors scored lower on knowledge. Most were ready to start programs. Missing guidelines, online learning, and management support were the chief barriers named.
pmc-11631449:
Uri Rosenblum and co-authors study balance recovery in 2024 when the arms are held back. Swinging the upper body helps people regain balance, but how it aids stability while walking was not clear.

Healthy adults walked on a treadmill that slid sideways under them, under three conditions: arms free, one arm held, and both arms held. Stability and upper body speeds were read from the first step after each slide. With both arms held, stability in the forward plane fell and trunk speed rose. Head and trunk often moved in opposite sideways directions. Trunk speed also often ran against the direction of the fall, which hints at an active righting strategy.
pmc-11631549:
A patient with a swollen pancreas formed an abscess deep in its tail, too far from the stomach wall for the usual drain route through the stomach. Ping Yue and co-authors report how they reached it anyway in a 2024 case report. The man, sixty-five, had heart stents placed a month before, which raised the stakes of any operation.

A scope passed into the pancreatic duct, but wires and tools kept jamming at tight narrowings in the duct. A cutting tool borrowed from cyst work, driven by electric current, burned the narrowing open. A drain tube then drew off a large volume of pus, and the abscess vanished within days. A stent followed, and the man recovered without incident. The authors offer the borrowed tool as a rescue when standard gear cannot pass.
pmc-11631749:
Yong Li and three co-authors assess how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped early breast cancer care in the United States. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Lockdowns and strained hospitals delayed screening and surgery across many cancers.

Using a national cancer registry, the team compared over one hundred forty-two thousand patients from twenty twenty with the two prior years. Diagnoses and surgeries both fell in twenty twenty. The stage mix shifted later, with fewer stage zero to one cases. Breast-conserving surgery and radiation shares dropped, while chemotherapy rose. Treatment delays, oddly, shortened. Survival for the twenty twenty group ran worse than for twenty eighteen patients. The authors document a lasting scar on early cancer care.
pmc-11631949:
Mateus de Castro, Mayana Zatz, and a team of co-authors hunt for why some exposed people never caught COVID-19. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, follows six women who lived with infected partners. The partners were sick and tested positive, some more than once. Yet the women stayed free of symptoms or infection.

Blood immune cells from the couples were prodded in the lab. One gene, switched on by interferon, stood out in the protected women alone. That gene, IFIT3, helps cells fight viruses. Its rise appeared only in the exposed but uninfected group. The team proposes it as a shield factor worth deeper study.
pmc-11632249:
Germaine Loo and Chi Keong Ching wrote an editorial in two thousand twenty-four on Japan's national registry for catheter ablation. Ablation treats faulty heart rhythms by scarring the tissue that causes them. Registries in several countries now track how the procedure is used and how safe and effective it is in real practice.

Rhythm disorders are rising with aging populations and better detection, and ablation volumes with them. Japan's registry grew from about forty thousand ablation cases in two thousand eighteen to over sixty-eight thousand in two thousand twenty-two. With ninety thousand cases in total, it is among the largest such registries reported.
pmc-11632949:
Xu and co-authors marry copper cobalt oxide sheets with peptide fibers for tumor heat therapy. Peptide fibers self-build and are kind to body tissue. The hybrid pairs those fibers with bimetallic nanosheets. Light-to-heat conversion hit 31.57 percent for the hybrid. That rate suits heat-based tumor cell killing.

The fibers cut the sheets' harm to normal cells. Heat killed over 95 percent of one lung cancer line. A second line lost over 90 percent of cells. A ranked score put total performance at 0.741. The authors say the peptide design guides future hybrids.
pmc-11633049:
Qintao Ma, Hai, and Shen hunt gene markers for thyroid-associated eye disease, a tangled autoimmune illness that bulges and inflames the eyes. Their angle is autophagy, the cell's recycling system. Comparing patients and controls, they found twenty-four such genes behaving differently, then let three selection methods compete to shrink the list to a diagnostic few.

Six genes survived all three screens and held up in a separate dataset. Together they split patients from controls with a score of 0.948, and a points chart built on them did better still. Each gene also tracked the mix of immune cells in tissue, hinting the set reflects the disease's immune invasion, not just its shadow.
pmc-11634749:
Jiang Liu and co-authors report in a 2024 case study a stomach cancer that should have answered immune therapy but did not. The tumor carried two traits that usually predict strong response: broken DNA repair and high instability, which load it with mutations and attract immune attack. The patient got a PD-1 blocker with a HER2 drug and chemotherapy.

The cancer failed to respond. Two further mutations, in the APC and PTEN genes, are the suspects, alongside the pattern of killer T cells in the tumor. The case warns that pathway mutations can veto an otherwise ideal immune profile and urges gene checks before such therapy.
pmc-11635249:
Xi and six co-authors studied a gene called PSMD11 in lung adenocarcinoma in twenty twenty-four. The gene helps run the proteasome, the cell's machine for shredding tagged proteins. It has been linked to cancer growth, but its value in this lung cancer type was unclear.

Using data analysis across many datasets, they found the gene far more active in tumor tissue than in normal lung. High activity tracked with DNA copying pathways and certain immune cell patterns. It correlated positively with some helper and regulatory T cells, and negatively with B cells and killer T cells. Links also appeared with genes tied to copper-driven cell death. Cell co-culture tests probed immune escape. The authors propose the gene as a possible drug target and marker.
pmc-11636049:
Savvina Leontakianakou and co-authors give in 2024 a better lab method to measure two sugar acids in wood xylan. The acids hang on the spine of hardwood xylan and can slow its break down. Color tests work on fake samples, yet real wood samples are far harder to read.

The team tweaks a charge based split method by adding a slope flow in place of a flat flow. That shift splits the two acids and kin wood parts in one run. Repeat runs gave steady scores, and a test curve stayed straight across a wide range. The method suits hard wood sample work.
pmc-11636249:
Hua Xiao and co-authors test in 2024 whether the mix of T cells in the blood foretells survival after stomach cancer surgery. The team studied patients who had radical stomach removal at three hospitals in China. Blood lymphocyte subsets are cheap to measure, and a good marker would help sort patients by risk.

Patients at the Hunan cancer hospital formed a training group of 231, and two Wuhan hospitals gave a check group of 159. The team found cut points for each cell subset against survival. Statistical models then picked which traits forecast survival on their own. A blood based risk score could steer follow up intensity and added treatment. The outside check group guards against a marker that works only at one site.
pmc-11638049:
Yang Luo and four co-authors present a 2024 meta-analysis on how two workout styles feel to people with excess weight. High-intensity interval training alternates hard bursts with rest, while moderate continuous training keeps a steady pace. Both help health, but which one people enjoy more was disputed. The team pooled sixteen studies with 537 participants, using standard scales for enjoyment and feelings during exercise.

Programs ran from one to sixteen weeks, with adults up to age seventy. The pooled result found interval training gave higher enjoyment than steady training. Felt responses during exercise were similar between the two. The authors conclude both styles leave people feeling positive, which matters because enjoyment keeps people exercising. Interval training's slight enjoyment edge, in shorter total time, may suit busy schedules. They still note wide variation across the studies pooled.
pmc-11638249:
Leonie Bossert, Tom Crompton, Anwesha Dutta, and Joni Seager wrote a 2024 article arguing that patriarchal norms weaken nature conservation. The field faces linked crises of species loss, habitat damage, and climate change. The authors say male supremacy and inequality sit at the root of much environmental harm, yet the topic is rarely raised in conservation debates.

They map how patriarchy shows up inside conservation itself. Women in the field often hold precarious posts, violence against animals is tolerated, and some forms of knowledge are pushed aside. Enforcement has grown more militarized, and nature is increasingly treated as a financial asset. The authors conclude that conservation programs must face these structures, or they will keep undercutting their own goals.
pmc-11638349: A set of answer keys from twenty twenty-four gives the right answers to short quiz sets tied to past journal articles. Each set has five questions, and the answers are listed as plain letter codes. The linked articles cover topics such as wrist scans, care for sick children, brain scans, and skin care during treatment. Health workers use these sets to claim learning credit for their own records.
pmc-11638449:
Gyu Won Kim and co-authors review how flat channel membranes pick lithium out of water, in a 2024 paper. Demand for lithium keeps rising with battery use, and seawater is a vast source. Two dimensional channel membranes can be tuned for which ions pass, and they already split lithium from magnesium well.

The harder split is lithium from sodium, the main similar ion in seawater. The review traces the physics: ions must shed their water shell, then diffuse through the channel. Channel size, surface charge, and binding spots set the energy hills that decide the race. The authors say the missing piece is a full rule set for how those factors trade off across the whole trip.
pmc-11638949:
Xinyang Lv and colleagues published a 2024 biotechnology study on making a human milk sugar. The sugar supports infant immune health. Formula makers increasingly add it to products. The team engineered E. coli bacteria to produce it. Earlier routes were too inefficient.

Genes that break down a key building block were deleted. New genes for building the sugar were inserted. Enzyme levels were balanced in modules. A helper chemical supply was recycled more efficiently. Transport proteins were screened to export the product. Output rose substantially. Fermentation could supply this ingredient at industrial scale.
pmc-11639849:
Sukyung Kim and co-authors test a microbe-based treatment for dry skin in this 2024 paper. The product, LP51, comes from a healthy vaginal microbiome. Dry, rough skin causes discomfort, and standard creams often help only a little. The team ran a blind trial with 43 people who had dry inner arm skin.

One group used a formula with the extract for four weeks, while the other used a placebo. The treated group gained much more skin moisture and lost less water through the skin. Lab tests backed safety and showed anti-inflammatory and related effects. The authors link gains to a rise in a skin-microbe index they define. They present the product as a fresh path for dry skin care.
pmc-11640149:
Alicja Fedorowicz and Artur Bartkowiak report a 2024 study of how butter type affects a probiotic bacterium through spray-drying and storage. The bacterium, Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG, was wrapped in a mix of starch, whey protein, soy lecithin, and ascorbic acid, with one of six butters added.

The team asked if the fatty acid makeup of a butter and its melting heat guard the cells as they dry. Survival was checked right after drying and through weeks of storage, in the cold and at room heat. Counts of live cells, water content, color, and shape were all tracked.
pmc-11640249:
Hui Zheng and co-authors test ways to process fiber from lotus leaves in a 2024 study. Lotus leaves yield an insoluble fiber that could serve as a food ingredient, but its raw form digests poorly. The team treated it three ways: shear blending, ball milling, and pressure cooking.

Ball-milled fiber freed the most plant compounds during simulated digestion and showed the strongest antioxidant power. During lab fermentation with gut microbes, the shear-blended fiber best supported microbe diversity. Pressure-cooked fiber fed one possibly harmful group the most. Fermentation also made useful fatty acids. The comparison helps food makers pick a treatment by the benefit they want most.
pmc-11640349:
Hiroharu Natsume, Shogo Okamoto, and Derek V Byrne present a two thousand twenty-four study predicting moment-by-moment liking of strawberries from changing sensations. Food tasters can record which sensation dominates over time. A parallel method tracks liking itself, but running both is costly.

A reservoir neural network learned to forecast liking curves from sensation curves. Strawberry data from an earlier study trained the models. Forecasts were often highly accurate. Two sensitivity measures ranked which sensations steer liking most. Sweetness led for strawberries. The method could let developers infer preference shifts from cheaper sensation testing alone.
pmc-11640549:
Lucia Biagini and co-authors test, in a 2024 poultry study, giving probiotics to chicks before they hatch. Live microbes delivered in the egg can meet the embryo early, and pairing them with the standard Marek's disease vaccine would simplify hatchery work.

One hundred five fertile eggs received the vaccine alone, or the vaccine carrying a multi-strain probiotic at two doses. Chicks were then raised for thirty-five days while growth, gut shape, and parasite shedding were tracked. A gut parasite, Eimeria, was monitored weekly in droppings, and intestinal tissue was checked for lesions at slaughter. The design weighs early probiotics against growth and gut health.
pmc-11640649:
Circular RNAs are rings of genetic material with no loose ends, which makes them hard for cells to break down. A 2024 review by Xiaocai Yin, Hongjun Li, and Yan Zhou surveys what these rings do during virus infection and how they might serve in treatment.

Both host cells and viruses produce the rings, and they can help or hinder a virus depending on the case. The review covers their roles across coronaviruses, herpesviruses, HIV, and others, their part in the host's antiviral defense, and their promise as markers that could flag an infection. The authors argue the rings form an overlooked layer of control in infected cells.
pmc-11640849:
Paula Cañaveras and co-authors study health gains among survivors who joined a support route after gender violence, in this 2024 paper. Gender-based violence harms health in deep and lasting ways. People who stand by victims can also face retaliation, a second form of abuse.

The MeToo route is a project that raises awareness and builds solidarity around victims. The team examine survivors who engaged with that route after first support. They look for signs that health improved following that engagement. Most past work stops at documenting harm, not recovery. Evidence of recovery paths can shape services for survivors. It also honors the role of community support in healing.
pmc-11641049:
Plants move salts through gate proteins in their cell walls, and one group of gates was long thought to haul sodium as well. Sam Henderson, Saeed Nourmohammadi, and Maria Hrmova test that view in 2024 with a grapevine gate. They model the gate's shape, trace its kin across species, and run power tests in frog eggs.

The gate's grip sites look like those of animal gates that haul potassium and chloride as a pair, with no sodium grip in sight. Frog egg tests fit that pair haul: chloride left the cells, and uptake of a stand in atom hung on chloride, not sodium. The team says plant gates of this group most likely work as potassium chloride pairs. That shift reframes their role in plant salt life.
pmc-11641549:
Zhenghui Ou and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether silencing one gene can stunt a notorious invasive weed. Mikania micrantha, the mile-a-minute weed, smothers farms and forests worldwide. Sprays and pulling are the usual defenses; gene silencing by RNA has rarely been tried on it. The team targeted the weed's version of a gene that starts root growth in embryos, guided by its kin in other plants.

They sprayed a matching double-stranded RNA onto the weed's roots. The target gene's activity fell by roughly a quarter to two fifths over the days that followed. The study tracks how that knockdown bears on root development and growth, as its title states. A working RNA spray could give land managers a precise, low-chemical way to slow this invader.
pmc-11641649:
Damián Pereira-Payo and co-authors study poverty and health in 2024 among middle-aged and older adults in the United States. Low income is known to track with worse health, but the team wanted the full pattern in one national data set. They used a decade of the national health survey program, covering over ten thousand adults.

Adults below the poverty line were more likely to be inactive, eat poorly, and have a history of heavy drinking. They also had higher rates of high blood pressure, diabetes, liver and kidney disease, arthritis, stroke, and heart attacks. The more of these diseases piled up in one person, the stronger the income link grew. The authors flag this group as needing targeted policy help.
pmc-11641849:
Orit Vidne-Hay, Amir Alhalel and Irina Barequet report long-term results of combining corneal transplant with vitrectomy, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. The paired operations tackle eyes where both the front window and the back of the eye are badly damaged. The team reviewed thirteen eyes followed for at least a year, on average over five years.

All eyes had severe corneal opacity, most from retinal detachment. Vision improved in just under half the cases, though it usually stayed low. Some eyes kept walking-level vision for years. The weak point was the transplanted cornea: most eyes needed repeat grafts, and graft failure was present in three quarters at the final visit. Still, the authors back the approach for saving complex eyes.
pmc-11641949:
Hao Yang and co-authors mapped the 3D shapes of sand grains in a 2024 study. A grain's shape and size steer how sand packs, flows, and bears load, yet shape reads were long stuck in flat views. The team defined a roundness score for full 3D form and scanned crushed and natural sands with X-ray micro scans, counting grains in the hundreds of thousands.

Grain sizes ran from silt fine to five millimeters. Shape marks such as length ratios, ball likeness, and the new roundness score were tied to grain size for each sand. Crushed and natural sands split clearly in their fine scale marks. Links among shape marks are laid out to feed fill and strength models, plus grain level computer sims.
pmc-11642049:
Julian Muller-Thyssen-Uriarte and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, neck muscle faults in neck pain and how dry needling shifts them. Most neck pain has no clear one cause. Faults are read by electromyography, a gauge of muscle work by skin pads. The team searched three data bases and kept 65 papers. The reads back odd muscle work in long neck pain, most in arm moves, loop work, violin play, neck force, and neck moves. Pain and muscle fault track each other in those tasks.

Needling an active sore knot in the top shoulder muscle can lift a deep neck bend task, the reads find. On calm knots, needling cut that muscle's work and wear in the short term after type tasks in sound folk.
pmc-11642349:
Aiko Ishizaki-Terauchi and colleagues published a clinical study in twenty twenty-four about small screws used to anchor teeth during orthodontic treatment. They looked back at records for Japanese patients who had screws placed in the upper jaw. All of the operators were right-handed and had several years of experience. The team compared screws placed by hand with screws placed using a motor, and they compared the right side of the mouth with the left side.

Hand-placed screws held less often on the left side than on the right side. Motor-placed screws held about equally well on both sides. Overall success did not differ much between the two methods. The authors link the left-side problem to the working position of a right-handed clinician, and they note that operator experience also mattered.
pmc-11642449:
Mariah Balmaceno-Criss and co-authors review how to spot a worsening neck spinal cord disease, in work from two thousand twenty-four. Wear and tear in the neck can slowly press the cord, causing nerve harm that grows with age in the population. Early, exact diagnosis matters because late finds can leave lasting damage.

Signs are often faint and vague, such as poor sleep, more falls, and trouble driving. That vagueness leads to missed or wrong calls. The review gathers history clues, exam findings, and look-alike diseases from recent papers. Surgery to free the cord is advised in most cases to halt decline.
pmc-11642649:
Gabriele Sebastianelli and co-authors present a 2024 study of brain excitability in chronic migraine patients who overuse acute pain drugs. Such patients show a hyped up sensory system. The team asked whether three weeks off the overused drugs could calm it, or whether the trait is fixed.

Nerve signals from the arm were read before and after withdrawal, and set against healthy volunteers. A habituation failure present at the start normalised after withdrawal. Fast signal components tied to relay and cortex both fell to healthy levels. One inhibition measure did not change. The results favour a brain state that withdrawal can partly reset.
pmc-11642949:
Sven Schwabe and colleagues published a 2024 protocol for a study of suicide assistance in Germany. Helping a person end their life is a multi-step process, from first talks about end-of-life options to care for grieving family. Who takes part varies by country and by local rules.

In 2020, Germany's top court lifted the ban on organized assistance, but the field stayed unregulated. No solid data show how such help is given in practice. The planned study will ask patients, families, and practitioners about their experience. It aims to map each stage of real cases. Clear facts could guide future rules and safer practice.
pmc-11643449:
Sylwia Olenska and co-authors evaluate new core layers for flooring materials in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. Shortages of familiar woods on the Polish market push makers to try new species and structures. The team tested plywood-like composites whose base layers use Scots pine veneers of varied thickness, some with alder interlayers.

They measured Young's modulus and stiffness, the properties that decide flooring suitability, and judged quality with statistical tools including control charts and distribution shape. Control charts show whether production stays stable and predictable, while the shape analysis shows how close values sit to the target. Thicker veneers in the base layer proved workable, which could simplify production and make it greener.
pmc-11643549:
Yujie Yu, Xiang Zhang, Chunjian Hu, Liangkun Liu, and Haibo Wang test how fatigue cracks grow in a weathering bridge steel and its welds. Their 2024 study covers Q370qENH steel, prized for rust resistance in highway and rail bridges. Weld joints are the weak point for crack growth in such structures.

Samples from base steel, weld metal, and heat-affected zones were grown under varied load ratios and plate widths. Welding heat refined grains and cut impurities, which slowed cracks in the treated zones. Base steel cracked fastest, while weld metal cracked slowest in steady growth. Crack speed rose with load ratio in every zone, most strongly in weld metal. Thick plates cracked a touch more slowly. The fitted law constants serve future bridge fatigue checks.
pmc-11643849:
Lee-Moay Lim and co-authors track how malnutrition and inflammation deepen as kidney disease advances toward dialysis. A combined score, the MIS, grades protein-energy wasting in dialysis patients, but how wasting grows across the earlier stages was unclear. Their 2024 study scores 3,659 patients across all five stages of chronic kidney disease in Taiwan.

Over about six years of follow-up, scores climbed steeply in the 1,124 patients who reached dialysis, with about half scoring eight or more at the start of treatment. Wasting by a global assessment rose from about ten percent at baseline to sixty-one percent just before dialysis. The pre-dialysis score tied to the starting score, age, heart disease, and cancer. The authors conclude that wasting is not a dialysis complication but a long build-up, and that the score can flag it early enough to act.
pmc-11643949:
Yan Zhang and co-authors pair fern goods with a germ drug to break piss tract germ films that shrug the drug off, in a study from 2024. The germ builds films by a loop good that grips a sway part. Dock math flagged three fern goods that fit that part.

Pairs of each good with the drug slew more germs than the drug alone, in dish and in sick drawn strains. Two goods lift the loop good, slow the sway gene, and cut film growth at set marks. Sim runs show the goods grip the part at two hinge spots with force. The pair path may crack drug proof films, the team hopes.
pmc-11644049:
Yang Peng and colleagues study how a rare riverside plant handles cadmium in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Cadmium is a toxic metal spread by industry and cities. It can stunt or kill plants. The plant here, Myricaria laxiflora, is rare and endangered. It grows along the upper Yangtze River, where cadmium pollution varies by site. How the metal stresses this plant was unknown.

The team raised seedlings and exposed them to cadmium. They measured growth, body chemistry, and the activity of thousands of genes. The combined data show how the plant senses and answers the poison. Such insight can guide efforts to protect wild stands of the species. It may also reveal tolerance tricks useful for cleaning polluted soils.
pmc-11644149:
Plastics riddled with tiny holes serve as gas stores, drug carriers, and filters. Ilsiya Davletbaeva and Oleg Sazonov review how the chains' own layout can carve those holes, in work from twenty twenty-four. Old routes to pore sizes in the five to fifty range take many stages and use up extra gear. Chain design offers a leaner path.

By shaping the polymer's own frame, makers can set surface area, hole size, and wall chemistry in one build. The review sorts the main design tricks and the frames they yield. Uses run from energy stores to cell scaffolds and proton membranes. The authors cast layout-first design as the road to plastics with bespoke pores.
pmc-11644349:
Bashar Esmail, Dustin Isleifson, and Lotfollah Shafai present a 2024 design for a compact high gain antenna for small satellites watching Arctic snow and sea ice. CubeSats leave almost no room, yet Earth sensing needs a strong beam. Their answer is a curved reflector, offset so its feed does not block the signal.

A flat patch array feeds the dish. Built and measured hardware matched simulations well, hitting strong gain at the target frequency with about half the aperture working usefully. The cylinder shape folds into a single unit cube with a simple deployer. Small satellites gain a serious ear without a serious volume bill.
pmc-11644649:
Pouya Mohammadnezhad, Alberto Valdés, and Alejandro Cifuentes optimize extracts of a Ferula plant and test them for brain protection in a 2024 paper. Plants in this genus have folk uses for many illnesses. The species studied had never been checked against the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease.

A pressurized liquid method extracted compounds from the plant's upper parts and roots using several solvents. Two solvents won, and fine-tuning their mix and heat gave the best yields. Upper-part extracts beat root extracts on most measures, including phenolic content and blocking of a memory-linked enzyme. Chemical profiling tentatively named 222 compounds across 66 families. The results set up the plant as a candidate source of protective compounds.
pmc-11644849:
Xuantuo Huang and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, a virtual training ground for sighted helpers who guide blind people from afar. In remote-sighted assistance, a helper watches live video and sends coded vibration commands, but video delay and imperfect execution make guiding hard to learn on real people.

Their platform, built in the Unreal Engine, simulates a visually impaired person following instructions in a realistic space. Helpers practice the vibration command set safely until it becomes fluent. Trained agents then guided people along the same route about thirty-two percent faster, with over half fewer bumps into surroundings, than untrained novices. The simulator offers cheap, repeatable practice.
pmc-11644949:
Wang, Wu, Wang, and Xia present a study from twenty twenty-four on a wider way to make pictures with light. Ghost imaging builds a picture from light patterns, not from a direct view of the object. It resists noise well, but its view range has stayed narrow. The team adds a second light path so the system can gather facts from a wider area. They feed both paths into a smart network that rebuilds the target picture.

The network also has a focus step that shifts weight to the most useful signals. Tests in simulation show the method works and rebuilds pictures well. The authors say the wider range makes ghost imaging more useful in real settings. It offers a fresh path for later imaging tools.
pmc-11645049:
Alessandro Mengarelli and co-authors test a way to gauge walking forces from muscle signals in 2024. The push of the foot against the ground guides balance and forward drive. Powered aids could walk more naturally if they used that force in their control loop. The team asked whether leg muscle signals alone could predict the downward part of the force.

They compared two deep learning models fed with signals from thigh and shin muscles. The models tracked the force while people walked freely, without lab limits. Good tracking would let aids react to each step in real time. The study supports more natural and comfy walking for people who use such devices.
pmc-11645449:
Perrine Burdeyron and co-authors tried repairing pig kidneys before transplant using tiny parcels shed by urine stem cells in a 2024 proof-of-concept study. A donor kidney suffers when blood flow stops and restarts, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Cell therapy might condition the organ during storage, but living cells bring risks.

Extracellular vesicles, the membrane parcels cells use to send signals, could deliver the benefit without the cells. The team perfused pig kidneys with vesicles from urine progenitor cells and checked the grafts. Conditioning an organ on the pump would fit real transplant workflow. A positive signal here justifies testing whether vesicles cut early graft failure in people.
pmc-11645549:
Arjun Srivatsa and co-authors build a principled way to plan cancer genome studies before spending on them, in a 2024 paper. Modern tools can read single cells’ genes and marks in many modes, each with its own cost and blind spots. For studies of how tumor cell families evolve, the mix of tools and sampling plans can make or break the result.

Their framework weighs what each design recovers about family trees of mutated cells against its price and limits. Somatic variation, where cell populations differ wildly, is the proving ground. A design chosen on paper with clear trade-offs beats the common habit of sequencing first and hoping later. Funders and labs can use such planning to stretch limited samples and budgets further.
pmc-11645649:
Mary Maldarelli and her team study air made foul by wild fires in Canada and the load of heart and lung ills in the east of the United States. Their 2024 case-just study uses files from a sick bay net in Maryland.

Meets on high foul air days in June twenty twenty-three were set next to matched days in two past Junes. On those days, fine bits in the air went past state norms. Finds took in stays, walk-in care, and rush room meets for heart and lung states. Checks were set right for side traits with known tests and math checks. Strong wild fires near homes come more and more, yet health acts of far smoke dose stay in doubt. The folk in the study were wide in life state and in group traits, which made the finds count for more folk.
pmc-11645749: Yang Pan and Takeshi Iwata write a 2024 letter that questions a study on a protein tied to eye disease risk at a known gene spot. The study gauged the protein in blood and eye fluid with a home-built glow test and found no tie to gene risk. The letter raises method flags. Two shop kits used for contrast have ranges that do not touch, so one sample cannot serve both. Curve math used a straight model where a log form fits, which may warp the null result.
pmc-11645949:
Yanling Zhang and co-authors use automated MRI segmentation to chart brain change in temporal lobe epilepsy. Their 2024 study covers 48 patients, split between those with hippocampal scarring and those with clean scans, plus 30 healthy volunteers. FreeSurfer software measured cortex thickness and hippocampal subfield sizes.

The scarred group lost clear volume in the hippocampus head, body, and tail against both other groups. Cortical thinning spread wider in the scarred group too, touching fifteen regions against controls. The non-lesional group differed in only six regions. Two regions split the two patient groups from each other. The authors back the tool for tracking disease type.
pmc-11646349:
Dan Shan and co-authors pool studies on whether COVID-19 infection raises the later risk of new dementia in older adults, in work from 2024. The link was suspected but unclear. Long follow up after infection is rare, so pooled evidence helps.

Searches covered studies in English from 2020 through 2023. Eleven studies qualified, with nearly nine hundred forty thousand COVID survivors and over six point seven million controls. Controls were split into those with other chest infections and those with unspecified health. Risk was tracked at three, six, twelve, and twenty-four months after infection. The split lets readers judge whether any excess risk is specific to this virus.
pmc-11647249:
Damla Gül Fındık and co-authors track in 2024 how a little studied protein changes as colon growths turn toward cancer. Colon cancer is a major health burden, and many cases start as benign growths in the bowel wall. Knowing which molecules shift along that path could sharpen early tests and forecasts for patients.

The team studied 60 tissue samples: cancers, two kinds of growth with low and high risk, and normal tissue next to the growths. They rechecked each sample's type and grade under the microscope. A staining method then showed where the protein sits and how much of it is present. They also checked how its level lines up with how fast the cells divide. Patterns like these may one day help doctors judge which growths need close watching.
pmc-11647349:
Han and co-authors lay out a plan to review trials that pair chemotherapy with immunotherapy for stomach cancer, in this 2024 paper. The pairing has become a new standard of care, yet reviews so far cover only parts of the field. A full account of benefits and harms is still needed.

The protocol follows standard reporting rules for review plans. The team will search three major databases and screen studies in two rounds by two authors. Only randomized trials in English that compare the pairing against chemotherapy alone will count, in both surgical and first-line settings. The finished review aims to guide care and future research.
pmc-11647549:
Julien Le Guevelou and co-authors review imaging for dry mouth after head and neck radiation in a 2024 paper. Radiation saves lives but often wrecks the salivary glands, leaving lasting dryness. New scans promise to measure that damage and even predict it. The team gathered studies using PET, MRI, and older tracer scans of the glands.

Saliva flow after treatment tracked the dose reaching both the cheek and under-jaw glands. Uptake values from PET scans matched the flow results. Models mixing early scan changes during treatment with clinical details could forecast later loss of function. Such forecasts could let doctors reshape treatment mid-course for patients headed for the worst dryness. Imaging turns a vague side effect into a measurable, maybe preventable, one.
pmc-11647849:
Fuel cells that run on hydrogen live or die by the water balance inside their membranes. Xin Zhan and co-authors studied that balance in 2024 by mapping electrical resistance across a working cell, a signal that tracks how wet or dry the membrane is. They paired three-dimensional simulations with local impedance measurements to check the model.

Simulated and measured resistance patterns agreed reasonably well. At high current, the driest point shifted upstream on the air side, thanks to the membrane humidifying itself. Water and heat patterns explained the uneven stress the membrane feels as load changes. The outlet region swung most. The authors say such maps can guide design and operation to extend cell life.
pmc-11648149:
Rodrigo Carrillo-Larco and Ian Hambleton describe the daily work of a cohorts consortium that pools health data across Latin America and the Caribbean. Pooled cohort data let small lands make region level risk gauges. The article came out in twenty twenty-four.

A steering group of regional experts set the project up. Members who agree to share person level data help set goals and coauthor papers. A systematic search found data holders, and a manual logs all steps. By the study year, the pool held dozens of units from over a dozen lands, with a vast total sample. Past outputs include region risk gauges for heart and metabolism traits.
pmc-11648249:
Heyue Jin and a team of co-authors map gene and protein shifts in placentas of small babies, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Babies small for their age face stillbirth risk and lasting harm, often from a weak placenta. The team paired gene readouts with protein measures in placental tissue.

Two linked modules of genes and proteins split small-baby placentas from healthy ones. Core driver molecules were traced to their upstream switches. A separate group of samples confirmed those drivers. The work names fresh targets that may drive the placenta's failure to feed the baby well.
pmc-11648549:
Zheng, Pei, and Huang map research trends on dexmedetomidine in perioperative medicine. The drug calms, eases pain, and cuts stress in surgical patients. It also shows anti-inflammatory and anxiolytic effects in that setting. The team pulled 1,652 papers from the Web of Science Core Collection. That set held 1,497 articles and 155 reviews. Output rose sharply after 2013 in this field.

China led output, with the United States second. One journal, BMC Anesthesiology, printed the most papers on the topic. Anesthesiology led on citations per paper and co-citation rank. Ji Fuhai was the most prolific author in the set. Hot topics were older patients and post-surgery confusion.
pmc-11648749:
Saeid Joveini and co-authors compare two plant compounds against chronic inflammation in rats in this 2024 study. Both compounds come from plants of the carrot family. Inflammation signals named in the title are the readouts of interest. Sixty male rats were split into ten groups. Once lasting inflammation was confirmed, treated groups got one compound by mouth for nine days. Tissue samples were examined after the course ended.

Body weight changes were tracked as a health sign. One compound at a set dose raised weight gain clearly. Blood levels of the two signal proteins showed distinct patterns per compound. The pair are not interchangeable, the results suggest. Such differences matter for picking a lead compound for arthritis research. The study is an animal experiment, not a human trial. Doses and effects are fully tabled in the article.
pmc-11650149:
Yen-Ting Lin and Yu-San Han survey glass eels in Yilan, Taiwan, in a 2024 study. Glass eels are the young stage of freshwater eels, and Yilan is the first place in East Asia where they arrive on ocean currents. Knowing which species arrive matters for ecology and fisheries.

The team netted eels in a river estuary twice a month for over thirteen years. Shape checks and a gene test identified seven species. Three species made up most catches, a few were rare, and two were new records for Taiwan. The count of eel species known there rises from five to seven.
pmc-11650349:
Seo, Jung, and Song discuss in twenty twenty-four a bladder-sparing option for a hard-to-treat form of bladder cancer. The cancer sits in the bladder lining and no longer responds to the standard bladder drug treatment. The usual next step is to remove the bladder, a major operation many patients decline or cannot face.

The authors review a trial plan that pairs focused radiation with a drug that makes radiation work harder. Patients keep their bladder while doctors check how many are clear of cancer at six months. They also weigh how long the effect lasts and how safe the mix is. The piece weighs this path against newer bladder drugs and body-wide treatments.
pmc-11650749:
Jie Zhang and co-authors study two immune genes, TLR2 and MyD88, in frogs and their relatives. These genes help the body spot invading germs. The team read the genes in a large treefrog and checked where in the body they switch on. Both were active in every tissue tested. Levels ran highest in the heart.

Across amphibian species, the genes are strongly conserved. Yet tests find clear signs of positive selection acting on both. Certain sites changed faster than chance would allow. The authors read this as adaptation to new germs faced on land. Amphibians moved from water to land and spread into many habitats. Their immune genes seem to have evolved under that pressure.
pmc-11650849:
Quentin Smith and co-authors widen the range over which scientists can measure how drugs slip into the brain. The blood-brain barrier lets fat-loving compounds through easily, but blood flow caps how fast uptake can be clocked in a living animal. That cap hides the true permeability of many approved brain drugs. The team perfused rat brains with salt fluid at higher flow and added blood proteins to slow extraction back into a readable range.

With those tricks they measured 125 substances across ten orders of magnitude in permeability. Seventy-eight showed no sign of being pumped back out. Famous drugs like diazepam came out far more permeable than older reports claimed. The results trace a straight line between lab fat-solubility and brain entry across the whole range. The method resets expectations for how quickly brain drugs actually cross.
pmc-11651449:
Li Chen and four co-authors test a blood protein as a liver cancer flag in a 2024 study. Pentraxin-3 rises with inflammation, and the team asked whether it also tracks primary liver cancer closely enough to help clinics.

They drew blood from 180 patients and 180 healthy people and measured the protein with a standard kit. Levels ran clearly higher in patients, and higher still with drinking history, larger or more numerous tumors, spread stage, and vessel invasion. A cutoff sorted patients from healthy people fairly well, though not perfectly. Survival tracking linked high levels to worse outlook. The authors pitch the protein as a useful extra marker, not a lone verdict.
pmc-11652049:
Yang and four co-authors tested image fusion for judging lung tumor ablation during the procedure itself in twenty twenty-four. Microwave ablation destroys early lung tumors with heat in patients who cannot tolerate surgery. During treatment, the tumor and the burned zone can look alike on CT scans, hiding whether the tumor is fully covered.

In twenty-nine patients with thirty-two lesions, a radiologist fused before-and-after CT images, a process taking about ten minutes with a ninety-seven percent success rate. Two physicians then judged the tumor's position relative to the ablation zone. On plain scans they were right only about eight to thirteen percent of the time. On fused images they reached about eighty-seven percent, and they agreed strongly. Judgments from fused images matched six-month follow-up perfectly. The authors call fusion a valuable intraoperative check.
pmc-11652549:
Yazan Alwadi and six co-authors measure heat's toll on Kuwaiti hearts in a 2024 paper. Kuwait is heating fast under climate change. Heart disease already leads its mortality statistics. Hospital records from 2010 to 2019 anchor the analysis.

Over two hundred sixty thousand heart admissions were recorded in that decade. About twenty thousand of them were attributed to heat. Risk climbed as temperatures passed forty one degrees. Statistical models adjusted for humidity and season. Future climates from global models extended the trend to 2099. Both moderate and extreme scenarios raised the projected burden. The authors warn health systems to plan for hotter decades. Their numbers give Kuwait a baseline for adaptation policy.
pmc-11652949:
Printed blood vessel tubes could treat heart disease, and Tianhong Chen and co-authors review the materials used to print them. Older ways of making vessel scaffolds carried risks of clots, lasting inflammation, and clogged arteries. Bioprinting builds the tubes layer by layer, and the ink matters as much as the printer.

The review compares natural, synthetic, and blended materials for printing implants that sit inside the body. Each type trades strength against friendliness to living tissue. The authors stress that a material must print well and behave well inside the body, and they point to gaps still blocking clinic use.
pmc-11653249:
Lisa Körtgen and Uwe Ruschewitz make and map a new family of crystal salts in a 2024 paper. The salts join alkaline earth metals with hydrogen acetylide units. No crystal structure for this family had been published before. The barium member was made from metal in liquid ammonia plus a gas.

Fine powder X-ray data gave the barium salt's full crystal structure. Its layers look much like two known mineral types. The strontium salt seems to share the same structure. The calcium salt formed with almost no crystal order. Light and gas tests confirmed the key anion in all three. Heating the barium salt with extra metal gave a pure carbide crystal.
pmc-11653549:
Slavka Porubcova and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, if pharmacists on the care team can cut drug problems for vessel surgery patients. Such patients take many drugs at once, which raises the risk of harm and clashes. The trial ran for one year at a specialist hospital in Slovakia. It held 105 adults with artery disease of the neck or legs, each on at least three drugs. Pharmacists checked drug lists at entry and at discharge, and flagged fixes to the doctor. Patients also got teaching on their drugs at discharge.

At entry, each patient had a mean of 2.3 drug problems. At discharge that fell to 1.6, a clear drop. Heart and vessel drugs drove most problems, at about 42 percent. The work backs a set seat for pharmacists in vessel care teams.
pmc-11653849:
Bleeding inside the brain is a rare and dangerous complication of a vessel inflammation disease once called Churg-Strauss syndrome. Pu Bai and Peitao Xie report the case of an 18-year-old student with the disease, now named EGPA. His scans showed both a brain hemorrhage and lung infiltration, with blood eosinophils climbing steadily.

The patient received three days of high-dose steroid infusion plus cyclophosphamide, then oral prednisone. At discharge, scans showed the brain blood clot largely absorbed and the lungs improved. The authors also reviewed 40 published cases of the same pairing, comparing features and treatments. Their message is that early recognition matters: prompt, strong immune-suppressing treatment improves the outlook. Doctors caring for these patients should stay alert for signs that the disease has reached the central nervous system.
pmc-11653949:
Ayaka Mitomo and co-authors report a young woman whose kidneys failed after she took a dose of caffeine large enough to kill. Their 2024 case report notes that caffeine poisoning is rising, yet kidney injury from it stays rare and its path unclear. She had swallowed an over-the-counter drug loaded with caffeine.

Doctors found kidney failure of the kind that still lets urine flow. A biopsy on day nineteen showed healthy glomeruli but hurt tubules, with casts of a muscle protein inside them. Filter treatment steadied her, and she went home on day thirty-four. The authors walk through how caffeine's grip on two receptor types may have driven the damage.
pmc-11654149:
Liu and co-authors (2024) surveyed clinical medicine students about blended learning in pediatrics. Blended courses mix online and classroom work, and schools need to know how students judge that environment and how independently they learn in it. The team polled 487 students at Wuhan University who had finished the blended pediatrics course, using two standard rating scales, and linked the answers with statistical models.

Students rated the environment and their own learning autonomy positively overall. Ratings of teachers came first among the environment parts, and social self-perception last. Among autonomy parts, learning strategies scored highest. Every part of the two scales correlated with the rest. The atmosphere of the course and students' academic self-perception stood out as significant predictors of learning autonomy. The authors recommend steady tuning of course content and environment to lift both satisfaction and independent learning.
pmc-11654249:
Ayelign Mengesha Kassie and five co-authors scope how well mother and newborn care truly lands in poorer countries in a 2024 review. Effective coverage counts not just visits but good care received by those in need, yet studies define it in clashing ways. The review gathers those definitions, the measures used, and what moves the numbers.

Thirty six papers made the cut. Most framed coverage as need met in equipped sites or as quality care actually received; some swapped need for raw use. Rates ran from zero for some post birth care to eighty four percent for pregnancy visits. Wealth, schooling, and town or country living all bent the rates. The authors call for one shared yardstick so countries can compare fairly.
pmc-11654349:
Xuelian Liu and six co-authors find, in a 2024 study, two genes that steer sepal and petal development in the lotus. The lotus is a prized aquatic plant grown for ornament, food, and medicine. Its blooms range from few petals to a thousand, which makes it a fine case for how flowers form. The genes are lotus counterparts of a well-known flower gene called APETALA2.

Both genes were most active in buds and petals, and their proteins sat mainly in the nucleus, as gene switches should. When the genes were switched on in a model plant, its blooms grew extra sepals and petals. Each gene also repaired the flawed blooms of a mutant that lacks its own AP2. Tests show the lotus proteins team with other flower organ proteins. The team say the pair shape the outer rings of the lotus bloom, a lead for breeders.
pmc-11654649:
Tariq Imran Khokhar and four co-authors report a rare set of brain abscesses in a boy from Pakistan. Their patient was 14 years old, with a healthy immune system, and had suffered seizures for six months along with fever, vomiting, and headache. Ear, nose, throat, and sinus exams were normal, which is unusual since most cases spread from those sites. Scans showed several space-occupying lesions in the left fronto-parietal region.

Surgeons removed the multiloculated, encapsulated lesion, which held yellow-green pus, through a modified pterional craniotomy. Culture grew Proteus mirabilis, a Gram-negative bacterium rarely behind such cases. The boy left hospital without complications, and the authors stress early surgical excision.
pmc-11655549:
Samantha Hartke and five co-authors introduce GARD-LENS, a high-resolution climate dataset built to separate forced change from the climate's own wobble, in this 2024 data paper. The set sharpens three big global model ensembles down to daily rain and temperature maps. Coverage spans the continental United States at twelve-kilometer grid size, Alaska at four, and Hawaii at one.

Two hundred ensemble members across one hundred fifty years give users deep statistics on trends and extremes. Because each parent model starts many runs from slightly different states, the dataset is the first of its kind to show natural variability at street-level detail. The authors aim it at scientists and planners who must budget for uncertainty in adaptation work.
pmc-11655649:
Tape measures and calipers give a rough picture of body shape, and their errors limit studies of weight and health. Magda Alexandra Trujillo-Jiménez and ten co-authors present a three-dimensional body data set in 2024, built from scans of a Patagonian population in Argentina.

The data set, called 3DPatBody, holds full body scans, point clouds, and matching hand measurements for 299 people, most of them women. The group is of special interest because its body pattern ties to both obesity research and local ancestry and environment. Shape measures from the scans predicted the classic indices well, while adding detail about body form that flat numbers miss. The authors offer the data as a reference for health and population studies.
pmc-11655949:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is usually sorted by stage and chromosome damage, but Gorkem Kismali and co-authors try sorting it by gene activity instead, in a 2024 study. They clustered gene expression data from 130 untreated patients and found the groups split cleanly by one gene's level: BTK, a signaling protein that modern leukemia drugs target.

The high and low BTK groups held up across five datasets totaling about seven hundred patients. High-BTK leukemia carried more disease burden and more of two immune signal molecules. Low-BTK leukemia showed weaker DNA repair messaging, more damage-response activity, and more self-destruct programming. Protein measurements matched the gene patterns. The authors suggest BTK level marks two biological styles of the disease that may one day guide treatment choice.
pmc-11656249:
Pengyin Li and four co-workers wrote a 2024 paper on a bone-healing gel made by linking a common polymer with resveratrol, a plant compound. Plain gels of this polymer are too soft for bone repair. Freeze-thaw cycles let the two parts bind through strong hydrogen bonds. No harsh chemistry was needed to set the gel.

The mixed gel was far stiffer than the plain one at the best ratio. Cell tests used young bone-forming cells from mouse skull. A low-dose gel boosted bone enzyme activity and mineral deposits. It also raised bone-growth gene levels. The gel nudged immune cells toward a healing type as well.
pmc-11656549:
Hatefi, Biglari, and Babakhani check if ankle bend range and stiffness predict landing balance. Both traits have been tied to non-contact injury risk. Twenty male amateur athletes joined the tests. Ankle bend was gauged with a weight-bearing lunge test. Balance was scored on one-leg landings with two index tools.

No clear link joined ankle bend, stiffness, and landing scores. A mid-level tie between bend range and stiffness did not reach significance. Bend range and time to steady stance also showed a weak tie. The authors say stiffness alone does not set landing balance. Sex, age, and task type may change the picture.
pmc-11656649:
Tingxiang Yan and co-authors report in a 2024 study that a protein tagging pathway runs weak in Alzheimer's disease brains. The tag, UFM1, latches onto other proteins and was lately shown to curb tau clumping in models. Whether the pathway falters in human disease tissue had not been checked.

Frontal and temporal cortex samples from donors with and without the disease were compared. Levels of pathway proteins were measured and tied to tangle and plaque marks. Regression tests with strict error control hunted links to tau measures and stress paths. Gene edited neurons then tested the stress links in living cells. The work frames the pathway as a fresh angle on tau harm.
pmc-11656949:
Carla Andreea Culda and co-authors surveyed parasites carried by ticks and other vectors in dogs in the Galapagos in 2024. The islands hold many unique native species that are at risk from new pathogens brought in with domestic animals. Dogs are a likely bridge for such spread.

The team collected blood from more than twelve hundred pet dogs on four islands in 2021 and 2022. Tests found heartworm in dogs on all four islands, at about two percent overall. Gene tests confirmed heartworm on two islands and found another parasite, Babesia vogeli, in about three percent of dogs. The work maps where these parasites sit so spillover to native mammals can be judged.
pmc-11657349:
Miaomin Ye and co-authors link bowel habits to fatty liver disease in a 2024 study of United States adults. Gut microbes tie the two together, but simple signs like stool form and toilet frequency had not been checked against the disease and its scarring stage.

They used national survey data from 2005 to 2010 covering nearly 10,000 adults. Models weighed stool type and movement frequency against disease status, with care for survey design. Both very rare and very frequent movements tied to higher odds of fatty liver disease in adjusted results. The trend analysis and subgroup checks held up. The authors suggest bowel habits may flag liver risk in clinic.
pmc-11657449:
Fei Xue and Yating Zhou link exercise patterns, including weekend-only workouts, to sleep apnea symptoms in US survey data, in a study from 2024. Many busy adults now cram their activity into one or two days, the so-called weekend warrior pattern. The team used national health survey data from three waves, covering 19,223 adults with self-reported activity.

Adults fell into four groups: inactive, not quite active enough, weekend warriors, and regularly active. After adjusting for other factors, both weekend warriors and regular exercisers had lower odds of apnea symptoms than inactive adults, by about 15 and 17 percent. The two active patterns did not differ from each other. Weekend benefits showed most in white, low-income, and male subgroups, while regular activity helped more broadly.
pmc-11657749:
Mengge Zhou and co-authors set fresh disability weights for 196 health states in Hubei Province, China, in a study from 2024. A disability weight grades how severe a non fatal health state is, from zero for full health to one for a state like death. Such weights feed into measures of total disease burden used to plan health spending.

Whether global weights fit a single province is debated, so the team gathered local judgments. A web survey drew paired comparisons from close to thirty four thousand residents. Statistical methods turned those choices into weights on the zero to one scale, anchored to a past global study. The new weights are then compared in value and rank with Chinese, global, and Japanese sets, to show where local views differ.
pmc-11658049:
Constanza Martínez-Valdebenito and co-authors hunt the animals behind scrub typhus in southern Chile, in a study published in 2024. The disease there is caused by a local Orientia species carried in nature by unknown hosts and vectors. The team trapped rodents at six sites on Chiloé Island, where human cases occur, and tested their tissues and the mites found on them.

Orientia DNA turned up in about a quarter of rodents across five of seven species, at rates that varied by place but not by the rodent's sex, age, or mite load. Mite sequences matched those from human patients in the same region exactly. A particular trombiculid mite therefore looks like the vector. Whether the rodents themselves are lasting reservoirs remains open.
pmc-11658149:
