Jonas Manschel and co-authors published this metasynthesis in 2024. Osteopathy, a hands-on manual therapy, is regulated very differently across Europe. Switzerland legally recognizes the profession, while Germany and Austria do not. The COCO project set out to learn how osteopaths themselves see their work in the three German-speaking countries. After a systematic search, the team synthesized thirty interview-based studies.

Practitioners described their core resources as manual treatment, a whole-person approach, and unhurried sessions. Teachers and prominent figures strongly shaped their outlook. The deepest challenge was identity: many struggled to define what osteopathy even is. Training paths and qualifications varied widely, the largest difference between the countries. Internal disagreements over standards added friction. On the bright side, osteopaths reported satisfying work and strong public demand. The authors say the field's future depends on settling its identity and training questions.
pmc-11658349:
Bin Xia and nineteen co-authors ask whether healthy eating patterns lower the risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Proof on diet and the two main forms of the disease, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, has been thin. The team followed nearly two hundred thousand adults in a British cohort who were free of the disease at the start. Four healthy diet scores were read from their food records.

Over the follow-up, 260 people developed Crohn's disease and 601 developed ulcerative colitis. Two diet scores, for a Mediterranean-style diet and a general healthy index, went with lower Crohn's risk but not colitis risk. Low body inflammation carried part of the benefit. The paper ties everyday eating to one form of the disease.
pmc-11658449:
Xuezhi Zhou and co-authors build an unsupervised AI signature to forecast rectal cancer outcomes in a 2024 paper. Rectal cancer is common worldwide and lacks good forecast markers. Whole slide images of tumors hold rich detail that computational pathology can mine.

From over two hundred patients in two data sets, the team first trained a model to find tumor areas. An autoencoder then turned tumor patches into deep features, and patches were clustered by those features. Cluster patterns formed a signature tied to progression-free survival. Tuning the cluster count sharpened the result. Such image signatures could help doctors sort patients by risk without new lab tests.
pmc-11658949:
Ni Shi and nine colleagues link pro-inflammatory and high-insulin dietary patterns to specific gut microbiome profiles, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Two empirical diet scores capture how strongly eating patterns drive inflammation and insulin response. Whether the colon's microbes mediate their disease effects was poorly understood. The analysis used over sixteen hundred adults in a British twin cohort.

Microbiome profiles were built from dozens of bacterial genera for each diet score. Higher profile scores tracked with higher insulin and insulin resistance. Six genera were shared between the two dietary patterns, some positive and some inverse. Predicted microbial pathways involved fatty acid building, sugar acid breakdown, and mevalonate metabolism. Those pathways also associated with the dietary scores themselves. The authors suggest diet may shape chronic disease risk partly through gut microbes.
pmc-11659249:
Xilong Wang and six co-authors review what is known about thinking problems in Moyamoya disease in this 2024 paper. The disease narrows the brain's arteries, and trouble with memory, planning, and general intelligence is common among patients. The authors note that knowledge of these mental effects still lags far behind knowledge of the blood-vessel side.

The review sorts the reported patterns of decline across mental skills, including executive function, intelligence, and memory. It also weighs surgery that reroutes blood flow to the brain, where studies disagree on whether thinking improves afterward. The authors find the research base thin and call for work on how the disease produces these effects in the first place. Long-term studies that follow the same patients over years are another priority they name.
pmc-11660149:
Batey and co-authors review how gut-wall toxin shifts brain chemistry in a 2024 perspective paper. Inflammation in the body and depression travel together, yet how body inflammation rewrites brain signals stayed murky. The toxin LPS, shed by bacteria, gives labs a fast, standard way to spark inflammation.

Across studies, the toxin lowered dopamine and serotonin in several brain zones while raising norepinephrine. The authors read this not as damage but as an evolved program: the body slows and turns inward to heal. Mood change, on this view, is part of the recovery script. The frame may reshape how depression with inflammation is understood.
pmc-11662649:
Yuki Ban and co-authors fish for proteins that grip a lesser-known DNA fold, and land on a famous nucleolar protein doing two opposite jobs, in a 2024 study. The fold is the i-motif, formed where DNA runs rich in cytosine; its better-known cousin, the G-quadruplex, has many known handlers, while i-motif handlers were scarce. The team built a DNA probe that tags nearby proteins for capture and ran it through HeLa cell nuclear extract.

The catch included known binders and fresh candidates. They characterized nucleolin, which binds the i-motif and relaxes it, unwinding the fold, while stabilizing the G-quadruplex instead. One protein thus pushes two rival structures in opposite directions. The authors present the probe as a general tool for mapping who handles folded DNA, and nucleolin as a regulator of the cell's high-order DNA architecture.
pmc-11662949:
Yangning Zhou, Yan Wang, and Limin Xu pick out risk factors for postoperative cognitive dysfunction. That state can come after vessel treatment, done as an emergency for stroke, with general anaesthesia. Their 2024 study builds a model to forecast it, from signs in patients.

Three hundred thirty-three patients with acute ischaemic stroke took part. About a third of them got cognitive dysfunction. Regression analysis picked two markers of inflammation and three signs of brain injury. They were used for a nomogram model used as a set. The measures picked took in a score for how severe the stroke was, a peptide tied to the heart, and a protein tied to brain injury. Checks of the model took in calibration and curves for how much use it is in clinics. Results also hinted at links through anaesthesia depth, cognitive impairment, and inflammatory response in these patients.
pmc-11663549:
Maric sums up recent work in twenty twenty-five on how plants remember cold stress. Plants that survive a mild cold spell can build a kind of memory at the gene level. That memory helps them cope better when cold strikes again, unlike plants that meet cold for the first time.

She explains two kinds of memory genes. Some stay switched at a new level after stress ends. Others return to normal, then react more strongly the next time. A study on young cucumber plants traced changes during the rest phase after cold. It found more work on making proteins and less on folding them. Marks on the gene packaging help hold these states in place.
pmc-11664049:
Onur Mutlu, Bengi Türk, and Furkan Asan report a rare seizure case in pregnancy in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Absence status epilepticus is a long stretch of blank, unresponsive episodes driven by seizure activity. It can appear for the first time in adults with no prior epilepsy.

Their patient was a woman aged twenty-two, pregnant, with no history of seizures. She arrived with reduced speech and a puzzled state. A brain wave test showed continuous, whole-brain spike-wave patterns at a steady rhythm. She improved after a sedative and a seizure drug. The authors say this is the first reported case of this condition starting during pregnancy.
pmc-11664249:
Majd Almech and co-authors survey medical students in Saudi Arabia on herbal medicine in a 2024 study. Herbal remedies are woven into the country's health culture, and its Vision 2030 plan promotes alternative practices with a stress on safety through education and research. Future doctors will meet patients who use these remedies daily, so what students know and believe about them matters.

The team surveyed students at three medical colleges over six months in 2024. They scored knowledge and perceptions and tested how the two vary with background traits. The title poses the paper's pointed question: should medical schools act now? Gaps in student knowledge, if found, would argue for teaching that covers benefits, risks, and drug interactions before these students prescribe.
pmc-11664649:
Kfir Rutman Moshe and co-authors rescue a subtle molecular effect from being mistaken for noise in a 2024 paper. In long, straight molecules, spinning couples with bending vibrations, splitting rotational levels in a phenomenon called l-doubling. Laser alignment studies, which set molecules spinning in step, had mostly left the effect out of their accounts.

The team traces what l-doubling does to the shared rotational dance of linear three-atom molecules at room temperature and above. Its signature unfolds across the first few hundred picoseconds after excitation, exactly the window where researchers usually blame collisions for fading signals. That resemblance is the warning: decay blamed on molecular bumps may instead be this orderly internal effect, misread. The authors argue that models of rotational dynamics, dissipative and coherent alike, must assimilate l-doubling to read their own data correctly.
pmc-11665549:
Jinoll, Workalemahu, and Adugna assessed mixed land-use planning in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in twenty twenty-four, asking what blending homes, shops, and leisure spaces does to a fast-growing city. Mixed planning promises shorter trips and livelier streets, but its full effects in the capital were unmeasured.

The team surveyed three hundred eighty-four households, forty planning specialists, and fourteen key informants in two sub-cities, drawing on data from twenty oh two to twenty seventeen. Effects on travel and access to services varied sharply from place to place. Planners and residents praised gains in economic life and social mixing, yet flagged real strains as well. The authors conclude there is no single recipe: each district's mix must fit its own conditions. Their recommendations aim at planning that supports growth without surrendering fairness or green space.
pmc-11666349:
Hongzhan Zhang and co-authors study thyroid function and ovarian reserve in infertile women in a 2024 paper. Low ovarian reserve limits success in fertility care. Thyroid trouble is common in women of childbearing age, and its link to reserve, apart from thyroid autoimmunity, needed a large test.

Near three thousand women starting their first IVF cycle at one hospital were grouped by thyroid status. Egg reserve was gauged by a hormone level and follicle counts. Women with underactive thyroid, even mild, showed lower reserve in the analysis, independent of autoimmunity. Fertility clinics may add thyroid checks to reserve workups on this evidence.
pmc-11666449:
Elena Campione and co-authors study fungal growth on psoriasis patients and how a drug changes it, in a 2024 paper. Yeasts such as Candida can trigger or worsen psoriasis in hard-to-treat spots like folds and nails. The team enrolled 70 patients with psoriasis in those areas.

At the start, 47 percent carried Candida, mostly in the mouth, and 39 percent had nail fungus. Blood markers and skin scores were tracked over a year of apremilast treatment. By week 52, the drug had cleared Candida fully in 83 percent of patients with a single yeast species. Mixed-species cases cleared more slowly. The study links a common psoriasis drug to a lighter fungal load and better skin outcomes.
pmc-11666549:
Jose DeAndres and co-authors, editors of a research collection on the topic, survey the state of neuraxial therapeutics for pain. The term covers drugs delivered into the spaces around the spinal cord, rather than swallowed or injected into a vein. The approach is widely used for pain and other spinal disorders, and thousands of papers on it appeared in just the past five years.

Writing as a perspective, the authors explain why interest runs so high and lay out the major themes in how the spine encodes pain signals. They discuss how spinal delivery can place medicine close to its target while sparing the rest of the body. The piece serves as an invitation and a map for the research collection they edit. It points toward open questions about dosing, safety, and new drug forms.
pmc-11668149:
Josef Finsterer and Sounira Mehri wrote a 2024 letter to a journal editor about a teenage patient whose case had been reported by another team. The boy had a kidney condition and, after a drug switch and a positive virus test, suffered seizures and brain lesions. The first team blamed a drug side effect called PRES, a swelling problem in the brain.

The letter argues that the PRES label rests on weak ground. The lesions were scattered, and the scan proof that PRES requires was not shown. The writers say an autoimmune brain inflammation tied to the virus fits the facts better, since the boy's course matched that pattern more closely. They urge care in telling the two apart, because the treatments differ and a wrong label can steer care the wrong way.
pmc-11668449:
Dinkar Yadav, Hunny Verma, Neha Yadav, and Kapil Bhalla report a child harmed by cough syrup in a 2024 case report. Cough is a reflex that clears the airways, and most cases need only basic care. Still, over-the-counter syrups are often used too freely in India, the authors note.

A six-year-old girl came to emergency care after taking a syrup with dextromethorphan and chlorpheniramine. She had lost consciousness and shown abnormal body movements. Tests of spinal fluid, brain scans, and brain wave records found no major problem. She stayed in hospital for five days and went home in stable condition.
pmc-11668549:
Qing Li and seven co-authors use a new ultrasound method to track which heart failure patients improve on treatment, in a 2024 study. The method draws a loop of heart pressure against wall strain, giving numbers for the work the main chamber does, both overall and by region. It needs no invasive probes.

The study enrolled 88 patients whose hearts pumped at 40 percent efficiency or less. All had taken heart failure drugs for six to twelve months. Scans supplied strain and work values, and improvement was judged by standard recommended criteria. Setting the work numbers beside who actually improved shows which measures track real recovery. Such a gauge could help doctors adjust drugs earlier for those falling behind.
pmc-11672249:
Yao Li and co-authors guard the brain's border wall in a 2024 sepsis study. Sepsis can scramble the brain partly by loosening the blood-brain barrier, and the team suspected a protective protein, Annexin A1, which septic mice had in short supply.

Mice lacking the protein suffered worse memory problems, leakier barriers, and more inflammation, with the molecular mortar between vessel cells, proteins like occludin and ZO-1, falling away. In cultured vessel cells, a fragment of the protein restored the mortar and blocked the leak, unless a growth signal overrode it. The work names a druggable defense for sepsis fog.
pmc-11672649:
Yusuke Ota and co-authors examine hospital wastewater to see which drug-resistance genes are active there, not just present. Their study appeared in 2024. Hospital drains gather resistant bacteria, yet gene surveys based on DNA alone cannot tell which genes are switched on. The team combined gene reading of both DNA and RNA from the water. They also tested the water for antibiotic traces.

They found several common antibiotics in the sample, which can push bacteria to switch resistance genes on. Genes for resistance to many drugs were the most common. Gene copies carried on plasmids, small DNA rings that jump between bacteria, showed high activity for their amount. The authors say watching active genes gives a truer picture of the risk hospital wastewater poses.
pmc-11672849:
Khury and five co-authors revisit antibiotic cement spacers for diabetic foot bone infection with long follow-up, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Diabetic osteomyelitis prevalence rises despite better living standards globally. Fifty-five patients with grade two B wounds receive debridement plus cement spacer fixation. Median follow-up approaches two and a half years.

Over half achieve primary eradication without further intervention. Another share succeeds after a secondary procedure. Most reoperations occur within a month of the primary procedure. Age, sex, and gentamicin-only cement correlate with reoperation risk. Staphylococcus infection correlates inversely with reoperation in this cohort. Most cured patients never need cement removal at all.
pmc-11672949:
Lee and co-authors examine muscle behavior in adult women who live with non-specific chronic low back pain. The study focuses on how their back and trunk muscles contract and how quickly those muscles tire during effort, measured with a technique called tensiomyography.

The researchers compare contraction properties and signs of acute muscle fatigue between the women in the study, looking for patterns tied to their pain condition. Muscles that tire fast or contract weakly can fail to support the spine during daily tasks, which may keep pain going. The results give physical therapists concrete muscle traits to target in exercise programs rather than treating all chronic back pain the same way.
pmc-11673149:
Roxanne Pillay and six co-authors map an unstudied pairing: intestinal worms and genital herpes in sub-Saharan Africa. The region carries a heavy load of both, with 232 million young children at risk of soil-transmitted helminths and herpes simplex virus type 2 widespread. Worm infections bend immunity toward a Th2 style, which can mute the Th1 and Th17 responses that fight viruses. Studies exist for worm pairings with HIV and HPV, but not for herpes.

That gap leaves the sexual and reproductive fallout unknown. The review lays out both infections' burdens and immune styles, then calls for joint research and combined screening in clinics.
pmc-11673249:
Marina Danalache and co-authors compared how two stem cell types respond mechanically to culture conditions, in a 2024 study. Cell behavior bends under physical forces, and growing conditions may reshape the cells meant for therapy. The team grew jaw periosteal cells and lab-induced stem cells under normal and low oxygen, with and without bone-forming cues, on two coatings.

Force microscopy measured each cell's stiffness and the stiffness of the mineral deposits the cells laid down. The induced cells stayed softer yet formed harder deposits in several settings. The two cell types answered the same conditions in opposite ways, a caution for standardizing cell products.
pmc-11673349:
Shinya Tanaka and co-authors test a feeding route for the smallest newborn babies, in a 2024 study. These babies often need breathing machines. Milk that flows back up and is breathed in can worsen lung harm. A tube that passes beyond the stomach may cut that risk.

The trial enrolled 39 babies with very low birth weight who were on ventilators. Each baby was assigned at random to the deep tube or a standard nose-to-stomach tube. The main measure was harmful breathing events. The deep tube group had a lower rate of such events. Babies in that group also went longer before an event. The results support the deeper route for fragile infants, within this small trial.
pmc-11673549:
Polina Klauzen, Liubov Basovich, Daria Shishkova, and colleagues review the role of macrophages in heart valve hardening in this two thousand twenty-four paper. In calcific aortic valve disease, immune cells, macrophages above all, help drive the valve's hardening. Macrophages inside narrowed valves show strong swelling activity, tilted toward pro-swelling types. Those cells release cytokines, chemokines, and microRNA that act straight on resident valve cells and push them toward hardening.

The review gathers proof that patient macrophages carry stronger pro-swelling traits. Soluble signals passed between cells shape them, but so do other forces. Notch signaling by direct cell contact also plays a part. Factors acting on parent cells as they mature matter too. The authors set out the data on these passed and contact-based signals. Their aim is a clearer picture of how immune cells steer valve disease and point to drug targets.
pmc-11673749:
Paulo Cezar de Freitas Mathias and a large research team published a rat study in two thousand twenty-four on how a mother's poor diet shapes her pups' metabolism. Mothers fed little protein while nursing can leave lasting marks on offspring. The team focused on stress hormones and sugar control in male offspring.

Rat mothers got a low-protein or normal diet for the first two weeks of nursing. At ninety days old, the male pups faced fasting or doses of a stress-hormone-like drug. Pups of low-protein mothers barely reacted to long fasting or to the drug given into the brain. Given the drug body-wide, both groups had blood sugar swings, but the low-protein pups reacted more strongly. The findings tie early diet to lifelong sugar handling.
pmc-11673849:
Yuqiao Dai leads a team on shape control of soft robots. Their work from twenty twenty-four uses neural networks for shape reading. Soft robots bend in a smooth line, unlike stiff arm robots.

To know their shape is hard, which blocks fine control. The team pulls outlines from camera views to get shape traits. A neural net learns how motor inputs map to shape output. A sim world then tests shape guesses and shape control. Results show the method can guess and copy soft shapes well. It offers a path to better soft robot control.
pmc-11673949:
Juliette Fouillet and co-authors teach the biology behind a scan that lights up a tumor's support crew instead of the tumor itself. Cancer-associated fibroblasts remodel the tumor's scaffolding, feed its blood supply, and muffle immune attack. They wear a marker, fibroblast activation protein, that nuclear medicine can target with labeled inhibitor molecules.

This didactic review walks through why the target makes sense and how the imaging agents are designed. The tracers shine where the standard glucose scan is weak, notably in liver and bile duct cancers with low metabolic activity. Newer derivatives sharpen scans further and hint at theranostics: the same targeting that finds the tumor could deliver radiation to it. The authors frame the protein as a precision oncology address worth mailing to.
pmc-11674049:
Betty Noergaard and co-authors teach ward staff five soft steps to ease heel prick pain in frail babies, in a study from 2024. Heel pricks feed blood tests but can leave blue or swelled heels and bad cuts. Near two hundred pricks ere and past the teach were scored for pain, strain, and harm.

The steps cost no cash: skin touch, cuddles, sweet feeds, warm heels, and sound staff pose. Past the teach, sound pain and strain scores in the prick rose by near a tenth. Past prick scores rose as well, while harm counts fell by a fourth, though that fall could be chance. Free rite tweaks cut baby pain, the team says.
pmc-11674149:
Sherlyne Jaimes-Díaz and co-authors test whether blood levels of vessel-growth factors can help diagnose a rare inherited bleeding disorder, in a 2024 paper. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia causes fragile vessels and nosebleeds, and faulty vessel growth drives it. Genetic testing confirms the disease but costs dearly and misses the mutation in up to one case in ten.

The team measured four vessel-related factors in blood from forty-four patients and nineteen healthy controls. Patients showed higher levels of one factor, TGF-beta1, and lower levels of another, ENG, than controls. Statistical checks, including cutoff analysis and combined models, weighed how well these cheap blood measures could flag the disease or hint at its course.
pmc-11674549:
Donatella Gambini and co-authors followed breast cancer patients diagnosed at eighty or older in a 2024 single-centre study; the catalog adds one author absent from the head byline. Care guidance for this age group rests on thin evidence, yet life expectancy can still be substantial. Eighty-eight consecutive patients were tracked for survival and disease course.

Five-year survival was about eighty-three percent, and freedom from progression about sixty-four percent. By eight and a half years, about half had died, a third of them from the cancer. Surgery, done in about seven in ten, linked to better early control. Added drug and radiation therapy were often skipped, and drop-out was high. Tailored, assessment-based care is urged.
pmc-11674749:
Mahmoud Abdallah and co-authors weigh a three-way drug alliance against advanced lung cancer: vessel blockers plus immunotherapy, with or without chemotherapy. Non-small cell lung cancer's local setting smothers immune attack, and drugs that prune its blood supply may loosen that grip. The review gathers past work on the pairing.

Their 2024 paper maps where the combo might serve: first-line care for spread disease, salvage after other drugs fail, mutated tumors that resist targeted pills, and brain spread before radiation. Stage three disease that cannot be cut out also enters the plan. The authors argue the alliance, timed well, could stretch long-term survival in more patients than now reach it.
pmc-11674849:
Vinod Kumar and co-authors show that the kidney risk gene APOL1 switches on the renin-angiotensin system in kidney filter cells, in a 2024 study. People carrying the G1 or G2 variants of the gene face higher risk of a scarring kidney disease. The team grew podocytes, the filter cells, engineered to carry the harmless G0 form or one of the risk forms.

Risk-form cells made more renin and more of the machinery that responds to it, while losing protective vitamin D receptor and key identity markers. The harmless form showed the opposite pattern. Silencing a partner protein raised renin, and a vitamin D activator restored the markers. The authors link a small RNA, miR193a, to the switch.
pmc-11675149:
Ruiz-García and co-authors read the genes of two South American tapirs in a 2024 study that reshapes their family tree. Tapirs are the largest land mammals of their region, yet their genetics remain thinly known. The team read full cell-power genes and three further genes in the Andean tapir and a claimed new species.

The Andean tapir came out as the youngest branch, sister to the lowland tapir, which flips the old view from body shape. The claimed new species fell inside the lowland tapir instead, not apart from it. The Andean tapir also held the least genetic variety of its kin.
pmc-11675349:
Hua Zhang and five co-authors line up stem cells on a gel using magnetism, coaxing them toward bone, in a 2024 paper. Many tissues are anisotropic, built in aligned patterns that give them direction-specific strength. Copying that alignment in soft wet gels is hard. The team let magnetic iron oxide particles self-assemble on a polyethylene glycol gel under a steady magnet. The particles formed ordered ridges a few hundred nanometers high and about ten micrometers wide.

Layer-by-layer building varied the ridge density and height, and tilting the field stacked patterns into three dimensions. Bone marrow stem cells grown on the patterns aligned and leaned into bone formation. Aligned scaffolds like these could guide regrowth of tendon, muscle, and bone along their natural grain.
pmc-11675449:
Sabuj Chandra Sutradhar and co-authors make hydrogels from a cellulose derivative and acrylic acid using gamma radiation, to remove dye from water, in a 2024 paper. Better wastewater treatment is a pressing need. The gels are tested for soaking up methylene blue dye.

Several acid-to-cellulose ratios were treated and exposed to varied radiation doses. The best gel formed at a middle dose. Swelling rose with acid content up to a point, and one mix reached the highest swelling. Spectra confirmed the grafting, and heat tests showed higher acid content raised stability. Pore size and grafting shaped the swelling behavior.
pmc-11675749:
Monika Jokubaite and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, whether water-based gels can unlock the skin benefits of caffeic acid. This plant compound fights oxidation and germs, which makes it attractive for skin care, but it needs a good carrier to reach the skin in useful amounts.

The team built gels from two common polymers and their mix, at varied strengths, and measured how fast the acid escaped each gel. Thicker gels released it more slowly, letting the team tune delivery. The finished gels killed a common skin bacterium and a yeast in tests. The work supports gels as practical carriers for plant compounds in creams and treatments.
pmc-11675849:
Mabel Diesel and co-authors ask how fast fitness fades in older adults when training stops. Their group had heart and metabolic risk factors, a common profile at that age. Breaks in exercise are common too, through illness, travel, or life events.

Eight adults, averaging about seventy years, were tested after one month and after three months without training. A standard battery timed chair stands, arm curls, reach, and a six-minute walk. Some scores, oddly, improved after the first month, which the team reports as found. Longer breaks told a plainer story of decline in key measures. Even small samples can warn clinics how quickly gains slip. The study argues for restart plans after any break.
pmc-11675949:
Julia Kutz and co-authors study a protein called HROB in this 2024 study. DNA copying must stay exact even when the DNA is damaged, so copy, repair, and damage response work as one system. HROB was known as a partner of a repair motor protein, and this team found separate clues that tie it to the copying process itself.

HROB levels rose and fell with known copying factors, peaking when cells copy DNA. Its shape is mostly loose, with one folded part that is old in evolution. Tests showed HROB sits close to parts of the copying machine. Adding too much HROB nearly shut copying down. The authors argue that HROB helps copying pass hard spots, such as crosslinks in the DNA, and flag it for deeper study.
pmc-11676049:
Pierre Bongrand and co-authors ask in 2024 if AI should keep a long term place in medical research and care. AI has spread fast in the past decade. The authors frame three questions. First, what blocks medical research most now? Second, what can AI add? Third, how well has it done so far in real tests?

They argue that research now deals more with complex systems than in the past. Older tools like theory and simulation have not fully met that need. AI is strong at sorting and predicting from many factors at once. Recent results put its skill near that of human staff in some tasks. They back a lasting role, mixed with older methods.
pmc-11676749:
Manal Khowdiary and a large team analyze the chemistry of a salt-tough desert shrub and test its extract against disease models. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The shrub, Nitraria retusa, survives drought and salty ground and has a history in folk remedies.

Chemical scans found three plant acids as the main contents. In lab tests the extract fought free radicals slightly better than vitamin C at matched doses. It slowed several cancer cell lines while largely sparing a normal cell line, with a colon cancer line the most sensitive. It also blocked two enzymes that break down starch and sugar, a sign of possible diabetes use. The authors present the shrub as a source of natural compounds worth deeper study for therapy.
pmc-11676849:
Ryo Uchimido and co-authors describe a 2024 study of how body chemistry shifts over time in severe COVID-19. A skewed metabolism is a known part of the disease, but its path across the weeks of severe illness was unclear. The team tracked blood samples from patients on breathing machines in one intensive care unit.

They grouped samples into three spans: the first days, the next two weeks, and the month mark. Hundreds of small molecules were read at each span. Early on, non-survivors showed raised fuel burning across sugar, protein, and fat paths. Later, fat and hormone paths split the groups in fresh ways. Some paths stayed skewed at all spans. The authors say timing shapes what care could target.
pmc-11677249:
Pitiwat Lueangwitchajaroen and colleagues teach a computer to name human actions in video using only ordinary color frames, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Action recognition feeds fields from health care to self-driving cars. Richer sensors help, but depth cameras and motion rigs are rare outside labs, so the team squeezed more from plain video.

From color frames alone, pre-trained tools pulled out two extra streams: skeleton poses and optical flow, the pattern of motion. Their method fuses the three streams at three depths of the network, early, middle, and late, rather than only at the end. Using a large public video set and an EfficientNet model, the fusion reached ninety-one point five percent accuracy, beating single-stream and single-view rivals. The authors say the cheap trick rivals far costlier setups.
pmc-11677349:
Luca Landini and co-authors followed four patients with late-stage age-related macular degeneration who received a tiny implantable telescope in one eye, in a case series published in 2024. The device, placed through a smaller cut than its forerunner, magnifies central images for people whose central vision is largely gone. The team tracked electrical responses of the retina as well as reading vision.

Six months after surgery, all four patients had gained in both distance and near vision scores. The retina's response density rose in every eye, most strongly at the center of gaze and fading outward in rings. Response strength also rose overall, with one dip in one patient's center. The authors call the early results promising while stressing the series is only four cases.
pmc-11677549:
Liyang Zhu and Tolgor Bau study how herbivore biodiversity drives species split in dung fungi, through the snow inkcap, in a 2024 paper. These pale inkcap mushrooms grow on the dung of grazing animals in pasture lands. Their true kinds were muddled, and wide sampling was needed to sort them.

Field work across China logged each find's place and the animal whose dung bore it. A four-locus family tree was then built from the samples. Fourteen species fall out of the tree, six of them new to science. Which animal's dung a fungus favors, the team argue, is one force that pulls the group apart into kinds.
pmc-11677649:
Mokgadi Makgobole and colleagues squeeze collagen from fish scales with a buffer borrowed from protein labs, and optimize the recipe statistically, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Fish processing waste is a sustainable collagen source if extraction cooperates. A Taguchi design varied acid strength, soaking time, and buffer volume to find the sweet spot with few experiments.

The optimum used half-molar acetic acid, a hundred milliliters, two hours of soaking, and ten milliliters of Tris-Glycine buffer. Temperature and buffer concentration proved the influential knobs. The product checked out as genuine type I collagen: infrared spectra showed the classic amide bands, and gel separation matched collagen's weight pattern. The amino acid mix was rich in glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline, the fibrous signature. Yield purity reached about seventeen milligrams per gram. The authors present the method as efficient and waste-cutting, pending scale-up validation.
pmc-11677849:
Lee and five co-authors study caffeine and gut aging in a worm model, in work from twenty twenty-four. Intestinal aging brings declining protein control as proteasome activity falls. That decline is a hallmark of age related disease.

Prior work showed caffeine improved gut integrity in aged Caenorhabditis elegans worms by reducing a yolk protein called vitellogenin. The new study traced the regulatory mechanism. Caffeine raised two proteasome related genes, pas-1 and pas-3. Higher proteasome action lowered the yolk protein load. The worm work names a pathway by which a common dietary compound may protect the aging gut.
pmc-11677949:
Justyna Podgórska-Bednarz and co-authors measure belly obesity in Polish children and teens with intellectual disability, in a 2024 study. Abdominal obesity is a serious health risk at any age. Children with intellectual disability may face added risk from medication, activity limits, and diet. Regional data for this group were scarce.

The study covered students aged seven to eighteen at care and education centers. Degrees of disability ranged from mild to severe. A matched comparison group without disability was drawn from local schools. Waist measures showed how common abdominal obesity was in each group. The results highlight a group needing tailored support. Schools and carers gain evidence for activity and meal programs.
pmc-11678049:
Muhammad Saqib and four co-authors tested coatings that slow the decay of magnesium implants in a 2024 study. Magnesium suits body implants since it is safe and dissolves over time, but it corrodes too fast. A plasma coating process can armor the metal, and the team tuned its bath mix and timing.

Samples were aged fast in flowing fluid that mimics body conditions at body heat. Imaging, surface reads, and weight loss tracked the decay. A added polymer coat over the plasma layer cut corrosion the most. The authors say the combined coat makes the alloy a stronger implant candidate. They also back the flowing test as a quick stand-in for long body trials of dissolving metals.
pmc-11678149:
Anthony Salib and co-authors checked whether CT scans of the heart arteries stay readable in patients with high body weight. Doctors often avoid this scan, called CTCA, in obese patients for fear the images will be too poor to judge. The team reviewed scans from 703 consecutive patients sent for suspected artery disease, grouping them by body mass index and grading image quality.

Nearly 94 percent of studies were fully readable. Among the few poor studies, nine in ten of the wide, near-heart artery segments could still be judged, and only seven patients had unreadable main segments. The authors conclude the scan remains a sound test for the segments that matter most to prognosis, whatever a patient's weight.
pmc-11678249:
Aleksandra Jóźwik, Agnieszka Wnuk-Scardaccione, and Jan Bilski compared in 2024 back pain and phantom pain in men with one lower leg amputated, split between amputee football players and non-athletes. Amputation brings lasting challenges, and pain in the back and in the missing limb is common. Whether adapted sport changes that pain was the question.

Phantom pain appeared in both groups at similar rates and similar strength. Back pain was far more common and somewhat stronger in the non-athletes, who also scored worse on disability and mobility measures. The players scored much higher on a standard mobility test. The authors conclude football training did not change phantom pain but was linked to less back pain.
pmc-11678349:
Mária Mörtl and co-authors test how bioplastic carrier bags break down at a full-size compost plant in a 2024 study. The bags were made of starch, additives, and a plastic called PBAT. Many past tests were small lab trials, so the team ran a large trial that matches real plant practice.

The trial mixed tons of manure and wood with tons of bags over twelve weeks. Heat in the piles peaked at seventy degrees and stayed high for weeks. By the last week, ninety-five percent of the bags had fallen apart. Tests with seeds showed mixed effects on sprouting, so the residue needs care. Lab checks traced how the bag material changed in form and makeup. The authors say the work can help sharpen compost rules.
pmc-11678849:
Wit Thun Kwa, Choon Kiat Sim, and co-authors grade three auto pull kits for gene stuff from human stool, in a 2024 study. Auto kits speed lab flow and cut hand work wobble in gut work. Kit picks bend what gene tales say, so head to head grades earn their keep.

A mock germ set and real stool bits run through all three kits. Beat steps lift yield past juice lone in stool runs for all kits. Beat runs pull more hard wall germs to light in the reads. Yield, wobble, and read tales part by kit in clear ways. Kit pick is a real call in gut gene work.
pmc-11678949:
Four authors, led by Xin Xie, fuse in 2024 a knowledge graph with a language model to diagnose faults in industrial sensor networks. Their graph packs expert knowledge about equipment into linked facts. A similarity measure built for long entity names fishes out the facts that match a live case.

The model then reasons over sensor text plus those facts to name a fault's cause and place. Trials on equipment systems backed the accuracy and speed claims. The authors pitch the method as a sturdier watch tool for plant operators, where a missed fault can halt a line.
pmc-11679249:
Kaiya Wang and co-authors review a family of bowl-shaped molecules called cavitands in work from 2024. These hosts, built on a ring base, can trap guest molecules and are prized for their shape and flexible design.

The review covers their many uses: speeding reactions, sorting and purifying mixtures, building polymer materials, sensing, battery materials, and drug delivery. Their clear structure and strong recognition of guests make them useful across these fields. The authors aim to give a full picture of how these hosts advance the study of weak bonds between molecules.
pmc-11679349:
Safa Melki and co-authors present a 2024 study of two pollutants on a sea squirt, a simple marine animal used as a coastal sentinel. They test bisphenol A, a plastic chemical, and tiny polystyrene beads, alone and mixed, on enzyme activity in three body parts. Exposure lasts just minutes in glass.

The enzyme was most active in the gut and siphons. The beads alone changed nothing, and mixing them with the chemical added nothing. The chemical alone blocked the enzyme in the gut, more at higher doses. Bead charge tests suggest the two pollutants do not stick to each other. The authors call for longer work on nerve harm in real coastal waters.
pmc-11679449:
Chunyu Jiang and four co-authors review in 2024 the state of portable powered exoskeletons for the legs. These wearable robots help users walk, lift, or recover motion. Their performance hinges on three choices: mechanism design, control strategy, and sensor suite.

The review sorts current designs by those three axes and weighs how well they fit together. Strengths and gaps of each approach are laid out side by side. Battery limits, weight, and user comfort recur as core hurdles. The authors close with future paths for research and product work. Students and engineers entering the field gain a compact map of what works and what still blocks daily use.
pmc-11679549:
Blue-green algae that bloom in lakes make toxins called microcystins, and tracking how fast the cells produce them matters for water safety. Kurmayer and Morón Asensio watch the synthesis happen in real time by feeding the algae marked building blocks.

Their trick is click chemistry: the algae's peptide assembly lines accept look-alike amino acids carrying chemical tags, so new toxin molecules come out tagged and countable. Two bloom species were fed three tagged amino acids in pulses over hours to a week. Tagged toxin share climbed to a plateau within a day or two, faster in faster-growing cells, and the share inside cells matched the share leaked into the water. The tagged fraction then fell in a straight line, showing the toxins leave mainly by dilution as cells divide, not by any triggered release.
pmc-11679649:
Jiadai Xue and co-authors published a 2024 study on polishing the metal molds used to shape X-ray telescope mirrors. The mirrors curve in complex ways, so a polishing tool must press evenly as the curve changes, or the surface ends up wavy. The team built a model that predicts how a soft, flexible tool removes material on such curved molds, tying pressure to contact size and angle.

The model draws on flat-surface polishing data and adjusts it for the mold's changing curve. The team also corrected the tool's effect in real time across several polishing rounds. Tests showed clear gains in surface shape, smoothness, and mirror performance. The work supports the fine optics needed for X-ray astronomy.
pmc-11679749:
Alexandros Sakkas and co-authors measure rain by microwave fading in 2024. Rain weakens radio signals, and abundant links could double as rain gauges. Most work uses high bands, where fading is strong; low bands fade so slightly that few try.

Their precision rig works at three low frequencies under ten gigahertz. It resolves power changes finer than a hundred-thousandth of a decibel in early tests. Fading followed a clean power law against rain rate at all three bands. Higher bands faded more, as expected. The authors offer the setup as a path to denser rain monitoring from existing networks.
pmc-11679849:
A new steel for hot-work dies must hold its shape at heat and under strain, or the moulds it makes will fail. Yasha Yuan and eight co-authors bake and squeeze a fresh chromium steel in 2024 to chart that act. Tests ran on a heat rig at heats from 950 to 1,200 degrees and at strain speeds across a wide span.

From the curves, the team built a law that links flow stress to heat, strain, and speed, with a fix that lets the law bend as strain grows. The law's forecasts hug the test data, with a match score near 0.99 and a mean error near three percent. A map of safe working zones, built by a set rule, joins the law. Steel makers gain a guide for forging this grade.
pmc-11680149:
A team of virologists compares epidemic and vaccine strains of orf virus in a paper from 2024. The catalog adds a ninth author absent from the head byline, so team framing is used here. Orf sickens livestock and sometimes people, and live vaccines guard herds. The epidemic and vaccine genomes proved ninety-nine point eight percent identical. Still, small changes clustered in telling places. The vaccine strain lost a stretch of non-coding DNA near the genome end.

Three point mutations changed proteins, and one frameshift broke another gene. Such terminal genes often tune virulence rather than growth. The authors argue these edits likely explain the vaccine's mildness. Matching vaccines to field strains could improve protection.
pmc-11680349:
Pauline dos Santos and co-authors test how one step in spay surgery affects stress in female dogs, in a study from 2024. Surgeons often snap a small ligament to reach the ovary more easily, but the snap may add strain. Twenty healthy dogs had the standard surgery, half with the snap and half without, with heat sealing used to stop bleeding in both groups.

Pain scores over the first day were much the same in both groups, though rescue pain relief differed. Heart rate and some blood cell counts did differ by group. Signs of cell stress stayed low in both groups. The authors conclude that the snap brings a slightly stronger stress response, a point vets can weigh when they plan the surgery.
pmc-11681849:
Clement Delage leads a team with a case of Alport syndrome in a family. Their report from twenty twenty-four uses full gene code reads. Alport syndrome harms the kidneys, hearing, and eyes over time in those affected.

Three kin in one family had the dominant form of the disease. Full reads found a new large change in a collagen gene. That change had not been seen as a cause before. The case shows full reads can work as a first test. Large gene changes are a key cause of such diseases.
pmc-11682549:
Raziyeh Barzegar-Bafrouei and four co-authors measure how often Salmonella bacteria contaminate traditional dairy products and raw milk in one Iranian province, and how drug-resistant those germs are. Their study came out in 2024. Salmonella food poisoning is among the most common foodborne infections worldwide.

From three hundred fifty samples, about one in fifteen carried the bacterium, confirmed by a genetic marker test. Contamination did not cluster in particular products or sources. Resistance was highest against an older antibiotic, while three stronger drugs still worked against over nine in ten isolates. The authors warn that both contamination and multi-drug resistance are rising in traditional dairy production there. Their findings argue for tighter hygiene in small-scale dairy supply.
pmc-11682749:
Young teeth that die before their roots finish growing are hard to save, since the root stays thin and open at the tip. Mohamed Abdelsalam and co-authors tested ways to regrow tissue inside such teeth in a 2024 animal study. They compared a plain blood clot with the same clot plus one of two soft gels used as a frame for new growth.

Sixteen young dog teeth were cleaned, treated, and checked under a lens three months later. All treated roots grew more tissue and showed less swelling near the tip than roots left alone. The gel made from a natural body sugar did not calm cell counts as well as hoped. Even so, the basic cleaning and clot method helped on its own, which keeps the simpler route in play for young patients.
pmc-11683049:
Ildiko Radvanyi and co-authors survey in this 2024 study whether heavy internet use worsens headaches in Hungarian university students. Of 550 respondents, about thirty-seven percent reported primary headaches, split between migraine and tension types, and eight percent met an internet addiction screen. Mood and sleep scales rode along in the survey.

Headache severity tied to being under thirty, childless, married, and online more than four hours a day, plus low mood and insomnia. Total screen time correlated weakly with severity. The link concentrated in tension headaches, where night use and addiction scores mattered. The authors call for campus health programs that treat sleep, mood, and screen habits together. Night use stood out as a habit to curb.
pmc-11683649:
Ajay Khopade and Nitin Chitranshi published a materials study in 2024. They built tiny drug-carrying particles with layered cores. The core pairs an antibiotic, tobramycin sulfate, with a fatty acid. Together they form thin repeating layers at nanoscale size. A common dispersing agent helped form separate particles. The team tuned mixing to control particle size. They named the core-shell particles lamellosomes.

Tests showed the layered core survived strong mixing. Particles carried a mild negative surface charge. They stayed separate in salty water at tested levels. Acid changes could clump or break them apart. The core could also hold a second drug, dexamethasone. That drug was released much more slowly. Such carriers could suit controlled drug delivery.
pmc-11685149:
Sandra Evans and co-authors argue in a 2024 policy brief that better data should drive national vaccine decisions. Vaccination across the whole lifespan, not just childhood, brings broad value that spans generations. Showing that value takes stronger data systems, teamwork across fields, and shared methods.

New tools such as machine learning and language processing can sharpen analysis and live tracking of disease and uptake. The brief backs a grading process for evidence, strengthened with real-world data from daily practice. Mixing many study types helps capture how behavior and local settings change results. Decision makers get a plan for evidence that keeps pace with fast outbreaks and uneven local needs.
pmc-11685749:
Qiangqiang Zhao and co-authors test a plant sterol against bone loss after the ovaries are removed in a 2024 study. Bone-eating cells drive the loss, and curbing them is a main line of care. The sterol, drawn from plants, had shown hints of slowing those cells, though the path was unclear.

In dish tests, the sterol cut the count and spread of bone-eating cells and blocked their grip rings. Key marks of the cells fell at both gene and protein levels. Two signal paths tied to the cells' birth were damped. In mice, scans and stains checked whether bone mass held up better under the sterol.
pmc-11687249:
Adam Grice and Hajira Dambha-Miller, editors of a primary care journal, reflect on the future of peer review as submissions hit record highs. Authors want fast decisions, yet standards must hold. Their 2024 editorial argues that journals guard knowledge by printing only sound, relevant work and by cutting research waste.

Waste, they write, includes weak designs, biased publication, and studies that repeat what is known. Reviewers help by spotting duplication and by giving feedback that lifts papers before print. Open access sharing of data and findings also helps new work build on old. The piece is a statement of editorial duty: select carefully, review firmly, and keep the literature worth reading.
pmc-11688749:
Kate Hamel asks if a course on aging can shift student views in a 2024 study. Kinesiology students often aim at health and fitness jobs with older clients, yet many enter with dim views of aging drawn from sport. Those views can color how they treat older adults and pick their paths.

Students in an aging elective across two terms filled surveys before and after the course. Scores for hopes about aging rose by the end, across body, mind, and mood parts alike. Kind acts toward older people held steady, while unkind acts fell. Hamel reads the course as a lever that can lift outlook and cut age bias in future staff.
pmc-11688849:
Miranda Kunkel and co-authors study how nursing home staff adapted a care program in 2024. The program guides one-to-one time with residents who live with dementia. Staff should bring a warm intent, good talk skills, and an activity the resident prefers.

The team drew on 78 talks with 23 staff who led the work in their homes. More than half said they made unplanned changes that still fit the program aims. They loosened structure or changed the setting, often due to time limits or resident needs. The authors argue such changes are a normal part of real care and should be welcomed, not hidden.
pmc-11689249:
Mariela Gutierrez writes alone in a 2024 study of work and memory in Mexico. Rich countries have shown that mentally demanding jobs track with sharper later cognition. Evidence from poorer countries stays thin. Gutierrez linked a national aging study of Mexicans over 50 with United States job descriptors, sorting each person's main lifetime job by its mental demands.

Memory change was tracked from 2001 to 2018, a long window for spotting decline. The question matters for policy in middle income countries, where schooling and job types differ from rich world patterns. If mental work protects memory there too, job design joins the list of levers for healthy aging. The study tests whether the rich country finding travels.
pmc-11689349:
Casey Brown, Jenna Wells, Claudia Haase, and Robert Levenson studied empathic accuracy in long-term marriages. Their 2024 paper compares middle-aged and older couples. Reading a partner's emotions well helps keep social bonds strong. Empathic skill may shift with age, but close relationships are rarely the test setting. The sample held 154 long-term heterosexual marriages.

Couples discussed a topic of marital disagreement for fifteen minutes in a lab. The talk was recorded on video for later review. Each spouse then rated their own and their partner's feelings moment by moment. Ratings used a dial from very negative to very positive. Accuracy was scored by how closely partner ratings matched self ratings. Age group differences sit at the heart of the analysis.
pmc-11689449:
Five authors study side strains on dementia carers and their view of home aid in a 2024 survey. Sixty-three carers filled web forms on care strain kinds, aid use feels, and mood ends. Path math tests if aid feels carry strain effects to those mood ends in a chain.

Kin fights tied to worse aid feels, which then tied to more load in full chain form. Hard finds of aid partly carried cash strain and role trap ties to load, low self-trust, and low mood. The read backs whole-life care for carer aid plans at all steps of the chain.
pmc-11689549:
Karen Kopera-Frye, Karen John, and Robynn Frank describe a traditional healing program on the Navajo Nation and how the COVID pandemic disrupted it. The program, running since 2007, gathers families in summits built on Navajo values of wellness. Two Navajo students and a faculty member led the project, using a community-based approach.

The authors frame the work with tribal critical race theory, which honors three kinds of knowledge. Those are cultural knowledge and Indigenous ways of knowing, knowledge of survival through change, and academic knowledge. The pandemic broke gatherings that carry cultural knowledge between generations. The study records how the program adapted and what it protected. It shows healing practice as a living system, not a museum piece.
pmc-11689649:
Matt Yousefzadeh gives an overview, from twenty twenty-four, of how aging changes the immune system. As people age, the immune system works less well. That loss makes it harder to fight germs. It also plays a role in many long-term illnesses of old age. A second process is steady, low-level swelling in the body even when no germ is present.

Yousefzadeh notes that much is still not known. Scientists do not yet fully grasp how immune aging talks to the rest of the body. The talk points to new work at basic, applied, and treatment levels. Readers get a plain map of two core ideas and the open questions.
pmc-11689849:
Lewis Lipsitz and Dae Kim preview a symposium of four editor picked papers on frailty risk and recovery in older adults. The set spans diet, smell, a supplement pair, and muscle energy, all tied to how elders lose or regain function. A guest voice will draw shared lessons.

One paper links a pro swelling diet to frailty in elders with low mood. One ties smell loss to frailty as a warn mark. One tests a two part supplement on aging marks and body function. One links muscle power plant output to leg power and fitness.
pmc-11689949:
Pengyuan Zhang and co-authors present a 2024 study of a hidden bias in research on thinking decline in old age. People who die before a study starts can never join it, so the joiners differ from the full pool in a set way. No data exist on the missing group, so standard fixes cannot be applied.

The team used the case of type 2 diabetes and thinking decline across lands. They simulated cohorts of 300,000 adults each for the United States, India, and China under seven causal stories. Each fake person got a life or death status before the study start. The sims show how much the bias can bend effect estimates, and why cross land compares are hard to read at face value.
pmc-11690149:
Turning back the clock in old brain cells may restore the birth of new nerve cells, which fades with age. Lucy Xu and co-authors tested brief gene-based reprogramming in old mice, in work from twenty twenty-four. The target zone lines the brain's fluid spaces and feeds new neurons and support cells through adult life.

Gene reads at single-cell level showed the share of young nerve cells rose after treatment of the whole body. Signs of aging in cell code also flipped back. Treating just the zone itself lifted both stem cells and young nerve cells. Old stem cells grown in dishes made more young cells after treatment too. The work hints that aging in this brain zone can be partly undone.
pmc-11690249:
Grief can begin before a loved one with dementia dies, and a 2024 study by Lauren Elliott and co-authors asks how that early grief ties to caregiver stress. Family caregivers of people with Alzheimer's and related diseases carry chronic strain, and strong pre-death grief forecasts worse depression after the loss.

Data came from sixty-five family caregivers, with an average age near sixty-nine. Each filled in standard scales for felt stress and for pre-death grief symptoms. Caregivers on average reported moderate levels of both. The two scores moved together: higher stress went with stronger grief before death. The link, missing from earlier work, suggests stress relief might soften grief's early grip.
pmc-11690349:
Jacqueline Mogle and co-authors ask why people fail to finish intended daily activities in a 2024 diary study. Completing chores, exercise, or work tasks draws on planning and other thinking skills. Yet when people explain a missed task, they may cite time, health, or forgetfulness rather than cognition.

More than two hundred adults kept evening diaries for a week. On about half of days, at least one of eight intended activities went unfinished. Not enough time was the most common reason. Older adults reported unfinished activities more often than younger adults, and also blamed lack of time more.
pmc-11690549:
Amal Wanigatunga, Hang Wang, and co-authors fuse sense and move marks in one score to flag soft mind loss risk, in a 2024 study. Sense plus move acts braid in plan and world touch tasks. How to sum that braid in one mark was the gap this work fills for risk hunts.

Six plain marks, from hear and sight to grip and pace, feed one score. Two long pools of old folks take the score and mind tests. Each step up in the score cuts soft loss odds by near half. Both pools show the tie at like force post term tweaks. Time proof of fall calls is still owed.
pmc-11690649:
Anna-Christina Kainradl writes, in twenty twenty-four, on the care stories of older migrants. Her paper is a theory and ethics piece, not a data study. She notes that race, sex, class, nation, and age can combine to block fair care. Most accounts of these lives come from staff or family, not from the older people themselves.

Kainradl uses a lens that looks at how those forces overlap. She applies it to stories told by older migrants and by care staff. She asks what the lens adds to the study of aging. She also weighs postcolonial views, which stress the lasting weight of empire, as a further tool.
pmc-11690849:
Vanessa Fabbre and co-authors set out principles for queer gerontology in a 2024 symposium paper. The field studies aging through a justice lens, with special attention to LGBTQ+ elders, building on recent work that brings queer theory into the study of later life.

Five principles anchor the approach: deepening visibility, applying critical perspectives, challenging oppression, engaging multiple ways of knowing, and fostering work across disciplines. The symposium's talks illustrate each principle with existing research, apply them to a fresh reading of older qualitative data, and reflect on the scholar-activist role. Attendees are invited to test their own projects against the principles.
pmc-11690949:
Cara Wallace and co-authors review why dying patients and their families join research studies in a 2024 paper. Hospice clinicians often shield patients from study invitations, fearing extra burden at a fragile time. Yet almost no evidence described what participation actually feels like.

From over 3,400 screened papers, 24 studies qualified. Participants commonly reported more benefit than burden, and even found value in studies that did burden them. Joining offered extra support and contact, plus the warm feeling of helping future patients, even without personal medical gain. The authors urge clinicians not to assume refusal: many patients welcome being asked.
pmc-11691049:
Chiung-Jung Wen and co-authors track what pushes older patients into or out of frailty in a 2024 prospective study. Frailty, the state of low reserve that makes a fall or illness dangerous, is not one-way: people worsen, hold steady, or improve. Little work had pinned down the factors behind those moves. The team recruited patients from a geriatric outpatient clinic at a medical center.

Frailty was scored at the start and again one year later with a modified standard checklist, next to background, health, and geriatric measures. Of one hundred forty participants, nearly half worsened over the year, a small share improved, and the rest held steady. After adjustment for other traits, the analysis names the factors tied to change. Knowing them lets clinics aim support at the patients most likely to slide.
pmc-11691149:
Shelbie Turner and co-authors sorted the problems that arise when family caregivers for people with dementia live with lasting pain, in work published in 2024. Pain can make lifting, bathing, and other care tasks hard, and can leave needs unmet. The team spoke in depth with twenty five such caregivers.

Three linked kinds of problems stood out. Some were physical, some were about worry and low mood, and some were about strain with family who did not help. Problems often fed each other and made both care and pain worse. Some caregivers also said pain gave them more empathy. The authors offer their sorting as a guide for programs that help caregivers manage pain.
pmc-11691249:
Theresa Allison, Alexander Smith, Jennie Gubner, and Kenneth Covinsky published a 2024 study of home dementia care, drawn from two ethnographic projects on music and daily life. The team coded interviews and field notes from 83 people: 38 living with dementia, 34 family care partners, and 11 professionals. Contact ranged from one phone interview to eight home visits over two years.

Families described a recurring mismatch: the help on offer did not fit the care actually needed. The gap bit hardest in the walking-around stages of dementia and when the care partner also had several illnesses. Spirituality stood out as a strong motive to keep caring. Solid social support and money were named as critical. The authors call for support designs that fit real home situations.
pmc-11691349:
Rodlescia Sneed and Elaina Reese present on research ethics in aging prisons in a 2024 abstract. State prisons hold a fast growing share of older adults. Studying their health can improve care, yet they are a vulnerable group. Review boards demand extra safeguards before such studies proceed.

Examples come from the pair's own multi site study of chronic disease self care. Topics include power gaps, pressure to join, and fair consent in custody. Choosing participants and paying incentives raise special issues behind bars. Protecting data also needs care, since records could harm participants if leaked.
pmc-11691849:
Suparb Aree-Ue and co-authors test a combined support program for knee arthritis in a 2024 study. The program mixes teaching, weight control, thigh exercise, and home visits. Older adults joined with either mild or moderate joint symptoms. Both groups followed the same twelve week program for fair comparison.

Most who finished were women in their late sixties on average. The moderate group started with worse joints and lower well being. Gains in weight and leg strength did not split clearly by group. The authors conclude the program helps joint function across severity levels.
pmc-11692049:
M K Kirsten Chui and co-authors present a 2024 study testing whether boosting a key cellular fuel calms the inflammation behind delirium in mice. Delirium, an acute confusional state often triggered by illness, has no effective drug treatment. It travels with inflammation and metabolic trouble. The fuel in question, NAD+, supports energy production and moderates immune activity.

The team gave mice a direct precursor of NAD+ alongside a bacterial toxin that induces sickness resembling delirium. Blood profiling followed. The supplement did not rescue the sickness behaviour or the metabolic disturbance, the authors report, but it did modulate the wider inflammatory response. The mixed result still maps where this lever acts and where it does not.
pmc-11692249:
High blood pressure among North Korean defectors links closely to age and depression, Sang Hui Chu, Oksim Kim, and Hokon Kim report in a 2024 study. Defectors arrive undernourished yet face rising chronic disease as their group ages. The team studied four hundred forty-nine defectors in three age bands, from under thirty to over sixty.

Trauma and depression were scored with a standard international questionnaire. Mental strain is common in this group and may push blood pressure up beyond diet effects alone. Age-split analysis aims to show where risk concentrates so care can be tailored. Clinics serving resettled defectors gain a reason to screen mood and pressure together, above all for older arrivals.
pmc-11692349:
Kyle Page and co-authors survey mental health care inside the Veterans Health Administration's nursing homes. These Community Living Centers house veterans with high rates of mental illness and behavior concerns, and psychologists must sit on their teams by rule. The team asked the centers' psychologists and psychiatric providers how care really runs.

About half of those invited answered. Supportive therapy, behavior therapy, and behavior management topped the list of helpful tools, with life review, relaxation training, and talk therapies close behind. Barriers to proven psychotherapies included the veterans' own thinking limits and illness. A third of respondents ran group sessions. Teamwork ran deep: colleagues observed, co-signed notes, and watched symptoms together, and a third of centers held regular behavior rounds.
pmc-11692449:
Ellis Dillon and co-authors count avoidable hospital stays among Connecticut Medicaid members who get care at home. Their 2024 study covers home and community services for older adults and people with illness or disability. Such programs aim to keep people well outside hospital walls.

Linked claims and assessment records cover 33,688 residents across six programs. Avoidable stay rates from April to September 2022 ranged from under one percent to near sixteen percent. People with avoidable stays made up over half of all who were hospitalized. One personal care program ran higher odds than the elder program, while a brain injury program ran lower. Odds rose with each step of a hospital risk score.
pmc-11692649:
Cristina de Rosa and Yu-Ping Chang published a study in 2024 on a mobile app teaching mindfulness-based stress reduction to older adults in underserved communities. Mindfulness practices involve calm breathing and focused attention. The community in the study was primarily African American and faced barriers to mental health care during the COVID-19 pandemic and afterward.

Seventeen adults took part in an eight-week intervention delivered through the app, then shared their experiences in interviews. Most participants were women aged around sixty-six. Four themes emerged. The app made participants open to the practice and broke down barriers to care. It helped them notice themselves and the world around them more clearly. They could draw on the practice whenever they chose, in calm times and in difficult ones. It also helped them build routines that kept them calm. The researchers found the app feasible and well liked.
pmc-11692749:
Ranell Mueller studied how growing old beside a dog changes men's views of aging in a 2024 paper. Little was known about the deeper meaning of aging alongside a companion animal. The author interviewed older men in depth and convened a panel subgroup repeatedly over three months. Transcripts were coded in stages to surface underlying patterns.

The men described empathy for their aging dogs that spilled over into empathy for themselves and other older adults. Watching their dogs age made them more sympathetic and understanding of the process in people. A sense of grace, toward themselves, others, and their dogs, emerged as a prominent theme. The author offers the findings as a step toward a theory of how dogs shape men's attitudes to aging.
pmc-11692849:
Joseph Shen and four co-authors measure how losing several senses at once relates to depression in older adults. Their study came out in 2024. Hearing, vision, smell, and touch each fade with age, and each loss alone has been tied to low mood.

The study covered just over eight hundred participants in their seventies to nineties with objective tests of all four senses. Most had at least one loss, and a small share had all four. Each additional sensory loss came with about a ten percent higher depression symptom score, after full adjustment. The effect stacked up sense by sense rather than appearing only at the extreme. The authors urge clinicians to treat combined sensory loss as a mental health risk worth acting on.
pmc-11693049:
Barbekka Hurtt and a team of co-authors explore running as part of healthy aging over fifty years, in two thousand twenty-four. Running is easy to start and has a low barrier for any age. Social and population shifts over that span may have changed what running means to older adults.

The team gathered surveys and interviews through social media, running groups, and marathon events. Older runners linked the sport to stronger bones, heart, and mood. All said their mood worsened when they took time off. Interviewees praised older athletes, yet most disliked the phrase about playing like an old person. Many wanted better local chances for older runners.
pmc-11693249:
Thi Vu and co-authors link internalized HIV stigma to cognition in older women living with HIV in a 2024 study. Internalized stigma means taking society's harsh views into one's own self-image, and it harms mental health.

Data came from a long-running women's HIV study, with stigma scored in mid twenty tens and thinking tested then and years later. Over seven hundred women took part, with an average age in the mid fifties. Higher stigma tied to worse overall thinking scores over time. Verbal learning was among the hit areas. The link held after adjusting for mood, income, and drug use. The work adds brain health to the case for stigma care.
pmc-11696749:
Eder Soares and a large team used in 2024 explainable multitask learning to hunt compounds against the parasite behind visceral leishmaniasis. The disease can kill, and current drugs are toxic, costly and losing ground to resistance. Their models predicted activity against three Leishmania species at once. They then screened about 1.3 million compounds from a commercial library.

Twenty candidates emerged, and nine killed the main target species in lab tests. Three stood out with strong potency and only moderate harm to human cells. Explanation tools showed which structural traits drove the predictions, guiding the next design round. The authors present multitask screening as a way to raise hit rates for neglected diseases. Their hits now await the slow work of turning leads into medicines.
pmc-11699449:
Thailand is chasing hepatitis elimination, and its hepatitis C hotspot province, Phetchabun, also carries hepatitis B that needed mapping. Nawarat Posuwan and co-authors pooled three population surveys from 2024, testing nearly eight thousand adults and young adults for the B virus surface marker. Prevalence differed sharply by age group and place.

Adults ran about six percent positive, while young adults in the worst districts ran three percent. Those born after Thailand's infant vaccination program began fell below one percent, a quiet triumph. Risk tracked age, schooling, injecting drug use, and family liver history, with patterns differing between generations. The authors say elimination plans must treat each age band differently.
pmc-11700249:
Catalin Gheorghe and Oana Panazan study how world tensions move the share prices of defense companies. Their sample covers seventy-five arms firms worldwide, tracked daily from 2014 to 2023. The authors treat Russia's seizure of Crimea in 2014 as a turning point for the industry, and they use wave-based methods to watch links at different time scales.

About half the firms reacted at once to the Crimea shock, led by companies in Europe, the US, and South Korea. The pandemic stirred about a third of firms, in a mild, negative way. The full war in Ukraine touched over four fifths of the sample. The Israel-Hamas war stayed local to Israeli firms. The authors advise investors to treat defense stocks with geopolitical risk in mind.
pmc-11700349:
Eren Arslan Davulcu and Suat Hilal Akı describe a seventy-one-year-old man whose chronic myelomonocytic leukemia kept appearing in his skin. This leukemia mixes features of two disease families and follows an uneven course. Skin spread in some forms signals a poor outlook. The patient, judged high risk, developed pink-purple nodules on his skin.

Treatment with azacitidine and hydroxyurea shrank the nodules. When the skin disease returned, treatment regained control without the illness turning into acute leukemia. The authors stress close watching and flexible treatment plans for such patients. Skin signs, they note, can flare and settle while the blood disease stays contained. The case adds a worked example of managing this rare presentation.
pmc-11701249:
Calhoun and six co-authors test human stem cell therapy in mice with mucopolysaccharidosis type I, in a 2024 paper. The disorder stems from lack of an enzyme that breaks down certain sugars. Current treatments reach the brain poorly, so nerve damage is hard to prevent.

The team made induced pluripotent stem cells from human cord blood and turned them into neural stem cells. In lab tests the cells moved well and corrected the enzyme lack in nearby cells. Transplanted into newborn mice, they spread through the brain and became glial cells. Enzyme activity partly returned, and markers of disease fell. The results support patient-specific cell therapy.
pmc-11701849:
Recent Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry went to work on machine learning, and Charles H. Martin and Ganesh Mani use those awards as a starting point. Their 2024 article asks what it means when three fields that once grew apart now grow back together. The prizes, they argue, reward tools built in one field that changed work in the others.

The authors trace the long history of neural networks, the computer models at the heart of modern AI. They show how ideas from physics and chemistry fed into those models over many decades. Their call is for schools and labs to train more people who can work across fields. Such broad training, they argue, could help close the gap between new theory and real use, and move the field toward more general AI.
pmc-11702349:
Abdulmalik Timamy and co-authors reported in 2024 a rare drug side effect: stubbornly low blood potassium during treatment with the antibiotic meropenem. Their patient was a seventy-two-year-old woman admitted after a fall with a broken hip, who was also receiving chemotherapy for lung cancer.

In hospital she developed sepsis with low white cell counts. When fever persisted and counts fell further on the first antibiotics, her treatment switched to meropenem. Low potassium then appeared and resisted correction while the drug ran. A few days after the course ended, her levels returned to normal on their own. The authors warn clinicians to suspect this link in hard-to-fix cases.
pmc-11704449:
Shahla Alalaf and co-authors ran a trial in 2024 of a blood-clotting drug for women whose placenta lies too low in pregnancy. The low placenta can bleed without warning and end a pregnancy early. The drug is known to curb bleeding in other settings.
