The trial ran at three teaching hospitals in Iraq and Egypt, with near one hundred fifty women split by lot. Half got the drug and half got a plain sugar drip, with neither side told which. Staff tracked whether bleeding stopped, how long the pregnancy held, and how mothers and babies fared. Such blinded tests give the firm proof doctors need before a drug joins routine care.
pmc-11704649:
Jimmy Wen and seven colleagues compare heavyweight weight-loss drugs head to head for people with obesity but not diabetes. GLP-1 drugs made their name in diabetes care. Which one trims the most weight in plain obesity, and at what side-effect cost, needed a direct answer.

The review gathered direct comparison trials of semaglutide against liraglutide and against efinopegdutide. Pooled results gave semaglutide a clear edge over liraglutide in mean weight lost. Against efinopegdutide the gap was not firm. All three drugs were tolerated much the same, with mostly mild to moderate gut complaints. The authors call for more direct trials against the newer multi-target drugs.
pmc-11707449:
Yousria Badawy and co-authors survey what Saudi women know and believe about preventing osteoporosis. Their 2024 study polls 406 women online, none with the disease. A health belief model sorts views into felt risk, felt severity, benefits, barriers, confidence, and cues to act.

Knowledge lands at a moderate level, as do most belief scores. Perceived barriers score low, the one weak construct. Knowledge ties positively to every belief construct except barriers, where the tie runs negative. Many women report cues that prompt action, like cost worries about care. Standard cut-off scales grade the levels. The authors say belief-aware education could lift prevention habits in a country where bone thinning is common among women.
pmc-11708949:
Sibel Kara and co-authors compare lung cancer in patients whose lungs are scarred by fibrosis, in a 2024 study from several centers. Lung cancer is a known companion of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the unexplained scarring form, but less is known about cancer in other scarring types. The team reviewed records from 2010 to 2022.

The study covers 251 patients, 164 with the idiopathic form and 87 with other forms. Most were older men with a history of smoking. Scan patterns differed: a honeycomb look marked the idiopathic group, while haze and air trapping marked the other. The most common cancer type was squamous cell carcinoma, then adenocarcinoma. Survival was short in both groups, with a median of about two years, and five-year death rates above 60 percent.
pmc-11709049:
Four Indian physicians propose a new discipline, community pharmacology, to make everyday drug use safer outside big hospitals. India has lengthened lives and built vast vaccine programs, yet rural patients still face irrational prescriptions, medication errors, and drug resistance with little oversight. The authors argue that pharmacology must leave the tertiary ward and work at street level.

Their network would watch side effects, police antibiotic use, and keep village formularies matched to local needs. It would manage supply, storage, and dispensing, and prepare essential medicine lists for each community. Public and private actors would share the work. The authors tie the proposal to global goals of health for all and to India's own development targets, arguing that safe routine prescribing is where most health is won or lost.
pmc-11709349:
Jee Wook Kim and co-authors track if liver marks foretell how Alzheimer harm grows in the brain. Past work ties a weak liver to the ill, but the brain path of that tie is dim. Their 2025 study draws on a Korean aging cohort that began in 2014. Just under three hundred and fifty older adults, from town and memory clinics, are seen at base and two years on.

Four liver blood marks form the lead facts. Brain scans of three kinds log clump, tangle, and fuel use at both meets. Mind checks ride with the scans. Ties from liver marks to scan change form the core read. A firm tie would cast the liver as a lever in brain care, not just a by-stander.
pmc-11709549:
Aina Comas-Alberti and co-authors study gene activity in blood from people with the inherited form of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 paper. This rare form runs in families and stems from faults in one of three genes. It makes up only a small share of all cases. Most gene studies focus on the common late-onset form and on brain tissue, not blood.

Earlier work by the group found nine genes whose activity differed in both brain tissue and lab-grown cells from patients. Here they test those genes, plus three genes tied to the disease, in whole blood. The goal is to find blood signs that track the disease and hint at how it harms the brain. Easy blood markers could aid early trials and diagnosis in these families.
pmc-11709649:
Learning the same task over many days may reveal Alzheimer's disease before symptoms show, and a 2025 study by Roos J Jutten and co-authors tests that idea. Earlier work showed that healthy older adults with amyloid buildup learn less across repeated tests.

The team gave 136 cognitively normal older adults a remote test battery, called BRANCH, on their own devices over many days. The battery joins memory tasks, such as linking faces to names and items to prices, with a speed task. This study asked how tau buildup, the second hallmark protein of the disease, relates to the shape of those learning curves. The goal is a cheap home test that flags risk early.
pmc-11709749:
Kate Foley, Erica Weekman, and Donna Wilcock probe why Alzheimer's antibody drugs sometimes injure blood vessels in the brain. Their 2025 paper concerns the first approved disease-modifying antibodies, which clear amyloid and slow decline. Their main side effect, ARIA, shows up as brain swelling or small bleeds on scans, and it blocks treatment for patients with heavy vessel disease.

Carriers of the APOE4 gene variant face the highest risk, with up to forty percent of double carriers affected. Using mouse models, the team gave antibodies systemically and directly into the brain. Immune cells called microglia switched on along amyloid-laden vessels, near the spots where microbleeds appeared. The work links vessel amyloid, immune activation, and the side effect.
pmc-11709849:
Daniel Chain and co-authors use a protein-folding AI to compare two forms of tau in a 2025 study. Tau tangles drive Alzheimer's disease and several related dementias, and the brain makes six versions of the protein, split mainly into 3-repeat and 4-repeat forms.

Each disease favors its own mix: Pick's disease leans on the 3-repeat form, while most other tau diseases lean on the 4-repeat one. AlphaFold 2 predicts the binding region of the 4-repeat form folds into a mostly ordered shape, quite unlike the 3-repeat version. The team pairs the modeling with lab tests to probe those shape gaps. The contrast may explain why the forms bind cell skeletons and clump so differently.
pmc-11709949:
Eating less extends life and sharpens the aging brain in many studies, but a gene tied to Alzheimer's risk may tune that benefit. Wenhui Qiao and co-authors tested the interaction in 2025 using mice engineered to carry the human APOE gene in its three forms. From middle age, half the mice ate freely and half ate thirty percent less.

Calorie restriction calmed anxiety and improved memory in the mice carrying the two common risk forms, and it switched on brain pathways that build cholesterol and insulation for nerve fibers. The protective form's mice showed fewer of those brain effects, though their blood fats shifted most. Gut microbe changes also split by gene form. The authors say prevention plans should weigh this gene.
pmc-11710049:
Marta Olah reviews a 2025 conference abstract on microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, and Alzheimer's disease. Two findings reshaped the field in the past decade. Many risk genes for the disease act mainly in microglia, and the cells come in far more varied states than once thought. Whether those two facts connect has stayed unclear.

Olah's team measured disease-linked proteins within single microglia subsets from aged and diseased human brains. The pattern of proteins differed by subset, which means the cell's state shapes what a risk gene does. The talk argues that future gene studies and drugs must reckon with this variety.
pmc-11710149:
Mathini Vaikunthan and José McFaline-Figueroa probe in this 2025 study how the company neurons keep changes their response to Alzheimer's-linked insults. Toxic amyloid and reactive support cells are both suspects, but their separate weights were unclear. Rat cell mixtures, neurons alone or with astrocytes and microglia added, faced twenty conditions of disease-linked compounds while single-cell sequencing read the replies.

Merely changing the cell mix shifted genes tied to late-onset Alzheimer's, and one early-onset gene rose in neurons. In high-microglia mixes, a receptor pair seen weakened in patients also faded. The authors argue cell interaction alone can mimic parts of the disease signature. Drug screens can use the same mixtures.
pmc-11710249:
Joy Ochai and co-authors test whether omega-3 fatty acids shield the brain of sleep-deprived rats. Lost sleep raises oxidative stress and inflammation, which build up a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer's disease. Thirty male rats were split into five groups; most were kept awake 18 hours a day for three weeks, and three groups got rising doses of omega-3.

Sleep loss slowed maze learning and raised the toxic protein, stress, and inflammation markers. Omega-3 groups kept better memory and showed less protein buildup and stress, with gains growing by dose. The authors back omega-3 as a guard for the memory center.
pmc-11710549:
Lucineia Danielski and co-authors describe a 2025 rat study of vitamin D and a memory drug after loss of female hormones. Low hormone levels after the change of life may raise dementia risk. Vitamin D has shown guard effects in the brain, so the team tested doses in rats.

Female rats had their ovaries removed and were then given vitamin D, the drug, or both for three weeks. Brain areas tied to memory and planning were checked for swelling signals. One month after surgery, two harm signals rose, and the higher vitamin D dose brought them back down. After eight months, one signal still rose and the same dose helped. The authors see a dose linked guard effect.
pmc-11710649:
Agnès Denève and co-authors compare psychiatric disorders with a behavioral form of frontotemporal dementia, in a 2025 paper. The dementia variant changes behavior and social conduct, and it can look much like a primary psychiatric illness. Social cognition tests were hoped to split the two, but newer results clash on how well they work.

The team reviewed all suspected dementia cases at a Lille memory clinic over eight years, with at least two years of follow up. Fifty six dementia and forty seven psychiatric cases were compared on mind tests in both score and error pattern ways, plus brain scans and biomarkers. Overall test scores for many functions were much alike across groups.
pmc-11710749:
Wen Zeng and Zhuohao He trace a chain from battered brain cells to the tau clumps of Alzheimer's like disease. Repeat head injuries correlate with tau buildup, but the link was missing. In mice, repeated injury sparked tau spread, and the cell's inner rails, microtubules, came apart in the process.

Drugs that wreck those rails triggered tau disease, while rail stabilizers rescued it. Rail damage also shattered the Golgi, the cell's shipping hub, and spilled contents that seeded tau fibers directly. Those fibers converted healthy tau in mouse brains and matched the folds seen in human disease. The authors propose guarding rails and Golgi as a therapy angle.
pmc-11710849:
Eight researchers describe a growing bank of stem cells for Alzheimer's research, in a 2025 paper. The national repository NCRAD builds lines of induced pluripotent stem cells, which can be grown into brain cells in the lab. The lines are open by request to researchers studying Alzheimer's and related dementias.

Each line passes quality checks, including full genome sequencing. Of the lines from 183 donors, 120 have passed sequencing review so far. The set includes lines from ninety donors plus thirty matched edited lines. Many carry known risk variants in genes tied to Alzheimer's, such as APP and MAPT. Blood-based gene typing confirmed each line's identity. Adding genome data lets researchers pre-screen lines before experiments, saving time and money. The bank keeps expanding toward more variant types.
pmc-11712049:
Waiswa and co-authors measure dementia among older people in Uganda's Tororo district, in a 2025 study presented as a systematic review of local evidence. They surveyed 434 people aged fifty and over, combining questionnaires, medical records, and a community screening tool.

Almost one in four screened as having probable or possible dementia. A past infection of the central nervous system came with nearly five times the odds of dementia. Age over seventy and chronic headache were also independent predictors. The authors argue dementia is a growing public health problem in African settings and urge investment in research and specialist services for older adults.
pmc-11712149:
Stephanie Young and seven co-authors test tablet and phone apps that screen thought skills in primary care. Yearly checks catch early thought loss, yet most cases are missed in busy clinics. One app runs on a tablet in the clinic, and one runs on a phone at home.

In ten clinics about a third of due patients finished the tablet check, with wide spread by site. Users flagged test strain, unclear steps, and a need for a Spanish form. All phone users finished twice at home, with sound steadiness and good ease scores. Tweaks could lift uptake.
pmc-11712249:
Roos J Jutten and co-authors ask whether a standard computer test battery tracks decline in Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The battery, the NIH Toolbox, was built to give research studies one shared, brief test set. The team used data from 178 adults in the ARMADA study across nine United States centers.

Participants fell into three groups: healthy, symptom-free with brain amyloid, and early disease with amyloid. The early disease group scored lower at the start on most thinking tasks. Over two years they also fell faster on speed and working memory tasks. The battery showed no gap for the symptom-free amyloid group. The authors say the tests suit early symptomatic disease better than silent disease.
pmc-11712349:
Aldana Lizarraga and co-authors study brain network links in the earliest stage of Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 report. They used data from 328 adults with normal thinking in the ALFA cohort, average age near sixty-one. Spinal fluid tests showed amyloid and tau status, and resting brain scans measured how regions sync their activity.

About thirty-eight percent had positive amyloid markers in their fluid. Low amyloid ratios went with stronger sync between visual areas and the default-mode network, a set of regions active at rest. High tau shifted links in other region pairs. The amyloid-linked sync pattern predicted later decline in memory and planning over about three years of follow-up. The authors say early network change may warn of decline before symptoms.
pmc-11712449:
Samantha Shah and co-authors report a dementia screening toolkit built into the electronic health record in this 2025 paper. Alzheimer's disease touches at least one in ten people over sixty-five, yet their hospital's records showed four percent of such patients carried the diagnosis. The gap fell hardest on Black and Hispanic patients.

The tool takes under five minutes: three questions about changes in language, memory, and personality for the patient and a family informant, then a memory test if needed. A Spanish version was shaped for the Hispanic community. Patients answer through the record system before visits, and results flow into the doctor's note with advice. In fourteen months at a diverse Los Angeles clinic, over a thousand patients were screened. Thirty-one received a dementia diagnosis and eighty-one were sent to neurology. The authors present the build as a model for fairer screening.
pmc-11712549:
Anjan Bhattarai and co-authors show how to measure tau build-up in the brain without drawing arterial blood. Tau clumps mark Alzheimer's disease, and PET scans with the tracer PI-2620 can picture them, but exact measurement normally needs blood samples taken during the scan. Using a total-body scanner, the team instead read the tracer's blood curve straight from the images, from a large artery in the chest.

Fifteen older adults, all without tau deposits, were scanned for 90 minutes. The image-based curve fed standard models that fit the brain data well across the regions most at risk in the disease. The study also tests how shorter scans change the estimates, a step toward gentler, simpler patient scans.
pmc-11712649:
Tevy Chan and co-authors study an odd scan pattern in a 2025 Alzheimer's paper. Some people show high tau signal on brain scans without the amyloid buildup that usually pairs with it. That pattern may mark a distinct age related condition driven by tau alone. The team profiled blood markers in people with this pattern to see how they differ.

Blood readouts could sort these cases without a costly scan. They may also show whether the tau only pattern carries the same risk as full Alzheimer's change. The work draws on a large Montreal based cohort and its stored samples. Sorting scan patterns by blood tests would help clinics judge what a lone tau signal means for a patient.
pmc-11712749:
Andrew Mao, Sebastian Flassbeck, Elisa Marchetto, Henry Rusinek, and Jakob Assländer test a brain scan method, published in 2025, that might track amyloid without tracers. The method is called quantitative magnetization transfer MRI. It senses large molecules in tissue, and amyloid is one of them. Earlier work suggested it could separate patients from healthy people. The team asked whether it works before symptoms start.

Fourteen people with no thinking problems took the special scan, which took twelve minutes. Standard scans mapped each brain, and past tracer scans gave amyloid levels. Two measures from the new scan fell as amyloid rose, most clearly in the temporal lobe. One of those links is new, since most methods fix that value. The size of the large-molecule pool did not change. The authors call the method promising but say a larger group must confirm it.
pmc-11712849:
Ying Xia and colleagues published a long-term study in 2025 on early Alzheimer disease, using data from a large Australian aging study. Hundreds of older adults without dementia had brain scans, memory tests, and amyloid imaging over many years. The team tracked shrinkage in a small brain region that supports memory and attention.

Adults with amyloid buildup lost volume faster in that region and in the hippocampus, and their scores fell faster too. Shrinkage helped explain how amyloid buildup connects to falling scores, with different regions mattering more for memory than for attention. The findings point to early brain change as a key link in the disease.
pmc-11712949:
Lloyd Tran, Zung Vu Tran, and Fern Vu present a 2025 paper linking two drug candidates, one for Alzheimer's disease and one for obesity. The first drug is said to protect nerve cells and support new cell growth and memory. The second is a close cousin that acts on three hormone signals tied to weight and blood sugar.

The paper reports a trial of the first drug in 112 people with mild to moderate disease, where scores improved more than with placebo over twenty-four weeks. It also reports a short mouse study of the second drug, with marked weight loss. The authors use both results to argue the two conditions share drug pathways.
pmc-11713049:
Swastik G Pattanashetty and co-authors describe a 2025 lab study that tests an old drug, terazosin, as a possible treatment for Alzheimer's disease. The drug is already approved for other uses, so its safety in people is well known. The team tested it in rats bred to develop the disease over time.

The drug works in two ways: it blocks one receptor and boosts an enzyme that helps cells make energy. Treated rats did better than untreated rats on tests of place learning and memory at nine and eleven months of age. The results support more study of the drug as a way to protect the brain.
pmc-11713149:
Eunah Cho and seven co-authors published a 2025 biomarker study from a phase 2 trial of an experimental Alzheimer's drug called CT1812. The drug targets the sigma 2 receptor and is designed to knock toxic amyloid clumps off synapses, clearing them into spinal fluid. Earlier work showed it restored memory performance in a mouse model of the disease.

The team ran deep protein and phosphorylation profiling on spinal fluid from the trial's first patients, comparing start and end of study samples. The drug maker and academic partners looked for molecular fingerprints of how the drug acts in people. Such signatures can guide dose choices and future trials. The analysis covers the first eighteen patients with paired samples.
pmc-11713249:
Slutsky-Ganesh and co-authors study how a year of exercise affects brain volume in adults at high risk for Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. A gene variant raises risk and speeds shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory hub. Exercise can grow that area in older adults, but midlife effects were unclear.

Forty-four inactive adults with a family history of the disease joined the trial subset. About half carried the risk gene. One group trained for a year while the other kept usual care. Scans at the start, middle, and end measured the memory hub. The authors test whether training helps, and whether the gene changes the benefit.
pmc-11713349:
Henry Bockholt and a large team of co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, brain network patterns in a hereditary small-vessel disease called CADASIL. The disease degrades brain arteries and is a model for how vessel damage disrupts brain communication. The team compare people who show symptoms with carriers who do not yet.

More than two hundred people joined the study despite pandemic hurdles, with brain scans on three-tesla machines. The symptomatic group was older and scored lower on thinking and daily function tests. Network analysis found clear gaps between the groups in both steady and shifting connection patterns, above all in visual and thinking-control networks. The patterns may yield markers that track the disease before symptoms strike.
pmc-11713449:
René Lattmann and co-authors watch brain activity shift along Alzheimer's path in a 2025 neuroimaging study. Task-based brain scans show abnormal activation early in the disease, but how those abnormalities evolve stage by stage, relative to the standard fluid and volume biomarkers, was unknown.

A progression model placed nearly five hundred participants, from healthy controls to suspected Alzheimer's, on a single disease timeline built from spinal fluid ratios, brain volumes, and cognition scores. Repeated memory-task scans over up to four annual visits then showed activation abnormalities tracking the modeled stage. The work positions functional scans as a progression marker in their own right.
pmc-11713549:
Tamil Iniyan Gunasekaran and co-authors study mixed test results in 2025 among older adults in a New York aging study. Blood tests can flag Alzheimer disease changes, yet some healthy people test positive and some patients test negative. The team asks what brain scans show in these mixed cases.

They tested 685 people and sorted them by thinking state and blood result. Scans measured white matter damage, memory-center size, and silent strokes, while a smaller group got scans for the two hallmark proteins. Healthy people with a positive blood test and patients with a negative one showed distinct scan patterns. The work may help doctors read blood tests with more care.
pmc-11713649:
Carla Abdelnour, a solo author writing in 2025, asks where Lewy body dementia fits in new Alzheimer's rules. The Alzheimer's Association has revised its criteria for diagnosis and staging. Care is moving from symptoms alone toward biology and lab markers. Many dementia cases in fact hold more than one disease process.

The new rules sort markers into core Alzheimer's markers, general markers, and markers for other common diseases. A test for synuclein can now reveal Lewy body disease during life. That may help cases once missed, in special those with both diseases. The piece also weighs how these rules could shape Lewy body trials.
pmc-11713749:
Kexin Yu and co-authors trace a path from personality to memory in old age in a 2025 study. Neuroticism, the tendency toward worry and low mood, tracks with weaker cognition late in life. The open question is the route: does the trait harm thinking directly, or through the gloomy feelings it breeds?

The data come from a trial of socially isolated adults aged seventy-five and up, some with mild impairment. Statistical mediation analysis points to negative affect as the bridge: the trait's link to cognition runs largely through day-to-day negative emotion, more than through depression labels or social ties. If feelings are the conduit, mood support becomes a plausible lever for protecting cognition.
pmc-11714049:
Wayne Chong, Nagaendran Kandiah, and Mohammed Azam lay out a 2025 trial plan on lifestyle and thought decline. Many habits that feed dementia can be changed, and past joint habit plans gave small gains in thought scores. Their plan adds a twist: each member's plan is shaped to their own life and risks.

The test runs as a chain of one-person trials, each open and split by lot. One member at a time gets the tuned plan or not, in set rounds. That design shows gains person by person, not just on average. The plan may sharpen habit care.
pmc-11714249:
James Russell Pike and co-authors reanalyzed a hearing trial in 2025 to see who gains most in thinking skill from hearing care. The trial gave older adults with untreated hearing loss either hearing aids and support, or health education, and tracked thinking for three years.

The hearing care slowed thinking decline by nearly half in participants drawn from a long running heart study, but not in healthy new volunteers. To test why, the team built a risk model from about 2,700 adults in that heart study who were not in the trial. The model explained most of the spread in decline over six years. Applying it showed the benefit was larger for those at high risk.
pmc-11714449:
Fedor Levin and co-authors test in 2025 whether a neural network can spot signs of Alzheimer's disease in a standard MRI scan. The cheap, common scan does not show the amyloid protein that marks the disease. A network that could infer its presence would save costly special scans.

The team had earlier built a network that flags the disease from MRI and shows which image traits drove its call. Here they ask if the same approach can flag amyloid itself. The work sits in a large German study of aging and dementia. A clear network, whose reasons a doctor can inspect, is more likely to be trusted in a clinic. If MRI based flags prove sound, they could sort who needs the dearer scan.
pmc-11714549:
Sharon A Savage and Eloise Trotter test whether a short video improves young adult knowledge and attitudes about reducing dementia risk. Dementia feels distant at twenty, yet early and midlife lifestyle choices shape later risk. Teaching modifiable factors early offers one route to lower future incidence.

The online randomized study enrolls 88 Australians aged 18 to 24. One group watches a five minute dementia video and the other a general health video, each with practical actions. Knowledge and beliefs are measured before and right after viewing. Baseline knowledge is limited, with mean accuracy of only 42 percent on risk factor statements. Just 27 percent know that midlife hearing loss carries risk, which shows the gap the video targets.
pmc-11714649:
Andrew Christopher Miguel and co-authors present a 2025 estimate of how much dementia goes unseen in Brazil. The number of cases there is set to triple by mid-century. Yet no national count of missed cases existed. The team worked from drug records in the public health system for one year. They combined those records with published shares for disease stage and drug use. That let them infer how many diagnosed cases there must be in total.

More than four in five people with dementia over age sixty appear to be undiagnosed. The share was highest in the north of the country and lowest in the southeast. Missed cases were more common in men than in women. They were also most common in the youngest old group, those aged sixty to sixty-four. The authors call the gap one of the highest in the world and urge faster action.
pmc-11714849:
Kensaku Kasuga and co-authors test blood markers for Alzheimer's disease in Japan in this 2025 study. New antibody drugs require biomarker proof of disease, but brain scans and spinal fluid tests are costly, scarce, or invasive. Blood tests promise cheap, repeatable screening.

The team studied two hundred seventeen patients who had spinal fluid testing, over half with an Alzheimer's clinical picture. A blood form of tau sorted disease from non-disease with high accuracy and tracked the key spinal marker well. Another blood marker separated Alzheimer's from a related vessel inflammation that mimics a drug side effect. The authors expect blood screening to guide who should get antibody therapy.
pmc-11715049:
Sofia Toniolo and co-authors test, in 2025, whether an online thinking test plus blood markers can spot Alzheimer's disease and mild subjective decline. Blood markers can flag the disease early, but tracking subtle thinking changes at scale needs remote tools. Their portal hosts validated tasks in memory, attention, and mental flexibility, plus two new visual memory tasks.

One hundred fourteen people took part: patients with the disease, people with subjective complaints, and healthy controls. The online test separated the complaint group from controls with fair accuracy, and all took standard in-person testing too. Blood measures of four markers were collected. The authors argue remote testing could support screening and follow-up at scale.
pmc-11715349:
Sapir Golan and thirteen co-authors studied how people at high risk of Alzheimer's disease reacted after learning their amyloid status in a 2025 paper. The work pooled two observational studies and two trials run in Israel, all using amyloid PET scans. Participants filled in questionnaires before the scan and again four to six months later, covering anxiety, depression, memory complaints, and drive to cut risk.

Among the 199 participants, the 178 who learned they were amyloid negative showed lower scores across every domain that was tested. The group was mostly in their mid-sixties, while the 21 amyloid-positive participants were older, with a mean age of 77. The authors used mixed models and logistic regression to hunt for what predicted a poor response to bad news.
pmc-11715449:
Jiao Wang and six co-authors wrote this 2025 study on whether a body's metabolic age predicts dementia. Metabolic age is read from hundreds of small molecules in a blood sample, using a machine learning method. A person whose blood looks older than their years may carry more wear than the calendar shows, and the team asked whether that gap tracks later dementia.

The study followed more than 153,000 adults in the UK Biobank who were free of dementia at the start. Over up to sixteen years, about three percent developed dementia. Each added stretch of metabolic age raised risk a bit, and people in the oldest metabolic group faced higher risk and earlier onset by nearly a year. Risk was highest of all in people who also carried a strong genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease. The two risks added up together.
pmc-11715649:
Seth Robey, Ka Lai Yee, and Julie A Stone build a mathematical model that lines up many Alzheimer's biomarkers on one shared disease clock. The clock starts when amyloid, the first hallmark protein, turns positive. The markers do not move in step, so a shared clock helps trials pick the right patients. Their 2025 model was trained on records from ADNI, a large shared database in the United States.

Training used 831 adults who were amyloid positive, with scan and test scores over time. The model placed scans for both hallmark proteins and three cognitive test scores on the shared clock. It recovered the order of disease stages with no outside guide. When fed only baseline data for 76 new adults, it matched their real course two to seven years later. The authors see it as a tool for trial selection and personal forecasts.
pmc-11715749:
Ariane Bollack and co-authors give guidance on a standard scale for brain amyloid in Alzheimer's care, in this 2025 paper. The Centiloid scale puts amyloid scan results on one tracer-free ruler. A European consortium gathered trials and studies to say what values mean in practice.

Against tissue checks and spinal fluid, the scale tracked true pathology well. Values under 10 rule amyloid out with high certainty; values over 30 mark it present on a cautious read. The band between means raised risk but needs more study. The method proved robust across pipelines, with small measurement wobble. The guidance was sent to regulators for endorsement.
pmc-11715849:
Leila Letica and six co-authors bred a mouse that carries both inherited Alzheimer's traits and a vessel disease gene, in a 2025 study. Small vessel disease scars the aging brain with tiny strokes and bleeds, and it often mixes with Alzheimer's disease. The team asked whether the two pathologies add up or amplify each other in the brain's sugar use.

They crossed a standard Alzheimer's mouse with a mouse carrying a Notch3 mutation that causes the vessel disease. Awake mice got a sugar tracer, and scans read how much each brain area took up. Whole-brain uptake ran lower in all three mutant lines than in normal mice at every age. The paper sets up the double model as a tool for tracing how vessel and amyloid damage interact over time.
pmc-11715949:
Gabriela Mantovani Baldasso and co-authors present a 2025 study of gene activity in brain cells in Alzheimer's disease. Some brain zones are hit hard by the illness, while others resist it, and the reasons are not clear. The team compared cell-level gene patterns in weak and hardy zones.

Public datasets covered zones such as the hippocampus and the cerebellum, from people with and without the illness. A sorting method split the signals by cell type, from neurons to support cells. The team then grouped the changed genes by their roles, to show which cell paths mark weak zones and which mark hardy ones.
pmc-11716049:
John Laporte and five co-authors scan for dying nerve fibers in mild memory loss and Alzheimer's disease using an improved imaging method. The method estimates neurite density, the thickness of the wiring in each brain spot, from diffusion scans. An earlier technique sometimes returned implausible values, even suggesting growth where loss was expected. The team's constrained version fixed those readings. They applied both methods to scans from a major Alzheimer's study.

The patient groups showed clearly lower density than healthy controls across wide brain areas. The constrained method spotted the subtler gaps too, between healthy and mildly impaired people and between mild impairment and full disease, where the older method missed or reversed them. Only the improved density scores tracked thinking-test results in the expected direction. The authors propose the measure as a sharper trial biomarker.
pmc-11716149:
Jose Luchsinger and co-authors compare two short tests for finding dementia in older adults in 2025. The study took place in primary care clinics in New York City. One test asks people to name smells. The other is a short test of memory and thought. The group had 600 adults aged 65 and older who had concerns about their thinking.

The memory test found dementia and other thinking problems better than the smell test. Using both tests cut false alarms and raised trust in a positive result. Most of the group were women, and many were Hispanic. The authors note that early finds matter more now that new drugs exist for early disease. Clinics could use both tests in a stepwise way.
pmc-11716249:
Yulu Pan and co-authors find gender splits in how daily rhythms track cognition in older adults with poor sleep in a 2025 study. Circadian strength, timing, and fragmentation each describe a different face of the body clock. Their links to thinking skills may not run the same in women and men.

Sixty adults aged sixty to ninety wore activity monitors for a week and slept one night in a lab. In women, steadier and less broken rhythms meant better cognitive scores. In men, earlier activity peaks and earlier sleep midpoints meant better scores. Rhythm height mattered only when everyone was pooled. The split hints at different clock-care advice by gender.
pmc-11716449:
A team led by Christopher Schwarz shares a large public data set from a long study of aging in Minnesota in a 2025 paper. The study tracks county residents over time, and the release covers the first fifteen years. It holds health facts, brain test scores, drug lists, mood and sleep notes, and risk facts for people aged thirty to ninety.

Brain scans come with it: three kinds of magnetic scans plus a scan for the protein clumps tied to memory loss. Faces were swapped out of the scans to guard privacy, and each was checked by eye. The open set aims to speed work on aging and dementia.
pmc-11716549:
Wei-Hsuan Chiu and co-authors studied blood markers in young-onset brain disorders and mental illness, in a 2025 report. Telling these two groups apart is hard, since both can start with mood, conduct, and thinking symptoms. The study ran at a Melbourne hospital as part of a larger multi-site project. Sixty people took part, with conditions that ranged from Alzheimer's disease to deep depression and anxiety, plus healthy controls.

Blood levels of five markers were measured, covering protein buildup, nerve damage, and support-cell activity. Mood and thinking were also scored with set tests. Early pilot results linked memory recall to a mix of the protein markers. Skill at planning and switching tasks tied more to the nerve damage marker. The full analysis was still in progress when the report was written, and the authors frame the work as a step toward cleaner early diagnosis.
pmc-11716649:
Guo and co-authors use genetics to test whether air pollution actually causes dementia, rather than merely traveling with it. Observational studies link dirty air to higher dementia rates, but they cannot fully separate pollution from poverty, lifestyle, and other risks. Mendelian randomization uses inherited gene variants as a natural experiment to get closer to cause and effect.

Drawing on large genetic databases, the team tested four pollutants against several dementia types. Coarser particles, PM10, and nitrogen dioxide showed causal links to Alzheimer's disease risk, while the finest particles and nitrogen oxides did not show convincing effects. The authors call for animal and long-term population studies to uncover how these pollutants harm the brain.
pmc-11716749:
Xinhui Wang and six co-authors ask in 2025 whether heart risk factors carry or change the link between a gene variant and late-life cognitive decline. The APOE gene shapes dementia risk, while midlife heart risks also track with worse cognition. Their interplay near the end of life is less clear.

Data follow 1180 older adults in two long-running aging studies, each with at least four cognition tests. Change-point models split decline into a slow phase and a fast terminal phase. Heart risks in view are depression, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and diabetes. The study tests whether those risks explain part of the gene effect or sharpen it. Findings could refine who gets early preventive care.
pmc-11716849:
Sara Aguilar-Navarro and co-authors build a simple eye-based scale to grade shrinkage in the rear top of the brain on scans. Their 2025 study runs in a memory clinic in Mexico City and uses one slice of a common scan type. The scale keys on a groove at the back of the brain tied to Alzheimer's disease. Files spanned near a decade of clinic care, and patients were sorted as healthy, mildly impaired, Alzheimer's, or other dementia.

Two readers agreed well on the scale, and score curves set how well it split the groups. The aim is a quick, plain tool for a change that scans show well but staff need to grade the same way each time. Links to the clinic's gold standard diagnosis were also checked.
pmc-11716949:
Naresh Damuka and co-authors present a 2025 study imaging the skeleton inside neurons as Alzheimer's disease unfolds. Microtubules are the rails that move cargo in brain cells, and tau protein normally steadies them. When tau falls away, the rails destabilize early in the disease, before plaques and tangles fully form.

A PET tracer built for microtubules let the team watch that change in living mouse brains over time. Two mouse models were followed, one for amyloid pathology and one for tau. Standard scans image the plaques and tangles themselves; this one aims at the earlier rail failure that links them. The longitudinal design tracks whether the signal grows with disease stage. An early marker could open treatment windows that current scans miss.
pmc-11717349:
Kanwar Parhar and co-authors pilot a peer coaching program for heart surgery patients, in a study from 2024. After heart surgery, rehab exercise cuts risk and aids survival. Yet only about a quarter of patients take part. The program paired new patients with a coach who had been through the same kind of surgery.

Ten patients joined and got four hour-long video sessions with the coach. Seven finished the program, and all of them went on to rehab. They averaged about nineteen rehab sessions each. Mood scores did not shift by a clear margin. Still, patients rated the coaching high for easing worry and for nudging them into rehab. The authors say the pilot shows promise but needs a bigger trial. A larger study with a control group could confirm the gains.
pmc-11725049:
Right-side belly pain screams appendicitis, yet a rare pouch disease of the appendix can mimic it. Youssef Assaad Ahmed and co-authors report such a mask in a 2024 case. Their patient was a middle-aged woman with high inflammation marks.

Scans read the case as plain, uncomplicated appendicitis. A camera probe found the swollen organ plus three small nodules. The appendix came out in the same session. Lab study showed pouch disease riding beside the inflammation. She healed cleanly, and her colon check ran normal. Tissue study, they stress, closes such cases.
pmc-11726849:
Chung-Che Tsai and co-authors review current methods to find and treat malignant tumors, in work from 2024. Cancer stays a top global health challenge with high death rates across many types. Its complex nature calls for many sided tools for both diagnosis and care.

The review covers molecular imaging, blood and tissue markers, and liquid biopsies that sample tumor material from blood. On the care side it traces surgery, chemo, and radiation, plus newer targeted paths such as immune therapy and gene therapy. The authors argue the future lies in precision care built for each tumor. Gaps and hurdles ahead are also named.
pmc-11727349:
Hansen Wu and co-authors review how the cell's powerhouses, mitochondria, go wrong in pituitary adenomas and how that weakness might be treated. These pituitary tumors are usually benign, yet they invade nearby tissue and disturb hormone output, and surgery, drugs, and radiation each have limits. Mitochondria steer metabolism and signaling throughout tumors.

Evidence links faulty mitochondria to how these tumors arise and grow. Several compounds that help against pituitary adenomas turn out to act on mitochondria. The review pulls together the genetic changes, the functional failures, and the drug leads in one place. Targeting the powerhouse offers a route around the limits of current care.
pmc-11727549:
Bondar and co-authors run in 2024 a pilot study of gender gaps in depression among patients with ischemic heart disease in Romania. Heart disease weighs on mental health, with unlike responses by gender. They recruited 183 adults with artery disease and depression at one hospital psychiatry unit from 2021 to 2024.

A self built questionnaire, paired with standard scales, profiled demographic, clinical, and social traits. Women showed higher emotional distress and more severe depression than men in the results. Women also reported greater social isolation and a stronger wish named in the head. Reliability of the new tool was checked by standard scores. The pilot maps where gender tailored support may help.
pmc-11728249:
Patricia Bermudez-Gomez and co-authors optimize in 2024 how mushroom stems can be turned into functional flour. Stems are a major waste product of mushroom farms. Two common species are studied, one whose stems stick to peat.

For the peat-stuck stems, abrasive peeling cleaned best, with low germ counts and good work rate. For drying, a dehydrator beat oven and freeze-dryer on color and energy use. Drying at fifty degrees for a day kept plant compounds as well as slower, cooler drying. The final process balances quality, cost, and speed for flour making.
pmc-11728449:
A rice-grown kefir product trimmed fat gain in mice fed a rich diet, and the gut seems to carry the tale. Takuto Kurakawa and eight co-authors dosed the mice in 2024 and watched weight, liver fat, and sugar handling. All three leaned the right way, sugar by a modest step. Droppings showed the gut crowd shift as the gains came.

Two germ clans tied to fatness thinned out, while two tied to leanness grew. A fat-burning acid in the droppings rose with the shift. Gene-path guesses from the germ mix pointed to sugar handling as the worked lever. The team read the product as a postbiotic, a germ-made good that works without live germs, and call for the chain to be traced link by link.
pmc-11728549:
Oscar G Marambio and co-authors design a polymer that meters out a plant-based agent on a schedule set by acidity. Their 2024 paper builds water-loving copolymers from two monomers, then grafts the herbicide 2,4-D onto the chains. The question is how fast the weed killer breaks free in water as the pH changes, a release measured by ultrafiltration, which also tracks how the gel swells.

On the acid side, release followed first-order kinetics, and the rate rose as pH climbed. On the basic side it ran at a steady zero-order pace, with the base itself speeding the split like a catalyst. Swelling grew with pH too, and release tracked the swelling. In distilled water at pH 10 the samples matched the profile wanted for farm hydrogels. The authors offer the system as a carrier whose timing can be tuned to field conditions.
pmc-11728749:
Wenxia Bu and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four review of how polystyrene nanoplastics harm cells. Tiny plastic particles from pollution collect in living tissue. Their small size lets them enter cells and disturb basic machinery.

The review gathers evidence on oxidative stress, power plant damage, and DNA injury. Inflammation and faulty self-cleaning also appear. Several distinct death programs can be triggered, from quiet cell suicide to fiery inflammatory death. Particle size, surface treatment, other pollutants, and protein coatings all change the harm. The authors urge more mechanism research and stronger rules.
pmc-11728849:
Erik Turner and co-authors asked whether the temperature a mosquito actually lives at, indoors or out, changes how fast Zika and chikungunya grow inside it, in this 2024 study. Weather stations miss that difference, yet Aedes aegypti mosquitoes prefer homes. Using temperature records from Neiva, Colombia, the team ran both viruses through mosquitoes under indoor and outdoor profiles.

Mosquito survival barely moved. Infection rates shifted only slightly, though virus amounts in the body differed at several time points. Modeling told a stronger story for chikungunya: indoor warmth produced a much taller, earlier outbreak peak than outdoor conditions. For Zika, both settings gave high spread odds but few cases. The authors urge finer temperature data in risk models.
pmc-11730449:
Katsuhiro Masago, Shiro Fujita, Eiichi Sasaki, and Yoshitsugu Horio discuss whether inherited variants change how well a class of lung cancer drugs works, in this 2024 article. The drugs block the epidermal growth factor receptor and are a mainstay for advanced lung cancers with certain mutations. The piece centers on a study by Guan and co-authors that singled out one variant in the gene USP36.

That variant raises the amount of USP36 a cell makes, which steadies a partner protein and helps tumors resist the drugs. The commentators praise the study's method, which hunted for variants that change how long a gene's message lasts, not how its protein is built. They also quibble with wording, noting variant is now the preferred term over polymorphism. A second, rarer variant in the same gene gets a close reading. The authors present the variant as a candidate marker for predicting drug response.
pmc-11734049:
Norma Nicole Gamarra-Valverde and co-authors report a lung tumor that reached into the heart. Their 2024 case, titled in full From Lung to Heart: Unusual Case of Pulmonary Myxoid Sarcoma, describes a seventy-seven-year-old man with cough, breathlessness, and vague malaise on top of several chronic illnesses. Scans found a mass in the right lower lung lobe and a shadow in the left atrium.

Heart ultrasound first suggested a clot. Deeper imaging showed a tumor over seven centimeters long, growing from the right lower lung vein into the atrium and across into the ventricle, where it choked the mitral valve. A lung biopsy named the culprit: primary pulmonary myxoid sarcoma, a rare cancer. The authors stress full heart imaging when a chest mass casts a shadow there.
pmc-11736349:
Li and co-authors review a form of cell death and its part in liver disease. The death mode, ferroptosis, is driven by iron and by damaged fats in cell walls. The liver, as the body's metabolic hub, is exposed on many fronts. The review, published with a Chinese title, walks through the mode's role disease by disease.

Speeding this death up worsens sharp liver injury, fatty liver, alcohol harm, and viral or immune hepatitis. In scarred livers and liver cancer, the same death can slow the disease instead. That split makes the pathway a tempting drug lever. The authors sum up fresh work and point to where targeted control might help patients.
pmc-11740749:
Noer Handayani and co-authors made rice-like grains from sago and corn flour in 2024 and tested their traits and taste appeal. Indonesia eats large amounts of rice and imports much food, so a local staple stand-in has real value. The team fortified the grains with black-eyed bean flour and skimmed milk powder to raise their food value.

The grains were shaped by hot extrusion, a method that forces a mix through a die under heat. Lab tests measured protein, carbohydrate, fat, water, fibre, and ash. Heat stability was checked with a scanning calorimeter, and grain structure was viewed with an electron microscope. Panels also judged how much people liked the product. Readers get a full profile, from nutrients to texture, of a rice analogue meant for daily use.
pmc-11753149:
William Schultz and Rosemary Ricciardeli survey, in a 2024 review, what prison work does to the health of the staff who run prisons. Officers and other front-line staff handle the daily work of a jail or prison, from safety checks to care of those held there. Research on this group has grown fast in the past ten years. The picture it paints is grim, the authors say, across body, mind, and social life.

Staff show high rates of poor body health, and signs of a mental health crisis, with high rates of illness and self-harm. Those rates top even other police-type jobs in some reports. Work culture and home life take a hit as well. The review ends with gaps to fill and next steps for research and reform.
pmc-11770049:
Six authors led by Diego Diaz-Guerra set out a protocol for AI-aided mind tests in older adults with mental illness, work dated 2024 in the study text. Mind tests in this group are hard, since symptoms mix and each case varies a great deal. Their plan pairs standard test sets with AI reads of the scores, case by case. Each profile is fit to the one patient, not to group norms alone.

The AI step hunts patterns across test lines that a human read may miss at speed. Output is a per-person mind map that flags strong and weak zones for the care team. The plan also probes spare paths the brain may use to work around harm. Gains claimed span sharper reads and care plans fit to each elder. Test proof of the plan comes next, the authors note.
pmc-11774649:
Omar Larentis and co-authors report, in a paper whose head is dated 2024, a joint study of three mummies kept at a cliffside sanctuary in Italy. The hermits' bodies date from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries and were revered locally, yet science knew little about them. Moving the bodies was impossible, so the team brought portable X-ray gear to the site.

Mobile digital X-rays let experts from many fields read cloth, past repairs, insect traces, bone traits, and disease signs in place. The approach trades the depth of a full body scanner for access where none exists. New facts about the hermits' lives and deaths emerged, bringing these figures into the scientific record for the first time.
pmc-11779549:
Maider Prieto-Vila and ten co-workers wrote a 2024 study on paths of depression after therapy in primary care. Patients got either usual care or usual care plus group cognitive therapy. The course of depression varies a lot between people. The team asked which paths each care type produced over a year.

Close to five hundred patients were tracked after care ended. Usual care split into two paths: improvement or none. The therapy group split into four paths, from full recovery to relapse. High starting symptoms and added illness linked to poorer paths in both groups. The therapy group shrank symptoms more overall than usual care alone.
pmc-11783849:
Angela Caroline, Martine Coun, Agus Gunawan, and Jol Stoffers review work on digital literacy, employability, and new ideas at work, in work from 2025 in the journal record. Modern work demands staff who can use digital tools, stay employable, and act in fresh ways that rivals cannot copy easily. The three traits are often studied apart.

Through citation mapping and a systematic review, the team joins the three strands. They sum up trends, measures, theories, and models in human resource research. They stress context, since the same skill can play out differently by setting. The review shows where the joined field stands and where it should go next.
pmc-11784049:
Anan Chaokaur and six colleagues published a goat feeding study in two thousand twenty-four on purple Napier grass silage. The purple pigment, anthocyanin, is a strong antioxidant. It may protect dairy animals from cell stress and lift production.

Nine milking crossbred goats were fed corn silage, plain Napier grass silage, or the purple version. Intake and digestion were tracked, and milk and blood were tested for makeup and antioxidant power. Goats on corn silage ate the most feed and fibre. Protein intake was similar across the three diets. The study sets up a comparison of whether the pigment-rich silage brings blood or milk benefits beyond the plain grass.
pmc-11798949:
Karen Sieben-Aduful leads a team in a study of how teachers in Dutch primary schools respond to racism and racist bullying. Children with a non-White skin color, or a non-Western cultural or faith background, can face racist acts from a young age. Since school fills much of their day, teachers hold a key role in keeping class safe and fair.

Yet a reply to racist bullying can be hard to get right. In-depth interviews with a set of teachers probed their past cases and how they acted. The study also asks how racism itself is talked about in class.
pmc-11803449:
Samantha González-Téllez and Meritxell Riquelme (2024) identified a helper protein that ships a wall-building enzyme out of the fungal cell's packaging center. Chitin gives fungal walls their strength, and enzymes called chitin synthases make it. In baker's yeast, a chaperone escorts one such enzyme from the endoplasmic reticulum onward. The mold Neurospora crassa carries two versions of that escort. Earlier work tied the first version to one synthase. This study tested the second, named CSE-8.

Deleting the gene for CSE-8 kept the class I synthase CHS-3 from reaching its work sites. The glowing tagged enzyme vanished from the growing tip and cross-walls. Sexual development also faltered in the mutant, and removing both escorts cut chitin content and slowed growth. Stress tests supported the picture of CSE-8 as a reticulum worker. The authors map a division of labor between the two escorts in filamentous fungi.
pmc-11808149:
Peng and eight co-authors study Chinese peony flowers as a new food ingredient, in work dated twenty twenty-four. The root of peony is a known Chinese herb. Its flowers are a major waste by product that may hold value.

Samples from four cultivars were profiled with a high resolution mass method in a three level strategy. One hundred fifty compounds were identified, more than fifty of them new reports for this species. Targeted measures split flower parts clearly. Cell tests and four chemical assays checked anti swelling and antioxidant power. Turning herb waste into a food ingredient could add income and cut waste.
pmc-11810649:
Parhati Tuerxun and co-authors take a first look in a 2024 study at body chemistry in people who have both migraine and a small hole between the heart's upper chambers. That hole, present from birth, is tied to migraine in ways that stay unclear. They read blood chemistry in eleven such patients around a closure procedure, and in healthy peers.

Six compounds stood out between the groups, among them dopamine and proline. Path maps pointed to protein handling and one amino acid path as key. Dopamine ran high in the migraine group. The small study marks paths worth a deeper look in larger groups.
pmc-11827849:
Yuri Kim and a large team of collaborators published a 2024 heart genetics study on a DNA enhancer that the heart needs to build its contractile machinery. Titin, the giant spring protein of muscle, is the most common genetic cause of heart failure when cut short by mutations. How the heart keeps titin production so high was unclear.

The team studied a conserved stretch inside the titin's first intron that opens up as heart cells mature. Deleting it from both gene copies killed mouse embryos, and deleting one copy cut titin output from that copy. A small fragment of the element alone could drive a reporter gene. Removing it in human stem cell derived heart cells lowered titin, broke sarcomere assembly, and weakened contraction.
pmc-11835849:
Catherine Wilkinson wrote this reflective paper, published in 2024 though the catalog lists 2025, on designing research with and for people who live with chronic pain. Wilkinson writes as a researcher who also lives with two painful long term conditions. Study designs often bend for participants' pain, with breaks for flare ups and quiet spells. The researcher's own pain is rarely planned for.

The paper draws lessons from that double view. It asks how methods can serve the bodies of both sides of the study at once. It also reflects on the bond between researcher and participant when pain is shared ground. The aim is research ties that are both kinder and more productive.
pmc-11836649:
Yuliya Tyravska and four co-authors review how the immune system and blood clotting shape each other, in a 2024 paper. The joint field is called immunohaemostasis. The team read across immunology and blood science to map the two-way links. They also weighed modern care for clots and bleeds in that light.

Immune cells and complexes switch platelets on, tune clotting factors, and speed or slow clot breakdown. In return, clotting parts help immune cells move to infection sites and guard tolerance of the body's own blood parts. Care options span blood thinners, platelet blockers, clot removal, and bleed guards. The authors say this two-way view can seed new immune-based care for clot and bleed risks.
pmc-11841449:
Dong, Niu, Jiang, Choi, and Li survey more than thirteen hundred city middle school girls in China on what support helps them stay active in sports. Social backing is known to matter for teen exercise, yet how much each source counts was unclear. Their 2024 survey spans sixteen regions and blends activity, support, and family wealth questionnaires.

Family support scored highest, ahead of teacher and then peer support, with emotional backing stronger than practical help. Activity in school slightly beat activity outside school. Girls' activity tied to their age, grade, family wealth, and parents' schooling. Oddly, richer families gave less emotional but more informational support, and better-schooled parents sometimes dampened activity. The authors urge schools to build support networks that fill family gaps.
pmc-11842349:
Rongjing Xu and co-authors explore what older adults in Shanghai know about mental health in a study published in 2024. Mental health literacy means knowing how to spot mental illness, hold sound views about it, and act to stay well. China's older population is growing fast, and gaps in this knowledge can delay care.

Twenty older adults from four city communities sat for deep interviews. Three themes came out of the talks. Knowledge of mental health and illness was thin. Views on keeping the mind healthy and preventing illness leaned negative, with stigma in the mix. Daily habits to guard mental health were patchy. The authors call for joint effort by people, families, and society to teach, to fight stigma, and to support healthy habits. They tie the work to a national healthy aging plan.
pmc-11855049:
Shin and Woo trace the careers of medical students at Jeonui-gam, a Joseon dynasty training office, in the late nineteenth century. Two rosters anchor the study. One lists 384 entrants with their enrollment facts, and the other, shown here for the first time, records an alternate entry path based on recommendations from other offices.

Many students enrolled at several technical offices at once, such as those for astronomy or state stores, which shows medical training sat inside a wider job-training web. A rule let younger brothers join elder ones, opening doors for families. About two thirds of the students became medical officials, while others became interpreters or took other state posts.
pmc-11877649:
Josephine Sabrina Jakubowski and five colleagues survey specialists who support children whose vision problems stem from the brain, not the eyes. These children, some diagnosed with cerebral visual impairment, form a growing group with complex needs. Care pulls in teachers, therapists, clinicians, and families at once.

Ninety-four people answered the online survey, most of them educators and rehabilitation staff. Nearly all shared two goals: connecting with the child and fostering learning. Beyond that, goals sometimes clashed between groups. Staff often named parents as their best source of insight, yet family members felt undervalued. Joint clinics drew praise as a model. Most staff who knew the CVI label still thought it underdiagnosed.
pmc-11881649:
Caleb Nault reviewed a 2024 book by Andrea Jamison on decentering whiteness in library collections. The book offers a framework for more inclusive collection management. It appears amid book bans and protests aimed at works by or about marginalized groups.

Jamison draws on long work in school libraries and teaching. The book gives practical steps to review collection policies for bias. Nault places it within wider efforts on diversity and fair hiring in libraries. He presents it as a useful guide for staff who want collections that serve all readers more fairly.
pmc-11883249:
Tuba Demirci Yildirim and co-authors weigh how well young patients move from paediatric to adult rheumatology care. Their 2024 study looks back on past cases. It covers moves of care in Turkey from 2013 to 2023.

Of more than twenty-five hundred patients who were sent on, about eight percent moved with success. That was set by their keeping up visits each year to the adult clinic. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and familial Mediterranean fever were the diseases seen in most cases. The median time for the move was four months. Close to half moved early. Use of biologic drugs was linked to an early move. Higher education, and one diagnosis, were linked to a late move. Care changed for about half the patients after the move. The study sets those changes out.
pmc-11888749:
Natarajan and co-authors review the case for quitting smoking as a shield against oral cancer. Smoking is a leading driver of these cancers, which remain a heavy global burden. The review gathers evidence on how stopping changes a smoker's risk, both soon after quitting and over the long run.

Quitting cuts exposure to cancer-causing chemicals and lets the mouth's lining heal, lowering the chance that malignant change takes hold. The benefit grows with time away from tobacco. The authors also survey public-health tactics that help people stop, from counseling to policy, and argue these belong at the center of oral cancer prevention. For smokers, the message is simple: stopping is the strongest step available.
pmc-11927549:
Qun-Qun Zhu and co-authors compare two ways of guiding a biopsy needle into lung nodules. The coaxial technique parks a guide tube so several samples pass through one puncture. In their retrospective series, two hundred nineteen patients had CT-guided core biopsies with or without the coaxial guide.

The coaxial group needed fewer needle paths, yielded more samples, and finished faster. Diagnostic accuracy was statistically the same in both groups, around ninety-seven percent, but the coaxial route produced a working diagnosis more often. Collapsed lung and bleeding rates did not differ. The authors conclude the guide buys efficiency and yield without costing safety, at least in experienced hands at their center.
pmc-11935349:
Bell and seven co-authors review workforce outcomes for substance use peer support workers in a paper published in 2024. Peer workers draw on their own lived experience of addiction. Their roles are growing, but their job outcomes are little studied.

Searches across major databases and grey sources yielded a small set of studies that fit. Supportive supervision and chances to grow skills were linked to job satisfaction and staying in the role. Low pay and stigma hurt retention. Personal strains such as boundary problems and poor self-care fed burnout. The authors call for long-term studies and clearer accounts of work settings. Better support may keep this workforce healthy.
pmc-11935549:
Zhendong Mei and a large team search blood metabolites for signs of plaque burden in heart disease patients already on cholesterol treatment, in a 2024 study. They profiled 175 metabolites in 2,560 newly diagnosed patients and compared them with angiography scores and a heart injury marker. Genetic methods probed which links might be causal.

Triglycerides and apolipoprotein B inside LDL particles tracked plaque severity more strongly than the standard LDL cholesterol test. Some large HDL parts pointed the other way. Two combined metabolite scores followed later heart events, with one raising risk about 15 percent per step. The authors say metabolite profiling could assess risk without invasive imaging.
pmc-11936749:
Can Guo, Ke-Wei Liu, Jing Tong, and Meng-Qiu Gao, published in 2024, study whether being undernourished worsens outcomes in tuberculous meningitis. This infection of the membranes around the brain kills many patients and leaves others disabled. Few effective treatments exist once it strikes. Poor nutrition is one risk factor doctors can actually change, but its link to recovery from this disease was unclear.

The team reviewed records for patients treated between 2010 and 2021. They scored each patient's nutrition risk with three standard scales, built from blood values such as albumin and cholesterol, plus body weight. Recovery was graded one year later on a standard disability scale. The analysis then asked how common nutrition risk was in this group, and whether patients flagged as at risk recovered worse than those who were not. The aim is a cheap warning sign that could trigger feeding support early in treatment.
pmc-11970149:
Geraldine Basanyukira and co-authors measure malnutrition in babies of teenage mothers in a 2024 Uganda study. Children of adolescent mothers face stacked risks, and poor growth is high on the list. The team worked at Mulago Hospital's children's department in Kampala.

Babies aged one to twenty-four months were examined with their mothers. Stunting hit thirty-two percent, wasting thirty-one, and underweight twenty-seven. Stunting linked to age over one year, chronic illness, low birth weight, rural homes, and partners who gave no money. Wasting linked to early birth, thin antenatal care, working mothers, and again missing partner support. The authors call the burden a concern for families and health services alike.
pmc-12008349:
Houyem Khiari and co-authors present a 2024 report from the Northern Tunisia Cancer Registry. Cancer is a leading cause of illness and death in Tunisia. The registry tallied estimated new cases for 2023 and projected rates out to 2040, giving planners a view of the coming burden.

Standardized incidence reached about 166 per 100,000 men and 141 per 100,000 women, counting skin cancers. In men, lung, colorectal, bladder, prostate, and stomach cancers led the list. In women, breast cancer led by a wide margin, followed by colorectal, uterine, thyroid, and lung cancers. The registry gathers cases actively from public and private care. Projections used an age-period-cohort model. The numbers guide screening and treatment planning.
pmc-12203749:
Oluwatoyin Famojuro and co-authors check drug-resistant germs in samples from a Nigerian teaching hospital in a study from 2024. Some bacteria make enzymes called ESBLs that break down key antibiotics. The study used high vaginal swabs from women with genital tract infections.

Women aged eighteen to fifty took part, both pregnant and not. None had taken antimicrobials in the prior two weeks. Bacteria grew in about four of five samples in each group. The team tested which drugs still worked on each isolate. They also checked how often ESBL genes appeared in the Gram-negative germs. Local data like this guide drug choice where resistance is rising fast.
pmc-12384249:
An and Yang study what drives fall prevention acts by long-term care nurses in Korea. Falls harm many older hospital patients each year. The survey held 136 nurses from four large care hospitals. Data were gathered in August 2021. Belief scales and safety culture scores were the predictors.

Safety culture views and age each predicted prevention acts. Perceived seriousness and action drive also added weight. Perceived barriers cut acts, with a negative weight. The full model explained 44.5 percent of the spread. The authors urge culture work plus belief-based training for nurses.
pmc-12450649:
Bicheng Zhang and co-authors, published in 2024, study what happens when a solid tumor spreads into the bone marrow. Patients in this situation usually have a poor outlook, yet some do notably better after aggressive treatment, so the authors look for factors that separate the two groups. They review 41 consecutive patients diagnosed by bone marrow biopsy at their center between 2016 and 2021, comparing clinical features and blood tests between them.

Survival in the whole group was short, with a median of just 23 days. Using standard survival curves, the team examines how symptoms, blood counts, biochemistry, and clotting measures relate to how long patients live. The goal is practical triage: to spot, at diagnosis, the minority of patients whose profiles suggest they could gain from aggressive therapy, and to spare the rest treatment that cannot help them.
pmc-12539549:
Alicja Nowak and Małgorzata Ogurkowska review how physical activity shapes bone health in a 2024 paper. Bone adapts to the loads placed on it, most where stress is greatest. The response differs between spongy and dense bone tissue.

Both mechanical forces and body-wide signals steer bone metabolism during exercise. Hormones, muscle factors, and immune signals all play a part. Bone-building cells burn much glucose, so nutrition matters when activity raises energy demand. Training effects vary with age and sex. The authors stress picking the right dose of intensity, duration, and frequency for each person.
pmc-12660949:
Hulls and co-authors asked business and industry experts whether 5G has kept its promises in European workplaces. They interviewed 14 specialists from companies and stakeholder bodies in the United Kingdom, Belgium, Spain, Poland, and Switzerland during 2023, using a semi-structured guide, then coded the transcripts for themes.

Views were mixed: 5G was described as still developing and not the cure-all once expected. Workplace uptake was small and mostly limited to pilot sites in farming, manufacturing, airports, and campuses, often backed by government schemes. Experts saw a natural evolution coming in factories but stressed the cost of upgrading every device to connect. Pandemic-era misinformation had also colored public views. The authors conclude that real deployment lags the hype and that more work is needed on how firms can adopt 5G well.
pmc-12661549:
Fan Luo and co-authors feed a gut germ to mice to learn how it lifts growth in a 2025 study. The germ had boosted growth in piglets in past work, and gut germs are known to shape how fast a beast grows.

Male mice got the germ by mouth for four weeks. Their weight gain ran a touch above the plain group, and one blood fat fell by a clear mark. The gut germ mix shifted, with two clans in step with growth and leanness on the rise. Most shifts faded once the germ was stopped. A scan of small compounds found fifty-three that moved, in four known paths. One germ clan tracked those moves most, and the authors cast it as the lead actor.
pmc-12661849:
Kajganic and five co-authors test a stimulation pattern for paralyzed leg muscles during cycling therapy, in work from twenty twenty-five. Functional electrical stimulation cycling moves paralyzed legs by stimulating the quadriceps. Muscle fatigue limits session length and power.

Spatially distributed sequential stimulation spreads the pulses across muscle sites in sequence. It had shown greater fatigue reduction and power in static contractions than conventional stimulation. The study applied it during motor assisted cycling, a more realistic therapy task. Better endurance in cycling sessions could raise the training dose that spinal cord injury patients can tolerate.
pmc-12662949:
Florence Leduc and co-authors review work that pairs tree-ring records with satellite data to watch forests, in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Rings track wood growth year by year, while satellite greenness tracks leaf activity and canopy cover. The two views differ in scale and can enrich each other.

Seventy-eight studies were sorted into three themes: links to climate, long-term growth trends, and responses to shocks. Ring and greenness records often moved together within single years. Over long spans they often split apart. Rings showed deeper, longer drops after shocks than greenness did. Scale mismatch remains a core hurdle.
pmc-12663249:
Tengyi Liu and Chuantao Li build a model in 2025 to judge and lift college students' skill at solving higher math problems. Judging that skill today is crude. Their system rates both thinking traits, like reasoning, and behavior traits, like time use. A hybrid neural model, tuned by an optimizer, scores students on both sides at once. Regression weights feed the network, keeping the score readable.

The model fit student data closely. Thinking traits carried most of the weight, with logical reasoning on top. Students given guided intervention improved over three times more than controls. The authors offer the framework as a tool that predicts skill and guides teaching at once.
pmc-12663549:
Tufa and co-authors test in 2025 how well drugs work in the lab against a parasite from patients in northwest Ethiopia. The parasite causes visceral leishmaniasis, and HIV co infection makes care hard, with relapse a common problem. Samples came from a treatment center in Gondar during 2020.

They tested 30 parasite isolates from first episodes and relapses, in patients with and without HIV. Three standard drugs were checked at one parasite stage, and ten isolates were retested at a second stage. Mean doses needed to halt growth are reported for each drug. Such profiles help judge whether drug resistance plays a part in relapse.
pmc-12664149:
Mehtap Gürler Balta and co-authors compare two nerve block methods for pain relief after breast removal surgery, in a randomized trial from 2025. Good pain control after surgery shapes how well patients recover. Both blocks numb the chest wall, but their effect on overall recovery quality was unproven.

Sixty-eight women having the surgery were split at random between the two blocks. Recovery quality was scored with a standard forty-item survey at one and two days after surgery. Pain scores, opioid use, and time to first pain request were also tracked. The two groups scored almost the same on recovery quality. The first pain request came after a long delay in both groups. The authors treat the blocks as near equals for this surgery.
pmc-12664249:
Mohammad Hassan Emamian and a large team track the safety of the Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine in young people in this two thousand twenty-five study from Iran. The vaccine had proved safe in adults and children, but data for teens stayed thin. The study followed children and teens aged five to eighteen in eight cities. Families joined after the first dose. Staff phoned them daily for a week after each dose.

The callers logged sore arms, fever, and other reactions. They also watched for breakthrough infections and serious events over a longer span. This style of study, called cohort event monitoring, catches side effects as they happen. The findings add real-world safety data for a vaccine given to millions of young people. Parents and health officials can use it to weigh risks.
pmc-12689649:
Abdel-hameed El-Aassar and co-authors build and test in a 2025 study a compact wastewater plant sized for farm villages that want to irrigate with the cleaned water.
