Big central plants cost too much for small communities. Their unit stacks four treatments: sieving, extended aeration, a moving-bed biofilm reactor, and membrane filtration.

Total dissolved solids fell by about half, and heavy metals dropped by a quarter to near total removal depending on the metal. Germ counts fell sharply as well. The output met Egypt's standards for watering edible crops, a practical route to reuse where water runs short.
pmc-12692749:
Stanisław Szlufik and co-authors hunt brain scan signs that predict thinking changes after deep brain stimulation in a 2025 study. The treatment eases Parkinson movement symptoms but can dull some mental skills. Thirty-eight patients took thinking tests and MRI scans before surgery and again within two years after.

Decline clustered in language: word fluency and object naming fell clearly, while memory, attention, and overall cognition held. Wider fluid spaces in the brain, the lateral ventricles, tracked with worse results across several domains. One left-brain width measure also linked to outcomes. The authors say simple ruler measures on routine scans could help select patients and counsel them before surgery.
pmc-12693549:
Martin Eckert, Thomas Ostermann, Jan Peter Ehlers, and Gregor Hohenberg test an open-world virtual reality program for people with dementia. Their 2025 pilot study builds on talking therapy that stimulates thinking, a drug-free aid for dementia care. Open virtual worlds that users can explore freely have been little studied for this group.

Three men with dementia took one seated session, moving an avatar with arm and head motions. All finished with no adverse events, and the average session ran close to half an hour. Surveys showed acceptance and a positive view of ease of use. Mood changed only a little, but reports told of deep immersion and memories being stirred. The small pilot supports larger tests of safety and benefit.
pmc-12693849:
Chun-Mei Lai and co-authors review new ways to change plant genes in a 2025 paper. Changing a plant's genes can raise crop yield and help crops stand up to drought, heat, and pests. The older ways of delivering new genes into plant cells can harm tissue, work in only some species, or succeed too rarely to be practical.

The review looks at tiny engineered particles that can carry genetic material into plant cells while shielding it from damage. These carriers can work across more species and may let treated plants regrow more easily. The authors also cover precise gene editing tools and how they pair with the particle approach. The field is still young, they note, but the mix of gentle delivery and exact editing could make crop improvement faster and more reliable.
pmc-12694149:
Salty soils already spoil about a fifth of irrigated farmland, and the share is set to grow. Sajida and co-authors review in this 2025 paper two helpers that shield crops from salt: helpful root bacteria and tiny particles of silicon, plus the newer idea of using both together.

Each helper on its own steadies plant ions, builds protective compounds, and switches on stress genes. Together they may do more, but trials at field scale are still scarce, and questions remain about particle stability and microbe compatibility. The review maps the mechanisms and case studies, and it marks where proof is still missing.
pmc-12694249:
Lauren Kness and Virginia Quick survey troubled eating behaviors and quality of life in young adults living with bowel diseases, in a study from 2025. Conditions like irritable bowel syndrome and Crohn's disease force constant attention to food. That vigilance can slide into unhealthy eating patterns, and daily life often suffers with it.

Seventy three young adults, most of them women, answered an online survey in 2022 and 2023. They reported about eleven physically or mentally unhealthy days in the past month. Scores on a standard eating disorder questionnaire ran well above healthy norms for both men and women. The study compares results by sex and disease type, and it argues that gut clinics should screen eating behavior, not just bowel symptoms.
pmc-12694549:
Alžbeta Bánovčinová and co-authors sort metabolic risk in Slovak children with obesity in a 2025 study. Children with obesity differ a lot in health risk, and insulin resistance is a core part of that risk. The team used body scans and fasted blood tests on 54 children with obesity and 33 peers.

Two markers split the group in distinct ways, and about a fifth of the obese group scored high on both, a rate well above peers. Low muscle mass for age stood out as a flag for the highest risk band. Matched pairs by age backed the same pattern. The authors urge body makeup checks, not weight alone, to rank risk in clinic.
pmc-12695949:
Yaqi Wu and five co-authors reveal the three dimensional structure of the machine that herpes simplex virus uses to copy its DNA, in this 2025 study. The machine, a three part primosome, unwinds the viral DNA and lays down starter pieces for copying. It is a prized drug target, but how it works had stayed murky.

Using electron microscopy, the team froze the machine holding a strand of DNA and read its shape at fine detail. The picture shows an open groove where DNA sits and tight contacts among all three parts. Follow-up tests mapped the active sites and the joints between parts. The authors propose the machine unwinds DNA through a two way rotation, switching between unwinding and starter making. The design is shared across the herpes family, which may aid broad antiviral design.
pmc-12699549:
Li Fu and co-authors use gene lots to test if blood chemicals cause major depression, in a study from 2025. Mood and metabolism are kin, but kin ties do not prove cause. Gene lots, dealt at birth, can mimic a trial: if a chemical's gene marks track the ill, cause is apt.

The pool set 871 blood chemicals against the ill in vast gene banks, more than a million souls for the mood side. Eleven chemicals passed the bar. Eight leaned guard, one a fat part of cell skins among them; three leaned risk, each by a hair. Twin-source checks and drug worth scans flagged which of the eleven could be drug leads. The team frames the list as a map for lab proof, not proof itself.
pmc-12699849:
Eight authors map mpox spread in a Congo health zone in a 2025 study of 160 firm cases. The zone, Kamituga in South Kivu, sits at the heart of the Congo wave of the clade I strain. Case data span nine months from late 2023 to mid 2024, with blood tests and life and symptom logs.

Cases ran young, with a mean age near 24, and women made up about 59 percent. Women who sell sex made up over a third of cases. Fever, wide pus rash, and swollen glands marked near all cases in the set. Late care and risky sex drove spread.
pmc-12700149:
Steinmann and six co-authors test if first grade takes shift by school race in this twenty twenty-five study. Young heal hands of far roots oft score low in ward grade rounds. First takes may stick or shift as act grades change in a meet.

Inside, medics watched tapes of school acts that rose or fell cross time. First takes at one mark showed no race gap in the grades. Rise acts won high end grades for far-root youth from young medics. Grade shifts tween first and end takes ran large for that band. Both rise and fall tapes drew those large shifts in the runs.
pmc-12700549:
Yue Li and co-authors find, in a 2025 mouse study, that a swollen spleen cell type actively feeds leukemia growth by rewiring the cancer cells' fat use. As the marrow fails in this blood cancer, the spleen takes over blood making. A marked class of young red blood cells ballooned in the spleens of sick mice.

Those cells poured out a signal protein that latched onto the cancer cells and switched on a growth pathway. The cancer cells then shifted their fat balance, hoarding whole fats over broken ones. Adding back the broken fats, or cutting a key gene, restored balance and blunted the tumor boost. The crosstalk names new drug targets.
pmc-12701049:
Chih-Chieh Hsu and co-authors uncover in 2025 how a mouth bacterium survives in the bloodstream during heart valve infection. Streptococcus gordonii can cause infective endocarditis. It carries a type VII secretion system that exports a protein called EsxA, whose role was unclear.

Deleting the export machinery stopped the protein's release; restoring it brought release back. In rats, bacteria lacking the protein survived poorly in blood and built smaller growths on heart valves. The secreted protein also made neutrophils cast out their DNA nets, and pure protein alone triggered the nets dose by dose. The authors conclude the nets, meant as traps, instead help the bacterium persist and grow.
pmc-12701649:
Neck surgery for a pinched nerve root demands cutting bone near delicate structures. Zhenfei Wang and co-authors compare two ways to make that cut through an endoscope. One group of patients received an ultrasonic bone scalpel, which shaves bone with vibration. The other received the traditional high-speed drill. Forty-one patients were followed for well over a year.

The ultrasonic tool opened the bone window significantly faster. Total surgery time and view-blurring episodes were similar. No complications occurred in the scalpel group, against one in the drill group, a gap too small to judge. Pain and function scores improved equally in both. The authors conclude the ultrasonic scalpel is a safe, efficient option for this precise operation.
pmc-12701849:
Hartleif and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on using a scope test to rule out a blocked bile duct disease in jaundiced newborns. The disease scars and closes the bile ducts, and early surgery gives the child's own liver its best chance. No blood or scan test can rule it out for sure, so open surgery has been the default proof. The team tested whether a camera passed into the bile duct could do the job.

Sixty infants at one German hospital were scheduled for the scope test at a median age of fifty days. The test worked in all but two. In twenty-three babies the ducts could not be shown, which pointed to the disease. In thirty-five the ducts looked normal and the disease was ruled out. The test caught every true case with no major side effects.
pmc-12704249:
Feyzi Sinan Tokali and co-authors synthesize new rhodanine compounds that block the two cholinesterase enzymes tied to Alzheimer decline. When cholinergic signaling fails, these enzymes chew up what little messenger remains, so blocking them is a standing drug strategy. The team builds Mannich-type variants with amine tails meant to grip the enzymes hard.

Their 2025 study finds two compounds that inhibit both enzymes at far lower doses than standard reference drugs. Cell tests show little harm to vessel cells at many times the working dose. Docking and energy calculations back the strong binding seen in the assays. The results mark the pair as leads worth refining toward a dual-action Alzheimer candidate.
pmc-12705649:
Gabriele Domaine and co-authors reported in 2025 the first sightings of a long-predicted family of exotic metals. In these crystals, paired electron bands cross along lines, and slicing them at the energy where electrons live at rest yields strange surfaces. Theory promised surfaces shaped like an eight-sided cage or a spindle-wrapped ring, but none had been seen.

Using photoemission mapping plus calculations, the team found the cage form in one layered crystal and the ring form in its cousin. Filling the bands tips one shape into the other. Strain or pressure should collapse them into an ordinary metal. The authors hail the pair as a tunable playground for the new physics. Graphene-like effects, magnified, may live there.
pmc-12705749:
Dexiang Li and five co-authors compare how an invasive water plant and a native water plant shift their root and leaf traits when nitrogen is added. Trait links across organs show how plants invade and adapt. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

A space for time design varied invasion degree and nitrogen dose. Added nitrogen grew both species, but the invader gained more mass and pushed the native out at mid and high invasion levels. Invasion, nitrogen, and their interplay moved most traits in both species, yet their root and leaf replies split sharply. Trait to mass links ran stronger in the invader.
pmc-12706049:
Butrint Aliu and seven co-authors report a 2025 study of a sugar-coated polymer built to clear harmful antibodies from the blood. The target is a nerve disease in which the immune system makes IgM antibodies against a sugar mark on nerve insulation. Those antibodies strip the insulation and cause numbness and weak balance. The polymer, called PPSGG, copies the sugar mark so the antibodies bind to it instead.

Tests show the long, strongly charged polymer is picked up by scavenger cells in the liver and spleen. It binds the harmful antibodies one-to-one or one-to-two, without forming clumps. The paired loads are then eaten and broken down by those cells, in mice and in human cells in the lab. No liver harm was seen, and the team calls it a path to the first targeted care for the disease.
pmc-12706649:
Edwige Noelle Roamba and co-authors assess two local food plants in Burkina Faso in a 2025 nutrition study, Crateva adansonii and Capparis corymbosa. Both are eaten locally, and the team measures their food value and plant chemicals.

Crateva leaves proved rich in protein, fat, minerals, and energy. Capparis fruits led on carbohydrates and vitamin A. Both plants hold nearly all standard amino acids, with most of the essential ones present. Leaf extracts carried high polyphenols and flavonoids and strong radical-scavenging power. Crateva leaves also topped anthocyanin content. The authors back wider use of both plants to enrich local diets.
pmc-12706749:
Carissa Lange and colleagues published a school environment study in 2025. They measured air and noise pollution in Accra schools. Children spend much of their day at school. Little data existed for African school settings before. Ninety schoolyards across Greater Accra were monitored. Measurements ran for a full week at each site. Fine particles, black carbon, and sound were recorded. Yard surfaces, greenery, and roads were documented. Over one thousand children answered noise surveys too.

Particle levels exceeded health guidelines by large margins. Pollution varied strongly between schools in the city. Nearby roads and yard features helped explain differences. Private and public schools faced different exposure patterns. Noise annoyed many children during school hours. Cleaner, quieter schoolyards could support learning and health.
pmc-12706849:
Zahid Ali, Jameel Ahmed Baig, Hassan Imran Afridi, and a team of co-authors build a sensor that can measure three toxic metals in a drink or water sample at once. Cadmium, copper, and manganese each harm health at high levels, and checking them one by one with lab gear is slow.

They coated an electrode with a coral-like mix of two magnetic nano-materials, giving a rough, porous surface with a large active area. The coated electrode picked up all three metals together at very low levels. The team then tried it on tap water, mango juice, and milk, and the readings matched expectations closely. They present the device as a cheap, portable option for routine safety checks.
pmc-12706949:
Zhicong Xu and co-authors built an AI that can fake an invasive eye scan from a painless photograph. Doctors use dye-based angiography to judge blood vessel damage in diabetic eyes, but the dye injection limits its use. Their system learns from 270 matched pairs of wide-field color photos and dye scans, covering every stage of diabetic retinopathy from mild to advanced.

Before training, a self-taught landmark finder lined the photo pairs up precisely. The generator then used wavelet tricks to keep fine detail and a transformer-based judge to keep structures believable. On standard image quality scores, the system beat three rival methods. The authors aim at clinics that could screen vessel damage from a plain photo alone. Human grading of the fake scans would be the next test of trust.
pmc-12707149:
Dongqiang Song, Xueyi Feng, Yingting Zhou, Yu Cai, and Tongchun Xue present a 2025 study on a combined treatment for liver cancer that cannot be cut out. The method threads a catheter into the tumor's blood supply and blocks it with drug-loaded beads plus an oily contrast agent called lipiodol.

The study enrolled 120 patients treated between December 2017 and August 2020. Median survival reached about thirty-one months, and three quarters of patients had their disease controlled for a time. About a fifth saw strong tumor shrinkage. Tumor size and later conversion therapy were the two factors that independently shaped survival. Side effects were mostly the expected post-procedure syndrome, liver tests wobbled briefly, and no severe grade four events occurred.
pmc-12707549:
Freja Eriksen, Sten Madsbad, Mogens Fenger, and Elin Carlsson track blood fats before and after weight-loss surgery in a 2025 study. The surgery, a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, often sends type 2 diabetes into remission, and shifts in fat chemistry may help explain why. The team measured eight free fatty acids plus two complex fat classes for up to two years after surgery.

Patients fell into three groups: no diabetes, diabetes that remitted, and diabetes that stayed. The no-diabetes group was by far the largest. At every check, free fatty acids explained more of the change in one complex fat class than in the other. Omega-3 levels tied more tightly to storage fats in the remission group. One omega-6 fat tracked both fat classes strongly in all groups.
pmc-12708649:
Simin Nie and three co-authors compute how doping changes superconductors in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Superconductors carry current with no loss below a transition temperature. Recent high-pressure hydrides revived the hunt for higher temperatures. The team used first-principles calculations on five pure elements: molybdenum, niobium, lead, aluminum, and zirconium. They added or removed electrons to mimic doping.

Both kinds of doping strengthened the link between electrons and lattice vibrations. That link sets the transition temperature, so it rose in each case. Softer vibrations and certain key phonons drove the gain. Each element showed a best doping level for the highest temperature. The study gives materials hunters a cheap screen before lab work.
pmc-12708749:
Pamela Alebna and four co-authors published a 2025 review of treating obesity in heart failure, where heavier patients oddly survive longer, the so-called obesity paradox. Once heart failure sets in, higher body mass seems protective in observational data. The review weighs fitness and lean mass as the deeper drivers behind that pattern, and examines new incretin-based weight-loss drugs.

These drugs cut weight and help some heart failure types, but their role in reduced-function hearts is unsettled. Big weight loss may also burn lean mass, a danger for frail patients. The authors urge judging treatment by fitness, walk capacity, and quality of life, not weight alone. They call for fresh studies matching modern drugs to the right patients.
pmc-12709749:
Yu Lu and co-authors test a composite yeast culture feed on immune gene expression in the spleens of weaned lambs. Their 2025 study asks whether the supplement improves immune status after weaning.

Eighteen healthy male lambs of similar age and weight were split into three groups. One got a basal diet, and the other two got the same diet with one of two daily doses of yeast culture. After a week of pre-feeding and forty days of the trial, spleens were collected. The team used tissue sectioning, ELISA, gene expression tests, and transcriptome sequencing. Spleen structure and immune gene patterns were compared across groups.
pmc-12710249:
Jennifer Gavin-Veyna and co-authors time a clotting step in heart bypass care in a 2025 lab study. During bypass, blood is thinned so the circuit stays clear, then a drug reverses the thinning at the end. Suction that pulls blood back must stop as reversal starts, or clots may foul the circuit.

Using pig blood kept on bypass for hours, the team tracked clot times as reversal drug was added. A small test dose cut clot times sharply in most samples. At a third of the full dose, nearly all samples fell to unsafe levels. The authors urge strict, shared timing rules for suction shut-off.
pmc-12714749:
Fatma Mohamady El-Demerdash and co-authors, in a 2025 study, tested whether omega-3 fatty acids can shield rats from harm done by two farm insect killers. Those chemicals are known to raise stress inside cells and hurt the testes. Omega-3 fats, by contrast, are known for calming swelling and fighting cell stress.

Rats were split into four groups, from plain controls to groups given fats, the chemical mix, or both. The fats were given by mouth an hour before the chemicals, each day for three weeks. In rats given chemicals alone, damage markers rose and natural defenses fell. Cell death signals in the testes also shifted. The team traced the fats' effect through gene paths that guide stress and cell death, to judge if the shield held.
pmc-12716549:
Frank Peinemann and co-authors present a 2025 review of two drug strategies for advanced melanoma with a BRAF gene change. One strategy pairs two immune drugs that free the body's own attack. The other pairs two targeted drugs that hit the tumor's growth path. Both are used as first care, and head-to-head proof is thin. The team pooled the trial proof on survival and harm.

The search found just two trials with 305 patients in all. Both trials used chance-based splits and full-group analysis. The reviewers graded how sure the pooled proof is and weighed bias in each trial. Sparse proof is itself a finding for such a costly choice. The review gives doctors a clear view of what is known and what is not.
pmc-12717049:
Patchana Jaidee and co-authors assessed what would happen if Thailand handed emergency medical services to local governments, in a study published in 2025. The policy aims to speed response and involve communities, shifting control away from the health ministry. Using a six-step health impact assessment, the team gathered views from 562 providers, patients, and policymakers in Chonburi Province. Interviews, focus groups, and surveys fed the analysis.

Expected gains included faster response, better teamwork, and more motivated staff. Expected harms included staff shortages, communication gaps, and tight budgets. The effects spanned dispatch, response, referral, and management work, and touched physical, mental, and social well-being. The authors recommend planned hiring, upgraded communication systems, stable funding, and shared monitoring. They present the assessment method as a way to turn local evidence into policy.
pmc-12717349:
Shaohui Jiang and seven co-authors investigate a long non-coding RNA that seems to restrain breast cancer and shape its response to immune therapy, in this 2025 study. The molecule, RERE-AS1, does not code for a protein; it regulates. Its role in breast cancer was essentially unknown.

Mining patient data, the team found the RNA sharply reduced in breast tumors, with higher levels tracking better outcomes. In two breast cancer cell lines, restoring it slowed growth, movement, and invasion, pushed cells toward death, and stalled their division cycle. Co-cultures showed it also changed how immune cells attacked the tumor. A mouse experiment then tested tumor growth and response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy with the RNA present. Molecules like this are doubly attractive: a marker that forecasts a patient's course, and possibly a lever that makes immunotherapy work where it currently fails.
pmc-12717449:
Butler and six colleagues map where a soft tick that can carry African swine fever lives in the United States in twenty twenty-five. The fever is a deadly pig disease not yet in the country. Wild hogs plus this tick could let it take root if it arrives. The team gathered tick records from papers and field work, mostly in Texas.

Six weather and land traits best predicted where the tick can live. The map runs from southern California to Texas, with a lone zone in Florida. Most of Texas looks highly fit for the tick. Host species were richest in Florida and central Texas, which the team flags for close watch. Ticks in warthog burrows raise the stakes.
pmc-12717849:
A genus of frogs that skip the tadpole stage holds more species than any other vertebrate genus, and Ecuador is a hotspot for finding new ones. Keyko Loza-Carvajal and co-authors describe a new species in this 2025 paper, from reserves in the eastern Andes of Ecuador. They also propose a new subgenus to hold two related species groups.

Gene, body, and map evidence place the new frog inside one of those groups, with clear genetic distance from its kin. The frog has a black to dark gray back and a marbled belly, and it lives only in one mountain range and the Llanganates region. The authors stress the value of comparing specimens from the exact home sites when drawing species lines.
pmc-12718149:
Brianna Bowden and co-authors compare bone strength in 2025 between children with two conditions that limit walking. Both cerebral palsy and spinal muscular atrophy raise the risk of thin bones and breaks, but through unlike paths. The team asked whether the bone loss itself differs between the groups.

Clinic records held 274 children with cerebral palsy and sixteen with the muscle condition, all aged five or more and unable to walk. Scans read bone density at the spine and at a thigh site. Spine scores, once height was counted, sat in the normal range for both. The thigh site ran low in both, and clearly lower in the muscle group, they report. Scan site choice matters: a spine-only check would miss the weakest bones.
pmc-12720449:
Seasoned nurses who guide new staff can shape whether those staff stay, and Waleed Alshehri and Abdulaziz Alodhailah asked nurses in Riyadh how such guidance feels, in work from twenty twenty-five. Talks with seventeen nurses from mixed backgrounds fed the study. The Saudi capital's wards blend many cultures, which colors how guidance plays out.

Four themes stood out: growth on the job, emotional backing, finding one's feet in a new culture, and feeling part of the team. The authors name a key idea, backed openness, for how guidance lets nurses be frank about strain while growing surer at work. Their advice aims to help hospitals build guidance that fits a mixed-culture staff and keeps nurses in post.
pmc-12721049:
Blood cultures take days and miss hard-to-grow germs, so Qichuan Fu and co-authors look for fingerprints in the fragments of DNA that pathogens shed into blood. Their 2025 study sequenced plasma from about one hundred patients with bacterial, viral, or parasitic bloodstream infections. Pathogen fragments ran shorter than human ones, and each kingdom had its own length signature.

Bacterial pieces averaged shortest, viral pieces a bit longer, and one virus that hides in a protein shell mimicked human lengths. Parasite pieces spread too widely to read by length. The authors see fragment patterns as a fast companion to culture, pending bigger validation.
pmc-12722049:
How a country treats its animals begins with what its people believe animals feel. Azadeh Jalali-Motahari and co-authors run the first broad survey of those beliefs in Iran in a 2025 study of three hundred twenty-five respondents.

The validated questionnaire covered farmed, companion, and wild animals. Most respondents rated animal welfare important and wanted practices improved. Support for protective laws was broad, despite uneven familiarity with different species. Over nine in ten agreed chickens feel pain, and four in five credited them with emotions, though scores varied by animal. Cultural, religious, and legal threads run through the answers. The authors offer the results as groundwork for Iranian welfare policy.
pmc-12722249:
Osteoarthritis wears down joints and has no cure, so new ideas such as tiny cell-made parcels called extracellular vesicles draw growing interest. Hongyu Xie and co-authors, in 2025, mapped the state of that research field. They combined a count-based survey of past papers with a topic model that sorts papers by theme.

Their survey traces how work on these parcels in joint disease has grown, which teams and countries work together, and which themes run hot. The topic model adds a view of how themes shift over time and where new ones form. The authors aim to give other teams a clear base for planning studies and for moving the parcels toward real care for worn joints.
pmc-12722749:
Mingwei Zhang and co-authors use soil depth on the Moon to count small impacts from the past. Their 2025 study focuses on the landing zone of a recent Chinese mission, the youngest dated plain of its kind. Small craters fade too fast to count directly, but the loose soil layer keeps a record of hits over time.

Fresh crater shapes point to a median soil depth of about 3.6 meters there. Models show that depth needs more small craters than past counts assumed, by a factor of about one and a half. The extra hits may trace to a breakup of space rocks about six hundred million years ago. Or steady drift of small rocks toward the Moon may have kept the rate high.
pmc-12723849:
Saeid Mirzaei and co-authors compared four drug treatment settings in Iran in a 2025 study. Drug use disorder is a lasting public health load in Iran, and several care types run side by side there. They range from daily methadone care and drop-in centers to live-in groups and forced care under a court rule.

The team followed clients in 15 routine centers in Kerman Province from May 2023 to May 2024. Of 493 who enrolled, 470 finished the follow-up span. Each setting was judged on its own change over the year. The side-by-side view may help Iran steer funds to the care forms that hold gains.
pmc-12725749:
An AI app that reads feeling from the voice was put to the test among nurses in a 2025 study at a medical center in northern Taiwan. The app scored the voices of 349 nurses who work in clinics there. Its calls were checked against standard surveys for anger, stress, joy, and low mood. A small group of 30 nurses took the test twice, so the team could see if scores held steady from one run to the next. Age, sex, work years, exercise habits, and past body signs were logged and stripped out of the links.

App scores tracked the survey scores at a fair level for all four feelings. Habits and health also split the scores: less exercise linked to more anger, and stomach ulcers linked to shifts as well. The team weighs where such an app could help staff well-being checks.
pmc-12727049:
Laura Giglio and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five study of brain predictors for whether aphasia therapy gains spread to everyday discourse. Naming practice helps word-finding, but conversation is the real prize. Brain integrity before treatment might forecast that transfer.

Eighty-eight people with chronic post-stroke aphasia received semantic or sound-based therapy. Lesion and white-matter maps were related to discourse measures before and after treatment, and months later. Baseline talking productivity tied to dorsal-stream language pathways. The design separates predictors of starting ability from predictors of generalization, guiding realistic therapy planning.
pmc-12727549:
Xianshui Mei and nine co-authors report a rare tumor case in a 2025 paper. A woman who had lost a breast to cancer came in with swelling and pain around her anus, worse at night. A smooth, oval lump could be felt in the rectum near the tailbone. Scans showed a mass in and around the lower spine bones.

Tests on the tissue showed a chordoma, a slow tumor that grows from leftovers of the early spine. Its cell marks fit that call, and a growth index sat near five percent. Such tumors at the tailbone rarely cause anal swelling on their own, the authors note. They urge doctors to keep this cause in mind when the usual ones do not fit.
pmc-12728349:
Joschka Spornberger, Petr Soukup, Andrea Meyer-Lindenberg, and Ingrid Allgoewer read the tear film of French bulldogs in a 2025 study. The breed's flat face strains its eyes, and a poor tear film can dry the eye's face to harm.

Sound dogs of the breed faced sound dogs of long- and mid-face kin in a full eye check. The flat-face pack made more tears by the strip test, and its tear pool stood near twice as tall. Yet its film's fat coat graded worse and its film broke in half the span. Salt in the tears ran the same both ways. The authors read the marks as a dry-eye flaw of kind, not of count: the film is there, but it thins and parts too fast.
pmc-12729149:
After heart bypass surgery, waking patients quickly and removing the breathing tube early helps recovery, but the muscle relaxants used in surgery must first wear off or be reversed. Matthew Ellison and six co-authors ran a trial in 2025 comparing two reversal drugs, neostigmine and sugammadex, in bypass patients. The aim was a safe tube removal in the operating room itself.

Patients on sugammadex had the tube out in about six minutes on average, against more than ten minutes for the other drug. Fewer of them failed a swallowing screen, and none needed the tube put back, while two patients in the other group did. Time in intensive care was a bit shorter too. The authors favor sugammadex for this use.
pmc-12729549:
The authors test a grape seed extract rich in plant compounds, sold under a trade name, for a bundle of health effects. They checked its action against germs, its shielding of gut cells under chemical stress, and its effects in mice fed the extract at two doses. Gut germs and gut-brain signals were tracked as well.

The extract slowed several harmful germs and shielded gut cells from damage and swelling signals. In mice, it raised antioxidant gene activity in gut and liver and shifted gut germ mixes in helpful ways. Signals that link gut and brain, such as GLP-1, also moved in a good direction.
pmc-12729749:
Mai Hanh Nguyen and co-authors built deep learning models in 2025 that read stomach cancer slides to sort patients by risk and likely response to immune therapy. Stomach cancer kills many people worldwide, and fewer than four in ten patients live five years. Immune checkpoint drugs help only a small share, so a slide-based guide has real value.

The team used whole-slide images from 292 patients in a large cancer atlas cohort. A network first found tumor regions, checked on a second data set, and malignant tiles were kept for the risk models. The models aim to predict a novel marker tied both to outlook and to drug sensitivity. Readers get a translational step: routine pathology images turned into a forecast that could steer who gets immune therapy.
pmc-12730149:
Zhao-Lan Hu and co-authors trial in 2025 a continuous flipped classroom for anesthesia teaching in an eight-year medical program. Flipped classes move study home and practice into class time. Whether a full-course flip shapes learning and career choice was unclear for this field.

Two hundred students split evenly between flipped and standard teaching. The flipped group scored higher on final exams and told of better satisfaction and active learning. They were also far more likely to pick anesthesia as their field. Score gains explained near half of that career shift in the path study. Results back the flip for skill and interest alike.
pmc-12730449:
Conan Juan and co-authors review the molecular landscape of triple-negative breast cancer in this 2025 paper. This subtype has the worst outlook of any breast cancer, partly because it lacks the targets that standard precision drugs aim at and often resists both chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Sorting it into finer subtypes has already taught researchers much about its biology.

The review argues that multiomic analysis, reading several layers of molecular data at once, can cut deeper into the tumor's variety. Those layers include the genome, the gene-activity record, proteins, and small metabolic molecules. By combining them, researchers hope to find new markers that predict the disease's course and new targets for drugs. The authors frame multiomics as the most promising route to therapies that finally move outcomes for this hard subtype.
pmc-12730949:
Madeleine Osborne and John Maher weigh off-the-shelf CAR cell care for autoimmune disease in a 2025 review. CAR care retunes immune cells to hit a set mark. Own-cell forms work but cost vast sums per patient. Shelf forms from donors could slash that cost. Risks ride with them: donor cells may hit the host, or the host may kill them. Gene edits and calm host cell kinds may dodge both.

The team swept three banks for clinic and lab reads, 107 in all. Cancer reads fill gaps where autoimmune data run thin. Marks look bright so far, they find. Safe build at scale is the bar to clear, the authors say.
pmc-12731449:
Swati Mamidanna and fifteen colleagues review the rise, fall, and partial revival of preventive brain radiation in small cell lung cancer. This aggressive cancer seeds the brain often. Irradiating the cranium after successful initial treatment once clearly extended survival, above all in limited-stage disease.

Newer trials with routine MRI surveillance found no survival benefit in extensive-stage disease. That makes watchful scanning, with salvage treatment if needed, a real alternative. Memory damage remains the chief cost, though hippocampus-sparing methods and protective drugs soften it. The arrival of immunotherapy scrambles the calculus further. The review maps where preventive irradiation still earns its place and where scans have taken its place.
pmc-12731549:
Hooman Soleymani Majd and a large surgical team describe a technique for a dangerous pregnancy condition in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In severe placenta accreta, the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall. Delivery can then cause catastrophic bleeding. Many centers use radiology balloons to cut blood flow, but that service is costly and not always at hand. The team's method instead ties off pelvic arteries step by step under direct sight.

The technique forms part of their approach to caesarean hysterectomy for these cases. The paper sets out the surgical steps in detail. It also compares short- and long-term outcomes against the radiology route. Direct ligation, they argue, is safe and workable where radiology support is scarce. Obstetric surgeons facing this emergency are the readers.
pmc-12731949:
Burçe Dörtkardeşler and co-authors check nutrient gaps in breastfed babies in this 2025 paper. Breast milk alone is the ideal food for the first six months, yet hidden shortages can slip in. The team tested 132 healthy six-month-olds at a Turkish clinic. Blood panels covered iron, several vitamins, zinc, and copper.

About four in ten babies were low on iron or anemic. Vitamin D deficiency hit about one in seven, and nearly three in ten lacked vitamin B12. Steady supplement use clearly lowered the rates. The mother's schooling, dress style, and smoking tied to the baby's vitamin D. The authors urge firmer supplement routines and checks for quiet deficiencies.
pmc-12732149:
Mei Chen and colleagues rethink twenty-five years of Hsp90 cancer drug trials, in a review from 2025. Blockers of this chaperone protein reached about ninety single drug trials since the late nineties. Nearly all failed, with toxicity blamed, yet one oral drug won approval in Japan.

Trial filings missed an extra effect known since 2004, the authors argue here. The same blockers also hit the outside cell form of Hsp90, which drives invasion. Trial outcomes thus mixed two drug actions that were never separated in patients. Which action caused the harm, and which the benefit, remains an open question. Answering it could reshape the next wave of Hsp90 drug design.
pmc-12732649: Fernandez-Ferreiro and Giralddez-Fernandez introduce a special issue on dry eye at the molecular scale. Dry eye disease is a common disorder of the eye surface with many causes. It shows as tear film instability, eye discomfort, swelling, and blurred vision that comes and goes. The issue gathers work on the molecular roots of the illness and on new ways to understand and treat it.
pmc-12732749:
Margherita Grasso and co-authors review glial cells and one signaling path in Parkinson disease in a 2025 paper. The disease slowly kills dopamine neurons in a deep brain area. Both genes and environment shape who is at risk. Support cells called glia react strongly, but whether they help or harm is still debated.

The review centers on astrocytes and microglia, plus the Wnt and beta-catenin signal path. A toxin model that harms dopamine neurons helped clarify many disease steps. The authors weigh how glial factors and growth signals drive repair after such harm. Their aim is a clearer map of protection and repair routes worth targeting.
pmc-12732949:
Nazlı Karimi Ahmadi and four co-authors measure immune signals in blood and spit from people with acne. Acne is a long-term skin condition with swelling, and signals such as IL-17, IL-19, and CRP are thought to play a role. Their 2025 study covered ninety-nine people aged fifteen to thirty, split into clear-skin, moderate acne, and severe acne groups. Lab tests measured the three signals in both blood and saliva, and the team checked links with acne severity.

Blood IL-17 ran higher in the clear-skin group than in either acne group, against what many expect. Spit levels did not split by group, though the two IL signals tracked each other closely in both fluids. CRP showed no group gap. The authors suggest IL-17 may calm as well as stir skin swelling.
pmc-12733049:
Magdalena Smereczańska, Natalia Domian, and their co-authors compared two tiny gene regulators in prostate cancer and in benign prostate growth. Their 2025 pilot study starts from a testing problem: the standard PSA blood test rises in both conditions, so it cannot separate them well. The regulators studied, two microRNAs, are known to affect a growth pathway called Wnt beta catenin.

Tissue came from 30 cancer patients and 30 patients with benign growth. The team measured the two regulators and four pathway parts, including beta catenin and cyclin D1, using staining and gene counting methods. Several pathway parts showed lower activity and gene expression in cancer tissue than in benign tissue. No earlier study had mapped these links in prostate tissue in this combined way.
pmc-12733449:
Maria Battistelli, Paola Riolo, and co-authors survey two moth pests in maize fields in central and east Italy, in a 2025 study. Both moths bore into maize and cut yield in both bulk and grade. The team used scent traps and cut open close to six hundred plants at harvest.

Traps with three scent blends caught males at like rates, so all blends are needed for checks. One moth was far more common, but both shared plants with no shift in where grubs sat. Grubs of both kinds were most dense low in the stalk. Both kinds reached ears too, so farm plans must treat both pests.
pmc-12733549:
Some patients with atrial fibrillation keep a fast, irregular heartbeat despite drugs. One last resort treatment burns the heart's electrical relay node. A pacing defibrillator device is then implanted to keep both sides of the heart in step. Bagdat Akhyt and co-authors followed one hundred one such patients for five years at one center. Thirteen cardiovascular deaths occurred in that time. The team used machine learning methods to find which measures best predicted death.

Five measures carried the signal. They were how strongly the main pumping chamber squeezes, walking distance in six minutes, pressure in the lung artery, a relaxation measure, and the leakage of one heart valve. A model built on them classified outcomes with high accuracy. The authors are careful to call the analysis exploratory. They present the factors as candidates for personal risk checks and for designing future studies, not as settled rules.
pmc-12733849:
Pablo Diaz-Calvillo and co-authors ask in 2025 how a skin cancer call reshapes feelings and daily life over time. Two cancer types are set side by side: melanoma and a squamous cell form. Mind and social costs of skin cancer got far less study than its care.

Thirty six patients, half of each type, gave deep talks that were taped and read for themes. Feelings, kin ties, and life shifts formed the three themes. Worry, relief, and fear of return ran through both groups. Kin gave both strong back up and fresh cause for concern, and work and self image shifted.
pmc-12733949:
Simina Moroz and co-authors study risk signs in valve replacement patients in 2025. Aortic stenosis narrows the main valve of the heart and strains it over time. A catheter based valve swap now offers a gentler fix for older or high risk patients. The team asked whether a ratio from heart scans helps flag who faces poor outcomes.

The ratio pairs right heart motion with pressure in the lung artery. Records for about one hundred treated patients were reviewed in depth. The authors link the ratio to later outcomes after the valve swap. A simple ratio could help doctors pick patients and tailor care after the procedure.
pmc-12734149:
Çakan Demirel and a large team check in twenty twenty-five whether blood scores for inflammation and nutrition predict survival in advanced voice-box cancer. Such scores help forecast outcomes in many cancers, but their value in this cancer was untested. The team reviewed close to one hundred and fifty patients treated over a decade and computed six combined scores from routine blood tests.

Median survival was about four and a half years. High scores on most measures tied to shorter overall and progression-free survival. One combined score stood out as an independent predictor alongside stage and response to chemotherapy, while surgery helped survival. The authors urge routine use of these cheap scores to sort patients by risk.
pmc-12734249:
Johanna Rehn and co-authors ask whether cannabis-like exposure in early teens leaves the adult brain extra sensitive, in a 2025 paper. Rats were dosed with a drug that switches on the main cannabis receptor during early or late adolescence, then tested as adults while researchers drove a key memory rhythm in the hippocampus.

The drug cut the rhythm's power in adults, and the cut ran deeper in rats exposed as adolescents, above all those exposed early. The team reads this as a lasting rise in sensitivity to the receptor's activation, planted during a window when the hippocampus's rhythm circuits are still being built. The findings echo concern about teenage cannabis use and later mental illness.
pmc-12734449:
Mariana Feijó and co-authors show that fat tissue around the prostate, once pushed toward an obese state by a pollutant, shields prostate cells from chemotherapy. Published in 2025, the study works with human tissue taken from patients. The fat pad touching the prostate talks to the tumor, and obesity already worsens that talk; hormone disrupting obesogen chemicals may corrupt it further.

Exposing the human fat to a model obesogen, tributyltin, swelled its cells into an obese look. Medium conditioned by that tissue then kept prostate cells alive better and blunted two standard drugs, docetaxel and cabazitaxel. The authors hunt the molecular messengers of this crosstalk, aiming at better disease management where metabolism and cancer meet.
pmc-12734949:
Ertugrul Gazi Alkurt and co-authors study stapler size and leakage after bowel surgery in a 2025 analysis. Ninety-nine patients had surgery for left-sided colorectal cancer at one center. Leakage at the join is a major complication of such surgery.

Patients were split by stapler diameter, small versus larger. Records ran from January 2020 to May 2024. Blood protein levels before surgery were also checked against leakage. The group averaged about sixty-six years of age. Most patients were male. Readers, mainly surgeons, learn whether a simple tool choice tracks a feared complication.
pmc-12735249:
Yihao Yang and co-authors pack a wide-band quantum light receiver into a hybrid chip. Their twenty twenty-five paper builds a balanced homodyne receiver, the meter at the heart of continuous-variable quantum links. Bulky bench optics and noisy electronics have capped its speed and clarity.

An adjustable optical path restores balance between the two arms. A quiet amplifier design cuts the hiss that usually swamps faint quantum signals. The unit reaches two and a half gigahertz of bandwidth with a clear margin over shot noise. Compact, fast receivers are what quantum communication needs to leave the lab bench and enter network racks.
pmc-12735849:
Andrea Carboni, Matteo Calvaresi, and Agata Kot-Wasik argue for a better way to test how anticancer drugs affect water life, in a 2025 paper. These potent drugs wash out of patients and treatment plants into rivers and lakes, where they are now found widely. Drugs built to stop cell growth can harm non target water species even at trace levels. Standard lab tests, though, often use one species and one outcome under fixed conditions.

Such tests miss how species interact, how food webs shift, and what long exposure does. The authors advocate mesocosms: middle scale, semi natural setups that mimic real exposure over long spans. These systems can track both what happens to the drug and what it does to living communities at once. They present mesocosms as the bridge between small lab tests and full ecosystem knowledge, fit to guide monitoring and rules.
pmc-12736249:
Xiaoting Sun and co-authors published this 2025 study on healing salty, alkaline soils with natural humus. Humus is rich, dark organic matter from decayed life. It is widely spread to improve poor soils, but its effect on the many jobs a healthy soil does was murky. The team varied humus doses and watched soil chemistry, fungi, and overall function.

Humus raised soil organic matter by up to about 46 percent and usable nitrogen by up to about 82 percent. Salt stress, read by conductivity, fell as well. Fungal diversity grew, and hardy fungi that use resources with care became more common. At the top dose, thirty tons per hectare, soil function peaked. The findings credit fungi as key drivers of the gain.
pmc-12736549:
Courtney Jensen and co-authors ask whether the stress of formal competition slows recovery in women soccer players. Thirty Division I athletes wore team tracking devices for thirty-five straight days. The devices logged exercise time, distance, sprints, heart rate, training load, and how long recovery took.

In their 2025 study, data came from practices and from formal matches. Recovery lasted far longer after matches than after practice sessions. A regression model found that competition added many hours of recovery on its own, apart from the physical work done. The authors say match stress itself carries a cost, a point coaches may use when they plan rest for women athletes.
pmc-12736849:
Pradeep Raja and co-authors test how design and fill density shape printed plastic parts in a 2025 study. Three-dimensional printing builds light parts whose inner fill can be tuned at will. The study used the common plastic PLA at a low, ten percent infill.

Four profile designs, drawn from beam and column practice, faced four load levels. Computer models in ANSYS tracked bending, stress, and strain under two support styles. Real three-point bending tests then checked the models against printed parts. One design stood tallest in both the virtual and real trials. Sparse fill can still serve, if the profile shape carries the load well.
pmc-12736949:
Arwa Badhib, Suhair Alshehri, Asma Cherif, and Ilsun You survey device login safety in federated learning in a 2025 paper. Internet of Things devices share huge data, but central training raises privacy fears. Federated learning lets each device train at home and share only model updates. That still leaves room for poisoning and fake device attacks.

Strong login checks are thus vital, the authors argue. The survey sorts past login schemes by their base tech, such as blockchain, cryptography, and artificial intelligence. It also weighs how well each works in practice. Open problems and next steps for safe, large scale systems are laid out.
pmc-12738549:
Devin Rocks and co-authors show that a single gene switch, Egr1, reshapes the female and male mouse brain in different ways. Brain sex differences trace largely to gonadal hormones, and estrogen swings remodel the adult female brain across her cycle. Yet the molecular drivers in females remain understudied. Their 2025 paper raises Egr1 levels in the ventral hippocampus, where the factor normally rises and falls with the cycle.

Raising it shifted chromatin openness, gene expression, and the physical shape of neurons — differently by sex. Behavior tied to that brain region changed in females specifically. Turning the gene down partly mimicked the low-estrogen brain state. Neuroscientists get a named lever behind hormone-driven plasticity, and a case for studying female brains on their own terms.
pmc-12738749:
Andrea Vitores-Calero, Vanessa Paredes-Gallardo, and eight co-authors checked if a vibrating mouth device heats the mouth, in work from twenty twenty-five. The device, AcceleDent, is sold to speed tooth movement with clear aligners. Backers say it stirs cells and bone. Heat was the key test here: if the device warms tissue, that might help explain its effects, or raise safety flags.

Twenty-two adults in aligner care wore the device on and off on two days. A heat camera read gum and tooth surfaces after each use. No gap in heat showed up between the on and off days, at rest or after use. The team calls the device safe on heat grounds.
pmc-12740749:
Rolf Weimer and co-authors report five year results on immune effects after kidney transplantation across blood groups in a 2025 prospective pilot study. Such transplants carry higher risk of severe infection and antibody mediated rejection. A drug called rituximab is used at induction, and its long term immune effects needed tracking.

Eighty five recipients were followed, including living donor groups with compatible and incompatible blood groups and a deceased donor group. Incompatible recipients had double the severe infections in two years. Their B cell subsets stayed deeply reduced, B cell responses were impaired, and T cell counts were lower at six months.
pmc-12740949:
Helmy Eldib and co-authors compare two access sheaths for clearing kidney stones from both sides at once in a trial from 2025. Flexible scopes remove stones through the urinary tract. A suction sheath that bends and navigates promises cleaner, faster work. Bilateral same-session surgery doubles the stakes for safety.

One hundred patients with stones under twenty millimeters on both sides were randomized. Half received the suction sheath, half the conventional kind. Ages ran from twenty-three to sixty-five. Stone-free rates differed significantly between the groups. Operative details and complications filled out the comparison. One-session treatment spares patients a second anesthesia, if the tools prove equal or better.
pmc-12741849:
Luís Felipe Tubagi Polito and five co-authors compare the hearts of futsal players by age group in a 2025 study. Futsal's bursts of sprinting remodel the heart, but how that remodeling builds from youth to pro level was unclear. Players from under-18, under-20, and adult elite squads all took heart scans, ECGs, and fitness tests.

The under-20 group posted the best oxygen capacity, edging out adults. Adults showed thicker walls in parts of the left ventricle and a larger left atrium than the youngest group. Oddly, the youngest players had the widest right ventricle measurement of the three groups. Pumping fraction and overall heart mass stayed similar across ages. The pattern suggests futsal's cardiac signature forms early, with wall and chamber changes still accruing into adulthood. Coaches and team doctors can use such baselines to spot abnormal hearts.
pmc-12742149:
Jyothi Shetty and co-authors systematically review what it costs families to raise a child with Down syndrome. Care spans health visits, therapies, schooling support, and parents' lost work time, yet the full burden is rarely summed. The review gathers studies of children under eighteen published between 2000 and 2024.

Searching seven databases plus gray sources, two reviewers screened and appraised the evidence independently. They collect both direct costs families pay and indirect costs such as forgone earnings, and parents' own accounts of financial strain. A clear cost map can guide benefits, insurance design, and family support services in countries where most care falls on households.
pmc-12743849:
Visnes and co-authors use a national registry to count two knee injuries found during ACL repair surgery in Norway. Meniscus repair during ACL surgery has grown more common. Two injury types draw special concern: root tears of the outer meniscus and ramp lesions. Past counts came from small, selected patient groups. Registry data from 2018 to 2023 covered isolated ACL repairs across the country.

The team compared traits of patients with and without these injuries. They also recorded how surgeons chose to treat each injury. Weight, age, sex, and activity data fed the comparison. The study gives a population-wide view of how often these injuries appear. It also shows current practice for handling them.
pmc-12744949:
Usama Abdelgwad leads a team that compares two pain blocks for hernia repair. Their study from twenty twenty-five is set at Dubai Hospital. Keyhole hernia repair often brings early pain from the belly wall.

One group got a sheath block before the cut was made. The other got local numbing drug in the wound after. Drug needs in and after surgery were compared by group. The block aims at nerve ends in the belly sheath. Sound guidance is used to place the block dose. Past compare proof for adults was thin.
pmc-12745449:
Ye and co-authors take the global pulse of a worm disease by counting infections in its mosquito carriers. Lymphatic filariasis, spread by mosquitoes, remains a major neglected tropical disease despite elimination campaigns. Pooling eighteen studies covering over 160,000 mosquitoes in ten countries, the meta-analysis finds a pooled infection prevalence of 0.7 percent.

Rates run highest in Asia, in Mansonia mosquitoes, and where the most sensitive test, RT-PCR, is used. Places without drug administration programs and warm regions between twenty-three and twenty-seven degrees show more infection, as do studies after 2016. Results vary enormously between studies, and publication bias is present. The authors urge stronger mosquito-based monitoring, especially with molecular tests, to reach the 2030 elimination goal.
pmc-12746349:
Anas Elyan and five co-authors give a full account of complications after robot-assisted bladder removal with internal urine diversion. The surgery is a major cancer operation, and their center used the study window to shift from open surgery to the robot method. Their 2025 paper reviews one hundred eleven patients treated in a row from 2017 to 2023. Every problem in the first thirty and ninety days was graded by a standard scale and sorted by cause.

Fine-grained counts show which setbacks are common, which are severe, and how each was handled. Such profiles help teams counsel patients with honest odds. They also show where a center in transition should watch most closely. The authors offer the data as a benchmark for other programs making the same switch.
pmc-12746749:
Xiao-Meng Huang and co-authors weigh a care model that joins treatment with prevention for older adults in a 2025 paper. The model serves people with long-term illness, mainly high blood pressure and diabetes. The team looks at costs and fairness, not just health gains. Their work feeds into a national plan for a healthier China.

The study covers 10,236 adults over sixty from nine areas in three provinces. Cost data were modeled in two stages, and staff also ran case studies and interviews. The team built measures for savings, efficiency, and fairness between city and country areas. Gaps for poorer regions and weaker groups are named plainly. The results can help leaders spread the model without deepening unfairness.
pmc-12747049:
Jessica Ortega-Balderas and co-authors report a rare brain tumor case in this 2025 case report. Primary yolk sac tumors inside the skull are uncommon, and their usual tissue patterns are documented. Their patient was a twenty-year-old man with a pure yolk sac tumor growing within the brain tissue.

What made the case unique was its sarcomatoid morphology, a tissue pattern not previously reported for a pure primary intracranial yolk sac tumor, the authors state. The case argues for keeping yolk sac tumors in mind when diagnosing midline masses in the brain, even when the histology looks unusual.
pmc-12747349:
Xiaowen Zhang and Tiegang Lv present a learning method for pharmacy robots in this 2025 paper. A medicine-picking robot must grasp each drug pack firmly and precisely. Its success depends on visual guidance that finds the right grasp point. In messy, unstructured settings that search can be slow and error prone.

Their method works in two steps, guided by detection constraints. First, it marks candidate grasp areas from the outline of each medicine pack. Then a deep reinforcement learning system, DDPG, learns the best grasp point from those marked images. It explores with added noise and feeds results back in real time. Tests showed a clear gain in grasp detection accuracy over prior methods.
pmc-12747549:
Anqi Lin and co-authors reviewed how DNA damage repair shapes cancer chemotherapy in 2025. Repair pathways decide how well tumor cells survive chemo drugs. Five core pathways handle most repair work in the cell.

The review maps how each pathway drives drug resistance and which breaks in repair make tumors drug-sensitive. Faults in the BRCA genes are a key example. Drugs that block one repair enzyme kill such faulty cells by synthetic lethality, passing over healthy cells. Blockers of damage sensors add force when paired with chemo. The authors also link repair faults to stronger responses to immune therapy. A combined data marker system for repair faults is proposed for sorting patients.
pmc-12748249:
Javier Goena and eleven co-authors mine fifteen years of social media posts about psychotherapy in two languages, in a two thousand twenty-five digital psychiatry paper. Public talk about therapy reveals cultural framings that clinics rarely see.

About one hundred three thousand posts on X from two thousand eight to two thousand twenty-two, three quarters English, covered four therapies. Cognitive behavioral therapy dominated mentions. English posts leaned toward professional promotion with fear the prevailing emotion. Spanish posts shared personal experience instead: joy led for acceptance therapy and narrative therapy, while anger, tied to misunderstanding, marked psychodynamic therapy posts. Volume surged after two thousand twenty. The authors urge culturally adapted mental health communication.
pmc-12748449:
Kaixuan Hui and co-authors trace how a long non-coding RNA helps bile duct cancer grow and spread. Cholangiocarcinoma is usually found late and carries a grim outlook, so fresh treatment targets are badly needed. The team focused on LINC00519, an RNA that does not build protein but steers other molecules.

Tumor samples from about two hundred patients gauged the RNA's link to outcomes. In two cancer cell lines, experiments showed LINC00519 works through a small RNA, miR-876-3p, and the gene GATA1 in one axis. Loosening that axis slowed the cancer cells' growth, movement, and invasion. The chain is a candidate drug target in a cancer short of options.
pmc-12748949:
Keying Su and six co-authors build a heat-responsive catalyst for formic acid fuel cells in a study from 2025. Single-atom catalysts are highly active but hard to switch off. Their design places single rhodium atoms on palladium sheets coated with a polymer that opens or closes with temperature, like a gate for the reaction.

Below the gate's switching point, near thirty-five degrees, the catalyst oxidized formic acid with high activity and strong resistance to poisoning. Above it, activity fell sharply. In a working fuel cell, power stayed high below the switch point and dropped above it, giving a built-in heat guard for the cell.
pmc-12749049:
Salma Hatem and three co-authors study printed dental crowns in this two thousand twenty-five lab study. Dentists now print crowns from hybrid ceramic material, but the best curing steps are not yet clear. The team asked how curing time and aging affect how well such crowns resist breaking. They designed one standard lower premolar crown shape on a computer. Then they printed eighty copies of it.

The crowns were split by curing time, ten or twenty minutes under UV light. Groups also went through heat-and-cold cycles that mimic aging in the mouth. The team then broke the crowns and studied the crack patterns. Their findings help labs pick curing and aging steps that yield stronger crowns. The work is lab work only, not a trial in patients.
pmc-12749849:
Jinmin Chen, Wenyuan Zhang, and Yongmei Yang ask whether low body heat raises death risk in sepsis, in work from 2025. Sepsis is a severe response to infection that fills intensive care units. Body temperature often swings during the illness.

The team searched a large hospital database and found near twenty thousand sepsis patients. About five percent had low body heat in their first day in intensive care. Those patients died at higher rates over six months and one year. The link held after matching patients with like traits and after weighting the data in a second check. The authors urge staff to treat low heat as a warning sign.
pmc-12750149:
Rebecca Merchant and a large team of colleagues report the full gene sequences of three viruses that infect soil bacteria, found in Socorro, New Mexico. Such viruses, called phages, were grown on two host germs taken from soil samples. Two phages came from one host species, and the third from another.

Gene content placed the first two in a known phage cluster, and the third in a different one. All three share the long-tailed shape typical of their kind. Short genome reports like this one build the catalog that lets scientists sort phage diversity and trace how these viruses relate.
pmc-12750449:
Greg Courville and co-authors describe an open-source robot system that splits and reseeds cell cultures in 96-well plates. Plate cell culture is slow hand work, prone to drift between people and days. Their Automated Cell Culture Splitter is built round an Opentrons OT-2 liquid handling robot. A camera-based counter sits on the deck and counts cells.

Because the system sees cell density well by well, it can correct for uneven growth across a source plate. It then seeds each new well with a set number of cells. In tests it cut hands-on time by 61%. Seeding was tight, with well-to-well variation under 11%, and the cells fared as well as with manual care. All code and designs are free under open licenses. A lab that can buy one robot gains round-the-clock, repeatable cell culture.
pmc-12750749:
Wenjie Zeng and co-authors test in 2025 whether disability before the pandemic predicted COVID-19 outcomes in older United States adults. Past work was mostly snapshots, which limits firm claims. A long-running health and retirement study gives a forward view for this question.

More than nine thousand adults aged fifty and up were tracked from a twenty eighteen base wave. Disability was scored by daily task limits at base. Outcomes span infection, emergency visits, hospital stays, and long post-illness signs. About sixteen percent told of infection, and most had been vaccinated. Weighting and learning methods weigh how disability and vaccine status act together.
pmc-12750949:
An eighty-year-old with a burst appendix is not a fifty-year-old with a burst appendix: frailty, multiple diseases, and vague symptoms raise both the danger and the diagnostic difficulty. Dezhuang Li reviews the research landscape of emergency surgery in older adults in 2025, covering the common conditions, the tools, and what decides who recovers.

Appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforation, and gallbladder disease dominate the case mix. Frailty and multimorbidity predict outcomes better than age alone, and risk scores help sort patients before the operation. For stable patients, a laparoscope-first approach meant fewer complications and shorter stays. The review pulls together what is known and marks where the evidence is still thin. Li argues the winning model is a team one: surgeons, geriatricians, and rehabilitation specialists planning together, with minimally invasive surgery where possible and recovery work starting early rather than after discharge.
pmc-12751249:
Edosa Amente Gutema and co-authors review in 2025 how funding cuts affect supplies for maternal and newborn health in low- and middle-income countries. Aid cuts strain already weak health systems and raise death and suffering. The review maps the challenges that shrinking funds create for basic supplies.

Searches of four databases yielded close to a thousand records, and fifteen articles passed full review. Weak domestic funding and supply chains made the cuts bite harder. Pregnant women and newborns face gaps in care when stocks run out. The authors present the findings in text, tables, and figures to guide response.
pmc-12751449:
Sonia Johnson and a large team published a feasibility study in two thousand twenty-five on preventing forced psychiatric readmissions. Compulsory admissions in England are rising and often traumatic. Joint crisis planning is the most promising counter, yet hard to deliver well.

The FINCH team, including service users and carers, adapted a Swiss approach into personal crisis plans with a year of follow-up support. Eighty people leaving compulsory admission joined a pilot randomised trial across three areas. Recruitment hit its target on time, and forty participants came from groups over-represented in detention. The study tested whether a full trial can recruit and retain people. Findings guide a larger definitive trial.
pmc-12751549:
Rosemarie Gideonse and colleagues publish the protocol for a Dutch trial of Beat the Kick, a motivation program for adults with mild intellectual disabilities who use substances in harmful ways. People with mild intellectual disabilities face raised risk of substance-use problems. Yet standard addiction treatment assumes thinking capacities they may not have. Beat the Kick is an adapted pre-treatment program built on motivation.

The open-label multicenter trial will take in one hundred thirty-eight adults from six disability care groups. Those who qualify have mild or borderline intellectual functioning with adaptive limits. They have long hazardous alcohol or drug use below dependence-treatment thresholds. A Zelen design assigns before consent, comparing the program with care as usual. The primary question is whether it raises self-driven motivation to enter substance-use treatment.
pmc-12752249:
Luise Holberg Lindgren and co-authors set out a trial plan for nurse-led self-care training in new inflammatory arthritis, in a protocol from two thousand twenty-five. New patients face body, mind, and social strain despite better drugs. One hundred thirty adults from three Danish hospitals will join by lot.

Half get the training plus usual care, and half get usual care alone. Training means three solo nurse sessions plus two optional group sessions over a year. Skill gain at one year is the main yardstick, with a two-year extension check. Fixed analysis rules and gap handling are set in advance. Readers get a full blueprint, with results still to come.
pmc-12752349:
Nicholas Awodele Awolola and co-authors tracked appendix disease over 16 years in a 2025 hospital study in Nigeria. The appendix can host a range of ills, with sudden inflammation the most common. Cases are rising in Nigeria, and wrong calls lead to healthy organs being cut out, so exact diagnosis and routine tissue checks matter.

The team reviewed every appendix cut out at their teaching hospital across the span. They charted how the mix of findings shifted over time and whether past claims about the pattern still hold. Such a long view helps surgeons judge when to act. It also shows where diagnosis can be sharpened to cut needless surgery.
pmc-12752449:
Reza Kalantari and three co-authors clock the delays and interruptions that steal time in operating rooms, in a 2025 Iranian study. Surgical suites are complex, and every pause raises the odds of error and harm. Over half of Iran’s hospitals are teaching hospitals, so their habits shape national care.

Observers watched 251 randomly chosen surgeries in five teaching hospitals during July and August 2025, timing with stopwatches and standard forms, without joining the work. They sorted causes of delay and interruption by directed content analysis. Knowing the top causes, from missing gear to late starts, lets managers fix the preventable share. Lost minutes in surgery are also lost chances for other patients waiting.
pmc-12753049:
Naoyuki Okamoto and co-authors test why people claim skill for wins but blame luck for losses when pay is unsure. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. A hand-move task let pay hinge on skill in some rounds and on chance in others. That split let the team watch how each result was judged.

Players gave wins to their own skill and losses to chance, and that slant shaped their next choices. Model work split the slant into two parts: a warped view of own skill and a rose view in skill rounds. Warped self-view drove acts but not trust. Blame sent outwards, not self-view, fed excess trust. The authors stress tight task design plus models to pull such slants apart.
pmc-12753649:
Shuo Yuan, Lingling Cai, and Man Su pool trials of natural antioxidants for ulcerative colitis in a 2025 analysis. The disease inflames the colon lining, and oxidative stress, an excess of reactive molecules, drives much of the damage. Antioxidant supplements promise to restore balance, yet trials disagree. The authors searched four databases for randomized trials against placebo.

Nine trials with six hundred twenty-four patients qualified. Supplements cut a key damage marker and raised three protective enzyme measures. A clinical activity score also fell, meaning calmer disease. Quality of life scores, though, did not improve in a clear way. The authors conclude that natural antioxidants strengthened the body's defenses and eased disease activity in these trials. They present the work as a basis for choosing add-on therapies, pending stronger trials.
pmc-12753749:
Hao Chi, Michele Carbone, and Youping Deng comment on new evidence that COVID-19 mRNA vaccines may help cancer immunotherapy work better. Their 2025 piece sums up a study in Nature by Grippin and colleagues. That study found the shots briefly reset the border between a tumor and the immune system, warming up cold tumors that normally ignore treatment.

In mice, the vaccine's fat-wrapped RNA woke up a first-line immune signal, type I interferon, which primed killer T cells and raised a marker that checkpoint drugs target. Blocking that signal erased the benefit, and swapping in a different antigen kept the effect, so the platform itself seems to drive it. The window of extra sensitivity is short, the authors note, so timing a checkpoint dose inside it may matter for patients.
pmc-12754049:
Po-Hung Lin and co-authors report, in a 2025 trial, results for prostate removal done with a single-port robot through one small cut. The robot sends a camera and three jointed arms through that one opening. Two surgical routes were used, a standard front route and a hood method meant to spare support tissue.

Every operation in the trial finished with the single-port system, with no switch to multi-port or open surgery. Patients reported less pain and left hospital sooner than typical reports suggest. Most needed no drain tube. Cancer control and continence recovery were much the same for both routes, and most men regained continence within three months. The authors call the approach feasible and effective.
pmc-12756149:
Yating Zhang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on how moxibustion, a traditional heat therapy, changes brain activity in vascular dementia. The illness follows blood vessel damage in the brain. The team had already seen the therapy lift test scores and wanted to watch the brain changes behind the gains.

Fifty-five patients were treated at three head and back points every other day, and fifty healthy adults served as a comparison group. After treatment, standard thinking scores rose clearly. Resting brain scans showed activity shifts in the memory hub and linked regions, and the wiring between areas changed too. The scans hint at how the therapy may act.
pmc-12756349:
Nursyazyla Sulaiman and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, spotting three weed species in rice fields from a drone carrying a special camera. Broadleaf weeds choke young rice exactly when competition hurts most. Finding them early, by species, guides targeted spraying.

Flights over a one-hectare Malaysian plot used a hyperspectral camera, which records many narrow color bands. Machine learning classifiers learned each weed's spectral signature. The three species differ subtly to the eye but more clearly across wavelengths. The drone flew at forty meters over a field known for heavy weed pressure. Species-level maps could cut herbicide use by treating patches, not whole fields.
pmc-12756849:
Jens Goldschmidt and co-authors present a 2025 instrument for reading the isotope mix of carbon dioxide in air. The ratio of heavy to light carbon in CO2 tracks sources and sinks of the gas. Firm reads at normal air pressure and bulk gas levels are hard to get.

Their dual comb spectrometer works in the mid infrared, where CO2 absorbs strongly. It reads three forms of the gas at a fine spectral step with a high signal level. Test values reached below one part per thousand in precision. The build starts from light modulation at a telecom wavelength and converts to the mid infrared, which makes the wavelength flexible for other gas targets.
pmc-12757349:
Wenbo Liu and co-authors build a three-in-one DNA test for bean root rot in this 2025 paper. The disease, driven by three Fusarium fungi, threatens red kidney bean crops in Shanxi Province, China. Until now no single test could spot all three culprits quickly in soil or roots.

Their assay targets a gene shared by the fungi, with primers and probes tuned to tell the three apart in one run. It proved specific and keen, finding tiny copy numbers of each target, and its repeat runs barely varied. Field sampling across the growing region fed a model that predicts disease severity from the total fungal DNA in a gram of soil. The authors offer the test as an early-warning tool to cut crop losses.
pmc-12757949:
