Chen, Murphy, Yeo, Serr, and Brown apply an ecology idea, the extinction vortex, to acute lymphoblastic leukemia in a 2025 paper. This leukemia is the most common childhood cancer. Modern multi-phase therapy now cures most patients.

Treatment starts with a strong induction phase, then shifts drugs often during consolidation, then moves to long maintenance. The authors argue this works like extinction therapy: each new strike hits the shrinking cancer before resistance can grow. Genetic diversity falls as the population contracts, pushing cells toward collapse. Single-drug care, by contrast, often lets the cancer rebound. The paper reframes a known success as an evolution-guided strategy.
pmc-12763949:
Carmen Cabezaolias and co-authors measured what happens to the opposing arm muscle when its partner is treated with focused vibration. Focal muscle vibration is used to tune nerve-muscle excitability, but its effects are usually checked with electrical tests that patients find uncomfortable, and its spillover onto antagonist muscles is little known. Thirty healthy adults did repeated elbow bends while sensors recorded the triceps, the muscle that opposes the vibrated biceps.

After five minutes of vibration, triceps activity fell and stayed reduced for up to twenty minutes, while a rest-only session changed nothing. Surface sensors proved sensitive enough to catch the effect. The authors say vibration of one muscle can quietly damp its antagonist, a finding that could guide rehabilitation dosing.
pmc-12764049:
Jiawen Chen and eight co-authors park engineered bacteria inside tumors and switch them on with light. The goal is more tumor-killing T cells, since immunotherapy lives or dies on CD8 expansion. Interleukin-2 grows those cells but poisons the body when given plainly. Their system loads a probiotic Escherichia coli strain, drawn to oxygen-poor tumor zones, with a light-triggered IL-2 factory inside a gel.

Near-infrared light starts local IL-2 release, and a tumor enzyme frees low-dose cyclophosphamide from the gel. In mouse liver tumors, CD8 and natural killer activity rose while regulatory T cells fell. Memory T cells guarded against rechallenge.
pmc-12764149:
Pankaj Aggarwal and co-authors report a bullet left in place inside a patient's heart, in work from 2025. A man aged thirty-seven was shot in the right chest, and the bullet lodged in the wall between the heart's lower chambers. Removal is the usual call, given risks of fluid crush, rhythm flaws, travel of the bullet, or infection.

Scans showed the bullet sat still, with no fluid around the heart and sound heart action. A joint team chose watchful care: a chest drain, broad germ drugs, and close checks. A year of follow-ups found no shift, travel, or infection. The authors back case-by-case calls for stable patients.
pmc-12764349:
Sattam Khulaif Alenezi and co-authors tested a plant compound, marmelosin, against diabetes in rats, in a 2025 study. Type 2 diabetes brings high blood sugar and wide metabolic strain, and standard drugs carry side effects that push interest toward natural options. Twenty-four rats were split into four groups for twenty-eight days. One group stayed healthy. One was made diabetic by a fat diet plus a pancreas-harming drug. The last two diabetic groups got low or higher oral doses of the compound.

Treated rats showed lower fasting glucose and lower long-term sugar markers, with more insulin and better insulin sensitivity. Blood fats improved, antioxidant defenses rose, and inflammatory signals fell. A cell-death protein also dropped, hinting at protection for tissues. The authors call marmelosin a multi-sided candidate for diabetes care, while the work remains at the rat stage.
pmc-12764849:
Isaac Bishara and co-authors track how a rare ovarian cancer shifts as patients get drug mist sprayed inside the belly in a 2025 study. The form of cancer spreads through the belly and often resists standard care. The spray method lets doctors take tumor samples again and again during care.

The team read single cells from samples of two patients, one who gained from care and one who did not. The tumor that resisted turned up growth and stress paths. The tumor that responded turned those paths down but woke other routes to stay alive. Immune cells also looked more held back in the resistant case. Even from two patients, the split shows why one plan fails some.
pmc-12766849:
Jiying Ling, Annie Kao, and Xining Yang ask whether living far from healthy food blunted a mindful eating program for rural families. Their study appeared in 2025. The data come from 154 low-income parent-child pairs at twenty-six Head Start centers. Parents reported habits, feeding attitudes, and food insecurity; children's growth and body fat were measured directly. Home food access was estimated by mapping zip codes to food outlets.

The children averaged about four years old; many parents were single, unemployed, or earning under twenty thousand dollars a year. The team tested whether food access changed the program's effects on eating and body measures. The authors say interventions cannot be judged apart from the food landscape families actually shop in.
pmc-12767049:
Eiman Wazwaz and co-authors tested a lower dose of a transplant drug in a 2025 study. Thymoglobulin wipes out immune cells to protect a new kidney, but dosing varies by center with no firm standard. In April 2022 their center cut the dose for low-risk recipients from 4.5 to 3 milligrams per kilogram.

The study compared 196 low-risk patients treated before and after the change, from 2020 to 2024. The reduced dose met the bar for noninferiority: the combined outcome of rejection, graft loss, or death was actually lower, at three percent versus eleven. Low blood counts and viral infections were also less common. The authors endorse the smaller dose as safer for this group.
pmc-12767249:
Jyoti Bajpai, Akshyaya Pradhan and their co-authors review tirzepatide for sleep apnea tied to obesity in 2025. The breathing disorder is common and often missed, and the standard airway pressure therapy suffers from poor long-term use.

The review searched major databases for trials and reviews on the drug in apnea or obesity up to a set date. Evidence from a named trial program showed large drops in weight, apnea scores and inflammation with tirzepatide. Sleep quality and heart risk factors also improved. The authors call the drug a promising add-on or alternative, while urging more long-term research.
pmc-12767449:
Julia Sonnleitner and co-authors check whether stem cells from arthritic knees still hold repair power and still answer chemical calls to migrate, in a study from 2025. In situ tissue engineering wants the body's own mesenchymal stromal cells to home to damage. Arthritis might dull those powers; past results conflict.

Cells from arthritic and healthy donors matched on making bone, fat, and cartilage lineages, and on aging markers, from enzyme activity to gene profiles. Arthritis cells carried the full set of chemokine receptors on gene and protein levels. Both cell types migrated toward the attractant CCL25 in a chamber assay. Gene-wide scans after exposure confirmed effects on movement and growth programs. The authors conclude the cells stay competent recruits for drug-guided repair.
pmc-12768649:
Ally Robert and Smarth Lakhanpal review how structured expert elicitation has been used in British reviews of rare disease treatments. The method gathers expert views in a formal, statistical way. It helps when trial data are thin, as with rare diseases and new technologies.

The authors screened twenty-seven submissions made through a special pathway for very rare conditions. Every one used expert evidence, and many mixed two or three methods, led by interviews and surveys. Most evidence backed core value measures such as healthy years gained. Claims about wider gains, like family impact, were less often accepted. Winning submissions explained why no other data source would do and used large expert pools.
pmc-12768749:
Priscilla Loze and co-authors draw lessons from four countries on moving care out of hospitals, in a 2025 conference report. Decentralized care treats people in simpler settings closer to home, which cuts travel and frees hospital beds. Belgium, the Netherlands, Singapore, and the UK served as benchmarks.

The team read government papers and interviewed senior hospital and state officials. Britain's integrated providers cut hospital admissions by 12 percent. Singapore's home program saved 7,000 bed days and lifted telemedicine use by 40 percent. A Dutch home scheme saved two million euros a year. The report folds such results into a framework other systems can scale, with patient focus as the stated core.
pmc-12768849:
Aldenora Rodrigues and co-authors review how Brazil judges new medical devices for its public health system in a 2025 paper. A national board weighs proof and cost before the system adopts each device. The team read board reports on devices that won approval over a decade.

Most reports leaned on pooled study reviews, and most heard public views. Few weighed what patients felt, and none used real-world care data. Cost-value math was common, yet many reports left the sums thin. Reliance on foreign data was a shared weak point. The authors urge more local proof, patient input, and watch for future devices.
pmc-12769749:
Marion Di Ciaccio and co-authors explore how people living with HIV in North Africa experienced the COVID-19 pandemic, published in 2025. The pandemic disrupted health care worldwide, including HIV services. Those disruptions deepened health inequality for groups already underserved, including people with HIV.

The team interviewed dozens of people living with HIV in Tunisia, Morocco, and Algeria during the pandemic years. A theme analysis used a syndemic lens, which treats diseases and social conditions as intertwined. Interviewees' experience of the pandemic was closely tied to their HIV status and to money and social limits. Living with HIV in a pandemic, the authors find, added to overall disease burden. They call for pandemic planning that takes such linked burdens into account.
pmc-12771049:
Kittipong Pinyosamosorn and co-authors study sex gaps in death after a heart artery procedure in Thailand, in work from 2025. Past studies found women die more often than men after the procedure, though both share the same main risk factors. The team used a national registry of 19,701 patients to test the gap with fresh data.

Women died in hospital at 3.5 percent, against 2.3 percent for men, they report. Risk models then split which factors drove death in each sex. Care and risk data of this size are rare, the authors note. A clear map of where the gap comes from, age, timing, or added illness, can guide fairer care. It can also show which part of the gap better systems could close.
pmc-12771849:
Takashi Oshio, Kemmyo Sugiyama, and Toyo Ashida follow middle-aged and young-old Japanese adults over nine survey waves. They track how the sense of social support changes with age, and how that links to mental distress. Support is a known key to aging well, but its dynamics were little studied. The data cover more than twenty thousand people born in the late 1940s and early 1950s.

Distress was far less common among people who felt supported. With age, family support tended to fade while support from others grew, largely keeping total support steady. More than half of the harm from losing family support was offset by support from others, for both men and women. The authors read this as a smooth handover between support sources.
pmc-12772549:
Laura Ojanpera and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-five, spacer devices that help small children inhale asthma medicine. A spacer is a chamber between an inhaler and the child's mouth. It holds the spray so the child can breathe it in slowly. Disposable paper spacers may suit some clinic uses, but data were scarce. The team tested two disposable spacers against three reusable chambers in the lab, using a child throat model.

They used three child breathing patterns, calm and blocked. One reusable chamber gave the highest fine dose that can reach the lungs. Blocked breathing raised throat deposits for all spacers. Reusable chambers beat disposable ones overall. Of the disposable pair, the valved one did better.
pmc-12775249:
Xinyi Zhao, Quan Zhang, Vivian Lou, and Siqing Tao sort older Chinese adults by their mix of caregiving loads, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Many juggle care for parents, a spouse, and grandchildren at once. Data followed 11,775 people aged fifty and up across seven years.

Four patterns emerged, from part-time care for all to full-time spouse care. Spouse caregivers, part- or full-time, showed more depressive symptoms years later. Full-time parent-plus-grandchild carers fared no worse than the light group. The authors urge services shaped to each pattern, not one plan for all.
pmc-12780449:
Jieqi Peng and co-authors (2025) followed patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to see how eosinophil levels predict flare-ups. Eosinophils are white blood cells whose counts in sputum and blood can run high in some patients. The team sorted patients by whether levels stayed low, stayed high, or swung between the two over three years. They then compared flare-up rates and lung function decline across the groups.

Patients with persistently high sputum eosinophils had more breathlessness and clearly more flare-ups, including severe ones. The unstable group also flared more than the stable-low group. Blood levels told the same story at smaller strength. Lung function decline, however, did not differ between groups. The authors conclude that a single measurement undersells the risk: persistence itself is the warning sign. They suggest repeated eosinophil checks should guide how closely COPD patients are watched.
pmc-12781649:
Seven authors pool trials in 2025 on game-based digital health tools for children and teens with autism. Drug options for autism are few, so playful digital tools draw interest for their reach. The review held 21 randomized trials with 1,050 young people, drawn from six databases through late 2024.

Pooled scores rose for emotion skills, social skills, planning, and motor skills, with motor gains the largest. Sensor-based games did best in split checks. No clear drop in behavior problems appeared. The authors call for sharper behavior measures and long trials to test lasting gains.
pmc-12782349:
Baptiste Chanel, Carole Cometti, and Nicolas Babault compare in 2025 how joint position changes tissue stiffness in grown men and in boys before puberty. They used shear wave measurements, an ultrasound method that reads how fast a ripple crosses muscle and tendon, as a window on stiffness.

Ten men and ten boys each took ten positions, crossing five knee angles with two hip angles. The team measured the two big front-thigh muscles and the kneecap tendon at rest in every pose. Their data show how much of an adult's stiffness pattern is already present in childhood and how much arrives with growth.
pmc-12785849:
Easan Anand and co-authors test AI-written summaries of scan reports in a 2025 study. MRI reports on anal fistulas are dense, and patients often leave clinic unsure what was found. A large language model might restate the findings in plain words, if it stays faithful.

Two hundred fifty reports were rewritten and checked by a specialist panel; invented content appeared in about one in nine. Sixty-one patients then rated paired original and AI versions, blind to which was which. The AI versions scored far higher on readability and grasp, and patients trusted them. Panel checks still matter, since the error rate was real. The study backs supervised use.
pmc-12786049:
Seven authors led by Qingjie Wu stack gene, cell, and learning reads to find marks shared by type 2 diabetes and artery clog. The clog is the top killer in that sugar ill, yet their shared code was murky. Bank gene sets for both ills gave an overlap pool for the hunt. Path and web reads then sorted which shared genes sit at cross roads.

Seventy-two shared genes made the first pool of the work. Three rose as hub marks with firm call worth across sets in the tests. Immune cell reads and lone-cell reads both point to swelling as the shared fire. Drug teams gain three marks to chase for twin care.
pmc-12786749:
Beatriz Agostinho and co-authors test greener catalysts for making plant-based plastics in this 2025 study. The plastics in focus are furan-based polyesters, a family that can come from plant sources rather than oil. Their usual making relies on metal catalysts that are hurt by air and water, and on harsh conditions.

The team tried two deep eutectic solvents, mixtures that melt far below their parts, as catalysts. The best mix joined urea with a zinc salt in a four-to-one ratio. It was used to make three members of the family. The products were checked for their structure, chain length, and heat behavior. The work offers a gentler route to these plastics.
pmc-12787049:
Theja V Channapragada and co-authors ask whether treating sleep apnea also heals a fatty liver. Their 2025 review covers the overlap of two common conditions: fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnea, which share metabolic roots.

Eight studies, from airflow masks alone to lifestyle programs, drugs, and surgery, met their criteria. The mask treatment, CPAP, used four weeks to three years, gave small and uneven drops in liver enzymes and modest gains in blood sugar and triglycerides. No trial showed real improvement in liver fat or scarring. One trial carried low bias risk and two raised some concerns. The authors rate the certainty low and call for longer, stronger trials.
pmc-12787349:
Elif Demirbas and co-authors review solid-state LiDAR sensors that steer light with flat surfaces in a paper published in 2025. LiDAR maps surroundings by timing light pulses, and self-driving cars need versions without spinning parts. Flat optical surfaces called metasurfaces can bend a beam by shifting its phase.

A fixed metasurface serves when the beam only needs one direction; scanning needs a tunable one that changes on demand. The review explains how these phase-shifting surfaces work and compares their fields of view. It also weighs them against other solid-state options, such as tiny mirrors and phased arrays. Tunable versions promise faster scans, higher reliability, and wider views in a compact form.
pmc-12788349:
Vourna, Falara, Ktena, Hristoforou, and Papadopoulos review a magnetic sensor method for testing materials in twenty twenty-five. The method listens to tiny magnetic noise from steel and other magnetic materials. That noise reflects grain structure, stress, and other internal traits. It allows testing without damaging the part.

The review covers theory, sensor design, signal processing, and industry uses. New sensors are smaller and can work in harsh settings. Modern methods, including deep learning, extract more information from the raw signals. Uses include factory quality control, railway checks, and health monitoring of structures. Reported accuracy is good for stress and hardness measures. The authors list open needs, such as common standards and more robust learning methods.
pmc-12788549:
Priyanka Patel and six co-authors compare outcomes for mothers sent to a big hospital against those who came on their own, in a 2025 study. Referred cases often arrive late and already in trouble, which raises the risk of harm. The study ran at a tertiary care center with 300 women admitted for delivery, split evenly between the two groups.

Cesarean delivery was far more common in referred cases, at 68 percent against 42 percent. Heavy bleeding after birth hit 10 percent of referred mothers against 3.3 percent of the others. Intensive care admissions also ran higher in the referred group, as did deaths. The gaps show how much rides on fast referral chains and readiness at the receiving hospital.
pmc-12789549:
Bin Ren and co-authors report a 2025 materials study aimed at very hot, very fast flight. Craft moving at high Mach numbers need coatings that soak up radar waves across a wide band while standing extreme heat. Past materials leaned on complex shapes to widen the band, because the key property shifts with heat and wave frequency in hard-to-control ways.

The team's trick is to tune that shifting property directly. They made ceramic composites from several high-heat borides and adjusted the oxide skin on each grain. The flat material, just a few millimeters thick, absorbed across a very wide band at room heat. Even at the highest test heat it kept a broad band once coated, a result the authors link to fast craft that must stay hard to spot.
pmc-12793949:
Juhui Han and co-authors report a 2025 study of a common virus infection after two strong blood cancer treatments. Both treatments, one using reprogrammed immune cells and one using dual-target antibodies, weaken the immune system. Data on how often this virus flares up after them was scarce.

The team reviewed records from a large hospital in Seoul for patients treated between 2018 and 2024. Of 179 patients, infection rates were higher after antibody therapy than after cell therapy. A small share of cases became serious or reached organs such as the lung. The results help doctors plan virus checks after these treatments.
pmc-12797949:
Awad Bin Naeem and colleagues apply convolutional networks to spot osteoporosis in spine scans. Their 2025 paper uses DXA images from clinical practice. Osteoporosis silently weakens bones until sudden fractures occur. Spine density scans help radiologists catch it early. The team built a 21-layer network for automatic detection.

The dataset held 174 spine images, most with osteoporosis. Augmentation expanded the data for stronger training. Four famous pre-trained models served as comparison baselines. The custom network beat them on the reported scores. Its F1 score and recall both ran very high. Transferable mining methods are the wider theme of the work. Clinics with few specialists could gain screening support.
pmc-12798049:
Zixuan Wang and co-authors built a deep learning system in 2025 to flag upper neck spine problems from X-ray images. Reading these images is hard because structures overlap and several problems can coexist. Their system uses three views of each patient — bending forward, neutral, and bending back. It first crops to the right region, then blends shape features with motion features across views.

A tuned loss function teaches the model how the six problems relate. On 249 patients, the system scored high on standard accuracy measures. The authors present it as a helpful aid for diagnosis, not a replacement for doctors. Faster, more consistent reads could improve care planning.
pmc-12801649:
Hyun Ji Park and four co-authors study quality of life in pregnancy in a 2025 paper. They ask how a woman's body weight before pregnancy shapes her well being during pregnancy, and what sits in between. The team surveyed two hundred forty pregnant women in Korea with self report forms.

Their path model fit the data well and explained over half the variation in quality of life. Weight before pregnancy had no direct link to quality of life. Instead, its effect ran through sleep problems, depressive symptoms, and how women rated their own health. Sleep mattered mainly through its effect on mood and health perception. The findings point to mood and sleep care as routes to better pregnancy well being.
pmc-12801949:
Anna Rogachevskaya and eight co-authors published a study in 2025 on a little-known gene, C1orf50, and its links to cancer behavior. The gene makes a small, ancient protein whose job is unclear. Screening public tumor data across many cancers, the team focused on ovarian cancer, where the gene's story looked strongest.

Copies of the gene were gained or amplified most often in ovarian tumors, and more copies meant more gene activity. High activity tracked with more mutations, weaker DNA repair, faster cell-cycle programs, and an immune mix tilted toward suppression. In ovarian samples the gene's activity rose step by step with clinical stage and traveled with changes in the famous BRCA repair genes. Whether the gene drives these patterns or merely reports them remains open.
pmc-12804749:
Rika Kakutani and four co-authors study the strength of knuckle bone in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2025 paper. These patients often get silicone joint swaps in the hand, and weak bone under the joint can let the implant sink. The team took 105 knuckle heads cut out during such surgery and measured their strength, density, and inner build.

Scans of the bone's tiny struts tied most closely to strength, and in their joint model only one scan measure, bone volume share, held up as the driver. Joints with weaker bone saw more sinking of the implant later. A steroid drug dose at surgery also tracked with strength. The authors urge keeping the illness quiet without steroids to guard the bone bed.
pmc-12804849:
Ravindra Singh and co-authors published this farm study in 2025 on cumin in dry Rajasthan, India. Sandy soils and fierce evaporation starve border-watered fields. The team tested drip lines that feed water and fertilizer together, over three years. Ten setups mixed three drip rates with three fertilizer doses, against a flooded control.

The top drip rate with a full fertilizer dose won on growth, seed yield, and profit, and lifted the spice's prized oil content. Leaner drip rates saved far more water and used each drop best. All drip setups cut seasonal water use by a fifth to over half against flooding. Year weather swayed which setup paid most. The authors back drip feeding as the sound path for spice farms in arid lands.
pmc-12807949:
Gracia Tian and Jayson Tuan report a vet case from 2025 in which bone growth from a badly healed break was reused as graft bone in the same cat. The cat was a young domestic shorthair from a rescue, with injuries to both back legs from an unknown cause. Scans showed a shin bone that had healed crooked with a large lump of new bone, plus complex harm to the other ankle.

Surgeons chipped bone from that lump and used it twice. It filled the repair of the crooked shin and the fusion of the other ankle joint. Later scans showed the shin sat straighter and the ankle had fused well. At three months, the cat moved well. The case shows that extra bone growth, often cut away and thrown out, can serve as a free graft source in the same operation.
pmc-12812049:
David Chou, Assad Zahid, and Ernest Cheng present, in a 2025 case report with a literature review, a tumor that hid in plain sight in a patient's pelvis. Schwannomas are benign growths from the cells that wrap nerves, and they almost never arise in the pelvis. Their patient was a sixty-five-year-old man being treated for rectal cancer.

A scan showed a lump on the right pelvic wall that looked like cancer spread to a lymph node. During keyhole surgery, the lump was cut out along with the rectum. Lab study showed it was a schwannoma, not cancer at all, and review of the surgery footage traced it to the obturator nerve. The case warns that not every new lump in a cancer patient is spread.
pmc-12812549:
Zixuan Yuan, Yutong Pan, Haodong Yuan, and Aihua Gong review a promising target for cancer immunotherapy, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The target is a receptor on T cells that, when switched on by its partner molecule, helps those cells multiply, survive, and attack tumors. It also damps the cells that normally hold immunity back.

Drugs that switch the receptor on were safe in early trials but shrank few tumors on their own. Weak binding, few T cells inside tumors, and leftover suppressor cells are blamed. Pairing the drugs with other treatments raised response rates but also raised severe side effects. The authors call for sharper drugs that act mainly inside tumors, to balance gain and safety.
pmc-12812649:
Xiaotao Cao, Jiaxing Xu, Mingyang Li, and Li Zheng compare clinical research nurse roles across countries. Their review deals with developed and developing nations. Trial quality leans on these nurses as core team members.

Role views, duty splits, and promotion paths are compared. China serves as the example developing country case. Blocks to nurse career growth there are analyzed. Role perception gaps stand among the contrasts. The aim is a reference for building the profession. Better training and management modes are the goals. High quality trial growth is the wider aim.
pmc-12813149:
Pingxiang Ouyang and co-authors built, in a 2025 study, a model to predict which eczema patients will stick with a biologic drug. Dupilumab works well for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, yet adherence had not been studied in a systematic way. The team followed a single-center group over time.

Quitting tied to age, sex, added therapies, and how severe the disease was at the start and how it responded. A learning model ranked response scores as the strongest signals. A final risk model kept age, baseline severity scores, and whether patients hit a set response bar. The team turned the model into nomogram charts that show each patient's risk at a glance. Such tools may help clinics support patients most likely to stop.
pmc-12815449:
Clara Voltarelli and co-authors report a rare heart tumor on the lung valve that threw clots into the lungs, in a case report from 2025. The tumor type, papillary fibroelastoma, is the second most common benign heart tumor. It usually grows on left-side valves, and lung valve cases make up under 8 percent.

The patient, a 60-year-old man, arrived with acute breathlessness and swollen legs. Scans showed a failing left heart and a small mobile mass, one centimeter wide, on the lung valve. CT confirmed clots in both lungs with tissue damage. Heart catheter tests ruled out blocked arteries. Given his high surgical risk, the team chose blood thinners and heart failure care first, and put surgery off until he stabilizes.
pmc-12815849:
Binhui Xiao, Jiaqian Zhu, and Yong Han test a nutrition linked index as a stroke outcome marker in a study published in 2025. The index joins blood fat, cholesterol, and body weight into one score. Past work on its tie to recovery after a blocked artery stroke was thin, so the team ran a cohort analysis.

Records covered one thousand seven hundred sixty four stroke patients at a South Korean hospital. Higher index scores linked to lower odds of a poor outcome at ninety days. The tie curved, with the strongest link below a clear turning point and a flat link above it. Checks in subgroups, such as patients without diabetes, held steady. The score may help flag patients who need closer follow up.
pmc-12816149:
Abdelmoneim Ali and co-authors test ways to catch pork fat hidden in ghee, the prized cooking fat made from buffalo or cow milk. Milk fat commands high prices, so fraud hurts buyers and trust. Their 2025 study spiked pure ghee with pork fat at levels from one percent up and ran three kinds of checks.

Fatty acid profiles shifted in telltale ways, with butyric acid dropping as pork fat rose. Volatile compounds and infrared spectra also carried clear signs, and a clustering analysis split pure from spiked samples cleanly. Detection worked even at the lowest spike level. Food safety labs get a combined method for guarding a high-value dairy product.
pmc-12816249:
Nacer Bellaloui, James Smith, Alemu Mengistu, and Hamed Abbas studied slow-wilting soybean lines in work published in 2025. Soybean seed supplies protein, oil, and sugars, and drought cuts both yield and seed quality. Slow-wilting lines hold leaf water longer, which may help under dry conditions.

A three-year trial in Mississippi grew two slow-wilting lines with and without irrigation, next to standard and fast-wilting checks. Under irrigation, the slow lines had lower protein and higher oil than checks, but yielded less in all years. Without irrigation, their protein and one fatty acid ran higher, while oil varied by year. The authors discuss leaf water holding as one way the trait may work.
pmc-12816649:
Gianmario Sambuceti and co-authors track how a cancer drug family harms the power plants of normal blood cells, in a 2025 study. The drugs, anthracyclines, gather inside mitochondria. A vicious cycle has been proposed: DNA damage and stress feed each other until function fails. The team tested that idea in lymphoma patients.

Blood cells were sampled from 23 patients before, during, and after a standard drug regimen. A matched healthy group gave a baseline. The team measured oxygen use and counts of mitochondrial DNA copies. Patients were chosen with good early scan responses. Tracking normal cells shows the collateral cost of a curative therapy, which may guide safer dosing.
pmc-12816749:
Xiaotao Ai, Yicheng Chen, and Yuzhou Huang ask whether a mine's waste mountain will slide, given how messily its rocks settle, in a 2025 paper. Open-pit mines stack soil-rock mixtures into ever taller dumps, and rolling sorts the particles as they fall, big and small segregating down the slope. Standard stability checks pretend the mix is uniform; real dumps are anything but.

The team coupled a cellular automaton, which grows the disordered particle layout, with a finite-difference solver that computes stability on it. For one fixed overall recipe, the strength numbers scattered widely from spot to spot, following bell curves for both cohesion and friction. Grading along the slope turned out protective: it shrank the strained zone, lifted the likely slip surface, and raised the computed safety factor. The framework gives engineers a stability check that respects the mess instead of averaging it away.
pmc-12817649:
Rohana Abdul Ghani, Firdaus Mukhtar, Barakatun Nisak Mohd Yusof, and Zubaidah Nor Hanipah published a survey study in 2025 on how Malaysian health professionals see obesity. Recognition shapes care, and the survey, part of a multinational project, asked 150 professionals and 53 decision-makers about the condition, their attitudes, and the system's readiness.

Only about twenty-seven percent recognized obesity as a chronic disease. Over half of both groups admitted bias against people with obesity, and over half called it a personal choice and responsibility, even while agreeing such patients deserve equal respect and care. Fewer than six in ten professionals judged current services adequate. The authors call for a coordinated system that treats obesity as a disease and tackles stigma head-on.
pmc-12817749:
Jia-Wei Wu and co-authors review ten cases of a rare, deadly link between the aorta and the gut, treated at one Chinese hospital from 2022 to 2024. Their 2025 paper covers aortoenteric fistula, an abnormal channel that lets blood leak from the body's main artery into the bowel. Most cases follow earlier aortic graft surgery.

All ten patients were men, most in their late sixties. Bleeding, belly pain, and fever were the common signs. CT scans found the fistula in every case, while a camera exam of the gut rarely did. All had open surgery to remove the weak artery section and repair the bowel. Half faced major complications afterward and two died. The authors stress fast scanning and prompt surgery.
pmc-12817849:
A team of co-authors reports a study from two thousand twenty-five on immune cells that help kidney cancer grow. The surroundings of a tumor shape its growth, spread, and response to drugs. In clear cell kidney cancer, the rules of that environment are still partly unknown.

Reading gene activity cell by cell, the team found a group of macrophages, a type of immune cell, marked by a protein called CD9. These cells were enriched inside the tumors, and CD9 levels ran higher in cancer tissue than in nearby healthy tissue. Turning CD9 down in experiments slowed the cancer. The cells seem to act through a receptor called Nor1.
pmc-12819749:
László Ózsvári and co-authors tally what dairy farms spend on vet drugs, with a focus on antibiotics, in a study published in 2025. Drug use in farm animals matters for public health, since overuse can breed resistant germs. The team surveyed 20 large dairy herds with more than eighteen thousand cows in five Central European countries, using cost data from 2019.

Antibiotics took the largest share of drug spending, about two fifths of the total. Udder infection, called mastitis, drove the most cost of any single problem. It also drew three fifths of all antibiotic spending. One drug family, the cephalosporins, led antibiotic costs by a wide margin. Costs per cow varied sharply by country and by herd, a sign that some farms may use far more drugs than they need.
pmc-12820149:
Ke Tian and co-authors web silver dust in a stretch gum to make a wire that bends, in a study from 2025. Soft wires for skin tech must haul charge like metal yet stretch like gum. The trick is the leap gaps twixt dust grains: slim and low, and charge pours.

A wash-and-grow way seeds fine silver dust in one step for any gum. Coat craft drops the leap wall to a hair. Big soft balls then squeeze the web, which thins the gaps past the key mark. The gum hit metal-class flow at half silver by weight, kept more than half its flow at full stretch, and hauled heat fivefold more. Web craft by gap math, the team shows, beats brute fill.
pmc-12821549:
Raquel García De La Peña and co-authors compare three treatments for fungal nail infection in a 2025 study. The fungus Trichophyton rubrum causes most cases, and drugs struggle to reach it through the nail, so relapse is common. The rivals here are strong nitric acid, a medical laser, and the two combined.

Patients with confirmed infection were assigned to one of the three routes and followed for twelve months. Scores tracked how the nails looked, whether lab tests still found the fungus, how fast nails cleared, and how often the infection crept back. All three groups improved on look and lab measures. The combined route answered fastest and held its gains best. The authors present pairing acid with laser light as the strongest of the three options tested.
pmc-12821649:
Michelle Tucci and co-authors test a liquid sealant that stops lung wounds bleeding and leaking air, in a 2025 study. Torn lungs that cannot be squeezed are a deadly gap in field care. The team cut wounds in pig lungs and compared a silicon-based visco-liquid, plain or loaded with kaolin or chitin, against gauze pressure and no care.

The plain liquid and the chitin mix sealed eight of ten wounds, in about two minutes and under ninety seconds, while gauze needed eight minutes. Air leaks stopped in every treated group. A spray-on seal that needs no pressure could matter for medics far from an operating room.
pmc-12821849:
Dipesh Kumar Yadav and eight colleagues compare laparoscopic ultrasound with gastroscopy done at surgery for finding stomach tumors, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Finding the exact spot is a hard step that persists in laparoscopic gastrectomy. The team looked back at fifty-eight patients who had radical laparoscopic surgery. Twenty-two were localized by ultrasound and thirty-six by gastroscopy.

Ultrasound matched the scope on success at finding the spot, at about ninety-six versus one hundred percent. It needed much less time to find the spot and cut the total operation time. Harm rates were the same, with like rates in both groups. Tissue outcomes were excellent in both arms. Short-term cancer results were also compared. The authors present ultrasound as a faster, safe swap for the standard scope. That matters for smooth running in stomach cancer surgery.
pmc-12821949:
Bhavika Baweja and co-authors mapped a web of gene regulators around BUB1, a cell-division checkpoint gene often overactive in lung adenocarcinoma. Working entirely with public cancer databases and computer predictions, they built a competing RNA network in which a long non-coding RNA soaks up a small RNA that would otherwise restrain BUB1. High BUB1 levels tracked with poor survival, especially in smokers, and tumor tissue showed much higher BUB1 than normal tissue. A known switch gene and the long RNA both rose and fell with BUB1.

Computer docking suggested a natural compound, hesperidin, binds BUB1 strongly. BUB1 levels also moved against helpful immune cell counts, hinting the gene may help tumors hide from immunity. The authors propose the whole axis as a possible marker for prognosis and a target for treatment. All findings are computational, so lab confirmation is still needed before any clinical use.
pmc-12822049:
Eliud Andrea Lukole leads a large team in 2025 in asking rural Tanzanian households how they feel about a new kind of malaria bed net. The nets carry two active insecticides instead of one, a design the World Health Organization backs where mosquitoes have grown resistant to older chemicals.

A net only works if people sleep under it every night, so taste matters: smell, feel, size, and trust all shape use. The team mixed surveys with interviews to learn what families liked and disliked about the dual nets. Their findings can guide how the nets are rolled out so that protection on paper becomes protection in bed.
pmc-12822149:
Zhi and co-authors test a teaching blend for chest trauma care that pairs case-based learning with a spaced online classroom. Standard teaching often fails to build hands-on skill or drive. Memory research shows recall fades fast unless review is spaced out. The team enrolled 43 fifth-year students in an eight-year medical program. Students were split at random into standard case learning or the blended form. Both groups studied chest trauma and closed chest drainage.

Baseline checks confirmed the groups started alike. After the course, exams and self-confidence surveys compared the two paths. The blended path spaces review in small timed doses online. The study asks whether that rhythm lifts both scores and confidence.
pmc-12822249:
Zaid Al-Azzawi and five colleagues survey Canadian physician-scientist trainees from marginalized groups about mentorship, in a twenty twenty-five study. These trainees study for both medical and research degrees and report high burnout and dropout. No work had mapped those who also carry a marginalized identity. The team used a national survey run in twenty twenty-one covering five identity grounds.

Seventy-eight percent of trainees held at least one such identity, and near half held two or more. Each group ranked its top needs differently. Trainees with a disability and those caring for others reported distinct gaps. The authors call for mentorship built around these specific needs, not a single template.
pmc-12822349:
Daifeng Li and co-authors build a tiny motor that attacks drug-resistant biofilms. Their 2025 paper tackles a hard problem: antibiotics cannot pierce the slime shields that bacteria build. Their Janus nanomotor carries an antibiotic and silver at once. One side is coated with silver particles that split peroxide fuel.

In the acidic biofilm setting, that split makes oxygen, which pushes the motor forward. The motor thus bores into the film and raises the drug's local level nearly fourfold. Silver ions add stress, break membranes, and hinder DNA copying in the bacteria. The motor also nudges immune cells toward an attack state. Tests support strong anti-biofilm action with good safety, the authors report.
pmc-12822849:
Florence Mutua and co-authors review how women living with HIV fare when cervical cancer is treated with radiation. These women face sixfold higher risk of the cancer, above all in poorer countries. The team pooled 18 cohort studies covering 2,790 HIV-positive and 4,064 HIV-negative patients, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa.

Survival ran about a third lower for the HIV-positive group, and their risk of death was higher still in relative terms. Full response to treatment also trended lower. Reports on side effects were too uneven to settle whether HIV worsened them, and no study showed whether HIV therapy changed the picture. The authors call the evidence thin and press for trials built for this group.
pmc-12824549:
Anupriyaa A and co-authors report a warty skin cancer growing out of a precancerous patch on a patient's lower back, in a 2025 case report. Verrucous squamous cell carcinoma is a slow, locally aggressive tumor, usually unrelated to HPV and demanding wide excision. Bowen's disease is its in-situ cousin, often virus-linked and sun-related, sometimes treatable without surgery. The two rarely share a lesion.

Here the verrucous tumor arose within Bowen's disease at a site unusual for both. Surgeons removed it widely and rebuilt the area with a Limberg flap. Microscopy confirmed the double diagnosis. The authors urge pathologists and surgeons to expect dual pathology in odd-looking lesions, because the pair changes the operation.
pmc-12825249:
Moon Modak, Arif Hasan Khan Robin, and five co-authors compare twenty enriched sweet potato lines. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, seeks types rich in key nutrients that also mature fast. Sweet potato already gives carbs, fiber, and vitamins. Lines high in orange pigment and purple pigment remain scarce.

Trials ran in a blocked field design with three repeats. Clear genetic gaps showed across most traits, from root count to yield. One line topped yield by a wide margin over the next best. Yield rose with root number and root mass. Five summary axes captured most of the variation. The best lines can guide breeding for short-season, nutrient-rich crops.
pmc-12827249:
Lisa M Ooms and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five breast cancer study on two brakes in a growth pathway. The PI3K pathway runs too hot in most breast cancers. Two enzymes, PTEN and PIPP, each trim its key signal lipid, but in different ways.

Whether the two brakes back each other up in living tissue was unknown. In mice already missing one PTEN copy, removing PIPP raised pathway activity further. Breast tissue showed more cell growth, thickened ducts, and overgrowth changes. The enzymes are not interchangeable, so losing both may push tissue closer to cancer.
pmc-12827949:
Vignesh Shanmugam and co-authors map the neighborhood around Hodgkin lymphoma's rare malignant cells at genome scale, hunting the signals that keep them alive, in a 2025 study. The cancer cells are a small minority in their own tumor, fed by surrounding immune cells. Spatial and single-cell profiling charted the niche cell by cell.

Thirty-one non-malignant cell types crowd the niche, rich in helper T cells and myeloid cells, poor in plasma cells. One secreted factor stood out: IL13. Adding it in the lab sped malignant growth, and screens across a thousand cancer lines found its receptor parts uniquely essential in Hodgkin cells. Blocking antibodies copied the genetic knockout. Since IL13 drugs already exist, the authors urge trials.
pmc-12828049:
Giacomo Gattoni and colleagues straighten out the family tree of an ancient gene that marks the front end of animals, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The gene, FoxQ2, is a forkhead transcription factor found across animals with heads, yet reports of it were tangled, with claims of fast change, losses, and duplicates. The team rebuilt its history from twenty-one animal phyla.

Gene trees plus neighbor-gene maps revealed three ancient copies in early bilaterians. All three reached the chordate ancestor, and vertebrates still keep two, a richer set than texts had credited. Expression tests in mollusks, acorn worms' kin, amphioxus, and zebrafish, plus staining in five chordates, showed two copies marking the front end as expected. The third copy works in the gut lining instead. The authors credit ancient duplication for the gene's fast evolution: freed copies could specialize.
pmc-12829249:
Yifei Xu and seven co-authors report a 2025 study linking heart rhythm to anxiety felt before stress begins. Fifty-nine adults were split by a short survey into low baseline anxiety, with thirty-two people, and high baseline anxiety, with twenty-seven. Each group then faced the same test sequence.

Heart signals were recorded at rest, during a social stress test, and during recovery. Six heart rate measures were tracked across three types of analysis. Under stress, the low group showed sharp shifts in several measures, while the high group changed on only one. In recovery, the low group's measures bounced back, but the high group's did not, leaving clear gaps between groups. The authors say high prior anxiety may blunt and prolong the body's stress response and limit how well it settles.
pmc-12831249:
Babies born early face higher infection risk, and their vaccine schedules often drift late. Ahmed El Beleidy and a panel of Egyptian experts produced a consensus statement in 2025 to standardize how preterm infants in Egypt are vaccinated.

Eighteen specialists in pediatrics, neonatology, and pharmacy worked through a modified Delphi process. They drafted 59 statements across fifteen vaccine topics from the literature, then voted on a five-point scale with a seventy percent bar for agreement. Statements that missed the bar were revised and voted on again. Most cleared in the first round. The final set gives clinicians shared, evidence-based rules for catching fragile infants up on time.
pmc-12834949:
Xiaojing Shen and five co-authors refine a method for extracting saponins from a ginseng relative, in this 2025 paper. Saponins are plant compounds of interest for medicines and supplements. The plant, Panax zingiberensis, is usually harvested for its roots, so its stems and leaves go to waste. The team targeted that waste stream.

They used ultrasound plus two enzymes to free the compounds, tuning each setting first alone and then with a response surface design. The best mix used a one-to-five enzyme ratio, a mildly acidic bath, a 55-degree bath, and about 29 minutes of ultrasound. The yield reached 37.12 percent of the material. Chemical fingerprinting then found 42 saponin compounds, most of them of the dammarane type found in ginseng. The authors offer the recipe as a base for using the whole plant.
pmc-12835149:
Querzoli and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on job exposures and cancer change in a benign nose tumor. The tumor can turn into squamous cell cancer in some patients. Virus links were studied before; work exposures may also matter. Thirty-two cases from twenty ten to twenty twenty-two are reviewed. Job histories come from a national nose cancer registry survey. About two in five cases report exposure to known or likely carcinogens. Most patients also have smoking histories. Active virus shows in just one case.

Simple tests find no direct link between exposure and cancer change. Grouping analysis still finds three patient types. One high-exposure, low-smoking group is entirely cancer cases. The authors urge targeted checks for exposed groups.
pmc-12835449:
Hae Won Kim and Saem Yi Kang tested a brief web program in 2025 for high-risk drinking among female college students in Korea. The goal was not only current drinking but future pregnancy safety, since alcohol in pregnancy harms the child. Twenty-three students took the program and twenty-three served as controls.

The half-hour online session covered prevention for future pregnancies, with a month of daily drinking tracking by phone app. Afterward, the program group held less positive attitudes toward drinking in pregnancy and stronger intentions to abstain. Their confidence in refusing drinks also improved. Attitude and intention gaps between groups held over time. The authors call the short format effective and worth wider use.
pmc-12836849:
Jielong Wu and co-authors link a combined state of muscle loss and excess fat to mild thinking decline in China. Their 2025 study uses a national aging survey with base data from 2015 and follow-ups in 2018 and 2020. Prior proof of the link over time was thin.

More than eleven thousand adults aged forty-five and up took part. The combined state was rare, found in well under two percent. That group scored lowest on thinking tests and had the highest rates of new decline at both follow-ups. Risk ran about twice that of other groups. Older adults and women were hit hardest. The authors urge early screening for the paired state to protect brain health.
pmc-12836949:
Vu Nhi Ha and thirteen colleagues report the first detection of occult hepatitis B among ethnic minority students in Vietnam. Occult infection means viral DNA is present while the usual surface antigen test stays negative. That hidden state threatens blood safety and escapes routine screening. Data on Vietnam's ethnic minorities were scarce. The twenty twenty-five study tested 267 antigen-negative students at a medical university in Thai Nguyen.

Blood samples were screened for hepatitis B antibodies, and viral DNA was amplified and sequenced. Sixteen percent of students carried core antibodies, a sign of past exposure. Fifty-seven percent were fully susceptible, having neither infection nor vaccine markers. Finding occult infection in this population argues for DNA-level screening where antigen tests alone are trusted. It also highlights vaccination gaps among minority students.
pmc-12837049:
Linjing Nie and co-authors study a uric acid ratio in chronic kidney disease in this 2025 paper. Uric acid links to kidney decline, but the connection is disputed. Their marker divides blood uric acid by the urate passed in urine over a day. Records covered 165 patients at a Shanghai hospital.

Kidney events meant losing half of filtration function, starting replacement therapy, or death. Analysis covered the whole group and subgroups by sex and diabetes status. The signal in the title appeared in men without diabetes. Higher ratios tracked with worse kidney outcomes there. Receiver curves tested how well the ratio separates patients who progress. A urine based ratio may flag risk that blood values alone miss.
pmc-12837249:
Jui-Ming Sun and co-authors wrote a 2025 review of how body state shapes oxidative stress in stroke. Oxidative stress, where harmful oxygen byproducts build up, is a core part of stroke damage. The review argues that its size and timing shift with age, metabolic strain, and body clock upset.

Aging weakens cell power unit upkeep and blunts a key shield response. Obesity and diabetes raise the burden through enzyme firing and fat damage. Clock upset narrows the hours when the brain can best resist harm, since shield enzymes lose their rhythm. The authors name shared signal hubs that join these inputs. They propose stroke care timed to the clock and tuned to metabolic state.
pmc-12837449:
Jiacheng Shen, Kun Fang, Yu Qiu, and Li Li study how frailty and ventilator strength combine to affect survival in intensive care, in a 2025 paper. Frail patients have little reserve, and strong breathing support can itself injure. Their joint effect was little explored.

Records for 17,881 critically ill patients came from two large databases. Higher ventilator power and higher lab based frailty each raised hospital death risk. Together they did worse than either alone would suggest. Each step up in power added about 8 percent risk per set increment. Frailty steps added about 18 percent. The pairing argues for gentler ventilation in the frailest patients.
pmc-12838449:
Kubra Sahan and Emre Boz published a sports study in 2025 on how music tempo affects athletes in traditional Turkish archery. The field is little studied, and the team wanted hard measures rather than opinion. Fourteen student athletes shot first in silence, then to music at slow, medium, and fast tempos. The team recorded heart rate, shot timing, shot count, scores, and draw form.

Faster music raised heart rates and shortened shot time. Shots without music took longest, while medium tempo gave the most efficient pace. Scores were highest with no music and with medium tempo, and lower at slow and fast tempos. Draw form did not change with music type. The authors suggest medium tempo music best supports performance.
pmc-12839249:
Kibrom Alula and co-authors show that a plant compound, celastrol, calms gut inflammation by waking a heat-shock switch in immune cells, in a 2025 study. Inflammatory bowel disease springs from a gut immune system off its leash. Regulatory T cells are the leash holders, and a master switch called HSF1, which guards cells against protein misfolding, had earlier proved to tune them. Celastrol is known to flip that switch.

In dishes, celastrol switched HSF1 on inside regulatory cells and sharpened their calming work. In mice it grew their numbers in the body. Two mouse models of bowel disease, a cell-transfer colitis and a genetic ileitis, both eased under the drug. Mice bred to lack the switch in their T cells tested the chain of cause. The authors read a clean line from switch to cell to calm gut, and flag celastrol as a lead worth clinical study.
pmc-12841149:
Paul Stănescu and co-authors make and test clay-based hydrogels in this 2025 paper. Hydrogels are water-swollen polymer networks used in medicine and industry. Adding nano clay as the crosslinker, instead of a chemical one, can make a gel far more stretchable and squeezable.

The team polymerized a formamide-based monomer in water with a synthetic clay and a heat-activated starter. Tests confirmed the gel's makeup. The clay gels swelled in two stages and reached over 90 percent compression and about 840 percent stretch, far beyond chemically linked or sister gels. Repeated squeezing showed better spring and stability too. The authors credit an even network of flexible chains.
pmc-12842649:
Baris Eren surveys the genetic diversity of alfalfa in Turkey's Aras Basin, in a solo study from 2025. The basin sits where three major gene centres meet, a crossroads for forage legume evolution. DNA fingerprints from 74 plants, wild stands and bred cultivars mixed, were scored with ISSR markers to map variation and group structure.

Variation ran broad, a sign of strong adaptive potential in this mixed landscape. Three genetic clusters emerged, splitting wild material from registered varieties, and plants from the western, central and eastern subregions grouped apart as well. Eren offers the results as a guide for breeding choices and for conserving the basin's distinct alfalfa heritage.
pmc-12844049:
Inci Boztepe, Shuaifei Zhao, Xing Yang, and Lingxue Kong present a 2025 review on designing better protein-purification membranes with computer simulation. Ion-exchange nanofiber membranes promise fast, high-throughput chromatography for making biologic drugs. Their binding capacity, though, is poorly understood, and lab tuning is slow and costly. The review argues meso-scale modeling, between atomistic and bulk, is the sweet spot for predicting how proteins meet fibers.

Such models can probe binding access, salt effects, and surface charge at longer timescales than molecular models allow. Obstacles remain: these messy pore shapes are hard to represent well, and adsorption models are often too simple. The authors propose pairing the models with lab tests to speed design while cutting cost. Their framework targets next-generation separations in bioprocessing and analysis.
pmc-12846349:
Andrei V Chaplin and fourteen co-authors introduce Adele, a newly isolated virus that kills Pseudomonas bacteria, in this 2025 study. Such viruses, called phages, are back in focus as drug resistant infections spread. Adele belongs to a known genus but counts as a new species, and the team profiles it from genes to behavior.

The phage wakes fast, bursting each infected cell in about twenty minutes with roughly fifty-nine offspring. It dissolved bacterial films and killed most tested strains of its target, a common hospital pathogen. In wax moth larvae it gave strong protection against infection. Family comparisons show an ancient, stable body plan dressed up by lineage specific tweaks, plus a rich kit of stolen metabolic and anti defense genes. The authors present Adele as both a therapy candidate and an evolution case study.
pmc-12846449:
Warisraporn Tangchang and four co-authors describe unusual growths inside lung blood vessels of wild Korean raccoon dogs, in a 2025 study. Such vessel growths are barely documented in animals. The team examined 13 cases found in this one species.

Under the microscope, finger like growths lined the thickened vessel walls. Stains showed a single cell layer over cores of muscle and collagen. Marker tests confirmed the growths were benign vessel lining, not cancer. Many dogs also carried heartworm or scabies, hinting at chronic vessel injury from parasites. The authors suspect these growths are underrecognized in raccoon dogs. More work is needed on what triggers them.
pmc-12848049:
Lei Bai and co-authors report a catalyst study on turning acetylene into polymer grade ethylene with electricity. The standard heat based route is costly, so an electric route draws strong interest. High current often drives wasteful hydrogen evolution instead, which cuts the share of current that makes ethylene.

The team built a copper palladium single atom alloy catalyst. It reached high ethylene efficiency at large current and stayed stable for many hours in flow cell tests. Tests in a membrane electrode assembly also showed long stability for crude ethylene purification. Spectroscopy and calculations point to direct hydrogenation through palladium hydride species. That path lowers the energy barrier and limits hydrogen loss.
pmc-12849149:
Mei-Yuan Teo and ten co-authors hunt death marks in ICU folks with blood ills from a drug-proof lung germ. Their past-look study appeared in twenty twenty-five. One hundred sixty-eight grown ICU folks at a Taiwan ward from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-one were read. All had breath fail on machines.

Death at one month ran past six in ten. The dead bore high germ and part-fail scores, more kidney swap care, more belly ills, low plate counts, and high flare reads. Flare reads and part-fail scores stood as lone death marks. One drug and fast fit drugs tied to life.
pmc-12849249:
Hitesh Chohan, Harisha Dewan, and eight colleagues test whether tooth desensitizers weaken the grip of fillings on dentin, in a laboratory study published in two thousand twenty-five. Desensitizers seal sensitive teeth, but anything painted on dentin before bonding might interfere with the adhesive a restoration depends on.

The experiment used one hundred forty-four freshly extracted, cavity-free upper premolars. Surfaces were etched, then split among three commercial desensitizers or none, and restored with two bulk-fill composites or a conventional one. The team then sheared the restorations off and measured the force required. Twelve teeth filled each subgroup, keeping comparisons balanced. Bonding strength decides whether fillings stay put for years or pop out early. A desensitizer that comforts the patient but loosens the filling trades one problem for another. This bench study quantifies that trade-off before it reaches the dental chair.
pmc-12849349:
Cynthia Quarshie and co-authors ask mental health service users in Ghana how they view the country's 2023 decision to stop treating attempted suicide as a crime, in a 2025 qualitative study. The old law dated to 1960. Reformers hoped removing it would free people to seek help, but the voices of those most affected had not been heard.

The team interviewed thirty adults with personal experience of suicidal thoughts or attempts at a teaching hospital in Accra. Views of suicide itself split: some called it an escape or a reaction to stress, and some defended its past criminal status while others rejected it. On the reform's effect, hopeful themes sat beside worried ones. The study traces how users expect help-seeking to change now that the threat of prosecution is gone, in their own words.
pmc-12849449:
Deborah Mitchison and co-authors describe a binational registry tracking eating disorder treatment in a 2025 paper. Australia and New Zealand spend heavily on eating disorder care yet lack shared outcome tracking, especially outside hospitals. The TrEAT Registry fills that gap across clinics, day programs, residential care, and wards.

From 2021 to 2025, 754 clients were invited to share their de-identified treatment data; about 88 percent agreed, and nearly all who agreed finished the starting survey. The group was mostly young and female. Standard questionnaires track symptoms, impairment, and distress at intake, during care, and at discharge. The registry aims to benchmark services and lift care quality.
pmc-12849549:
Mary Tabit tells how a collegiate recovery program was built from scratch in two thousand twenty-five. Such programs back students healing from substance use disorders, a risk that peaks in the college years. No single gold-standard model exists, so each campus shapes its own.

Tabit writes as a co-director who spent a year launching one at a four-year United States institution. The account covers setting priorities, drawing in campus partners, and gauging student needs. Handouts and tools made along the way are included. Lessons stress patience: the build is slow, resource-hungry, and keeps evolving. Fitting the program to campus culture, she argues, matters more than copying any template.
pmc-12849749:
Xiaomei Zhu and co-authors published this study in 2025. It reports real-world results for risdiplam, a daily oral drug for spinal muscular atrophy. Trials had shown the drug works; clinic data from China were scarce. One children's hospital followed twelve patients with types 1 to 3 of the disease, treated between 2021 and 2024. Motor scores, milestones, breathing, and feeding were tracked for eight to eighteen months.

Eleven of the twelve children improved in motor function. Nine reached new motor milestones, after about ten months on average. Younger children and those treated earlier gained the most. Side effects were mostly chest infections, blamed on the disease rather than the drug. No child stopped treatment or died. The authors back the drug's value in daily practice, and stress early diagnosis.
pmc-12852549:
Sousan Heydarpour and three co-authors test hypnosis for easing distress linked to premenstrual syndrome in a 2025 trial. The study enrolled sixty female university students living in dormitories in western Iran. Half received the treatment and half received none, allowing a direct comparison.

The treatment group took three weekly group hypnosis sessions of one hour each. Both groups filled a standard distress survey before treatment and three months after the last session. After treatment, scores for depression, anxiety, and stress were all clearly lower in the hypnosis group. No serious adverse events were reported. The authors conclude that hypnosis helped this group, while noting the trial was not blinded for participants or staff.
pmc-12852749:
Ahmed Abdou and co-authors assess industrial pollution in the Nile River at Aswan, Egypt, in a 2025 study. The river supplies drinking water, irrigation, fishing, and tourism, yet untreated factory waste flows into it. The team combined water sampling with map-based interpolation to see pollution patterns between sampling points.

Two standard water quality indices rated water near factory outflows as poor to very poor. Upstream and downstream stretches away from outflows rated good. The worst sites carried high loads of oxygen-demanding waste, solids, murkiness, nitrogen, and phenol. The authors say spatial mapping caught gradients that spot sampling alone would miss. They support enforcing Egypt's water protection law and link the work to global clean water goals.
pmc-12853249: Cheon, editor of the journal Ultrasonography, thanks the journal's peer reviewers in a short 2026 notice. The piece names the winners of the 2025 Best Reviewer Awards. Awards rest on the quality, speed, and volume of reviews done across the year, and each winner gets a certificate and a letter of congratulations. The board also thanks the full pool of reviewers for their care and expertise, which it credits with upholding the journal's standards.
pmc-12853749:
Lingxiao Gao and co-authors measure what happened to stroke care bills when a large hospital in northeast China moved to diagnosis-based lump payments. Under the new system, hospitals get a fixed sum per case group instead of billing item by item. The reform aims to slow cost growth and protect insurance funds.

Records ran from 2018 through 2024, spanning the switch. Matching methods paired like patients across the change, and a difference-in-differences design isolated the policy's effect. Stay length, cost makeup, and the patients' own share of bills were all tracked. Payment rules quietly steer ward behavior. This study shows the steering in numbers.
pmc-12853849:
Duygu Gozen and co-workers survey Turkish neonatal nurses on tube feeding of premature babies, in a 2025 study. Nurses run this feeding day to day, yet their knowledge had not been measured. Three hundred intensive care nurses in eight Istanbul hospitals took a forty-item knowledge test.

The average score was about sixty-seven out of one hundred. Older age, longer unit experience, more education, and certification each came with higher scores. Weak spots included tube size choice for the smallest babies, positioning, placement checks, flow rate, and sterile technique. No unit in the study used a standard feeding protocol. The authors call for evidence-based training and shared protocols.
pmc-12858849:
Yaodong Yu and a large team build a palladium-carbon catalyst that turns carbon dioxide into formic acid. Their study from twenty twenty-five works under acidic conditions. Acidic conversion promises high rates but suffers low efficiency and short catalyst life. Solving all three problems at once is the challenge.

Tiny carbon atoms sit inside the palladium crystal structure. That placement softens how the surface binds key intermediates. Formic acid then forms and leaves without poisoning the surface. Computer models and lab characterisation agree on the mechanism. Intermediate coverage improved while the product escaped cleanly. Current densities reached industrially interesting levels in the work. Carbon recycling gains a sturdier catalyst design.
pmc-12859849:
Hung Mai Trong and co-authors compare early and late blood infections in preterm babies in Vietnam, in work from twenty twenty-five. Blood infection still causes much illness and death in babies born early. Few local studies have set the early and late forms side by side. The study runs at a large birth hospital and uses proven culture results. Babies treated over close to two years are included.

Late infection made up most cases and hit the smallest babies hardest. Those babies showed worse breathing and heart signs. Early cases linked more to birth weight and to fever or infection in the mother. Blood tests and spinal fluid tests also split by timing. Germ types split too, with one germ leading early and another leading late. Knowing the split can speed first treatment where resources are tight.
pmc-12859949:
Shadi Hazhir and co-authors (2025) reviewed studies of health chatbots built for underserved and vulnerable people. Chatbots are cheap to reach and always available, which suits groups the health system serves poorly. The team searched six databases with no date limits and followed scoping review rules. Eighteen studies qualified. Most appeared after 2020, and the largest share came from the United States. Adolescents and women were the main audiences.

Mental health and sexual health dominated the topics. Most bots followed fixed rules rather than learning models. Social media and web pages were the main delivery channels. Only nine studies formally evaluated their bot, mostly for acceptability and feasibility. The authors find the field young and thin outside a few countries. They see real potential for closing access gaps. They urge researchers to build and test more bots with these populations in the design room, not only as end users.
pmc-12860049:
Atif Adnan and co-authors present the first full mitochondrial genome study of two groups in northern Pakistan in a 2025 paper. The Gilgiti and Kohistani peoples live at a crossroads of past migration, yet their genetics are little studied. Past work looked only at a small control region of the mitochondrial DNA, which is passed down the mother line.

The team read 120 complete mitochondrial genomes with modern sequencing. Both groups showed high diversity. One group bore signs of balancing selection, and the other of recent growth. The team also found variants tied to a hereditary eye nerve disease, which are known to cause harm only in some carriers. The data serve both history and health aims.
pmc-12860149:
Roselyne Clouet and co-authors ran a 2025 study on whether playing music helps dental students start with stronger hand skills. Dental work needs fine hand control, good spatial sense, and steady technique. Music training uses like skills, so the team tested whether student musicians start ahead.

The study enrolled 85 first-year dental students with no past clinical training. Of these, 33 were musicians and 52 were not. Each student took a mental rotation test, a hand precision test, and a timed task on a printed tooth model. Students also rated how hard each task felt. Musicians did better on the tooth task, which asks for a correct pulp opening. The results hint that music practice may give new dental students an early edge.
pmc-12861649:
Marianne Novak wrote a short paper in 2025 on the names doctors give to functional disorders. These are real health problems where scans and tests do not show clear damage. The paper centers on one such condition that affects movement and the senses. Novak weighs the word functional against other terms doctors might use in its place.

The paper looks at what a label should avoid, such as names that are wrong or that split mind from body. It also weighs how a chosen name shapes the care a patient feels they get. A label can affect how a person views their own illness. It can also affect what services are offered to them. The piece gives clinicians a clear frame for picking words with care.
pmc-12864749:
Marie-France Jilderda and colleagues checked whether a gene-based test can safely flag breast cancer patients whose chance of distant return is truly minimal. The Breast Cancer Index had earlier suggested that about a fifth of postmenopausal patients with early, hormone-sensitive, node-negative cancer face under a five percent ten-year risk even without hormone therapy. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team validated the adjusted test in two large sources: a Dutch national registry cohort and an international trial cohort, all treated with five years of hormone therapy.

About fifteen percent of patients landed in the minimal risk class in each cohort. Their distant recurrence risks over ten years stayed in the low single digits, well below the higher classes. The score added information beyond standard clinical factors. The authors say the validation supports using the class to guide treatment discussions.
pmc-12865949:
Jessica Gronsbell and co-authors critically review the algorithms that guess a patient's gender from electronic health records. Records often lack gender data, so computational phenotyping fills the hole from diagnosis codes, prescriptions, and notes. The tools were meant to make trans and gender-expansive patients visible in research.

The authors argue the outputs can be misused and the inferences can misfire in ways that harm the very populations they aim to serve. Their narrative review collects the methodological and ethical problems and the recommendations already on the table, then proposes priorities. Inference about identity demands more care than inference about lab values.
pmc-12866349:
Jinchuang Li and co-authors present a 2025 study on a blood index that predicts survival after ischemic stroke. The index, EASIX, combines three routine labs tied to vessel lining stress: platelet count, creatinine, and an enzyme level. The team mined a large intensive care database for its link to death rates.

They enrolled 3,625 patients and split them into four bands by the index. The top band died far more often: thirty-two percent within thirty days and about half within a year, against fifteen and twenty-nine percent in the lowest band. After full adjustment the top band still carried roughly 1.29 times the thirty-day risk and 1.25 times the one-year risk. The authors propose the index for sharper risk sorting.
pmc-12868849:
Fuxin Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 materials paper on ultra-thin films that filter organic solvents for industry. Solvent filtering saves energy compared with boiling methods, but membranes must be both picky and tough, and hard to make at scale. The team built films under twenty nanometres thick by a standard coating reaction.

Into the film's backbone they wove twisted, fluorine-rich segments alongside flexible, water-loving parts. The mix forms a rigid yet flexible pore network with two faces of character, which the authors call a Janus framework. The structure steers both how solvent dissolves into the film and how it travels through, aiming at durable, selective filtering.
pmc-12870249:
Nan Zhou and co-authors test a plant compound for polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2025 study. The syndrome is the most common hormone and fuel disorder in women of child bearing age. The compound comes from a root herb used in Chinese care, and the team trace how it may act.

Fluid and cells from patients showed low levels of a gene called FDX1, tied to cell growth. In mice with the syndrome, the compound fixed cycle timing, egg sac growth, sugar handling, and ovary shape. It also raised FDX1 and a growth marker in the ovary. Cell tests that cut or boosted FDX1 confirm its role in the effect. The chain runs through a known growth signal path in the cells.
pmc-12872849:
Lershito Antonio Pasamba and nine colleagues test a phone app that nudges Indonesian schoolgirls to take their weekly iron tablets. Anemia stalks adolescent girls, and weekly iron-folic acid pills fight it, but adherence lags worldwide. The Jaga Diri app sent weekly reminders and short lessons on anemia and the supplements.

Eighty-two girls at two senior high schools in Maluku took part for four weeks, one school on the app, the other on routine services. App users finished with clearly higher anemia knowledge scores. Adherence, counted as taking at least three quarters of the tablets, was checked by self-report with hemoglobin backing. The team argues cheap digital nudges can move a stubborn habit.
pmc-12883649:
Peng Lu and seven co-authors find a blood protein pattern that warns who will fall ill with tuberculosis, in a 2025 study. The catalog lists the paper under 2026, while the text itself gives 2025 as the year. Today's immune tests show infection but cannot tell who will progress to active disease. The team ran deep protein scans on blood from sixty exposed students in Jiangsu, China, forty of them infected.

Over two years, twenty-one of the infected students developed active disease. A model built from baseline samples picked out a protein signature tied to actin and clotting pathways. That signature predicted progression with strong accuracy. A test of this kind could target preventive therapy to the few who truly need it.
pmc-12892849:
