Shabaev and co-authors test a dissolving drug-coated stent covering in sheep, a stand-in for human arteries. pmc-12901449:

pmc-12904149:

pmc-12906749:
Lujaw Ratna Tuladhar and co-authors present a 2025 observational study of poisoning and overdose cases reaching one Nepali teaching hospital's emergency department. pmc-12913849:
Miguel Gonzalez-Lozano and Jose Alberto Cano-Buendia review chitosan nanoparticles as carriers for DNA vaccines in animals. Chitosan is a natural polymer that breaks down safely in the body and sticks to wet tissue. The review came out in twenty twenty-five.

Recent work shows strong body and cell defense, plus defense at wet surfaces, in farm stock, poultry, fish, and shrimp. Targets range across many virus ills. Doses have gone in by nose, muscle, belly, or mouth, which suits mass use.
pmc-12915349:

pmc-12916049:
José Rosas-Díaz and co-authors compare two coverings for gum graft donor wounds under the microscope in a study from 2025. The palate supplies most connective tissue grafts in gum surgery. pmc-12918749:
Behnam Oboudi, Robert Book, and Ekaterina Glebova reviewed sexual harassment in sport across studies from 2020 to 2025 in a 2025 paper. The problem persists as a safeguarding failure in clubs and federations. The review sorts risk factors, guiding theories, and prevention ideas into one account.

pmc-12958149:
Margaret Wallhagen asks what makes a health system kind to old age in a 2025 commentary. The piece replies to a review that built a frame for the idea, as lands plan for more and more older adults.

Hard data on outcomes are scarce, and the core parts of a kind system are still argued over. Wallhagen probes what the word friendly should mean in care. She asks how the frame can sit inside a view of health that spans the whole life, not just the late years. The piece urges care in how the label is used and what it claims.
pmc-13002549:
Zulal Keles and co-authors search for the genetic causes of inherited retinal diseases in a Turkish patient group. These diseases slowly destroy vision and can stem from faults in more than three hundred genes. Clear culprit variants turned up in twenty-four patients. Four of the faults had never been reported before. One patient carried a fault in a gene usually tied to wider body syndromes, yet showed eye disease alone. Another had a rare form of Usher syndrome, which joins vision and hearing loss. The authors say broad gene reading sharpens diagnosis and opens the door to gene-based treatment planning.
pmc-13037649:
Yahia Hassan Ali and co-authors survey a livestock virus in 2025 in northern Saudi Arabia. Pestivirus infects sheep and goats and harms herds, but its current local spread was unclear. The team tests blood from 850 animals, mostly sheep, collected at a slaughterhouse in Rafha.

About a quarter of all animals carry antibodies, with goats higher than sheep, females higher than males, and adults higher than the young. One breed reaches nearly half. Statistical tests tie infection to species, sex, and breed. The authors conclude the virus is spreading in the north and across the country, and they call for control steps.
pmc-13059849:
Fernanda Paulino and co-authors set out a protocol to map tools that measure caring culture in health services in a 2025 paper. Findings will be charted by tool design and setting. Since only published sources are used, no ethics approval is needed.
pmc-13087449:
Felipe Ponce-Fuentes and co-authors test, in a 2026 trial, if a cuff that limits blood flow boosts the pain relief that shoulder exercise gives after rotator cuff repair. Twenty-three adults who had keyhole repair of a worn cuff took part. Each did three shoulder holds that squeeze the muscle with no move. In one session the holds came with the cuff; in the next, the holds came alone. The order was set by chance, and each person crossed to the other arm of the trial.

Fear of move, function loss, and life quality were logged for links to the pain shift.
pmc-13094649:
Yuetong Liu, Ge Hong, Tianjun Liu, and Hong Liu test a light-based therapy that wakes up the immune system against breast cancer, in a study from 2026. pmc-13099449:

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but blood-rich tumor of teenage males that usually causes nose symptoms. This patient, a 19-year-old, showed only a bulging eye for seven months.

Unusually, its main feeding artery came straight from the external carotid artery rather than the typical branch. pmc-13118349:
Wenxian Wen and co-authors trace how hepatitis B pushes the liver toward scarring through a sugar byproduct that tags a metabolic enzyme. pmc-13127149:
Chen-Ran Wang and a large team of co-authors checked if lung cancer screening rules miss young and never smoking patients. The set held patients with no signs whose cancers were cut out, at twenty-six top hospitals since twenty fourteen. Gaps showed where the rules leave real cases out. Readers who set screening rules get proof for a wider net in a changed disease.
pmc-13127249:
Shreya Tiwari leads a 2026 review of molecularly imprinted polymers for targeted cancer therapy. pmc-13128349:
Ming Jin and six co-authors present a 2026 survey of Traditional Chinese Medicine nursing skills among clinical nurses in Guangyuan City, China. Such nursing joins classic Chinese methods with standard care. The team asked how strong these skills are and what shapes them, to guide training plans.

pmc-13128649:

pmc-13130049:
Cheewita Suwanchawalit and co-authors study tunable bismuth oxyhalide pairs for breaking down dye under visible light in a 2026 paper. pmc-13132549:

pmc-13136449:

pmc-13136849:

pmc-13139249:

pmc-13141449:

pmc-13144549:

pmc-13144749:

pmc-13144849:

pmc-13145549:

pmc-13145849:

pmc-13146249:

pmc-13146749:

pmc-13147049:

pmc-13147149:

pmc-13147349:

pmc-13147449:

pmc-13147749:

pmc-13148749:

pmc-13151649:

Surgery went smoothly, and recovery went well. The authors call the approach promising, while asking for more studies to set standard practice.
pmc-13202049:
Hearing loss is a leading modifiable risk factor for dementia, and a 2026 study protocol by Lisa M Shulman lays out a three-year comparison of two hearing treatments. The protocol describes the ARCH study, which follows older adults using cochlear implants or hearing aids at an academic medical center.

The study will enroll 210 older adults in six subgroups defined by hearing level, device use, and cognitive status. Its main outcome is change in real-time, patient-reported listening experience gathered through ecological momentary assessment in daily life. Laboratory hearing and thinking tests, plus measures of loneliness, mood, and quality of life, support the comparison through completion in 2029.
pmc-13202249:
Marianne Månsson and her three co-authors, publishing in 2026, dig into a puzzle inside Europe's big prostate screening trial. Overall, screening cut prostate cancer deaths by about 20 percent over sixteen years. But the two centers they compare diverged wildly: Sweden's cut reached 37 percent, Finland's just 9. The teams started with very different sizes, about 65,000 Finnish men against 10,700 Swedish.

The screening recipes differed too. Swedes were invited every two years with a lower biopsy threshold; Finns every four with a higher one. Screening raised cancer detection in both, 44 percent in Sweden and 21 percent in Finland. The key surprise sat in Finland's control group, whose death rates ran unexpectedly low from the start. The authors blame widespread informal testing blurring the trial's contrast, a warning for screening research everywhere.
pmc-13202849:
People living with HIV now age on therapy, yet their brains show Alzheimer-like changes, extra amyloid and tau, more often than expected. Biju Bhargavan, Narendran Annadurai, and Georgette Kanmogne ask in 2026 whether the virus alone drives that, or whether an older drug, azidothymidine, still used where resources are thin, adds to it.

In humanized mice they measured virus levels, immune suppression, and brain markers. The list included phosphorylated tau at three sites, amyloid levels, neuron counts, and the gate proteins of the blood-brain barrier. Two transporters that move amyloid in and out were also tracked. HIV raised tau and amyloid and lowered a protective transporter. Cell tests added the viral protein Tat to the mix. The design separates drug effects from virus effects.
pmc-13203449:
Didier Serteyn and co-authors inject in a 2026 study a horse's own muscle-grown stem cells into its arthritic joints and track the outcome openly. Evidence for the horse's own cells as a stand-alone therapy is thin. Thirteen horses with chronic osteoarthritis each got one injection per sore joint, dosed by joint size.

Lameness and inflammation scores fell significantly by six and twelve weeks. Seven of thirteen horses met the responder bar, several losing their lameness entirely. Reactions were mild, brief, and needed no treatment. The open design cannot exclude placebo-like effects, but the safety and signal justify a controlled trial.
pmc-13203749:
Huichi Qian and co-authors study in 2026 how feeling like an underdog at work can push employees toward nasty behavior toward coworkers. Underdog expectations mean sensing that others rate your chances low, a cue that can sting and steer conduct. A three wave survey of 221 employees tracked these feelings, two inner states, and later behavior over time.

Feeling underrated predicted more interpersonal harm, through two paths at once: a loosened moral brake, and a weaker sense of being an insider. Oddly, strong pride in the organization made both paths stronger, not weaker. The authors say low expectations can wound through both ties and thoughts, and that pride can sharpen the sting.
pmc-13205249:
Lu Qiu and three colleagues present a 2026 economics study mapping how housing price shocks travel between Chinese cities. Treating cities separately misses the contagion pattern. So the team fused a spatial gravity model with a time-series method that measures directed information flow over finite windows. They fed in prices from 296 cities.

The resulting network is hierarchical. Eastern coastal cities and the national core act as the main radiating hubs. Regional stories differ: the north settled from many centers into one dominated by Beijing. The east kept several strong centers anchored by Shanghai. The south moved from Guangzhou alone to a trio with Shenzhen and Nanning. The map can guide regulators watching for regional housing contagion.
pmc-13205649:
Newer tobacco products are popular with teenagers, and a 2026 analysis led by Jinyoung Kim links them to asthma diagnoses in South Korea. Drawing on the national Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey from 2022 to 2024, the study compares asthma prevalence across patterns of cigarette, e-cigarette, and heated tobacco use.

The dataset held more than one hundred fifty-nine thousand students in grades seven through twelve. Asthma was uncommon overall, yet odds were higher for every user group than for non-users after adjustment in the authors' models. Teenagers using both e-cigarettes and heated products showed the highest odds, and the authors stress the design cannot prove these products cause asthma.
pmc-13205949:
Xingdong Yang and co-authors build a fast test for a deadly food toxin in a 2026 study. Bongkrekic acid comes from a bacterium that spoils fermented rice and wheat foods, snow fungus, and black fungus. It attacks breathing at the cell level and has caused fatal outbreaks. A quick on-site screen could stop poisoned food before it is eaten.

The team raised a monoclonal antibody that binds the toxin tightly and built a glowing enzyme test around it. In the competitive format, toxin in the sample dims the glow in proportion to its amount. The test reads down to a few picograms per milliliter, works across a wide range, and runs many samples at once. They target two risky foods named in the title: tremella fungus and rice noodles.
pmc-13206149:
Tetsuya Nakajima and co-authors, in a 2026 study, hunted for gene regions that control leaf color in bunching onion. Dark green leaves sell well, so the trait matters to growers. Yet the genes behind it have been poorly known. The team used a meter score for leaf green, called SPAD, as a stand in for color.

They crossed a dark green line with a light green line, and built a map of the offspring's genes from RNA based markers. The map held 765 markers across eight groups. Leaf scores differed clearly between the parent lines, and most of that gap traced to genes. Strong gene regions turned up on two chromosomes, each explaining a large share of the color gap. Helpful variants came from both parents, the team found.
pmc-13206449:
Brain scans must correct for head size, and a 2026 study led by Aliza Brzezinski-Rittner asks which correction method distorts sex differences least. Working with UK Biobank imaging, the authors compare four ways of adjusting for total intracranial volume when estimating how male and female brains differ.

They built a reference standard by matching men and women on age and head size, removing the confound directly. Against that benchmark, simply adding head size as a covariate in the model performed best across brain measures and brain regions. Common smoothing of the imaging data could itself bias the estimates, a caution the authors raise for the field.
pmc-13206649:
Masaki Ishida and co-authors compare gene testing paths in advanced lung cancer in 2026. Picking the right first treatment hinges on finding driver gene changes in the tumor. Clinics test either gene by gene or with one broad panel at once. The team reviewed outcomes across many centers for both paths.

Single gene testing found a key growth gene change more often in this study. That path also led to more use of matched targeted drugs and longer survival. Broad panels may miss some changes that single tests catch. The findings matter most where that gene change is common in the population.
pmc-13206949:
Ondřej Sobotka and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, a new way to prove poisoning by the diabetes drug metformin: testing the energy machinery of blood platelets directly. The poisoning floods the blood with acid and is usually inferred from side markers. A direct measure could confirm it faster.

The patient, sixty-five, had overdosed on purpose on several drugs at once. Dialysis cleared the drug and the acid, yet low blood sugar raged for six days. Platelet testing on day two showed deep shutdown of the first energy complex even as blood levels fell. The authors call that gap a toxicodynamic lag. Recovery showed by day seven.
pmc-13207349:
Arjumand Fatima and Onaiza Maqbool build a dataset of software advice from Stack Overflow in a 2026 paper. Developer forums hold rich tips on which tools to pick. Mining those tips could fuel advice systems for coders. A clean, large dataset is the first step toward that goal.

They used the full Stack Overflow dump from October 2025. Keyword filters caught questions, answers, and comments about recommendations. The set holds tens of thousands of such questions. Millions of answers and comments also matched the filters. Extra user and tag data can enrich the raw set. The data is shared on Figshare and GitHub for reuse.
pmc-13207549:
Drugs that block one of the brain's cannabis-style switches, while staying out of the brain itself, are hoped to help several diseases without mental side effects. Patryk Remiszewski and co-authors check what such a blocker does to blood pressure in a 2026 short report. Their rats had a hormone-and-salt form of high blood pressure, and the team tested the body's own cannabis-style signals on top.

The blocker alone did not move blood pressure. It did blunt both the rise and the fall caused by a stable copy of one body signal. A drug that raises the body's own signal lowered pressure, and the blocker erased that drop in the high-pressure rats while boosting it in normal ones. The authors warn that heart effects of this drug class swing with the model used.
pmc-13207749:
Şenay Demir Yazıcı, Ecem Ersungur, and Nazan Öztürk study an eight-week evening aerobic exercise program for university students in a 2026 paper. Poor sleep and low mood are common in student life and drag on its quality. Movement is a drug-free aid for both, but proof for steady evening exercise in young adults was thin.

Dozens of students were tested before and after the program. Sessions ran for an hour, three days a week, in the evening hours. Sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and each student's lean toward morning or evening were scored at both ends. The shifts are read as one set, to judge what the evening habit changed.
pmc-13207849:
An old blue dye might guard aging brains through surgery, and a 2026 review authored by Yu Wu builds the case for methylene blue. The article pulls together early and clinical evidence on perioperative neurocognitive disorders, which strike a large share of elderly patients after surgery and raise later dementia risk.

Proposed mechanisms converge on mitochondria: the dye can shuttle electrons, switch on antioxidant defenses, calm brain-cell inflammation, block tau clumping, and protect the blood-brain barrier. Small randomized trials report that one dose by vein during surgery cut delirium after surgery sharply in older patients having major non-cardiac surgery. The authors call for large trials at many centers to confirm dosing and benefit.
pmc-13207949:
Two decades of pancreatitis research are mapped in a 2026 bibliometric analysis authored by Chenlu Huang. The study retrieves basic research on acute pancreatitis causes and therapies published between 2003 and 2025 from the Web of Science, then visualizes authorship, institutions, journals, and keywords with standard mapping tools.

Six hundred thirty-two publications formed the dataset for the analysis. China produced the most papers while the United States carried the greatest citation impact in the field. Enduring themes included oxidative stress, a master inflammatory switch, and premature enzyme activation, while gut microbes, autophagy, and two forms of cell death emerged as recent hotspots for therapy ideas.
pmc-13208249:
Mohamed Ali and nine co-authors studied valve size mismatch after a heart procedure in a 2026 paper. In the TAVI procedure, a new aortic valve is threaded into place. If the valve is too small for the patient's body, blood flow suffers, a problem called mismatch. Most past work looked at patients with small valve rings, not large ones.

At one British center, 353 patients with large rings were analyzed. Some mismatch appeared in thirty-eight percent, and severe mismatch in fifteen percent. Severe cases were younger, larger-bodied, and more often given balloon-expanded valves. After about three years, deaths were somewhat more common in the severe group, though the gap was not statistically firm. The authors say even large-ring patients face real mismatch risk, and sizing choices deserve care.
pmc-13208549:
Lihua Chen and seven co-authors present a 2026 study predicting the bursting pressure of pipelines with two neighboring corrosion pits. Real corrosion comes in clusters, and nearby pits tug on each other's stress field, changing how the pipe fails. Standard assessment codes simplify the pair into one defect, which can overshoot or undershoot the true danger.

Using a common pipeline steel, the team built computer models of twin uniform pits in two layouts: side by side along the pipe, and around it. They varied pit spacing, depth, and length to see which combinations weaken the pipe most. The results feed a failure pressure prediction that respects the interaction.
pmc-13208649:
Nishioka, Azma, Mieda, and Mio study how cold storage makes blood cells shed clot-promoting particles in a 2026 paper. Whole blood is returning to trauma care, raising questions about cold-stored white cells. The particles carry tissue factor, a clotting trigger.

A human monocytic cell line was chilled, then rewarmed, with shedding tracked by flow methods. Tissue factor release rose during chilling and surged after washing and rewarming. The particles were actively shed, not leaked from dead cells, and differed from apoptotic debris. An enzyme complex generating superoxide drove the process. Antioxidant enzymes could suppress the release. The authors suggest a way to tame clotting side effects of stored blood. Trauma transfusion practice is the backdrop.
pmc-13208849:
Sorana Maria Bucur and four co-authors compare two kinds of molar bands used in braces for teens. Standard steel bands can fit poorly, trap plaque, and inflame the gums. Their 2026 trial gave one hundred eighty teens either standard bands or bands made to order by computer design and milling. Gum health was checked at the start and after one, three, and six months.

The made-to-order bands won on every measure. At six months, plaque scores and bleeding were about half those seen with standard bands, and gum pocket depth was lower too. The authors credit the snug fit of the custom bands. They present custom bands as a way to guard gum health during long brace treatment.
pmc-13210249:
Júlia dos Santos Fonseca and co-authors published a 2026 review of how worm-fighting fungi are formulated so they survive to do their work in the field. Such fungi are an environmentally friendly way to cut gut worms in farm animals and root worms in crops. A formulation must keep the fungal spores alive through manufacture, storage, and delivery. That is the hard part.

In animal care, a predatory fungus consumes the young of the worm after it passes through the gut and germinates in dung. Egg-killing fungi strike the eggs and hard cysts. The two kinds complement each other, so formulations that combine them could hit hard. The review names the commercial products on sale, and the obstacles to farm adoption: dose, route of delivery, and habit. In crops, solid formulations dominate one market, because dry stock lasts. Liquid and oil formulations serve particular tasks.
pmc-13210449:
Carlos Carpio-Cevallos and co-authors compare milled versus printed dental resins in a 2026 review. Digital fabrication now makes many temporary dental restorations. Milling and printing are the two rival routes. Which yields mechanically stronger parts remained disputed.

The review followed standard reporting guidelines with a registered protocol. Five databases were searched for head-to-head lab studies. Hardness pooling covered four studies with many specimens. Milled resins proved significantly harder on average. Printed resins trailed on bending strength too in three studies. Heterogeneity was high for hardness, modest for bending. Signs of small-study effects appeared in funnel plots. Bias was checked with a tool built for lab studies. The authors favor milling for mechanical performance today. Printing still wins on other practical grounds in clinics. Methods are detailed for anyone updating the pooling.
pmc-13210749:
Jian Shen, Hanye Liu, Zhilin Chen, and co-authors present a vision system that traces the outlines of gravel pieces on a conveyor belt in this 2026 paper. Rock plants need particle counts and sizes, read from depth maps of the moving load. Factory depth data is messy, with weak breaks, holes, and speckle.

Their framework pairs a compact transformer encoder with depth-based cues: the raw depth, its slope strength, and a second response that marks edges. A light local branch and a gated fusion step sharpen the trace, and a final pass restores full resolution. On their main dataset the scores neared the top of the scale. A test set shot under changed conditions scored nearly as well with no retraining. Repeated scans of fixed objects agreed to within a third of a pixel. The system runs at about forty-nine frames per second, fast enough for live belts.
pmc-13211149:
Shuai Li and co-authors automate the search for stable gene therapy virus formulas. Adeno-associated virus products need recipes that keep them potent in storage. New capsid types multiply the recipe space past what hand work can cover. Their platform mixes ninety-six formulas in forty minutes flat.

One plate of virus compounding takes twenty minutes more. Acidity, buffers, and virus strength are set with tight control. A proof run screened 128 recipes for the AAV1 type. Winners held high strength through frozen, chilled, and room storage. The system saves scarce virus while widening the search a great deal.
pmc-13211449:
Magdalena Druszczynska, Beata Sadowska, and their co-authors review links between the tuberculosis vaccine and brain health. Their 2026 review covers the BCG vaccine, made to prevent tuberculosis, which also retrains the innate immune system in lasting ways. That retraining changes how the body handles inflammation long after the shot.

Such immune shifts may reach the brain, where they can alter the activity of microglia, the brain's own immune cells, in pathways tied to diseases like Alzheimer's. Long infections such as tuberculosis, by contrast, keep inflammation simmering and may prime the brain toward damage. The review searched five major sources and preprint servers. It weighs the evidence that an old vaccine could protect the aging brain.
pmc-13212849:
Hongrong Zhang and four co-authors are named in a 2026 retraction notice from Discover Oncology covering their 2025 paper on a gene called BRCA1 in gastric cancer. An institutional review at a Chinese medical university triggered the withdrawal.

The review found the first author had sent in the article without a co-author's consent. It also found false details for that co-author, and a list of authors that did not match who did the work. Zhang acknowledged misrepresenting authorship. The editor-in-chief therefore lost confidence in the article's reliability. All authors agree with the retraction, which closes a case about credit and consent rather than data fabrication.
pmc-13213049:
Jacob Sampson leads a large team mapping in 2026 how genetic differences tune gene activity in the human retina. They paired whole-genome sequencing with gene activity readings from two retinal tissues taken from 201 donated eyes.

Millions of small genetic variants influenced nearby genes, far more in the light-sensing layer than in its supporting layer, though many effects were shared. The team also flagged over a thousand people whose gene activity sat far outside the usual range. Rare variants plausibly explained more than a quarter of those outlier cases. The catalogue should help interpret genetic findings in both common and rare eye diseases.
pmc-13214149:
Elisabeth Larsen Engholm and four co-authors ask patients in Denmark how it feels when a lone paramedic answers their emergency call, in a 2026 study. The single responder unit was launched in 2022 to treat more people at home and ease pressure on ambulances.

The researchers rode along on twelve shifts and later spoke by phone with twenty-two patients. Most callers said they just needed help and felt unsure what would come. Overall, patients voiced satisfaction with the unit. They valued being treated on the spot instead of being carried to hospital. The study gives a patient's-eye view of a care model that more regions are copying.
pmc-13214349:
A rare lung germ came back three times in one man because he kept quitting his drug early. Huifen Zuo and co-authors prove the relapse with gene reads, in work from twenty twenty-six. The man, in his seventies, had long bronch trouble, fever, and cough. A first drug course helped, then he stopped.

Over three years, fresh bouts sent him back to hospital again and again. Gene reads of germs from the first and third bouts matched near in full, which proves the same strain returned. A full six-month course at last cured him, with five clean years since. The case warns that sticking to the drug counts as much as naming the germ.
pmc-13215049:
Hanze Du and a large team chart in 2026 how a simple insulin-resistance index, built from fasting glucose and triglycerides, varies by age and sex across China. Reference ranges matter, because a value that is ordinary at one age may signal risk at another.

Data from a national health survey covered 4,621 adults aged twenty to eighty. Men ran higher on body mass, fats, glucose, and the index itself, with male values peaking around age forty. Women's lower range overtook men's near age fifty, and after sixty their upper range sat higher. The crossover pattern gives clinicians age-aware cut-offs for judging sugar and fat metabolism in Chinese adults.
pmc-13215549:
Josphat Kosgei and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of hepatitis B infection among people living with HIV in four sub-Saharan African countries. The data come from the African Cohort Study, which follows patients at twelve clinical sites.

Among 4,241 participants with valid test results, hepatitis B prevalence was 4.7 percent in people with HIV and 4.2 percent in those without. Rates varied sharply by place, reaching 11.1 percent among Nigerian participants with HIV against 2.6 percent in Kenya. Male sex, Nigerian residence, and age over forty each raised the odds of co-infection. The authors recommend routine hepatitis B screening inside HIV programs, especially for older men.
pmc-13215749:
Danilo Pelaes de Almeida, Amanda Maria Picelli, Carolina Romeiro Fernandes Chagas, and Lucio André Viana wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It describes a new species of blood parasite found in green iguanas in the eastern Amazon of Brazil.

The parasite belongs to Lankesterella, a group of coccidian blood dwellers in reptiles. Under the microscope, the new species showed a strange flexible nucleus that changes shape and packing depending on where it sits in the host cell. It infects red blood cells and two kinds of white cells, warping their nuclei in the process. Gene sequencing placed it among other lizard Lankesterella, and a second, unnamed relative turned up in the same iguanas. The authors argue that pairing microscopy with DNA work is essential for sorting out these neglected parasites.
pmc-13217449:
Daniella A. Spittle and Alice M. Turner present a 2026 review of alpha-1 antitrypsin, a blood protein best known for shielding the lungs from digestive enzymes released by immune cells. When the protein is missing or overwhelmed, that protection fails and lung tissue is slowly destroyed.

The review covers the protein's wider talents beyond enzyme blocking: calming inflammation, steering immune cells, and resisting cell death and oxidative stress. Deficiency-driven emphysema is the proven indication for replacement therapy, which is already in clinical use. The authors then examine whether the same treatment could help in bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, and interstitial lung diseases, where protease burden runs high even without the genetic defect. They weigh the emerging evidence for widening its use.
pmc-13217849:
Jonathan Brutti and co-authors present a 2026 surgical study asking whether adding a nerve block to the standard painkilling injection cocktail improves the first day after knee replacement. The design is a natural experiment: one surgeon's patients received injection alone in year one and injection plus adductor canal block in year two.

The final sample held 188 patients, 104 with the block and 84 without. The block group used less opioid in the first twenty-four hours, averaging 31.6 morphine milligram equivalents against 42.5, and reported lower average and peak pain scores, with a summed pain measure of 40 against 54. Differences survived adjustment for age, sex, body size, and anaesthetic risk class. The authors conclude the block earns its place in the regimen.
pmc-13217949:
Yaning Shi and colleagues report in 2026 that celastrol, a compound from the root of the thunder god vine, slows atherosclerosis in mice. The disease builds fatty plaques inside arteries, and one driver is pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death in macrophages, the immune cells inside plaques. The study tests whether celastrol can quiet that process.

The team combined a mouse model of atherosclerosis with cultured macrophages exposed to oxidized LDL, the cholesterol form that triggers pyroptosis. Celastrol reduced cell death in the dishes and eased plaque growth and instability in the animals. Tests of binding and signaling showed that celastrol blocks the receptor TLR4, which lowers STAT3 activation and in turn switches off the NLRP3 inflammasome that drives pyroptosis. The authors propose celastrol as a candidate drug for atherosclerosis, though all findings so far are preclinical.
pmc-13218149:
Qindan Du and colleagues report a 2026 study uncovering a second, non-burning role for the protein gasdermin D in prostate cancer. The protein's front fragment is known to kill tumor cells by pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. What the full-length protein does in prostate cancer, particularly for immune evasion, was unexplored.

Using deletion models, the team found removing gasdermin D sped tumor growth, shortened survival, and created an immune-suppressed environment with fewer killer T cells. The protein binds a laminin subunit called LAMC2 and tags it for destruction. Without gasdermin D, LAMC2 accumulates and pushes macrophages into their M2 state. That state releases a chemokine, switching on growth signals and suppressing T cells. In human tumor samples, gasdermin D levels rose alongside T-cell infiltration and fell as suppressive macrophages rose. Activating the protein, the authors suggest, could thaw cold tumors and help immunotherapy.
pmc-13218249:
An old folk remedy smashes fresh dandelion onto sores, and Shenyu Tan and co-authors rebuild that remedy as a modern wound dressing in a 2026 study. Their film blends bubble-like particles from dandelion juice with fibers spun from the plant's own leftovers. The aim is the stubborn wounds of diabetes, which stall in inflamed tissue.

The film nudged immune cells from attack mode to repair mode and spurred new blood vessels. Loaded densely into the film, the juice particles released on demand. Treated wounds in animals closed almost fully within two weeks, far ahead of untreated ones, with better collagen layout and vessel regrowth.
pmc-13218349:
Siyu Long, Marie-Hélène Boudrias, and Georgios D. Mitsis examine bursts of beta brain waves and the blood-flow responses that follow them, in a 2026 neuroscience study. Beta oscillations are rhythms in brain activity tied to holding back movement, arriving in short bursts rather than a steady hum. Where these bursts occur during movement, and how they relate to the blood oxygen signals seen in brain scans, was unmapped.

Eleven adults performed a handgrip task at rest and during movement while electroencephalography and MRI recorded. During transitions between phases, the background electrical components and beta bursts grew stronger compared with steady squeezing. Bursts over the motor region were followed by positive responses during movement but negative ones at rest, while other regions showed negative responses. The authors describe this flip as a new detail in how electrical events become scan signals, calling for larger studies.
pmc-13218649:
Small cysts in the brain's fluid factory may mark the failing cleanup system of liver driven brain disease, suggests a 2026 scan study by Li Chen and co-authors. The team imaged three groups: patients with hepatic encephalopathy, patients with cirrhosis but clear minds, and healthy controls.

Every encephalopathy patient carried the cysts, against six in ten with cirrhosis and about a quarter of controls. A scan index of the brain's waste flow fell step by step across the groups, and cyst load tracked worse thinking and more shrinkage. The authors propose the cysts as a visible sign of a deeper drainage failure.
pmc-13218849:
Quanping Yan and co-authors link cooking habits and smoke pollutants to platelet traits in rural China. Their 2026 study draws 2,124 people from the Henan Rural Cohort. The pollutants, called PAHs, arise from burning fuels and oils, and they usually act as mixtures rather than alone.

Blood tests measure ten PAHs and standard platelet traits such as size and count. Single-pollutant models tie some PAHs to lower platelet counts and larger platelet size. The ten-part mix links to wider size spread and higher size-to-count ratios. Two named pollutants drive much of the mix effect. Links persist in men who neither smoke nor cook, a subgroup that helps split cooking smoke from cigarette smoke as sources.
pmc-13218949:
Bosworth and eight co-authors surveyed trainees in primary care research about the obstacles in their path, in this 2026 study. Primary care research is growing, and its trainees are the field's future workforce. Their frustrations, if unaddressed, become everyone's shortage later.

The online survey drew sixty-nine usable responses, mostly medical students and residents, spread across the United States, the Netherlands, Canada, and Uganda. The team paired statistics with themes drawn from open-ended comments. Trainees described familiar strains: scarce mentorship, funding uncertainty, and the difficulty of building a research career inside busy clinical training. The paper's title states its hope, that naming problems precisely is how a field turns them into progress. For program directors, the findings list where support would count most for keeping young researchers in primary care.
pmc-13219549:
Michal Paret and co-authors review infections caused by a family of bacteria called Fusobacterium, in a paper from 2026. These germs live without oxygen and colonize the mouth, gut, and other sites. Illness ranges from throat and soft tissue infections to blood poisoning with no clear source. One species can trigger a grave clotting infection of the neck vein.

The review walks through the germ's traits, the syndromes it causes, and how each is treated. Blood infections are rare but carry a high death rate. One species strikes the young and healthy after neck infections, while another hits older patients with cancer. Most strains still yield to common antibiotics, though resistance to two drugs is rising. Since labs rarely test these germs, strong first-choice drugs are the norm for severe cases.
pmc-13220249:
Hong Wei, Da Yong Sun, Xiang Yu Wang, and Dan Wu report one case of draining a fluid sac on the pancreas with a home-adapted tube, in a paper from 2026. The sac formed after a bout of pancreas swelling and caused clear symptoms. Standard drains and stents can be costly.

Doctors reshaped a standard nose-to-bile tube into a curled drain and placed it through the stomach wall with a scope. The steps for making, cleaning, and checking the tube were recorded in full. A month later, scans showed the sac was gone and symptoms had cleared. At six months there was still no return, and the patient was back to farm work.
pmc-13220349: The Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation issued this short correction in 2026 for a case series by Andrea Demofonti and co-authors on tailored rehabilitation after lower limb soft tissue sarcoma reconstruction. The notice is a correction only. In the original version, one author's given and family names, Marco Morelli Coppola, were wrongly ordered, though the name was right in all versions when published. The original article has now been corrected. Its results and conclusions stand.
pmc-13222049:
Zirong Liu and colleagues survey patients with venous thromboembolism about long-term blood thinner use, in a 2026 cross-sectional study at a Shandong hospital. Three hundred eighty-nine patients completed a questionnaire covering knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice around anticoagulation. Younger patients made up a large share, with a mean age near forty-six.

About half of respondents met the preset bar for adequate knowledge, while majorities showed positive attitudes and proactive habits. Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores all rose together in correlation analysis. Patients under forty-five scored higher on knowledge and attitude than older groups. The gaps suggest education should target older patients, whose understanding lagged despite years of potential treatment ahead.
pmc-13222949:
Xu Jia, Jun Xie, Fang Chai, HaoBo Jiang, and Rui Shi offer a two thousand twenty-six case study of digital prescription review in Sanya, China. Irrational drug use wastes money and harms care quality. Small clinics often lack the pharmacy expertise of big hospitals.

A centralized electronic review platform linked the region's facilities into one checking system. Artificial intelligence with retrieval support backed the reviewers. Over four hundred thousand prescriptions from one year were analyzed. Trend tests tracked safety, cost efficiency, and consistency of service over time. The Sanya model is offered as a route to fairer pharmaceutical care.
pmc-13223049:
Edwin Solares and co-authors teach computers to tell male from female red abalone by ultrasound in a 2026 study. Knowing sex matters for breeding in both wild recovery and farm programs. Checking by eye means prying the shellfish off surfaces, which can hurt them or trigger early release of eggs or sperm. The team built a set of 246 clear ultrasound images from forty-four animals.

Seven network designs were tested, with care taken to keep all images of one animal in a single data split. A design called YOLOv8 scored best, at about eighty-six percent correct on held-out images. pmc-13223149:

pmc-13224049:

pmc-13225449:

pmc-13226249:

pmc-13226849:

pmc-13228149:

pmc-13228849:

pmc-13231049:

pmc-13231349:

pmc-13232849:

pmc-13232949:

pmc-13233349:

pmc-13233649:

pmc-13233749:

pmc-13233949:

pmc-13234249:

pmc-13234449:

pmc-13235049:

pmc-13235149:

pmc-13235249:

pmc-13240249:

pmc-13240349:

pmc-13240549:

pmc-13244949:

Mothers who felt less control did fewer care tasks and had less contact. The authors say giving parents more say may help both mother and baby.
pmc-13271149:
Niek Stevenson is lead author of a 2026 journal article presenting an open-source toolbox for joint modelling of brain scans and behaviour. Joint modelling fits behaviour data and MRI data, which track brain activity, together in one model. It accounts for measurement error and for differences between people.

Built into an R software package called EMC2, the toolbox streamlines building behaviour, brain, and joint models. The authors show it on a perceptual decision task done inside a scanner. They explain how to set up design tables, prior guesses, and brain-behaviour links. Joint fitting steadied weak values and cut a known bias that shrinks brain-behaviour links, they report. Code examples are included.
pmc-13271349:
Yi Zhou is lead author of a 2026 review on Fusarium oxysporum forma specialis vasinfectum race 4, shortened to Fov4. That is a highly damaging fungus that causes wilt disease in cotton, especially in the United States. The review gathers what is known from field disease through to the pathogen's genome.

Fov4 genomes are larger and richer in repeated DNA than those of related races, the authors note, though their chromosome layout is still unresolved. Studies have flagged candidate attack factors, including race-specific effector proteins and chemical-making genes. Because the fungus persists in soil and adapts genetically, control relies on mixing resistant cotton varieties, farming practices, and close monitoring, they conclude.
pmc-13271549:
Nakul Verma and coauthors describe in 2026 the features and outcomes of cavitary retinoblastoma, a child eye cancer that forms hollow spaces inside the tumor. Retinoblastoma is the most common eye cancer in young children. The cavitary form is less often described, so its behavior under treatment matters to care teams.

Records covered 40 children with 43 affected eyes, most diagnosed near age two. White pupil reflex was the most common first sign, and nearly all eyes received chemotherapy through a vein. Every eye achieved tumor control at final follow-up, with no spread or deaths. The results support standard chemotherapy for this tumor form.
pmc-13271849:
Lori Birder, Joel Stern, Robert Moldwin, and Edwin Jackson review a candidate drug for bladder pain. Their 2026 paper deals with cystitis, which brings bladder pain and urgent, frequent urination. Two forms are covered: a pain syndrome with no clear cause, and a form tied to infection or cancer treatment. Good drug targets for the pain remain scarce.

The candidate, 8-aminoguanine, blocks an enzyme that turns protective purines into damaging ones. Patients with the pain syndrome show skewed purine levels that match that path. In rats with drug-induced cystitis, the oral drug prevented all seen harm, from tissue damage to raised urination. The authors argue it could cut pain and guard the bladder in patients.
pmc-13271949:
Rong-rong Zhang and coauthors follow in 2026 wound healing in people with diabetic kidney disease who take SGLT2 inhibitor drugs. These drugs protect heart and kidneys, yet sugar in the urine raised worry that wounds might heal more slowly. Clinicians lacked direct evidence for patients with active wounds.

The study enrolled 247 adults at a wound care center and matched 102 drug users with 102 similar non-users. Median healing time was nearly identical, at about thirty-three days in both groups. Infection and kidney outcomes at six months also showed no clear difference. The results ease concern about continuing these drugs during wound care.
pmc-13272149:
Heng Chen and coauthors estimate in 2026 how emergency policy changes affected regional emergency logistics capacity across China. Contingency plans are meant to make disaster response faster and better stocked, but hard evidence of their effect is scarce. The 2006 national master plan for public health emergencies serves as a natural experiment.

Panel data from thirty provinces between 2005 and 2022 fed a difference-in-differences analysis. Provinces whose plans matched the national text closely gained a measurable rise in response capacity, about forty-seven percent on the study's scale. Matching the text alone did not guarantee strength, though; weak alignment reliably went with weak capacity.
pmc-13272249:
Lena Marie Süß is lead author of a 2026 journal article on blocking P2Y6 receptors to slow kidney fibrosis. Fibrosis is the scarring that drives chronic kidney disease. That disease affects over 850 million people worldwide. Signals from released nucleotides through P2 receptors help activate the fibroblast cells that lay down scar tissue, but their role was poorly understood.

Using precise RNA staining, the team found P2Y1 and P2Y6 receptors in kidney interstitial fibroblasts, with P2Y6 sharply raised in several mouse fibrosis models. Cultured fibroblasts moved more when stimulated by a nucleotide signal. In a mouse kidney disease model, a selective P2Y6 blocker cut expression of a scar-cell marker and of collagen I, a main scar protein. They propose P2Y6 blockade as a new anti-fibrosis strategy.
pmc-13272349:
Chen Yuhang and coauthors sort in 2026 older adults in two Chengdu districts by how well their basic mental needs are met or blocked. Needs for choice, skill, and close ties shape mental health late in life, yet people mix met and blocked needs in distinct ways. Grouping those mixes can help aim support where it fits.

Surveys from 430 residents, gathered in late 2025, supported four groups. The largest group, near half the sample, had its needs well met, while a small group had them broadly unmet. Life satisfaction, distress scores, and social support helped explain who fell in each group. The authors use the groups to guide local mental health work with older adults.
pmc-13272449:
Ran Meng and coauthors review in 2026 hydrogel therapies that deliver healing cargo directly into heart muscle damaged by heart attack. About seven million heart attacks occur yearly, and surviving muscle often scars into heart failure that drugs and devices cannot reverse. Injectable gels suit the heart because they are water-rich, body-friendly, and can carry living cargo.

The review traces the path from blocked artery to scarred, failing heart, then compares gels loaded with drugs, bioactive molecules, cells, or exosomes. Each cargo class attacks a different step, from calming inflammation to growing vessels. The authors judge hydrogels a promising repair platform still proving itself clinically.
pmc-13272549:
Ellis Eikenboom, Helena van Doorn, and Anja Wagner wrote a 2026 authors' reply about womb surveillance in Lynch syndrome in the Netherlands. Lynch syndrome raises cancer risk, and their earlier paper questioned whether regular checks of the womb lining help Dutch carriers. The reply answers comments on that paper.

They explain why the subtype of overgrown womb lining did not change their advice, since surgery is advised for any such growth. They note that more growths and cancers were found in the checked group, yet cancers were not less advanced in a way that cut later treatment or improved survival. A much larger study is needed, they argue.
pmc-13272749:
Fang Zhang leads a 2026 study of a protein called SEMA6A in colorectal cancer, cancer of the colon and rectum. The protein was lower in cancer tissue than normal, and low levels linked to more aggressive tumors and a poorer outlook. The team tested what raising SEMA6A does in cells and in animals.

Raising SEMA6A slowed tumors and boosted killing by CD8 T cells, the immune cells that attack cancer. It acted by lowering a protein called ISG15, which otherwise helps stabilize TGF-beta, a signal that shields tumors. Patients with high SEMA6A and low ISG15 responded better to immunotherapy, and raising SEMA6A improved anti-PD-1 treatment in mice.
pmc-13273349:
Santi Poungcharean and colleagues described early life development in seven wild mouth-brooding fighting fish in a 2026 study from Thailand. These small air breathing fish hold eggs and young in the father's mouth for protection. Knowing how each species grows helps tell them apart while young.

The team bred fish gathered from type localities and followed their young through larval and juvenile stages. Most species released their young at a set stage about eleven days after fertilization, though one took up to twenty days. Young then reached the juvenile stage within a month of release. Counts of body segments and fin rays differed by species, as did pigment bands on the head and stripes along the body. A step by step identification key with illustrations sums up the differences.
pmc-13274149:
Yujie Chen and co-authors study why bowel growths return after removal, and how gut microbes differ in those cases, in work from two thousand twenty-six. Such growths can turn into bowel cancer, so spotting return risk matters. Thirty people with returned growths were compared with fifteen without.

More growths at first and a smoking history stood out as lone risk factors for return. Overall microbe variety was much the same in both groups. Some harmful bacteria ran higher in the return group, while two helpful types ran lower. Fat-linked pathways were more active in the group without returns. The authors link return to a skewed gut mix.
pmc-13274349:
Dattesh Bala Saranga and a large team engineer a soil bacterium to make plant scent compounds. Their twenty twenty-six study uses Azospirillum brasilense Sp7. Sesquiterpenes serve in many commercial products, but plant extraction has limits. Microbes could make them if yields were high enough.

The chosen bacterium already moves much material through a pigment pathway. That flow passes a shared building block for sesquiterpenes. The team improved strains and growth media step by step. Pigment output rose sharply, and cells tolerated the target compounds well. Adding the needed enzymes produced two model compounds at low levels. Further pathway and export changes raised output more than tenfold.
pmc-13274549:
Xiaocui Ma and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on what shapes bird diversity in a small Chinese nature reserve. Louzishan, in Liaoning Province, offers a test of how plant productivity and habitat variety affect birds across seasons. The team surveyed bird communities in summer breeding season and in winter, scoring greenness from satellites as a stand-in for productivity.

In summer, greener sites held more bird species and more varied bird traits, and species replacement along the greenness gradient drove community differences. Winter flipped the pattern: habitat variety related negatively to species counts, and distance between sites drove differences instead. The authors read this as environment filtering birds in summer but limited movement ruling in winter.
pmc-13274849:
Madisen S Mason and co-authors present a 2026 protocol article for growing a deadly childhood brainstem tumor in mouse embryos. Diffuse midline glioma of the pons is considered universally fatal, and few animal models capture how it starts. The method zaps DNA into the developing mouse pons while the pup is still in the womb, using three electrodes for precise aim.

A single engineered DNA package carries the cancer's signature mutations, including the histone change H3.3K27M, into the progenitor cells lining the fourth ventricle, a fluid space in the brainstem. The embryos then develop large, diffuse brainstem tumors resembling the childhood disease in their molecular makeup. The protocol aims to speed study of the tumor's origins and of candidate treatments.
pmc-13274949:
A brain-wave cap with many sensors gives more data than most tasks need, and the extra channels cost time and add noise. Neda Abdollahpour and four co-authors pick the channels that count in 2026, by how much each one drives the rest. Their score rates each channel by its causal pull on its peers.

The pick needs no labels: it reads the web of pull among channels and keeps the hubs. The team tests it on three known brain-wave sets across four kinds of task, scoring the pick with five gauges of causal pull. A leaner cap set that keeps the signal's spine could make brain-wave tools faster and cheaper to run. It could also sharpen what the reads say about how the brain talks to itself.
pmc-13275249:
Andrea Nana Ofori-Boadu and Rabiatu Bonku built a theory of professional identity in women studying architecture, engineering, and construction in a 2026 study. These fields are male dominated, and women must negotiate clashing expectations as they become professionals. Earlier work mostly took snapshots rather than following the process over time.

The team interviewed 78 undergraduates at five United States institutions across seven rounds, comparing accounts as they built their theory. Women moved gradually from isolating clashing parts of themselves to blending them into one professional identity. A shared coping pattern also emerged, which they name with a new term: women drew on collective resilience, aiming at influential, helpful roles that widen inclusion. The framework ties identity content, process, and setting together.
pmc-13275349:
Hend M. Al-Atif and co-authors surveyed body art knowledge and practice among young adults in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Piercing and tattooing have moved from tradition to mainstream self expression, yet safety habits lag. Their online questionnaire reached people who already had body art across all regions of the country.

The final group held 1,472 participants. More than three quarters knew body art carries health risks, but only about a third recognized non-infectious complications. Most doubted the hygiene standards of the procedures they had used. Ear piercing was by far the most common practice, while tattoos were rarer, and interest among newcomers was low. Age and gender shaped risk views. The authors call for public teaching and stricter regulation of practitioners.
pmc-13275449:
Efrah Ahmed Ibrahim offers a 2026 systematic review of radionuclide therapy across 54 African nations. Cancer cases on the continent are projected to double by 2040, yet these targeted radiation treatments remain scarce. The review measures availability, travel access, staffing, and cost in one combined analysis.

The author screened thousands of records and kept 47 studies, alongside data from global cancer and atomic energy sources. Radioactive iodine for thyroid cancer existed in only about half of the countries. A newer prostate treatment was present in just seven, and specialist doctors were far scarcer than in Europe. Local production cut drug costs by more than ninety percent, which supports regional hub investment.
pmc-13276049:
Giorgia Picci and a large team report a 2026 brain study of how cortical structure and activity stay linked across life. They used magnetoencephalography, which records magnetic signals from brain activity, in one of the largest lifespan samples of its kind. Participants numbered 388 and ranged from age six to eighty-four.

Coupling between local rhythms and cortical thickness changed with age in distinct frequency bands. Sensory and motor networks showed strong, steady coupling, while higher association networks showed weaker and more variable links. The pattern followed a gradient from basic sensory areas toward complex association areas. The authors frame the results as a baseline map for healthy brain ageing.
pmc-13276349:
Yuchen Ping and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on why a prized Chinese medicinal herb tastes of place. Atractylodes macrocephala, one of the famous Zhejiang herbs, varies in potency by region. Traditional thinking credits local soil, but the microbes living around roots may matter more.

The team transplanted herbs across China's four major producing regions. Soil from Pan'an, the classic home region, strongly boosted the active compounds in plants sourced from Bozhou. Gene sequencing of root-zone microbes showed moving reshaped the community and raised its diversity. Eleven bacterial groups stood out as keystone members, rising with the move. Their abundance tracked with root growth and active compound levels. The authors say soil nutrients, microbe-driven carbon and nitrogen cycling, and plant resource shifts together create the herb's regional authenticity.
pmc-13276449:
Dian Kusuma and Hario Megatsari present a 2026 journal article on whether local tobacco laws can cut teen smoking where national action lags. Indonesia has some of the world's highest smoking rates, especially among boys and men. Bogor City tightened its local tobacco rules from 2014 while national enforcement stayed weak.

The team compared Bogor with a synthetic control, a blend of similar districts among nearly five hundred nationwide, over a decade of data. Current smoking among boys fell by about fifteen percentage points versus the control, a cut of over two fifths. Ever smoking dropped by about twelve points. The gaps grew over time, suggesting lasting impact. Adult men showed smaller gains, and their current smoking stayed above the control. The authors back local action plus stronger national measures.
pmc-13276749:
SM Tawhid and colleagues publish a 2026 dataset of budgerigar flight filmed in stereo for collision-avoidance research. Small birds dodge each other in flight with ease that robots still struggle to copy. Frame-level three-dimensional tracks of real flocks can teach engineers how they do it.

Three hundred sixty synchronised video pairs were recorded indoors at high frame rate. Flights covered solo birds and head-on meetings in one-to-one, two-to-two, and three-to-three groups. Every bird was hand-labelled in both views with a body box and four key points. Reconstructed three-dimensional trajectories, calibration files, and processing scripts are included, with quality checks such as reprojection error reported.
pmc-13277249:
Nevra Koç leads a 2026 study of appetite hormones and body weight in children with inherited metabolic diseases. The diseases covered, including phenylketonuria and maple syrup urine disease, force strict low-protein diets that can blunt appetite. The team compared 43 affected children with 40 healthy children aged one to eighteen.

Two hormones, peptide YY and adiponectin, were higher in the patient group. Other appetite hormones did not differ overall. Yet ghrelin, a hunger hormone, was highest in the thinnest patients. The authors link the shifts to diet, toxic buildup, and organ strain. They urge regular hormone checks and personal diet plans for long-term care of these children.
pmc-13277749:
Seyedeh-Zeynab Hosseinian leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of FODMAP foods and indigestion symptoms. FODMAPs are fermentable sugars and related compounds, found in many foods, that gut bacteria break down with gas. The team gathered trials, through October 2025, that compared a low-FODMAP diet with a high-FODMAP diet.

Twelve studies qualified. The low-FODMAP diet eased bloating and early fullness at meals compared with the high-FODMAP diet. Abdominal pain scores, though, ran higher on the low-FODMAP diet in their pooled result. Results varied a great deal between studies, and the authors rate the certainty of evidence as very low. More well-run trials are needed before firm diet advice can rest on this base.
pmc-13278449:
Yannick Elysée Ewane Epée leads a 2026 survey of snail harvesters along Cameroon's Atlantic coast, where giant land snails are a key protein source and income earner. Farming in the region uses more pesticides, raising fears for snail stocks and human health. The team interviewed 211 harvesters across six localities and observed their work.

Fifty-eight percent believed pesticides shrink snail size, while sixty-one percent saw no effect on snail numbers. Collection peaked at night and in October. Statistical links between beliefs and reported harvest amounts were weak, with perceived effect on quantity the only clear predictor. Despite knowing the risks, sixty-three percent had no interest in snail farming, preferring wild harvest.
pmc-13278749:
Payam Shabestari and a team of co-authors map brain network signatures of tinnitus using a whole-graph learning method, in two thousand twenty-six. Tinnitus is hearing sound with no outside source. Older connectivity methods compare brain regions two at a time, which misses the shape of the whole network.

Their method estimates the full connectivity structure from all signals at once, and works even on short recordings. Learned connectomes identified individuals across repeat sessions better than correlation-based ones. Patients showed altered connectivity across several frequency bands and networks, including hearing, vision, and default mode systems. Each patient's profile was highly individual, which the authors say supports personal treatment models.
pmc-13279049:
Tallal Hashmi and co-authors combine trials on blood pressure after stroke treatment in a 2026 meta-analysis. After a clot is pulled from a brain artery, doctors must choose how hard to lower blood pressure. Trials have differed on that choice. The team searches three large databases for randomized trials on the question.

Six trials qualify. Pooling them, tight control linked to fewer good recoveries at ninety days and more deaths. Low blood pressure episodes were also more common under tight control. No clear gap appeared for best-level recovery or for bleeding in the brain. The proof was strong for function outcomes, the authors say.
pmc-13279149:
Sangho Lee and co-authors report a 2026 case, in letter form, of a skin flare tied to a drug for eczema. The drug is dupilumab, and the flare is generalized pustular psoriasis, a rare skin illness with widespread pus filled spots. Their patient was an eighty two year old man with a two year history of eczema.

Two weeks after he started dupilumab, red plaques with pustules spread over his trunk, back, limbs and scalp. Skin biopsy, meaning a small skin sample test, showed changes that fit pustular psoriasis. Swabs found no germ cause, and blood tests were near normal apart from mild shifts. Past reports of this switch are rare, so the case adds a clear warning for skin doctors.
pmc-13279749:
YanLing Yang and colleagues give a 2026 review of safety risks from oral nicotine products. Oral nicotine products, like pouches held in the mouth, form a new tobacco product class. As tobacco rules tighten and health awareness grows, their safety draws more focus. Regulators still lack long term data and full data on additives. The review joins chemical, animal, cell and human group data.

First pages list the main products on sale and their types. Next sections weigh harmful substances found in them and their levels. Health effects on the mouth and on the heart and vessels get systematic checks, with paths of harm traced. Gaps guide future work the authors propose. Clear risk sums can help users weigh use, and help firms and regulators set sound policy to cut health harm.
pmc-13280649:
De Mello and co-authors compare two fat-tailed peptides used in skin care. Their 2026 paper studies C16-KTTKS, sold commercially as Matrixyl, and a variant called C16-RTTRS in which one building block is swapped. Both molecules are reported to boost collagen, the protein that firms skin, but their assembly in water was less clear.

The authors measured how each peptide arranges itself across acidity levels and in two salt forms. The original peptide formed flat nanotapes across most conditions and round micelles only in strong acid, while the variant switched shapes depending on its salt partner. Both peptides were gentle on fibroblast cells at low doses. Each also stimulated collagen production in human skin fibroblasts at very low concentration, with no clear difference between salt forms.
pmc-13281349:
Haoran Zhang and co-authors test in 2026 if the low point of blood potassium after a heart valve swap links to death in the next month. Valve swaps are big heart work, and salt balance can swing in the days that trail. A large care data base holds the case set.

Two thousand eight hundred seventy seven patients from that base form the group. Death risk traced a U shape as the low point rose and fell. A set line split the safe zone: below it, death risk jumped in a clear way. High low points tied to low death odds in the tuned model.
pmc-13281449:
Joseph Emmanuel Dela Cruz and Laufred Hernandez study in 2026 antibiotic misuse among adult residents of Rodriguez, Rizal in the Philippines. Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat, and public habits drive part of it. The study uses a mixed methods design, with a survey first and interviews second.

The survey covered 384 residents aged eighteen to fifty-nine without medical training. It measured knowledge, attitudes, and practices around antibiotics, plus personal background. Nine residents then took part in depth interviews. Most survey respondents were young adults, and about a third held bachelor's degrees, the abstract reports.
pmc-13281549:
Negash Wakgari and four co-authors trace how women move through abortion care in health sites in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Care that fits the person is a goal, but stigma and few method choices still block good care worldwide. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The team spoke in depth with sixteen women who sought induced abortion care at seven sites. The talks were held across a few months. Notes were coded and sorted into themes by what the women said. Five themes arose, on social and felt support, on moral views that shape care, and on access and service flow. Two more covered trust in staff skill and the bodily and felt effects of abortion.
pmc-13281949:

Standard drugs and hands-on care often give only mild relief. Herbal formulas vary widely in Korean practice. The trial asks whether a flexible herbal strategy is no worse than standard Korean hands-on care. One hundred fifty patients with pain for at least three months will join many centers.

Half get herbal care fitted to each patient for thirty days. Half will get hands-on care twice a week for five weeks, such as needles, cupping, and heat. Raters scoring pain and disability will not know who got what. Scores run to week seven, with cost and harm checks. As a protocol, the paper reports no results. Its value is a fair test design for real-world herbal practice.
pmc-13282049:
Michele Francesco Chiappetta and co-authors tell of a 2026 case of a very rare cancer of the pancreas, the organ behind the stomach that aids digestion. The tumour type carries large, bone-like cells called osteoclast-like giant cells alongside shapeless cancer cells. Scans cannot reliably tell it from other pancreatic masses, so tissue proof is often needed. The patient was a fifty-seven-year-old woman with belly pain and cholestasis, a blockage that slows bile flow.

A first needle sampling guided by endoscopic ultrasound, an internal sound-wave scope, gave no clear answer. A second procedure at a specialist centre used a fine-needle biopsy, which takes a small core of tissue. That sample showed the tell-tale giant cells and a matching pattern of cell stains. The authors say the biopsy route can secure this hard diagnosis before surgery, guiding the care team and sparing guesswork.
pmc-13282549:
Mehrzad Mirzania and co-authors present a 2026 study comparing two chemotherapy sequences given before surgery for locally advanced breast cancer in Iran. One sequence gives two drugs first, then a third; the other gives all three together. Real-world comparisons in Middle Eastern patients were scarce. The team reviewed one hundred eighteen women with stage three disease treated in Tehran, seventy on the sequential plan and forty-eight on the combined plan.

The combined plan, though, kept distant recurrence away significantly better at ten years. Disease-free and local control outcomes were similar. After adjustment, hormone receptor positivity, not the drug sequence, independently predicted better survival. The authors support choosing the regimen by patient profile and tumour biology.
pmc-13282849:
Dalia Hyzam and co-authors present a 2026 study of health care in Yemen during ten years of war, epidemics, and COVID-19. Formal leadership structures stayed in place the whole time. The team asked whether those structures made the system able to withstand shocks. They interviewed health leaders and experts, and traced four periods from before 2014 to after the pandemic.

Before the war, rule was stable but centralised, and planning for shocks was weak. During the war, planning collapsed, rival authorities split control, and aid groups carried most services. COVID-19 brought brief gains in teamwork that were never made permanent. Later, foreign funds fell, and fixes such as WhatsApp groups stayed local and informal. Lessons were rarely written into routine practice. The authors say structures on paper do not create strength. Real resilience needs ready plans, home-grown emergency funds, and learning built into daily governance.
pmc-13283449:
Eric Canton and colleagues asked in 2026 what really drives scores when wrist wearables stage sleep. Many teams credit their model choice, yet datasets differ so much that fair comparison is hard. The group built a new dataset pairing Apple Watch motion data with lab sleep studies in 28 people with sleep apnea, then trained networks on it plus two older datasets.

A very simple wake detector, based on smoothed movement, explained much of every model's score on every dataset. Periods that are easy to class as wake can inflate results. Training with apnea patients included helped when test sets held people with suspected sleep disorders. The authors urge shared benchmark sets and honest checks of how separable a new dataset is.
pmc-13284049:
Lokman Koçak surveyed adults in 2026 on fear of missing out and cyberstalking, the repeated online monitoring or harassment of another person. The study asked which inner patterns carry the link between that fear and stalking behaviour. A total of 540 adults aged eighteen to forty-eight, mostly women, answered measures of fear of missing out, two early maladaptive schemas, and phubbing, which means snubbing people nearby for a phone.

All the study variables were significantly related. Both schemas, one centred on abandonment fears and one on weak self-control, helped carry the fear-to-stalking link, and phubbing carried part of it too. The author reads the abandonment path as attachment vulnerability and the self-control path as a regulation problem. The findings point future work toward mindful technology use.
pmc-13284749:
Mark M. Gulman, Yurii I. Glazachev, and Sergey A. Dobrynin propose a new route, published in 2026, to make shielded piperidine nitroxides. Current methods mostly give symmetric forms and cannot easily add useful groups next to the reactive center. The new acid-driven ring building starts from beta-aminoketone acetals and ketones to form a varied piperidine frame. Later steps add diverse groups, including ones with extra chemical handles, and optional steps can saturate side chains. Decay tests in antioxidant mixes gave rates near those of a known shielded standard. The route widens design choice for future probes.
pmc-13284849:
Anika Lipinski and co-authors report a 2026 cohort study on long-term effects of DRESS, a severe drug reaction with rash, high eosinophils, and organ harm. The team sent follow-up surveys to patients in a German registry from 2003 to 2023 with definite or probable DRESS.

Thirty-six replies were analyzed, split evenly between mild and moderate-to-severe cases. Every patient reported some long-term problem, with skin disorders most common and hair or nail issues also frequent. Blood and liver test faults appeared often, more so in severe cases. Many patients feared new drugs and avoided them. The authors stress lasting burden across severity levels.
pmc-13285449:
Atefeh Mir and co-authors reported in 2026 a mild case of a rare developmental syndrome in a nineteen year old Iranian man. The cause was a new spelling error at the very start of a gene that helps organize chromosomes. The syndrome usually brings marked growth delay, learning disability, and distinctive features.

Whole exome sequencing found the error at the gene's start signal, where protein building should begin; neither parent carried it. His learning problems were milder than in typical cases where the gene is fully broken. The authors suggest the cell may start building at a backup site, softening the blow. Checks against population databases found the variant nowhere else. The case widens the known range of the syndrome.
pmc-13285549:
Gut viruses in people living with HIV differ in fine detail from those in HIV-free peers, Ji Zhang and co-authors find in a 2026 pilot study. Both tools agreed on broad patterns, though one named more species. Most viruses were unclassified kinds, and bacteria-eating viruses ruled the known set. Patient samples split from controls at species and genus level and varied more within the group. Sex shaped the mix no matter the HIV state. Links also tied some virus kinds to immune counts and treatment length.
pmc-13285649:
A shape-shifting guard protein helps cells resist division-blocking drugs, Mar Mora-Santos and co-authors find in a 2026 cell study. One spot on the protein, threonine 552, sets how freely it moves. A stuck version that cannot take a phosphate tag moved sluggishly, weakened checkpoint shouts, and let cells shrug off anti-division drugs. Loose, lively hSpindly kept the guard strong. The authors name the protein a drug target lead for beating resistance to mitotic blockers in cancer care.
pmc-13285749:
Alejandro De la Cadena leads a 2026 report on a new light source for label-free microscopy of living tissue.
