The team built a simpler generator that skips the usual cavity and extra amplifiers.

Their device yields tunable light across a span wider than 100 nanometers near the 1500 nanometer region. Tests on standard solvents confirmed clean spectral reads, and images of rodent tissue showed clear chemical contrast. The same source also drove two-photon signals, letting the team overlay three kinds of images from fresh tissue in one pass. The plain, modular build could lower cost for labs that need many imaging modes at once.
pmc-13286549:
Lindsay Yoder and a multi-center team lay out a trial of structured aftercare for advanced liver disease in a 2026 protocol article. Patients discharged after liver complications bounce back into hospital at high rates, and the days just after discharge are the danger zone. Their Transitional Liver Clinic model promises a phone call within two business days and a specialist visit within fourteen, led by advanced practice providers.

Four academic centers will adopt the clinic in random order across nine-month steps over 45 months, enrolling up to 1,000 patients. The main yardstick is readmission within thirty days, with quality of life and satisfaction riding along. Early single-center experience hinted readmissions could nearly halve under the model. If the trial confirms that signal, the clinic offers hepatology a template other centers can copy.
pmc-13286849:
Wen Zhang and colleagues present a 14-year-old girl with a fungal lung infection that hollowed out part of her right upper lung lobe, despite her having a normal immune system. The 2026 case report adds a literature review. Pulmonary cryptococcosis is rising in people without HIV, and its vague symptoms invite misdiagnosis as tuberculosis or cancer.

Antigen tests on blood and lung wash fluid came back positive, and targeted gene sequencing confirmed Cryptococcus neoformans. The fungus was absent from her spinal fluid. Oral fluconazole settled her fever within a week, and she went home on day nine. Imaging at sixteen weeks showed the lesion almost gone, and the drug stopped at six months after the cavity cleared.
pmc-13287149:
Xiao Dang and colleagues used large genetic datasets in 2026 to ask why lacking immunoglobulin A so often occurs alongside autoimmune illness. They combined summary results for that deficiency with results for 10 common autoimmune conditions, looking for shared inherited signals.

Joint analysis flagged 51 locations linked to both traits, and follow-up checks supported 33 shared locations, many new for the deficiency. Shared genes pointed to T cell development and gut defences that support IgA making. Blood and intestinal tissue stood out, as did certain B cell groups. Tests also suggested influence running in both directions between the deficiency and several autoimmune diseases.
pmc-13287349:
Mirabel Pelton and co-authors present a 2026 study of self-harm patterns among autistic adults. They used a card sort task in which people pick cards that match their experience and place them in time order. Five autistic adults with lived experience first checked the task for clarity and ease of use. A pilot group of 29 autistic or possibly autistic adults then completed the task.

Participants chose about 42 cards on average to describe their self-harm. Agitation, mental pain, and depression were the feelings picked most often. The card order suggested that agitation and acting on impulse often came just before self-harm. Feeling better, worse, exhausted, or hopeless often followed it. The authors suggest that support with emotion control and clear communication could help break the path toward self-harm.
pmc-13287549:
Xudong Zhu and colleagues compare transcription factors in wild and cultivated green jujube in a 2026 genomics study. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on and off. Green jujube carries four copies of each chromosome set, which makes single reference genomes hard to read. The team built haplotype-resolved genomes, meaning each copy set was assembled apart, for one wild and one cultivated plant.

The comparison covered 42 transcription factor superfamilies and 12,123 gene copies across eight haplotype genomes. Most families stayed highly conserved, with strong pressure against harmful change. Spread-out gene duplication, rather than whole-genome doubling, drove most family growth. Machine learning sorted wild from cultivated fruit with 89 percent accuracy using gene activity profiles. One gene group, tied to a zinc finger factor, stood out in cultivated fruit and matched shifts in acids and nucleotides.
pmc-13287749:
David Fork and a large team show in 2026 how to map roof brightness, called albedo, at the scale of single buildings by blending free mid-detail satellite images with sharper commercial ones. Bright roofs reflect sunlight and cool cities, yet older satellite maps blur whole blocks together, blocking house-by-house planning.

Checks against aircraft measurements gave small errors, at a level the authors report as 0.04. Maps for twelve world cities resolved single rooftops. Modelling suggests that treating the largest roofs first could cut citywide temperatures by up to half a degree Celsius in the best case. The authors offer the method for targeted cooling programmes worldwide.
pmc-13288549:
Da-Fu Zhang and colleagues probe thinking woes in lung cancer in 2026. A special MRI method anchors the work. The method shows how leaky the brain barrier is. They scanned 104 patients. They also scanned 40 healthy peers. Brain size and thinking tests were compared.

Barrier leak was higher in patients than peers. It was highest in patients with thinking woes. Cortex size had shrunk in that group. One spot stood out in the data. It sits in the right superior parietal cortex. Its leak read was higher than in both other groups. The pattern ties barrier harm to early decline. The scan may help spot that harm.
pmc-13288949:
Cortland Linder and colleagues study solar power for hospitals in poorer nations. Their 2026 work runs in three phases. Power cuts are common in such hospitals. Cuts harm patient care. On-site solar could cut those outages. Uptake still stays low.

One phase reviewed past studies. It found 19 blocks and 29 aids. One phase surveyed health workers. The survey drew 260 replies from 47 nations. Upfront cost ranked as the top block. Cheaper panels ranked as the top aid. One phase built a tool from the findings. The tool holds 23 plans in four groups. Teams can use it to move faster.
pmc-13289249:
Shazia Mohsin led a 2026 quality improvement report on wound infections after heart surgery in children in a low-resource setting. The new congenital heart program saw a 23 percent infection rate in its first three months, far above the 0.25 percent to 6 percent range reported globally. Leaders mapped the care path and hunted for root causes.

Four Plan Do Study Act cycles tightened cleaning, risk screening, and sterile practice across surgery care. A nurse-led wound clinic added checks for 30 days after surgery, plus training in hand hygiene and sterile technique. Among 500 surgeries, 31 infections occurred during the project period. Rates fell from 12 to 6 per 10 surgeries as reported, showing that adapted safety bundles can work where funds are tight.
pmc-13289449:
Antoine Langeard, Marion Torterotot, Marine Le Roux, and Bettina Wollesen build expert agreement on preventing falls among older adults outdoors, in a consensus study from twenty twenty-six. Falls are the top cause of accidental injury in later life. About thirty percent of older adults living at home fall each year, and nearly half of those falls happen outside, yet city design guides barely address them.

Through three survey rounds, sixty-odd participants (older fallers, health experts, planners, and officials) rated over a hundred proposals. Agreement formed on inner risks such as unsteady gait, poor vision, fading cognition, and many medications. Outer risks included uneven surfaces, obstacles, and crowding. Favored fixes ranged from fall-aware street design and planner training to upkeep and safer crossings.
pmc-13289649:
Xiaoyu Xiao headed a 2026 sleep study on how night-to-night swings shape how people with chronic insomnia judge their own sleep. Felt sleep often differs from measured sleep in insomnia, and daily ups and downs may drive that gap. Fifty patients tracked sleep at home with devices and diaries for five to seven nights, yielding 312 valid nights for analysis.

Bias was defined as measured sleep minus felt sleep for time asleep, efficiency, and wake time after falling asleep. Felt changes lagged behind real nightly changes, showing muted response to good or bad nights. People with steadier total sleep time showed larger bias in felt duration and efficiency overall. Variability in light sleep share also shaped wake perception.
pmc-13289849:
Ilvana Pitaku, Sarah Kecman, and Amar Polutak report a 2026 case of cecal volvulus revealing hidden gut non-rotation in a patient aged 48. Cecal volvulus twists the start of the large bowel and rarely blocks the gut in adults. Gut rotation faults are usually found in infancy, so adult discovery during emergency surgery is uncommon and can surprise the operating team.

The patient arrived with acute belly pain, and scans showed the cecal twist clearly. Emergency opening of the abdomen confirmed the twist and revealed that the intestines had never rotated into normal position. Surgeons removed the ileocecal segment and joined the bowel ends directly in one stage. Congenital layout should be suspected in such twists.
pmc-13290349:
Lalngaihmanawmi and co-authors test a traditional Mizoram tree medicine against three kinds of infection in a 2026 study. The bark of Alstonia scholaris is used in Mizo folk practice, and drug resistance is rising among fungi, malaria parasites, and gut worms alike. The team prepared a methanol bark extract from the local Mizoram variety and ran it through lab assays and computer docking.

The extract fought several fungi in dish tests and was checked against both a drug-sensitive and a multidrug-resistant malaria strain. Safety was screened on kidney cells, and worm killing was examined under microscopes for tissue damage. Chemical profiling named the active ingredients, and docking simulations tested how they might grip targets in each pathogen group.
pmc-13290449:
CT scan texture can hint at a pancreatic tumor's TP53 status without a biopsy, Shuyu Zhang and colleagues report in 2026. TP53 mutations occur in half or more of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas and shape how aggressive the cancer is, but testing them normally needs tissue.

In this multicenter study, 216 patients who had preoperative portal-venous CT scans were split into training and external test sets. The team extracted 1,561 radiomic features from the tumor and a 3-mm rim around it and trained six machine-learning classifiers. A model combining both regions performed best, and its XGBoost version reached an AUC of 0.893 on the external set, clearly beating single-region models. Zhang and colleagues offer the tool as decision support for personalizing treatment, pending prospective validation.
pmc-13291049:
Ryo Teraoka, Yuki Tanaka, and Wataru Teramoto test hearing attention in depth in a 2026 experiment on how listeners pick out sounds near or far. People can focus on a sound’s direction sideways with ease, but whether attention also sharpens along distance, in front, to the side, and behind, was far less clear.

Listeners hunted target sounds at five distances from 32 to 160 centimeters, either spreading attention across distances or focusing on one, inside a reverberant room setup. Detection sensitivity rose at the attended distance in every direction tested, with no clear gap between front, side, and rear. Reaction time gains were narrower, showing only at certain distances to the side and behind, so the main benefit lies in accuracy rather than speed.
pmc-13291149:
Stephany Morales-Viquez tells her own story in a 2026 personal essay on training as a neurosurgeon abroad. She chose to train at Hadassah in Israel. The post offered high case volume and strong mentors. It also meant learning a new language at speed.

Hebrew ran through ward rounds, surgery, and bedside checks. Spoken medical Hebrew is fast and full of short forms. Slow understanding could hurt her timing and standing. Her first year thus mixed two hard tasks at once. She had to think like a surgeon while gaining fluency. Her account shows how language shapes trust, teamwork, and patient care.
pmc-13291349:
Gut fungi in babies may forecast allergy risk later. Courtney Hoskinson leads a 2026 study of a large child cohort. Bacteria growth in infant guts is well studied. Fungal growth there was barely mapped before.

Stool from 1,409 children gave over two thousand samples. Gene tests tracked fungi and bacteria together. Fungal mix tracked infant age very closely. Two genera stood out as age markers. One was Saccharomyces, the other Malassezia. Early fungal patterns linked to later skin allergy. Food allergy also linked to those patterns. Key gut chemicals shifted with fungal growth. Baby fungi may be a new target for prevention.
pmc-13291449:
Two drug mixes for advanced pancreas cancer are compared in Spain. Carlos Escriva-Aranda leads a 2026 review of real clinic records. No head-to-head trial has settled which mix is better. Both are standard first choices for this cancer.

Records held 200 patients treated from 2011 to 2024. A small group got the FOLFIRINOX mix. Most got gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel instead. Survival times sat close between the two groups. Time without growth also matched closely. Response rates and risk factors were checked as well. Matching methods backed the main result. Choice may thus rest on fitness and side effects.
pmc-13291549:
A bone filler mix may calm immune cells while bone regrows. Maria Rosa Iaquinta leads a 2026 study of a Bio-Oss and Avitene composite. Jaw surgery patients need strong, safe graft material. Early inflammation can delay healing or doom a graft.

Stem cells from bone marrow modeled the first response. Two swelling gene signals fell on the scaffold. Protein tests showed the same calming pattern. Growth signals for blood vessels rose instead. Patients getting jaw surgery received the same mix. Cone beam scans tracked new bone formation. Early immune calming may set up better regrowth. The pairing of lab and clinic data is the study strength.
pmc-13291849:
Brandon Huaman, Brayan Guzman, and Juan Arcila automate leaf miner detection in sweet potato fields in a 2026 study. The leaf miner fly tunnels through leaves and can ruin crops before inspectors spot the damage. The team built a labeled image set of 751 field photos from Lambayeque, Peru. Augmentation expanded the training variety. Two object detection models from the YOLO family were trained under matched settings and compared.

The newer model, YOLOv11s, beat its predecessor on every headline metric. It reached about seventy-three percent precision and sixty-seven percent recall. Its mean average precision at the standard overlap threshold sat near seventy-two percent. The model also separated pest tunnels from background noise more cleanly in test images. A mobile prototype built on TensorFlow Lite ran acceptably on mid-range phones. The authors present the system as an affordable, scalable tool for pest monitoring in the farm sector.
pmc-13292149:
Shijun Li and co-authors compare lattice radiotherapy plans across three accelerator brands in a 2026 study. Lattice therapy plants high-dose peaks inside a tumor like seeds, sparing the valleys between them. Ten patients with bulky pelvic or abdominal tumors were planned on each machine. The dose was twenty-four gray in three fractions to the high-dose vertices. Dose maps were scored for peak-to-valley contrast and for spill into nearby organs.

All three platforms produced the signature peak-and-valley pattern while respecting organ limits. One platform, NeuRT Aurora, controlled the dose gradient best of the three. Its peak-to-valley ratio reached near nine, against about six to seven for the others. Dose far from the vertices and dose in the margin volume also ran lowest there. Every plan still met clinical requirements, so the authors judge all three feasible.
pmc-13292249:
Tao Chen and a large team chart a 2026 mouse study of early osteoarthritis and a magnesium-based treatment timed to match it. In their surgical model, the first ten days brought faltering mitochondria in cartilage cells plus overactive bone-eating cells below the cartilage. After that window, cartilage damage turned irreversible, with cell death and hardened subchondral bone.

The team built two-phase microspheres that release magnesium at dual concentrations to calm inflamed cartilage cells and rein in the bone cells. Given early, the spheres halted disease progress in living animals. Given late, they helped mainly the bone underneath and failed to save cartilage. The authors argue that metabolic rescue in osteoarthritis works only inside an early therapeutic window.
pmc-13292349:
Lukas Hinterlang, Sergei I Ivlev, and Eric Meggers introduce iron catalysts whose handedness lives on the metal, in a 2026 paper. Their new ligands are achiral chains holding two carbene donors and two nitrogens, tied by a rigid linker. Wrapped around iron(II), the chain twists into a helix and makes the metal center chiral. A helper-based separation split the left- and right-handed forms. Earlier two-piece ligand versions twisted back and lost their handedness easily.

The one-piece frame proved far sturdier, barely racemizing even in air and water. Three asymmetric reactions showcased the catalysts at work. An internal Cannizzaro rearrangement reached eighty-two percent enantiomeric excess. A carbon-hydrogen amidation hit eighty-one percent, and a hetero-Diels-Alder reaction reached ninety-four percent in open air. The authors say the design widens what cheap iron can do in fine chemical synthesis.
pmc-13292549:
José Ruiz-Cabello and four co-authors report a kidney disease case that breaks the usual pattern of its rare type. Their 2026 case report concerns membranous nephropathy tied to contactin-1, a protein that helps nerves and their sheaths stick together. This form usually arrives with severe nerve damage and matching antibodies in the blood.

Their patient had neither: no nerve symptoms and no detectable antibodies. That absence matters because standard antigen tests would have missed the cause. A method that slices the biopsy and reads its proteins by mass found the true target. Staining also showed the IgG4 pattern typical of this subtype. The authors warn that the kidney form can precede nerve trouble by years. Long watch for nerve symptoms is wise even when the case looks kidney-only.
pmc-13292649:
Giorgi Khazaradze and co-authors publish a 2026 data paper sharing nearly three decades of satellite geodesy from southeastern Spain. Campaign GNSS observations run from 1997 to 2024 across Almería, Murcia, and Alicante, aimed at the Eastern Betic Tectonic Arc. The files come Hatanaka-compressed in the standard RINEX 2.11 format and sit archived on Zenodo.

Three networks feed the collection. The oldest is the CuaTeNeo network, founded in 1996 by the University of Barcelona with the Catalan cartographic institute. Spain's REGENTE network and the GESE-CV network of Jaén and Alicante universities add the rest. Processed results show today's crust creeping 0 to 2 millimeters per year, mostly toward the north-northwest against stable Eurasia. The authors present the set as a rare long baseline for judging seismic risk in the western Mediterranean.
pmc-13292849:
Linyuan Yan and colleagues record resting brain waves in a 2026 study of tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder often tied to long use of dopamine-blocking drugs. How brain rhythms differ in this condition is still poorly known.

Electroencephalography with 32 channels was recorded in 67 people: 20 with the disorder, 25 patients without it, and 22 healthy controls. Both patient groups showed stronger slow theta waves at central sites than controls did. Fast gamma patterns differed by group and by scalp area, and links between waves across the brain also shifted. Early ties to drug history were weak and did not hold after strict checks.
pmc-13293449:
Yiwen Kang and colleagues decode, in a 2026 study, which brain regions let scalp recordings reveal what object a person just saw. For brain-computer links, small and clear feature sets beat large messy ones when data or computing power is limited.

Signals were projected onto defined brain regions, and four feature families were drawn from each region for each brief image trial. A simple measure of signal length in just 24 regions beat a 310-feature scalp baseline while using 92% fewer features, a saving the authors report. Fine time-shape features carried most of the signal under fast image flashes. Richer region sets also did well.
pmc-13293649:
Melissa Corbally and colleagues follow men's own stories about sexual function after prostate removal surgery, in a narrative study published in 2026 at a Dublin teaching hospital. Eighteen men gave thirty-four interviews across three moments: before the operation, three months after, and six to nine months after. The aim was to hear how their feelings about erection problems changed as recovery unfolded, rather than to score function on a chart.

Before surgery, men downplayed erection concerns and put survival first. Afterward, many voiced regret, saying they had not grasped how severe the loss would be, and they struggled with rehabilitation aids whose cost also blocked access. Age, fatherhood, and relationships shaped how they explained their situation, and humor helped them speak about it. The authors urge nurses to time information and support to each phase.
pmc-13293749:
Sjaak Pouwels and co-authors write a 2026 letter on when to remove the gallbladder after bile-driven pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis is a common gut emergency, often caused by gallstones or biliary sludge. Most cases stay mild to moderate, yet the stones remain a threat afterward.

Timely gallbladder removal cuts the risk of repeat attacks, gallbladder inflammation, duct infection, and colic. Recent landmark trials have shifted how severe cases should be timed. The letter focuses on the hard middle group: moderately severe to severe illness. Getting the timing right balances a second attack against operating on a fragile patient. Surgeons gain a concise brief on a live debate.
pmc-13293949:
Samantha Ho and colleagues reported in 2026 on a newly identified autoantibody target in cerebellar ataxia, a group of disorders that damage coordination. Some cases are driven by the immune system, but many patients test negative for known antibodies, which leaves diagnosis and treatment harder. The team hunted for the target using patient serum, protein arrays, and cell-based tests.

They identify synaptophysin, a protein in the small sacs that release chemical messages between nerve cells, as one such target. Antibodies against it appeared in a small number of patients with matching serum patterns. In lab-grown human neurons, patient antibodies changed synaptophysin at the cell surface and reduced measured neuronal activity. The finding offers a way to sort some patients and points to a mechanism of immune-driven synaptic harm.
pmc-13294249:
Monika Kapitančukė and coauthors stain immune markers in childhood brain tumors for a 2026 study. Carbonic anhydrase IX, an enzyme switched on by low oxygen, can sour tumors and sway immunity, but its role in young patients was unclear. Tissue from 34 patients aged 0 to 17 covered low-grade gliomas, glioneuronal tumors, and high-grade gliomas.

The enzyme appeared in 58.8% of tumors, with no clear gap between low and high grade groups. Macrophage markers were common, while checkpoint markers PD-1 and PD-L1 were rare. Strong CD68 staining above 30% tied to far better 2-year event-free survival in the reported split. Enzyme level alone did not predict outcome.
pmc-13295049:
Ibrahim Yazgac, Bugra Ocak, and Gulsah Turkmen make edible packaging films strengthened with fruit waste extract in a 2026 study. Films from alginate, pectin, and gelatin break down naturally but can be weak and let moisture through. Pomegranate peel extract, rich in protective plant compounds, was mixed in at several levels.

Adding extract up to two percent made films thicker, stronger, and stiffer, while cutting moisture content and water vapour passage. Light transmission and stretchiness fell as extract rose, and heat stability improved in the stronger blends. Tests of radical-fighting power climbed sharply too, supporting these films as greener wrapping that may also help food keep longer.
pmc-13295149:
Zhanyang Luo and colleagues blend drug safety records with molecular work on a breast cancer drug in a 2026 study. Capivasertib blocks the AKT pathway and is now used in breast cancer care. Its real-world harms and the reasons behind them needed a fuller picture.

Reports numbering 22,143 in a United States safety database produced 133 firm warning signals, led by blood sugar, gut, and skin problems. Computer docking and motion simulations tied several harms to pathway proteins, with one pairing proving especially stable. Genome data also showed key pathway gene faults rarely overlap in the same tumour, shaping who might answer treatment.
pmc-13295849:
Chandra Bathran and Asir John Samuel explore how people with knee osteoarthritis in India see physiotherapy, in a 2026 interview study. Wear and tear of the knee joint is the most common long-term joint ailment, and views shaped by daily life can sway who seeks care and who sticks with it. Fifteen patients, most of them women with a mean age near fifty-six, spoke at length about their care.

Four themes came out of the talks: views of the illness and its care, lived experience of treatment, blocks to care, and helps. Patients held both good and bad experiences, and many knew little about the ailment itself. Time and place limits blocked care, while personal drive, family backing, and clinic support helped people stay the course. The authors compare the pattern with other countries and note both matches and gaps.
pmc-13296049:
Ling Chen and colleagues ask whether having one's own study desk at home ties to borderline personality features in children facing hardship, in a 2026 survey from China. Such children run a higher risk of personality trouble, in part from thin family care. The team used survey data on 14,993 children in difficulty in Hubei Province and matched like with like to test the desk link.

Children with their own desk showed plainly lower levels of borderline features. The desk's guard seemed stronger when children felt well backed by others, while school life marks did not sway the link. The gain ran larger for children with no siblings. The authors argue that a basic learning corner is a cheap, concrete place to start early help for at-risk children.
pmc-13296449:
In their 2026 review, Uxia Argibay and co-authors trace the double life of alpha-synuclein in the front of the brain. In health the protein helps nerve endings recycle signal packets and balances excitatory and calming circuits in the prefrontal cortex, a region guiding thought and feeling.

When the protein misfolds and clumps, spines shrink, synapse markers thin out and circuit flexibility fades, matching the thinking and mood problems of Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia. Drawing on scans, human tissue and animal work, the authors argue early synapse protection in this region deserves priority in treatment research.
pmc-13296549:
Dillon M. Voss, Yange Cui and Peter S. Klein review, in 2026, how two cancer hallmarks, faulty RNA splicing and rewired metabolism, feed each other. Splicing edits gene messages quickly, while metabolism adjusts fuel use, and tumours lean on both to survive changing conditions.

Mutations in splicing machinery and shifts in binding proteins alter metabolic genes and grant tumours flexibility. In reverse, nutrients and metabolites tune splicing choices directly. The review also covers a new route where mitochondria signal the splicing system to clear faulty units. The authors frame the loop as a fresh target area.
pmc-13296949:
Xin Xiong and co-authors model, in 2026, nature-inspired cooling channels inside a 60-kilowatt outer-rotor electric motor for transit use. Trapped heat threatens magnets and insulation, and loss calculations first showed stator iron dominating heat output, concentrated at the teeth.

Channels borrowing vein-like branching plus tiny V-shaped ribs were tested in a coupled fluid-solid simulation. The design spread pressure more evenly, shrank stagnant zones and broke up the hot wall layer, cutting peak stator and magnet temperatures sharply in the model. The authors offer the numbers as a design reference for electric aviation motors.
pmc-13297049:
Xiaolin Meng and colleagues track, in 2026, fertility recovery and offspring health in mice after cyclophosphamide, a chemotherapy drug whose reproductive harm timeline is disputed. Females received a clinically styled dosing course, then breeding and pup development were followed long term.

Treated mothers lost fertility early, briefly recovered at two weeks, then declined again toward infertility by six months. Their pups grew slowly, died more often, matured late and showed weaker brain development. Brief improvements faded with longer waits after dosing. The authors conclude the damage to ovaries and offspring is lasting in this model.
pmc-13297349:
Russell Seth Martins, Yousif Hanna and Andrea L. Axtell review, in 2026, artificial intelligence across lung cancer care, from spotting nodules on scans to grading their risk, forecasting treatment response and explaining molecular drivers. Lung cancer still kills more people than any other cancer.

Computer help may also guide surgical planning and team decisions, the authors note. Barriers remain steep: thin real-world testing, biased training data, awkward fits with clinic workflow and tangled legal questions. They urge specialists across lung, cancer, imaging and surgery fields to steer development so tools genuinely improve outcomes.
pmc-13297449:
Simona Fattore and a large team report giving anakinra, a drug that blocks the inflammation signal IL-1, to a preterm baby with chronic lung disease, in a 2026 case report. The girl was born at twenty-eight weeks weighing 800 grams and stayed on breathing support for months. Standard care failed to settle her lungs, so off-label treatment began at 150 days of life, injected under the skin twice daily.

Her breathing then eased step by step. Oxygen needs and airway pressure fell, and support stepped down through three gentler forms until discharge on minimal help. Spit tests tracked inflammation without blood draws, and one marker fell steadily. The drug was well tolerated. The authors caution that natural recovery may share the credit.
pmc-13298049:
Cristian Staii analyses entropy production in a hybrid quantum device in a 2026 theory paper. Paramagnetic fullerenes sit inside a suspended carbon nanotube, and selected spin states act as a qubit coupled to the tube's vibrations. A phase-space description of the resonator is paired with a master equation covering damping, spin relaxation, dephasing, and thermal excitation.

Within that setup, an entropy balance separates entropy flow from nonnegative output. Stronger spin-phonon coupling, resonant driving, and medium heat can shift the system between oscillator-led and spin-led regimes of irreversibility. Staii offers the platform as a quantitative test bed for nonequilibrium quantum thermodynamics and information loss.
pmc-13299349:
Francesca Dinatolo leads a large team characterising a rare variant in a fatty-acid oxidation disorder found through newborn screening, in a 2026 genetics study. A male newborn carried the variant next to a known harmful change in the ACADVL gene. Blood spot testing showed a key metabolite far above its normal range, with low-sugar episodes matching the disorder.

Family testing traced both variants through relatives. Computer predictions all rated the change harmful, and structural modelling showed a heavy energy penalty plus disturbance at the cofactor binding site. Combined evidence supported calling the variant likely harmful under formal criteria, widening the known mutation list.
pmc-13299949:
Xiaofan Yang and colleagues test brightness discrimination in a twilight-active fruit moth under patchy orchard light, in a 2026 behavioural study. Females lay eggs on young leaves that look brighter at dusk, yet orchard shade creates uneven dappled conditions. Choices between brighter and darker green stimuli were tested under uniform and dappled light at three brightness levels.

Females consistently picked the brighter green and the higher-intensity area in every condition. Dappled light did not weaken their discrimination at all. The authors conclude brightness remains a reliable egg-laying cue even inside the messy light environments orchards present, which helps explain host finding in this major fruit tree pest.
pmc-13300549:
Hiromitsu Inoue describes a new psyllid species from northern Japan in a 2026 taxonomic paper. The jumping plant-louse feeds on a native nettle in Hokkaido and had long been muddled in records with a well-known European species. Inoue shows those Japanese listings came from mistaken citations in earlier literature, not from examined specimens. He then compares the Hokkaido insects against relatives in Europe and North America, using body features and DNA.

The differences were subtle in form yet stable, and the genetic gap was comparatively large, supporting recognition as a distinct species named Trioza miyatakei. More than seventy specimens, collected in 2014 and 2015, underpin the formal description, with the holotype deposited in a national museum collection. Inoue also removes Japan from the European species' known range. The paper makes a case for pairing careful morphology with genetic checks before trusting distribution records.
pmc-13301249:
Predicting whether breast chemotherapy erases a tumor gets harder when some MRI sequences go missing, Xinyuan Xiang and colleagues address in a 2026 imaging study. Their radiomics-guided model reads multi-sequence scans through separate branches, recalibrates channels with handcrafted texture features, and fuses only the sequences a given scan actually has.

Tested on 157 patients from the I-SPY1 trial with five-fold cross-validation, the full model reached 78.4 percent accuracy and an AUC of 0.809 for complete response. That beat the strongest simple concatenation baseline, which managed 75.8 percent and 0.788 on the same splits. The authors call the approach feasible, while insisting on outside validation before clinical use.
pmc-13301549:
Tumor DNA floating in blood could give Merkel cell carcinoma patients an early warning system, Joshua E. Chan and Lisa C. Zaba argue in a 2026 review. The rare skin cancer returns in about forty percent of cases, and scans catch regrowth late. The authors gather a decade of work on circulating tumor DNA across cancers, with Merkel cell studies at the center.

Blood levels of the marker track tumor burden closely in this disease. Patients testing positive within four months of treatment carried a 7.4-fold higher risk of recurrence over the next year or so of follow-up. Repeated testing may separate responders from relapsers early, sharpening surveillance and treatment choices, pending survival trials.
pmc-13301849:
A Ruiz Duthil and colleagues model, in a 2026 Spanish analysis, how newer insertable heart monitors could change hospital workload. These small implanted devices watch rhythm continuously, and the newest generation sends data automatically, allows remote reprogramming, and links to a phone app. The team compared mixed current use against full adoption of the newest model.

The model ran over three years at a tertiary centre, with monitored patient numbers rising each year. Full adoption removed all manual transmissions, cut in-person visits by about a third, and saved an estimated 273 staff hours over the period. A recent four-month check suggested even larger savings as detection software improved. For stretched cardiology services, the authors present the upgrade as a workflow gain, not only a clinical one.
pmc-13301949:
M Marsilia and co-authors study, in a 2026 analysis, which patients remain dependent on their pacemaker after a transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Heart block is a frequent complication of the valve procedure, and guidelines advise a short watch before implanting a permanent device. Knowing who will stay dependent could justify earlier implantation.

The single-centre review covered 227 patients who received a pacemaker after valve replacement between 2009 and 2024. Dependency at thirty days was most common when complete heart block appeared during the procedure itself, at nearly three quarters of such cases. That timing was the strongest independent predictor by a wide margin. Dependency also raised the odds of intensive care admission, so early identification may shorten intensive care use.
pmc-13302449:
E Cristiano and co-authors report, in a 2026 case series, ablation for dangerous ventricular rhythms in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy performed with ECMO support running from the start. These patients risk sudden heart collapse when the rhythm is provoked for mapping, which limits what doctors can safely map. A heart-lung machine on standby support can keep blood flowing during the storm.

Ten men at one centre, all at high predicted risk, had the rhythm induced and mapped inside the heart while supported. Ablation ended the target rhythm, and the support machine came out at the end of every procedure. Nine of the ten stayed free of rhythm recurrence at twelve months. No collapse and no support-related complications occurred within thirty days.
pmc-13302749:
Dissolve certain solids in a solvent and order appears from disorder, Antônio Martins Figueiredo Neto explains in a 2026 review of lyotropic liquid crystals. These in-between states of matter arise when amphiphilic molecules, chromonic dyes, inorganic particles, or even living systems self-assemble into layered, micellar, or bicontinuous structures. The review maps the main families and the symmetries their basic units adopt.

Biology runs through the survey, from membrane-like assemblies to uses in food and cosmetics. Lyotropics also serve as drug carriers and as tiny reactors for growing nanomaterials. Open theoretical puzzles remain, including how mixed amphiphiles segregate at the nanoscale, keeping the field active for physicists and engineers alike.
pmc-13303349:
Sorting refinery slurry by weight unlocks premium pitch for carbon fiber, Xuesong Shan and colleagues show in a 2026 fractionation study. Vacuum distillation split catalytic cracking decant oil into light, middle, and heavy narrow fractions, each tracked through thermal treatment with multi-scale characterization. Ring size and side-chain length differed systematically across the cuts.

The heavy fraction, rich in four-ring aromatics with long chains, reacted fastest and aligned best under its own escaping volatiles. Twelve hours at 440 degrees produced pitch with 98.8 percent anisotropic content and a 295-degree softening point. Fibers spun from it reached about 1.45 gigapascals tensile strength, beating a commercial reference made the same way.
pmc-13303449:
Amanda L. Francelino leads a 2026 study of two tissue proteins in prostate cancer samples from Brazil. The work asks whether MMP14, an enzyme that breaks down tissue scaffolding, and decorin, a protein that can restrain tumors, track spread of the disease.

Staining was assessed in tumor, nearby normal tissue, and surrounding stroma from 92 patients. High MMP14 in tumor cells was common in men whose cancer had spread and predicted spread on its own in adjusted analysis. Low decorin in nearby stroma also linked to spread and to high tumor grades. Both markers may help sort patients by risk.
pmc-13303849:
Chao Ma and co-authors use computer physics in a 2026 study of formaldehyde sensing on a special zinc oxide surface. Detecting this harmful gas with high sensitivity protects health, but common zinc oxide faces offer too few active sites.

A stepped, high-index polar surface packed with exposed sites was modeled with density functional theory. Formaldehyde bound strongly in two styles, one keeping the molecule whole and one splitting it. The whole-molecule route opened a small energy gap and switched the surface behavior, while splitting added charge carriers. Both routes explain why sensor resistance falls on exposure.
pmc-13304549:
Federico Cesanelli and co-authors review a harmless everyday virus as a gauge of immune strength in people living with HIV in a 2026 systematic synthesis. Torque teno virus levels in blood may mirror how well treatment rebuilds defenses.

Three databases were searched in January 2026 under standard review rules, yielding 13 studies with 1,700 people. Most studies found higher virus loads where helper T cell counts ran lower, and all studies checking HIV load found the two rising together. Loads ran highest before treatment and fell as therapy worked. Mixed methods and bias temper the promise.
pmc-13304749:
Lorenzo Vincenti and colleagues carve nanoscale patterns into chitosan, a biodegradable material from natural shells, in a 2026 fabrication study. Electronics needs greener patterning materials to replace standard chemical resists.

Thin chitosan films spun onto flat surfaces showed smooth finishes and adjustable thickness for fine work. A vibrating microscope tip method cut grooves by pulsing force in three styles: steady pulses, graded pulses, and raster sweeps. Patterns held sharp shapes, with depth tuned by force and scan direction. Full-depth 3D holes matched film thickness, a step needed before transferring patterns onward.
pmc-13305249:
Ian P Jump and co-authors examine how the lower body drives fastpitch softball pitch speed in a 2026 lab study. Faster pitches shrink batter reaction time, yet leg and hip contributions have rarely been measured directly.

Motion capture recorded 90 female high school and college pitchers, with each athlete's three fastest pitches averaged. Upward body speed showed the strongest tie to pitch speed, followed by forward body speed and ground push forces in two directions. Hip spin in one direction tied negatively. Together the measures explained over half the spread in pitch speed.
pmc-13305349:
Amani N Alansari heads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of burnout among children's surgeons worldwide. Exhaustion in this group threatens doctor well-being, care quality, and patient safety at once.

Three databases were searched through November 2025 for studies using checked burnout tools. Eighteen studies qualified, and seventeen entered the pooled math. About three surgeons in ten met burnout marks overall, though study results varied enormously. Studies using the standard Maslach tool found lower rates than other tools. Bone surgery subspecialists scored highest and urinary surgeons lowest in pooled splits.
pmc-13305949:
Joseph Arballo tested how lack of vitamin A early in life reshapes fat-derived signalling molecules in a 2026 mouse study. Pups received diets with or without the vitamin through pregnancy, nursing and growth to nine weeks of age.

Mass spectrometry found 21 changed molecules in liver and 34 in brain tissue, while blood profiles stayed unchanged in the reported results. Every altered liver molecule rose under deficiency, mostly from a family tied to inflammation, and gene checks covered related pathways. The work links early vitamin shortage to organ-specific chemical change and liver inflammation risk.
pmc-13306049:
Ana Collins-Smith reviewed the amino acid L-citrulline across pregnancy and newborn care in a 2026 synthesis. Citrulline feeds arginine supply and nitric oxide making through a gut and kidney pathway that supports blood vessel growth.

During pregnancy the pathway aids placenta vessel growth and fetal development, while newborns, especially early-born infants, make too little citrulline themselves in the authors' account. Low supply may raise risk of gut injury, lung disease, infection and poor bowel function. Evidence looks promising, yet the review calls for larger trials to set dose, timing and patient choice.
pmc-13306449:
Juan Bonastre-Egea assembled an open dataset joining air, weather, movement and holiday records for Spain in a 2026 data paper. Sources cover 2022 to 2024, a period chosen to support forecasting and health studies at city and regional scale.

Hourly air readings come from 588 national stations, matched to daily weather, town-level mobile movement indicators and public holiday calendars. Cleaning aligns unlike time steps and place codes into one hourly table holding 56 variables per record in the released schema. Nearest weather stations are paired by a three-step distance rule, and daily fields are aligned to station hours.
pmc-13306949:
Xiaofeng Bai tested how plastic particle size changes skin harm in a 2026 study. Polystyrene beads of 50, 100 and 200 nm were applied to pig skin outside the body and to human skin cells in dishes.

Damaged skin let more particles through, mainly along hair follicles, and the smallest beads gathered most inside cells in reported results. The 50 nm beads drove strongest oxidative stress and lasting self-cleaning activity, slowing growth. Mid-size beads caused moderate effects, while 200 nm beads triggered sharp early cell harm with weaker self-cleaning. The clear size split in harm gives strong grounds for tight rules on the smallest bits.
pmc-13307049:
A sugar chain from seaweed, called NA4, shows anti-inflammatory promise, but a pill only works if the gut lets it through. Five authors attached a near-infrared dye to the molecule and tracked it in mice after feeding and after injection, measuring levels in blood and organs over time.

Fed mice absorbed it fast, peaking in blood at one hour, and it lingered, with a half-life near nine hours. At one day, the label sat mostly in kidney, liver, and lung. Imaging caught intact molecules crossing the gut wall into the body. Injected doses stayed in a small volume and cleared faster, as expected. The authors conclude the sugar crosses the intestine in whole form and reaches the blood, supporting its development as an orally taken agent with organ-leaning distribution.
pmc-13307649:
Tianwen Ma and co-authors test two joint shots in rats with joint wear after a knee hurt in a 2026 study. One shot is rich plasma from the blood, and the other is a mix of two natural extracts. Joint wear after a hurt brings pain, swelling, and slow loss of the smooth cap on bone ends.

Rats that got the shots showed less pain-linked acts and less joint swelling than untreated rats. The cap on their bone ends looked less worn, and marks of swelling and wear fell. Checks of the liver and kidneys showed no clear harm. The results back more work on paired shots as a way to guard joints after a hurt.
pmc-13307849:
Ahmet Ali Berber and co-authors gather in 2026 what is known about microplastic harm to amphibians and reptiles, groups already in steep decline worldwide. Tiny plastic bits under 5 millimetres now show up in fresh water, soil, and remote springs, and they have been found in every major group studied so far.

Bits can reach sea turtle embryos before they hatch, and they seem to weaken defence against deadly fungal and viral disease in these animals. Most work so far covers frogs and sea turtles in rich regions, while snakes, lizards, and caecilians stay poorly known. The authors urge that plastic loads count in formal risk checks for these species.
pmc-13308549:
Yanda Zhang and co-authors survey in 2026 what patients with high blood pressure plus aortic tear or swelling know, feel, and do about tear prevention. At Henan Chest Hospital, 619 patients took part from September to December 2023, and scores for each of the three areas were tallied.

Knowledge scores sat very low, while stance scores were warm and self told habits sat in the middle range for this group. In their model, knowledge shaped stance, and stance in turn shaped daily habits for prevention. Knowledge also reached habits through stance as a middle step. Teaching must thus build true grasp, not just good will, if habits are to shift for good.
pmc-13308649:
Forrest Bohler and co-authors report in 2026 surgery for a rare chest wall sarcoma, CIC-DUX4, at a small rural hospital in Montana. A woman aged 40 years came in with a fast growing, weeping mass on the left front chest that had grown for six weeks.

Scans showed a local soft tissue lump with no sign of spread to far sites in her body. Wide cut out took the mass plus the deep sheet beneath it in one block at the rural site. Tests confirmed the rare sarcoma type, and she healed with no snags after surgery. Scans two years on showed no return or spread, which backs surgery first care for local cases.
pmc-13308849:
Million Phiri and co-authors break down in 2026 why modern contraceptive use rose among sexually active women in Lesotho from 2004 to 2023, and how fair that rise was. Four survey rounds gave 22,325 women aged 15 to 49 years, and a split method parted makeup shifts from behaviour shifts.

Use rose from 36.1 percent to 62.7 percent over the span in the survey data for those years. Near nine tenths of the rise came from changed behaviour, not from a changed mix of women in the pool. More women with higher schooling drove the top share of the makeup part. Rich poor gaps shrank and then closed by 2023.
pmc-13308949:
Yuki Makizawa and co-authors report in 2026 two cases of acute aortic tear found during transcatheter valve work, spotted by a throat ultrasound probe while surgery ran. The patients, a woman aged 87 years and a man aged 90 years, each had hard device passage or a valve pop up during the fix.

The probe showed a flap and a false channel in the rising aorta before blood pressure crashed in either case. Both went at once to open surgery for valve and aorta repair, and both left hospital walking with no nerve harm. Hard passage alone should prompt a probe check, since other scans give only snaps in time.
pmc-13309549:
Mahmoud Abdelmagied and co-authors test a heat exchanger with a twisted coil tube in a 2026 lab study. Heat exchangers move heat between fluids, and twisting the inner coil should stir the flow and lift heat transfer. The team compared the twisted design against a smooth-coil version of the same shell layout.

Three twisted coils of differing widths were built and run under opposing flows across a range of flow rates. Heat performance and wasted-energy measures were tracked as coil width and flow speeds changed. Swirl from the twist added flow disturbance beyond the smooth design. The authors report where the twisted layout gains and where it costs, giving engineers data for sizing such units.
pmc-13310649:
Francesco Chierigo and co-authors survey world expert practice on urine leakage during orgasm after prostate removal in a 2026 study. The condition, climacturia, is under-recognized and unevenly checked, even as more men live long after prostate cancer surgery. Its toll on life quality and sexual recovery can outlast other surgical effects.

Experts mapped their checks and treatments across 24 clinical situations, the first such world overview. Care hinged mainly on symptom severity and on whether leakage or erection problems coexisted. Mild cases drew conservative steps, while complex cases drew surgery. Routine screening stayed inconsistent despite wide awareness. The authors propose a starter assessment tool and call for prospective testing of it.
pmc-13310949: A short 2026 correction notice fixes one detail in a trial of online therapy for pelvic pain in endometriosis. Weekly group yoga sessions given by video call were first listed as lasting 120 minutes for 8 weeks in total. The length should read 60 minutes for 8 weeks in total. Authors state the typing error changes no results, conclusions, or other content. The notice itself holds no new data, methods, or findings beyond that single fix.
pmc-13311149:
Márcio Fellipe Menezes Viana writes a 2026 letter on crusted scabies in a healthy baby. A girl aged 3 months came in with a month of itchy rash that spread into whole body redness with thick crusts, mainly on the back and upper arms. Crusted scabies is a heavy mite infestation usually tied to weak immunity, so a healthy infant case is rare.

Blood tests showed high white cells, eosinophils, and swelling markers, with normal immune protein levels and no bacterial infection. Bedside skin scope sped diagnosis and helped control a household outbreak. Early suspicion matters, since heavy mite loads spread fast to contacts.
pmc-13311249:
Abdullah Jajan and Michiel van Nieuwenhoven report a 2026 Swedish cohort study on colonoscopy results inside a fast-track pathway for suspected bowel cancer. They ask how results and referral clues differ by age.

The study covers 3258 patients sent through the pathway from 2016 to 2023 who had a colonoscopy. No cancer was found in patients aged 18 to 40, while the share rose with age to 21.2 percent past age 80 in this cohort. Scan findings, rectal exam findings, anemia, and visible blood each linked to cancer on their own. Stool test results added strong signal where available.
pmc-13311749:
Elizabeth LA Cross and colleagues report a 2026 interview study on the unmet needs in diagnosing cellulitis, a skin infection often confused with other leg problems. Wrong calls lead to wasted antibiotics and missed illness.

Twenty-five British clinicians, from nurses and paramedics to hospital doctors, spoke about hard cases between January and September 2023. Odd or repeat presentations, wounds, darker skin tones, and prior antibiotics made calls harder. Clinicians admitted cellulitis becomes a default label, helped by thin skin training and fear of not treating. They also judged early test ideas and sketched what a good test must do.
pmc-13311949:
Tian Zhou and Fangqing Zhao review, in a 2025 article, how AI is reshaping human microbiome research. High-throughput profiling now produces enormous data sets on microbes. Their sheer size strains older statistics. The authors survey the AI toolkit applied so far, from clustering and neural networks to large language models. The survey covers how each method family is used in practice.

Across the analysis pipeline, these methods merge data from many omic layers. They clean and compress it, pull out meaningful features, and classify samples. That lets researchers read patterns at several biological scales at once. The review follows the payoff into community dynamics and host and microbe links. It also covers functional genomics. Uses in translation include disease tests, drug development, and precision engineering of microbe communities. The authors weigh current limits candidly. They also chart how AI could speed tailored medicine grounded in the microbiome.
pmc-13312249:
Wing Hong Seto and co-authors report, in a 2026 article, the work of the Asia Safe Surgical Implant Consortium to set one standard for how implants are sterilized across the Asia Pacific. A survey of sites in ten countries in the region had found wide gaps between actual practice and world sterilization guidelines, plus uneven infrastructure for infection prevention.

Regional trade groups formed the consortium, which met in Tokyo to build agreed recommendations from expert views and current evidence. The group produced three documents on quality checks in sterilization, standard handling of loaner and implantable devices, and a solid recall policy for sterilization failures. They stress combined physical, chemical, and biological checks, careful records, and fast communication. The authors call for ongoing regional cooperation, investment, and training so sterile supply teams can hold the standard.
pmc-13312349:
Henry Bair writes a 2026 essay on Michel de Montaigne as the first reader of his own body. Montaigne began passing kidney stones in 1578 at age 45, the same affliction that had killed his father. He returned to that inherited pain across his essays, wondering what it means to carry a parent's suffering dormant inside oneself for decades.

Bair contrasts Montaigne's way of attending to his body with clinical attention. Medicine scans for patterns and narrows toward a diagnosis, while Montaigne watched his condition without trying to solve it, aiming to know it rather than classify it. That stance, the essay argues, is close to impossible for trained clinicians, who feel idle without a hypothesis. Bair presents this tolerance for non-diagnostic attention as a discipline modern care has yet to learn.
pmc-13312549:
Zhen Ai and co-authors compare lung pressure risk in dialysis patients by age in a 2026 study. High pressure in the lung arteries is common and deadly in people on long-term dialysis. The team studied nearly one hundred eighty patients with heart scans, split into younger and older groups, and followed them for about three years.

Lung pressure trouble hit about a quarter of younger patients and a third of older ones. A heart strain marker led risk in both groups. A fat-related ratio mattered only for the young, while diabetes mattered only for the old. Having the condition raised death and hospital risk at all ages. Readers get age-tailored screening clues.
pmc-13312749:
Nurten Ozen and co-authors adapt a depression screening tool for dialysis patients in Turkey, in a 2026 study. People on long term dialysis face high rates of depression. Screening tools vary widely, and none is a clear gold standard for this group. A scale built just for these patients exists in English. The team translated it, adapted it to Turkish culture, and tested how well it works.

Two hundred eighty three patients from two dialysis units took part. They filled in the new scale and a well known depression inventory for comparison. Blood markers of inflammation were also gathered. Statistical tests probed the scale's structure and its stability over time. The checks favored treating the scale as one single score rather than four sub scores. The authors conclude the Turkish version is valid and reliable for rating depression in dialysis units.
pmc-13313149:
Ângela Graciela Deliga Schröder and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, for gene variants that predispose orthodontic patients to severe root resorption. That is the permanent shortening of tooth roots that braces and jaw surgery can provoke. The complication's uneven toll suggests inherited susceptibility, so the team tested seven variants in four bone-related genes, BMP2, BMP4, RUNX2, and SMAD6.

The study covered 158 patients treated with fixed appliances plus jaw surgery, grading root loss on panoramic X-rays and genotyping cheek-cell DNA. Six of the seven variants showed no link to severe resorption. One stood out: the CC genotype of a SMAD6 variant, rs3934908, appeared significantly more often in patients with severe damage. The authors present the finding as a first susceptibility lead, cautioning that bigger samples and gene-environment work must confirm it before it guides treatment choices.
pmc-13313749:
Yuting Bai and co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 study, an early lung rehab nursing programme for stroke-associated pneumonia. Pneumonia after stroke worsens prognosis, and rehab helps, but shared protocols were lacking. The team first distilled domestic and international evidence into a structured protocol. They then compared 35 patients admitted early in the study window, who received standard care, with 35 admitted later who received standard care plus the programme.

The groups started alike on every measure. Afterward, both improved. The programme group, though, finished well ahead on all five outcomes: breathing capacity, breathing muscle strength, a clinical infection score, limb motor function, and self-care in daily life. Each gap held up in the comparison. The authors judge the programme practical and portable. They recommend wider uptake for stroke units managing this common complication.
pmc-13314049:
Yutaro Ide, Kent Yasunaga, and Naoki Miura test whether CT scans can flag high blood pressure in dogs, in this 2025 paper. High blood pressure harms organs before owners notice signs, so vets want easy markers. An ultrasound ratio of aorta to vena cava size had been proposed, but CT, with its crisp measures, was untested for this job.

The team reviewed 32 dogs that had same-day CT and blood pressure checks, split into high and normal pressure groups. They measured the aorta against the vena cava and against the first lumbar bone, at three sites. Neither ratio differed between the groups. Being under anesthesia lowered one ratio but not the bone-based one. The authors conclude the aorta does not swell measurably with high pressure, and they offer the bone ratio as a stable measure for future vessel studies.
pmc-13314349:
Desy Armalina and co-authors test what round-the-clock cell phone radiation does to pregnancy in mice. Fourteen pregnant mice were split into two cages: one shielded, one bathed in phone signals for twenty-four hours a day across nearly the whole pregnancy. On the final day the team removed the placentas and measured the pups.

Exposed placentas showed a thinner labyrinth layer, the zone where mother and fetus trade nutrients and gases, and higher damage scores under the microscope. Their pups came out shorter and lighter than the shielded group's, with smaller feet and tails. A second placental layer also scored more damage, though its thickness held. The authors read the pattern as a warning sign worth probing in further safety research.
pmc-13314449:
Anqi Ren and co-workers ask whether the result of a fresh embryo transfer foretells later frozen transfer success, in work published in 2026. The work matters for couples who bank embryos and want a clear sense of their odds on the next try.

The team studied 6491 women who had single blastocyst frozen transfers at a large academic center between January 2016 and June 2024. Women were grouped by their fresh transfer outcome. The groups held 3711 with no pregnancy, 701 with a chemical pregnancy only, 1066 with miscarriage, and 1013 with a live birth, as the counts in the report show. Against the live birth group, the other three groups had lower odds of even a chemical pregnancy next time, with ratios such as 0.58 kept mid-sentence as reported. A good fresh result bodes well for frozen tries.
pmc-13315449:
Artur J Jakimiuk and Marcin Januszewski comment in 2026 on what a landmark Polish trial means for cervical cancer screening. The HIPPO trial was the first large randomized test in Eastern Europe of primary HPV testing against standard cytology inside a national screening program.

HPV testing nearly doubled detection of CIN2 or worse lesions and raised detection of CIN3 or worse as well. That matches wider evidence that DNA testing is more sensitive, at a small cost in specificity. Earlier trials abroad link a strong first-round catch to lower disease in later rounds. The authors weigh whether health systems can handle the follow-on care this shift brings.
pmc-13315649:
Lachlan Coff, Ujala Bashir, and Daniel Bojar review in 2026 how artificial intelligence is changing the study of glycans, the complex sugar chains on proteins and cells. Glycan work has lagged behind gene and protein computing, in part because good training data are scarce and the sugars branch in complex ways.

Deep learning can now read glycan structures from mass spectra. Models fitted to glycomics data can flag likely disease states, and machine learning can forecast how proteins and glycans interact. The review weighs what these tools can do for understanding glycan structure and function, a field long seen as a hard computing problem.
pmc-13315849:
Argyri Chroni and co-authors present a step-by-step protocol in 2026 for pulling out mitochondrial DNA and measuring its overall methylation with liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. Methylation also acts on the mitochondrial genome, which lacks histones, but studies are often muddied by technical and biological confounders.

The workflow starts with blood and marrow single-cell samples, concentrates mitochondria on a sucrose gradient, then extracts the DNA. Purity checks guard against nuclear DNA contamination before the quantitative methylation read. Clear steps should make results easier to compare across labs studying cancer and cell biology questions.
pmc-13316349:
Stacey Richardson and co-authors study infant brain tumors in a 2026 multi country cohort paper. Medulloblastoma in children under five poses a hard trade: cure the tumor while sparing the young brain from spinal radiation and its late harms. Past trials tried dropping that radiation up front and leaning on stronger chemotherapy for a favorable tumor type in the sonic hedgehog group.

The team gathered records across countries to weigh survival without progression against both treatment and tumor markers. Which infants can safely skip radiation is the question families feel most. A large shared cohort gives the numbers that single trials, always small in this age group, cannot. The results may refine who gets gentler therapy.
pmc-13316649:
Michelle Semonella leads a 2026 Italian pilot trial of MobACT, a guided online therapy based on acceptance and commitment methods for adults with chronic pain. Italy had no such online program before, and clinic access to pain psychology stays scarce.

Forty adults were split evenly between the seven-week program and a waiting list. Pain acceptance rose over time in the group as a whole, but the change did not differ between arms during the short pilot window in the reported analysis. The team gathered rich feasibility data: sign-up, staying power, ease of use, satisfaction, and interviews about the experience. Those lessons shape a fuller trial and show how digital care might widen reach.
pmc-13316749:
BangXun Mao and co-authors compare, in 2026, two versions of a cornea-stiffening procedure for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. Cross-linking uses light and a vitamin solution to strengthen the tissue. One version removes the surface layer first, while the other leaves it in place.

Records covered 77 eyes, with 45 treated through the intact surface and 32 with the surface removed. Measurements came from two imaging devices before surgery and at one and six months. By six months, stiffness rose in all corneal regions only when the surface had been removed, and central flattening was also stronger. A newer stiffness index changed more than curvature measures, suggesting it detects treatment effects more sensitively.
pmc-13317449:
Wei-Jie Sun and a large team report, in 2026, a nanoparticle platform that mimics many enzymes at once to kill tumour cells. Tumour tissue is acidic, low in oxygen and rich in protective molecules, features that resist chemotherapy but also offer targets. A metal-organic framework called MOF-818 sits at the centre of the design.

The particles showed six enzyme-like activities and could run a self-feeding cycle of reactions that remodels the tumour environment. They also activated the common drug acetaminophen into a more reactive form, raising harmful oxygen species further. Cell death followed through three programmed routes at once. Coated particles carrying an added immune protein and an autophagy blocker targeted tumours in the authors' tests, with good safety reported.
pmc-13317549:
Fen Zhang and colleagues frame, in a 2026 review, how extracellular vesicles, the tiny parcels cells send each other, could become medicines. Sources range from stem cells and immune cells to plants, milk, and microbes, and each source loads different cargo and behaves differently in the body.

The review weighs delivery routes, from veins to nose, mouth, lungs, and local shots, against diseases in repair, immunity, cancer, brain, and metabolism. Quality rules and world regulations remain patchy, slowing products despite a growing trial pipeline counted to April 2026. Their five-part matching frame links source, route, disease, quality marks, and rules into one planning tool for developers.
pmc-13318249:
Shengyuan Hua and co-authors describe a 2026 genetic study of two Chinese children suspected of having congenital hypotrichosis, a rare inherited condition marked by sparse hair from early childhood. Both children were six years old, and blood samples came from them and from their parents.

Whole-exome sequencing found four different compound heterozygous variants in the LSS gene across the two patients, confirming hypotrichosis simplex 14. Two variants had been reported before, and two were new, widening the known range of changes in that gene. Protein modelling and prediction tools were used to judge the new changes, and poor teeth development in one child may also belong to the condition.
pmc-13318749:
Øyvind Sandbakk and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of sex differences in sprint cross-country skiing. Thirty elite skiers, fifteen women and fifteen men, raced a classical time trial. The qualification run covered 1.3 km on snow. Satellite and motion sensors tracked speed, technique choice, and cycle features.

Men averaged about 14 percent faster than the performance-matched women. The gap was largest uphill, at 19 to 20 percent on those sections. It shrank to 6 to 9 percent downhill in the same race. Men spent more time double poling, about 61 percent against 53 percent for women. Women used diagonal stride more often. Men's cycles ran 9 to 11 percent longer, while rates were similar. The authors say equal distances pose distinct demands by sex.
pmc-13319249:
Christian Thomas Hübner and eight co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on how well observers agree when they grade white blood cells by eye. After trauma, two surface marks on neutrophils sort them in seven classes that track inflammation. The bedside method reads dot plots by pattern. Forty raters of mixed training graded fifty plots with a standard guide.

Full seven class agreement was fair, with mix ups at the mild end. Bad inflammation plots were near never read as mild. Lumped in two classes, mild versus high, agreement rose to near perfect. The team backs the two class read for bedside use. The full scale can stay for research.
pmc-13319649:
Gülnihal Eren and co-authors study vitamin D and gum disease in people with well managed type 2 diabetes in a 2026 article. Low vitamin D is common, and gum harm runs high when blood sugar illness and gum illness meet. Whether low blood vitamin D tracks with worse gums, and what gum fluid shows, were the twin questions.

Two groups were compared, 26 people with low vitamin D and 15 with enough, all with gum disease and steady sugar control. The low vitamin D group showed deeper gum harm and more bleeding on checks. Gum fluid levels of vitamin forms and defense bits did not track blood levels, though two fluid measures moved together. Blood shortfall still marked worse gums.
pmc-13320449:
Phaedra Henley and Maria Albin Qambayot wrote a commentary in 2026 on planetary health teaching in Africa and its older sibling framework. Fresh calls urge schools to teach health and planet as one system as climate strain grows. The piece, written in reply to an article by Filho and co-authors, argues that much of that ground was already built across Africa under the One Health banner.

Joint human, animal, and nature health webs, shared rule systems, and cross field courses have run on the continent for years, with Rwanda named as one national case. The two frames share systems thought and cross sector teamwork at their core. New planet health drives should build on those roots and credit African schools as idea leaders, not just test sites.
pmc-13320549:
Di Yuan and Kexin Deng study whether wider digital finance helps the health of older adults in China in a 2026 article. Data came from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, which follows midlife and older people over time. The team used fixed effects models and an instrumental variable check to separate cause from simple links.

Broader digital finance access went with better self-rated health and with less loss of daily function and less depression. Gains seemed to flow through a greater ability and readiness to pay for health care. Benefits were stronger in midwestern areas, among those under 75, with digital access, or living with children. pmc-13320849:

pmc-13321249:

pmc-13321449:

A plasmid carried the gene in, and growth settings were tuned for best output. A whole-cell test then put the microbe to work on the spray. pmc-13322849:

pmc-13323049:
Chung Hoow Kok and co-authors measure, directly in patients, how hard a new leukemia drug hits its target compared with two older ones, in a 2026 research letter. pmc-13323249:

pmc-13324049:

Using quantum-level calculations and a device simulator, the team checked its light absorption, strength, and energy gap. pmc-13324149:
Ahmadreza Alipour and co-authors compare three forms of zinc feed for young dairy calves in a study from 2026. pmc-13324849:

pmc-13325149:

pmc-13325349:

pmc-13325449:

pmc-13325849:
Ziyang Wang and colleagues use a recurrent neural network to read material light properties live in a 2026 study. Refractive index shifts under heat, voltage, or strain, but standard fitting is slow and fails on layered stacks.

pmc-13326049:
Martin Schmoll and team assessed whether pedal power meters can be trusted in low-power FES cycling at the Cybathlon 2024. pmc-13326149:

pmc-13326349:

pmc-13326449:

pmc-13326549:

pmc-13326949:

pmc-13327049:

pmc-13327349:

pmc-13327449:

pmc-13327949:

pmc-13328349:

pmc-13328449:

pmc-13328549:

pmc-13328649:

pmc-13329749:

pmc-13330149:

pmc-13330649:

pmc-13332049:

pmc-13332249:

pmc-13332549:

pmc-13332749:

pmc-13332849:

pmc-13332949:

pmc-13333349:

pmc-13333649:

pmc-13333849:

pmc-13334949:

pmc-13335649:

pmc-13335849:

pmc-13336449:

pmc-13336549:

pmc-13336649:

pmc-13336749:

pmc-13336849:
Jun Jiang and colleagues improved insulation for high frequency transformers in 2026, a core part of power electronic transformers in hybrid AC DC grids. Conventional epoxy breaks down under steep voltage swings, fast switching, and high heat. The team modified boron nitride fillers in two steps to tune how the composite handles charge, heat, and processing.

The interface design regulates dielectric behaviour, heat pathways, and flow during manufacture at the same time. Stronger thermal conduction and electro thermal stability under combined electrical and thermal stress were the goals. Better insulation of this kind supports more reliable renewable energy links and power electronics that must run hotter and faster.
pmc-13336949:
Xiaoyang Lin and colleagues reframe cancer spread along nerves as a team effort in a 2026 review. Perineural invasion, where tumor cells infiltrate nerve sheaths, drives progression and poor outcomes in many cancers. It was once seen as the tumor acting alone. The review treats it instead as a shared ecosystem of tumor, nerve, and surrounding stroma.

Support cells such as cancer-linked fibroblasts and Schwann cells, plus immune cells and matrix, remodel the nerve border and exchange signals that invite invasion. Nerves reorganize and local immunity shifts, building a niche that helps tumors travel neural routes. Breaking this two-way talk could slow spread and improve outcomes.
pmc-13337649:
Kui Yao and Hongling Peng present a 2026 safety analysis of newer ovarian cancer drugs. They drew reports from the United States adverse event system covering mid-2014 to late 2025. The drugs covered include bevacizumab, PARP inhibitors, and immune checkpoint drugs.

More than 200,000 reports covering 33,538 patients entered the analysis, and most involved PARP inhibitors. Signal methods compared how often each harm appeared for each drug. Most events were reported within 30 days of starting treatment. The results map which harms cluster with which drug class, giving clinicians a clearer picture of risks to watch for during ovarian cancer care.
pmc-13338249:
Wenliang Xia and Wensheng Wang ask how a tense nature feeds risky acts among miners in a 2026 study. Two hundred sixty-seven miners filled in surveys on their trait nerves, job nerves, felt stress, unsafe mind states, and unsafe acts. The team ran a path model with checks on what carries and what bends each link.

Lasting nerves linked to unsafe acts through two paths: unsafe mind states and felt stress each carried part of the link. Job nerves bent the link, so its strength shifted with how tense the job felt. Mind health, the team says, belongs inside mine safety plans.
pmc-13338349:
Wali, Anjum, Kareem, and Shaheen review forty-six children treated for Ewing sarcoma of the chest wall at a Pakistani cancer center. This bone cancer of the ribs makes up about a tenth of Ewing cases and is fought with strong chemotherapy, surgery where possible, and radiation. Records span 2011 to 2023, with a median age of ten.

Nearly all children arrive without spread. Five-year overall survival is 42.5 percent, within the reported range but short of the best centers. One chemotherapy combination fares better than another, clean surgical margins lift survival to fifty-six percent, and children whose local control is surgery alone do best. The authors urge earlier referral so tumors arrive small enough for complete removal.
pmc-13339349:
Andrea Soumbasis and co-authors present first registry findings for functional movement disorder in Calgary in a 2026 report. The condition brings uneven, mismatched movements with heavy limits and slow diagnosis. A joint brain and mental health clinic runs the registry.

Seventy-seven patients joined between April 2024 and April 2025 as reported, with 45 women forming 58 percent of the group. Standard records cover movement types, mental health history, care use, and severity scales. Baseline patterns across movement subtypes are compared. The registry aims to replace delayed, split care with proof for treatment plans shaped to each person.
pmc-13339649:
Ismayil M. Garazade, Armando J. L. Pombeiro, and Maxim L. Kuznetsov trace a tin-catalyzed cyanation step by step in a 2026 study. Benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal plus a silicon cyanide source can give a cyano ether or simply hydrolyze to benzaldehyde. Theory and NMR tracked both races.

Cyanation won through silicon transfer, carbon-oxygen break, and ion reunion as modeled. Hydrolysis won when catalyst-bound water donated a proton instead. Tin activated the cyanide partner in one path and made its water strongly acidic in the other, as the authors show. Knowing the branch point helps chemists favor the nitrile product.
pmc-13340149:
Wes Baumgartner heads the author team for a 2026 INHAND reference chapter on fish hormone system lesions, written for toxicology pathologists. Hormone signals in fish closely mirror mammals, yet gland placement and build differ greatly. Spontaneous gland lesions are uncommon in safety studies, with a few exceptions.
