Major tissues covered include pituitary, thyroid follicles, pancreas islets, pineal gland, and corpuscles of Stannius. Ultimobranchial gland tumors in zebrafish are noted as a known exception. Standard finding lists and species contrasts help pathologists judge whether a change came from treatment. Shared wording across labs makes safety reading stronger across studies.
pmc-13340249:
Owens and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a rare germ infecting a false bulge in the aorta. A 60-year-old man arrived with three days of chest pain. Scans showed fluid around the root of his aorta, a sign of a leaking pseudoaneurysm. Blood cultures stayed negative, and surgeons repaired the aortic root.

Cultures from the surgery grew an odd rod-shaped germ that standard tests could not name. Gene sequencing at an outside lab identified it as Paenibacillus pueri, a soil germ that rarely harms people. The case shows how alike this germ looks to common Bacillus types under the microscope. The authors stress gene-based tests when cultures puzzle the team.
pmc-13341649:
Giammarino and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an enzyme-blocking compound called MC1568 can boost the standard antifungal fluconazole against non-albicans Candida yeasts. These species now cause a large share of Candida bloodstream infections and increasingly resist standard drugs. The team compared three approved blockers of histone deacetylases, enzymes that help switch genes, plus the selective compound MC1568, alone and paired with fluconazole.

The MC1568 pairing stood out, working in synergy to cut biofilm growth, the slimy layers yeasts form, and to strengthen killing against three species, including Candida tropicalis. In wax moth larvae, a stand-in host, the pair raised survival in tropicalis infection by about 70 percent over controls. Tests on human retinal cells showed low toxicity for three dose pairings. The authors propose MC1568 as an add-on therapy worth refining for hard-to-treat yeast infections.
pmc-13341749:
Genevieve Van de Bittner and co-authors hunt for the best molecular flags that reveal a T cell has met the COVID virus. T cell activation assays mark pairs of surface proteins that switch on after stimulation, but dozens of candidate pairs exist and no one had raced them head to head. The pandemic supplied the perfect samples: donors known to be naive and known to have recovered.

Thirty-five marker pairs were compared on a fifteen-marker flow panel. The strongest pairs fed a machine learning classifier that sorted donors as recovered or naive. The winning recipe could sharpen immune monitoring for vaccines, and the same approach extends to cancer reactivity testing.
pmc-13342049:
Removing a whole lung by robot is reported in the largest single-center series yet, by Ammar Asban and co-investigators in a 2026 study. Their consecutive series covered 21 robotic pneumonectomies performed from January 2019 to December 2024, drawn from a prospective database.

Median age was 70 years; cancer drove 17 cases, and 76% of those patients had prior drug or radiation therapy. Only two cases (9%) converted to open surgery as planned, chest tubes lasted a median of one day, and hospital stay five days. Thirty-day mortality was 0% and 90-day mortality 5%, far below historical figures for minimally invasive attempts at this operation.
pmc-13343149:
Binbin Su and colleagues tested lenslet array spectacle lenses in 2026 for refractive and corneal astigmatism in myopic children. The secondary analysis drew on a randomised, double masked trial of LARI lenses for myopia control in children aged six to twelve. Data from 209 participants in the earlier two phase LARI study were retrieved and analysed.

In phase one, children wore LARI or single vision lenses for twelve months, while phase two gave all children LARI lenses for another twelve months. Children who wore LARI lenses for two years formed the LARI group, while switchers from single vision formed the comparison group. The analysis tests whether lenslet lenses shift astigmatism as they slow myopia progression.
pmc-13343349:
Run-hua Li and co-authors lay out a 2026 trial protocol comparing single-use and reusable endoscopes for a reflux treatment called endoscopic cardia constriction with ligation. Reusable scopes need reprocessing and carry contamination worries, while disposable scopes may cut infection risk, but proof they handle demanding therapy equally well is thin.

Ninety-eight adults with stubborn reflux will be randomized evenly across centers, with symptoms tracked at three and six months. The main goal is a symptom score drop of at least four points, alongside checks of procedure feasibility, safety, device faults, and later acid drug use. Results will guide whether disposable scopes can take on therapeutic upper gut work.
pmc-13346649:
Brain waves may reveal how severe a person's Parkinson's disease is, as Sahil Chilukuri and co-authors show. Doctors rate severity with a standard scale, but that scale says little about the faulty circuits underneath. The team recorded brain signals from 47 patients during deep brain stimulation surgery.

They fed 110 signal features into two kinds of models. A plain linear model failed to predict the severity scores. A forest of decision trees succeeded, drawing on rhythm bursts and links between cortex and deep brain areas. Severity seems written across the whole network, not in any single signal.
pmc-13346849:
In-Sung Luke Yeo argues, in a 2026 editorial on prosthodontic care, that clinical judgement must stay anchored in science rather than habit alone. The piece opens with winemaking, where talk of wind, soil, and season can hide the measured choices about ripeness, acidity, and timing that shape a good vintage.

Dental restoration is framed the same way, since anatomy, jaw movement, materials, lab work, and patient response all vary and cannot be fully controlled at once. Experience is treated as vital but not enough on its own, because uncontrolled variation makes tested principles more needed, not less. The editorial calls for treatment choices that rest on understood evidence.
pmc-13347049:
Tiantian Wang, Difei Yao, Lingyan Yu, and Donghang Xu build a scoring system for stomach cancer drugs in a 2026 paper. The drugs are immune checkpoint inhibitors used first for advanced gastric cancer that lacks HER-2. Hospitals need a fair, numeric way to judge such drugs for use and listing.

The team starts with a pool of measures from past papers. Two rounds of expert input and a ranking method then set the weights. The final system has four main measures and many sub-measures. Effectiveness counts most, then safety, with cost and drug traits smaller. Side effects and clinical benefit weigh most below that level.
pmc-13347349:
S. Altun and co-authors make zirconium diboride powder by a gel route and test it in solid-state supercapacitors, in a study from 2026. Powders were checked by diffraction, microscopy, and surface tools, then run in salt solution across wide scan rates to separate charge stored on surfaces from charge stored by chemical change.

Chemical storage led at slow scans while surface storage led at fast scans, showing mixed behaviour in the reported split. A solid paired cell kept 90.7 percent of its capacity after 5,000 cycles, and a zinc-ion hybrid version reached 230 mAh per gram at the stated rate. Low resistance and a 1.4 V working window support use in compact storage devices.
pmc-13347949:
Benedetta Felici and colleagues review how genome scan hits are turned into treatments and biology at many scales, in a review from 2026. Nearly twenty years of scans have piled up variant links. So recent work is traced from picking drug targets and reusing old drugs, through gene control inside cells, to the inherited shape and workings of whole organs.

Key studies are highlighted at each scale to show where translation already pays off in clinic-ready leads and where gaps remain between a variant flag and a safe therapy. With the human genome draft near twenty-five years old, the authors present genomics as a working engine for new care, not just a catalogue of risk.
pmc-13348049:
Brandon Maughan and co-authors published a methods paper in 2026 on how emergency doctors judge lung clot risk. Guidelines list tests for a suspected clot in the lung, but little is known about how doctors decide to suspect one. The team built an online survey that varies patient traits to expose those choices.

Each case vignette came in eight versions, flipping sex, race, and one clinical fact. Doctors rated their suspicion on a slider and picked tests they would order, without knowing the design. Repeat scores from sixteen doctors matched closely over time. In pilot use by sixty-one doctors, mid-risk cases drew higher suspicion than low-risk ones, as they should. The authors say the tool is a sound way to study testing choices.
pmc-13348249:
Shichu Liu and co-authors forecast in 2026 a sharp north-south split in sunlight reaching Earth's surface under warming. Polar dimming pairs with mid-latitude brightening in the Northern Hemisphere. Surface solar radiation drives surface energy. Yet how its map and seasonal cycle shift with warming was poorly grasped.

Across models, the split peaks in local summer. It weakens the seasonal cycle by about fifteen percent in the Arctic and seven percent in the Antarctic. It slightly lifts the cycle over northern mid-latitudes under a high-emission path. Fewer clouds brighten mid-latitudes, while wetter clouds dim the poles. The pattern reshapes hopes for solar power, snowmelt, and ecosystems in a warmer world.
pmc-13348749:
Rafaella Henriques Cavalcanti Torres de Melo and colleagues test a growth-path marker for outlook after liver surgery for spread bowel cancer, in a cohort study from 2026. A total of 64 patients operated from 2012 to 2022 at a northeast Brazil cancer centre had metastasis tissue stained for eight markers. Survival was tracked at one, three, and five years. Standard curves and models did the tracking.

Median overall survival was 23 months in the reported follow-up, a sober base for judging any marker claim in this group. Only the S6 marker, positive in 20.7 percent of cases, tied clearly to worse disease-free survival at all three time points, marking active growth signalling as a warning sign after liver surgery.
pmc-13348849:
Ana C Siquara-de-Sousa and colleagues review 26 years of nerve biopsies for nerve-only leprosy in Brazil, in a clinic study from 2026. Brazil carries the second highest leprosy load worldwide. So 819 biopsies from 1997 to 2023 at a specialist clinic were checked, covering patients with nerve signs but no skin marks, using stains and molecular tests on saved tissue.

Leprosy was confirmed in 529 cases, a share of 64.6 percent, with 207 pure nerve cases inside that total. While other finds included vessel inflammation, diabetic nerve harm, and amyloid disease. Feeling loss led symptoms, and hand and leg nerves were sampled most, backing biopsy when clinic signs alone cannot settle a hard case.
pmc-13349749:
Yoshito Koyanagi and colleagues test how age shapes gene finds in inherited retinal disease, in a clinic study from 2026. A total of 506 patients with retinitis pigmentosa had an 83-gene panel at one centre and were split into six age bands from under 40 to 80 plus. Solved genes were tallied for each band. First symptom ages were compared across each solved gene group.

Gene solving fell steadily with age, from 39.7 percent under 40 years to just 3.0 percent at 80 years or more, a sharp trend in the reported counts. The EYS gene led solved cases at 42, and onset ages split by gene, so older unsolved patients may carry genes outside the known panel or non-gene causes.
pmc-13349849:
Jianhua Guo and colleagues reviewed zebrafish as a test platform for traditional Chinese medicine in 2026. Herbal treatments use many ingredients acting on many targets, so researchers need a whole-animal system that works fast.

Clear bodies and easy genetics let scientists watch effects live, such as heart rate shifts, immune cell movement, and tumour glow, across heart, brain, metabolic, and cancer studies. The review also covers safety testing that traces how harm develops, not just whether it occurs. Limits remain, such as following how combined formulas act over time and place. Pairing fish with organoids, single-cell data, and AI analysis is proposed as the next step.
pmc-13350049:
Yang Chen and a large team searched blood for immune signals of type 1 diabetes in a 2026 multi-dataset study. In this autoimmune disease the body destroys its own insulin-making cells, and current risk tools based on genes and antibodies predict progression poorly.

Combining bulk, single-cell, and spatial gene data from human pancreatic tissue, they traced how macrophages, a type of immune cell, change inside the islets. Machine learning distilled tissue and blood gene sets marking inflamed macrophages, and models built on them separated patients and risk groups in several blood cohorts. Checks in donated blood cells and mouse tissue backed the picks, offering candidate markers for earlier warning.
pmc-13350149:
Yang and eight co-authors build a scoring chart to predict deep pelvic endometriosis from ultrasound and symptoms, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The disease grows tissue deep behind the uterus and is hard to confirm without surgery. They propose a new ultrasound ratio based on wall thickness at a uterine neck point. The chart blends that ratio with other scan signs and symptoms.

They study three hundred sixty-two patients who had both scans and surgery. Four factors drive the final chart, led by the new ratio. The chart separates cases from non-cases with excellent skill. Its scores match real outcomes well in internal checks. The tool may speed referral to specialists from general clinics.
pmc-13350349:
Alessio Elia and co-authors reviewed nickel across farm and food systems in a 2026 article. The metal arrives from natural rock and soil sources and from industry, fuel burning, and phosphate fertilisers, entering the food chain mainly through plants.

In plants, nickel is a needed trace nutrient for nitrogen handling, yet slightly higher amounts poison growth and disturb nutrition. In people, diet is the main exposure, and sensitised individuals can react even to low doses with body-wide skin and allergy symptoms. New European limits set maximum levels in several foods in 2024, and the review weighs what that means for growers and consumers.
pmc-13350449:
Jiayou Wang and Yanqiao Zhang edited a 2026 collection on HDL, the so-called good cholesterol, and cardiovascular disease. High HDL levels track with lower heart risk, yet trials that simply raised HDL with drugs failed to cut events, and genetic studies find no causal protection from the level itself.

Laboratory work still shows HDL particles directly protecting vessels and aiding metabolism in liver, immune, vessel wall, and pancreas cells. The collection shifts focus from how much HDL circulates to how well it works, gathering mechanisms, clinical relevance, and treatment ideas. Function-based measures may explain the trial disappointments and point to better targets.
pmc-13350549:
Placing a drain tube into a dog's chest is a core emergency skill, and Katrine Gillett and co-authors compared two ways of teaching it to veterinary students. Thirty students placed small wire-guided tubes into sixteen cadaver dogs with air or fluid artificially added to the chest. Half the placements were guided by point-of-care ultrasound and half by surface landmarks, in a randomised crossover design. Tutors timed each try and later checked placement at dissection.

Landmark placements were clearly faster, sometimes by half. Complication rates did not differ between methods, and about eleven tubes ended outside the chest space in both groups. Students felt much more confident they were in the right space when using ultrasound. The authors sum up the trade-off: guidance slows novices down but reassures them, without yet cutting errors.
pmc-13351849:
Beatriz Alonso de Castro leads a 2026 real-world analysis of the HER2DX gene test in early HER2-positive breast cancer. The test aims to tailor care, and the team checked how it links to full tumour clearance and time free of invasive disease. Records cover 156 patients with stage I to III disease treated from February 2015 to May 2022 in A Coruña.

All patients had dual HER2-blocking treatment before surgery, and the test was run on 111 tumours in the cohort. That count works out to 71.2 percent of all tumours assessed in the study. Full clearance occurred in 51.3 percent of patients across the whole treated group. Hormone-sensitive disease linked to lower clearance, with an odds ratio of 0.25 in the adjusted statistical model. Findings help judge where the gene test adds value beyond standard clinical traits.
pmc-13351949:
Zipeng Wu leads a 2026 cohort study of treatment after third-generation EGFR drugs fail in advanced lung cancer. Lung cancer causes the most cancer deaths worldwide, and resistance to these targeted drugs always develops. Immune-based plans widen later options, but direct comparisons are scarce. Records held 225 patients treated at Jiangsu Cancer Hospital from 2017 to 2023.

All had EGFR-mutant adenocarcinoma and received further multi-line treatment after resistance. One group of 131 patients got immune checkpoint drugs, while 94 did not. Subgroups included immune therapy with bevacizumab and chemotherapy. The team compared results across plans and searched for traits marking who gains most from each route.
pmc-13352849:
Claudia Vanney and Belén Mesurado build a questionnaire that measures two neglected sides of a flourishing life: feeling intellectually well and morally well. Standard flourishing scales cover emotion, relationships, and general psychology, but leave out the life of the mind and of conscience. The authors tested Argentinian university students in two rounds. A first sample of 560 students shaped a 20-item scale with five factors, adding the moral and intellectual dimensions to the usual three.

A second sample of 427 students confirmed the structure, with fit statistics the authors describe as good and overall reliability of 0.86. The new subscales held up less strongly but acceptably. Scores rose alongside personal growth, study engagement, and perseverance, supporting validity. The five-factor version beat rival structures, which the authors take as evidence that moral and intellectual well-being are distinct parts of flourishing.
pmc-13353149:
Ismail Shaleh and co-authors build a Hanwoo cattle cumulus cell line for heat stress research in 2026. Heat stress cuts cattle fertility, yet reproductive cumulus cells lack good lab models and deep molecular data. Cells from fresh Hanwoo follicles were made immortal with a piggyBac system carrying SV40T, reaching 99 percent CD44-positive purity.

Heat settings were tuned with reactive oxygen checks and stress markers over 4, 12, and 24 hours. Reactive oxygen rose by 4 hours, stress proteins HSP70 and BiP jumped early, and defence genes peaked at 12 hours. Profiling found 754 changed genes and 357 changed proteins tied to heat. The line gives cattle breeding research a reusable heat model.
pmc-13354949:
Amritava Ghosh and co-authors set out a 2026 trial plan to test four weeks versus six weeks of antibiotic care for diabetic foot bone infection treated without surgery. Foot bone infection is a common and serious problem in diabetes, and the best length of drug care is still in doubt. Current guides allow up to six weeks.

Patients will be split at random into the two groups, with 52 people planned in each. Wound care, pressure relief, and blood sugar control will run alongside the drugs. The team will check healing, signs of infection, scans, and any need for amputation six months after drugs stop, to see if the shorter course works as well.
pmc-13355249:
Chunhao Mo and co-authors pooled trials in 2026 on drug therapy to help pass kidney stones stuck in the lower ureter. Two drug types that relax the tube were tested together versus one type alone. The team searched five databases through late 2025 and found eight trials with about 1,200 patients.

Stones passed more often and faster with the paired drugs, and patients needed fewer pain drugs. Headache, dizziness, and low blood pressure did not differ between groups, though a hint of more back pain needs care in reading. The authors say the pairing looks useful for stones under ten millimeters, while pain results varied too much for firm claims.
pmc-13358849:
Janani S Reisenauer and co-authors report early results from the VIGOR study in a 2026 case series. Patients with early lung cancer set for surgery first received immune therapy plus chemotherapy. The study added a new step: pulsed electric fields, short bursts of energy delivered to the tumor to kill its cells before removal.

Five patients received the energy treatment, and it reached the target in each case. No serious device-related problems occurred, and surgery went ahead as planned. The team also examined the removed tissue to see how much tumor the combined treatment had killed. Early safety like this justifies testing the approach in more patients.
pmc-13359549:
Liting Wang and co-authors aim drug loaded nanoparticles at both cancer cells and their helper fibroblasts. In triple negative breast cancer, fibroblasts feed the tumor signals and lay down collagen roads for invasion. Their particle carries a homing peptide and a chemotherapy drug, targeting receptors that both cell types display.

Patient data first confirmed fibroblasts as a worthy target. The particles entered receptor rich fibroblasts eagerly and killed them more than normal ones. Crosstalk signals between the two cell types fell, collagen patterns loosened, and the invasion program in cancer cells dimmed. Mouse tumors echoed the dish results. The authors pitch dual targeting as a way to stall spread.
pmc-13362649:
The journal Molecules issued a 2026 correction to a 2023 paper by Zhengguang Xu and colleagues on hordenine, a barley compound, in a mouse model of ulcerative colitis. The notice fixes Figure 4, which tests how gut cells move to close a scratch wound after treatment. One image had been placed in the wrong panel through a file name mix-up, and another came from the single best run rather than a typical one.

The corrected figure now uses images whose wound closure sits near the average of three runs, and the legend says so plainly. The notice states that the data behind the chart and the paper's conclusions stand unchanged. The editor approved the fix, and the original paper has been updated to match.
pmc-13362749:
Fernando Espuny-Ruiz and colleagues present a 2026 study that adapts a knee quality of life questionnaire into Spanish. The survey, with 26 questions, covers physical and emotional effects of kneecap pain, a stubborn condition that limits daily life. No Spanish tool of this kind existed. The team translated the survey with care for culture and wording, then tested it on 104 native Spanish speakers with the condition.

The Spanish version kept a clear five-part structure and matched well with other knee scores. Repeat answers two weeks apart were steady, and every patient could complete it without trouble, with no pile-up at the top or bottom scores. The authors say clinics and studies can now measure life impact fairly for Spanish-speaking patients.
pmc-13363449:
Ah Young Hwang and a large team report a 2026 trial of two probiotic blends mixed with plant nutrients for gut health. Adults took one of two blends, built from different sets of lactic bacteria, or a placebo for eight weeks. They kept stool diaries and gave samples for microbe-made chemicals, barrier markers, and gut microbe reads. Neither the team nor the patients knew the assignments.

Both blends raised the share of normal stool types versus placebo and lifted levels of helpful short-chain fatty acids, above all butyrate. A barrier leak marker fell in the mid-weight subgroup. Microbe diversity held steady while friendly groups gained ground. The authors say such blends may ease bowel habits and feed the gut lining well.
pmc-13363749:
Ayman Termanini and colleagues present a 2026 review that scores the datasets used to train intrusion detectors for industrial control systems and connected factory gear. Detector quality hinges on training data, yet surveys usually compare sets in words only. This team graded 23 public datasets on seven measured axes, mapped their attacks to the standard MITRE playbook for industrial systems, and built a decision rubric to help buyers choose.

Most sets come from physical test rigs, a point for realism, and nearly all map to the attack playbook. Gaps show too: one factory protocol dominates while others are scarce, and multi-stage attack stories are rare. The authors advise pairing a realism-strong set with a reproducibility-strong one.
pmc-13363849:
John Kenneth Hoober and colleagues present a 2026 perspective on chlorophyll b, the second green pigment of plants and green algae. This pigment builds the antenna arrays that catch light for photosynthesis. The article centers on the enzyme that makes its precursor, chlorophyllide a oxygenase, which carries a stable tyrosyl radical and seems to work as a paired unit with its substrate.

Drawing on work in a model alga, the authors argue that pairing lowers the substrate's redox potential, letting the enzyme act fast and letting chlorophyll b pile up as chloroplasts develop. They set out the enzyme's likely structure and radical-driven mechanism, and its place in the plant. The piece gathers scattered clues into one testable picture.
pmc-13364149:
Yuliya Genievskaya and colleagues present a 2026 study of seed variation in sand rice, a drought-hardy desert grain, across five wild populations in Kazakhstan. As deserts spread, this psammophyte draws interest as a future food crop. The team measured seed size traits and chemistry, above all amino acids, and used combined statistics to rank the populations for breeding value.

Seed shape traits varied mildly and moved together, while amino acid levels swung widely between sites, showing metabolic flexibility. Protein held fairly steady, reaching about a third of seed weight in the best lines. Two populations stood out as breeding picks, one most distinct overall and one with the largest seeds. Size and chemistry barely tracked each other, so both can be selected at once.
pmc-13365249:
Miranda Türkal and co-workers test in 2026 a block on a two part cell protein pair as a cure path for fatty liver scar. Fatty liver can move to swell and scar, and scar sets death risk. The pair helps wake scar cells in the liver, the team held.

A drug that breaks the pair cut wake marks and scar genes in lab liver scar cells. In lab grown mini livers with the ill, it cut scar and glue lay down, with no shift in fat load. The block works through a route clear of the main scar path. A new aim stands out.
pmc-13367049:
Gracious Donkor and Jan-Ulrik Dahl sum up in 2026 how germs bear harsh oxygen and chlorine foes, from their own growth and from host or drug attack. These foes scar cell parts of all kinds. Each foe has its own hit list and its own germ shields.

The pair set the two foes side by side: what they scar, how germs mop them up, and how they feed drug proof and drug kill force. Plans that break germ shields could boost old drugs, a key need as proof climbs and new drugs lag. The map guides such hunts.
pmc-13367149:
Gemma C Stevenson and others put forward a plan for outside vesicle miRNA moving in multiple scarring, in 2026. Outside sacs carry distinct miRNA sets that differ across ills with multiple scarring, hinting working roles in harm. Yet whether sacs truly traffic miRNA to targets, divert it, or retain it stayed debated.

Three moving modes were put forward: hand-off of miRNA to target cells, detour away from its target, and holding within the parent cell. The idea plan orders clashing sightings into testable modes. Multiple scarring teams gain a conceptual tool for interpreting vesicle miRNA data and designing tests that distinguish hand-off from detour.
pmc-13369749:
Agnieszka Bruzda-Zwiech and Julia Durka survey stress in 2026 among dental students treating children. Children's dentistry during training is widely felt as the hardest rotation: young patients fidget, fear runs high, and students work under watchful supervisors. Studying abroad may color the strain further.

One hundred fifteen students at a Polish university, local and international, rated stressors and overall stress. Polish students reported higher general stress, while training-specific stress matched across groups and tracked general levels. Root canal work and numbing injections stressed students most. Polish students blamed the child's attitude first; internationals blamed the supervisor. Few in either group planned to specialize in children's dentistry.
pmc-13370249:
Siqi Li and co-authors trace how fine dust in air scars the heart, in a 2026 study. The dust, called PM2.5, is known to drive heart disease, and scarring of heart muscle is one route. The team tested a chain of cell events. Stress in a cell compartment raises a protein called TXNIP. That protein fires an alarm complex, NLRP3, which can kill cells by a fiery route called pyroptosis.

Dust exposure raised harmful oxygen byproducts, cell stress, and TXNIP in both immune cells and heart muscle cells, and both cell death routes followed. Blocking the stress step or TXNIP sharply cut the death and the switch-on of scarring cells. The chain, the authors argue, sits at the core of dust-driven heart scarring and offers targets for drugs.
pmc-13371549:
Van Niekerk and co-authors use a Dutch heart registry to compare two ways to replace a worn aortic valve in younger patients who had prior heart surgery, in a 2026 study. One route goes through a vessel with a catheter, the other is open surgery. Prior surgery shapes both the choice and long-term results.

They analyze 1,284 patients aged fifty to seventy-five treated from 2015 to 2020. Models identify what drove the treatment choice and how outcomes played out over time. The registry base gives a real-world view across Dutch centers. Readers get a profile of who receives each route and what follows, which can inform shared decisions in this group.
pmc-13371649:
Berke Temel and co-authors sort cases of diabetic eye swelling by shape and by inner marks, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Eye scans from over seven hundred eyes were grouped into three forms: diffuse swelling, pocketed swelling, and a worn, pocketed form. Eight scan marks were checked in each eye.

The pocketed form was most common, and the worn form rarest. The worn form had the worst sight and the most damage to outer eye layers. Some marks clustered by form: fluid and bright dots favored the pocketed form, while layer damage favored the worn form. Several marks also tracked with poorer sight.
pmc-13372849:
Alexander Brückner and co-authors compared two forms of stiff heart valve disease in a 2026 study. One form comes with a valve of two flaps from birth, and one with the usual three flaps. Both stiffen and clog with lime over time, but the paths may differ.

The team used a film trick to slice hard, lime-rich valve tissue thin for clear stains. Gene reads and stains showed more new vessel growth, more swelling, and a higher lime share in the two-flap form. The split hints that the two forms may need distinct care plans, not one shared plan for all stiff valves.
pmc-13373249:
Neil McMillan and co-authors evaluate a virtual reality training program that teaches community health practitioners to assess diabetes-related foot disease among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Their 2026 pragmatic case series was run alongside three Aboriginal community-controlled health organisations across regional South Australia.

The program presented five virtual patients and interactive assessments covering essential examination and triage skills. Forty-one primary healthcare staff took part; thirty-four had matched before-and-after surveys and twenty completed at least three scenarios. After training, participants reported higher self-efficacy for the key assessment and triage skills. Feedback from thirty-nine users found the experience engaging, acceptable, and valuable for clinical education. The authors conclude the tool was workable and confidence-building in this setting, while noting the small, self-selected sample and the potential for virtual reality to upskill remote practitioners.
pmc-13374249:
Xiang Dong and co-authors assemble the mitochondrial genome of a mullein plant in a 2026 study. Great mullein is valued in folk medicine and ecology, yet its mitochondrial DNA had never been reported. Mitochondria carry their own small genome, and its shape tells how the plant's energy system evolved.

The genome forms a circle of about four hundred seventy eight thousand letters with a balanced base mix. It holds thirty six protein genes plus transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. Hundreds of editing sites rewrite its RNA after copying, and a slice of its sequence matches the chloroplast genome, a fossil of past transfers. Family trees place the plant firmly in its expected order.
pmc-13374349:
Neck surgery from the front — disc out, bones fused — heals well but the road in can bruise throat and nerve. Zihua Ding and five co-authors trace how smaller roads evolved in 2026, and race them against the open way. The line runs from scope-aided mini cuts to full camera work through a straw.

Studies that compare the ways head-to-head feed the pooled sums; lone reports fill the tale of the craft's growth. Short-term scores are the stake: pain, blood, days in ward, and early snags. The review was run by the standard reporting rules. A patient choosing a road in deserves both the history and the score sheet, and that pair is the offer.
pmc-13375549:
Marc S Raab and co-authors tried a two-tag immune drug first in myeloma in a 2026 trial. The cancer is a marrow growth with strong first care, yet most see it come back. The new drug links immune cells to the cancer and is famed for late-stage wins.

The phase two trial tests it up front in fit, swap-ready new cases, mixed with two more drugs. A pooled look at three arms held 49 patients on the main mix. First reads will show how deep the gains run and what harms show. Deep first gains could push back the near-sure return of this cancer.
pmc-13375749:
Fumiki Takahashi and ten co-authors build a sensor that screens for a cough drug with high selectivity, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. The sensing method glows with great sensitivity but poor aim, since many chemicals can trigger it. The team added a plastic molded around the drug itself, so only that shape fits snugly and gets counted.

The mold was grown on an electrode by electric means, which locked the template firmly in place and tripled sensitivity. X-ray probes at a synchrotron hinted at how the drug grips the mold, through several weak bonds acting together. The sensor measured the drug in store-bought and prescription products and in urine. Its readings matched a standard lab method, backing it as a practical screen.
pmc-13376649:
Seven authors led by Asghar Estaji spray friendly bacteria on tomato plants to shield fruit from drought harm. Tomatoes lose quality fast when water runs short, and picked fruit keep that harm in store. The bacteria used are the lactic kind found in many foods. Plants in a glasshouse trial got full water, short water, or short water plus the spray, then fruit sat in cold store for 20 days.

Sprayed fruit held a steadier acid level and softened more slowly in store. Their stock of health-linked plant compounds rose, and three defence enzymes worked harder. A cell harm mark fell in sprayed fruit, which shows their skins held up better. The team reads the spray as a primer that wakes fruit defence before harm hits. Shelf life gains are charted day by day.
pmc-13376749:
Jiakang Zhang and co-authors slip a crosslinked polymer skin between two layers of a perovskite solar cell and reap a record device. The weak point of these cells is the junction where the electron-carrying tin oxide meets the perovskite: flaws there eat current and loosen the bond. The team's interlayer locks the two sides together mechanically and soaks up stress. Its chloride ions also heal flaws on both faces, and it bends the energy levels into a graded slope.

That slope cut the junction's energy mismatch by 0.24 electron volts, easing charge flow and trimming losses. The finished cells converted 26.34 percent of sunlight to power, with a certified 26.27 percent, and a palm-sized module reached 22.03 percent. The authors present the multi-job interlayer as a template for stable, efficient cells.
pmc-13377649:
Lienne R Sethna and others coin and review that mixing, the full mixing of a layered lake with oxygen-free bottom waters, in a 2026 review. Climate change is changing lake layers and mixing, yet mixing outside yearly mixing has drawn little review. The paper reviews earth and life consequences of that mixing events.

Climate-driven shifts in temperature, wind, and storms may make that mixing more frequent, altering nutrient, contaminant, and carbon cycling, flux, and storage. Mixing may also reorganise food webs, favouring fast-growing phytoplankton and cyanobacteria and shifting energy transfer upward. Current lake care barely addresses anoximixis and may sometimes promote it. The synthesis calls for tests of its predictions to improve lake water quality management.
pmc-13378349:
Charles Q Jia and Donald W Kirk argue in a 2026 paper that direct air capture is a weak answer to climate change. The technology pulls carbon dioxide straight from the air, and it is often promoted as essential. The authors say the energy it needs makes large-scale use deeply impractical.

Current systems need far more energy per tonne captured than capturing the gas at its source. Meeting even modest removal targets this way could swallow over half of all electricity generated in the world today. That would divert clean power from cutting emissions directly. The authors favour preventing emissions first, supporting plant growth that absorbs carbon, and using proven options such as biochar.
pmc-13380049:
Hideki Funou and seven co-authors study how a fat-based signal helps cells clear worn-out parts. The signal starts with an enzyme that makes a compound called C1P. The team worked with human cells and with mice that lack the enzyme. Cells without it held less of LC3B, a protein cells need to form the sacs that haul waste to be broken down.

Adding C1P back restored the protein, and a gene switch that guards cells played a part in the effect. Without the signal, starved cells died more readily. The paper names this path as one that keeps cell cleanup going.
pmc-13380449:
Mateus Oliveira Machado and colleagues found Trypanosoma cruzi, the Chagas parasite, in anteaters of southeastern Brazil, in a 2026 molecular study. As people reshape land, wildlife, pets, and humans meet more often, redrawing parasite transmission webs. Anteaters may host the parasite within forest transmission cycles, but data from São Paulo State were scarce.

Blood from 26 anteaters was tested by PCR for the 18S rRNA gene, then sequenced. Parasite DNA appeared in 42.3 percent of samples, and all sequences clustered within the Trypanosoma cruzi clade with low diversity. No link emerged with species, sex, age class, or season. The findings place anteaters inside the sylvatic cycle and flag wildlife surveillance for Chagas risk.
pmc-13380749:
Xiaosi Chen and co-authors published a 2026 study on whether a simple blood-based index can predict outcomes after emergency repair of a torn aorta. The tear type studied affects the descending aorta and is treated with a stent placed inside the vessel. The index, called EASIX, reflects blood vessel lining activation and stress.

Records for 1,090 patients who had the repair were analysed. About one in six had a serious short-term problem, and about one in five died during follow-up of around seven years. Higher index values were linked with greater risk of kidney failure needing dialysis, organ blood loss, and early death. The index may help doctors spot patients needing closer care.
pmc-13381749:
Malekzadeh and co-authors studied how regional traits drive seven kinds of human movement across Europe. Studies often treat mobility as one thing. Yet lasting migration, student stays, seasonal work, commuting, and living in two places may answer to different forces. The team combined labor survey data, Erasmus exchange records, and social media data to compare the types region by region.

Each type responded to its own mix of money, nature, and social factors. What attracts long-term students does not always draw seasonal workers or cross-border commuters. The authors argue this rules out one-size policies for regional growth. They close with targeted ideas for making regions more attractive in the ways each kind of movement rewards, supporting more even growth across Europe.
pmc-13381949:
In-Won Lee and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on how mitochondria arrange themselves in egg cells. Mitochondria are the cell's power units, and in mature egg cells they gather on the spindle side. That lopsided layout has long been known, but how it forms was a mystery.

Live imaging and modeling revealed two mechanisms at work. First, flows in the cell fluid, driven by actin fibers, carry mitochondria within the spindle hemisphere. The flows are stirred by the DNA mass itself. Second, a motor protein called MYO19 channels mitochondria from beneath the spindle toward the cell edge in both directions. Together, the two paths create rich and poor zones of mitochondria. The findings explain the polar pattern and may inform fertility science.
pmc-13382049:
Mohsin Hossain and co-authors present a 2026 computer study on identifying microscopic fungi from images, with explanations for its decisions. Fungal infections are a growing risk, yet diagnosis is slow and specialists are scarce. Early, accurate identification matters for effective treatment.

The team fine-tuned a well-known image network, adding a new activation method whose threshold learns during training. The model classified fungi with accuracy above ninety-five percent in their tests, beating comparison methods. Explanation tools showed which image features drove each call. Such a system could support labs that lack expert staff, provided its performance holds up on independent image sets from other sources.
pmc-13383549:
Ecem Dogan and co-authors test dental adhesives for leakage in a 2026 lab study. Class II fillings sit at the back teeth, where gaps at the edge let fluids and bacteria creep in. Universal adhesives promise one bottle for many jobs, but their chemistry differs by brand.

Standard cavities were cut in more than one hundred pulled human molars. Twelve groups mixed adhesive type with etching style, from full etch to self-etch. A chemically cured universal adhesive got special focus in the design. Fillings used one nanohybrid resin across all groups for fairness. Leakage scores tell dentists which pairing seals best before human trials.
pmc-13384449:
Ketnipa Ratanakul's team tested speech perception and sound skills in Thai children with speech sound disorders, in a 2026 study. Research in tonal languages was thin. The team compared 32 children with SSD and 44 typically developing peers, all in preschool levels 2 to 3 and aged 4 to 6 and a half years. Tasks covered phonemic discrimination, lexical and phonetic judgment, and sound skills.

After accounting for age and word knowledge, children with SSD performed no differently from peers. Age forecast telling sounds apart and rime skill in the SSD group, while word knowledge forecast only rime skill there. Speaking accuracy forecast scores in neither group, hinting that hearing and speaking develop on partly separate paths.
pmc-13385449:
Xiuying Peng and colleagues show how high uric acid exhausts gut stem cells through a mitochondrial protein in 2026 work. Raised uric acid, common in metabolic syndrome, harms many organs, but its gut effects were little known. The team found the damage centers on intestinal stem cells that renew the gut lining.

Uric acid binds directly to the mitochondrial protein CCDC90B, sparking excess harmful oxygen species inside cells. That stress fires an inflammasome and a fiery cell death path, draining the stem cell pool. Blocking the protein restored stem cell function, which nominates it as a target for gut damage tied to high uric acid.
pmc-13385849:
Soumabrata Majumdar's team designed a lab-made catch bond that strengthens under pull, in a 2026 chemistry study. Catch bonds, whose spans grow under load, drive living force sensing but resisted lab copying. The team's design uses HEP triesters, where pull suppresses neighbor-group help.

Blocking that within-molecule help raises the reaction barrier and prolongs bond life. Density functional theory showed that tension hinders the shape change needed for neighbor-group help. Single-molecule force tests showed triester spans rising over threefold at 400 pN. The trick opens routes to force-tuned polymer networks and adaptive matter.
pmc-13390049: Li replies to Zhang's letter about the prognostic nutritional index in cancer, in 2026 correspondence. Li clarifies that the original work was an umbrella appraisal of meta-analyses, graded with AMSTAR and GRADE frameworks rather than pooled against staging variables. It covered 64 reviews and meta-analyses comprising 265 syntheses, 68.8 percent rated high quality and 45.7 percent backed by high-certainty evidence. Li concedes discrimination and reclassification remain limited, but cites nomogram studies with C-index values up to 0.816 as signs the index adds value beyond staging.
pmc-13390349:
Timnit Kefela's team soaked plastic films in suboxic marine mud from a methane seep to learn what settles on sinking plastics and whether they degrade. Glass jars with venting mud held three plastic vinyl alcohol films, a PET film, and a plant-fibre acetate film, plus glass controls, sampled over six months.

All films gained germ groups of their own, apart from seawater and mud, moving over time from Gammaproteobacteria lead to Bacteroidota. Plant-fibre acetate attracted its own kinds including sulfur reducers and showed light-based signs of core breakdown, while other plastics showed minimal material change despite settling.
pmc-13391349:
Shaun Khanna's team pooled eleven studies together to test whether SGLT2 blocker blood-sugar-illness drugs shrink heart-surface fat, the energy-active depot around the heart linked to heart disease. The drugs protect hearts beyond glucose cutting, and heart-surface fat change was one lead workings.

Across 284 patients tracked by heart scans, CT, or heart MRI, SGLT2 blockers beat standard therapy with a large standard drop in heart-surface fat. Within-group analyses also showed clear shrinkage from start. Both thickness and volume gauges fell, backing fat drop as one pathway of heart benefit.
pmc-13392249:
Masato Kanai and five co-authors linked leader behavior to worker well-being and profit in a Japanese home builder, in a 2026 study. Four years of company-wide survey data were analyzed at branch level. Nine leader behaviors were rated by staff. Models tracked effects across years in both directions.

Three behaviors tied to higher branch well-being. Developing employees, clear communication, and sustainable work pace all helped. A different behavior tied to profit targets: setting clear strategy and goals. Over time, the arrow ran the other way than expected. Happier branches later rated their leaders higher, not the reverse. Leader behavior did not predict later well-being in their models. The authors discuss how firms should split limited leadership effort. Well-being and profit may need different levers, they suggest.
pmc-13392649:
Charlie O Coward and Jennifer L Howell audited how United States hospitals talk about pregnancy care on their websites, checking whether the language welcomes transgender patients or shuts them out. Coders reviewed obstetrics pages from one hundred seventy-eight hospitals spread across all fifty states during late 2025. Pages were scored for inclusive wording, pictures, symbols, and resources aimed at transgender readers.

Inclusive touches proved rare, while wording addressed to women alone or neutral second-person phrasing dominated nearly everywhere. The pattern held across regions and across university and religious ownership, though hospitals in states with stronger legal protections and university hospitals scored somewhat higher. Even welcoming pages often mixed inclusive and exclusive terms side by side. The authors argue hospitals need clear, service-level standards so mixed signals stop confusing patients choosing where to give birth.
pmc-13392849:
Hyunwoo Kim leads a national check on mosquitoes at Korea's doors, trapping at forty major airports and seaports through sixteen rounds from March to November 2025. Climate change plus swelling travel and trade raise the odds that foreign disease-carrying species slip in. Every catch was identified by form and screened for six major viruses with a combined genetic test.

Traps took more than thirty-seven thousand mosquitoes across eighteen species. Total numbers fell by about a fifth against the year before, yet three extra species appeared, widening diversity. One house mosquito dominated the catch, and the capital region logged the densest counts while the south held the richest species mix. No sample carried any target virus. The authors advise airports to watch hardest for new arrivals, while seaports track overall numbers.
pmc-13392949:
Hongnian Wang, Mingyang Zhang, Xiong Ke, Zichao Wang, and Lijuan Wu measured the toll of rheumatoid arthritis across one hundred twenty-nine low- and middle-income countries. They used Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2023, with projections onward to 2050. Countries were grouped by national income so gaps between poorer and richer settings could be tracked over time.

In 2023 the disease affected about twelve point six million people in those countries, Recorded prevalence in upper-middle-income settings ran over four times the low-income level. That gap widened across the study years, even as death rates drew closer together. Forecasts show deaths falling in low-income countries but rising in middle-income ones. The authors argue poorer settings chiefly need better diagnosis, since cases there likely go uncounted, while middle-income systems must make modern arthritis drugs affordable.
pmc-13393149:
Ga-Young Suh and five colleagues modelled how the aorta reshapes after repair of a torn inner lining in the descending aorta. The repair uses a stent graft plus a bare extension meant to press the layers together, a method shortened to PETTICOAT. Twenty patients at one centre, mostly men in their mid-sixties with tears of varying age, had scans before and after treatment. Computer models built from each patient's scans measured length, curve, and width along the whole aorta.

Within the first month the true channel widened markedly, the arch and descending aorta straightened somewhat, and the abdominal aorta lengthened a little. The clotted false channel shrank in half the patients early and in most by two years, Its cross-section barely changed on average. Total aortic width grew only in the chest segment. One patient died early; the rest needed no further procedure.
pmc-13393249:
HuiLing Xu and coauthors report a 2026 laboratory study of synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive cancer of soft tissue. The work asks how a small RNA molecule, miR-29b-5p, affects tumor growth and stem-like behavior in this cancer through a signaling route involving TGF-beta and the gene EP300.

The team predicted a link between miR-29b-5p and EP300 with computer tools, then tested it in cell experiments. Tumor spheres grown in the lab showed low miR-29b-5p and high EP300, along with stronger growth, movement, and invasion. Raising miR-29b-5p curbed sphere formation, which points to a possible control point for future treatment research.
pmc-13393949:
Jingjing Liu and coauthors test whether folic acid in pregnancy affects mothers' later thinking skills in a 2026 cohort study. Folic acid supports nervous system function at all ages, but its long-term effect on postnatal maternal cognition had never been tested.

From the Ma'anshan Birth Cohort follow-up, 182 women with prenatal supplement records completed Stroop, digit-symbol, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment tests after birth. Supplement use in each trimester was recorded prospectively by questionnaire. The paper offers early evidence that pregnancy nutrition may shape maternal brain health well beyond delivery.
pmc-13394149:
Vansh Maheshwari, Shyamashree Das, and Saurav Basu estimate heart risk among older adults in India, in a 2026 study. Heart disease is the top cause of death there, in a fast aging population. Early spotting of high risk people can guide timely steps to prevent events, but broad estimates with sound tools were scarce.

The team used a national aging survey with more than sixty four thousand adults aged forty to seventy four. A World Health Organization chart, using age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, and body mass, sorted risk for the next ten years. Close to a third had risk of ten percent or more. Alcohol use, past high blood pressure, and widowhood raised odds, while college and work lowered them.
pmc-13394449:
Adrien Robin leads a 2026 study of how the heart and blood vessels cope when gravity shifts and blood volume drops. Sixteen healthy adults lay on a tilting table, from head-down to head-up in small steps. They repeated the test after a drug made them pass more urine and lose fluid. The team tracked heart rate, output, and vessel tone at each angle.

With less fluid, heart rate and vessel tone rose while each beat moved less blood. Pressure stayed steady, and heart rhythm signals shifted toward stress patterns. The tilt curve let the team place Moon and Mars gravity levels on one chart. Space crews and doctors may both use the map.
pmc-13394849:
Sabrina Atha Shania and co-authors design, in 2026, a phone app to guide stroke recovery in Indonesia. The country carries one of the heaviest stroke loads in its region, with too few therapists for home care. The team spoke with ten experts and eight stroke survivors, then built the app in three rounds of design and testing. Each round sharpened the prototype.

The app offers training plans for movement, speech, and daily tasks, with progress tracking. It adds video lessons, reminders, targets, games, and links to staff for chats and home visits. Test users rated the design as good overall. The authors offer the plan as a guide for clinics and rule makers.
pmc-13395749:
Yuwei Li and co-authors find, in 2026, a guard that keeps myelin-making cells safe from rust-like death. Cells that wrap nerves face heavy strain as they build fatty sheaths. A tagging enzyme named RLIM marks a cystine porter for keeping at the cell surface. That porter feeds production of glutathione, a master shield.

Mice lacking RLIM in these cells lost porter from the surface, made fewer cells, and formed poor myelin. Their movement, social acts, and thinking slipped in ways that echo human cases. Most harmful human variants broke the porter grip. Extra glutathione rescued mice in the tests. The authors pitch the shield as a therapy lead.
pmc-13395949:
Stylianos Kapetanakis and co-authors reviewed records of older patients who needed repeat vertebroplasty, a procedure that injects cement into broken spinal bones, in a study published in 2026. The patients were 75 to 85 years old and had osteoporosis-related fractures in the chest and lower back.

All had earlier vertebroplasty and came back for repair at three or four levels in a single session, between August 2019 and November 2023, at one center. Pain scores and a disability index were recorded before surgery and at one, three, six, and twelve months after. The authors set out to judge pain relief, daily function, and safety for a group that earlier reports rarely covered.
pmc-13396349:
Geethamani Rajamani and Jaganathan Subramani offer a map-based graph net for city food safety under climate strain in a 2026 study. Climate shocks and soil wear threaten soil-free farms, and food-juice wobble in water-grown and mist-grown crops needs early flags.

A Pi-based sensor web tracked sky traits, plant health, and food-juice levels as map points, while a tuned multi-scale graph net forecast growth from lettuce trials. Plant color signs flagged strain early, before crops failed. City growers gain a watch frame for tough soil-free farms in a hot, rough climate.
pmc-13396449:
Yuchen Lin and colleagues build a textile interface that decodes silent speech for people who cannot speak aloud in a 2026 study. People with impaired vocal organs face profound communication barriers, yet subtle multi-muscle activity remains even when audible speech is absent.

The team created a scarf interface that imperceptibly captures those muscle signals and decodes silent speech robustly, fusing electromagnetic physiological communication with metamaterial embroidery. The design reconciles spatial selectivity with fidelity in noisy environments. The paper offers a wearable path back to conversation for people with speech loss.
pmc-13396649:
Abdalrahman G. Al-Gamal and co-authors decorated graphene and carbon nanotubes with extra atoms and measured how the decorations change the materials, in a 2026 study aimed at cleaner energy devices. Three additions were tried: fluorine, bromine in a carrier compound, and lithium fluoride.

Graphene oxide was fluorinated with hydrofluoric acid and brominated through a salt treatment, while multi-walled nanotubes took up lithium fluoride. A battery of imaging and spectroscopy tools confirmed each structure, and light-based and electrical tests tracked the changes. Because each dopant altered conductivity and light behavior differently, the comparison guides which decoration suits which energy job.
pmc-13396849:
Alexandre Araujo Pereira and co-authors borrowed a heart procedure to fix a leg artery fork, and report the first such use in a 2026 case. A 46-year-old man had lifestyle-limiting leg pain on walking from a heavily calcified narrowing where the iliac artery splits toward the pelvis and the leg.

The double-kissing double-crush method, routine for coronary forks, stents both branches of a split in a choreographed sequence that keeps each branch open. Applied here across the common, internal, and external iliac arteries, it restored flow. At twelve months the man remained free of symptoms with the stents open, evidence that heart-born techniques can travel to the pelvis.
pmc-13397949:
Yash Jawale and team projected how many skilled health workers rural India will need by 2030 and what closing the gap would cost. Their 2026 study tracks doctors, nurses, and midwives at rural primary-care and community clinics, using national Rural Health Statistics from 2009 to 2019. India already faces a shortage, and rural shortfalls had not been weighed against global development targets.

Skilled worker density grew about 2.59 percent per year and is set to rise from 8.85 per 10,000 people in 2019 to 11.47 per 10,000 people in 2030. Even so, India would still face a shortfall of roughly half a million workers at the low end and 1.83 million at the high end, costing an estimated 1.46 trillion rupees at the low end and 4.96 trillion at the high end to close. The authors argue that cost equals about 15 percent of government health spending, making scale-up feasible. The result is a state-aware planning baseline, not a hiring plan.
pmc-13398249:
Francesco Liuzza and colleagues report results of cement-free hip replacement in patients whose hip sockets formed poorly from birth. Their 2026 study reviews eight women, mean age near 53.9 years, treated at one centre between 2019 and 2025. Developmental dysplasia warps the joint's anatomy, making it hard to restore leg length, stability and natural mechanics.

Alongside the cementless implant, surgeons balanced soft tissues and, where needed, rebuilt the socket using bone from the patient's own femoral head. Hip scores including the Harris Hip Score and the WOMAC index tracked pain and function, while X-rays checked implant position and healing. The series offers ground-level evidence for tackling moderate to severe dysplasia in one operation.
pmc-13398349:
Two water channel proteins in pancreatic cancer balls are tested by Catarina Pimpão and co-authors in work dated 2026. This cancer kills late-found and drug-proof. The channels, AQP3 and AQP5, run high in such tumors. The team grew two tumor lines as balls and blocked or silenced the channels. Ball size, area, and life signs were tracked.

Blocking AQP3 shrank balls and cut their life signs. Silencing either channel in one line shrank balls and killed more cells. Roundness shifted in the second line under the block. Both channels now stand as drug targets worth chase.
pmc-13398649:
Rodolfo Carneiro and Fernando Palhano study a decay route for messenger RNA in human cells in a 2026 paper. In yeast, codons that lack matching transfer RNAs make messages decay faster. Human cells use a related but distinct route that depends on certain arginine codons sitting in a key ribosome site while decoding stalls nearby.

By mining public data sets, the authors find a surprise: messages rich in those trigger codons tend to last longer, not shorter. They suggest the human route trims the life of otherwise long lived messages, acting as a regulator rather than a cleanup crew for weak messages. That role differs sharply from the yeast system.
pmc-13398749:
R. J. Lowes and colleagues tested how much digital joint-motion results depend on choices made while building the starting pose. Their 2026 paper concerns range-of-motion analysis for extinct vertebrates, where joint mobility limits which limb poses are biologically plausible. Digital workflows are growing, yet no thorough sensitivity study had checked how subjective setup steps change the viable poses.

The team ran a complete six-degree-of-freedom automated workflow on guinea fowl ankle and foot joints, varying each stage of reference pose assembly. Outputs proved sensitive to variation, especially the choice of joint surfaces and the shape used to define the joint center. Single-study conclusions based on maximum rotations may survive, but cross-study and cross-species comparisons could mislead. The authors urge future studies to publish full joint models.
pmc-13399049:
Martínková and Trnka review, in 2026, tunnelling nanotubes, the hair-thin membrane bridges that let cells pass cargo between their interiors, with a focus on cancer. Found a little over two decades ago, these bridges have since been found across body function and disease. The review sums up their structural and molecular features and the cytoskeletal machinery that builds them. It covers the striking range of freight they carry, from nucleic acids and proteins to organelles, pathogens, and drugs.

Mitochondria transfer gets attention: in a classic experiment, healthy pheochromocytoma cells donated mitochondria through nanotubes to ultraviolet-stressed sister cells, rescuing them from early apoptosis. The authors also weigh newer evidence for mRNA transfer changing recipient cell behavior and ribosome transfer implying cells can share protein-making capacity. In tumors, such cooperation supports metabolic sharing, stress adaptation, and treatment resistance, making them both a biological curiosity and a therapeutic target.
pmc-13399149:
Ashish Heerani, Muskan Bai, and Noor Un Nisa wrote this 2026 letter questioning a proposal to screen everyone with Hashimoto's thyroiditis for a diabetes antibody. The discussed article suggested routine testing for glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, called GADA, so latent autoimmune diabetes in adults might be caught early. The letter writers accept the link between the two autoimmune conditions but dispute the screening logic.

Their first objection is that no prospective evidence shows screening changes the course of this diabetes; the drug data cited come from relatives at risk of type 1 diabetes, a different group. Second, a positive antibody result in thyroid patients has not been shown to predict who later develops autoimmune diabetes. Third, without prevalence and test-performance figures for the actual screening population, the value of routine testing cannot be judged. The authors ask for long-term studies before such screening is adopted.
pmc-13399349:
Marwa S. Ibrahim, Ibrahim A. Naqid, and Ghadeer Suaifan surveyed Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in the wounds of diabetic patients in Duhok Province, Iraq, in a 2026 study. This bacterium is a frequent wound invader in diabetes and often resists many drugs. Between June 2024 and July 2025 the team collected 141 wound swabs from adult diabetic patients.

The bacterium grew from 44.68 percent of the samples, as the laboratory results showed. Most patient traits showed no clear link to infection. Wound location did matter. Infections in the leg region carried nearly four times the odds, with an adjusted figure of 3.94 reported by the authors. Resistance testing found high multidrug resistance, especially against aztreonam and ceftazidime. Colistin kept the best activity against the isolates, followed by the carbapenem antibiotics. The authors urge early testing and careful drug choice.
pmc-13399449:
Alfonso Trinidad and colleagues reviewed a quarter century of research on teaching swimming in schools, in a 2026 systematic review. School programs are the main route to aquatic literacy, the mix of knowledge, skill, and confidence that keeps children safe in water. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, SportDiscus, and Web of Science following PRISMA guidance, covering programs from early childhood through secondary school.

Sixteen studies met their criteria and were quality-checked. Most programs took a technical, utilitarian approach, drilling specific strokes and skills with little connection to the wider curriculum. Research clustered in infant and primary years and thinned out sharply at secondary level. Program length, session frequency, content, and assessment tools varied so widely that comparisons were difficult. The authors conclude that school swimming has progressed but still lacks systematic implementation. They call for stronger backing, better teacher training, and stage-appropriate teaching.
pmc-13399649:
Cheng-Wei Kuo and co-authors published a 2026 study on whether nutrition scores predict survival in advanced liver cancer. The scores combine blood protein levels, immune cell counts, and body weight into one number. Patients with better nutrition tend to withstand treatment better. The team tested two such scores in people receiving a standard first drug, lenvatinib.

The study covered 276 patients with advanced disease. Those with high scores lived much longer without their cancer growing: about seven and a half months versus four. Overall survival roughly doubled as well, near nineteen to twenty-one months against under ten. High-score patients also responded more often and had fewer severe side effects. They were more likely to receive further treatment after the first drug. Both scores predicted death risk on their own, and together they did slightly better.
pmc-13399749:
Ayu Hidaka and co-authors evaluated a shortcut test for lupus anticoagulant, a clotting-related antibody central to diagnosing antiphospholipid syndrome, in a 2026 laboratory study. Their proposed method takes one ratio: clotting time with a high-sensitivity reagent divided by clotting time with a low-sensitivity reagent, both from the familiar APTT test family.

The team checked the ratio against guideline-based testing in plasma from 57 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and 74 patients with prolonged clotting times. They also used samples deliberately spiked with anticoagulant drugs. Agreement with the standard pathway was good overall. Five patients whom the guideline route called negative showed elevated ratios, a discrepancy the authors flag for cautious follow-up rather than dismissal. They position the method as a screening sieve: a negative result makes lupus anticoagulant unlikely, while positives still require the full confirmatory workup.
pmc-13400049:
Matteo Tacelli and nine co-authors built an AI model in two thousand twenty-six to grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours from ultrasound video. Grade, set by cell division counts, drives care choices, yet needle sampling misgrades up to a quarter of cases. Their model, GradAINet, reads contrast-enhanced endoscopic ultrasound recordings instead.

The study drew one hundred fifteen patients from a Milan centre of excellence. More than two hundred fifty thousand video frames were split into training, validation, and test sets. The model reached a sensitivity of zero point eight for spotting higher-grade tumours in the reported results. The team presents video AI as a support for grading, not a swap for tissue proof.
pmc-13400249:
Ran Svirsky and colleagues mapped germline genetic findings among men with prostate cancer in a real-world, multicenter study. Their 2026 paper asks whether broad next-generation sequencing adds value beyond testing for known founder variants, inherited changes common in a population. Genetic results can guide treatment and family screening, yet testing patterns in routine care had been unclear.

Among 293 tested men, 39, or 13.3 percent, carried a positive finding, including 18 with high-penetrance genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and ATM, and 21 with risk variants. One third of disease-causing variants found by sequencing were unique rather than founder variants. Family history of cancer was the only demographic or clinical factor tied to positive results. The authors argue for broad sequencing regardless of ethnicity or stage.
pmc-13400549:
João Victor dos Anjos Almeida and co-authors review, in 2026, prebiotics and probiotics in animal nutrition and what they mean for food safety and greener farming. Prebiotics feed helpful gut microbes, while probiotics supply live beneficial microbes directly. Interest has grown as producers seek alternatives to routine antibiotics.

Across poultry, pigs, cattle, fish and shrimp, these additives can improve digestion, gut wall health and immune strength while suppressing harmful germs such as E coli and Salmonella. Trials link them to better growth, feed efficiency and carcass quality, plus less reliance on antibiotics. The review also highlights turning farm waste streams, like fruit pomace and cereal bran, into useful feed substrates within circular production systems.
pmc-13400649:
Anthony W Sali and colleagues issue, in 2026, a correction to their 2025 study of how sustained attention affects readiness to move the eyes. A stimulus error had cut the last trial of each run short for some people. For others, the response was not recorded. A few worked-out measures also held mistakes.

The team cut the faulty trials and fixed the counts, then ran the tests again. One key interaction, between shift likelihood and attention state, kept the same direction but weakened. It no longer cleared the usual threshold for a firm finding. The results and discussion text was softened to match. The authors say the overall pattern and conclusions stand.
pmc-13400749:
Calvo-Sánchez and colleagues studied liver cancer risk after hepatitis C cure in a multicentre cohort study published in 2026. Clearing the virus lowers risk, but some patients still develop hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The team asked whether longer use of metformin, a common diabetes drug, was linked to lower risk after cure.

They followed 1,531 patients who had cleared the virus with direct-acting antiviral drugs, and 50 developed liver cancer over a median follow-up of about six years. With models that track metformin use as it builds up, each extra year of use was linked to about half the cancer risk. The pattern held in patients with type 2 diabetes. Portal hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and a high fibrosis score each raised risk. The findings support trials of metformin as a cheap preventive after hepatitis C cure.
pmc-13401649:
Davis Ngarashi and co-authors carried out a 2026 cross-sectional study of noncontact infrared thermometers in healthy Black African adults, asking how much the body site and room temperature shift the readings. These forehead-style devices screen quickly at a distance, a virtue during infectious emergencies, but their accuracy varies and evidence from African populations was thin.

In an environmental chamber, 216 adults were measured at the forehead, neck, temple, and wrist. Readings came first at a cooler setting and then at a warmer one, in a fixed order. Statistical tests compared sites and conditions, while Bland-Altman plots and kappa statistics judged agreement between readings. The repeated-measures design isolates how much of a thermometer's answer comes from where it points and how warm the room is, rather than from the person being measured.
pmc-13401749: Andrés Fernando Montalvo Vásquez and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction notice in AIDS Research and Treatment for their 2025 article. It covers how migration movements shape the epidemiology and clinical profile of HIV infection in Quito, Ecuador. The notice is a correction only: the article was first published with the wrong article type, labelled a Review Article when it should have been a Research Article. The first author's name was stated incompletely. The article has been updated and the publisher apologises.
pmc-13401949:
Ram B Basany and colleagues describe making silicone finger prostheses for people who have lost fingers, in a 2026 case series. Traumatic hand injuries damage far more than grip: dexterity, work capacity, social ease, and psychological well-being all suffer, and losses can also follow birth defects, infection, or disease.

The team presents their work designing and fabricating custom hand prostheses tailored to each patient. A well-made silicone prosthesis restores appearance convincingly and can support some function, though it cannot fully replace a natural hand. Their reported gains centre on aesthetics, confidence, independence, and reintegration into daily and social life. Success, they argue, rests on clinical expertise, careful treatment planning, and a compassionate approach as much as on materials. The series documents their fabrication efforts and what the devices meant to the patients fitted with them.
pmc-13402249:
Akhilesh M Wodeyar and co-authors review how glowing dyes could sharpen robot surgery done through the mouth for head and neck cancers. The robot route, called TORS, cuts harm and preserves function, yet the surgeon loses touch and depth sense, which makes judging tumor edges hard. Fluorescence imaging, where tissue lights up under special light, offers real-time sight of the tumor instead.

The review weighs a general dye, indocyanine green, against tumor-targeted agents such as panitumumab-IRDye800CW, checking fit with the da Vinci Firefly camera system. Targeted tracers gave the strongest contrast in the sensitive imaging mode, but results hinged on settings: camera angle, light output, field evenness, and autoscaling all mattered. The authors add lessons from their own operating rooms and call for shared protocols and stronger trials before the method becomes routine.
pmc-13402649:
Pritam Bera, Rajesh Raju, and Debodipta Das compare lung tumors with the lung cancer cell lines labs use to model them, working at pathway level rather than gene by gene. They set 513 lung adenocarcinoma tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas against 45 cell lines from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia. Each sample was scored across hallmark gene sets, and a penalized model hunted for separating patterns.

Five pathways split the two groups cleanly: E2F targets, interferon-gamma response, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coagulation, and the G2M checkpoint. Cell lines ran hot on growth pathways and carried higher mutation loads, with more TP53 and STK11 changes, while true tumors kept immune and surrounding-tissue programs that lines have lost. The same split held in lung squamous cancer. The authors offer the five-pathway test as a yardstick for picking cell models honestly.
pmc-13402849:
Muhammad Usman and co-authors report a 20-year-old Marshallese man whose tuberculosis had spread body-wide, striking skin, brain vessels, and clotting at once despite a healthy immune system. He arrived with trouble swallowing, weight loss, and confusion after a fall, and imaging found disease in lungs, pleura, and the skin by his left ear. He tested negative for HIV, and clotting workups found no inherited cause.

His course worsened with a large stroke in the left middle cerebral artery territory, with mild bleeding into it, plus a pulmonary embolism in the left lung. Pleural fluid markers strongly supported tuberculous pleuritis, yet PCR tests on lung washings and blood stayed negative, deepening the puzzle. The authors blame a tuberculosis-driven clotting state and urge suspicion for spread disease in young patients from high-burden regions.
pmc-13403149:
Vishwadeepak Rajput, Vishavdeep Kaur, and Ankalayya Bobbara compare heart rate variability at rest and after step exercise in 200 young adults split evenly between normal weight and overweight. Extra fat in youth can tilt the autonomic balance before heart disease declares itself, and variability in beat timing reads that balance noninvasively. Volunteers aged 17 to 25 stepped on a 23 centimeter stool at 40 steps a minute for up to five minutes.

At rest the overweight group already showed lower variability across time-domain measures and higher heart rate, all with p values below 0.001 in the reported tests. After exercise their recovery values, including SDNN, RMSSD, and high-frequency power, stayed lower, and adjusted models tied overweight status to lower fitness index scores too. The authors read early autonomic strain in overweight youth, detectable with a stool, a stopwatch, and an ECG.
pmc-13404049:
Benoit Caullery and co-authors ran a pilot study of supersaturated oxygen therapy after severe heart attacks in 2026. The therapy feeds blood loaded with extra oxygen into the heart artery after the blockage is opened. It shrinks heart damage, possibly by easing poor flow in the smallest vessels.

The method is cumbersome: it needs a leg artery puncture and an hour in the procedure room. The pilot asked whether the therapy improves small-vessel function in front-wall heart attacks. A scan-based index of small-vessel resistance was measured before and after the hour of therapy. Knowing who gains most could guide the therapy to the patients who benefit, the authors argue.
pmc-13404149:
