Anna Szlachcic and Nadinath B. Nillegoda probed in 2026 how mixed helper proteins team up to dissolve toxic protein clumps in animal cells. Clumps threaten cell health and build up with age and disease. The clearing machine pairs a workhorse protein, Hsp70, with helper proteins from two classes.

The team muted each helper's grip on the workhorse in turn, while keeping the helpers paired. Teamwork gains vanished when either partner could not engage the workhorse. Size-sorted tests showed the mixed pair handled clump types that neither class managed alone. Both helpers thus pull workhorses in together, widening what the machine can clear.
pmc-13404249:
Shiinoki and colleagues teach a model to read lung function from moving chest X-rays. The aim is patients who cannot do the forced breathing tests demand. Spirometry, the reference test, fails with children, frail elders, and people with poor cognition. Their 2026 study reuses chest radiography, a low dose image sequence taken while a patient breathes, in 151 patients. It extracts image features at breath phases and from a motion map. Models are trained to predict standard lung values.

Models built on the multiphase images and motion map beat the formula that estimates lung function from age, sex, and height alone. The approach predicted both breathing volumes and sorted patients by the ratio used to flag high risk obstruction. Because the study is one center and looks backward, the authors call for validation elsewhere before clinics trust it. An X-ray that reports function could reach patients spirometry leaves untested.
pmc-13404849:
Huayue Zeng and colleagues built a single test that finds three chicken viruses at once, reporting in 2026. Avian leukosis virus, chicken infectious anaemia virus and fowl adenovirus cause tumours, weak immunity and heavy losses on poultry farms. Testing for each separately costs time during outbreaks.

Their triplex crystal digital RT-PCR copies and counts genetic material from all three viruses in one run. After tuning reaction settings, the test showed strong specificity, sensitivity and repeatability. On 1,211 farm samples it agreed with reference methods in at least 98.18 percent of cases in the reported checks. The team offers the assay for routine flock screening where the three viruses circulate.
pmc-13405449:
Ali Ijaz, Kin Mun Lau and Andrew CF Hui write in 2026 with two objections to a recent study of dermatomyositis diagnosis in 14 patients. The original authors concluded that electromyography, a test of electrical activity in muscle, can exclude the disease. They also proposed that every suspected patient should receive the test.

Both claims overreach the data, the letter argues. Abnormal results appear in 70 to 90 percent of inflammatory muscle disease, yet some classic cases with raised muscle enzymes showed no such pattern in the study itself. A test that misses real cases cannot rule the disease out. The correspondents ask for the conclusions to be softened to match the small, real-world series.
pmc-13405649:
Serena Stigliano and co-authors compare two scope routes for draining the gallbladder in patients too frail for surgery, in a 2026 Italian series. Ultrasound-guided drainage through a metal stent serves people with gallbladder inflammation or blocked bile ducts from cancer. The scope can pass through the stomach wall or the duodenum, and which is better is debated.

Seventy consecutive patients treated between 2020 and 2026 were reviewed, with an average age of 77. Technical success reached 98.5 percent in the reported results. The stomach route was used in 48.5 percent of cases. Success, complications, readmissions and repeat procedures are compared between the two routes to guide route choice.
pmc-13407349:
Zhaoxi Wang and co-authors survey, in 2026, heat shock proteins and protein housekeeping in worn spinal discs, a leading source of low back pain. Heat shock proteins act as chaperones that refold stressed proteins, and in disc tissue they can protect cells or, in other settings, feed the damage process.

The review tracks members such as HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27 across the disc. They appear in its gel-like centre and its fibrous outer ring. The authors tie them to inflammation, cell death, and matrix turnover. Tuning these chaperones could pair with biomaterials, physical stimulation, or regenerative approaches. Direct disc-specific evidence for some family members is still scarce, a gap the authors flag for future work.
pmc-13407449:
Laura Valentina Klüner and co-authors, in 2026, scanned child-sized head models to compare two CT detector technologies for children's brain imaging. Photon-counting detectors are newer than standard energy-integrating ones, and the team varied image quality settings on models representing ages one, five, and ten, recording dose, noise, and signal clarity.

Photon-counting scans needed lower radiation dose at every age, with the biggest saving, about 9 percent, in the ten-year-old model at clinically used settings. Signal clarity ran higher for both brain tissue and bone, by up to roughly 20 and 50 percent across the full range tested, and image noise was lower in the younger models. Organ doses were highest in the smallest model under both systems. The results support gentler, clearer paediatric head scanning.
pmc-13407849:
Yan Wei and co-authors report, in 2026, turning a water pollutant into a recoverable polymer without gumming up the catalyst. Oxidation-driven linking can convert pollutants into useful products. Reactions on solid surfaces coat catalysts with polymer and stall, though. The team moved the key bond-forming steps out into the water itself. A facet-cut bismuth oxyiodide catalyst with peroxide did the work.

The catalyst steers peroxide activation toward freely diffusing iodine, a moderate oxidiser that polymerised the target chlorophenol mainly in solution. A record 73 percent of polymer product stayed in the aqueous phase for recovery. Specialised microscopy watched iodine form and react in place, and calculations showed one crystal facet's hydrogen-bonding arrangement favours iodine generation while another favours radical routes. Fouling-resistant cleanup coupled to resource recovery is the promise.
pmc-13408049:
Alexander R. Markes and James P. Bradley describe, in 2026, a combined arthroscopic operation for massive rotator cuff tears that cannot be sewn back. Two fixes are paired. The first rebuilds the cuff's cable, the load-spreading structure along the tear's edge, with heavy non-absorbable suture anchored at the bone. The second resurfaces the bone knob, tuberoplasty, capped with a dermal graft from donated tissue.

The operation suits multi-tendon tears with heavy retraction where complete repair is impossible and pain persists despite conservative care. Published results for the components separately show fewer re-tears, better shoulder mechanics, and pain relief. Combining them aims to restore partial biomechanics and soothe pain through the biological interposition graft. Joint replacement is avoided. Portal placement, graft rolling for insertion, and anchor choice by bone quality are covered as key technical points.
pmc-13408149:
Simone Nascimento Santos Ribeiro and co-authors build, in 2026, a camera-based system that counts newborn breathing without touching the baby. Contact sensors and subjective observation limit neonatal monitoring, especially for preterm infants. The team therefore trained a vision model to segment the chest-abdomen region in video. It then extracted the breathing signal from motion between frames, counting peaks only while a pose tracker judged the infant still.

Twenty-three recordings of spontaneously breathing newborns, three to fifteen days old, supplied 3,387 hand-labelled frames. Segmentation precision exceeded 94 percent on the reported metric, and estimated breathing rate missed the simultaneous clinical reference by an average of 2.1 breaths per minute. The single-centre sample was small, so the authors present technical feasibility and call for multicentre prospective validation.
pmc-13408349:
Seenivasan Subramani and Muthu Chidambaram discuss in 2026 why everyday care for bronchiolitis, a viral chest infection of infants, still drifts away from published guidance. The illness fills paediatric wards every season, respiratory syncytial virus causes most cases, and care is supportive only: fluids and oxygen, with no drug proven to help much.

Drawing on a survey of practitioners, the authors catalogue how often inhalers, steroids, adrenaline, antibiotics, and scans are still used despite guidance advising against most of them. Premature babies face several times the risk of severe disease, which may encourage intervention. Readers get a clear map of the gap between guidance and habit, and a reference point for audits aiming to standardise supportive care in busy children's hospitals.
pmc-13408949:
Yangxiang Zhou and team propose 6HAN, a graph attention network algorithm to make IPv6 scanning targets for prefixes with no seed addresses. Their 2026 work takes on a core web measurement snag: the IPv6 space is vast and sparse, and past generators lean on seed patterns, failing on nonseed prefixes. Prior nonseed methods used single traits, underused Whois data, and could not handle missing Whois fields.

6HAN builds a mixed graph from IPv6 prefixes and Whois metadata. It learns prefix codes by joining Whois traits with structural traits, and fills missing Whois fields by graph guessing before moving patterns from like seed prefixes. Sending 50 million probes, it lifted hit rates by 13.81 to 201.05 percent and prefix coverage by 17.41 to 233.58 percent over two rival methods. The work offers a stronger tool for IPv6 measurement, with scanning ethics and authorization still required.
pmc-13410549:
Ping Han, Yiwei Wu, and Lin Cai survey in 2026 why flooded phone users sometimes step back from their screens on purpose. Endless feeds tire the mind, yet fear of missing news keeps people scrolling. That push and pull sits at the heart of the study.

Questionnaires from 2,508 people in Sichuan Province, China, fed the analysis. Feeling overloaded tied directly to more reflective breaks from phone use. Social media fatigue carried much of that link, passing the effect along. Confidence in handling threats changed the pattern, with links weaker among the highly confident. Students low in confidence leaned hardest on stepping back as a shield against overload.
pmc-13411149:
Kaijiang Pan, Xinyu Lin, Shengqi Huang, and Caihua Huang build in 2026 a risk framework for chatbots that give exercise and health advice. Small shifts in a tool's claims, users, or automation can slide it from casual wellness help into regulated medical territory. In exercise care, a bad call can overload a body or delay needed treatment.

Anchored in China's device rules and informed by European and American frameworks, their matrix scores six dimensions, from intended use to update pathways. Green, yellow, and red coding uses strict aggregation, so one bad dimension cannot be averaged away. Three raters applying the rules to seven made-up scenarios agreed completely. A governance checklist and lifecycle path round out the package.
pmc-13411349:
Lăcrămioara Ionela Butnariu and co-authors present in 2026 clinical and gene data on neurofibromatosis type 1 in a Romanian cohort, the first such molecular survey in the country. The inherited condition varies enormously between patients, even within families. Fifty-four clinically diagnosed patients were examined, though gene testing reached only twelve.

Coffee-colored skin spots appeared in every patient, with eye nodules and skin-fold freckling also common. Sequencing found a spread of variant kinds, mostly shifts that truncate the protein. One brand-new complex variant appeared in a patient with severe disease, including a malignant nerve tumor. Over half the tested cases were the first in their families, which strengthens the case for early genetic screening where funds allow.
pmc-13411749:
Bhargavi Rajarathinam leads a team reviewing in 2026 how antibiotic classes differ in their power to stir up inflammatory bowel disease. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis arise from genes, immunity, environment, and gut microbes in tangled ways. Antibiotics, which bulldoze microbe communities, stand out among environmental suspects.

Risk tracked the drug class, total exposure, age at exposure, and how many microbe kinds a drug kills. Broad-spectrum and anaerobe-killing drugs showed the strongest links to later disease. Damage runs through lost helpful bacteria, skewed microbial chemistry, and a leakier gut wall. Counter-moves surveyed include careful prescribing, stool transplants, and tailored diets. Matching antibiotic choice to microbiome cost is the authors' central plea.
pmc-13412149:
Marie Saint-Dizier and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that embryo laboratories should copy how the female body picks sperm. In vitro embryo production underpins cattle breeding, yet only about a quarter of fertilized eggs become transferable embryos, and pregnancies lag behind natural conception. In the body, fewer than one in ten thousand sperm reach the egg, filtered by junctions, a storage reservoir in the oviduct, and guided swimming.

Bench methods such as swim-up and density gradients capture only part of that filtering. Newer tools, including microfluidic chips and systems lined with oviduct cells, mimic the tract more faithfully and have lifted embryo yields in trials. Throughput and standardisation still limit routine use, the authors note.
pmc-13412349:
Kennedy Nye and co-authors simulate blood supply for front-line surgical teams in future wars in a 2026 study. Bleeding is the top preventable cause of battlefield death. Past wars allowed steady blood resupply, a luxury big wars may deny. Walking blood banks, where soldiers donate on site, may plug gaps.

A day-by-day Monte Carlo model runs a thirty-day conflict. Stock starts at one hundred twenty units, restocked every three days. Casualty waves of rising intensity draw it down. A hundred-donor walking bank joins in some runs. The team measure how fast shelves empty and how much donor augmentation helps. The results warn planners that current stocks bend quickly under mass casualties.
pmc-13412549:
Huixiao Yuan and colleagues follow a large Chinese cohort in 2026 to test whether two blood-and-vessel markers jointly predict death. One marker blends inflammation and insulin resistance into a single index; the other estimates artery stiffness from age and blood pressure. The prospective study drew 7,183 participants from the CHARLS 2011 survey, with a second cohort from 2015 used to check the findings.

During follow-up, 906 deaths occurred in the main cohort. Each unit rise in the combined index came with 56 percent higher mortality risk, and stiffer estimated arteries added risk of their own accord. People high on both markers faced the greatest danger, with risk about 73 percent above the low group. Each marker explained a small slice of the other's effect.
pmc-13412649:
Emily T. Skrocki and colleagues report in 2026 a quality improvement effort that brought intensive lifestyle treatment for child obesity into a busy primary care clinic. Such programs improve weight and related conditions, yet few clinics deliver them at the recommended intensity. At their large urban academic clinic, referrals, participation, and session dose all started low, so the team ran repeated plan-do-study-act cycles testing provider teaching, tailored materials, and a hybrid visit format.

Participation and treatment intensity both shifted upward in a sustained way on control charts, and the gains held over time. Referral volume, by contrast, mostly wobbled within its usual range. The authors present the hybrid model, mixing office visits with technology-supported contact, as a workable route for similar clinics.
pmc-13416149:
Chan-Young Kwon and colleagues followed 92 cognitively impaired patients in 2026 through four months of Korean medicine home visits at several centers. The program aimed at pain, dementia-related behavior, thinking, and caregiver strain, with checks at baseline, two months, and four months.

Pain scores fell from a median of 4 to 2 and behavior severity eased, while memory test scores held steady and caregiver burden trended down without reaching significance. The paper supports adding home-based Korean medicine to community dementia care, while calling for controlled trials to confirm the gains in larger groups.
pmc-13416749:
Przemysław Kurek reports field work in a Polish oak and hornbeam forest on where birds drop seeds, in a 2026 study. Birds often leave droppings at perch sites, so seeds they carry collect in those spots. He tested whether decaying logs act as perches that shape this seed rain inside a forest.

Traps sat under logs or at random floor spots across three seasons from 2021 to 2023. Of 524 droppings, about three quarters fell near logs, and about four fifths of all seeds landed there too. Total seed input was low, yet logs clearly guided where new plants could start.
pmc-13417649:
Antony Bologna and colleagues test whether a brief trauma screen's total score fairly reflects overall burden, in a 2026 psychometric study. The Global Psychotrauma Screen asks about 17 symptom items spanning intrusion, avoidance, anxiety, low mood, and sleep problems. Data came from 6,930 Italian adults surveyed online during the COVID outbreak.

Statistical checks supported treating the items as one broad dimension. A two parameter model fit best, and items varied in how sharply they separated levels of burden. Precision was best from slightly below average to high burden. Results back the total score as a first line screen, with clinical sample replication still needed.
pmc-13417849:
Yi Fang and co-authors map symptom webs in women who cannot conceive in a 2026 study. Primary infertility lifts distress, yet which symptoms hold the web together was unclear. The team polled 1,062 women at four Chinese fertility centers in 2025 with seven standard scales.

About one in ten met the depression bar and one in twenty the anxiety bar. Trouble relaxing sat at the web core among symptoms. Public stigma led the social factors, tied hard to family stigma. Felt stress bridged social strain to symptoms most, with guilt the key bridge symptom. The hubs mark where help bites first.
pmc-13418049:
Qingqiao Fu and co-authors trace ordering inside a complex ceramic used for microwave devices, in a 2026 materials study. The ceramic's metal sites follow a one to two ordering pattern, and disorder at several scales can spoil performance. A multiscale toolkit tracked order from micrometre domains down to sub atomic detail in a barium based model system.

Ordered domains carried strong lattice strain tied to exact cation arrangement. Oxygen vacancies grew with hotter annealing, and local composition wobbled from spot to spot. Together these flaws scatter sound like vibrations in the lattice, shortening their life and hurting dielectric quality. Controlling order, defects, and strain together is the proposed design path.
pmc-13418249:
Johannes Raedler and a large team report that donor stem cell transplantation can cure CARMIL2 deficiency, a combined immune disorder, in a 2026 study. About 120 patients are known. The condition brings infections, gut and skin inflammation, poor growth, and virus linked smooth muscle tumours, with only about 60 percent surviving to age 40 under standard care.

Transplanted patients saw immune failure, dysregulation, and the virus driven tumours addressed substantially, the team reports. Replacing the blood and immune system removes the faulty gene's effects where they matter most. The authors urge offering transplantation soon after diagnosis rather than after years of damage accumulate.
pmc-13418549:
Cari R Levy and co-authors evaluate a programme to improve life sustaining treatment documentation for veterans in home based primary care, published in 2026. United States Veterans Health Administration policy asks teams to record patient wishes, yet home care rates lagged. Eleven low performing programmes received monthly feedback reports plus tailored facilitation help over a phased rollout.

Documentation rose by an average of 21 percentage points beyond expected trends across the intervention sites. Gains held through a 12 month sustainability phase after support ended. Feedback alone often fails, the authors note; pairing data reports with hands on facilitation made the change stick and supports goal aligned care.
pmc-13418649:
Camila Badell and three co-authors told the story of a 95-year-old woman in a 2026 case titled The Blue Delirium. She arrived with lethargy and weakness after a fall, on top of months of mental and functional decline and new persecutory delusions. Her history included heart disease, back pain, bladder symptoms, and many medications. One drug stood out: a urinary pain product sold as urogesic blue.

Two of its ingredients drive the lesson. Methylene blue, which turns urine blue-green, blocks an enzyme and can trigger serotonin toxicity with common antidepressants. Hyoscyamine blocks acetylcholine and can cloud thinking in older adults. The case shows how one bladder drug can stack both risks in a frail patient.
pmc-13418749:
Hengrui Zhang and colleagues compare how two unlike subduction zones handle carbon carried down into the Earth. One site, Colombia, runs hot, while Tonga in the Pacific runs very cold. Sinking slabs drive deep carbon cycling, yet how well each zone frees that carbon has stayed in dispute. The team paired detailed heat and rock modeling with gas and chemistry data from volcanoes above each zone.

The hot zone freed more than 15 percent of its slab carbon within a fairly narrow depth band. Melting added a second release route on top of the main chemical one. The cold zone freed only about 1 percent, spread thinly across a much deeper span, mostly by slow dissolving. The contrast shows why some arcs return carbon to the air far faster than others.
pmc-13418849:
Liisa Lutter and colleagues show that a single atomic force microscope image can yield a three-dimensional model of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The microscope method scans surfaces at tiny scale and is often used to describe biological material. Their approach rebuilds single particles in 3D from just one surface image, paired with matching against known electron microscope maps.

The test case was a lab-made form of the spike, the same protein family used in vaccine and drug work. A fast structural check like this can flag bad batches during protein production long before slower methods finish. Results showed the reconstruction worked at single-particle level with strong image quality. The pairing of the two microscope routes opens a quicker path for quality control in structural biology labs.
pmc-13420549:
Gaurav Lakhani and colleagues walk through a tricky heart tracing: a wide, chaotically irregular fast rhythm in a 69-year-old man with a weak heart and an implanted defibrillator. The tracing mimicked atrial fibrillation, the common impostor in such cases, yet several clues favored a ventricular origin, the far more dangerous reading. A standard decision algorithm, morphology signs, and proof that the upper and lower chambers beat apart all pointed the same way.

His heart ultrasound showed pumping strength down to 30 percent of the expected measure in the reported figure. The rate swung between 100 and 150 beats per minute in the tracing shown. Getting this call wrong risks fatal treatment errors, since drugs for the harmless mimic can collapse a true ventricular rhythm. The case teaches the discriminating steps in order.
pmc-13421249:
Nyoni and colleagues tested in 2026 whether road-traffic measures can stand in for personal air pollution exposure in Africa. Fine particles called PM2.5 harm health, yet ground sensors are scarce across the region. The team used year-long personal exposure measures from 343 new mothers in The Gambia, Kenya, and Mozambique. They checked three road proxies: weighted road density, distance from highways, and distance from main roads.

Single road proxies linked weakly to measured exposure and often pointed in opposite directions across countries. Road density correlated with exposure only in Mozambique, while highway distance flipped sign between Kenya and the other sites. Combining all three proxies improved prediction in Kenya and Mozambique but not beyond the best single proxy in The Gambia. They advise local checks plus data on weather, land use, and household fuels.
pmc-13421349:
Brennan Undseth and nine colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 paper, a silicon quantum computer chip in which electron spins are physically shuttled between stations. Moving qubits along a bus gives the long-range connections that quantum error correction needs, and the team built four interaction points along one such bus.

They populated the array, tuned every one- and two-qubit operation, and measured spins without disturbing them, largely without charge sensors. The resulting five-qubit processor performed the parity checks at the heart of surface error-correcting codes, up to checks involving four qubits. They also prepared a genuinely entangled five-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. The authors present the work as a route to calibrating larger sparse spin-qubit arrays.
pmc-13421549:
Wenhua Zha and four colleagues simulate, in a 2026 study, how a single pre-existing crack steers failure in red sandstone. Understanding crack growth matters for tunnels and slopes cut through such rock, and the angle of the crack relative to loading is the variable they isolate.

Using discrete-element software, they compressed virtual sandstone blocks uniaxially across a range of crack angles. As angle rose, the crack faces clamped tighter, so damage began later and at higher stress; peak strength rose too. Microcracking shifted from the crack's middle toward its tips, and the eventual fracture path followed high-stress zones more closely at steep angles. The authors derive staged patterns linking stress fields to crack evolution.
pmc-13421749:
Selleyitoreea and Rahman surveyed 1,410 retirees aged 60 and older across nine districts of Sarawak, Malaysia, asking how psychological distress, self-determination, and social connections relate to quality of life in retirement. They also measured catastrophic health spending, where medical costs consume a large share of a household budget, using standard questionnaires.

Their statistical model explained 56 percent of the variation in quality of life among the retirees surveyed. Self-determination, meaning a felt sense of relatedness, competence, and autonomy, showed the strongest positive link, followed by social capital from bonding and bridging relationships. Distress was tied to lower quality of life largely through eroding self-determination and social capital, with significant indirect effects along both pathways. Catastrophic health spending showed only small, non-significant direct links with quality of life in this sample.
pmc-13422349:
Needham and colleagues reviewed in 2026 studies of how lithium, a main treatment for bipolar disorder, affects the human retina. The retina is the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye, and its nerve fibre layer thins in some mental disorders. They gathered seven structure studies and ten function studies and judged each for bias.

Two larger studies found no difference in that layer between lithium users with bipolar disorder and healthy controls. Among studies comparing lithium with another drug, valproate, four of six found a thicker nerve fibre layer in lithium users. Every function study found lithium changed at least one measure, such as electrical responses of the eye. The authors conclude lithium likely affects the retina, but all studies had limits.
pmc-13423049:
Yue Zhang and four colleagues describe a planned multicentre study in China that will create a fairer measure of how hard a colonoscopy is to insert. Cecal intubation time is the usual stand-in for difficulty, yet it shifts with the operator's experience, the scope used, and the hospital, which limits fair comparison between patients.

About 3,000 adults having sedated colonoscopy at six centres will have their insertion times recorded alongside patient traits, operator experience, and scope type. Three standardisation methods will convert raw times into a standardised score, and machine learning models will then predict difficulty. The group hopes the metric supports training, scheduling, and quality checks across hospitals.
pmc-13423149:
James Dodington and Christopher Morrison argue, in a 2026 commentary, that research on hospital-based violence intervention programmes should be judged by goals patients set for themselves, not only by reinjury rates. Their piece discusses a study of 263 participants in the Life Outside Violence programme, which supports mainly firearm-injured patients.

Such programmes, now spread across the United States, offer intensive case management after injury and mostly serve Black and Hispanic patients, yet research on how they work remains thin. The discussed study measured completion of each participant's own treatment-plan goals, placing success inside a person's wider social world. The authors present that person-centred lens as a fairer test of recovery support.
pmc-13423449:
Uido Yeo and six colleagues compare haemorrhoid surgery outcomes between patients aged 65 to 79 and those aged 80 or more, a group surgeons often worry about. Their single-centre review covered consecutive open haemorrhoidectomies under spinal anaesthesia performed between April 2024 and May 2025, tracking complications for six months.

The cohort held 693 older and 68 very old patients. Early complications such as constipation, bleeding, and recurrence occurred at similar rates in the two groups. Urinary catheter placement was commoner in the very old group, at 45.6% against 31.0%, and no severe complication occurred among them. Intravenous patient-controlled pain relief was linked with lower catheter need, informing gentler care for the oldest patients.
pmc-13424449:
Sutiono and co-authors describe a difficult newborn case in this 2026 report of aplasia cutis congenita, a rare condition where a baby is born missing skin, here in its most dangerous form. The full-term girl had a midline scalp defect measuring 7 by 6 centimeters. The underlying skull bone was also absent. So was the brain's protective dura. That left the great vein of the brain exposed under a thin membrane.

After sterile dressings and broad-spectrum antibiotics, surgeons operated on day eight of life, laying a synthetic dural patch and rotating a scalp flap over the defect. Healing went smoothly. But at six months she developed cystic hydrocephalus, abnormal fluid accumulation in the brain. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt relieved it. By the 24-month follow-up she was hitting normal developmental milestones with a good cosmetic result, though the authors stress lifelong vigilance after such repairs.
pmc-13424649:
Takatoshi Matsuyama leads an eleven-author prospective study of colorectal cancer patients whose disease had already spread to the peritoneum at diagnosis. This is the group with the bleakest outlook. All had surgery that removed every visible tumour. Thirty-six patients across several institutes were followed to learn which features predict who does well after such complete clearance.

Recurrence struck twenty-six of the thirty-six patients, 72%, over a median follow-up of thirty-four months, most often back in the peritoneum. Two features marked better survival: a low level of the blood marker CA19-9 before surgery, and a right-sided primary tumour. Patients with both advantages fared best of all. The authors offer the pairing as a practical guide for counselling and follow-up intensity.
pmc-13424949:
Wei and colleagues report a 2026 study linking a diet-and-lifestyle score to gallstones in United States adults. The score sums how diet and habits tip a person toward or against oxidative stress. Using national survey data from 2017 to 2020, the team compared scores with gallstone history and gallbladder surgery, after adjustment for demographic and health factors.

Higher scores meant lower risk. Each added point on the score came with a few percent lower odds of gallstones, and a slightly larger drop in the odds of having had gallbladder surgery. The pattern held across subgroups and rose in a smooth dose-response shape, which strengthens the case that the link is not a fluke of one group. The score rests on changeable habits, so daily-life steps may lower risk, though a survey cannot prove cause.
pmc-13426349:
Yong-Hong Ma and coauthors compared a statin-related gene in Tibetan patients with type 2 diabetes at high altitude in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Their sample held 156 patients at Yushu People's Hospital between September 2022 and December 2023, split evenly between normal and abnormal blood lipids. Genotyping targeted two SLCO1B1 variants, 521T>C and 388A>G, using PCR-based methods.

The 521TC genotype appeared in 30.8 percent of the abnormal-lipid group versus 14.1 percent of the normal group, alongside higher triglycerides, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol. Both variants tracked with lipid differences, suggesting genetic screening could inform lipid management in this population.
pmc-13426449:
Emmanuel Ndaba and Vukosi Baloyi compare kidney injury after heart surgery between rich and poorer countries in a 2026 focused narrative review. Injury rates look broadly similar across income settings, yet severity at presentation and survival differ markedly. Their review gathered contemporary observational studies reporting incidence, severity, dialysis use, and death after adult cardiac surgery through PubMed searches and hand-checking references.

System-level factors in resource-limited environments, such as late presentation and scarce dialysis capacity, emerge as contributors to excess deaths. Naming those drivers points health systems toward fixes beyond individual patient care.
pmc-13426949:
Simon Holzinger and coauthors introduce the nucDetective pipeline for mapping chromatin in the malaria parasite in a 2026 methods article. The software evaluates nucleosome positioning, occupancy, fuzziness, and array regularity from sequencing data at high resolution. Benchmarking used Plasmodium falciparum through its red blood cell development cycle, a hard case because its genome exceeds eighty percent AT content and its nucleosomes are unusually unstable.

Standard analysis tools struggle with such genomes, so a dedicated pipeline producing stage-specific nucleosome profiles fills a real gap. Parasite researchers gain a way to study gene regulation architecture across the erythrocytic cycle. The pipe line can be run by any lab with the right kind of reads. The maps can be laid side by side for each stage of the germ's life in the blood of man, which aids checks of each claim in the text.
pmc-13427049:
Nan Cheng and colleagues tested Feiwei Heji, a traditional Chinese herbal formula, against lung cancer in tumour-bearing mice. The formula is used for lung cancer patients marked by low energy and dryness in traditional practice terms.

Chemical tests found four main active parts, including naringin and chlorogenic acid. Fed by mouth, the formula slowed tumour growth and switched on pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death that alerts the immune system. It also raised the share of killer T cells inside tumours and boosted their activity signals. The effect ran through a gene regulator called MLL4, since forcing MLL4 back up largely cancelled the benefit.
pmc-13427249:
Aldemir and colleagues report a 2026 study of two microRNAs in the blood during the first three days of sepsis, the body's dangerous overreaction to infection. Fifteen adults meeting modern sepsis criteria and fifteen healthy controls gave blood on day one and day three. The team measured miR-101 and miR-146a, small RNA regulators of inflammation, and compared them with standard severity and inflammation markers.

On day one, miR-101 ran markedly higher in sepsis patients than in controls, a clear statistical gap. MiR-146a ran lower but not significantly. Neither marker changed much between day one and day three. MiR-101 tracked procalcitonin, a standard infection marker, in positive correlation. An early stable signal could help bedside judgments, though fifteen patients is pilot-sized.
pmc-13427649:
Shah Faisal and co-authors explore, in a 2026 study, why killer T cells lose strength inside liver tumors. Exhausted CD8 T cells, a class of immune cell, limit how well checkpoint drugs work in hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The team focused on a gene switch called NR4A2. They reused public human datasets covering single-cell gene activity, chromatin access, tissue maps, and survival records.

At coarse resolution NR4A2 was not a tidy exhaustion marker, since it appeared widely and peaked in another immune cell type. Finer views tied it to the fully exhausted T-cell state and to nearby macrophage-rich zones. Learning models that show their reasoning helped sort the signals. A survival score adjusted for T-cell numbers links the pattern to patient outcomes, offering a candidate marker for further testing.
pmc-13427749:
Ul Ain and colleagues compared oil extraction methods for Pakistani Cinnamomum cassia bark in 2026. They tested superheated steam extraction against standard water and steam distillation. Firms want natural options to replace synthetic preservatives, which can harm health. The team identified over ninety-nine percent of the oil's components, then tested germ-killing power against eight bacteria and fungi and measured antioxidant strength in several assays.

The superheated steam oil won on every front. It gave the highest yield, just over two percent of the bark mass. It also showed the strongest antimicrobial effects in plate, dilution, and biofilm tests, and the top antioxidant scores, clearing about ninety-four percent of test free radicals. Its chemistry was dominated by sesquiterpene hydrocarbons, a class of plant compounds. The authors strongly recommend superheated steam over both traditional methods for this bark.
pmc-13428249:
Kyungseok Jung, Ron A. Adelman, and Ji Liu study, in a 2026 review of records, a laser treatment for eye pressure that stays high after anti-VEGF injections. Those injections treat several retinal diseases, yet in some eyes the pressure inside the eye remains raised. Selective laser trabeculoplasty, a gentle laser to the eye's drain, is one answer. Records covered 33 eyes of 31 patients treated at one academic center between 2013 and 2022.

Pressure fell significantly after the laser at every check, though the number of pressure drops patients used did not fall. Success thinned over time, from about half the eyes at six months to about a quarter at two years. One factor predicted success: eyes that had received anti-VEGF injections more often did better. The laser looks like a useful add-on while its benefit lasts.
pmc-13428549:
Sonia Osorio and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, building 3D-printed anatomy models with an interdisciplinary team in a setting short on cadavers. Anatomy teaching suffers where donated bodies are scarce. Engineers, designers, and teachers worked in three phases: first finding what students struggled to grasp, then printing models from medical imaging data, and finally testing them in class. Two models resulted, one of the trigeminal nerve and one of the lower airway.

Students and teachers rated the prints well for usability, design, fit with course materials, and help in understanding structure. The survey itself held together consistently under statistical checks. The authors present the workflow as proof that local teams can manufacture their own teaching aids cheaply. Controlled studies with measured learning gains are the stated next step before stronger claims follow.
pmc-13428749:
Świdrak and colleagues map where people feel pleasant and unpleasant touch when they only watch it happen to others. Touch on screen can still stir echoes, and earlier work mostly asked where touch feels welcome. Their 2026 study shows volunteers videos of positive and negative touch. Volunteers paint the sensations on a body map tool, separately for physical feelings and for emotions. Each map is scored for strength and spread.

The two kinds of touch painted different bodies. Positive videos scored higher on physical sensation than on emotion, as if the skin itself answered. Negative videos flipped the pattern, with emotion spread wider than physical feeling. People who avoid touch showed muted maps for positive touch. People living with pain showed lower maps overall, though positive touch partly spared them the drop. Body maps, the authors argue, can grade how touch lands without a single probe.
pmc-13429849:
Yanyan Li and five co-authors review past studies in a paper whose head gives the year as 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. The topic is a blood protein that trims a clotting factor into smaller, less risky forms. Low levels of the protein may raise the risk of stroke caused by a blocked artery, but past studies did not agree.

The team searched four large databases and pooled 18 studies with 8,993 people in all. They compared protein levels in stroke patients and controls, and checked how levels linked to clot-removing care. The pooled results help weigh whether this protein can flag risk or guide care after stroke.
pmc-13429949:
Christoffer Jørgensen and co-authors built machine learning models in 2026 to predict which hip and knee replacement patients can go home the same day. Same-day surgery is growing, but limited capacity means clinics must pick the patients most likely to succeed. Data came from six Danish departments with shared protocols.

Three models of rising complexity were tested on thousands of eligible patients. All three predicted only weakly, barely better as they grew more complex. The scores did separate patients who went home from those who stayed, a little. The gain from using the models at current capacity was small, though it grew when capacity was tighter, the authors report.
pmc-13430749:
Aonan Wang and colleagues summarise scan patterns for lesions of the outer trigeminal nerve branches, which carry face feeling through skull-base openings. Their winding paths and rarity make radiology diagnosis hard, even though the branch pattern should guide the call.

Eighteen patients from 2008 to 2022 with tissue-proven lesions were reviewed, covering schwannoma in ten, neurofibroma in three, and one each of several rarer tumours and inflammatory conditions. Multi-plane CT and contrast MRI were the tools. Radiologists get a pattern guide for distal nerve lesions that most will meet only a handful of times.
pmc-13431349:
Byrnes, Collins, and Elliott examine hidden genetic variants in Australian children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in this 2026 study. The disorder follows prenatal alcohol exposure and causes lifelong neurodevelopmental impairment, but genes may influence which exposed children are most affected. The team reviewed records and chromosome microarray results from a statewide diagnostic service for children diagnosed between 2015 and 2022.

A rare copy number variant was found in 38 of the 157 children who received microarray testing. That is roughly one in four of those tested. A copy number variant is a missing or duplicated chunk of DNA. Four children carried a recognizable neurodevelopmental syndrome, including a variant of the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Most variants, about eighty-five percent, remain of uncertain significance, and several involved calcium channel genes tied to developmental disorders.
pmc-13432849:
Yadav and colleagues use in 2026 an immunosuppressed pig model to ask whether hepatitis E virus infects the male reproductive system during chronic infection. The virus is increasingly recognized beyond the liver. Viral RNA had been found in the semen of chronically infected men even without virus in blood or stool.

The team found infectious virus inside mature sperm cells from chronically infected pigs, and the virus altered the sperm's swimming and shape. Virus recovered from sperm could still infect human liver cells in culture. The accessory glands of the reproductive tract showed active viral replication, immune cell infiltration, and cell death, and infected pigs had lower testosterone. Even when a drug treatment lowered virus in blood and feces, sperm carried high viral loads, raising concern about sexual transmission.
pmc-13433349:
Salem Alalwani studied end-of-week school absence in 2026 as a shared social pattern shaped by how the school week is built, drawing on 411 teachers, students, and parents across Saudi regions. Counts weighed each driver's weight, while talks sorted themes by hand. Eleven linked drivers rose from the mix.

Named drivers span week-end tiredness, week shape, group-planned skips, digital chat habits, lax watch, and dull halls. The last day of the week carries shared hopes that pull seats empty in a group rhythm, not as lone rule breaks. Week time frames and crowd hopes press hard on the choice to show up. Alalwani frames the pattern as a joint act born where set time meets daily social life, with stakes for school reach and trust.
pmc-13433749:
Vedrana Aljinović-Vučić, Marin Vučić, and Renata Jurišić Grubešić surveyed adults in 2026 in two Croatian cities on self-dosing with drugs, a habit that can turn risky when it skips a doctor's eye. Forms reached 402 drugstore shoppers in Zagreb and Rijeka in spring 2025. The form probed picks, views, side harm, and home storage ways.

Pain and fever pills led by a mile, named by near all takers. Germ drugs and calm pills, both meant for script care, drew near a third and a quarter of takers. Higher school levels tied to more self-dosing overall. Most bought shelf drugs at drugstores. Women bought more shelf drugs and told of more side harm. A quarter could not say whether home stocks held poison risk.
pmc-13433949:
Ashish Kumar and colleagues design a compact multi-band MIMO antenna with a frequency-selective surface for sub-6 GHz wireless use. Demand for fast, reliable wireless links has pushed antennas toward multiple bands with better radiation performance in small packages.

Their slotted MIMO antenna operates at 3.4, 6.68, and 8.4 gigahertz, covering sub-6 GHz 5G, C-band, and X-band systems. Slots cut into the radiating patch shape surface currents into varied resonant paths, giving multi-band operation, while the MIMO layout lifts channel capacity, diversity, and link reliability. A periodic frequency-selective layer adds further control, giving device makers a compact antenna for crowded wireless bands.
pmc-13434049:
Yi Gong and co-authors found a rare-earth catalyst pair in 2026 that adds cyanide to ketone kin with near-perfect hand pick, opening a short road to a famed brain drug. Twin-armed end products of this kind anchor drugs and farm sprays. Yet face pick across wide stock has fought chemists for years. The two arms on the start carbon look near alike.

A tight ligand with a sulfur cap steers the rare-earth heart. Both fat and ring ketone starts gave end goods at top hand purity. The route reached the brain drug in four steps at a fat overall yield, the shortest such path yet. One end good killed cotton aphids at a dose on par with shop sprays.
pmc-13434149:
Juuso Takala and colleagues test a deep-learning tool for spotting sudden brain bleeds on head scans, outside the hospitals where it was built. The tool was tried on 901 plain head scans from two Swiss hospitals, judged against radiologists' reports.

Of 81 scans with sudden bleeding inside the brain, in its fluid spaces, or under its coverings, the tool found 74, for a 91.4 percent hit rate. In Zurich, hits ran 88.5 percent with 89.7 percent correct clears, while in St. Gallen hits ran 100.0 percent but correct clears only 47.5 percent. Resizing St. Gallen scans to a standard 512 grid was then tried, showing how scan format can swing outside performance.
pmc-13434249:
Shi-Ya Xie and a large team show in 2026 that a tumor far from the ovary can still harm egg supply in mice. The mice carried a skin tumor, and two cancer treatments were tested for side effects on the ovary. One treatment was an immune drug and the other was a whole cell vaccine.

Tumor growth cut ovary health in many ways. The vaccine largely restored health, while the immune drug did not. Blood tests pointed to one signal protein that rose most with harm and fell most with rescue. That signal binds a partner in the ovary and drives scar growth, early egg use, and swelling. Blocking the pair restored health.
pmc-13434449:
Chuan-Chin Huang and colleagues follow tuberculosis risk after prison release in Lima, Peru, in 2026. The study covers 3,658 adults with new lung disease plus 6,335 household contacts. About five in one hundred patients had left prison within the past five years.

Former prisoners came to care with worse disease and had poorer treatment results. Most new cases in that group arose within two years of release. Household contacts with a prison past also carried more infection at first check. The pattern held after checks for age, health, and income. Care that follows people home after release could cut spread.
pmc-13434549:
Vinay Kusuma and a large team show in a 2026 study that sewage checks can track a drug resistant fungus in Abu Dhabi. The fungus, Candidozyma auris, spreads in hospitals, resists many drugs, and can kill. It falls into family groups called clades, each with its own drug traits.

Over one year the team took more than twenty three thousand sewage samples across Abu Dhabi and Al Ain. They grew ten true isolates, about four per ten thousand samples. Nine were from the known first clade, and one was from a new sixth clade, the first found in the region. All ten resisted at least one drug, so the authors back sewage checks as a support for hospital watch.
pmc-13434749:
Alessandro Larcher and a large team build a pre surgery score for kidney cancer deaths in 2026. Surgery cures many kidney tumors that have not spread, yet outcomes still vary a lot. Data from 2,536 patients trained the model, with 580 more patients held for a fair test.

Just eight facts known before surgery drive the tree based score. Tumor size, lymph node signs, and general fitness count among them. The score beat a standard rival on the held out group, with strong accuracy in year one. A web tool puts the score in clinic hands. Patients can weigh surgery with a clearer personal risk.
pmc-13435149:
Soloway, Kärpänen, and Guy published a 2026 study on the hidden cost of catheter infections. Some line infections in hospital patients can be prevented with good care. The team compared matched patients with and without these infections in United States data. Records covered stays during 2022 and 2023 from a large hospital database.

Patients with these infections stayed about six weeks longer than matched peers. Their care cost roughly four times as much, near 187,000 dollars in 2023 figures. Death rates ran far higher too, at 12 percent versus 2 percent that year. Fewer infected patients went straight home after discharge from the hospital. The authors estimate that stopping one case could save about 100,000 dollars.
pmc-13435849:
Bao-Jie Wang and coauthors grow a ring by one carbon using violet light in 2026. The targets, naphthoquinones, serve medicine and materials, yet classic routes need noble metals and harsh heat. A chlorine bearing carbene source supplies the extra carbon here.

Light frees the carbene, which first forms a three member ring, then expands it. No metal catalyst or ligand is needed at all. Yields run fair to good across a broad set of starting diketones. Selectivity stays high under mild terms. Skeletal editing by light offers a cleaner path to a valued ring family.
pmc-13436949: Flávio Pereira-Costa and co-authors are named on a 2026 correction that concerns only the funding note of their earlier study on gut bacteria and digested wheat gliadin. The notice is a correction only. It restores a missing funder, the 2022 Beyond Celiac Established Investigator Award. The full corrected funding statement also lists Portuguese science funding for the Coimbra Chemistry Centre and several named researchers. No findings, methods, or results change, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13437149:
Chang and co-authors followed 11 patients with advanced cubital tunnel syndrome, ulnar nerve compression at the elbow graded IIB or III, who received a supercharged nerve transfer alongside standard decompression and transposition. The transfer grafts a nearby healthy nerve branch end-to-side onto the ulnar motor nerve to speed reinnervation across the long regrowth distance.

Electrical testing showed the little-finger muscle's response amplitude significantly improved by 12 months compared with before surgery in this small prospective series. Newborn motor unit signals, the earliest sign of reinnervation, appeared in 8 patients, all within the first 6 months after surgery. Sensory responses returned later, with most first recordings landing at the 12-month visit for patients who initially had none. Key-pinch strength and arm disability scores improved significantly, while overall grip strength did not, supporting early motor benefit from the transfer.
pmc-13437549:
Jiarui Cui and colleagues tested a soil bacterium as a cleanup crew for atrazine, a stubborn weedkiller poisoning bean crops planted after maize. The strain, G1-N1A, had shown promise in liquid tests, yet soil is a harder arena. Their 2026 study ran soil jars, community surveys, and bean pot trials. Residues were tracked chemically, soil enzymes measured, and bean leaves checked for stress damage.

The strain cleared over eighty-five percent of a standard atrazine dose from living soil within a day, ending at a breakdown product called cyanuric acid. Soil enzymes atrazine had suppressed bounced back, and the bacterial community grew richer and healthier. Bean seedlings in treated soil grew heavier, kept their green color, and showed less oxidative scarring. The authors pitch G1-N1A as a triple-duty helper removing the pollutant, restores soil life, and shields the next crop, field trials still lie ahead.
pmc-13437749:
Rugmani Meenambal and nine co-authors report a 2026 lab study on tiny cerium oxide particles tuned to both guard nerve cells and show up on scans. Such particles are known to shield neurons in disease models. Adding gadolinium, a scan contrast metal, could let one particle treat and image at once, a pairing called theranostics.

The doped particles were stable, gave contrast that grew with dose, and did not poison cells. Cells took them up fast. In a human nerve cell model of Parkinson's disease, they matched the plain particles at blocking damage from two toxins. The authors present the doped form as a candidate for tracking and treating brain decay in one agent, pending tests in animals.
pmc-13438149:
Sarah Heissler and co-authors captured the folded, switched-off shape of nonmuscle myosin-2, a motor protein letting ordinary cells crawl, grip, and pull. The motor rests as a compact unit, called the 10S form, with energy use, actin binding, and assembly all muted, then unfolds to work. Their 2026 paper reports frozen-electron microscope images of the protein in four related poses.

The pictures show the long tail folding back in three segments, tucking away the surfaces the motor needs to grab actin and join filaments. The two heavy chains and their light chains sit unevenly, an asymmetry shaping the whole fold. This layout explains how marks and mutations could tip the balance between rest and action. Faults in this motor family underlie hearing loss, brain disorders, and cancer spread. The authors offer the structures as a base for drugs that nudge the switch deliberately.
pmc-13438549:
Przymuszała and colleagues modeled Becker muscular dystrophy heart disease in a dish. They grew heart muscle cells from stem cells of two patients. Next to them sat gene-fixed versions of the same cells. Becker dystrophy makes a cut-down dystrophin protein. Heart damage drives much of the disease burden, yet its cell-level causes stay poorly known.

The patient cells showed raised reactive oxygen species. Their pools of free iron were shrunken in both cytoplasm and mitochondria, against fixed controls. A mitochondria iron-handling protein called mitoNEET was reduced. Genes for iron storage, uptake, and export all shifted levels in the patient cells. Fixing the dystrophin mutation with CRISPR gene editing undid these faults. It brought back full-length dystrophin and the iron readings. The authors conclude full-length dystrophin is vital for keeping cardiac iron balance. The work builds on their earlier Duchenne findings.
pmc-13439149:
Whitney N. Kuwamoto's team updated multimodal analgesia guidance in 2026 for surgery pain care, building on their 2018 review. Combining drugs, regional techniques, and non-drug methods that hit different pain pathway points can cut opioid reliance and side effects, yet evidence, techniques, and agents have moved since 2018. The update surveys trends, new regional methods, and novel drugs including suzetrigine, plus tailored plans for opioid-tolerant patients and those with opioid use disorder.

Continued opioid-sparing emphasis stands, with expanded options and special-population guidance for patients at higher risk of poor pain control. Anesthetists and surgeons get a current clinical guide for building patient-specific pain plans. The review synthesizes evidence rather than testing a new regimen, so local protocols still need adaptation.
pmc-13439349:
Yen and colleagues test whether a mosquito-borne virus could be linked to rheumatoid arthritis in Taiwan in this 2026 cross-sectional study. Chikungunya virus can cause chronic joint inflammation resembling rheumatoid arthritis. That resemblance raises a question: does the virus help trigger the autoimmune disease itself? The team tested blood from 98 arthritis patients and 200 healthy controls with two commercial antibody kits and a laboratory neutralization assay.

Neutralizing antibodies, the most specific sign of past infection, appeared in two arthritis patients and in no controls, a difference that reached significance on one statistical test but not another. The commercial kits agreed poorly with the neutralization assay and with each other, in some comparisons no better than chance. The authors conclude the study was too small to establish any causal link and warn that the available serology tests are unreliable for this question.
pmc-13439449:
Researchers test a traditional Chinese herbal formula in mice with Alzheimer's disease in a paper from 2026. The formula is called Bushen Yijing Formula. The mice were bred to build up the sticky brain protein linked to the disease. One group got the formula by mouth daily for twelve weeks, while other groups got salt water.

Treated mice did better on learning tests and had less of the sticky protein in the memory center of the brain. Gene readings found dozens of genes changed by the treatment. pmc-13446349:

pmc-13446549:

pmc-13448549:

pmc-13449349:

pmc-13449449:

pmc-13449649:

pmc-13459749:
