Two bacterial groups dominated every sample, together covering about four fifths of the census. Community makeup still differed sharply by country, with diversity scores splitting by location. Gambian flies carried far more of one wound-linked bacterium, while Chinese samples held more Pseudomonas. The survey shows the same fly species can ferry different microbial cargo in different places, a point local disease control should weigh.
pmc-13508549:
Three doctors review how artificial intelligence is changing heart ultrasound in a paper from 2026. The test, called echocardiography, is the main way doctors image the heart. In the old workflow, a worker scans the heart, takes each measure by hand, and an expert reads the results. Rising demand and staff shortages now strain that slow process.

The review shows that smart software can cut exam time and take many measures on its own. New tools also judge heart muscle texture and blood flow, not just chamber size. The authors warn that most proof comes from single hospitals. They call for wider testing before clinics trust the tools fully.
pmc-13511149:
Alexander Blagov and five co-authors review a cell signal path as a drug target for artery clogging in a 2026 paper. Clogged arteries drive most heart attacks, strokes, and leg artery ills. Fat build-up, vessel wall strain, long swelling, and poor repair all feed the clog, and the Notch path steers each cell type in play.

That path can guard arteries in one cell and harm them in the next, based on which parts pair up and where. Such two-faced acts have slowed drug work. The review sorts the proof by cell type and setting, to show where blocking or boosting the path may help.
pmc-13511549:
Chuhan Shao and colleagues review evidence that a mother's diet in pregnancy can reprogram the energy factories of her children's cells. Those factories, the mitochondria, sit at the hub of cell metabolism and pass effects across generations.

The changes differ by organ rather than failing evenly, the review finds, hitting placenta, liver, muscle, heart, and brain control centres. The review screened studies in two large databases published up to July 2026. Offspring mitochondria shift their growth, copying, and energy output, ending in weaker energy supply, more oxidative stress, and insulin resistance. Fixes under study include diet changes, exercise, drugs, and even transplanting healthy mitochondria. Shao frames organ-specific mitochondrial damage as the key link carrying metabolic syndrome from mother to child.
pmc-13511849:
Roman Skrypnyk and colleagues present a case of salivary gland problems in long COVID, paired with a literature review. Their 2026 report describes an elderly patient with severe generalised dry mouth and facial swelling.

The swelling involved the submandibular gland, an uncommon site since the parotid gland is usually affected in COVID-related cases. Ultrasound showed marked duct dilation without gland tissue changes. With other causes absent and repeated past infections noted, the diagnosis was post-COVID duct inflammation. Conservative symptomatic treatment led to recovery despite the patient's frailty and many medications. The authors argue COVID history belongs in the differential diagnosis for salivary gland inflammation.
pmc-13512249:
Christian Spiegel and six co-authors test whether fluid draining after soft tissue sarcoma surgery can warn of an unplanned return to the operating room, in 2026 work. Wound trouble after removing these tumors is common, and standard risk models lean on patient and tumor traits. Records covered 95 patients treated at one center between 2021 and 2025, of whom 23 needed unplanned revision surgery.

Drainage volume after surgery stayed tied to revision risk after other factors were counted, and the volume of fluid given during surgery was the only in-operation factor that held. Among patients without a planned second-stage reconstruction, drainage sorted future revision cases well, and a high cut-off point was rarely crossed by patients who healed cleanly. The authors present drainage watch as a cheap early marker, while calling the single-center findings exploratory.
pmc-13512549:
Wallace Pereira Silva and six co-authors study what shapes the usability of remote assessment for people with interstitial lung disease in Brazil, in 2026 work. Video-based checks can widen access for these patients, yet owning a device does not settle whether remote care works. Thirty-one adults from four regions joined a mixed study pairing a usability questionnaire with semi-structured interviews.

Income, whether patients felt remote checks were clinically fitting, and how strong their access barriers ran each tracked with usability scores. The authors name digital inequity, meaning unequal skill, connection, and means, as a driver of who can use remote care well. Interview material fleshed out the numbers with daily obstacles. Recommendations stress digital literacy support, attention to social conditions, and clear rules for when remote assessment is appropriate in chronic lung care.
pmc-13514549:
Hatice Sevim and colleagues report a retrospective study, published in 2026. It covers pancreatic shrinkage during treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer. The drug is bevacizumab. It blocks blood vessel growth. The team reviewed paired CT scans from 105 patients at one Ankara hospital. Pancreatic volume was measured before and during therapy. The change was related to survival.

Average pancreatic volume fell measurably on treatment. Patients who lost more volume progressed sooner. Their overall survival was also shorter in the main analyses. The link to progression held up more consistently in sensitivity checks. Scan-measured volume loss may be an early warning sign during this therapy, the authors propose.
pmc-13515549:
Yong Jun Choi and seven colleagues test a liver blood marker against heart artery calcium in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The marker, M2BPGi, reflects scarring in the liver and rises in fatty liver disease tied to metabolism. The question was whether it also flags silent coronary disease in the same patients. Records covered 6,514 adults with the liver condition who had health screening between 2020 and 2025, sorted into four marker bands.

Calcium in the coronary arteries grew steadily more common from the lowest marker band to the highest, rising from about thirty-nine percent to about fifty-seven percent. After adjusting for age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, sugar, and fats, the top band still carried clearly higher odds of calcium, and of worse calcium grades, than the bottom band. Choi's team proposes the marker as an extra flag for hidden heart risk in fatty liver patients, alongside standard risk checks.
pmc-13516849:
Giulia D'Alvano and five colleagues report how fast a targeted antibody works in hard-to-treat myasthenia gravis, in a 2026 single-centre study. Eight older patients, averaging seventy-three years, were scored for daily function and muscle strength before treatment, at five weeks, and at three months.

Improvement came quickly. Daily-living scores fell by roughly three-quarters within five weeks, and strength scores fell by about three-fifths, both shifts being large and statistically firm. Gains held at three months. The drug was well tolerated in this small group. D'Alvano's team reads the speed as clinically valuable for frail, elderly patients who need early relief. Eight patients at one centre still make a narrow evidence base.
pmc-13518849:
Ewelina Grochowska and six colleagues test in 2026 whether spraying selenium on spinach leaves can enrich the crop while it grows in salty soil. Salt-affected farmland is spreading worldwide, and selenium is a nutrient many diets lack. Their pot trial under field-like conditions used the Matador spinach variety at two salinity levels.

Leaf spraying raised selenium levels in the plants roughly tenfold without hurting yield, even at the higher salinity. Treated plants carried more phenols and antioxidants, tolerated salt better, and gained dry matter plus sulfur, zinc, and manganese. Selenium uptake tied closely to sulfur metabolism. Grochowska and co-authors see foliar feeding as a workable way to upgrade spinach grown on salty ground.
pmc-13518949:

Everyone practiced 324 kicks over two days from three distances. During learning itself the groups looked alike, aside from gains in the stricter algorithmic group. pmc-13519449:

Gum disease touches about half of adults worldwide, so AI tools for reading X-rays and planning care could matter widely.

Worries about data privacy and job displacement surfaced in two fifths of replies. The gap between warm views and thin use points to missing training, ethical rules, and access rather than hostility. pmc-13519649:
Kaida Huang and co-authors built a living micro-robot in a 2026 paper on deep tumor care. Drugs often fail to reach cancer cells buried deep in a tumor, past dense walls and odd blood flow. The team sought a carrier that swims on its own and homes in on the tumor core.

The coat helps it dodge body defenses and adds immune-calming effects. It hauls a chemo drug as cargo, earning the team's truck label.
pmc-13520149:
Elif Nur Özen and Ali İbrahim Hatemi survey eating habits in 2026 among 50 patients with inflammatory bowel disease at an Istanbul hospital. They link diet patterns to gut symptoms, mood, and quality of life. Thirty patients had Crohn's disease and twenty had ulcerative colitis. Intakes of fiber, several vitamins, and minerals fell below recommendations. Meal skipping, commoner in Crohn's patients, tied to worse gut symptom scores. pmc-13520449:
Mutita Wongsuwanlert and colleagues assess in 2026 whether non-surgical gum treatment helps people with chronic kidney disease over three months, tracking mouth bacteria, inflammation signals and kidney measures together. After three months, gum pathogen counts fell by roughly one to ten fold, pro-inflammatory signals fell, while a calming signal rose. Kidney markers improved in roughly six to nine of ten patients depending on the measure. Longer trials would be needed to prove lasting kidney benefit.
pmc-13520749:
Yiwei Rao and co-authors turn waste plastic into prized chains in a 2026 study. The waste is a soft plastic used in packs and medical goods. To burn or bury it wastes its carbon, so a lift to higher worth is the aim.

Four acts run in the pot in a set dance, which the team maps in full. Green chemists gain a lift path for a common waste.
pmc-13521549:

pmc-13522049:

pmc-13522249:

The headline result favours peer-reviewed guides as the top pick. Full shares with error ranges fill the result tables. Teachers gain a base line on pro fact habits as AI tools spread through clinics.
pmc-13522449:

pmc-13522549:

pmc-13522749:

Cross-kingdom tests may inform regenerative medicine.
pmc-13523249:

pmc-13523349:

pmc-13524049:

pmc-13524149:

pmc-13526249:

pmc-13527949:

pmc-13528049:

pmc-13528149:

pmc-13528949:

pmc-13529249: Doaa Filali and co-authors extend fixed point results for a class of contractions in a 2026 paper. The setting adds a binary relation with local transitivity to the metric space. pmc-13529649:

pmc-13529849:

pmc-13530149:

Field tests showed modest forecast error at day 30 and lower emission intensity per unit of fertilizer.
pmc-13530249:

pmc-13530649:

pmc-13538149:

pmc-13561149:

pmc-13561749:

pmc-13561949:

pmc-13562349:

pmc-13562549:

A swinging model captured how forces change as the cable moves, not just when it sits still.

pmc-13562649:

The authors present the work as a mechanistic basis for improving goat lactation by managing silage fermentation.
pmc-13563049:

pmc-13563549:

pmc-13563849:
Ruoyu Li and four colleagues model how MRSA, the drug-resistant staph bacterium, spreads through Alberta's hospitals, including the carriers nobody flags at the door. Patients can carry the germ without symptoms, and arrivals quietly seed wards. Their 2026 study built a Bayesian compartment model of 106 hospitals, splitting patients by where the germ was acquired and whether it merely colonised or infected. Calgary's hospitals showed the highest transmission, rural hospitals sat in the middle, and Edmonton's ran lowest, though the uncertainty ranges overlapped. Assuming more hidden carriers nudged transmission rates up slightly. The authors say the model gives teams a map of where spread pressure concentrates, and a way to test screening policies before paying for them.
pmc-13563949:
Nils Orth and co-authors study the microbes around apple roots for clues to replant disease. Some rootstock types tolerate the soil better, and the team asked whether their root microbes explain why.

The disease changed the outer root community most, while rootstock type shaped the inner one more. The most tolerant rootstock carried a richer, more distinct set of microbes. The authors say microbes likely help tolerance, but other factors must also play a part.
pmc-13564049:

The authors urge clinicians to keep these infections on the list when a treated patient sickens, and call for proper studies of the link.
pmc-13564149:
Abdul Shadab and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, lipid nanoparticles that hitch a ride on albumin, the common blood protein, to deliver messenger RNA more safely. Standard particles tend to collect in the liver and can harm it, while older fixes such as surface coating have stopped yielding much improvement.

The authors frame the shift as a biological alliance rather than chemical camouflage. Drug developers get a concise tour of a delivery strategy that could widen where mRNA medicines can safely go.
pmc-13564249:
Mingyue Wang and eleven co-authors name a membrane protein as a driver of cell aging in a 2026 paper. The protein, PTCHD4, had no known role in aging before this work.

pmc-13564749:
Yuerong Lv and Xiang Gao map where climate favors brucellosis, a fever passed from livestock to people, in Xinjiang, China, in a 2026 journal article. More than eighty percent of world cases sit in dry lands, yet the weather links were fuzzy. The study spans cases from 2015 to 2025.

Rain in the driest month led the drivers, then wind speed, then how much heat swings by season. High risk zones sat in dry, mid wind steppe. The model scored high on tests of its calls. The authors say scarce water and wild heat swings frame the risk, a guide for dry land health plans.
pmc-13564949:
Elena Coyago-Cruz and co-authors profile cherry tomatoes of five colors as they ripen in Ecuador. Small tomatoes are prized for their nutrients and for plant compounds that may help health. The team asked how those traits change from unripe to ripe, and how the colors differ.

Tests measured minerals, vitamin C, acids, color compounds, and germ-fighting strength. Ripe fruit from some lines held high levels of potassium and of the color and health compounds. Extracts from the fruit slowed four kinds of bacteria, though they did not stop two yeasts. The authors read the results as proof that these tomatoes carry strong food and health value.
pmc-13565049:
Denise Faustman and co-authors review, in 2026, an old tuberculosis vaccine being repurposed against autoimmune diabetes. The review extends the story to a slower adult form of the disease.
pmc-13565149:
Teerapat Monvises and co-authors reformulated the soaking solution used in shrimp processing to cut its sodium. Treated shrimp matched the standard soak on yield, color, and water-holding, and microscope images showed a relaxed muscle structure holding more water.

Tasters accepted the low-sodium shrimp, and an electronic tongue found better saltiness and umami notes. The authors present the swap as a route to reduced-sodium seafood that keeps the quality processors and buyers expect. Dose choice lets producers trade sodium cuts against cost.
pmc-13565249:

Laboratory work focused on one gene, ANXA1, and its effect on macrophages. The protein pushed macrophages toward a tumor-friendly state in co-culture and animal models. The authors tie the death program to an immunosuppressive tumor environment.
pmc-13565449:

pmc-13565849:

pmc-13565949:

pmc-13566249:

pmc-13566549:

pmc-13566949:
Vanessa Pellicorio, Raffaella Colombo, and Adele Papetti review light-based food checks in 2026. Food fraud and contamination grow more clever worldwide, hitting costly and common products alike. Classic lab methods are accurate but slow, solvent-heavy, and fussy to run.

pmc-13567349:

pmc-13567749:

pmc-13568449:

pmc-13568549:

pmc-13569849:

pmc-13570349:

pmc-13570849:

pmc-13570949:

pmc-13571149:

pmc-13571449:

pmc-13571549:

pmc-13571749:

pmc-13571949:

pmc-13572149:

pmc-13572449:

pmc-13572549:

pmc-13572749:

pmc-13572849:

pmc-13572949:

pmc-13575949:

pmc-13576349:

pmc-13576749:

pmc-13577149:

pmc-13578049:

pmc-13578249:

pmc-13578449:

pmc-13578749:

pmc-13578949:

pmc-13579049:

pmc-13579149:

pmc-13579249:

pmc-13579449:

pmc-13579749:

pmc-13579849:

pmc-13583849:

pmc-13585449:
Violaine Harris and six co-authors wrote a 2026 study on spinal fluid markers that shift after stem cell treatment for progressive multiple sclerosis. The therapy injects a patient's own bone marrow stem cells, grown into neural progenitors, into the spinal canal. These cells calm immunity and support tissue, but their biological footprint was unclear.

The team analyzed spinal fluid from two groups: 50 people in a phase 2 trial and 43 in an expanded access program, all with progressive disease and repeated doses. A protein screen nominated candidates, and validation confirmed four markers that changed in spinal fluid but not blood. Two standard damage markers did not change, though both tracked with age and disability scores. The panel offers a way to confirm the treatment is biologically active.
pmc-13585849:
Nikolaos Pyrgidis and others put out a 2026 study of prostate surgery problems across Germany. Enlarged prostate surgery is very common in older men. Narrowing of the urinary channel sometimes comes with it. National hospital data covered nearly two decades. Over one million surgeries were counted.

About thirteen percent had a linked narrowing. Most narrowings were opened during the same operation. Annual case numbers fell over the period. Patients with narrowing had slightly higher problem rates. Repeat operation rates were also a bit higher. Leakage rates differed only a bit. The huge data set gives surgeons real risk figures for advice.
pmc-13586449:
Saber Soltani and co-authors study small RNA molecules in COVID-19 patients with and without stroke in a 2026 paper. COVID-19 can bring brain complications, including stroke. MicroRNAs, tiny regulators of gene activity, may shape the inflammation behind those events.

One hundred people joined the study: patients with both conditions, patients with COVID-19 alone, and healthy controls. Blood levels of three microRNAs were measured with a precise lab method. Levels of one marker differed clearly across groups in the report. Such markers could one day help flag which infected patients face higher stroke risk, though more work is needed.
pmc-13586549:
Kanu and co-authors explore in 2026 how nerve growth factor treatment affects the cornea's outer layer through tiny released vesicles. The lab made growth factor heals slow corneal wounds and binds two receptors. Cell level paths are well studied, but signals between cells were less clear.

Vesicles released after growth factor dosing lowered the viability, growth, and movement of corneal cells in their tests. One small RNA was enriched in those vesicles yet reduced inside the cells. Blocking that RNA raised the cells' own growth factor output, a feedback hint. Media from blocked RNA vesicle treatment boosted cell growth. A target gene in the pathway was named.
pmc-13586649:
L M Guedes and colleagues dissect the tiny galls that mites raise on the leaves of a Chilean tree. The tree, Crinodendron patagua, grows in dry coastal forests and has tough, leathery leaves packed with defense chemicals. Such armor should repel leaf feeders, yet small eriophyid mites settle in and reshape the leaf into a shelter. The team compared galled and clean leaves in structure and chemistry.

Inside the gall, the mites thinned the upper cell walls and stocked the feeding cells with proteins and sugars for their young. Around the gall's mouth, hairs hardened into a guard, outer cells swelled with thicker walls, and bitter polyphenols rose in the tissue. Some tough leaf traits grew stronger under the mites' control while others stayed put. The picture is of a leaf reprogrammed to feed and shield its tiny tenants.
pmc-13586749:
Mengru Han, Hanghang Hou, Honglu Wang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It compares black and yellow highland barley as they ferment, tracking the microbes, the chemicals formed, and the antioxidant power of each.

Both grains lost microbe variety as fermentation went on, while helpful lactic acid bacteria grew and one yeast family took over among fungi. Helpful plant compounds such as phenolics rose in both. The black barley kept more of two prized compound groups and fought free radicals more strongly. The yellow barley gained more in total phenolics and overall antioxidant capacity. The team also mapped which microbes traveled with which compounds. The results show the two grains ferment along shared lines but end with different strengths.
pmc-13587149:
Itzel Astiazaran-Rascon, Joseph Lau, and Francois Benard wrote a 2026 review on tuning drug like tags for a cell receptor called CXCR4. Paired agents can both image a disease site and treat it with radiation, based on the isotope they carry. The receptor is a prime target since it shows up in cancer and many other illnesses.

Clear maps of the receptor shape, plus years of structure and activity work, sped up the design of new tags. Small changes to a tag can raise how tight it binds and how the body clears it. One peptide pair has reached early trials in patients for both scans and therapy. The review sums up the field and the build traits that work best.
pmc-13587349:
IgA nephropathy is the most common kidney disease of its kind in the world, and it can slowly lead to kidney failure. Yuanyue Lu and co-authors review, in 2026, how doctors might track the disease with layered blood and immune markers. Standard checks such as protein in urine and kidney function tests show damage only after it has built up.

The review explains how faulty IgA proteins form clumps that lodge in the kidney and trigger harm. New drugs act at set points in that chain, so doctors need markers that match each step. The authors weigh what each marker can and cannot show, given wide gaps between tests and patient groups. Layered marker checks could help doctors judge if a treatment is working for each patient.
pmc-13587649:
Radu-Ioan Onija and colleagues used quantum calculations to ask why biology chose cobalt for vitamin B12 and nickel for coenzyme F430. Both cofactors stabilize super-reduced metal(I) states, in which the metal holds an extra electron, during catalysis. The team modeled porphyrin, corrin, and corphin rings holding cobalt, rhodium, iron, manganese, or nickel, and checked the available spin states.

Porphyrin rings gave no clear metal(I) picture, instead pairing metal(II) with ring radicals, matching the fact that biology does not use porphyrin for super-reduced chemistry. Corrin yielded a clean cobalt(I) ground state and no clear super-reduced state for neighboring metals. The least conjugated ring, corphin, yielded a clear nickel(I) state, explaining each cofactor's metal choice.
pmc-13588149:
Ze Fan and co-authors show that support cells in one brain area help drive chronic itch in mice, in this 2026 study. The anterior cingulate cortex shapes itch and the feelings that come with it. Neuron circuits there are increasingly well mapped, but astrocytes were largely ignored.

A chemical skin treatment created lasting itch in the mice. The team measured scratching and signs of negative emotion. They imaged astrocyte shape and recorded calcium signals from astrocytes and neurons. Changes in these star-shaped cells tracked the itch state. The work adds glial cells to the itch circuit story. It may suggest new drug targets for patients whose itch will not stop.
pmc-13588249:
Gary Grove and colleagues compared two fingertip oxygen sensors in healthy adults in laboratory studies published in two thousand twenty-six. Sensors stuck to skin for hours can injure it when peeled off, a known problem in hospitals. One sensor uses a silicone-based adhesive; the other uses an acrylic-based adhesive.

Volunteers wore each sensor while the team measured skin water loss, protein stuck to the device, and peel force on repeated removal. The gentleness trial found no significant difference on its main skin measure in the portion reported. Nurses and device buyers get head-to-head evidence on comfort and reuse for a sensor used on nearly every patient.
pmc-13588349:
Shengxiang Ma and Wei Jiang mine subway accident reports to find which failures matter most. Their 2026 study applies an integrated method to seventy-six Chinese subway accident reports. A structured accident model extracts risk factors, and association mining finds which factors travel together. Network analysis then ranks their importance by how the web of risks holds together.

Four factors topped the network: unclear safety responsibilities among employees, managers' own safety responsibility, weak oversight of subcontractors, and safety training that lacks targeted content. Notably, all four are organizational, not mechanical. The authors offer the ranking as decision support for subway operators deciding where safety money bites hardest. As systems grow more complex, accident reports become data; this paper's contribution is a repeatable way to read them as a system rather than as isolated stories of blame.
pmc-13588949:
Jonathan Liu and co-authors compare gut bacteria in treatment resistant schizophrenia and healthy people in this 2026 paper. About one third of people with schizophrenia do not respond to standard drugs. Clozapine helps many of them, but it carries metabolic and immune side effects. Gut bacteria may shape both the illness and the side effects.

The pilot study matched 25 patients on long term clozapine with 25 healthy controls. Matching covered age, sex, body mass, and smoking. Stool samples were analyzed for bacterial makeup. Participants also reported symptoms, eating behavior, diet, and metabolic measures. Work on this group has been scarce. The study sets a base for asking whether gut changes track with drug effects.
pmc-13589049:
Michael R Williamson and colleagues hunt the brain changes behind memory trouble in childhood sleep apnea. In this condition, the airway collapses repeatedly at night, and the front-line fix, removing tonsils and adenoids, often fails to restore learning. Working in a mouse model that mirrors the illness, the team read gene activity cell by cell in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub.

Gene programs were disturbed in every cell type, most sharply in glia, the brain's support cells, and in neural stem cells. Six genes showed matching drops at the protein level across four cell types. Insulation of nerve fibers, the myelin wrapping laid by glial cells, was measurably impaired, glial shapes looked abnormal, and stem cell numbers in their nursery zone had thinned. The authors frame glial failure as a core driver and publish the full cell atlas for others to mine.
pmc-13589349:
Lina He and co-authors study folded DNA shapes in the hepatitis B virus genome. Their 2026 paper focuses on G-quadruplex structures, which can act as control points for gene activity. Proteins that bind these folds can lock, steady, or unwind them. The virus has few good treatments, so new targets matter.

The team found two working folds in a key control region of the virus. Breaking either fold lowered the activity of that region. One fold drew a host protein that boosted activity in a fold-dependent way. A drug that steadies folds strengthened that link. Another binding protein raised viral output by a separate path. The work maps how these folds help the virus make its proteins.
pmc-13589549:
Yong-Le Zhang and eight co-authors find a cold-linked protein that helps plants defeat a virus, in a 2026 study. Plants fight viruses with RNA silencing, a system that chops viral RNA using small guide RNAs. A helper protein, SGS3, gathers into droplets that build those guides, but what controls the droplets was largely unknown.

The team shows the dehydrin protein COR15, best known from cold hardiness, binds a citrus virus protein called p20. That binding strips away p20’s power to suppress silencing. COR15 also shields SGS3 from being destroyed at the virus’s bidding and helps its droplets form. Plants with this defense resist the citrus tristeza virus better. The find links cold biology to antiviral defense in a surprising way.
pmc-13589849:
Polymnia Louka and co-authors review how mood drugs affect bone health in a 2026 paper. Low mood links to thin bones and more breaks, through stress, swelling, and brain signals to bone. Old mood drugs have tied to worse bone ends in human studies, the team notes.

Fast mood drugs of a newer kind shift bone marks in mixed ways. Some rodent work shows bone saved under stress, while other lab work shows harm to bone growth. No long human bone data exist yet for the new kind, so the team calls the proof early.
pmc-13590049:
Tongyan Sun and Hua Zhang surveyed young people in China in 2026 about what they know, feel, and do regarding heart and brain vessel diseases. Such diseases are rising among the young, yet prevention habits in this age group are poorly mapped.

The online survey drew 636 people from three regions of China in late 2025. Overall scores were middling, at about sixty-three percent of the top mark. Attitudes scored highest and daily practice lowest, a clear knowing versus doing gap. Women, people rating their health better, and the overweight scored higher overall. Exercise and good sleep raised knowledge and attitude scores, while smoking and drinking lowered them. The authors urge teaching aimed at habits, not just facts.
pmc-13590149:
This 2026 document collects the contributed papers of the Canadian Health Libraries Association conference, a bilingual bundle of short research reports from health librarians across Canada. No single study unites them; together they survey a profession in transition.

Among the contributions, one team studied how closing the British Columbia physicians' college library in 2024 affected doctors. Those doctors lost literature search and document delivery services, and the team interviewed seventeen physicians about the change. Another compared human screeners' key concepts against machine indexing for finding records. A French-language report from a Quebec health network describes reinventing a hospital library around five projects, including embedding a librarian inside clinical services and supporting artificial intelligence use. Other papers cover grey literature publishing at a Quebec occupational health institute and further service redesigns.
pmc-13590249:
Tanya Leduc and co-authors studied brainwave patterns in mice lacking a synaptic protein in two thousand twenty-six. The protein, Neuroligin-2, shapes inhibition between brain cells and is linked to developmental disorders. The team focused on the aperiodic part of the brain signal, long treated as mere background noise.

Mice without the protein showed higher values of a decay measure across wake and sleep states, with stronger daily swings. After six hours of sleep loss, the patterns changed in ways that differed from normal mice, by state. Mutant mice also showed hypersynchronized, seizure-like events with even higher values. The findings support a role for the protein in shaping this brain activity property.
pmc-13591049:
Chukwumbana Faith Okirie wrote a 2026 letter on breast surgery after drug care given before an operation. A large study had counted how many women kept the breast and how many lost it. Okirie warns that a count of who kept the breast does not show who could have kept it in the first place.

The letter lists what shapes the true choice: scan results, calcium spots, tumor size next to breast size, and the woman's own wish. It urges future audits to log who was fit for each path, what the care team advised, and why the breast was lost. That shift would turn a plain count into a fair test of good care.
pmc-13591149:
Huzhe Cui, Zhengri Piao, and Songnan Zhang review medical imaging in the evaluation of immunotherapy response in a 2026 paper. Drugs that free the immune system have reshaped cancer care. But the patterns they cause, such as growth that is fake, split, or too fast, fit poorly with the size rules of the standard RECIST scale.

The review traces how scoring moved from that scale to immune-tuned forms, then to scans of function and molecules. The last step is AI models trained on scans over time. The authors stress one line: such models sort risk, they do not diagnose hyperprogressive disease.
pmc-13591549:
Zhixi Huang and co-authors test stem cell treatment in a 2026 study on Crohn's disease. Stem cells from support tissue can calm the immune system and have eased Crohn's symptoms in past work. A form of cell death driven by iron, called ferroptosis, also plays a part in the disease, but the link between the two was unclear.

The team screened for genes tied to both the cell death path and Crohn's, then checked them in patient colon samples. Mice with induced gut inflammation got stem cell treatment by injection. A rescue test then probed one gene, CBS, as the hinge of the benefit. The work maps a route for cell therapy in gut disease.
pmc-13591649:
Didier Bouhassira and Nadine Attal answer critics in a 2026 reply letter about their proposed rewrite of how nerve pain is diagnosed. The current grading leans on proving a lesion caused the pain, a link often hard to show. Their convergence model instead weighs several signs together. The critics granted the worry but raised hard cases.

A lesion patient whose pain truly stems from joint wear could pass their test wrongly, the critics note. Classic nerve pains like phantom limb pain might fail it, lacking the usual signs. The authors accept both as limits, arguing rare boundary cases should refine, not sink, the model.
pmc-13591749:
Kenneth Boe Krarup and colleagues studied how in situ drills, training in the real ward setting, affect learning versus off-site drills. Cross-training, where staff adopt other jobs' roles, is common but disputed. Their interview-based study in a Danish critical-care unit mixed watching, field notes, and 16 talks with doctors and nurses, read by theme.

Four themes emerged: realism, feel-safe factor, transfer, and cross-training. In situ drills felt more lifelike and gripping than off-site drills, aiding deeper buy-in and learning. Safety grew with known teammates, limited watching, and skilled, polite leading. Transfer to practice seemed stronger, sometimes changing ward routines. Most staff, above all juniors, liked true-role training best, saying cross-training hurt safety and learning. The authors urge setups centred on true roles.
pmc-13592149:
Nigel Sherriff leads a multinational team building a scale to grade how ready health workers are to care well for LGBTQI+ patients. Such patients still meet stigma and thin knowledge in clinics, which delays care and breeds mistrust. Experts first drafted 100 candidate items, then a Delphi panel of specialists trimmed the pool to 39 test items. The survey ran online across three countries: the United Kingdom, Italy, and the United States.

Over 1,300 health workers and trainees finished the survey, alongside two older comparison scales. Analysis began as the protocol paper closed, with results due later. Sherriff and the team expect the PRIDE scale to prove sound in both English and Italian, giving trainers a firm yardstick for teaching and for judging workplace climate.
pmc-13592349:
Myriam González and three co-authors review in 2026 how to fight infection in chronic skin ulcers. Such wounds linger for months, affect one to two percent of people in rich countries, and carry heavy costs and amputation risk. Germs living in films on the wound, plus drug resistance, defeat standard care in many cases.

The review weighs clinic-ready add-ons, from ultrasound and electric current to light therapy and oxygen, against lab-stage nano tools. The add-ons can shrink wounds, cut germ load, and ease pain alongside standard care. Nano platforms of metal, polymer, and mixed types show early promise against wound films.
pmc-13592849:
Shu-Mei Tsai and co-authors propose a urine marker to separate heroin use from a legal cough remedy in a 2026 forensic paper. Heroin is a Schedule I controlled substance with severe legal consequences, while liquid Brown Mixture is a legally prescribed cough remedy in Taiwan. The remedy contains opium tincture, so its users can produce urine results that look like heroin use.

Heroin itself vanishes quickly from urine, and its main metabolite is hard to detect, so labs lean on morphine levels and the morphine-to-codeine ratio. The team examines urinary antimony as an added biomarker for telling the two apart. A reliable extra marker could protect patients who took a legal medicine.
pmc-13593549:
Xianjin Hu and co-authors present a patient whose early extra heartbeats arose next to the His bundle, the heart's central electrical relay, and kept coming back after radiofrequency ablation. In their 2026 report they turned to focal pulsed-field ablation, which uses brief electric pulses rather than heat, in a spot where burning tissue risks permanent damage to the conduction system.

During energy delivery the patient briefly showed a junctional rhythm and even complete heart block. The authors say such changes may not signal lasting injury. They still warrant an immediate pause and close watching. A right bundle branch block persisted after the procedure, which they attribute to a mix of mechanical trauma from the catheter and the electrical effect of the pulses. Patients should be warned about such risks beforehand, the team concludes.
pmc-13593749:
Xuesong Du and co-authors survey Chinese trade school students in 2026. They ask how strain at home, taken as a whole, links to a student's sense of meaning in life. Self-esteem may carry part of that link, and support from labor classes may shape it.

More than fifteen hundred students filled out four scales for the study. Greater family strain went with lower meaning in life. Self-esteem carried a clear part of that link in the tests. Support from labor classes changed the strength of two links in the chain. The authors discuss the pattern through two named models of how support works.
pmc-13593949:
Navneet Prakash and co-authors test the agreement of over-the-counter glucose monitors with finger-stick meters in young adults without diabetes, in a research paper from 2026. Such monitors are now sold for lifestyle, sport, and screening use by people without diabetes. Independent accuracy data in that exact group were missing until this study.

Thirty-nine adults wore the monitors across sessions of rest or exercise, with a sugar drink or placebo. Average error sat near thirteen percent, with a small low bias. Agreement worsened after sugar intake, and when glucose changed fast. Exercise had no steady effect. A five-minute delay shift improved the error rate. The paper guides research use of the devices.
pmc-13594449:
Marie R Biondi Ryan leads a sixteen-author coalition from universities, industry, and government weighing how to make infant formula more like human milk. Human milk is a living, changing food packed with active components. Those components protect and develop the baby. Formula has gained ingredients over thirty years. It still does not match milk in composition or in outcomes for infants.

New ingredients could come from other species' milk, from precision fermentation, or from cultured mammary cells, the review notes. Getting them into formula is the hard part: doses must track milk's natural variability, safety must be reasonably certain, and researchers need agreed ways to test both safety and real functional benefit. The authors argue the field advances only if academic, industry, and regulatory scientists settle these questions together.
pmc-13594549:
Anna Schantz and co-authors studied the diet and parasites of invasive Egyptian geese in central Germany in 2026. The African goose, brought to Europe as an ornament, now thrives and is listed as an invasive concern. Over four years the team examined one hundred geese from one region. Their diet was mostly plants — corn, grasses, and grains — with some animal matter like mussel bits.

Checks found six outer and eleven inner parasite species, several present every year. Seven were first records for Europe in this host. Pairing diet with parasite data revealed earlier meals and local food webs. The study widens knowledge of the species for managers weighing its impact.
pmc-13594749:
Souradip Dasgupta and co-authors published this 2026 study counting how many antibody classes can sit on one HIV particle at once. Broadly neutralizing antibodies are leading candidates for treatment and prevention, but each class misses some viral variants, so cocktails are the plan. The team watched single virus particles with fluorescence correlation spectroscopy and energy-transfer readouts.

Three labeled antibodies aimed at different envelope sites, the CD4 binding site, a glycan patch, and the trimer apex, were mixed with virus from several strains. Particles carried one, two, or all three antibodies in varying shares. The share wearing all three tracked the neutralization strength of the cocktail significantly. The authors argue such single-particle counting should grade antibody combinations before clinical bets are placed.
pmc-13594849:
Yuji Sun and co-authors kept laying ducks under steady heat in 2026 to trace how hot weather cuts egg output. Long heat waves are a standing problem for duck farms, hurting both the birds and the eggs they lay.

Sixty young ducks were split between a mild room and a hot room kept near thirty-five degrees around the clock. The hot group ate less, laid fewer and lighter eggs, and showed poorer egg quality. Blood tests showed lower egg making hormones and signs of strained metabolism and liver stress. Enzymes that digest food in the gut weakened, and the liver's defense chemistry slipped out of balance. The authors map a chain from gut to egg.
pmc-13594949:
Sven Uthicke, Maria Gomez Cabrera, Maria Byrne, and Steven Purcell measured how long an endangered sea cucumber lives, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The species is fished heavily despite its at-risk status, and managers lacked basic life data. The team used genetic fingerprinting to re-find the same animals after a long gap.

A full twenty-four years later, most animals sampled were genetic matches to the first round. That means adult deaths are very rare each year, average lifespan runs to decades, and some live past a century. Recaptured animals had barely grown. The authors warn that current harvest models assume faster turnover and so overstate safe catches. Fishing at present rates, they argue, cannot last.
pmc-13595049:
Yi Chieh Chang, Cherng-Shyang Chang, and Chung-Kan Tsao engineered a living wrapper for cartilage scaffolds. The wrapper is a sheet of fibroblast cells. It shields the implant from the host body after surgery. Cartilage engineering often fails because host tissue invades the scaffold and disrupts new cartilage, while sealing the scaffold off completely starves it of exchange with its surroundings.

Implanted in mice, the plain fibroblast sheet did block invasion, yet cartilage matrix inside the scaffold fell, showing the cost of a purely defensive barrier. Adding endothelial progenitor cells, which encourage blood vessel growth, to the sheet changed the balance: matrix formation recovered and vessels grew richer around the scaffold. The authors present the cell sheet as an active interface rather than a mere wall, letting the implant negotiate with host tissue instead of hiding from it.
pmc-13595149:
For adults with phenylketonuria, a metabolic disorder policed by diet, the right blood target for phenylalanine stays contested. Lubout and co-authors listened in 2026 to eight adults inside a drug trial whose levels swung both ways. Levels rose during a washout week off their old medicine, then fell on the new drug sepiapterin. The patients narrated their mood and daily functioning through the swings.

Higher-than-usual levels came with worse self-reported functioning; lower-than-usual levels with better. The authors suggest the lived data support tighter targets, and that diet-free lowering drugs now let science test optimal levels person by person.
pmc-13595349:
Semwanga and six co-authors test whether scanned slides can strengthen breast cancer diagnosis in Uganda, where pathologists are scarce outside cities. The team digitized 100 biopsy slides and built a web system for viewing them remotely. Two experienced pathologists read each case on screen and under the microscope.

Agreement between the two readers was high on the digital platform, especially for the cancer call and its type. Finer judgments, like counting dividing cells, matched less well, and microscope reads still inspired more confidence. The authors say digital reading can spread expertise to rural areas. Scanners, internet, storage, and training remain the price of wider use.
pmc-13595749:
Maryam Shahdoust, Rosa Aghdam, and Mehdi Sadeghi present SimMapNet, a method for inferring which genes regulate which others. A simple hunch guides it. Genes with similar documented functions are likelier to be wired together. Their 2026 Bayesian framework folds Gene Ontology similarity directly into the statistical prior of a network model.

Tested on a bacterial DNA-repair pathway and on fruit fly data, SimMapNet reconstructed networks more accurately than three established methods on the standard F1 score. It also runs fast enough for large networks. The clearest advantage appeared when samples were few, the setting where purely data-driven inference usually starves. Simulations backed that strength. The authors offer the tool as a principled way to let accumulated biological knowledge steady network building when experiments are small.
pmc-13597049:
Farshid Danesh and colleagues mapped nearly a century of research on a rare inherited skin disorder in 2026. The disorder, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, comes from chronic HPV infection in people born with the faulty genes. It causes widespread skin lesions and raises the risk of skin cancer. Rather than run new experiments, the team measured the field itself, gathering every indexed paper on the disorder from 1931 to 2025.

The collection held 1,489 documents, drawn from the Web of Science. Software charts tracked publication trends, citation networks, and country teamwork. The United States, Germany, and Great Britain earned the most citations, and three pioneers stood out as the most cited authors. The team urges more studies of how common the disorder is and which HPV types matter most.
pmc-13597149:
Ludwig Lettenmaier and a large team studied how roe deer and forest canopy gaps together shape native earthworm communities, in a 2026 paper. Deer numbers and canopy openness are both rising in European forests. Earthworms drive soil mixing and nutrient cycles, yet their response to deer had mostly been studied in North America with foreign worm species.

The team worked across seventy-five forest patches, some with fresh canopy gaps, each with fenced and open plots, five years after gap cutting. Under closed canopy, deer cut worm density and biomass. Where deer were absent, gaps alone changed little. Where deer browsed, gaps raised worm numbers, working through plant growth and moister soil. Young worms gained most from the deer effects. The pattern runs opposite to North American findings, a contrast the authors highlight for forest managers.
pmc-13597349:
Samadhi Patamatamkul reports a case from 2026 of a Thai woman whose skin lesion pointed to a hidden immune fault. She arrived with fever and chest pain a week after walking barefoot in floodwater, and scans showed abscesses in her chest glands, liver, and spleen. The cause was melioidosis, a soil and water infection that surges after floods.

A painful lump under her skin darkened into an eschar-like sore, a sign seen in only six earlier published cases. Her germ also resisted a standard antibiotic, so treatment switched and she recovered. Tests then found antibodies attacking her own interferon, an adult-onset immune weakness that explained the severity. The author urges doctors to suspect both the infection and the immune fault after flood exposure.
pmc-13597849:
A swimmer's disinfectant nearly cost a 76 year old man his lungs, and mask support plus lying face down saved them, report Yu Xue and co-authors in a 2026 case study. Gas from a pool chemical flooded his airways and triggered acute respiratory distress syndrome, with oxygen levels meeting the formal definition on arrival.

There is no antidote for chlorine poisoning, so the team leaned on support: noninvasive ventilation, awake prone positioning, steroids, and close watching. He recovered completely without a breathing tube. The authors present the case as proof that early, layered support can carry such patients through.
pmc-13598349:
Abd Elbasset Tamersit and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six study of medicinal compounds in Halogeton sativus, a plant eaten around the Mediterranean. Extracts were screened for several possible health effects at once. Lab tests were paired with computer modelling of the active parts.

Fifteen compounds were isolated and identified from the plant. One extract beat a reference drug at blocking a starch-digesting enzyme. Another extract scored strongly on antioxidant tests. All extracts protected red blood cell membranes and showed moderate germ killing. Drug-likeness calculations rounded out the profile of a multitarget folk plant.
pmc-13598649:
Wenjun Xia and five co-authors give a step by step protocol for making platelet parent cells in the lab. Platelets come from large bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes. Faults in how those cells grow and mature can cause low platelet counts, clots, and some blood cancers.

The protocol starts with stem cells taken from umbilical cord blood, a source prized for strong growth and high yield. Steps cover sorting the stem cells by a surface marker and then growing them with two growth factors. The culture yields mature megakaryocytes that express key markers at high levels. Labs can use the method to study platelet production and diseases linked to low or faulty platelets.
pmc-13598749:
Jie Mao and co-authors reviewed computer aid for finding throat cancer in two thousand twenty-six. The cancer type they cover grows in the food pipe and is often found late. Doctors find it by passing a camera scope down the throat. Flat early growths are easy to miss, and tired eyes add risk. Smart software trained on images may help doctors spot them sooner.

The review weighs software used with several kinds of scope images. Tasks covered include finding growths and drawing their edges. The software also helps judge how deep a growth has spread. It can sort patterns in tiny blood vessels as well. The authors sort strong proof from weak proof. They note where trials in real clinics are still needed.
pmc-13599049:
Dandan Xia and co-authors study a sugar drug in a 2026 paper on diabetes in pregnancy. The drug is a known stand-in for insulin, but how it guards the placenta was not clear. High sugar can drive a kind of cell death by iron and rust in the birth sac cells.

In dish cells and in rats made high-sugar, the team tested whether the drug blocks that death. It does so by damping one switch and waking a guard path that fights rust. Marks of the rust death fell as the guard path rose. Birth teams gain a path tale for a drug in wide use.
pmc-13599149:
Sureyya Bayayoglu and co-authors run a randomized trial that sets coordination training next to aerobic exercise in children of school age. Their 2026 study asks which form of activity backs working memory and selective attention more.

Seventy-eight children aged ten to twelve were split into three groups. One did aerobic exercise, one did coordination exercise, and one was the control group. Both plans ran for forty minutes, three days a week, for fourteen weeks. They were matched for how hard they felt. Coordination training adds calls on how things are seen, on choices, on plans for moves, and on holding back a move. Those calls go past aerobic intensity on its own. Results took in working memory, and how much a child could work through on a test of attention. The plan tests if moves that engage the mind give gains more tied to that work.
pmc-13599249:

pmc-13599649:

pmc-13600649:

pmc-13600949:

pmc-13601249:

pmc-13601749:

pmc-13602049:

pmc-13602449:

pmc-13602549:

pmc-13602849:

pmc-13603249:

pmc-13609649:

pmc-13610749:
Vinayagam and co-authors compare two platelet drugs for effects beyond clot prevention in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Both drugs, prasugrel and clopidogrel, are paired with aspirin after coronary stent procedures for acute heart syndromes. How their effects on inflammation and oxidative stress compare was not clear.

About one hundred patients aged eighteen to sixty-five took part in two equal study groups. Blood markers of inflammation and antioxidant capacity were measured at the start and again at four weeks. The group on the newer drug showed a much larger drop in the inflammation marker. The paper also reports how antioxidant capacity changed in each group.
pmc-13610949:
Ghazal Basirinia and seven co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, tiny star-shaped gold particles as tools against cancer. Gold nanostars soak up light strongly, can be tuned in shape, and turn light into heat with high efficiency. Those traits suit them both for scans that locate a tumor and for treatments that attack it.

The review covers their use in Raman, glow, CT, MRI, and sound-based imaging, plus heat, light, and radiation treatments. Joining diagnosis and therapy in one particle could let doctors watch treatment as it happens. The authors also weigh the blocks to wider use: weak tumor targeting, safety questions, hard large-scale making, and how the particles behave in the body.
pmc-13611049:
Cheolwoo Lee and Taemyoung Yin validated a walk-through gate that screens railway staff before duty without touching them, in a study published in 2026. Fitness checks must be fast and objective so operations are not disrupted. The gate combines ID cards, infrared temperature, camera-based pulse reading, and a breath alcohol sensor, with signal checks and on-site processing. Three hundred adults took both gate and reference measurements of temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and alcohol.

Average biases sat near zero for all five measures, and agreement statistics ran from strong to near-perfect. After correction for multiple testing, errors did not consistently track age, sex, body size, skin type, or glasses. Two measures' errors did grow with the true value's size. The authors call the integration feasible indoors, with field validation still owed before real deployment.
pmc-13611149:
Salahaden Sultan and Adel Alzahrani ask in 2026 whether smoking changes how stiff fatty plaques in the neck arteries are. Smoking is known to alter what these plaques are made of, and stiffness may say something about how risky a plaque is.

Working with ninety-three patients, the pair used a sound-wave method called shear-wave elastography to measure stiffness in one hundred thirty-two plaques without any surgery. Forty-five patients were current smokers and forty-eight were not, and their plaque readings were compared side by side. The study tests whether a quick, painless scan can reveal effects of smoking that matter for stroke risk.
pmc-13611249:
Jing Long, Haiyang Zhang, and Chenglin Wen propose a prediction-enhanced polynomial Kalman filter. Their 2026 paper aims to improve state estimation in dynamic systems. The classic Kalman filter predicts in a first-order state space only. That limits its use of higher-order links between states. Predictive statistical structure also goes partly unused.

The new filter lifts one-step prediction into higher-order polynomial spaces. Kronecker augmentation builds those expanded representations. The higher-order values act as extra predictive pseudo-observations. A weighted least squares step fuses them with the standard prediction. The usual measurement update then completes each cycle. Simulations showed better estimation than the classic filter. The physical state model stays linear throughout the design.
pmc-13612349:
Ferdaus Ibne Aziz leads a six-author team building a brain tumor classifier meant to survive contact with real hospital data. MRI scans vary by scanner and site, tumor classes are imbalanced, and black-box models strain clinician trust. Their NeuroTrustNet framework fuses three views of each scan: convolutional networks, vision transformers, and handcrafted radiomic features. An adaptive attention stacking mechanism blends them, weighting features case by case rather than with fixed rules.

On a large multi-dataset corpus, heavyweight ensembles peaked at 96 percent accuracy externally, while NeuroTrustNet reached 94 percent. The trade was deliberate: the fusion stage cost roughly 80 percent less computation than full ensemble training. Lightweight baseline models filled out the comparison across budgets. A post-hoc layer adds visual attribution maps and plain-language summaries for clinicians. The authors pitch the system as decision support for settings that cannot afford datacenter-scale inference.
pmc-13612449:
Mikie Ebihara and co-authors ask when peer-led crisis planning changes psychiatric ward culture in a 2026 paper. Japan's wards hold the world's highest bed rate and a long habit of restraint. Crisis plans should be written by the service users themselves, but staff usually write them. The team interviewed thirteen nurses, managers, and peer support workers at two hospitals, analyzing the material twice for causal mechanisms.

Change took hold where three things combined. The hospital, not the lone nurse, owned clinical risk. Peer workers' lived knowledge entered gradually through a bridging staff member. And staff dropped the stance of managing the person, returning plan authorship to users. Roles then reversed, with users asking for care and staff responding. At a site without peer workers, the same practice faded back into routine.
pmc-13612949:
Liu and co-authors ask why some stroke patients turn disgust toward themselves in this 2026 survey study. Feeling cut off from social life may feed that disgust, while confidence in handling daily tasks may buffer it. The team surveyed 207 stroke patients on social ties, self-confidence, and self-disgust.

Patients with stronger social ties and higher confidence reported less self-disgust, and the two factors moved together. A mediation test showed confidence carried about 43 percent of the link between social ties and disgust. In plain terms, belonging seems to protect partly by restoring a sense of capability. The authors suggest rehab programs build both social contact and confidence together.
pmc-13613249:
Philipp Braun and colleagues test a free-breathing MRI scan for measuring fat in the pancreas, as part of the LION lifestyle study of adults with obesity who were losing weight through diet. Fat stored in the pancreas is tied to diabetes risk, so tracking it matters, yet the standard scan asks patients to hold their breath. The new scan lets people breathe freely and takes just under three minutes, against 16 seconds for the breath-hold version.

Eighteen adults had both scans at 3 tesla field strength. Software first outlined the pancreas, and staff then fixed the outlines by hand to keep out nearby belly fat. The team also checked how well one reader repeated the hand fixes after three months. Their results show whether the more comfortable scan can match the standard one, which would help patients who struggle to hold their breath.
pmc-13613349:
Seon Young Song, Jiyeong Kim, Yu-Mi Kim, and Joo Yeon Ko report a 2026 nationwide study of cutaneous lupus in Korea. This form of lupus affects the skin. It can stay limited there or spread to the whole body. Using national health insurance records from 2005 to 2020, they found 32,337 patients, with an average age near 43 years and women making up 72.5 percent. About 16.6 percent already had body-wide lupus at the same time.

Discoid lupus, the type that leaves round, scarred patches, was the most common form. The authors tracked how many skin-only patients later developed body-wide disease and looked at links with skin growths that can turn cancerous. Readers in a field short on Asian data get firm national rates for how often this skin disease appears and how often it deepens into a wider illness.
pmc-13613449:
Shivabalan Arun Prabha and co-authors build lab membranes from real cancer cell skins in 2026. Bubbles shed by cells carry the true mix of a living membrane, unlike simple synthetic films. Holding such films steady for long studies needs a tethered setup with room beneath.

Blebs from a lung cancer line were fused onto gold with the help of anchor molecules. Far more anchors were needed than for synthetic bubbles, and their chains stood upright, aiding fusion. A cancer drug was then tested on the platform. Imaging showed it loosened the membrane like a detergent, supporting the platform for drug screening.
pmc-13614049:
Maureen M. Kitheka, Yan Jing, Yan Yao, and Puja Goyal report a 2026 study on predicting how organic molecules pack into crystals, using a fast computer method called density functional tight-binding. Guessing crystal packing matters for drug and farm chemical design, and for battery materials such as quinones, whose charged forms are hard to pin down with X-ray methods. Full quantum calculations are accurate but slow and costly.

The lighter method used here skips the need to rebuild force fields for each new chemical species formed as a battery charges and drains. The authors show their prediction routine succeeding on test cases at a fraction of the computing cost. For labs screening many candidate materials, a cheaper route to reliable crystal guesses can speed the search for better batteries and medicines alike.
pmc-13614749:
Skin grafts around the eye traditionally need a bolster or a stitch that holds the lid still, both awkward for patients. Ahmed Wanas and Raman Malhotra describe a simpler dressing: quilting sutures that tack the graft down, plus adhesive strips as a splint. They review sixty-seven patients and seventy full-thickness grafts done this way.

Graft survival hit 98.6 percent, and complications ran about fourteen percent. Lid measurements improved clearly for both upper and lower grafts. Three quarters of grafts graded perfect to good on color and edge. Patients needed barely more than one visit in the first six weeks. The 2026 series offers a cheaper, lighter aftercare path.
pmc-13615249:
Huan Tang and colleagues ask in 2026 whether one scan timing predicts poor recovery after stroke treatment. The treatment successfully reopens a blocked artery. The timing in question is how long contrast dye takes to reach the large veins of the brain during a final scan. This sad outcome, called futile recanalization, means the vessel is open yet the patient still fares badly at three months. The team studied patients whose front-brain artery blockage was cleared by a catheter procedure.

The vein filling time runs from the first dye arrival in the neck artery to the first showing in the brain's veins. It stands in for how well tiny vessels in the brain are flowing. Statistical models tested whether a slow time flagged patients heading for poor function. Such a sign, read during the procedure itself, could warn teams early and guide closer care after the operation.
pmc-13615549:
Michail Zoumpoulakis and co-authors set oral health, hygiene, and nutrition side by side, in people with disabilities who live in institutions and in people who live with family. Their 2026 cross-sectional study takes in more than two hundred people.

Data took in questionnaires, dental indices from clinics, signs of how the mouth works, and measures of the body. Those in institutions were about sixty years old, on average. Those who lived in the local area were a bit older. Both groups showed a high need for dental care, and nutrition that was not sound. Those in institutions had oral hygiene that was more poor. They had more tooth decay, and they hung more on caregivers. Those who lived in the local area had better oral health. But their nutrition profiles were less good. Links that count showed between measures of the body and signs tied to the mouth.
pmc-13615849:
Carmen Ariño-Palao and thirteen co-authors check whether immune cells inside breast tumors line up with a commercial genomic risk test. MammaPrint sorts early hormone-sensitive tumors into four risk tiers, from ultralow to high 2. The team reviewed 492 such cancers with test results in hand, scoring stromal immune lymphocytes and their spatial patterns, plus CD4 and CD8 staining on tissue arrays.

High-risk tumors, 41% of the set, carried higher grade, faster growth markers, more vessel invasion, and less progesterone signal. Inflamed immune patterns and median lymphocyte levels also rose in that group. Genomic risk and immune heat, the data suggest, travel together.
pmc-13616049:
Junqin Mao leads a team describing in 2026 an artificial membrane for covering the brain after surgery, modelled on the layered build of a dragonfly wing. Real dura, the tough sac around the brain, is hard to replace: patches must be strong, stop tissue sticking, and vanish as healing completes. Their two-layer design pairs a strong polymer sheet outside with a gel fibre layer inside carrying bioactive glass and cerium oxide particles.

In lab tests the best version was gentle on cells, mopped up harmful oxygen waste, and calmed inflammation in a timed sequence. Implanted in animals, it spurred new dura growth and blood vessel growth while limiting scarring and sticking, and it broke down on a schedule that matched natural repair. Neurosurgeons may one day reach for a patch that works with the healing clock instead of fighting it.
pmc-13616549:
Lazaros Nikolaidis and co-authors report a heart transplant in a patient with three diseases at once in a 2026 paper. Each disease stiffens the heart by filling its muscle with abnormal material. Two are forms of amyloidosis, with distinct proteins building up. The third is sarcoidosis, a growth of immune cell clusters. Pairs of these have been seen, but all three together are almost unheard of.

Advanced scans and protein analysis of heart tissue confirmed all three in the same patient. The team says this is the first such triple case to receive a new heart. The removed heart confirmed the findings. After a transplant, the mix poses hard choices for drug care, since each disease may still act elsewhere. The case warns that one diagnosis does not rule out the others.
pmc-13616749:
Wu-Chul Song tells of a jaw bulge that rose in a deep sheet of the chew muscle post a two-tier calm shot. Such bulges are oft blamed on spare top threads that pull hard when kin rest. His 2026 case had both tiers dosed by plan, yet the bulge grew from the deep part of the top sheet. Sound scans at clench show the split: the outer sheet lies still and thins, while the inner sheet swells fat past a clear inner wall.

A deep re-dose by scan aim clears the bulge whole. Sheet-split build of the chew muscle is the tale's core. Scan checks earn their keep when a bulge shrugs off the first fix.
pmc-13616849:
Gozde Aydin and four colleagues evaluate a wellbeing questionnaire built for people with disability, called the Disability Wellbeing Index. They compare it with two versions of the Adult Social Care Outcomes Toolkit, a widely used measure of social-care quality of life. Their data come from an online survey of Australian disability insurance participants aged fifteen and older, carried out in 2024.

Nearly nineteen hundred people answered, and the two tools agreed moderately for young respondents and strongly for adults. Agreement was strongest on safety questions and weaker on dignity, and factor analysis showed the tools overlap only partly. Both measures separated groups in expected ways, such as by self-rated health. The authors conclude the new index is valid, while stressing that it leans toward general wellbeing where the toolkit leans toward care outcomes.
pmc-13616949:
Yuxiao He and co-authors measure grief and self-compassion among intensive care nurses in Chinese tertiary hospitals. Their 2026 study addresses a workforce that faces patient suffering and death daily. Grief tied to the job can build quietly, yet evidence from China on its level and its links to self-kindness was scarce.

Self-compassion ran modestly above the scale's middle. The two measures moved in opposite directions: nurses kinder to themselves reported less grief. Layered models explored which factors stayed linked after adjustments. The findings support training and support programs that build self-compassion as one buffer against the emotional cost of intensive care.
pmc-13617049:
Domenico Cristiano and co-authors walk through the diagnosis of a chest tumor first found by chance, in a 2026 case report. A man in his sixties had a chest scan for breathing symptoms. Reviewers spotted a mass near the airway junction in the chest. It first looked like dead lymph node tissue, a far more worrying sign. Schwannomas, nerve sheath tumors, are the usual benign culprits in that region.

Extra scans and a needle sample through the airway settled the question. The growth proved to be a schwannoma with cystic change. That change had mimicked necrotic nodes and even cancer on imaging. The report lays out each diagnostic step. Chest doctors gain a template for incidental mediastinal finds. Careful workup spared the patient a wrong cancer label.
pmc-13617749:
Rahul Shah and nine colleagues survey caregivers in a children's hospital emergency department about firearm safety counseling. Firearm injuries are the leading cause of death for American children over age one. The prospective survey, run from November 2020 to May 2022, asked parents whether they remembered receiving safety counseling in the past two years. It also asked whom they trusted to give it, and how they would prefer to receive it.

Eight hundred twenty caregivers answered. Only about a quarter recalled any firearm safety counseling, yet more than half said pediatricians ought to provide it. About one in six reported a firearm at home, and those caregivers were more likely to have received counseling recently. Police departments and pediatricians ranked as the most trusted sources. The authors conclude parents are receptive to counseling from pediatricians and could benefit from learning the American Academy of Pediatrics storage guidelines.
pmc-13618049:
Joshua M. Courtney and Phillip C. Stancil design a quantum computer algorithm that simulates low-energy scattering between two helium atoms in real time. Scattering calculations underpin reaction rates and spectra across chemistry and astrophysics, but classical machines pay steeply rising costs as systems grow. Their product-formula algorithm evolves a Gaussian wavepacket directly, skipping any precomputed energy states, and applies the interatomic potential through closed-form circuits.

From the tracked wavefunction they extract phase shifts and then the deflection function, scattering amplitude, and differential cross section that experiments measure. For identical helium bosons, total cross sections matched trusted classical benchmarks within about six percent, with a small localized discrepancy in the s-wave channel. The design handles any potential built from inverse powers of distance at no extra gate cost, scales toward multichannel problems, and offers a ground-truth operator for testing simpler quantum simulations.
pmc-13618249:
Crystals built around cheap metals could become the guts of light-based electronics if their structure explains their behavior. X-ray work reveals layered networks held by stacking rings and hydrogen bonds to water and chloride guests. Surface maps measure which contacts dominate.

Both crystals absorb visible light with band gaps near two electron volts. Turned into simple diodes, the iron version rectifies about 66-fold and conducts far better than the cobalt one. Computer calculations trace the gap to how the networks stack. The authors argue the pair shows how crystal architecture can be tuned for devices.
pmc-13618949:
Hawa I. Obaje and a large evaluation team assess Liberia's National Community Health Assistant Program, which posts assistants to serve villages more than five kilometers from any facility. The program rolled out across Grand Bassa County between 2018 and 2022. The staggered rollout enabled a stepped-wedge evaluation. A 2022 census collected birth and death histories from twenty-two thousand mothers covering thirty-three thousand young children.

The headline result: under-five mortality did not differ before and under the program, with an adjusted hazard ratio at one. Care patterns shifted, though. Seeking care from providers for fever, diarrhea, or breathing illness doubled to over half, while drugstore and black-market care collapsed, and facility-based deliveries rose from forty-one to fifty-seven percent. Full vaccination puzzlingly fell. The authors conclude the program improved treatment coverage and care-seeking quality, but more is needed to move mortality itself.
pmc-13619449:
Israel Osmond and co-authors squeeze ice to extreme pressure and watch its inner order change. Their 2026 paper uses a diamond press plus X-ray and light tests to track the change. Plain ice had long been known to settle into a neat cubic form under pressure. Theory said that still higher pressure should warp that form into a slanted one.

Past a threshold near three hundred gigapascals, the team saw a clear shift to a new phase. They name the new phase ice XXII and give its slanted structure. The new phase held firm to at least the top pressure they reached. The result settles a long open question about dense ice.
pmc-13620149:
The Atlantic's great overturning flow wobbles in its deep southward limb, and where that wobble starts matters. Jia-Jia Chen and Susan Lozier trace it through the Labrador Sea in a 2026 study. Models join data from a subpolar observing program.

The strongest wobbles sit on dense layers below the overturning peak. They reflect flow shuffled within the limb, not new forcing. Dense water leaving the sea mirrors what entered it closely. Inflow and outflow swings largely cancel in basin totals. Reading single moorings as climate signals can mislead. Density-wise bookkeeping, they argue, is the safer lens.
pmc-13620449:
Yakup Ozbay questions predictor directions and outcome definitions in a study linking thyroid ultrasound to low thyroid function after partial thyroid removal. Kang and colleagues built an ultrasound tissue score from routine pre-surgery scans, yet Ozbay finds their tables point opposite ways. His 2026 letter flags three mismatches between group differences and reported odds ratios.

Higher ultrasound scores and lower thyroid-stimulating hormone appeared in the wrong outcome groups relative to odds ratios above one, and larger remnant volume paired with a protective odds ratio below one. Defining low thyroid function by levothyroxine use at two years, rather than by blood hormone levels, may also blur two distinct states. Ozbay calls for clarification before clinical use.
pmc-13620849:
Hallie Arno and seven colleagues asked whether escaped farm salmon are quietly eroding wild salmon's ability to adapt to a warming climate. They then compared wild fish with aquaculture stock at climate-linked spots in the genome.

Climate adaptation in wild salmon turned out to rest on many genes, including one large flipped chromosome segment already tied to climate response. At those climate spots, wild and farm fish differed about twice as much as they did across the genome overall. Differences also grew with distance from the southern farm source. The authors warn that interbreeding may dilute exactly the variation wild salmon need, compounding climate harm in a way single-threat plans miss.
pmc-13623549:
Dandan Wu and co-authors show everyday materials quietly punching holes in the immune system's front line. Treating mouse macrophages with a range of materials, including laundry detergent, the team measured torn membranes with a damage stain.

Damaged macrophages ate fewer microbes but fused with each other more. In living mice, airway detergent exposure blunted the call-up of macrophages and other defenders to the lung. It also weakened the T cell responses that fight fungi, leaving the animals more open to Candida infection. The authors conclude that membrane damage is an underappreciated route by which household and environmental exposures disarm host defense.
pmc-13623749:
Xinlei Wu and Zhigang Song studied what helps team members share leadership well, in a 2026 paper. Shared leadership means members take turns guiding the team, and the skill to do it well must itself be developed. The authors look at the quality of exchanges between people as the root of that skill.

A two wave survey, two weeks apart, collected matched answers from 411 team members in 104 teams and their 104 leaders. Strong exchange ties with the leader and with fellow members both predicted stronger shared leadership skill. A team level focus on learning goals strengthened both of those links. The study shows how everyday working relationships grow into team wide leadership capacity.
pmc-13623849:
Rotem Mandil and co-authors study the jump from junior to senior sport in Israel in a 2026 paper. Young athletes face new physical, mental, and social demands at the top level. Team and solo paths may differ sharply. Swimming and basketball supply the contrast here.

Nineteen male athletes aged fourteen to twenty gave deep interviews. All trained at senior level while still in youth leagues. Five themes emerged, from entry routes to support and hindsight. Swimming ran on set selection and boarding cohesion. Basketball ran on market deals and pecking order pressure. Military service loomed over both as a fixed constraint. The study maps where support systems should differ by sport type.
pmc-13623949:
Garp Linder and colleagues watch single molecules to learn how a chromatin remodeler called INO80 finds its workplaces on DNA.
