INO80 places them with unusual precision, and the team asked whether the shape of the DNA itself guides it.

Using a technique that stretches rows of DNA like laundry lines under a microscope, the researchers observed INO80 binding, searching, and remodelling in real time. DNA shape features common at promoters and origins strongly controlled how well the machine bound and worked. INO80 also slid along DNA in one-dimensional searches and hopped between segments, yet it could not slip past nucleosomes or a barrier protein. The authors conclude that roadblocks pen the remodeler into promoter regions, raising its contact with the spools it must position.
pmc-13624149:
Yesim Andiran Senayli and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six validation study of a children's weight estimation scale in Türkiye. Emergency care doses medicines by weight, but weighing a child is not always possible. The scale predicts weight from arm circumference, height, and body build.

Nearly five hundred children from a surgery clinic took part. Estimated weights were checked for closeness to true weights. Accuracy was judged by how many estimates landed within set percentage bands. Age and sex differences were examined. A reliable scale helps emergency teams dose quickly and safely when scales or time are lacking.
pmc-13624449:
Dongmiao Cai and three co-authors report a surgical emergency during a womb procedure, in this twenty twenty-six case paper. A woman of forty had a planned operation to remove a fibroid through a scope. During surgery, fluid used to rinse the womb flooded into her blood, a known risk of this operation.

Her oxygen fell and her blood turned acidic as her lungs filled with fluid. Monitors also showed a sudden rise in a gas marker, hinting at bubbles in the veins from the surgical tool. Care teams limited fluids and supported her breathing. The case warns scope teams to watch fluid totals and gas markers closely.
pmc-13625349:
Fateme Asadollahi and colleagues tested a phone-health app for promoting healthy habits in pregnancy. Healthy habits matter for mother and baby, yet many pregnant women struggle to adopt them. App users improved significantly on every healthy-habit subscale, scoring about 30 points higher overall than controls. Gains held across demographic subgroups. Asadollahi and colleagues present phone-health tools as a practical prenatal add-on, pending wider trials.
pmc-13625649:
Matej Rakusa and Tomaz Kocjan present a 2026 case report on a young woman with a rare bone and phosphate disorder. Her gene fault makes the kidneys waste phosphate, which softens bone. Low iron can worsen the fault by raising the hormone that drives the waste.

The patient, aged nineteen, had severe soft bone, iron poor blood, and a thigh bone break that failed to heal on standard care. A newer drug that blocks that hormone was used as a bridge. Pain and stiffness fell fast, and she walked on her own within four months. Bone density rose a lot over the next year. Phosphate levels swung and needed dose care with iron. The authors give the first full report of this use.
pmc-13625949:
Shinya Kawano and three co-authors let an artificial intelligence model that folds proteins around drug candidates pre-screen a chemical library for them, in this 2026 study. Their target is an enzyme called AKR1B10, overproduced in several cancers and therefore an attractive drug target. Starting from 867 candidates in a diverse library, the co-folding model Boltz-2 scored how each molecule would sit against the enzyme. The team then picked forty compounds, favoring chemical variety, for real laboratory testing. Twenty-eight of the forty, seventy percent, genuinely inhibited the enzyme at useful strength, and several were potent at below one micromole with brand-new chemical skeletons. A hit rate like that turns AI screening from a curiosity into a working instrument.
pmc-13626249:
Atsushi Kohyama and colleagues rechecked data from a Japanese rectal cancer trial in 2026. The Ultimate trial tested keyhole surgery for very low, early rectal tumors. It ran at many centers in the twenty fourteen to twenty seventeen period. Front-facing tumor position is a known risk in advanced rectal cancer. Its role in early, very low tumors was unclear. The team split nearly three hundred patients by tumor position.

Groups looked similar in surgery results and tissue findings. Front tumors came back locally far more often within three years. The gap was driven by slightly deeper early tumors. In that subgroup, front tumors recurred at a much higher rate. Overall survival stayed high and similar in both groups. Local control and freedom from recurrence also looked alike overall. The authors urge closer watch and sharper treatment plans for front tumors.
pmc-13626949:
Guoliang Zhou and colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 materials paper, a new way to grow indium arsenide quantum dots exactly where wanted on indium phosphide. The team patterned regular nanohole arrays by electron-beam lithography and etching, regrew indium phosphide, then formed dots by droplet epitaxy, crystallizing indium droplets trapped in the holes. Light measurements on a 14 by 14 array showed single-line telecom emission. Lines were narrow, near the instrument limit, for about sixty percent of dots. Single-dot occupancy reached over eighty percent of holes. The design suits fiber-based communication and chip integration.
pmc-13627149:
Spruce chromosomes look much alike, so telling species apart takes fluorescent tags that light up known DNA spots. Goryachkina and co-authors map two ribosomal DNA families across seven spruce species from Eurasia and East Asia, adding dye bands that stain bright regions. Two species get their maps for the first time, and five are checked from new locations.

All species shared a core pattern on one large chromosome, while the count of strong ribosomal signals ranged from five to eight per genome set. Extra minor sites and stray B chromosomes turned up as well. The authors use the maps to identify nearly every chromosome and weigh diversity within the genus.
pmc-13627949:
Agustina Godino and co-authors scale up factory production of a cholesterol-testing enzyme and prove it in a real diagnostic kit, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, type II cholesterol oxidase from a soil bacterium, reads cholesterol in blood samples. Its built-in cofactor makes it extra stable, a prized trait. The team brewed it in Escherichia coli with a protein tag at either end, in a defined broth, then scaled to fed-batch tanks.

Both tag forms grew dense, beating flask output more than twentyfold. The tail-tagged form won, hitting the highest yield yet reported for this enzyme. One-step cleaning gave stock pure enough to match trade products. Kits built on the home enzyme read straight and true, with fast kinetics, and passed Europe's lab quality bars. After a year in the cold the kits still performed in full.
pmc-13628249:
Simona Lanzillotta and co-authors study how lacking an enzyme called BVRA leaves the brain open to harm from a fatty diet, in this 2026 paper. The enzyme helps cells handle stress, and its loss varies by sex and brain region. Enzyme loss alone caused insulin resistance in the cortex within a week, matching eight weeks of fatty feeding in normal mice. The frontal cortex suffered earliest and worst; the memory center lagged. Female mice showed thinking problems as strong as males' despite milder cell changes. After the diet ended, males partly recovered while females kept declining. The authors call this a metabolic memory written into the brain.
pmc-13628549:
Ryushi Kawakami and co-authors uncover how a heat-loving microbe switches on genes to use mirror-image amino acids, in work published in 2026. Feeding it that form strongly raises an enzyme that converts between the two forms.

The enzyme's gene sits in a cluster beside a transporter gene and a regulator gene. The team showed the unusual food switches on both the enzyme and the transporter. The regulator protein grips the transporter's promoter when the normal amino acid is present, and the mirror form breaks that grip. Crystal structures showed how each amino acid reshapes the regulator. The response touches only this cluster, a precise local switch.
pmc-13628949:
Jamie Penner, Sylvie Lambert, and Robin Cohen test, in a 2026 study, if a home move plan fits the kin who care for late-stage cancer patients. Care work wears the health of such kin. Move time is a known health boon, yet its worth for this group was not clear. The plan, My Ten, was built for each home and tuned to each carer. Its aim was to lift good mood and health, and to ease ill mood and wear. Ten carers joined for six weeks and gave week notes on its form. A last talk read their whole stay.

Eight of ten saw it through. All held the plan fit: no change was called for but a small form tweak to the log. Thanks for care of their own health ran through the notes.
pmc-13629049:
Anushka Reddy Marri and five colleagues examined how India's first COVID-19 lockdown, imposed in March 2020, affected nutrition across wealth groups. They drew on the country's fifth National Family Health Survey, conducted across 2019 to 2021, and measured underweight adults, wasting in young children, and anaemia, each broken down by household wealth.

After adjustment, most indicators improved after the lockdown, yet the gains clustered in richer homes, and the poorest gained least. Near-poor men were the exception, showing a rise in underweight. Child wasting fell in every group but least among the poorest, and anaemia declined everywhere while staying highest at the bottom. The authors caution that the design cannot prove cause, and they call for nutrition systems built to protect the vulnerable during crises.
pmc-13630449:
Designing a DNA test for a germ still takes hand work that ages fast as the germ evolves, and an automated pipeline aims to keep pace. Phillip E Davis, Colin W Price, Taylor Otwell, Anshika Kapoor, Vita Domnenko, and Joseph A Russell present TAPPR in a 2026 paper. The pipeline hunts shared marker stretches across huge genome sets without alignment. Settings tune how wide or narrow the catch should be.

Tests were designed for four targets spanning viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Computer checks and lab runs judged each design's aim and sensitivity. Several beat the fielded tests they were compared with. The authors pitch the tool for outbreak response and watch lists.
pmc-13630649:
Thi-Bich-Van Tran and Ngoc-Anh-Thu Pham measure how model base height changes clear aligner thickness. Their in vitro study from twenty twenty-six uses Zendura FLX dual-layer material. Heat forming thins aligner plastic in uneven ways. That thinning can change how an aligner fits and performs.

Forty aligners were formed over printed upper jaw models. Four base heights were tested, with ten aligners in each group. Thickness was checked at several teeth, from front teeth to molars. Average thickness fell steadily as base height rose. The tallest bases gave the thinnest aligners in the results shown. Dental labs can use these findings when they set model height for dual-layer aligners.
pmc-13630949:
Qi Li and Xinrui Yin pool studies on doomscrolling and mental health in teens and adults, in work from 2026. Doomscrolling is the sticky habit of paging through bad news that is hard to stop. It overlaps with, but is not the same as, general heavy social media use.

The review followed standard reporting rules and was registered in advance. Nine source types were searched. Forty-four studies qualified, and a subset fed the pooled math with forty effect sizes. The habit tied to worse mental health and lower well-being across outcomes. Quality and certainty grading were built in. The authors frame doomscrolling as its own risk, worth naming apart from screen time at large.
pmc-13631949:
Di, Li, and Jin review how brain imaging reveals waste-clearance problems in sleep apnea in this 2026 article. The glymphatic system flushes waste from the brain along vessels. Obstructive sleep apnea seems to impair that flushing, and the fluid spaces around vessels then enlarge.

Enlarged perivascular spaces mark small-vessel disease and hint at glymphatic failure. The review links apnea severity and sleep structure to where these spaces appear. It then walks through imaging tools: structural scans, diffusion methods that track water along the spaces, contrast scans, flow imaging, and blood-oxygen scans. Each method gives a different view of the same clearance failure. The authors map what each technique can and cannot show.
pmc-13633149:
Matteo Aulicino and ten colleagues published this 2026 comparison of robotic versus open surgery for a major pancreas operation. The operation, pancreatoduodenectomy, removes the head of the pancreas together with nearby organs. Robot assistance promises smaller wounds, yet the technique is hard to learn. The team studied patients treated at one busy center from 2020 through 2025. They compared the fifty most recent robotic cases with matched open cases, setting aside the early learning period.

Robotic patients lost less blood and left the hospital about two days sooner. Their operations took far longer, even though times had dropped since the team's first fifty robotic cases. Rates of major complications were similar between the groups. One leak type, involving lymph fluid, occurred less often after robotic surgery. Tracking charts placed the team's turning points just past fifty cases. The authors judge the robotic approach safe and workable in expert hands after the learning curve.
pmc-13633549:
Forming an ultrasound image from raw echoes is a computing problem, and neural networks are rewriting how it is done. Hamza Hadri and co-authors review that shift in this 2026 paper, sorting the model families on offer: convolutional networks, adversarial pairs, transformers, and hybrids. Classic methods are fast but leave images grainy and blurred.

Learned beamformers beat them on sharpness and detail in study after study. The review is frank about the brakes: small and narrow data sets, black-box decisions, and overfitting. Hardware answers get their own tour, from programmable chips to cloud-edge splits that keep frame rates live. The authors ask for shared benchmarks and validation rules before clinics can trust the new images.
pmc-13633649:
Opemipo Dosumu reports a case of lip swelling tied to a flu drug in a patient on a common blood pressure medicine in a 2026 paper. The flu drug oseltamivir is usually well tolerated beyond nausea. The blood pressure drug family, ACE inhibitors, is a classic cause of sudden swelling, sometimes after years of quiet use.

A seventy-three-year-old man with influenza A developed acute lip swelling soon after starting oseltamivir, while on long-term lisinopril. Stopping the antiviral settled the swelling. Untangling which drug, or the virus itself, caused the episode is the report's main puzzle. Dosumu walks through the diagnostic reasoning and the management stakes, since airway swelling can turn dangerous fast.
pmc-13634049:
Aleš Maver and a large expert team published this 2026 consensus on genetic testing reports for rare neurological diseases. Modern sequencing can hunt disease genes quickly, yet lab reports vary in quality and completeness. A European quality scheme the authors helped run exposed those gaps. From its findings, the team listed twenty-eight topics that needed shared guidance, grouped under clinical information, interpretation, methodology, and reporting.

Thirty-one experts rated every topic important or very important across two survey rounds. Working groups then drafted recommendations, and the full team approved nearly all of them by consensus vote. The guidance covers which genes panels should include, quality minimums, known blind spots such as repeat expansion disorders, and sharing of variant readings between labs. One topic resisted agreement: who should be offered testing, since national health systems differ. The authors expect the shared standards to make reports easier to compare across laboratories.
pmc-13634649:
Jamie Cowley and colleagues tested brain-penetrant drugs that block a receptor driving inflammation after head injury. Traumatic brain injury kills and disables people worldwide; no drug is approved to treat it. Much of the lasting damage comes from inflamed brain immune cells. A receptor called P2X7 acts as a trigger for releasing inflammatory messengers. The team built two human test systems: lab-grown microglia-like cells and living slices of human brain tissue.

A chemical activator made both systems release the inflammatory messengers IL-1β and IL-18 in rising amounts. Clinical-stage blocker drugs stopped that release in a dose-dependent way, at levels relevant to real dosing. Blockers of a partner complex or its enzyme also worked, confirming the pathway. Because the findings come from human cells and tissue, not animal models alone, the authors argue the case for trying these blockers in injured patients strengthens.
pmc-13634749:
Fangfang Peng and four co-authors present a complete genome of the white mulberry tree, in this 2026 research letter. Mulberries matter as fruit, medicine, and the food of silkworms. The white mulberry is the most widely farmed species, yet its genome still had gaps, especially around chromosome centers and ends. The team's new assembly runs from one end of each chromosome to the other, with no missing stretches.

A gap-free genome lets them trace how mulberry chromosome sets evolved, since species in the group carry either seven or fourteen chromosomes. It also sharpens the hunt for why one farmed variety, Zhenzhubai, grows white fruit while its relatives grow dark, pigment-rich berries. Comparing the complete sequence against pigmented cousins can pinpoint the gene changes that switched off the color. Breeders and mulberry researchers gain a reference map with nothing left blank.
pmc-13635249:
Michael Warchol and six colleagues studied how chemical tags re-tune the cell's cargo-hauling motor. The motor, cytoplasmic dynein, drags loads along cell tracks via adaptor proteins gripping one of its chains. The team asked whether phosphate tags, added by a cell-division enzyme, change which adaptors grip and how tightly. They tagged the chain's tail in the lab and read the effects with magnetic resonance methods revealing protein shape and contacts.

Tagging did not rebuild the tail's loose structure, yet it rearranged the tail's long-range contacts. One adaptor, BICD2, touched the tail differently afterward, with little change in grip strength. The tags also opened a high-affinity docking site for the shape-editing protein Pin1. Once Pin1 sat down, it selectively loosened BICD2's grip while leaving two other adaptors alone. The authors describe a tag-and-editor switch fine-tuning cargo loading during busy cell periods.
pmc-13635549:
Eva Piscator and three co-authors report how a Swedish hospital improved its paperwork for decisions to limit life-sustaining treatment, in this 2026 study. Such decisions, for example not to restart the heart or use a ventilator, must be documented in set ways under national rules. At the Stockholm hospital studied, records often missed required elements, which can leave later care teams unsure what was decided and why.

In June 2023 the hospital made three changes: a revised digital form, brief teaching for doctors, and an updated internal protocol. The team then compared one hundred randomly chosen records from before the change with ninety-eight from after. Full compliance with the rules leapt from one in a hundred records to sixty-three in a hundred. The reasons behind decisions were well recorded both before and after. The study shows a light-touch package can fix a quiet but serious documentation gap.
pmc-13635849:
A cyst growing in the wall of the knee's artery can squeeze it shut, and open surgery has long been the standard fix. Tsz Him Pang and co-authors report a through-the-skin alternative in this 2026 paper. The cyst's thick gel keeps pressing after simple ballooning or stenting, causing early relapse. Their approach lines the artery with a covered stent, then reinforces it with a woven metal stent.

The double layer resists the cyst's squeeze from outside. The authors report good short- and mid-term results, the first such success in print. Blood-thinning therapy continues afterward. Regular clinic and ultrasound checks watch that the artery stays open. Rare diseases advance one careful case at a time.
pmc-13635949:
Al-Khazraji and co-authors test how well simple body measures stand in for deep belly fat in a Canadian group. Deep fat around the organs and fat in the liver drive much of the health risk of weight gain. The usual height-weight index cannot see that deep fat at all.

The team compared four measures with scan-measured fat: the index, body fat share, waist size, and waist-to-hip ratio. Each person got a detailed scan that maps fat by site. The question was which cheap measure tracks the risky fat best. A good stand-in matters for clinics that lack scanners. It also matters for large studies that must sort thousands of people by risk. The results can guide which tape-measure value deserves the most weight.
pmc-13639249:
Farnoosh Khamseh and three colleagues report a case of COVID-19 lasting far longer than usual in a woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. The sixty-nine-year-old patient kept testing positive for the virus for 127 days after her illness began.

She arrived with fever and cloudy patches on her chest scan, and blood tests showed liver and kidney strain beside very high lymphocyte counts. Standard treatments, including dexamethasone and remdesivir, did not clear the virus, and she died from lack of oxygen. The authors blame the leukaemia's weak antibody defenses and urge tailored care for such patients.
pmc-13639649:
Takaaki Konishi and nine colleagues explain Japan's High-Cost Medical Expense Benefit System in a 2026 review. Even under universal coverage, patient co-payments can grow ruinous, so this system, created in 1973, caps what households pay each month.

The cap varies with age and income, costs can be pooled across family members, and special rules cover chronic care such as dialysis. A 2024 government proposal to raise the ceiling drew criticism for ignoring patient voices and was withdrawn. The authors describe the program as essential for keeping advanced care within reach of ordinary life.
pmc-13640849:
Serin Moghrabi and three colleagues report a 2026 imaging case that warns against misreading a new cancer scan tracer. A patient recovering from major pancreatic surgery showed fat necrosis, a benign healing change, in the operated area.

A standard glucose scan showed only mild activity there, while the newer fibroblast-targeting scan lit up intensely, a pattern that could be mistaken for returning cancer. A benign adrenal tumor in the same patient stayed quiet on both scans. The authors stress that this tracer reflects healing tissue activity, so results must be read alongside surgical history and anatomy scans.
pmc-13641049:
Cifuentes-Acebal and co-authors test whether tiny RNA strands from food plants survive cooking and digestion. Food is a source of foreign RNA found in human samples, but whether it survives the gut and enters cells is debated. The team used cauliflower as their test food.

They cooked the plant, ran it through a lab model of digestion, and measured its RNA strands. Most RNA was destroyed, with over ninety-nine percent lost. A small share packed inside the plant's own tiny parcels survived and could still be detected. Those parcels also endured digestion, though they clumped. Gut cells in dishes took up some of the surviving strands. The work shows survival is rare but real, which bounds claims about food RNA effects.
pmc-13641249:
Justine Perrin led a 2026 laboratory comparison of two radioactive microsphere agents for liver cancer radioembolization: holmium-166 and yttrium-90. Both deliver beta radiation to tumors through the arteries, but their biological effectiveness had never been directly compared, leaving isotope choice uninformed by biology. The team exposed three human liver cancer cell lines to equal absorbed doses of 1.5 or 2.5 gray over twenty-four hours, tracking survival and DNA damage.

Both agents cut survival in a dose-dependent way across all cell lines, with only a modest, non-significant trend toward greater toxicity from holmium-166. Holmium-166 produced fewer but larger DNA damage spots at earlier times, hinting at subtle differences in damage complexity or repair speed. At equal dose, the agents proved comparably toxic in dishes. Clinicians get a practical steer: injected activity, microsphere makeup, and distribution likely matter more than isotope choice alone.
pmc-13641449:
Nan-Su Huang and eleven colleagues present a 2026 study of how depressive symptoms change around kidney transplantation. About forty percent of people with end-stage kidney disease report such symptoms, and depression predicts worse outcomes even after a transplant.

The team drew on a multicenter prospective cohort of 4,661 adults being evaluated for transplant and 1,215 recipients, enrolled across many years. Their stated goals were to measure symptom change before and after transplantation and to test whether the path differs by patient traits such as age, sex, and support at home. The work aims to guide screening and targeted psychological support.
pmc-13642249:
Lars Meinertz Byg and six colleagues present a 2026 study testing the Barker idea that poor fetal growth programs later metabolic disease. Genetic studies had challenged that idea by showing birthweight genes can affect adult risk directly.

The team followed 1,167 offspring from pregnancy to age twenty-seven, comparing each person's actual birthweight with the birthweight their genes predicted. A mismatch in either direction came with more central fat or insulin resistance in young adulthood, while cholesterol and blood pressure showed no such pattern. The authors argue that falling short of, or overshooting, genetic growth potential is what carries the risk.
pmc-13643549:
Patrick Zamora and co-authors tell how they fished a stray stent out of a heart in a 2026 case report. The stent had been placed in a liver vein to treat Budd-Chiari syndrome after liver surgery. It slipped free and rode the blood to the right ventricle. The team reached it through a wide vein port in the leg, sewn shut by plan before the sheath went in.

A three-loop snare caught the stent in the heart and drew it past the valve to a large vein. There a plain snare lost its grip. The team built a rail of three wires, one through the stent and two beside it, and slid the snare down that rail. The snare caught the far struts and pulled the stent out whole. The report warns of traps: stent break, valve snag, and bleed at the port.
pmc-13645549:
Emily A. Stevens, Lexie J. Pfeifer, and Matt P. Malcolm survey occupational therapists about barriers that rural stroke survivors face when seeking outpatient therapy. Their electronic survey went out by email as a gap analysis. Twenty-six therapists answered. The paper reports what those therapists see as the main blocks to care.

Therapists named distance to the clinic, weak family or caregiver support, insurance limits, transport problems, cost, and low health literacy among the barriers. The top problem in treatment itself was a lack of clinic equipment suited to brain-focused therapy work. The authors note the sample is small and call for larger work that also asks stroke survivors directly. Their findings still map the practical gaps rural clinics must close.
pmc-13647049:
Guo-Ji Yan and co-authors report a 2026 study on a small gene regulator and its role in Alzheimer's disease. The disease moves slowly from mild memory loss to dementia, and its causes are still not fully known. The team focused on a short molecule and a nerve protein it controls, testing their link in several mouse models.

In the mice, the protein was off balance, along with changes in nerve connections and memory. Raising the small molecule eased memory problems, while blocking it made them worse. Tests showed its effects ran through the protein. The pair may offer a target for future treatments that protect memory.
pmc-13647149:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues report a pelvic cyst in a woman in her mid-thirties that scans misread as an old blood collection. She had months of left-sided lower belly and pelvic pain after pregnancies and miscarriages. Ultrasound and MRI showed a cystic lump in front of the lower womb, and its features suggested a chronic hematoma. Continuing symptoms led to keyhole surgery.

Inside, dense adhesions bound womb, cervix, and bladder together. Clearing them revealed a cyst in the space between bladder and womb, filled with dense whitish-yellow material. Tissue study showed a fibrous wall with chronic inflammation but no true lining, which makes it a pseudocyst rather than a cyst or blood pocket. Her recovery was smooth and symptoms eased greatly. The authors warn that inflammatory pseudocysts can perfectly mimic blood collections on scans.
pmc-13647349:
Alexandre Tavartkiladze and ten colleagues test whether low output of a sleep hormone's breakdown product tracks with unhealthy blood fats in adults with dyslipidemia. The product, measured in urine over a full day, reflects melatonin made the night before. Five hundred seventy-seven adults at a Tbilisi institute each gave three separate day-long urine collections between 2020 and 2025. Lower hormone output went with higher harmful LDL cholesterol, higher triglycerides, more inflammation, and lower protective HDL cholesterol. A bile-related signal ran high in most participants and also climbed as the hormone fell. Several gut microbe groups rose with higher hormone output. The authors keep the analysis exploratory and refuse causal claims from a single snapshot. Still, the pattern ties sleep chemistry to fat and inflammation inviting follow-up studies.
pmc-13648749:
Chen and co-authors build a rule-based system that finds fatty liver disease in the records of patients who also have type 2 diabetes. The liver condition is very common in this group. Yet its traces are scattered across coded fields and free-text doctor notes, so simple searches miss many cases.

The system joins five rule sets drawn from known liver scores and blood markers. A light text-reading tool scans notes for signs of the disease, while watching for words that negate a finding. The team tested the system across several sites. It is built to scale, so large record systems can flag likely cases for review. Finding these patients matters, since early care can slow liver damage.
pmc-13649449:
Yang Ou and eight colleagues pooled case-control studies on a gut-made chemical called TMAO and its link to clogged-artery heart disease. Gut microbes make this chemical from foods such as red meat, and past studies clashed on whether high blood levels spell real risk.

Nine studies fed into their pooled math. People with the highest TMAO levels had higher odds of disease than those with the lowest, and the link ran stronger in groups studied before any first event. One type of pooled result swung wildly between studies, though, so dose claims are shaky. The authors grade the proof as low and oppose routine screening for now, while backing diet shifts that cut TMAO sources.
pmc-13649749:
Xia Sun and four colleagues asked whether starting weight or weight change over a year tracks heart gains in people with a stretched, weak heart muscle. Of 600 records screened, 322 patients had full paired measures at entry and at twelve months.

Most patients lost weight over the year, and few gained. Starting weight showed no firm link to change in pump strength, a stress marker in blood, or symptom class. Greater weight loss, by contrast, moved with all three in the good direction: stronger pumping, lower stress marker, and better symptom class. The links held after checks for drug access. The authors stress that shared timing bars any claim of cause.
pmc-13650149:
Chao Kong, Qin Zhong, Dinghua Liu, and Boyang Liu tune catalysts for a cleaner route to butyrate esters, in a 2026 study. The reaction joins propylene with methanol and carbon monoxide, wastes little, and makes products used across industry. Which end of the propylene reacts decides the product's shape, and steering that choice is hard. The team tested palladium catalysts carrying different phosphine ligands, pairing bench work with theory.

The ligands steered speed mainly through their electronic effects and product shape through their bulk. The best catalyst ran about fourteen times faster than a standard one and favored the straight product nearly sixteen to one. Calculations showed the first hydrogen step fixes the outcome. The authors say the design rules fill a gap and can guide future catalysts for this reaction.
pmc-13650649:
Gareth Roderique-Davies and fourteen co-authors assess a Welsh pilot service that pairs trauma-informed mind support with long-acting injectable buprenorphine, a monthly shot that treats opioid use disorder. The injection steadies drug levels and clears mental fog, yet that clarity often unearths buried trauma and pain that substances had masked.

Nine service users described the program in guided interviews, studied for recurring themes. Clients said the switch to shots felt life-changing but left them emotionally bare. Fast, steady access to a non-judgmental therapist was essential for staying abstinent. They credited the support with stronger self-direction, steadier moods, and reconnection with daily life. They linked relapse prevention straight to having psychological help beside the medication. The authors urge weaving such support into injection pathways, while noting that wider transfer and long-term effects still need study.
pmc-13650749:
Anne L Donovan and six colleagues listen to mentees in one academic anesthesiology department about what mentorship and sponsorship actually feel like from below. Thirty-eight faculty members joined focus groups sorted by gender, career stage, and identity. Their discussion settled into three themes: lifting mentorship toward higher impact, building formal structures so sponsorship does not depend on luck, and installing a structured program to hold both. Subthemes were organized around practical questions meant to turn reflection into design. The authors note their themes match published literature while adding design principles drawn directly from faculty across career stages. The single-institution scope is stated plainly as the boundary of the findings.
pmc-13651149:
Lucía Cortés and five co-authors present a 2026 study adapting a therapy program for teenagers with emotional disorders. Anxiety and depression often arrive together in adolescence. The Unified Protocol treats their shared roots rather than each diagnosis alone, but it is usually delivered one to one. The team reshaped it into a group program and tested it at a public mental health center in Spain.

Thirty-one adolescents, most of them girls, joined sixteen group sessions, with three extra sessions for parents. About four in five finished the program. Teens and parents reported high satisfaction and strong trust in their therapists. Emotional symptoms and coping skills improved, parents saw fewer depressive signs, and clinician ratings showed better functioning. The authors judge the group format workable and welcome in public care. They call for randomized trials to confirm the gains.
pmc-13651249:
Mantis shrimps split into smashers and spearers, and their guts should keep the receipts of that dietary split. One species' transcript library was built fresh for the work.

The stomachs differ plainly. One species packs the densest filter bristles and narrowest pores. Another grows the thickest stomach wall and strongest exit muscle. The third has the tallest hindgut folds and the largest digestive gland. A family of protein-cutting enzymes tells the same story in counts, forty-five versions in one species against fifteen in another. Form and gene family both track what each animal eats, the authors argue, a two-level fossil of niche splitting.
pmc-13651649:
Francesca Barion and three colleagues map what is not known about two kidney diseases: lupus nephritis, kidney inflammation driven by lupus, and membranous nephropathy, an antibody attack on the kidney's filters. Both can end in kidney failure, yet their full burden across countries had never been assembled.

A targeted search of the literature from 2013 to 2023 across six countries found only twenty-six usable articles for lupus nephritis and eleven for the membranous disease. Lupus nephritis incidence estimates came solely from the United States, with risk concentrated in older people, women, and African Americans. A large share of patients reach kidney failure within a decade, at punishing monthly cost. The membranous disease looked rare everywhere, with sketchier data still. Quality-of-life evidence was thin, and generic questionnaires missed kidney-specific suffering. The authors call for broader geography, longer follow-up, and disease-specific outcome measures.
pmc-13652449:
Sed and Warsame report a rare birth defect case in a 2026 paper. Their patient was a fifteen-month-old girl with an abnormal channel between rectum and vagina, a defect called an H-type fistula. Her anus sat too far forward and was narrow, yet the defect hid behind a near-normal look. That hidden form often delays diagnosis, above all where scans are hard to get.

The girl had passed feces through the vagina and suffered constipation since early infancy. Doctors made the diagnosis by examination, since money limited imaging, and an X-ray showed a loaded colon. Surgery split the channel and rebuilt the anatomy in one operation. Recovery went smoothly, and at two-year follow-up the child had age-fit control with no return of the problem.
pmc-13652849:
Ahmad Alsarraf and colleagues report the first Middle Eastern real-world results for brentuximab vedotin in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, a skin-homing blood cancer. The drug is a set therapy for relapsed CD30-positive disease, yet data came almost only from Western and Eastern groups. Records covered nineteen adults treated at the Kuwait Cancer Center from 2018 to 2025.

Most patients had advanced-stage disease, and nine in ten had the mycosis fungoides subtype. Median CD30 levels were twenty percent. One in five had no prior therapy, while near two thirds had already had three or more treatment lines. The letter sets out this hard-treated group's makeup as the base for judging the drug's local performance.
pmc-13654049:
Hortsch and co-authors respond to a letter about their world survey of anatomy teaching. The letter praised the survey but questioned why Iran was grouped with South Asia. The survey appeared in a teaching journal in January 2026.

The team explains the grouping was a practical choice to keep the survey manageable. It was not meant to claim a shared geography, culture, or teaching style. The letter raised a second point about Iran's own place in global anatomy training, which the team also takes up. Such exchanges refine how world surveys draw their maps. The reply thanks the letter writers for a fair critique. It also pledges care with regional labels in future editions of the survey.
pmc-13654349:
Prudvi Tarun Betha and two colleagues report a rare and dangerous complication of heart catheterization through the wrist. Entering through the radial artery is now the preferred route because it bleeds less and lets patients walk sooner than the groin route. Their patient instead developed a large hematoma inside the mediastinum, the central chest compartment, after an attempted wrist-access angiogram, with the pooled blood pressing on nearby structures.
