This one reminds intervention teams that a routine access choice can still produce a chest emergency needing two kinds of rescue.
pmc-13655449:
Casey Nash and co-authors report a rare emergency after a freezing procedure for atrial fibrillation. A 47-year-old man had cryoballoon treatment to isolate his pulmonary veins. During the work his heart tracing showed a warning blip that faded on its own. Soon after, the blip returned and worsened.

His heart slipped into a deadly rhythm and stopped. Emergency imaging showed both coronary systems clamped in diffuse spasm, with no blockage. The spasm released by itself and circulation returned before nitrate drugs were given. Heart function normalized within a day. A nerve injury followed, and stress symptoms persisted. Two years on, the fibrillation has not returned. The authors urge close monitoring after ablation.
pmc-13655849:
Liping Ye and co-authors report a large trial of a traditional Chinese pill for stomach trouble in infants and toddlers in a 2026 paper. Many babies show gut discomfort that does not meet standard diagnostic rules, leaving doctors few options. Chinese experts have named this pattern a functional dyspepsia syndrome of infancy.

Across fifteen hospitals in China, children aged one to thirty-six months got the pill or a placebo twice daily for a week, with follow-up to two weeks. The main measure was a combined symptom success rate at day seven. The pill has a long record in older children with indigestion, but proof in this younger group was lacking. The trial tests both effect and safety under blinded conditions.
pmc-13657849:
Xin Lin and co-authors test a blood pressure drug as a cancer helper in a 2026 study. The cancer is colon and rectum cancer of a type that resists immune drugs. Those immune drugs free the body's defenses, yet this tumor type hides well from them. The blood pressure drug blocks a hormone signal that tumors also use to grow and hide.

In lab grown cancer cells, the drug lowered a shield protein that tumors use against immune attack. It also slowed cell movement across a test barrier. In mice, the drug alone slowed tumor growth, and pairing it with an immune drug worked better. Tumors in the paired group held more immune cells inside them.
pmc-13659249:
Daniel Sanin-Ramirez and co-authors check babies' airways with a tiny camera just before a high-stakes delivery procedure. Their 2026 study reviews nine fetuses with suspected airway blockage treated between 2013 and 2025. The EXIT procedure keeps the baby on placental support while doctors secure the airway, and a fetoscopic look comes first.

Growths on the neck, teratomas and lymphangiomas, caused most of the suspicion. In one case the camera showed the airway was open, so the team stepped down to a normal cesarean. Seven babies were intubated through the guided path and one needed a tracheostomy. Every baby survived the delivery room; one died before discharge. The authors call the preview a safety and planning gain.
pmc-13660449:
Yanfeng Liu, Yanan Gao, and Chuanli Zhao report a circular RNA in blood plasma that marks and drives a fast-growing lymphoma, in a 2026 study. The RNA, named hsa_circ_0080018, was clearly higher in plasma from newly diagnosed patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Its level also helped sort the lymphoma into its two main cell-of-origin subtypes.

The team traced how the RNA acts. Carried in tiny plasma vesicles into the tumor's surroundings, it soaks up a small regulatory RNA. That frees a growth pathway in immune cells called macrophages. Those cells then shift into a state that helps the tumor grow. Blocking or tracking this RNA could give doctors a blood test for subtype and a fresh drug target, the authors suggest.
pmc-13662249:
Özgür Avci and co-authors test whether an angle measured on front-view X-rays can estimate pelvic tilt in patients with severe hip deformity who are receiving a new hip joint. Pelvis movement affects whether the new joint stays in place. In these patients, one leg is shorter and side-view films often cannot show the pelvis clearly enough for standard measures.

The team reviewed thirty-two patients with neglected severe deformity on one side. They measured the candidate angle before surgery and computed pelvic tilt from other angles. The candidate angle tracked tilt strongly in their data. A front-view measure that works when side views fail could make planning safer for these complex cases.
pmc-13664449:
Aritra Halder and co-authors build a new stats method in a 2026 paper. The method finds zones where a surface changes fast across both space and time. Such zones can mark the edge of a storm, a polluted area, or a brain region at work. Older tools handled curves well but struggled with full surfaces that shift over time.

The new method uses a Bayesian model, which blends past knowledge with new data. It tracks rates of change on the surface and draws the fast change zones from model results. Tests on fake data checked that the method works as hoped. The team then used it on brain scans, climate data, and pollution data with good results.
pmc-13664849:
Ibraheem Alsawalem and Abdulmalik Alkhunini studied barriers to services for Syrian refugee children with disabilities in two thousand twenty-six. The children live in a refugee camp in Hatay Province, Turkey. The authors drew only on the views of psychologists who work with them there.

They spoke with ten Syrian psychologists and grouped the barriers into five linked areas. These were trauma and mental health, limited health care, and papers, language, and school hurdles. Poverty and child labor, plus unsafe living conditions, completed the set. Families also faced heavy care and money strain. The authors call for inclusive, trauma-aware services, early screening, family support, and joint work across sectors.
pmc-13669749:
Jasmine Ho opens a special issue on dentistry with a personal editorial in 2026. Ho is an oral and maxillofacial surgeon qualified in both medicine and dentistry, a specialty that bridges the two fields. She took an unusual path, qualifying in medicine first and returning to dental school later as a mature student.

That journey, she writes, exposed gaps she had never noticed from the medical side alone. Four observations from it shaped the issue's topics, starting with the divide between medicine and dentistry. The editorial aims to demystify dental services, training, and the patient experience for a mainly medical readership, arguing that the two professions understand each other far less than they should.
pmc-13672249:
Yuyang Wu leads a team that tracks tryptophan in live animals over time. Their study from twenty twenty-six makes fast, long plasma measures. Past theories came from lab, post death, or cell work.

No direct proof in live subjects backed those theories. Measures at fine time steps ran for many hours. They proved a joint action seen in cells holds in vivo. A key enzyme is steadied by tryptophan itself, they show. A model with steady supply from tissues fit the data. Flux and enzyme boost rates are given per subject.
pmc-13672949:
Masahiro Suzuki and Md Jahirul Islam studied police responses when abuse victims choose to stay with their partner, in this 2025 paper. Domestic and family violence is a growing public health concern. Victims who keep the relationship pose hard choices for officers.

Survey data showed officers generally took active steps to protect victims. Interview data showed many used a victim-centered approach. Some officers, though, showed limited grasp of why victims stay, such as fear, dependence, or hope for change. The authors call for better training so officers can handle the layered dynamics of such cases with more skill and care.
pmc-13673149:
Kirby Lampe, Victoria Sarata, Aileen Har, and Fernando Zapata report a rare case of Ogilvie syndrome in a child, in a 2026 paper. In this syndrome the large bowel balloons outward even though nothing blocks it, causing a swollen belly, nausea, vomiting, and constipation. It usually strikes men over sixty and centers on the first stretch of the colon.

Their young patient had a complex medical history and arrived with major belly swelling, which X-rays confirmed as gas-filled bowel. Standard care — rest, fluids, and medicines such as neostigmine — failed to shrink the bowel. Doctors finally relieved the pressure with a scope passed into the colon. The case reminds clinicians to keep this adult disease in mind for children too.
pmc-13673549:
Industrial solid waste is piling up worldwide, and China holds a large share of it. Qiuxia Zou and co-authors argue in a 2026 article that old mines offer a place to put that waste to work. Global generation passed sixteen billion tonnes in 2022, with China producing about a quarter, and more than thirty-two billion tonnes sit in Chinese stockpiles.

Filling worked-out pits and underground voids with treated waste can restore mined land while shrinking the piles. Demand for waste in building materials has weakened, and new landfill space is scarce. China's 2026 action plan for solid waste sets standards and oversight for such backfilling, with funding to follow. The authors present China's mix of progress and problems as a reference for other resource-heavy economies.
pmc-13675349:
Senna and co-authors test obeticholic acid against arthritis in rats. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease marked by joint inflammation, oxidative stress, and slow destruction of cartilage and bone. Activation of the farnesoid X receptor has emerged as a possible brake on immune inflammation.

Obeticholic acid switches that receptor on. In rats with adjuvant-induced arthritis, the drug eased disease through FXR-driven control of a TGF-beta signaling chain in joint tissue. That chain runs through TAK1, MKK3, and p38 MAPK proteins. The treatment also cut inflammation and oxidative stress in the joints of the treated rats.
pmc-13675449:
Rui Zhang and co-authors engineer safer cell therapy for acute myeloid leukemia in a 2026 study. CAR-T cells aimed at the CLL1 marker can kill this blood cancer, but CLL1 also sits on healthy neutrophils, so treatment can wipe out those key defenders. The team built a two-key lock to spare them.

Their synthetic Notch design fires only when a T cell meets both CD123 and CLL1, a pairing found on leukemia blasts. In dish tests the gated cells killed blasts harder and spared neutrophils more. They also showed fewer signs of exhaustion and kept a younger profile. In mouse models they expanded better and lasted longer. Dual gating may widen the safe use of CAR-T in this leukemia.
pmc-13675649:
Masami Tsuchiya and co-authors use health claim records to study cancer care during pregnancy in Japan. Their cohort study covers births from 2005 to 2024 and finds 500 cases where cancer was noted during pregnancy. Care could mean drug treatment, surgery, or radiation, and the team tracked early birth and birth defects.

Only 16 of the 500 women got anti-cancer drugs, and 46 had surgery, while none had radiation. Most drug treatment began in the middle third of pregnancy. Early birth and birth defects were noted more often in the cancer group than in other births. The authors stress that these rates alone do not prove the drugs caused the outcomes.
pmc-13677049:
Tielyr Creason and co-authors turn printed plastic patterns into durable optical masks by burning them to carbon, in this 2026 paper. Grayscale lithography carves smooth three-dimensional relief in one step, but good masks are costly and hard to make. Their method starts from patterns printed by standard multiphoton tools.

Heating collapses the pattern from micrometers to nanometers thick while it clings to its base. Sideways dimensions grow slightly, yet the overall layout holds faithfully. The carbon left behind is chemically inert and mechanically tough. A mask can thus survive repeated exposures and cleanings. The authors frame the trick as turning single-use prints into reusable production masks.
pmc-13677549:
Yingying Fan and Xutao Liu review dance programs for brain and mental health across the lifespan. Their 2026 review follows standard reporting rules and a registered protocol. Dance blends movement, thinking, emotion, and social contact in one activity, which makes it a rich candidate for health gains.

Six databases were searched to August 2026 for controlled trials of dance at any age. Twenty-two studies with 1,645 people aged 4 to 94 met the bar. Varied designs ruled out pooled sums, so the team sums up study by study. Gains show for overall cognition, memory, and attention in selected studies. Executive function results split both ways. Some studies also report lighter depression, anxiety, and stress after dance programs.
pmc-13677749:
Zhuopin Sun and co-authors map the genes behind the shape of the upper spinal cord in this 2026 paper. The cord carries movement, feeling, and body control, yet its genetics were barely explored. The team measured cord shape from brain scans of over eighty thousand UK Biobank volunteers. Measures included cross-section area, widths, and roundness.

They found 179 separate genetic variants tied to cord shape. Heredity explained a fair share of the differences, and some signals differed by sex. Cord measures also linked to many conditions, from multiple sclerosis and nerve damage to diabetes and attention disorders. The authors present the cord as a new window on health and disease.
pmc-13678549:
Paul Versteegh proposes a new lens for stubborn face and jaw symptoms in this 2026 paper, writing alone. Some patients keep feeling pain, odd sensations, or bite problems that tests cannot explain. The feelings stay pinned to one spot and resist treatment.

His framework, source-bound perceptual persistence, measures how strongly a suspected source organizes a patient's perception and behavior. It also shapes treatment seeking and clinical reasoning. Four literatures on sensory signals feed the idea. The paper is theory, offered to generate testable claims rather than report data. It may help clinicians discuss unexplained symptoms without dismissing them.
pmc-13679149:
Chlorinated pollutants linger in water and resist cleanup, so engineers want catalysts that are strong and reusable. Monika Dubey and co-authors built a magnetic nanocomposite of iron oxide and cerium oxide, riddled with pores and oxygen vacancies. A magnet can fish it back out of treated water.

The material removed nearly all of two test pollutants, chlorobenzene and a dichlorophenol, within seventy minutes at near-neutral acidity. It kept about ninety-eight percent of its power after five reuse cycles. Hydroxyl radicals did most of the attacking. Machine learning predicted performance across conditions, and quantum calculations explained the partnership's stability. The 2026 study layers experiment, theory, and AI into one cleanup design.
pmc-13680349:
Badr Othman measures the bone around lower molars to judge where instant implants can safely go. Placing an implant straight into a fresh molar socket shortens treatment and cuts surgeries, but the anatomy at the back of the jaw can crowd the work and raise risk. His 2026 study reads that anatomy from 3D cone-beam scans.

The study covered 25 adults and 100 molar sites. Six measures were taken at each site, including cheek-side bone thickness, ridge width and height, and the gap between the root tip and the nerve canal below. Two readers agreed closely on every measure. Second molars had thicker cheek bone and wider ridges, while first molars had more vertical bone and wider root spacing. The map helps dentists pick sites where an instant implant fits, and where waiting is wiser.
pmc-13680549:
Emilie Gheyle, Edouard Duquesne, Yves Roisin, and Denis Fournier report a genetics study from two thousand twenty-six on an invasive termite in Guadeloupe. Cities are reshaping tropical habitats fast, but how urban life affects gene flow in invasive social insects is murky. The team compared termites from three paired city and forest sites.

They genotyped over four hundred workers from fifty nests at eighteen new marker sites. Genetic diversity measures matched between habitats: city termites were no poorer in variation. Yet populations split clearly by habitat within each site pair, with habitat explaining fourteen to twenty-two percent of variation. Distance alone predicted differences weakly. Colonies were mostly extended families in both settings, with no mixed-family nests. Habitat mosaics thus structure the gene flow without eroding diversity.
pmc-13682449:
Jingyu Zhao and five co-authors frame immune aging as a treatable driver of brain decay in a 2026 review. As immune cells age, they drive Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease through four linked paths. The paths are steady swelling signals, stress from shifted cell fuel use, failed cell clean up, and broken talk between brain and immune system. Standard care only eases signs by tuning brain signals, which cannot halt the slide.

The review tours fixes aimed at the aging cells: drugs that clear them, fuel and stress modulators, clean up repair, and tiny carriers that ferry drugs to targets. Early tests, in labs and first trials, slowed disease in these frames. The authors add AI guided target hunts, carrier craft, and gut microbe work as the next layer of a many front plan.
pmc-13684449:
Joshua Brown and co-authors show that the visual cortex must loosen its inhibition for fear memories to last in humans. Their 2026 study combines brain stimulation, EEG and MRI scanning, and machine decoding. Volunteers learned fear associations, and their memory traces were tracked minutes, a day, and a week later.

Memory patterns appeared from the earliest sensory stage onward. Learning strengthened a rhythm change in visual areas that marks loosened inhibition, and that change predicted later memory strength. Stimulating the visual cortex to force inhibition erased the rhythm change. Consolidation and week-later retention suffered, while first learning stayed intact. The authors name early sensory areas as targets for treating stubborn fear.
pmc-13684649:
Leehyeon Kim and co-authors used cryo-electron microscopy to reveal how an enzyme called MBOAT1 reshapes a key membrane fat. Cells constantly remodel their membrane lipids: one enzyme clips off a fatty chain, and MBOAT family enzymes attach a new one, tuning how the membrane behaves. How these enzymes pick their partners was unknown.

The target lipid, phosphatidylserine, sets the membrane's surface charge, recruits signaling proteins, and marks dying cells. Its remodeling also helps cells resist an iron-driven death. The structures show how the enzyme recognizes both the donor chain and the acceptor lipid, and how the product leaves. Those details explain the enzyme's selectivity atom by atom.
pmc-13686249:
Six authors measure what people with intellectual disabilities know about menstrual health. This group faces steady barriers to health education and care, yet no study had checked their knowledge on this topic. The team surveyed Special Olympics athletes with a short set of questions from a standard socio-sexual knowledge test. Seventy-five athletes took part, with an average age of 37.3 years, and 72 gave usable answers.

Scores ran from 0 to 8, with a middle score of 5. Only 25 participants, 35 percent, could answer the hygiene practice questions correctly, while 65 percent answered them wrong. The authors call the gap a clear call for teaching materials and health resources built for this population. They frame menstrual health knowledge as basic health literacy that should not be left to chance.
pmc-13687549:
Manuel Dohla and co-authors set out a 2026 framework for keeping medical devices available when systems break down. Device supply is usually seen as a buying or cleaning problem. Wars, disasters, pandemics, and attacks have shown it rests on a wider web of linked resources. If those links fail, even devices on hand may become unusable. The authors name five domains of dependency that keep devices in service.

On that base, they build a seven-part response plan summed up as 7R. The parts start with moving devices to where they are needed and buying anew. Further parts, named in the full text, cover other adaptive moves. The plan aims to guide choices by risk when conditions degrade. Framing device supply as a system capability is the core idea. Hospital planners and policy makers are the intended audience.
pmc-13690449:
Cheng-Han Wu, Chin-Lung Kuo, Shang-Liang Wu, and Wen-Huei Liao studied sudden hearing loss in 2026. Predicting who will fully recover from a sudden drop in hearing is hard. Early gain in hearing may be a simple sign, but its link to full recovery was not well measured.

The team reviewed adults treated at a Taiwan hospital between 2012 and 2022 for a first case on one side. Two hundred forty patients were split evenly between those who fully recovered and those who did not, matched by starting severity. Early gain was the change in hearing within two weeks. Younger age and faster start of treatment raised the chance of full recovery, and each unit of early gain added to that chance.
pmc-13690849:
Tomoki Shimokawa and a large team report national figures on keyhole heart surgery in Japan in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Minimally invasive cardiac surgery avoids splitting the breastbone, easing recovery. This annual report covers operations done in two thousand twenty-three. Data came from the national cardiovascular surgery database. Procedures include mitral and aortic valve work, bypass grafting, hole-in-heart closure, and tumor removal.

The report sets benchmarks for deaths and major complications around surgery. It also traces trends from two thousand twenty-one to two thousand twenty-three in case numbers and case mix. Such benchmarks let hospitals compare their results fairly. They also show how fast the gentler approach is spreading. Cardiac surgeons and health planners are the readers.
pmc-3961149:
Kamvar, Tabima, and Grünwald introduced poppr in 2014, an R package built for a hard case in genetics. Many microbes, fungi, and water molds copy themselves or mix cloning with sex, so they break the rules that standard tools assume. Few programs at the time were made with such groups in mind.

Poppr gives users ways to study these mixed groups without forcing them into a simple sexual model. It helps track clones, measure diversity, and test how genes are shared across a sample. For labs that work on plant disease and other clonal life, it filled a clear gap in daily analysis.
pmc-4060849:
Cherry, Olschowka, and O'Banion reviewed neuroinflammation in 2014, with a focus on microglia. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain, akin to macrophages elsewhere in the body. Interest had grown in whether they, like other macrophages, switch among several activation states.

The review weighs the good and bad sides of the M2 state, which is often linked to calming inflammation and repair. Work on macrophages outside the brain does not always carry over to microglia, the authors note. Their balanced account helps brain researchers judge claims about microglia states in injury and disease with more care.
pmc-4302049:
Love, Huber, and Anders introduced DESeq2 in 2014 for RNA sequencing data. A basic task in such studies is testing read counts per gene for real changes between conditions. Small sample numbers, count data, and a huge range of values make that testing tricky.

DESeq2 improves how fold changes and dispersion, a measure of spread, are estimated. It borrows strength across genes to steady estimates when replicates are few. That moderated approach cuts false claims while keeping power to find real changes. The package became a standard choice for labs asking which genes turn up or down in disease, treatment, or development.
pmc-4489249:
Salentin, Schreiber, Haupt, and their team presented PLIP in 2015, a profiler of protein-ligand interactions. How a small molecule binds a protein is essential knowledge for structural bioinformatics, drug discovery, and biology. Full tools for this task were not freely available to researchers at the time.

PLIP works in a fully automated way on a protein-ligand complex. It detects and reports the key contacts, such as hydrogen bonds and stacking, in text and images. Drug designers use such profiles to see why a compound binds well or badly. A free, thorough tool widened access beyond groups with paid software.
pmc-7619449:
A Ben and two colleagues compare heat risk in two lizard species that share the same dry landscape in southern India. Global warming pushes cold-blooded animals toward their temperature limits, yet living side by side does not mean facing the same danger. The study covers Calotes versicolor, a tree-dwelling generalist, and Psammophilus dorsalis, a rock-dwelling specialist, measuring the temperatures each actually experiences and tolerates.

Copper models placed in open and shaded spots recorded the heat on offer in each microhabitat, while field readings captured the body temperatures of active lizards. Performance and tolerance tests completed the picture. The two species came out differently vulnerable despite similar overall exposure, a result with a general lesson for conservation. Climate risk must be judged species by species, through behavior and physiology, not from weather maps alone.
pmc-8443449:
Valery Feigin and the Global Burden of Disease collaborators analyzed in 2021 the worldwide burden of stroke and its risk factors over three decades. Planners need current figures on how often stroke occurs, how many people live with its effects, and how many die, broken down by stroke type. The analysis draws on the Global Burden of Disease Study for the years 1990 to 2019.

The team reports trends in incidence, prevalence, death, and disability, and weighs the risk factors behind them, such as high blood pressure. Their results show stroke remaining a leading cause of death and disability even where rates improve. Health systems use these numbers to argue for prevention programs and to plan rehabilitation capacity.
poe-von-kempelen-and-his-discovery-1849:
Edgar Allan Poe put out Von Kempelen and His Discovery in 1849. The tale is a brief hoax in the dress of news. A man named Von Kempelen is held by the law in New York. In his rooms the law finds a craft that turns lead to gold.

Gold falls in price in the tale's world as word of the find spreads. Poe plays the whole thing dead straight, with dates and trade facts. He had just scored with a hoax on a chess craft years past. The tale is a sly probe of crowds, news, and greed.
project-grudge-report-1949:
In August 1949 the United States Air Force closed its second official study of flying saucer reports and issued this final report. Project Grudge had taken over from Project Sign at the start of 1949. The work was run by Air Materiel Command, the Air Force branch in charge of planes and research.

Inside are case files on sightings from across the country, with radar reports, pilot accounts, and staff study of each event. The officers leaned toward plain answers such as weather balloons, stray planes, and hoaxes. Later the report was declassified in full. It now stands as a key record of how the Air Force first handled the UFO question, before Project Blue Book began.
project-sign-report-1949:
Project Sign was the United States Air Force's first true study of flying saucers. Its tech report of February 1949 sums up the first year of work. Air Materiel Command ran the study from Wright Field. The report was kept from the press at the time and freed much later.

Case by case, the staff weigh pilot tales, photos, and bits of proof. Some tales get plain causes, while a few stay unexplained in their lists. Staff talk hints that some men leaned to a bold view of the craft. The report is the root file of the state's saucer work.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol5-1849:
Quicherat closed his five-volume Joan of Arc edition in 1849 with the papers a reader needs to use the rest. Volume five gathers legal opinions on the trials, letters tied to the case, and a full index. The long work of 1841 to 1849 ends here.

The opinions show how church lawyers of the time judged the verdicts of 1431 and 1456. The letters add the voices of kings, kin, and towns. The index turns five dense volumes into a tool a scholar can truly work with day by day. With it, the whole record of Joan's two trials stands open to any reader.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-biography-m:
William Smith, a British classical scholar, edited his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology across the 1840s. Volume One appeared in its standard form in 1849. Smith gathered the leading scholars of the age as contributors.

Entries give the lives of Greek and Roman statesmen, poets, generals, and philosophers, drawn from the ancient sources. Gods, heroes, and mythic figures stand beside real men and women, each with its tale and lineage. Smith's careful method made the set the Victorian age's great classical companion. Students of the ancient world still reach for these volumes first.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5049:
George W. Bush gives eight yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from February 27, 2001, to January 28, 2008. Three stars part each address from the next. The first counts it a great privilege to speak. He will lay out a new budget and a new way of governing. He thanks Congress for its call to speak. The house had to call him by formal vote, he jokes.

Many members have come to the White House at his call. They talked over grave themes in those meetings. He will keep meeting them and asking their views. Their candor has made a new president feel welcome. The last time he stood at the Capitol, he took an oath. On its steps he pledged to honor the Constitution and laws. He asked Congress to join him in a tone of respect for Washington.
storm-immensee-1849:
Immensee, Theodor Storm's novella of 1849, is given here in the German original. No English translation of the tale is in the public domain. Old Reinhard, looking back, recalls Elisabeth, the friend of his childhood and the love of his youth at the lake estate of Immensee.

School, travel, and slow years apart let another man win Elisabeth's hand. A late visit to her home shows both what was lost and what duty built instead. Water lilies, songs, and the lake itself carry the story's feeling. The tale made Storm famous across Germany. It became the model of the German novella: brief, lyrical, and sad without despair.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
The issue of October 14, 1897 is No. 49 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item takes up a rumor about the Seal Conference. England, it was said, had refused to take part. Her reason was that Russia and Japan were to be admitted. At the British Foreign Office, officials gave out that Canada lay behind the trouble.

Ottawa, the paper says, much disliked the thought of Great Britain taking part. It asked the mother country to withdraw, and to leave the settlement to the colony most interested. The rumor surprised officials in Washington. Mr. Foster had been in London in July, fresh from St. Petersburg, where the Czar consented to send a representative. The Prime Minister left an ambassador's note unanswered from July until September.
the-gringos-a-story-of-the-old-californi: B. M. Bower wrote The Gringos, a story of the old California days in 1849. Anton Otto Fischer made the pictures. The book is dated 1913. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, an author's note, and the start of a contents list. The note thanks George W. Lee, a Forty-niner. He furnished data and color for the story. The heads open with The Beginning of It and The Vigilantes. They name The Lord of the Valley. No chapter text is present.
the-secret-city-pg12349: Hugh Walpole's The Secret City is presented here in the same 1919 Doran edition found in a sibling record. That sibling carries the novel's opening pages. This record stops earlier, at lists of Walpole's other books, the title page, and the dedication. Walpole dedicated the novel to Major James Annand for his friendship. An anonymous Cock-Crow Song from the first century B.C. serves as epigraph. The title page calls the work a novel in three parts. No contents or chapter text appears here.
the-treasure-of-heaven-a-romance-of-rich:
Marie Corelli's Treasure of Heaven, published by Dodd, Mead in 1906, carries in this record her unusual author's note about the frontispiece. At her publishers' special request, a photograph taken by Gabell in spring 1906 faces the title page. Corelli professes reluctance: the portrait has nothing to do with the story, and an author's real being shows in the work, not in mere physiognomy. She doubts her pictured personality can interest her readers.

Then she explains the real reason. Gross, libellous, fictitious misrepresentations of her had been circulated by lower sections of the pictorial press across Britain, the colonies, and America, striving to alienate her readers. An authentic likeness was the publishers' remedy. The note is a small drama of celebrity itself, from a novelist whose romance of riches follows after it.
the-woman-with-the-fan-pg8549:
Robert Hichens opens The Woman with the Fan in a cool London drawing room. Guests listen to a soprano singing in an inner room. Most faces turn eagerly toward the voice. One small dark-haired woman instead plays with a scarlet fan. She watches a thin elderly man beside her. His hands twitch on his knees as if longing to grasp something.

Her faint, malicious smile suggests old tensions between them. Hichens builds the scene from glances and small movements. Nearly everyone present hangs on the singing. Two people plainly have other matters on their minds. Readers get a society novel where desire and resentment simmer under polite manners.
the-works-of-john-dryden-now-first-colle: Volume four of John Dryden's collected works, edited with a life by Walter Scott, shows only its title page here. William Miller published the eighteen-volume set in London in 1808. James Ballantyne and Company printed it in Edinburgh. A contents heading for the fourth volume begins, but no contents follow. Nothing of Dryden's writing appears in what is shown here.
thoreau-civil-disobedience-1849:
Henry David Thoreau published Civil Disobedience in 1849, first as Resistance to Civil Government in print. The essay states the duty to resist unjust government and charters nonviolent civil disobedience for later ages. Thoreau wrote it after a night in jail for refusing a poll tax in protest.

He protested slavery and the Mexican War, which he saw as a slave power land grab. The essay holds that conscience outranks statute, and a just man must break an unjust law openly. Under a government which imprisons any unjustly, he wrote, the true place for a just man is prison. Gandhi and King both drew on its logic in their campaigns of nonviolent mass action later. Its brevity and moral force make it Thoreau's most influential single piece of prose.
thoreau-week-on-the-concord-1849:
Henry David Thoreau published A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers in 1849, his first book. The river journey with his brother John fills its seven days of rowing, camping, and talk. The elegy contains the seed of Walden in its praise of wildness, friendship, and simple days outdoors.

Thoreau printed the book at his own risk, and most copies came back unsold to his attic. John had died of lockjaw in 1842, and the voyage of 1839 became a memorial in prose. Each day mixes natural notes with essays on books, friendship, history, and the soul's quiet hours on rivers. Hindu scriptures and English poets float beside fish, locks, and New Hampshire hills in its wide-ranging pages here. Unsold in its day, it is now read as the overture to Walden's fame.
tob-13149:
Four hundred twenty-three verses present the Buddha's teaching in its briefest classic form in the Dhammapada. Taming the mind, the danger of anger, and the path out of suffering recur as its central concerns. The verses are grouped by theme, so a reader can turn directly to folly, vigilance, or happiness.

Monks have chanted the Dhammapada daily for two millennia, and householders keep it by the bed, according to long tradition. Its advice is concrete: watch your thoughts, guard speech, and expect deeds to return. V1 evidence calls it the place to start with Buddhist scripture, and its brevity and clarity make that advice easy to follow.
tob-13749:
Jeanne Guyon, a French widow of deep prayer, published her Short Method of Prayer in 1685. She taught what became known as quietism: stop striving, rest in God's presence, and let love itself do the praying. Her gentle manual won followers across France, including the famous Fenelon.

Guyon gives simple steps for beginners: read a little, then pause and be still before God. She warns against forced feelings and showy methods. Church leaders condemned her teaching, and she spent years under arrest and suspicion. The small book still attracts readers who long for prayer without strain or display.
tob-4049:
Volume one of William Wordsworth's Poetical Works, in an eight-volume collected edition, gathers his early and middle poetry. The Lyrical Ballads years stand behind it, when Wordsworth and Coleridge taught England to find sublimity in daffodils, beggars, and leech gatherers. Nature, memory, and the growth of the poet's mind form the great themes.

Early experiments give way to the confident lyrics and narratives that made Romanticism's fountainhead. Wordsworth revised his poems across his long life, so collected editions also record a poet arguing with his younger self. Readers starting the full set will watch plain speech about common life become, volume by volume, a philosophy of feeling.
tob-4149:
Edward Henry Palmer, a Cambridge orientalist of rare gift for Arabic, translated the Qur'an for the Sacred Books of the East in 1880. Volume one, volume six of the series, holds the first half of Islam's scripture. Palmer's English is vigorous and plain where other versions turn stiff.

Scholars used his rendering for decades, and general readers found it the most approachable of its age. His introductions treat the Prophet and the text with the respect his period allowed. Verified from the 1919 edition, Palmer's first volume remains a landmark of Victorian Arabic studies, whatever later translators have improved.
tob-4249:
Rudolf Steiner put out An Outline of Occult Science in 1910. It gives his whole scheme of world history in one dense book. Man, he says, has grown through great world ages named for Saturn, Sun, and Moon. The Earth age is the fourth. More ages, and a path of training for seers, lie ahead.

The scheme is dense, strict, and strange, and Steiner owns that it rests on his own occult sight. Those who grant his claim get a full esoteric world view in one volume. Those who do not still get a core text of his school, Anthroposophy, in its full form. Later work by his pupils takes this book for granted.
traite-anatomique-physiologique-et-criti: A French treatise on physiognomy, anatomical, physiological, and critical in approach, shows a garbled title page naming Brussels and Amsterdam sellers. Physiognomy means judging character from bodily and facial form. A Boston Medical Library stamp and a 2010 digitisation note from the Internet Archive, Harvard Medical School, and Open Knowledge Commons precede the title. The printed year on the page reads 1840, although this record's identifier carries 1849. The damaged title page is what is present here, so the treatise itself does not appear.
un-ga-res-a-69-49:
Fifty-four states had ratified the Arms Trade Treaty when the UN General Assembly took up Resolution A/69/49 at its sixty-ninth session, in late 2014. The treaty, which sets shared rules for cross-border sales of standard arms, was set to enter into force on 24 December 2014. Mexico had offered to host the first meeting of treaty parties in 2015.

The Assembly calls on all states that have not yet signed or ratified the treaty to do so as soon as they can. States that are able should give aid, in skills or in funds, to states that ask for help putting the treaty to work. The catalog year of 2006 on this record is wrong; the text is from 2014.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/49 (2014) is a short progress note on the Arms Trade Treaty, the first global treaty regulating transfers of conventional weapons. The Assembly welcomes the treaty's 54 ratifications and its entry into force on 24 December 2014. It thanks Mexico for offering to host the first Conference of States Parties in 2015. It calls on states that have not joined to sign and ratify as early as possible. It calls on those able to do so to fund technical help for others.
un-sc-res-1349:
Western Sahara's mission was renewed again in the spring of 2001. On 27 April 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 June 2001. The Secretary-General had reported days earlier. His envoy was still trying to save the Settlement Plan. Deep differences over the plan's main terms remained. The Council voiced full support for the envoy's mission.

The parties were expected to keep working under his guidance. They had to try to solve the plan's many problems. The Council also hoped they might agree on a political solution to the dispute. A fresh assessment was due before the mandate ended. Two months later the envoy brought forward a draft framework instead.
un-sc-res-1449: Year 2002 in the catalog holds Resolution 1449, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1549: Resolution 1549 is one of the Security Council's formal texts, held here in its official-record wording via Wikisource. The document speaks for fifteen governments at once, which is why its verbs are chosen with care. Demands, authorizations, and requests appear in numbered paragraphs after the opening findings, and the entry preserves that full structure.
un-sc-res-1649:
On 21 December 2005 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1649 on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Foreign armed groups in the east still had not laid down their arms. Their attacks threatened civilians and the coming elections. Stolen natural resources and arms trafficking kept the fighting fed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council stretches travel bans and asset freezes to new targets. Leaders of foreign armed groups who block disarmament now fall under the measures. So do Congolese militia leaders backed from abroad, above all in Ituri. The measures start on 15 January 2006 and run to 31 July 2006. A full plan for disarming and sending home foreign fighters is due by 15 March 2006.
un-sc-res-1749: Kept under number 1749, a Security Council resolution is preserved in official-record form through a Wikisource transcription. The Council's charge under the Charter is the maintenance of peace and security, and resolutions are its written instruments. This instrument is kept entire: recitals, decisions, and the closing machinery of reports and review dates.
un-sc-res-1849:
The Yugoslav tribunal needed more temporary judges than its rules allowed in 2008. Fourteen ad litem judges were already assigned to trials. A 2008 resolution had let the total reach sixteen, but only until year's end. On 12 December 2008 the Security Council loosened the cap again. The Secretary-General could appoint extra ad litem judges at the tribunal president's request. The appointments had to fit within existing resources.

The extra judges would finish trials under way or start new ones. The usual limit in the tribunal's statute would not block them. The change served the court's completion strategy. More benches meant more trials could run at the same time. The Council stayed seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1949: Resolution 1949 is a Security Council decision preserved here in the wording of the UN's official record, via Wikisource. The Council's output is cumulative, and each numbered act assumes the ones before it. This entry preserves its act completely, so the accumulation the collection documents has no missing link at this number.
un-sc-res-2249:
In a vote on 20 November 2015, the Council passed Resolution 2249 on the Islamic State group. The group held wide stretches of Iraq and Syria. Its attacks had just killed hundreds in Sousse, Ankara, Beirut, and Paris, and over the Sinai. The Council called the group a global and unprecedented threat to peace.

The text condemns the attacks in the strongest terms. It calls on states with the capacity to take all necessary measures, within international law, on Islamic State ground in Syria and Iraq. The aim is to crush the group's safe haven and stop fresh attacks. States must also choke off foreign fighter travel and terror funding, and the sanctions list should be updated fast.
un-sc-res-349: Catalogued with a 1964 date, Resolution 349 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-449:
The Golan Heights observer force was renewed in May 1979. On 30 May 1979 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 30 November 1979. The Secretary-General had reported on the force. The text follows the mission's set form. The parties must carry out resolution 338 at once. A report on events is due when the term ends.

One member, China, did not take part in the voting. The observers kept watch in the separation zone between Israel and Syria. The disengagement deal of 1974 still held. Each renewal restated the same hope for a wider peace. The Council handled the item as routine, but the force's presence prevented a fragile line from slipping back into war.
un-sc-res-49:
Open war in Palestine forced a cease-fire call in Security Council Resolution 49, passed on 22 May 1948. Past Council calls on Palestine, the text notes, had not been kept, and armed work ran on across the land. Israel had been proclaimed a week before, and the armies of the Arab states had moved in.

All states and chiefs are called to shun all hostile armed acts in Palestine. Each must order its troops and armed bands to cease fire within 36 hours of midnight, New York time, on 22 May. The Truce Commission in the land must give first place to a truce for the City of Jerusalem. It must report back on how the call is kept.
un-sc-res-749: Under number 749, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1991 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Nauru, one of the world's smallest countries, is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 1249, adopted on 25 June 1999. The Council had examined the Pacific island republic's application, filed as document S/1999/478. Nauru had been independent since 1968 but waited three decades before seeking a UN seat.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Nauru, following the Charter's two-step pattern for new members. When the Assembly acted, Nauru gained a vote equal to that of the largest states, a striking feature of the system. The tiny phosphate island's admission also reflected a late-1990s cluster of Pacific microstates deciding that a UN seat was worth having.

Guides that call this an Ethiopia text have the wrong war. The land at stake is Western Sahara. A UN team, MINURSO, stood ready to run a vote on its fate. That vote had been pledged for a decade. Deep rifts over who could vote blocked it still. Resolution 1349 passed with no dissent on 27 April 2001.

MINURSO won a short stay, to 30 June 2001. The chief's envoy would keep the sides at the table. The hope was plain: crack the old rifts, or find a deal both could take. The chief's report of 24 April had set out the snags. A fresh check on the state of play was due before the term closed. The text backs the 1991 peace plan, but its tone admits the plan was stuck.

Candidates for permanent judge posts at the Rwanda war crimes tribunal are forwarded on 24 December 2002. The tribunal, created in 1994, prosecutes those responsible for the Rwandan genocide and related crimes. Its permanent judges are elected by the General Assembly from a list the Council sends.

The text sends the Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received, as the tribunal's Statute requires. The list names 23 candidates from countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean. The Assembly would elect the judges from among them. Those elected would sit in the tribunal's trial and appeals chambers for the cases still moving through its courts.

Upper Volta, the West African country now known as Burkina Faso, won independence from France in August 1960. Its leaders applied for UN membership at once. Resolution 149 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The Council considered the bid at its crowded 891st meeting, alongside other African applications that day.

The members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Upper Volta. Admission followed that autumn. The country took the name Burkina Faso in 1984. Its UN seat, though, traces back to this text. The resolution belongs to the 1960 wave that transformed the UN. New African votes shifted debates toward ending colonial rule worldwide.

Liberia's Panel of Experts is re-established on 17 June 2004. The panel checks whether sanctions on arms, diamonds, and timber are being obeyed and breached. Liberia's transitional government had appealed for the sanctions to be lifted and asked for an expert visit to judge its performance against the Council's conditions.

The new panel, of up to five experts, would work from 30 June to 21 December 2004. Its tasks include a follow-up visit to Liberia and nearby states to study how the sanctions are being applied and where they are still broken. The Secretary-General is to appoint the experts in consultation with the sanctions committee and arrange the funding for their work.

Congo's armed-group leaders face targeted sanctions in Resolution 1649, adopted on 21 December 2005. Foreign armed groups in the east — the FDLR, the Palipehutu-FNL, the Lord's Resistance Army — had refused to disarm past the 30 September 2005 deadline. The deadline was set by the region's Tripartite Plus Joint Commission. Their attacks threatened civilians and the coming elections. MONUC was acting against them in hazardous conditions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the travel ban and asset freeze of Resolution 1596 (2005) to political and military leaders of foreign armed groups. It extends them to Congolese militias backed from abroad, above all in Ituri, who block disarmament and demobilization. The measures take effect on 15 January 2006 unless the Secretary-General reports disarmament is being completed, and are reviewed by 31 July 2006. A full strategy for disarming and repatriating foreign combatants is due by 15 March 2006.

The last notification rules on arms transfers to Rwanda's government are ended on 28 March 2007. The measures dated from 1995, passed after the genocide, and required notice of arms supplies to Rwanda. Rwanda's government had asked for them to be terminated, and the sanctions committee had reported on the question.

The measures are terminated with immediate effect. States in the region must still cooperate to prevent arms from reaching illegal armed groups, which the remaining embargoes on such groups address. With this step, the special arms restrictions built around Rwanda in the mid-1990s are fully wound down, twelve years after they began.

The Hague war crimes court needed more judges than its rulebook allowed. Trials from the Balkan wars were still stacked up in 2008. Fourteen stand-in judges were at work. More cases were set to start. Resolution 1849 passed on 12 December 2008. It drew on a plea from the court's president, sent that November.

The Council let the Secretary-General name extra stand-in judges on request. The total could climb to sixteen at a time. The cap in the court's statute was twelve. This break was meant to be brief. By 28 February 2009, the count had to fall back to twelve. The aim was clear: clear the docket and meet the plan to wind the court down by 2010.

Guinea-Bissau, a small country in West Africa, faced fresh instability in late 2010. Soldiers had detained officials on 1 April that year, and some people were still held without due process. Drug trafficking through the country was feeding corruption and organized crime. Resolution 1949, adopted on 23 November 2010, responds to that situation.

The Council extended the United Nations peacebuilding office in Guinea-Bissau, called UNIOGBIS, until 31 December 2011. It urged the armed forces to respect civilian rule. Those detained in April had to be released or given a fair trial. The government was pressed to finish its inquiries into the political killings of 2009. Reform of the security forces and action against the drug trade run through the whole text.

Islamic State terrorism draws a call to arms in Resolution 2249, adopted on 20 November 2015, a week after the Paris attacks. ISIL, also called Da'esh, had struck Sousse, Ankara, a Russian airliner over Sinai, and Beirut in 2015. It held parts of Iraq and Syria, destroyed cultural heritage, and drew foreign fighters from around the world. The Council calls it a global and unprecedented threat.

The Council condemns the attacks in the strongest terms and says those responsible must be held accountable. It calls on member states with the capacity to take all necessary measures, in compliance with international law, on ISIL-held territory in Syria and Iraq. They are to prevent and suppress terrorist acts by ISIL, the Al-Nusrah Front, and other Al-Qaida-linked groups, and to destroy their safe haven. It urges stronger action against foreign fighter flows and terrorist financing, and promises to update the sanctions list.

Resolution 249, adopted unanimously on 18 April 1968, deals with the application of Mauritius, filed as document S/8466. The Indian Ocean island had become independent from Britain the previous month, in March 1968. Its government applied for United Nations membership almost at once.

After examining the application, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Mauritius. The sentence is short because admission votes rarely involve debate in the Council itself; agreement is usually reached beforehand. Yet the formality mattered: without this recommendation the Assembly could not act. The resolution records the moment Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar, began its life as a member state of the world organization.

Ten years after it first arrived, the Cyprus peacekeeping force came up for a new term on 29 May 1974. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 May, said the force was still needed if peace was to be kept. Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 15 June. Resolution 349 records the renewal.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also told to speed up their joint efforts toward the Council's goals. The island's calmer climate was to be used well. The force's stay was extended to 15 December 1974. The Council expected that progress toward a final solution might then allow the force to withdraw or be reduced.

The label on this file can mislead. Some notes tie Resolution 449 to the settlement debate. The text itself renews a peacekeeping force. Fourteen members voted yes on 30 May 1979. China took no part. The Secretary-General's report on the force, paper S/13350, sat before the members.

The force was UNDOF, the UN team on the Golan Heights. Its mandate grew by six months, to 30 November 1979. The Council paired the renewal with its stock demand. Israel and Syria had to act on Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. A fresh report was due when the term ended. By 1979, these Golan renewals formed a fixed rhythm of the Council's year.

A week after the State of Israel was proclaimed, war was under way in Palestine. Earlier Council resolutions on Palestine had not been obeyed. Fighting continued on all sides. Resolution 49 was adopted on 22 May 1948.

The Council called on all governments and authorities to stop hostile military action in Palestine. They had to issue cease-fire orders to their forces within thirty-six hours. The order was given without prejudice to any side's rights, claims, or positions. The Truce Commission and all parties were told to give top priority to a truce in Jerusalem. Winning it and keeping it came first. All sides were also told to help the United Nations mediator do his work. He had been appointed only days earlier.

A United Nations force for Croatia, approved in February 1992, received the order to deploy in full that April. The force was called UNPROFOR, the United Nations Protection Force. Its advance teams were already in place. Fighting kept breaking the cease-fire in the areas where the force would be based. Resolution 749 was adopted in April 1992.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 2 April 1992. It decided to authorize the earliest possible full deployment of UNPROFOR. Everyone involved was urged to help cover the force's costs. Its aircraft had to be given complete freedom of movement. All parties were called on to stop the violence. That call applied above all where UNPROFOR would be based. The Council also appealed for cooperation with European efforts toward a cease-fire and a political settlement in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s457-149: Section 457.149 of Title 1 of the federal rules bars bias in program reach. The body bound is the National Capital Planning Commission. No fit disabled person may be shut out of its programs. The bar holds where the shut-out stems from hard-to-reach sites. A person may not be denied the gains of a program on that ground. He may not be kept from taking part in it at all. One linked section sets out the sole free cases.
uslaw-cfr-t1-s500-149: Section 500.149 of Title 1 of the Code of Federal Regulations sits in the part on nondiscrimination on the basis of handicap in programs of the National Commission for Employment Policy. Its heading is program accessibility, and its rule is that discrimination is barred. No qualified handicapped person may, because agency facilities are hard to reach or use, be denied the benefits of a program. Nor may such a person be shut out of a program, or otherwise face discrimination under it.
uslaw-usc-t2-s149:
Section 149 of Title 2 lets the Librarian of Congress pass surplus books to other libraries. From time to time, the Librarian may transfer books and material to other governmental libraries within the District of Columbia. The Public Library is expressly included among the recipients.

Two judgments must line up for a transfer. The material must, in the Librarian's judgment, be no longer necessary to the uses of the Library of Congress. And it must, in the judgment of the custodians of the receiving collection, be likely to be useful to them. The Librarian may also dispose of or destroy material that has become useless. A firm proviso follows. No records of the Federal Government may be transferred, disposed of, or destroyed under this authority. The section sits in Chapter 5 of Title 2.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1849: Section 1849 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the pay of a set of posts. It sits in Chapter 28, on the Architect of the Capitol, in a part on pay for staff. The Architect of the Capitol may set the base rate of pay for no more than 32 posts. The rate set may not top a named cap. That cap is the top full rate of pay for the Senior Executive Service, for the place in view, under a set part of Title 5.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2049:
Section 2049 of Title 2 of the United States Code allows loans to keep the Senate Restaurants running. It sits in the restaurants subchapter of the chapter on running and maintaining the Capitol complex.

With the approval of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, the Architect of the Capitol may borrow from the Miscellaneous Items account inside the Senate contingent fund. The loans support the work of the 1961 joint resolution that handed the running of the Senate Restaurants to the Architect. The committee sets each loan's amount and term. The Secretary of the Senate makes the loan on a voucher approved by the committee's chairman. Money paid back on a loan returns to the same account and is credited there for future use.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5349: Section 5349 of Title 2 of the United States Code caps printed law books for the House. No funds made open in any fiscal year may be used to give House offices more than a set total of printed copies. The total is fifty printed copies of any edition of the United States Code, across all offices of the House of Representatives. The cap applies from fiscal year 2019 onward. It is a small money-saving rule for the print age's end.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5549:
Section 5549 of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up an office for the interns of the House. It sits in Chapter 55, on House officers, in a part on the Chief Administrative Officer. The office set up is in the Office of that Chief Administrative Officer. Its name is the House Intern Resource Office. The office is to be led by a man with a set name. He is the House Intern Resource Coordinator.

That man is to be hired by the Chief Administrative Officer. The hire is to be made with the aid of the views of two men. They are the chair and the head of the minority of the Committee on House Administration. A second clause deals with the duties of the new office.
zoist-vol-07-1849:
The Zoist reaches volume seven with the months from March 1849 to January 1850. Elliotson's journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism keeps its double brief. Reports of trance surgery now compete with news of chloroform's spread. Mesmerists argue their method is safer and gentler in reply.

Clairvoyant cases, cure narratives, and sharp editorial combat fill the volume. The society of contributors spans Britain's industrial towns and villages. Across thirteen volumes the journal preserves the movement entire. Volume seven shows the cause in its mature, embattled phase. Historians of hypnosis quarry these pages constantly. The voices are those of the practitioners themselves.
